15601-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly for boys and girls, for May 27, 1897, number 29 of volume one, cost five cents, at two dollars fifty a year. William Beverley Harison published it from West 18th Street, New York. The front again offers a special inducement: a Rand McNally 1897 Atlas of the World for any subscriber who sends two dollars fifty for a new yearly subscription.

The atlas holds 160 pages of colored maps from new plates, size eleven and a half by fourteen inches, printed on special paper with a marginal index. Its regular price is two dollars fifty. The editors warn that an old atlas is no better than an old directory: countries change, and knowledge grows. Non-subscribers may send five dollars for a friend's subscription and their own, and win the atlas either way. The number shows the paper selling news with maps.
16673-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This September 29, 1920 number of Punch, volume 159, leads with Charivaria jokes on strikes, measles, the cost of living, and Dean Inge meeting the Food Controller. A sporting paper's cure for strife, a brace of MPs, and an artist lashed to a mast for a sea storm all get the Punch treatment in short squibs.

Punch keeps its dry London wit aimed at the week: workers, prices, strikes, and churchmen all come in for a poke. The jokes are short, topical, and sharp, with cartoons to match. The issue gives a quick, funny window on Britain in the autumn of 1920, best read a page at a time for its targets and tone.
17061-class-of-29:
Orrie Lashin and Milo Hastings wrote Class of '29 as a play in three acts, issued by Dramatists Play Service for nonprofessional stages. The service leased it to college, university, and little theatres across English-speaking lands, beside Broadway hits of its day. Its advisory board names Howard, O'Neill, Kaufman, Barry, and other stage leaders of the age.

The play itself belongs to the school and youth drama of its time, made for student casts and plain staging. This text gives the acting edition as theatres used it, with the service's notes on rights and use. Drama fans and theatre historians will find a neat sample of how plays reached amateur stages in the early 1900s.
30343-a-discourse-concerning-ridicule-an:
Anthony Collins examines ridicule and irony in writing in a discourse from 1729. The Augustan Reprint Society reprints it as publication number 142, from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles in 1970. Edward A. Bloom and Lillian D. Bloom supply the introduction, with William E. Conway, George Robert Guffey, and Maximillian E. Novak as general editors and David S. Rodes as associate editor.

Advisory editors from Michigan, Columbia, Virginia, Chicago, Princeton, Minnesota, and London support the series, with Edna C. Davis as corresponding secretary and Roberta Medford as editorial assistant. The reprint gives Collins's early eighteenth-century argument in a clean scholarly form, for readers who want period criticism on laughter, irony, and the proper use of wit in prose.
3826-rise-of-the-new-west-1819-1829:
Frederick Jackson Turner, the historian of the frontier, wrote this volume of the American Nation series on the decade after the War of 1812. The new west of the title means the lands beyond the mountains filling with settlers, speculators, and state banks. Government policy, Turner argues, fed reckless buying, as state bank notes were taken for public land while the banks took only nominal steps toward resuming specie payment.

Pioneers spent their funds on first payments and then borrowed from wild cat banks to finish, a system that bred booms and busts. The southwest chapters trace the same pattern toward the Gulf. Turner writes with a scholar's care for policy and a storyteller's sense of movement. Readers who study American expansion will find a clear account of how land, credit, and politics built the west.
5932-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Courtly debate fills chapters thirty-two through thirty-five of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter thirty-two gives the reply Quixote made his censurer, with other grave and droll incidents, as Quixote rises trembling like a man dosed with mercury and speaks in a hurried, agitated voice. The place, the presence, and the respect due to his hosts frame his defense of knighthood.

Chapters thirty-three through thirty-five continue the duchess's delectable discourse, the learning of how Dulcinea may be disenchanted, and further instruction for that task. Readers get the duke's court as a debating hall, where courtesy and mockery test Quixote's ideals. The part suits readers deep in volume two, since its disenchantment plot drives Sancho's famous self-whipping bargain.
6767-formation-of-the-union-1750-1829:
Albert Bushnell Hart traces the formation of the Union from 1750 to 1829, as the second volume of Epochs of American History. His preface states his method: study causes rather than events, and show an American nation growing from scattered, quarreling colonies. Throwing off English control, widening popular rule, and resisting foreign sway form one long process.

Maps, reading tips for teachers, and bibliographies aid the short text, which treats a mighty growth only in its elements. Hart writes with a teacher's clarity. Formation of the Union is a compact, classic survey of America's road from colonies to nation.
all-s-well-that-ends-well-pg1529:
William Shakespeare's comedy is laid out here with a full contents table, scene by scene, from Rossillon to Paris, Florence, and Marseilles. Helena, raised in the Countess of Rossillon's house, loves the Countess's son Bertram hopelessly. The person list ranges from the King of France to a widow in Florence, showing the play's wide road.

Helena cures the King and claims Bertram, who scorns the match and runs to war. In Florence she schemes with the widow and her daughter Diana to meet the terms Bertram set her. The five acts close at Rossillon with riddles answered and a marriage accepted, if not quite celebrated. The play's uneasy mix of fairy tale and realism still provokes argument.
angus-religious-quests-1929:
Samuel Angus was an Australian scholar whose Religious Quests of the Graeco-Roman World appeared in 1929. The book studies the spiritual hungers of the ancient world on the eve of Christianity. Angus asks why the old civic cults left so many hearts unsatisfied.

He surveys mystery cults, astrology, magic, and the philosophies that promised rescue from fate and death. Converts, he shows, sought a savior, a sure hope after death, and a brotherhood that crossed nations. His account helps readers see the soil in which the early church grew, without preaching for or against it.
arxiv-2412-00229:
Del Castillo, Henniart, and Lomeli prove key claims about smooth models of symmetry groups in twenty twenty-four. The groups act over local number fields where the counting base is a prime. Past proofs of these claims worked only when that base was zero in a key sense. The authors extend the results to the harder case.

One claim says a key function tied to a calm model has no bad poles in a stated range. Another says a model built as a short form is in fact the full form. For split classic groups, they add a result on a tame part of the spectrum. The work closes a gap in the theory of these groups.
arxiv-2412-03229:
Kunal Dutta and Indra Dasgupta propose a route to persistent spin textures in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A persistent spin texture keeps electron spins aligned in a fixed pattern, which suits spin-based devices. They target nonpolar chiral systems, a class not used for this effect before.

From symmetry analysis, bands of the right orbital character near a high-symmetry point can carry a single spin-dependent term that yields the texture. Two interaction types, allowed by the symmetry, must be of comparable strength. Quantum chemical calculations then identified two real compounds that show the texture, one in its conduction band and one in its valence band. The result widens the material pool for spin-orbitronics.
arxiv-2412-04329:
Tomáš Hale, Brayden Hull, David Kubizňák, Robert Mann, and Jana Menšíková wrote a 2024 physics paper reinterpreting a famous black hole solution. The BTZ black hole is a simple model of a black hole in three-dimensional spacetime. In their celebrated 1992 paper, Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli proposed a charged, rotating version supported by a static vector potential.

That proposal satisfies Einstein's equations, but the Maxwell equations of electromagnetism fail because of the special form of the field. The authors show that a generalized Einstein-Maxwell system, recently proposed by Deshpande and Lunin, repairs the problem. Within that system the original charged BTZ spacetime gains a consistent interpretation, rescuing a thirty-year-old solution.
arxiv-2412-04929:
Gaurav Shrivastava and Abhinav Shrivastava present a new way to predict future video frames in a 2024 paper. Diffusion models excel at making still images, but video prediction is harder because they treat a video as separate frames. Extra fixes are then needed to keep motion smooth across time.

Their model treats video as one continuous process across space and time instead of a stack of frames. This design also needs far fewer steps to produce a new frame, about a quarter of the usual number. On four standard video data sets, covering lab scenes, robot arms, human motion, and action clips, the model set new best results. The project page shares example videos for readers to inspect.
arxiv-2412-05829:
Naizhu Jin, Zhong Li, Yinggang Guo, Chao Su, Tian Zhang, and Qingkai Zeng wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. Its head author line adds one name to the catalog list. It shows how a backdoor can be planted in code models that reason step by step.

Their attack, SABER, picks a bad output by mutating code. It finds the tokens tied to it through self-attention scores in CodeBERT, then crafts a natural trigger that mimics a user. On test sets the attack fired far more often than prior tricks. Auto detectors missed most of its poison, and human checkers caught almost none. The work warns that chain-of-thought code models need safety study of their own.
arxiv-2412-06029:
Zhenghong Zhou, Jie An, and Jiebo Luo brought in Latent-Reframe in 2024, a way to steer the camera inside videos made by diffusion models without retraining them. Precise camera control matters for generated film and animation. But current methods fine-tune the model on extra data sets pairing videos with camera paths, which is costly and can distort what the first model learned.

Latent-Reframe works entirely at generation time. It repositions the internal latent codes of the frames so they line up with the requested camera path, using time-aware point clouds to keep the geometry steady. Inpainting and harmonization steps then clean up the adjusted latent space so the final video stays sharp. Tests showed camera control and video quality matching or beating training-based methods, with no fine-tuning and no extra annotated data needed.
arxiv-2412-06429:
Shai Chester and De-liang Zhong computed a key scattering size in string theory. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with the Virasoro-Shapiro amplitude on a curved space with flux. The space joins anti-de Sitter and sphere parts. They worked out the size for dilaton scattering in type IIB string theory with pure flux of one kind. The result holds to all orders in one small term, in a small curve expansion.

They got there by matching the flat space limit of a dual field theory result to a guessed form. The first curve fix was fully pinned this way and passed checks. Readers in string theory get sharp forecasts for dual data at strong coupling. Those can guide later work on exact methods.
arxiv-2412-07429:
Javad Seraj and three co-authors align an open language model's judgments with one particular human evaluator, using cleverly chosen data rather than more data. Personalized judging matters because evaluation is subjective, and a model that mimics an average rater may not match your rater. Labeled examples for one person's taste are, by nature, scarce.

Their augmentation technique selects the most effective samples from the limited pool for training. On a mathematical reasoning evaluation task, correlation with the reference judge rose about seven percent over the baseline method. Against the untouched base model, the improvement was about thirty percent. The study shows careful sample selection can beat brute-force fine-tuning in low-data personalization.
arxiv-2412-08829:
Elizabeth Mone and co-authors went trait hunting in 2024 for the birthplaces of the first giant black holes. Most galaxies carry a supermassive black hole, and some are already in place absurdly early in cosmic history. In the direct collapse case, the core of a pristine atomic cooling halo collapses into a dense group hosting supermassive stars, which leave behind a heavy black hole seed. The question is what distinguishes a halo that can do this from the normal crowd.

Using the Renaissance cosmological models. The authors built thirty-five likely host halos from the universe's first few hundred million years and weighed them against non-likely halos across eighteen measured traits of the halos, their centers. And their settings. Numeric study and machine learning methods then ranked which traits truly separate the candidates, sharpening the search rules modelers use to find direct collapse sites in larger volumes.
arxiv-2412-10729:
Kirill Boguslavski, Paul Hotzy, and David Müller tackle a stubborn computing problem in this two thousand twenty-four physics paper. The complex Langevin method can handle the sign problem, which blocks many simulations in physics. But left alone, the method often settles on wrong answers. Past work links this failure to structures called Lefschetz thimbles. The authors use that link to steady the method.

They add weight regularizations shaped by the thimble structure. They then correct the bias these weights bring in, so the true answers come back. The fix worked on a chain model and on several scalar models. It held across a wide range of couplings where the plain method had failed. The authors also discuss how the idea may extend to gauge theories.
arxiv-2412-12829:
Elena Bueno-Benito and Mariella Dimiccoli tackle global action segmentation, the task of grouping frames that show the same action across videos of mixed tasks. Past work dealt mostly with videos of one task, where action order is much the same. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

The pair use task labels to teach action features with weak guidance. Their learning plan works on video pairs and checks three things at once. Frames in one video must split by action, while frames across videos and across tasks must join when the action matches. A paired network built on sparse transformers judges if two clips share a task. Tests on two hard video sets beat prior methods.
arxiv-2412-13629:
Capozziello, Capriolo, Carleo, and Lambiase asked in twenty twenty-four how to spot far-reach twists to gravity in waves from paired stars. Base gravity theory has deep flaws, such as points where it breaks down. Far-reach twists fix some flaws but blur where acts take place.

They solve the field rules with such a twist and get a new form for wave loss in a pair. The base four-pole rule for wave power shifts in a non-plain way. That shift could leave a sign of far-reach acts in real wave data. A faint extra wave mode might just be seen by a next-wave scope in a thin band.
arxiv-2412-14829:
Gongbo Tang and Christian Hardmeier improve pronoun translation in a 2024 paper. Pronouns point back to earlier mentions, and languages differ in how they use them, so machine translation often gets them wrong. Mentions, the phrases a pronoun may point to, sit closer to the pronoun than other words do. Their model adds a module that pays extra attention to source mentions during translation.

Two small classifiers teach the model to spot mentions, and their output guides the extra attention. The decoder also uses target-side context. On an English-German benchmark, the model beat a strong baseline on pronoun measures and overall quality. The additions did not hurt general translation.
arxiv-2412-15129:
Alexander Kolesnikov, André Susano Pinto, and Michael Tschannen revisit a class of generative image models called normalizing flows, in two thousand twenty-four. Flows can compute the exact likelihood of an image, generate quickly, and stay structurally simple. They fell from favor because their samples looked worse than those of rival model families.

The team rework the classic coupling design by testing each old choice and swapping in blocks from the Vision Transformer. The result is a much simpler architecture with top quantitative and qualitative scores for its class. Visual quality still trails the best rival models. The authors argue that strong flows can serve as parts of more powerful generative systems.
arxiv-2412-15829:
Shuai Wang, Peter Bloem, Joe Raad, and Frank van Harmelen present SUBMASSIVE, an automatic method for repairing cyclic subclass relations in very large knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs record class subsumption with subclass-of assertions. Publicly available graphs, the authors found, contain many potentially erroneous cycles in those assertions, a problem worsened when graphs are integrated as linked open data.

Their approach encodes the cycle-resolving problem for a MAXSAT solver, letting automated reasoning choose which triples to remove. It is tested on the LOD-a-lot dataset and compared against a semi-automatic version of the same algorithm. The comparison exposes a trade-off: the number of removed triples balances against the efficiency of the algorithm. Cleaning subclass cycles matters because reasoners drawing inferences over a cyclic hierarchy can derive nonsense. SUBMASSIVE offers a scalable way to keep integrated knowledge graphs logically usable.
arxiv-2412-16029:
Nairne proves that a broad class of groups can be embedded into products of binary trees in this 2024 mathematics paper. The groups are relatively hyperbolic, meaning they behave like hyperbolic groups outside certain well-behaved subgroups. Here those subgroups are virtually abelian, close to simple grid-like groups.

An earlier result gave such embeddings for fully hyperbolic groups. Nairne's embedding is quasiisometric, so it distorts distances only in a controlled way. His method grows out of the earlier proof's diary idea. He builds a general theory of diaries and linear statistics around it. That machinery upgrades embeddings into products of wide-branching trees into products of binary ones.
arxiv-2501-00029:
Gupta catalogs recent language technology research for South Asian languages in twenty twenty-four. The sweep covers text, speech, and multi sense work from early twenty twenty-two to late twenty twenty-four. A spotlight falls on twenty-one low resource languages, from Saraiki to Telugu. Large models helped sort and cluster the flood of papers.

Trends, gaps, and next steps are mapped for each strand. Low resource tongues lag far behind rich ones in data and tools. The guide aims at researchers entering the area. It offers a breadth first map rather than deep dives, by design.
arxiv-2501-01629:
Nithyasri Narasimhan and Sagarika Singh build a pipeline in a 2025 project that translates Indonesian comics into English on its own. Manhwa, Korean comics read worldwide, are usually translated by hand, a slow craft. Most automated work targets Japanese comics. This team takes on Indonesian as the source, a language with far fewer digital resources.

The pipeline chains three tools. A vision model, fine-tuned for the job, finds the speech bubbles on each page. A text recognition engine reads the Indonesian words inside them. A translation model, also fine-tuned, renders the words in English. Each step scored well in their tests, and the joined system translated pages efficiently. The work aims to open more comics to a global audience at a fraction of the manual cost.
arxiv-2501-02629:
Yang Ouyang and co-authors propose, in twenty twenty-five, a defense that patches language models against jailbreak attacks. Jailbreaks trick models into harmful outputs despite safety training. Their insight: certain layers tend to emit affirmative tokens, the yes-like starts of compliant answers, when fed harmful prompts. The method, Layer-AdvPatcher, exposes those layers with self-made attack data to map their weaknesses. It then makes the model unlearn the harmful responses at those layers. Safe query behavior should stay intact.

Experiments covered two models, four benchmark data sets, and several state-of-the-art attacks. The framework cut harmfulness and attack success rates, they report. Utility on benign queries was not compromised, per their results. The defense works at layer level rather than by filtering inputs or outputs.
arxiv-2501-03529:
Alice Pelosse and Heinrich Jaeger stirred oversized grains into a tiny grain suspension and watched its thickening soften in a 2025 paper. Dense suspensions can jam abruptly under shear, a abrupt thickening that plagues and protects various processes. Starting from a fumed silica suspension that thickens in abrupt jumps on its own. The authors added grains tens of times larger than the tiny grains, varying their size, amount, and face character.

Thickening began at lower shear rates, yet its strength faded, sliding the actions from abrupt to steady thickening. Sphere-based nanosilica suspensions behaved the same, suggesting breadth, while cornstarch suspensions do the opposite. The authors blame the huge size ratio: giant big grains spread local shear rates and break the force-chain fabric thickening needs.
arxiv-2501-03629:
Li and a team including Xu present CFFormer in twenty twenty-five, a model that outlines organs and tumors in medical scans. Scan quality varies a lot by machine and body part, which blurs edges and hides targets. Past models used gaze like weighting on space alone. The new model mixes two designs, one for local detail and one for broad context.

Two new parts link the designs: one blends their channel cues, and one merges their space cues smoothly. Tests spanned eight data sets across five scan types. The model beat the best past methods and stayed sharp on poor quality scans. The team shares its code in public for other groups to use.
arxiv-2501-04829:
Obridko, Shibalova, and Sokoloff review parts of the solar activity cycle that dynamo theory alone does not explain. The dynamo describes how the Sun's magnetic field excites itself as traveling waves. The authors instead track how the surface field splits into patterns of different symmetry.

They sort the field into zonal, sectorial, and tesseral harmonics and follow each share of magnetic energy through a cycle. Early on, tesseral patterns hold the largest share, not zonal ones as simple accounts assume. Sectorial patterns peak after sunspot maximum at well over half the energy. The same sequence repeats across cycles regardless of strength.
arxiv-2501-06729:
Ankit Gangwal, Mauro Conti, and Tommaso Pauselli propose a defense for federated learning, where many users train one shared model without handing over their private data. The weak point is poisoning: a bad actor sends crafted updates that drag the shared model's accuracy down. Their defense, called KeTS, watches how each client's updates evolve over time.

Using a density-based method, KeTS sorts clients into trust groups and cuts out the malicious ones, even when some honest clients look odd. The team tested it against six strong poisoning attacks on four datasets and compared it with four known defenses. KeTS won in every setting, beating the best rival by wide margins, and it adds no extra work for clients. They also sketch an extension for attacks that flip signs or labels.
arxiv-2501-07629:
Yue and eight co-authors test whether a quasar's radio glow tracks the mass of its central black hole. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, is the second in a series using a Bayesian model. Quasar radio waves come from two sources mixed together. One is star birth in the host galaxy, and the other is the active black hole itself. Pulling the two apart is the hard part.

The team models radio data from the LOFAR sky survey for Sloan quasars. Their two-part model splits the star and black hole shares for each object. They find no link between black hole mass and star birth rate at any mass. The same holds for the black hole's own radio activity once other factors are fixed. The result bears on how black holes feed back on their galaxies.
arxiv-2501-11229:
Sagnik Bhattacharya and co-authors propose, in twenty twenty-five, a joint channel estimation and data detection algorithm for wireless links with low-rank channels. Receivers must infer both the channel and the sent symbols. Prior diffusion-model methods excel with many-antenna setups, whose channels are full-rank. They fail when users outnumber access point antennas, the low-rank case. Their method pairs successive interference cancellation, which peels off decoded users one by one, with a generative diffusion model. The diffusion process estimates score gradients for partial channels, then updates channel parts and source estimates in turn.

Simulations show the method beating baselines on channel error and symbol error. The gain holds in both full-rank and low-rank settings, at varied signal-to-noise ratios, and is strongest in low-rank cases.
arxiv-2501-11329:
Chong Zhang and five co-authors design a cascaded device that builds and boosts quantum links between light, microwaves, and magnons. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses optomagnomechanical systems, which mix all three carriers with rich nonlinear play. Such rigs are prized for hybrid quantum networks. The scheme chains two subsystems so entanglement can grow across the full set.

Within each part, light-microwave and light-magnon links are charted against tuning knobs. Detuning, decay, coupling strength, and transfer yield all shift the scores. In a set range, the second cavity's links grow far stronger than a lone rig's. Tuned well, four-way entanglement spans the whole cascade. The results give a theory base for steering entanglement in such stacks. They also aid magnon state transfer across unlike physical parts.
arxiv-2501-11729:
Rando and co-authors probe choice in state space tools and build SeRpEnt on that base. State space tools, SSMs, rose of late as a swap for Transformers. They dodge two flaws of care tools: square cost and long tie loss. The Mamba form matches Transformers with no care at all. Its edge rests on a choice step for state marks in the form. Choice was scored by tests lone, and its cause stayed dim.

Their read ties choice time spans to facts flow in runs. Choice spans act as straight near-forms of facts in the flow. SeRpEnt then uses choice to squeeze runs by facts load. A re-pick step groups bits by their facts load in the run. Tests on the Long Range set and word tasks show gains. The re-pick step drives those gains in the score reads.
arxiv-2501-13229:
Gratzer, Weinberger, and Buchholtz built in twenty twenty-five a key map tool in a typed frame for vast group theory. The frame blends shape theory with group theory for groups with end-less stacks of rules. Work in it can be less hard than with plain groups, since the frame hides those stacks.

They build sets of maps into a fixed group, called pre-sheaf sets, in that frame. They prove the Yoneda map that sends each item to its map set, with its full trait. They add rules for paired maps and stretch maps, and prove a known claim in that frame. The work grows the frame's base.
arxiv-2501-15829:
Tharindu Hewage and co-authors address a hidden cost of cloud computing for large language models. Making and shipping servers creates embodied carbon, emissions locked in before a machine ever runs, and much of it sits in the processor chips. Replacing chips sooner wastes that carbon, but running them longer risks failures as silicon ages. The team studied how inference servers actually use their cores and found many sit idle.

Their management method rests idle cores so they stop aging, and spreads work across active cores so wear stays even. In simulations built on real Microsoft Azure traces, the method cut yearly embodied carbon by about 38 percent and idle waste by 77 percent, with little loss in service quality.
arxiv-2501-16829:
Ankit Kumar, Sudhakantha Girmohanta, and Hajime Sotani model neutron stars that harbor dark matter as a second fluid, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In their picture, ordinary nuclear matter and dark matter coexist in the star, coupled only through their shared gravity.

They scan nuclear equations of state from soft to stiff and use a self-interacting, asymmetric fermionic dark matter model. Two structures emerge: stars where dark matter sinks into a core, and stars where it puffs into a halo. Observations then referee. Gravitational waves from a merger, X-ray timing of a pulsar's surface, and the heaviest known pulsar masses each carve the allowed parameter space. Halo-dominated stars survive the mass and radius checks but fail the tidal deformability bound from the merger event. Core-dominated mixtures remain viable. The combined limits squeeze dark matter's properties from several directions at once.
arxiv-2501-17129:
Rafael Ribeiro de Sousa and four co-authors revisit where ecliptic comets come from if a hidden giant planet exists. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Distant objects beyond Neptune show oddly aligned orbits. A proposed Planet-9 could explain the alignment. Early work gave it a hefty mass. So heavy a planet would tilt comet orbits too much, clashing with what is seen.

The team simulates the young solar system's instability phase. They track trans-Neptunian objects and the forming Oort cloud. Their Planet-9 is lighter and tilted, matching revised estimates. The lighter planet sculpts the distant belt without wrecking comet paths. The study checks the Planet-9 story against comet evidence. It narrows the planet's allowed traits if it exists.
arxiv-2501-19229:
Liu, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, proved a stability theorem for triangle-free hypergraphs. A hypergraph generalizes a graph: its edges can join more than two vertices. Mantel-type results ask how many edges such a structure can have without containing a forbidden pattern, here a specific three-edge triangle.

Stability theorems say that near-extremal examples must closely resemble the exact extremal construction. Liu proves an Andrásfai–Erdős–Sós-type stability result for this setting. A corollary is that, for large numbers of vertices, the unique best triangle-free construction is the balanced complete multipartite hypergraph. This answers a question posed by Mubayi and Pikhurko in a stronger form. The proof combines a recent entropy-based technique with a framework from earlier extremal combinatorics work.
arxiv-2502-00529:
Arijit Khan, Xiangyu Ke, and Yinghui Wu wrote this survey, published in two thousand twenty-five, on the two-way trade between graph data management and graph machine learning. Graphs power drug search, fraud hunting, and question answering, and each field has tools the other needs.

One direction: good data management makes graph learning better. Cleaning, scalable embeddings, vector stores, and explainability methods all lift neural models that run on graphs. The other direction: learning helps manage the data, as in answering queries over knowledge graphs. The survey walks the full pipeline, from storage to training to serving. It ends with open problems and research directions the authors judge most pressing. The piece is a map for two communities that often publish past each other.
arxiv-2502-01429:
Siddhartha Parupudi and Gourab Ghatak design an algorithm for finding the best option when tests can be batched, in a 2025 paper. In the classic bandit problem, a fixed budget of trials must identify the best arm, one pull at a time. Their variant lets the agent probe a subset of arms per round and see only the subset's average reward, as in pooled medical or sensor testing.

Batching widens the view but blurs individual arms, and grouping many poor arms can inflate a group's average deceptively. The algorithm forms a logarithmic number of groups, tests each for the presence of the champion with a likelihood ratio test, then decodes the pattern of answers to name a single winner. An error bound is derived through a new hardness measure. In identified regimes it beats leading single-play methods.
arxiv-2502-01829:
Daniel Adler and co-authors interview mental health clinicians about the data systems behind value-based care, in work from 2025. Value-based programmes pay for results rather than visits, so they depend on outcome data. What data to collect, how to gather it without burden, and how to use it well were all unclear.

The team spoke with thirty clinicians across the United States. Clinicians wanted outcome measures that serve both payment and actual care, not just billing. They saw phones and personal devices as aids to collect data between visits. They also weighed how outcome data could hold clinicians, insurers, and social services to account fairly. The authors close with design advice for tools that support value-based mental health care across all parties involved.
arxiv-2502-02029:
Mokshagna Karanam and co-workers taught image matching to respect group anatomy in a 2025 paper. Aligning medical scans needs warps that are smooth, reversible, and typical of the group. Yet common smoothers impose only smoothness, letting warps drift into anatomies no real patient has. Their MORPH-LER setup learns the stats of warps across a group and uses them to guide an unsupervised matching network toward plausible warps.

A narrow point encoder computes the main log of each warp field through repeated square-root forecasts. The forecasts land in a flattened latent space. There, two-way traits like composition and inversion behave well. Inverse consistency is imposed alongside. Group-aware warps should make atlas studies and long-term checks more trustworthy.
arxiv-2502-03429:
Ming Liu and co-authors audit unified multimodal models for demographic bias in image generation, in work from twenty twenty-five. Unified models both read and make images in one pipeline. That mix may open new bias paths beyond those of generation only models.

Benchmarks showed most such models carry strong gender and race bias in their images. By auditing each part, the team traced the bias chiefly to the language model core. A striking split appeared: bias in reading images looked small, yet bias in making them stayed large. A balanced preference method, trained with synthetic data, cut the bias while keeping image meaning true. The authors urge whole system checks for this model class.
arxiv-2502-05029:
Maria Aguareles and Francesc Font check that simple one-dimensional models capture how filter columns trap pollutants, in a 2025 paper. Such columns clean water and gas by holding pollutants on porous material. Engineers design with averaged one-dimensional equations, trusting that they mirror the three-dimensional reality inside the grains.

The authors built a full three-dimensional model: flow through the pores, drift and spread of the pollutant, and uptake set by a nonlinear law on the pore surfaces. Tests across microstructures with equal porosity showed that the inner layout barely matters, most of all across the column's width. Using homogenization theory, they then derived the one-dimensional model from the full one. Its two effective coefficients, dispersion and permeability, carry marks of the inner layout. Profiles and breakthrough curves matched the full results closely, and a finer layout closed the remaining gap.
arxiv-2502-05729:
Mohammad Jahid Ibna Basher and a large team build the first speaker-adaptation speech synthesizer for Bangla, a major language with thin technology support. The system learns a new voice from very little audio. It builds on a multilingual architecture, adjusted for Bangla's sounds and structure. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team pre-trained on thousands of hours of labeled Bangla speech. They then evaluated both zero-shot cloning and few-shot adaptation on a new test set built for the purpose.

Few-shot adaptation markedly improved the speech. Listeners rated it higher on naturalness, clarity, and speaker similarity than existing Bangla systems, the authors report. The gap the work closes is practical: hundreds of millions of Bangla speakers had no adaptable synthesizer. The framework is offered as a base for richer Bangla voice tools.
arxiv-2502-06129:
Jinyuan Liu, Pranav Puthan, and Sutanu Sarkar simulate turbulence behind underwater terrain in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Flows that are layered by density and rotating, as in the ocean, form complex wakes behind three-dimensional bumps. The fine scales of these wakes matter for geophysical models but are poorly understood.

Using high-resolution simulations, the team separates two drivers of energy loss in the near wake. One is shear instability, strengthened under strong layering. The other is a spinning instability that peaks at mid-level rotation and weaker layering. Strong rotation damps the first, and strong layering shrinks the second. The authors derive predictive links between conditions and which driver rules.
arxiv-2502-06929:
Anowar Shajib and Joshua Frieman test a physically grounded family of evolving dark energy models against the latest sky data. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Fresh supernova and sound-wave results have revived interest in dark energy that changes over time. The simplest such models use a thawing scalar field, frozen early and rolling lately.

For this family, one number, today's equation-of-state value, captures the whole history. The team fits that number using many data sets, from the microwave background to galaxy surveys. The best fit sits clearly away from the constant dark energy of the standard model. Statistical evidence favors the thawing family substantially. Combining just the sound-wave and supernova data sharpens the tension most. The models ease one cosmic tension slightly while worsening another. Forecasts for near-future surveys close the paper.
arxiv-2502-08629:
Timothy De Deyn and co-authors formalize how a key property of triangulated categories passes down to smaller pieces. Their 2025 paper works in algebraic geometry, a field that studies shapes through equations. The property is strong generation, which says a whole category can be built from one object in a bounded number of steps.

Their framework recovers several known results from the literature in one sweep. As new uses, they show that strong generation for the singularity category of a scheme is a local property in the Zariski sense. They also prove a strong generation result for the derived category of a class of algebraic stacks. The paper gives geometers a shared method for descent-style proofs, rather than each result being built from scratch.
arxiv-2502-10229:
Jens Andersen and Mathias Nødtvedt wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It maps the phases of dense quark matter in a low-energy model that joins quarks, mesons, and paired quarks, at zero heat but varied quark and isospin load.

The map shows four phases: empty space, a phase with condensed pions or paired quarks, plain quark matter, and a color superconducting phase. The authors sort the light waves that arise in that last phase and track the speed of sound in two clean cases. In both, the speed peaks and then nears the conformal limit from above as density grows. Rules that force charge balance, local or global, shift the picture only a bit, and a mixed phase is weighed at the end.
arxiv-2502-12129:
Mohammad Aamir Sohail, Touheed Anwar Atif, and Sandeep Pradhan reformulate a compression problem where classical data comes from measuring a quantum source. The decoder may use quantum side information to reconstruct the measurement results within a bounded error. Classical rate-distortion language fits this awkwardly.

Their new formulation replaces the distortion observable with a posterior channel and imposes a block error constraint instead. A parallel formulation handles the purely classical side-information problem. For both, they derive inner bounds on asymptotic performance in terms of single-letter mutual information quantities of the posterior channel. A bridge result shows a rate-channel protocol can attain the optimal rate-distortion function for a matching distortion measure. The paper connects two theories that usually stay separate.
arxiv-2502-12429:
Peilin Du, Jing Zhang, and Rongguo Yang propose a compact route to fault-tolerant quantum computing with light, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The route is one-way quantum computation, where the computing is done by measuring a large entangled cluster state one qubit at a time.

The bottleneck is building big three-dimensional cluster states that stay compatible with error-correcting codes. The authors' scheme builds canonical three-dimensional cubic clusters from the combined space and color modes of an optical parametric oscillator. Adding Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states, which encode a qubit in an oscillator, brings full fault tolerance within reach. The scheme also lowers the squeezing threshold that the light must meet. Its main selling point is simplicity: far less optical hardware than rival designs. The authors argue this compactness paves the way to practical optical quantum computers.
arxiv-2502-13029:
Rion Glenn Nazareth, Gayathri Santhosh, and Luke Chamandy apply a galaxy model in twenty twenty-five. Spiral galaxies host magnetic fields as strong, in energy terms, as their gas motions. Yet measured field traits had rarely been set against theory in a direct, quantitative way. In an earlier paper, the team built a simple axisymmetric dynamo model fed by observed data.

Here they run that model on four nearby galaxies: M31, M33, M51, and NGC 6946. Outputs include field strength and pitch angle profiles, gas velocity spread, and scale height. They also compute turbulent time and length scales and the sizes of supernova remnants. Scaling factors absorb known imprecision. Despite its simplicity, the model matched galaxy profiles fairly well.
arxiv-2502-15329:
Degott and four co-authors read star spots from wave bands in light curves in this twenty twenty-five paper. Low-mass stars wear spots that shift their light as they spin in view. Spot-by-spot fits in time can tie one curve to more than one true tale.

Inside, a new form reads the low wave band of a curve's spread for spot marks. It pulls spot force and mean spot life when spin peaks show in the band. Fake curves first prove the form, then real curves from a big sky set feed it. Tens of thousands of stars sort into peak and no-peak bands by that read. A hot act zone shows for light stars in one spin band of the set.
arxiv-2502-15829:
Christopher Johann Clarke presents LACTOSE, an algorithm that lets neural networks use if-then branches. His paper appeared in 2025. Training by gradient descent cannot pass through a branch, since the choice flips rather than slides. That blocks conditional logic inside learning models, such as sound processors that should react differently to loud and quiet inputs.

LACTOSE stores trained settings for each user-set numeric range and loads the right settings when a value lands in that range during use. Errors are kept apart by range, so learning still flows. Clarke demonstrates it on a simple digital signal processing task. The paper's main point is broader: a working if-then step for a family of audio tools that learn. The trick could matter wherever models must switch behavior by threshold.
arxiv-2502-17629:
Sepehr Assadi and Helia Yazdanyar simplified a key trick for graph coloring in a 2025 paper. Coloring a graph so neighbors differ takes at most one more color than the highest degree, but doing it with very little data or memory is hard. A known sparsification theorem says random short color lists, sampled per vertex, almost surely still allow a full coloring, powering near-optimal fast algorithms in several models.

That theorem's proofs are heavy and the coloring step is complex. The authors prove a weaker, asymmetric version that dodges both drawbacks while keeping algorithms of similar quality. Simpler proofs and simpler recovery make a central sublinear tool easier to teach, check, and reuse.
arxiv-2502-18229:
Mirsad Cosovic and colleagues released JuliaGrid in 2025, an open-source software framework for estimating the state of electric power systems. Modern grids are large and complex, mixing rising demand with many kinds of energy sources. State estimation, the calculation that turns meter readings into a consistent picture of voltages across the grid, is computationally demanding and needs fast tools.

Written in the Julia language, the framework covers observability analysis, two kinds of estimators, bad data detection, and phasor measurement algorithms. It also includes power flow and optimal power flow calculations, which can generate the measurements the estimators consume. The authors report that it solves large systems across all these methods with speed competitive against other open-source tools, and that it targets steady-state style analysis.
arxiv-2502-19229:
Ye Xing, Zhi-Peng Xing, and Yu-Ji Shi work out how exotic four-quark states with a strange flavor fall apart. These states bind four light quarks into one particle with set spin and parity. Symmetry alone dictates much of their decay menu. The study covers four charge patterns built from up, down, and strange quarks.

Flavor symmetry sorts the states into families, a decuplet and a larger twenty-seven member set. For each family the allowed two-body and three-body decays are listed. A molecular approach, treating the states as loose pairs of mesons, then sizes each channel. Two named states earn total widths of several million electron volts in the math. The results give search experiments concrete targets: which decays to watch, and how strong each should be.
arxiv-2503-00029:
Zhang, Hong, and Yu teach a language model to grade its own words as it writes in this twenty twenty-five paper. Word-by-word tools can not see ahead, so they can miss the best line. Look-ahead hunts fix that, but they lean on a split grade model that costs much.

Inside, the core model gains a word-grade skill of its own, which cuts the split tool out. A stream-fit hunt then uses those grades to pick the next word with care. That hunt also runs in parts side by side, which keeps the stream fast. Tests on three broad sets show wins in most bouts with the plain greedy mode. With a fine-tune step added, the win rate climbs more.
arxiv-2503-00129:
Erdogan and Tzirakis study the Zakharov system, a coupled wave model from plasma physics, on the upper half plane with data given on its edge, in work from twenty twenty-five. Boundary value problems for such systems are delicate, since waves meet the wall. Low roughness solutions were not known in two dimensions.

They prove local well posedness at low regularity, meaning rough starting data still give one short lived solution that depends on the data in a stable way. Tools mix a restricted norm method with a Fourier and Laplace approach to the boundary. The nonlinear part of the solution lands in a smoother space than the data. The authors claim a first for this system.
arxiv-2503-00929:
Xueping Gong and Jiheng Zhang design a pricing algorithm that learns as it goes in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Dynamic pricing in e-commerce and transport must explore how demand responds while exploiting what it already knows. Existing methods often assume exact knowledge of the demand function's smoothness and scale parameters, which real sellers rarely have. The authors remove that assumption.

Their Parameter-Adaptive Dynamic Pricing algorithm partitions the demand function's domain and uses a linear bandit structure on the pieces. Regret, the revenue lost while learning, is managed efficiently without prior parameter knowledge. The paper reports improved regret bounds over existing methods and extensions that use contextual information about customers or products. Numerical experiments backed the theory, showing the adaptive method beating its rivals. The contribution is practical: pricing that adapts both to demand and to its own ignorance about demand.
arxiv-2503-01129:
Haoyang Liu and co-authors solve mixed-integer programs with a neural loop that predicts, checks, then fixes only sure values. Learning models can guess a solution fast, but fixing wrong guesses ruins the result. Their Apollo-MILP alternates a prediction step with a correction step each round. A trust-region search polishes the guess into a reference solution.

Comparing guess and reference yields an uncertainty bound for each value. Only values with high confidence get frozen into the smaller problem. The rest stay free for the solver to decide. Benchmarks show over fifty percent cuts in the solution gap versus rival learning methods. Quality gains hold across the standard test sets.
arxiv-2503-02129:
Hao Yu argues that double descent in neural network error is shrinkage at work, not overfitting, and proves matching bounds for path-regularized multilayer networks. The paper from twenty twenty-five builds a nonasymptotic generalization theory with no caps on width, depth, or loss size. Under- and over-parameterized regimes are bounded separately, which is what lets the curve bend twice. An open approximation problem in generalized Barron spaces is settled en route.

Lower bounds at every minimizer meet the upper bounds, proving the error itself, not just its estimate, dips, peaks, and dips again. A slow-rate oracle inequality shows variance plays no part once regularization passes the noise level. The peak is the price of shrinkage the small regime demands.
arxiv-2503-02229:
Martin Landriau and a large collaboration check the reliability of emission-line identifications in the HETDEX galaxy survey using DESI spectroscopy, in a two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. HETDEX usually sees one emission line and must guess whether it is Lyman-alpha from a distant galaxy.

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument re-observed HETDEX candidates in two pointings, securing confident redshifts for over a thousand sources. The comparison tuned the classification method to meet the survey's contamination target of under two percent. It also validated that ninety-six percent of true Lyman-alpha emitters get the correct redshift. Line wavelengths, fluxes, and widths agree between the instruments within uncertainties.
arxiv-2503-02329:
Stella Koch Ocker, Mandy Chen, Peng Oh, and Prateek Sharma probe tiny swirls in gas around galaxies. That halo gas is hard to gauge at the small scales where swirls fade. Fast radio bursts pick up small swings in plasma density as they pass. Quasar light gives a read on the same swirls at larger scales.

From quasar data, the team infers the strength of density swings for hot and cool halo gas. Both values sit far below those in Milky Way gas at like scales. Hot gas would delay bursts by a negligible amount, while cool gas could broaden or twinkle them. Joint reads of one galaxy by both tools can bound the fade scale. Early checks put that scale at no less than about seven hundred fifty kilometers in cool gas.
arxiv-2503-03129:
Li presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on interpretable healthcare classifiers built from neural differential equations. Deep learning's black-box style breeds distrust in medicine. The proposed models process data as continuous flows instead. That flow view makes their inner steps easier to trace. Text data is handled continuously, a first for this model family. The architecture aims to keep predictive power while opening the hood. Healthcare groups needing transparency are the target users.

The paper is a proposal and exploration of the design. It argues differential structure suits readable classification. Future research directions are sketched throughout. Trust, not raw accuracy, is the headline goal.
arxiv-2503-04929:
Kehan Long and co-workers built learned safety barriers for robot arms in a 2025 paper. A manipulator working in clutter must pla fast and promise it will not collide, even as the scene moves. Their approach learns a configuration-space distance function, a score that says how close a pose is to hit. Turns it into a barrier that steers control away from danger while cutting hit checks sharply.

Because the barrier is learned from live point-cloud sensing, model error and sensor noise must enter the safety math. A distributionally robust version handles both without assuming a known error spread. Mock runs and a real six-joint arm confirmed fast planning and safe control in messy, changing scenes.
arxiv-2503-07529:
Stalport and a large team of co-authors confirm two planets crossing the star TOI-1453 in two thousand twenty-five. The star is a cool dwarf watched by the TESS space telescope in its northern zone. Ground data from photos, spectra, and sharp images back the space data.

One hundred high-grade spectra from the HARPS-N tool, taken over two seasons, pin down each planet's size, mass, and orbit. The inner planet is a super-Earth on a four-day orbit, slightly larger than Earth and light for its size. The outer one is a sub-Neptune on a six-and-a-half-day orbit, about twice Earth's size. Their period ratio sits near three to two, though the pair is not locked in resonance.
arxiv-2503-08029:
Tianyu Li, Sunan Sun, Shubhodeep Shiv Aditya, and Nadia Figueroa wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents Elastic Motion Policy, a way for a robot to learn a skill from a single shown run and still adapt when the scene shifts.

Plain behavior cloning copies a teacher but fails off its training ground, with no promise of success. The new frame is a dynamical system, so motion is ruled by equations with convergence built in. Laplacian editing warps the taught path in full hand pose space, and an online learner reshapes a Lyapunov function as the scene changes. Real robot tests show firm, quick work with obstacle dodging and multi-step tasks.
arxiv-2503-08629:
Joseph Jachinowski, Hassan Alnatah, David Snoke, and Peter Littlewood study coherence in two dimensional Bose gases in two thousand twenty-five. The gases are made of polaritons, part light and part matter. Their light part makes them easy to probe with optics. Interferometry can read the first order coherence of the gas.

The team derives a universal curve for the coherent share of the gas. It fits a calm, noninteracting gas in balance. Real data match the curve near exactly at low density. At high density, standard weak interaction theory fits. Finite size smooths the sharp phase shift seen in the bulk limit.
arxiv-2503-08929:
Hrishikesh Viswanath and co-workers rebuilt outdoor scenes from laser scans with a smoothness-seeking neural method in a 2025 paper called HessianForge. Robots map their surroundings from LiDAR point clouds, but noise and sparsity leave reconstructed faces bumpy and torn. The authors frame mapping as physics-informed energy tuning: learn a signed distance field whose face pays an energy penalty for sharp ridges. Gauged through second derivatives, so smoothness is imposed as a real preference rather than a post-process.

An octree coding feeds multi-scale networks that refine the field coarse to fine. A test-time step repairs shape-based glitches in the final mesh. Large outdoor scenes come out as clean, artifact-light manifolds suited to navigation and mock run.
arxiv-2503-09029:
Boyang Xue leads a team teaching language models to practice hardest on the problems they find hardest. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Self-training lets models learn from their own answers. Standard schemes sample easy questions far more than tough ones. Hard problems thus get too little practice. Ceiling performance suffers exactly where it matters.

Their DAST framework first estimates difficulty by sampling. It then augments data around the challenging queries. A training stage mixes supervised fine-tuning with preference optimization. Math tasks supply the test bed. Gains hold across settings in their experiments. The lesson is simple: difficulty should steer self-training, not be averaged away.
arxiv-2503-09229:
Thi Thanh Mai Ta, Quang Huy Nguyen, and Phi Hung Pham sharpen the error bounds for a method that solves heat-type tasks on a grid over both space and time. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The method cuts the task, set with start and edge values, into small space-time cells. Past work had set error bounds on neat grids. The team works on rough, free-form grids and gains higher-order bounds in three norms. One bound is in a norm stronger than the space the method works in, and is of the best rate. They close with worked cases that show the theory in use.
arxiv-2503-11329:
Marvin Kahra and Michael Breuß tackle a basic problem in color image processing: colors have no natural total order. Morphological filters need to pick the largest or smallest value in each neighborhood, which is trivial for gray levels but ambiguous for colors. Every existing scheme sacrifices some desirable property.

Their ordering starts from the log-exp-supremum of color matrices, which supplies a reference color under the Loewner semi-order. Colors are then pre-ordered by their distance to that reference. A lexicographic cascade breaks remaining ties, guaranteeing a total order with a unique result. The aim is a supremum analogue that keeps the original colors and satisfies as many wanted properties as possible.
arxiv-2503-13129:
Anne Morgen and six co-authors used a fast atom loss process to observe a slower one in a cold atom cloud, in a paper published in 2025. Their cloud is a Bose-Einstein condensate with impurity atoms near a tuned resonance point. There, three-body losses run faster than any clock can track directly. A still faster two-body loss, though, can be measured, and the team worked back from it.

From the fast measurements they rebuilt the number of atoms in the cloud over time. That gives the three-body loss rate and how it scales as the resonance tuning shifts. The two ways of counting the cloud agree well. Each loss event was found to cost the cloud more than two atoms, a sign of secondary collisions in the dense gas. The method opens a new probe for loss physics.
arxiv-2503-14929:
Yufan Sheng and six co-authors present ACE, an attention based gauge for the result size of queries over set valued data. Size gauges are core to databases, but most handle numbers or classes, not sets. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Set valued data fill search and recommendation tools. Past gauges favor common elements or assume partial freedom, which limits use. ACE first boils the data set into a compact matrix with a distillation encoder. An attention based query reader then catches links among query elements. A pooling step handles any query size, and a small network gives the final count. Tests on three data sets beat top rivals in exactness and speed.
arxiv-2503-15929:
Payel Patra, Daniele Di Pompeo, and Antinisca Di Marco build a framework for judging the judges of FAIR research data. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. FAIR data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, and many tools now score how well platforms meet those aims.

The authors evaluate twenty-two such assessment tools against open science platforms. Their framework exposes where the tools agree, where they fall short, and where they waste effort. Better scoring, they argue, leads to better sharing and tidier research artifacts, from data to code and documentation. The study is aimed at platform builders who want honest measurement before claiming openness. It also seeds ideas for the next generation of platforms.
arxiv-2503-16329:
Xiao Chen, Thomas Lettau, Ulf Peschel, Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean, and Silvana Botti wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It simulates, in real time, how short infrared laser pulses stir the electrons of crystalline zinc oxide.

The aim is to learn what fills the conduction band well enough for light-pumped lasing. Two pulse colors are tried, near and mid infrared, across a wide range of strengths where data exist. Three methods are set side by side: the Keldysh model, the semiconductor Bloch equations, and time-dependent density functional theory. The last proves a sound first-principles tool. The middle regime blends tunneling within bands with multi-photon jumps between them.
arxiv-2503-17129:
Omar Hussein and Yuri Mishin model how a metal alloy might freeze its grain size forever instead of coarsening, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Nanocrystalline metals are strong because their grains are tiny, but grains tend to grow, especially when hot. One hope is that solute atoms segregating to grain boundaries could drive the boundary energy to zero and halt growth.

Their model couples a Potts model of grain orientations with a lattice gas for the solute's thermodynamics and diffusion. Kinetic Monte Carlo evolves the alloy with nonlinear barriers between states. Stable polycrystalline states do appear, but only when solute atoms repel each other. The winning structure is not frozen: it holds a dynamic equilibrium between grain growth and grain refinement. Triple junctions vanish as small grains embed in a larger matrix. The result gives alloy designers concrete conditions to chase for thermally stable nanostructures.
arxiv-2503-19529:
Omid Esrafilian, Rakesh Mundlamuri, Florian Kaltenberger, Raymond Knopp, and David Gesbert wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reports first results on finding where ground users are with the help of a drone that carries radio gear, in a fifth generation mobile network.

The drone picks up signals from users at set spots, and the travel time of each signal gives a range. Since the drone's own place is not known with care, users and drone must be found at once. The team uses a least-squares mapping method that joins the range data with GPS reads. They built the setup with an open radio platform and checked it in real-world tests.
arxiv-2503-21829:
Ivan Diaz and eight co-authors build a cut net that learns straight from MRI scans took at grades that do not match. Care scans shift by who made the gear, by site, and by run type. The stock fix scales all scans to one grid. That fix brings in flaws from fills and drops fine points. Their net aims at cuts of sores from a brain and cord ill.

The build sets its core shapes with round wave terms at a fixed real size, through the e3nn frame. Cores can then be scaled to each scan's cell size, so no scan scale step is need. Trained on data from more than one site and from its own site, it beat stock U-Nets. That held in most test cases through both train plans. It also held for grades not seen in train.
arxiv-2503-24129:
Dominik Schnaus, Nikita Araslanov, and Daniel Cremers ask whether image and text models can be matched with no paired data at all. Their study from two thousand twenty-five starts from a simple claim. As models and data grow, the gaps inside each type of model start to look more alike.

The team frames blind matching as a math task and builds a new search method that beats older solvers. They also find test cases where a real match is likely to exist. Across four data sets, many image and text sets could be matched with no labels. A test classifier built this way scored well with no image-text training pairs.
arxiv-2504-03329:
Francesca Ronchini and three co-authors tuned the prompts that make synthetic sound sets for hearing training, in a paper published in 2025. Text-to-audio models can create clips on request, but the craft of the request steers how true the clips feel. Their tests ran two sound classification sets through two such models, with a spread of prompt plans, from bare to task tuned.

Task-tuned prompts beat bare ones by a wide step. Mixed sets from both models beat a lone set grown large. So the gain came from variety of kind, not bulk. The authors present prompt craft plus model mixing as a cheap data boost for sound classification. The route suits fields where true clips are costly.
arxiv-2504-06329: Mingjie Li and Simon Horsley calculate propagators for relativistic wave equations in two thousand twenty-five. A propagator tells how a field spreads through space and time. Their route borrows the view used for the Rayleigh-Sommerfeld diffraction integral. They apply it to the Klein-Gordon equation and the Dirac equation. Both equations get propagators this way. Their results cast fresh light on the Feynman checkerboard model. Some traits of that model, as used for the Dirac case, seem missed.
arxiv-2504-07029:
Ran Zhang and co-authors distill a big text-guided image fusion model into a small one that needs no text at run time. Fusing several images into one rich view helps in low light and clutter. Text-guided giants do it well but cost heavy memory and time. A teacher-student setup passes the giant's skill into a lean network.

A cross-fusion module blends the text lessons across space and channels during training. The student keeps about ninety percent of the teacher's quality. It runs on a tenth of the size and time. Tests show it beating current state-of-the-art fusion methods. Code will be shared as an open resource.
arxiv-2504-07529:
Niklas Elmqvist and Clemens Nylandsted Klokmose set out a research agenda for AI in data visualization, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Generative AI is reshaping computing, and charting and visual analysis tools are changing with it. The authors ask how AI that keeps people at the center can reshape the field for the better.

Their framework crosses four things AI can do for people with four stages of making sense of data, from first viewing to final reporting. For each crossing they survey current tools, imagine next steps, and flag risks and ethical traps. The grid is offered as a shared plan for researchers and builders. It also shows, in reverse, how visualization can serve human-centered AI work.
arxiv-2504-08429:
Brosda and a large team work in twenty twenty-five toward exact readings of quantum dot groups through electric measurements. Quantum dots are tiny islands that trap charge, and groups of uneven dots are probed by tracking how their charge storage shifts with voltage. Peaks in those curves shift with temperature, which models explained, and with signal frequency, which they did not.

The team measured peak shifts across temperatures and frequencies. They then built a refined model that accounts for how tunnelling rates depend on energy. The model matched the data in both cold and warm regimes, for different reasons in each. The findings sharpen tools used to build light sources and spin-based quantum bits.
arxiv-2504-11729:
Jiahong Ning and co-authors published a 2025 paper on running large language models inside future 6G mobile networks. Network operators hope these models will help manage the network and add smart services. Standard model designs, though, are slow and can leak data, and long inputs make both problems worse. Sixth-generation networks demand quick, safe responses.

Their framework, EdgePrompt, splits work between the cloud and edge devices near the user. It stores and reuses parts of the model's attention work in a distributed way, tuned to network conditions. That speeds up answers and raises throughput. A privacy step keeps sensitive information apart during processing, cutting the risk of leaks. Tests on a public dataset showed better speed and lower delay than the standard setup. The authors present the design as a workable base for language models in 6G settings. It targets the strict timing and security needs of live networks.
arxiv-2504-12929:
Kuzikova and co-authors watched, in extreme slow motion, how laser light flips the magnetism of an iron borate crystal. The material is a canted antiferromagnet, whose two magnetic sublattices tilt slightly toward each other. A laser pulse drives it through a ninety-degree spin reorientation, a sudden rotation of its magnetic order. The team found the switch is steered by that small tilt, called canting.

Within picoseconds the pulse disturbs the interaction that sets the tilt, tipping the crystal into a hidden phase no steady stimulus can reach. Heating then launches the full rotation. Because canting and heating share control, the final state mixes original and switched regions over a wide range, far wider than the sharp switch produced by ordinary heating.
arxiv-2504-13629:
Lin Cong and Wu Zhu study how researchers adopt large language models for writing in a 2025 paper. Tools such as ChatGPT are reshaping how academic papers are drafted and revised. The team built a data set of over six hundred twenty seven thousand papers from a public preprint server, and trained classifiers to detect text revised in the style of ChatGPT.

Adoption varied widely by field, gender, native language, and career stage. Use of the tools improved clarity, brevity, and formal style, with gains differing by revision type. Writing styles across scholars converged after adoption. The strongest shifts came from early adopters, men, non native speakers, and junior scholars, whose style moved toward that of established researchers.
arxiv-2504-14629:
Ivan Mikhailov finds new geodesic lines in the space of all metric spaces, near the cloud of the real line. The paper from twenty twenty-five works with Gromov-Hausdorff distance, a way to gauge how alike two spaces are at large scale. A geodesic line is a shortest-path curve through that vast class. Mikhailov builds one from any unbounded part of the line crossed with a scaled bounded space.

The scaling runs from zero upward without end. A second result blocks a tempting rival curve. Integer lattice scalings jump in distance, with a stated floor. That jump makes the lattice curve discontinuous, so it cannot be a geodesic. Scaling all spaces near Euclidean space proves jumpy as well. The work maps where smooth paths through the space of spaces can and cannot run.
arxiv-2504-14729:
Garg, Oliveira, and Sengupta proved rank bounds for a family of arithmetic circuits in twenty twenty-five. Arithmetic circuits compute polynomials through layers of additions and multiplications. Identity testing asks whether such a circuit secretly computes zero; fast deterministic tests are a central open problem in complexity theory.

The authors prove a nonlinear version of the Edelstein-Kelly theorem, a geometry result about lines and planes, for polynomials of any fixed degree. This settles a stronger form of a twenty fourteen conjecture and extends earlier work that handled only quadratic polynomials. As a consequence, depth-four circuits with top fan-in three have constant rank bounds when they compute zero. Combined with known results, that yields the first deterministic polynomial-time identity test for this circuit class.
arxiv-2504-16529:
Yang, Ku, Lou, Tenny, and Hsu propose in twenty twenty-five a network design that fuses communication and computing at the network edge for future 6G services. Today's edge setups treat the two as separate worlds, which strains the tight delays that live AI chat services need. Their framework puts computing inside radio network nodes and manages bandwidth and compute power jointly.

Queueing maths showed the fused design nearly doubles service capacity over the split design, at a fixed standard for on-time jobs. Simulations with real AI workloads, chip specs, and priority scheduling confirmed a large gain, though smaller. The authors pitch the design as a cheaper path to real-time AI services on 6G. Costs and rollout questions remain open.
arxiv-2504-17729:
Michele Botti, Daniele Prada, Anna Scotti, and Michele Visinoni discretize Biot's poroelasticity equations with a fully-mixed virtual element method. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets coupled deformation and fluid flow in saturated porous media. The fully-mixed form pays off twice: sharper Darcy velocity and stress fields, plus exact local conservation of mass and momentum. Their four-field scheme imposes stress symmetry directly in the discrete space.

No extra Lagrange multiplier is needed for that symmetry. A full error analysis shows robustness as material properties hit their limits. First-order convergence is confirmed in three-dimensional tests with backward Euler time stepping. A standard poroelasticity benchmark checks speed and toughness. Groundwater, geomechanics, and biomechanics codes are the audience.
arxiv-2504-17829:
Vlad Vasilescu, Ana Neacșu, and Daniela Faur published a 2025 paper on protecting image dehazing models from attack. Dehazing cleans up hazy satellite and aerial images so objects are easier to detect. The authors first show that leading dehazing models are fragile: changing a single pixel can cut image quality sharply.

They then propose two light fine-tuning methods that harden a trained model without retraining it from scratch. Clean-image quality stayed about the same, while resistance to attack rose a great deal. Tests on two remote sensing settings showed the protection held on unfamiliar data too. The authors share their code for both the attacks and the defences.
arxiv-2504-18629:
Jessy Han, Kristjan Greenewald, and Devavrat Shah ask, in a 2025 paper, whether risk scores tell the whole story of racial gaps in reoffending. Most fairness work treats reoffending as a yes-or-no outcome and audits the algorithm's predictions. These authors instead study time until reoffending, inside a causal framework that lets race, the score, and life context interact. They build a formal survival test for whether the score fully explains racial differences.

Run on the well-known COMPAS data, the test finds no racial gap inside risk groups over short horizons. In the low-risk group, though, a significant gap emerges after about nine months and survives finer score bands, score noise, and a competing-risks check. The authors read this as evidence that housing, work, and support, not the algorithm alone, shape who returns. Fairness, they argue, is more than algorithms.
arxiv-2504-18829:
Jiayi Chen and three colleagues wrote a 2025 robotics paper on how robot hands grasp objects. A good robot hand must pick the right grip for each job, from a firm wrap to a fine pinch. Building data for all grip types by hand is far too slow.

Their system, called Dexonomy, makes grasp data on its own for any grip type, object, and jointed hand. It starts from one human-marked example per grip and hand. First it reshapes the object to fit the hand's pose, then it fine-tunes the hand in a physics test bed. The grasps it makes are rich in contact, with no overlap errors. The team also adds a check for grasp quality.
arxiv-2504-19729:
Maxime Flin and Magnús Halldórsson speed up the task of keeping a changing network properly colored. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. In graph coloring, linked nodes must differ in color, and edges here appear and vanish over time.

Their randomized algorithm maintains a coloring with one more color than the highest node degree. It runs against an adaptive adversary, meaning each change can react to the algorithm's past choices. The update time beats a very recent rival result and reaches a natural barrier for this problem. The gains come from the densest parts of the graph. The authors borrow structural ideas from distributed computing, where many machines color a graph together.
arxiv-2505-01929:
Valentin Guichard leads a team of fifteen authors generating entangled states of up to six photons for photonic quantum computing. Their scheme uses a linear optical circuit with a fiber delay loop acting as memory, fed by a bright semiconductor quantum dot source. Watching entanglement form without ruining it is the practical problem they address.

They produced two, three, four, and six photon entangled states at steadily falling rates, averaging a factor of about forty-six per added photon. A monitoring method based on partial measurements reads the visibility of selected outcomes. That signal faithfully tracks the entanglement process in real time. Such live control matters for measurement-based photonic quantum computation outside the laboratory.
arxiv-2505-02929:
Arrazola, Bertet, Chu, and Rabl engineer protected links between quantum bits and a cavity mode, in two thousand twenty-five. Low-frequency noise can badly weaken the coupling in such cavity setups, which blocks clean exchange of excitations. Their answer is a train of short pulses, timed to cancel the noise while letting the exchange proceed.

By shaping the pulse train, they can select unlike coupling types on demand. The cavity can also mediate links between the bits themselves. A close analysis of leftover flaws shows the effective strength of the system rising by orders of magnitude. Operation fidelity for key quantum tasks should rise with it, they argue.
arxiv-2505-03529:
Kailash Reddy and three colleagues present SKALD, an algorithm for anonymizing very large datasets, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Privacy law and practice favor k-anonymisation, which hides each person inside a group of lookalikes. Standard tools, though, must fit the whole dataset in memory.

Big datasets get chopped into chunks, and chunk-by-chunk anonymisation loses quality. SKALD instead extracts sufficient statistics from each chunk and combines them. The global picture guides anonymisation even under tight memory limits. The authors claim multi-fold performance improvements over standard methods. Utility of the released data is also better preserved. The algorithm targets releases of sensitive tabular data at real-world scale.
arxiv-2505-04929:
Yair Caro and Zsolt Tuza prove new bounds in the style of a classic graph result, for a measure of how dense a graph's densest part can be. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The classic result bounds the sum and product of the color counts of two parts that split a full graph's edges. Caro and Tuza take up splits into any count of parts, and swap the color count for the max mean degree. They find a clean cap that the true value nears as both counts grow. They pin the exact value for splits in two, and for splits that leave a small count of edges out. They also give uses for the bounds in past work.
arxiv-2505-05529:
Ahmed Zahari Abdou Damdji and Bouzid Mosbahi sort pairs of small algebra systems that can work side by side, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Each system has two ways to multiply that must fit a shared match rule. The survey covers complex systems with size below four.

For each class the team works out a long list of traits and maps. Those include rate-of-change maps, centers, symmetry groups, and several named operator types.
