The full tables let other researchers look up a pair and read off its traits at once. Readers who study abstract algebra get a compact reference for a niche but growing topic.
arxiv-2505-06029:
Sarah Damerow and Stefan Kehrein test a bold extension of the adiabatic theorem in two thousand twenty-five. The classic theorem says a system changed slowly enough stays in its ground state. The proposed extension covers sudden changes, called quenches, that stay inside one phase.

The claim is that the start ground state overlaps most with the new ground state after such a quench. In one standard magnet model, the claim held in both phases, by proof and by numeric checks. In a second, richer model, the team proved a special case and tested the rest by computer. The work probes how far a core quantum rule can stretch.
arxiv-2505-06729:
Zhu and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on guiding robots to find objects indoors. Image-and-text models bring rich prior knowledge to this search task. Yet they struggle to grasp a full room layout, and asking them at each step wastes time. The team's system builds a layered map as the robot moves. The map holds viewpoints, object nodes, and room nodes in a clear structure. Search then runs in two stages, high-level planning and close exploration.

Tests on three fake indoor benchmarks gave top scores for success and path thrift. Gains held on both counts over prior methods. The team also ran the system on a real robot in ten rooms. It handled fifteen search tasks with strong steadiness. The authors back layered maps for robot search.
arxiv-2505-07829:
Ofer Dekel presents Blockbuster, in a 2025 preprint, a framework for fusing AI operations during inference. Fusing steps into one kernel saves trips to memory, the true bottleneck on modern chips. Blockbuster works on any machine with tiered memory, from graphics cards to AI accelerators. Workloads are drawn as block programs, which track exactly how chunks of data move between memory levels. Fusion candidates are picked first, then each is fused by a rule-based algorithm. That split suits the huge programs now common.

The paper centers on the fusion algorithm itself. As a sanity check, it rediscovers the famous Flash Attention kernel on its own. It then fuses normalization with matrix multiplication into single kernels. One mega-kernel swallows three multiplications plus several smaller operations. Dekel argues that modeling data movement directly is what makes the fusions unusually powerful.
arxiv-2505-08029:
Rohit Kumar Shukla, Rajiv Kumar, Ujjwal Sen, and Sunil Mishra study how to charge quantum batteries best, by tuning the split between the battery's own dynamics and the charger's. Quantum batteries store and give energy in many body quantum systems. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Battery and charger roles are given to distinct parts of one spin system's rule set. By dialing down the battery's own part during charging, stored energy and charging power can rise a lot. How much gain comes depends on how spins link and over what range. In open settings with energy loss and phase fade, scores mostly drop, but some systems gain, and the tuning gain stays robust.
arxiv-2505-08729:
Aditya Ghosh and Dominik Rothenhäusler tackle a quiet weakness in observational studies: nobody knows which background factors must be adjusted for. Their paper appeared in 2025. Often several adjustment sets look plausible, and ignorability, the key assumption, cannot be tested. Different choices can flip the estimated treatment effect, and common fixes give intervals that never narrow with more data. The authors propose a procedure that stays valid when at least one candidate adjustment is right.

Their trick shifts the target to a nearby reweighted population where robust inference is possible, echoing how overlap problems are handled. The method returns one estimate and an interval that shrinks at the usual statistical rate. Tests on synthetic and real data gave far tighter intervals than the safe convex-hull approach, with correct coverage.
arxiv-2505-09629: Runbo Li proves that a function sitting below the prime-counting indicator can still track primes well inside arithmetic progressions with smooth moduli. Minorants are the workhorse underestimators of sieve theory. A good one stays at or below the prime indicator everywhere, yet captures a known share of primes along progressions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Li constructs such a minorant with distribution level ten nineteenths, for progressions whose moduli have only small prime factors. The result refines earlier work by Baker and Irving and by Stadlmann.
arxiv-2505-09729:
Shuchen Zhu and Yu Tong proposed a variational quantum algorithm with a graceful failure mode in a 2025 paper. Ground state preparation underlies quantum chemistry and materials simulation, and adaptive variational methods build circuits step by step, yet they can stall without physical meaning. The authors' state-space gradient descent lowers energy at each step using only local physical operations, chosen from gradient and curvature information measurable on the device itself.

If the true ground state escapes, the result is still a genuine local minimum, often a real metastable state of the system rather than numerical junk. The method provably avoids barren plateaus, the flat landscapes that paralyze many variational algorithms, and simulations confirm the reliability claim on typical systems.
arxiv-2505-10929:
Alexander Litvak, Mathias Sonnleitner, and Tomasz Szczepanski study how points spread over a sphere in a two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. Given points on a sphere, some cap region will always be empty. The minimal dispersion measures the largest such empty cap, in the worst case over arrangements.

The authors track how this quantity behaves as the number of points and the dimension grow. They connect the problem to sphere covering and to approximating the Euclidean ball by inscribed polytopes. Random point choices yield upper bounds, sometimes improved by adding well-separated points. Intersections of caps get their own dispersion analysis. Old and new results are presented in a unified framework for researchers in geometric probability.
arxiv-2505-11329:
Raja Gond, Nipun Kwatra, and Ramachandran Ramjee speed up shared inference in twenty twenty-five. Running a large language model across many graphics cards splits the work, but the cards must talk to each other. That chatter can eat about a fifth of the time, even on fast links. One fix is to split work into small tasks and overlap talking with computing.

In practice, serving systems keep batches small for low delay, so splitting hurts more than it helps. The talking also steals processors from computing. TokenWeave is presented as the first system to overlap the two well in this setting. Readers who run model serving get a way to reclaim lost time on their hardware.
arxiv-2505-11629:
Taylor and Ritz studied light paths around a charged, spinning black hole sitting in a steady magnetic field in twenty twenty-five. The setup is known as the Ernst-Wild geometry. They traced how light bends near the hole, where rings of light can form, and what shadow the hole would cast for a distant viewer.

Using computer ray tracing, they show that spin and the magnetic field each change the light rings and shadow, and the two effects partly cancel. They also expand the math in small steps in the field strength to find how the shadow shifts from the plain spinning case. The work links the decay rate of light rings to the tones a disturbed black hole rings with.
arxiv-2505-14029:
Laura-Sophia von Hirschhausen and eight co-authors publish a large stereo image dataset of apple orchards across a growing season, in a 2025 paper. Precision farming models starve for realistic training data: orchards are dense, messy, and change weekly, and flat images cannot support three-dimensional reasoning about yield.

One part holds over ninety-three hundred high-resolution stereo pairs from a Brandenburg farm, spanning six validated growth stages over a full cycle. The other holds eleven hundred densely annotated images from two farms, with more than thirty-one thousand labeled apples. Stereo pairs enable depth reconstruction of trees, while growth-stage labels support timing analysis. The dataset extends an earlier public orchard collection and targets fruit detection, yield estimation, and structural modeling for orchard robotics.
arxiv-2505-14429:
Jonas Arruda and co-authors scale neural Bayesian inference to layered models with vast data in two thousand twenty-five. Amortized inference trains a network once to answer later data fast, but layered models demand giant simulated sets that choke the training.

Their fix extends a divide-and-conquer score method: split the data, update in parts, then merge. A new error-damping estimator cures a wobble the old merge showed with many parts. Stability held up to one hundred thousand points on a bench test. On a layered time-series model the method matched direct training on small sets while using less than one full simulation on big ones. A microscopy puzzle with over seven hundred fifty thousand parameters closed the proof.
arxiv-2505-15229:
Qihan Wang, Shidong Pan, Tal Linzen, and Emily Black propose multilingual prompting to make language model outputs more diverse, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Models underrepresent cultures and viewpoints in everything from opinions to factual answers.

The method rewrites a base prompt with cultural and linguistic cues from several cultures, samples responses to each version, and combines them. Because models store language-specific knowledge, the cues activate a broader range of their training. Across GPT-4o, its mini variant, and two LLaMA sizes, multilingual prompting beat high-temperature sampling, step-by-step recall, and persona prompting. Benefits varied with language resources and model size, and matching cue language to culture reduced hallucination.
arxiv-2505-15329:
Anqiao Ouyang, Hongyi Ke, and Qi Wang present a neural encoder that squeezes data about flows into a compact code without losing the ability to rebuild it. Their design, FINE, mixes reversible filters and steady-rising activation curves with a Fourier cutoff, so compression respects the shift symmetry of the data.

The team tested the encoder on interacting waves in one dimension, a turbulent one-dimensional system, and a two-dimensional turbulence set. FINE rebuilt the data with errors five to nine times lower than standard convolutional autoencoders, while using only a fifth or less of their parameters. The authors offer the design as a principled, light-weight route to shrinking data from physical systems while keeping it readable.
arxiv-2505-15429:
Pritam Anand wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It reviews and extends ways to say how unsure a support vector machine is about its own forecasts, a need the field has mostly left to neural networks.

Support vector machines give stable, sparse, and readable answers, but few tools attach honest error bars to them. The paper sums up existing methods for building prediction ranges in this setting and scores them against what an ideal range should do. None kept the answer sparse. The author then proposes a sparse quantile method that builds ranges by solving two linear programs, plus a feature-picking step that drops many inputs while improving the ranges on wide datasets. A final part wraps these models in conformal methods, which add firm guarantees on test data.
arxiv-2505-17329:
Hossein Adeli, Minni Sun, and Nikolaus Kriegeskorte modeled the visual brain with focus in a 2025 paper. Standard brain coding fits a huge linear map from a neural network's traits to each brain site. Ignoring the layout of traits in both systems, while factored versions assume fixed receptive fields that suit only early vision. Their model brain encoder instead routes retinotopic traits dynamically, using focus to send the right image information to category-selective areas downstream.

Across feature backbones and recording modalities, the focus model foretold brain activity during natural scene viewing by a lot better than rivals. Better still, its routing signals can be visualized per category area for any image, making the model's account of high-level vision straight inspectable.
arxiv-2505-19629:
Hassan Sartaj and a team of co-authors set out a research agenda in twenty twenty-five. Their topic is software engineering for robots that adapt on their own. Such robots work in changing, uncertain places and must watch themselves in real time. Unlike robots with fixed logic, they use AI, machine learning, and model-driven methods to keep adjusting.

The agenda runs along two lines. One follows the software life cycle, from requirements and design to testing and operations. The other covers enabling tools such as digital twins and AI-driven adaptation. Those tools support runtime monitoring and fault detection. Readers who build adaptive robots get a map of open problems and where effort should go next.
arxiv-2505-21229:
Jose Rodriguez and David Manlove study how to assign students to courses with credit loads in a stable way, in work from twenty twenty-five. Courses carry unlike credits and may clash in time, and students have their own wishes. A stable match leaves no student and course pair with a reason to break away.

The authors test several meanings of stability for this credit setting. For each, they give fast methods or hardness proofs for three tasks: checking a match, finding a stable match, and finding the largest stable match. Variants with ranked master lists and minimum class sizes add more results. The work maps where course allocation stays tractable and where it turns hard.
arxiv-2505-21329:
Allaa Boutaleb, Bernd Amann, Hubert Naacke, and Rafael Angarita found something fishy in the benchmarks for table union search in a 2025 paper. Union search finds, inside a data lake, tables that can be stacked onto a query table to enrich it, and representation learning methods compete on standard benchmarks meant to measure semantic understanding. The authors' audit shows prominent benchmarks have flaws that let simple baselines perform surprisingly well, sometimes beating sophisticated methods.

Scores, they argue, are driven heavily by dataset-specific quirks rather than genuine semantics, so the benchmarks fail to isolate what the methods actually learned. The paper proposes essential criteria for future benchmarks so progress in semantic table union search can be measured realistically and reliably. It is a cautionary tale for any field grading itself on inherited test sets.
arxiv-2505-22029:
Jinming Zhang and co-authors wrote this speech research paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on spotting stumbles in speech, like repeats, blocks, and stretched sounds. Such detection aids diagnosis and language checks, but labeled recordings of real dysfluent speech are scarce.

The team built LLM-Dys, a synthetic corpus where a large language model helps script the stumbles that speech software then speaks. The set covers eleven kinds of dysfluency, at both word and sound levels, with more varied contexts than past synthetic sets. They also improved an end-to-end detector trained on the corpus. Tests give it state-of-the-art scores. All data, models, and code are posted in public. The authors aim to free the field from its data bottleneck while keeping the fake speech natural enough to learn from.
arxiv-2505-23029:
Si Wu and Sebastian Bruch showed in 2025 that two qualities of words long studied by psychologists can be read off text alone. Imageability, how readily a word summons a mental picture. And concreteness, how perceptible its referent is, were before estimated with image-caption collections or multimodal models, on the starting claim that vision had to be involved. The authors bet that normal text figures carry the signal by themselves.

Their hypothesis is shape-based: in a text encoded form space, the area of a highly imageable or concrete word is more sharply peaked than that of an abstract word. They turn that sharpness into an unsupervised measure, the Area Balance Measure, needing no labels and no spread starting claims. Across tests it tracked human ratings more strongly than earlier unsupervised methods and forecast the two traits well in classification tests, with code and data put out publicly.
arxiv-2505-23829:
Xiaoqing Cheng, Ruizhe Chen, Hongying Zan, Yuxiang Jia, and Min Peng wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It presents BiasFilter, a tool that trims social bias from a language model's answers while the model is writing, with no retraining.

Most debiasing methods are costly, work weakly, or fail to scale. BiasFilter instead watches the text as it forms. Every few tokens it scores the partial answer for fairness, keeps a set of promising continuations, and drops the segments that score worst. A reward model, trained on a fairness preference dataset the team built, supplies the scores. The filter works with both open and commercial models. Tests across several models showed bias fell while answer quality largely held. The authors offer it as a practical add-on for fairer generation.
arxiv-2505-24129:
Wisnioski and five co-authors compiled this astronomy study in twenty twenty-five on how galaxies spin and stir their gas. A galaxy disc rotates, but its gas also moves at random speeds, called dispersion. Telescopes have mapped these motions in nearly one thousand far-off galaxies. Mixed methods and samples had led to clashing claims about how dispersion changed over cosmic time.

The authors gathered published measures for two hundred thirty-seven disc galaxies across a wide span of cosmic ages. They compared the data with stability models for discs. Once galaxy mass and tracer type were accounted for, dispersion changed little across most of the span. Ionised gas showed about twice the dispersion of cold molecular gas. The study cleans up a confused corner of galaxy research.
arxiv-2506-00329:
Muhammad Adnan and co-authors present Foresight, a method that speeds up text-to-video generation by reusing work the model has already done, in a 2025 paper. The big transformer models behind video generation repeat a costly denoising process many times, and attention over space and time makes each pass heavy. Fixed caching of past results helps, but a rigid schedule wastes chances or harms quality.

Foresight watches the generation as it runs and decides, layer by layer and step by step, which outputs can safely be reused. It adapts to the video's resolution and noise schedule instead of following a fixed plan. Applied to three open video models, it cut end-to-end generation time sharply while holding quality at the baseline level. The authors release the code for others to use.
arxiv-2506-02029:
Boris Zilber reframes the basic rules of quantum mechanics in a branch of logic called continuous model theory, in work from twenty twenty-five. The classic form of the rules came from Dirac and von Neumann. Zilber asks how those rules look when stated in a strict logical frame.

He shows the classic form can be restated in that frame with little loss. He also builds a new algebra for general structures, in the spirit of an older algebra for first order logic. Under mild limits, the new algebra takes the form of a Hilbert space with operators. The source structure can then be read back from it. The note links physics rules and logic in a fresh way.
arxiv-2506-02229:
Manas Mehta and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a lean way to teach a small network to read placenta photographs, with a big network as its teacher. An examination of the birth sac after delivery can flag risks to mother and baby. Recent tools pair photographs with the written reports of specialists to detect illnesses. Those tools are too big to run on thin equipment.

The new way anchors the teaching in the text side: the small network learns to match the text-first readings of the big network. A first teaching round on plain large natural image sets warms the small network up. The small networks then matched or beat the teacher on the placenta calls. They ran in far less size and time. Low-quality photographs gained most. The team presents the way as a path to placenta readings where equipment is thin.
arxiv-2506-02729:
Salih Kibaroğlu and Mustafa Senay build a deformed scalar-tensor gravity from Verlinde's entropic view. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. In that view, gravity springs from entropy rules, not from a basic force. They blend it with a q-deformation from statistics.

The result reshapes the Brans-Dicke frame, an old scalar-tensor theory, through a deformation factor. That factor acts as a fixed rescale of how strong gravity couples. They derive the field equations of the new frame and check that standard gravity comes back in the right limits. The frame keeps its key symmetries, though it does not stray far from plain Brans-Dicke. Next steps point to cosmic runs of the new equations.
arxiv-2506-02929:
Chang and a large team present a paper from twenty twenty-five on a large model framework for processor chip design. Chip architecture bridges software and hardware, from compilers to circuit layouts. Traditional design leans on manual expertise and fragmented tuning. Rising design space size makes that path costly. Automated methods help but focus on single stages with thin data. The team propose a language-model-driven frame for end-to-end automated design. It runs in three levels, from human-centric to model-governed. A three-dimensional graphics workload tests the first level.

Software-hardware co-design illustrates the frame in action at that level. Results support the approach's effectiveness there. Paths to the higher autonomy levels are discussed in depth. Challenges for full automation are also analyzed.
arxiv-2506-03429:
Vahid Nourozi wrote a 2025 paper on measuring how much information a noisy quantum channel can carry. Noise limits every quantum link, and past a certain level no quantum message gets through at all. Finding that capacity exactly is hard, because the best strategy may use many channel uses together. The author attacks the problem from two sides, theory and simulation.

First, a new technique embeds the channel into a larger space with extra flags attached. That embedding yields clean upper bounds on both quantum and private capacity from a single channel use. The bounds sharpen older results and mark where transmission must vanish. Second, a simulation framework searches over input states to estimate capacity in practice. Two classic channels are worked through: one that drains energy, and one that scrambles states at random. The simulations confirm the bounds and catch the sudden drop to zero capacity at high noise.
arxiv-2506-04629:
Mousa, Moghaddaszadeh, and Nouh present a study from twenty twenty-five on a smart surface that thinks with waves, not wires. The surface is a stack of tuned waveguides that bend elastic waves as they pass. A shake at one edge sends waves through the stack. The stack reads the traits of the shake and names its class, like a neural net in hardware.

Past such surfaces could do one task alone, since wave travel in a finite block has hard caps. Their surface does two tasks at once. The trick is to run the two tasks on split carrier tones, set by a clock based tweak of the guides. The work opens a path to wave based chips that do parallel work.
arxiv-2506-05029:
Simone Rusconi and co-authors propose, in a 2025 paper, a general recipe for slimming down complex physical models. Big models carry many parameters and scales, and one cure is to drop the terms that barely matter. Their method needs no peeking at the model's equations: it works only from the scales and dimensions in play, and it watches against keeping too many parameters.

The approach also gives numbers, not just hunches: thresholds on parameter values mark where a simpler model keeps the predictions that count. The authors show the recipe on the classic projectile model, a friendly test case. They note a side benefit for fitting models to data, since fewer parameters mean steadier estimates. The work speaks to modelers across physics and engineering who face bloated descriptions.
arxiv-2506-05529:
Rodney Sanchez and co-authors give a learning agent an inner fear signal so it learns to avoid death states, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Death ends many game-like tasks with no feedback, so agents cannot learn from it directly. Their signal is modeled on early fear wiring in the animal brain.

A memory-augmented network builds the fear signal from past states. Agents then steer away from fatal states, much like animals after fear conditioning. Raising or lowering the fear threshold produced a range of styles, akin to anxiety patterns. Tests ran in a sidewalk world with sparse rewards.
arxiv-2506-06129:
Tuovinen and Pavlyukh develop theory for thermoelectric energy conversion in molecular junctions out of equilibrium, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Time-resolved quantum transport matters for ultrafast nano devices. Steady-state methods miss the transient dynamics needed for control. Their Green's function approach uses an iterated Kadanoff-Baym ansatz beyond wide-band limits.

Charge and energy currents follow from the Meir-Wingreen formula. The wide-band approximation shows unphysical divergences that finite bandwidth removes. The method benchmarks well against full Kadanoff-Baym theory. A cyclobutadiene junction illustrates time-resolved thermopower and efficiency. Finite-bandwidth effects prove essential for realistic predictions.
arxiv-2506-06429:
Cowan and Coull-Neveu wrote in twenty twenty-five about choosing targets for the Ariel space mission's exoplanet survey. Ariel will measure atmospheres of many planets around other stars. Population studies look for trends, like how air composition varies with planet mass. The precision of such trends depends on target count and spread. The pair define a leverage measure combining both factors. It predicts trend precision well in their analysis.

They test schemes for picking targets over a three-year survey. Planets are sorted into classes by size, temperature, and star type. Picking the easiest target in each class in turn builds the sample. More classes boost leverage on one axis but weaken it on others. They advise a modest number of classes, and urge confirming candidate planets soon.
arxiv-2506-09229:
Sungwon Hwang, Hyojin Jang, Kinam Kim, Minho Park, and Jaegul Choo fine-tune video generators so each frame remembers its neighbors. User-level fine-tuning of video diffusion models is under-explored and hard: attributes must stick across every frame. A recent image technique aligns a model's hidden states with features from a pretrained vision encoder. Ported naively to video it speeds convergence but lets frames drift apart in meaning.

Their method, CREPA, aligns each frame's hidden states with external features drawn from neighboring frames instead. Cross-frame coherence becomes a training objective, not a hope. On two large video models, paired with parameter-efficient tuning, the method improved both visual fidelity and semantic consistency across frames. Varied data sets with different attributes confirm broad applicability. Video, the work insists, must be regularized as video, not as a stack of photographs.
arxiv-2506-11329:
Park and seven co-authors managed cache memory in data centers in this paper from twenty twenty-five. A server's last-level cache buffers fast transfers from network and storage devices. High-speed devices can flood it and crowd out running programs. The team probed Intel server chips and found two hidden sources of contention.

Data placed by devices in special cache ways migrates when cores read it, clashing with ordinary data. Storage devices also gain little from the fast path yet jostle network traffic there. Their framework, A4, uses hidden chip controls to calm both problems. Priority workloads sped up by about half, with little cost to background jobs. The authors say the fix uses features already in the chips.
arxiv-2506-14329:
Schulte, Rügamer, and Nagler asked in twenty twenty-five when traits drawn from pre-trained nets can clean bias in cause-effect reads from pics or text. Such traits can hide the true drivers of both care and outcome. Skipping them risks wrong claims, but their use needs care.

They state the rules under which net traits give sound bias fixes and error bars. High size and loose identity of the traits break stock fast-rate claims, they show. Nets seem less hurt by those flaws than plain sparse models. Nets can still hit fast rates by fit-ting the true low shape of a task.
arxiv-2506-14829:
Majumdar and three co-authors ask why AI for good causes stalls short of real use in this twenty twenty-five paper. The field pairs AI craft with social science to hit world goals on health and air. Yet most works stall at the proof stage and never reach real streets.

Inside, talks with more than two dozen workers in the field feed the team's map. Their themes span team shape, funds, talk, trust, and day-to-day run snags. Finds stress that a keen lab mate who will co-build and field a tool is rare. Best acts drawn from the talks are cast as a field guide for new teams. The team notes its view leans to north labs and says so plain.
arxiv-2506-16029:
Zhenting Qi, Fan Nie, and colleagues built a suite of language models to expose how training choices echo through later stages in a 2025 study. Modern training runs in stages, from pretraining through fine-tuning to reinforcement learning, and downstream developers rarely see how early decisions shape final behavior. The suite trains over one hundred models from scratch at two sizes.

Each model is scored on upstream skills and downstream tasks after every stage. Continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning get the same transparent treatment. With the full record public in spirit, teams can trace a final weakness back to the stage that caused it instead of guessing.
arxiv-2506-17329:
Pedro Lui and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on the performance of cyber-biomedical features for intrusion detection in connected health care systems. Modern health care runs on interconnected sensors and medical devices. That connectivity opens new paths for cyber attack, and security models that read network traffic alone can miss clues carried in biomedical data.

The researchers applied explainable artificial intelligence to a data set combining network traffic with biomedical sensor data. One leading classifier achieved near-perfect scores for benign traffic and for data alteration attacks, and a strong score for spoofing attacks. The explanations showed that network features did most of the work in detection. Biomedical features still contributed to spoofing detection, where body temperature was the strongest such clue. The work supports security tools that can explain why they raised an alert.
arxiv-2506-20429:
Wolf-Dieter Richter published a 2025 maths paper on quadratic equations whose roots are not plain numbers. A quadratic equation sets a squared term against lower terms, and school maths solves it with real or complex roots. Some such equations have no root of that kind at all.

Richter works with a method that pairs the unknown with helper variables, turning one equation into a vector form. Roots of the vector form then give new kinds of answers. He sorts these into round, stretched-round, and wave-like families. Known answers gain sharper forms along the way. The paper closes by noting that the same path, pushed to cubic and higher cases, may reshape how we think of number systems.
arxiv-2506-22029:
Nikhila Chandran and Tijs Karman study how gases absorb light when atoms collide, in a 2025 paper. Such absorption matters for modeling the air of planets and stars. It is computed from first-principles data, and the team asked how good that input data must be. Surprisingly, even the cheapest calculations proved accurate to within a small margin at room temperature, and better when hotter.

They also found a new double-peak shape for a helium-neon pair that simple common models cannot capture. Which distances between atoms matter shifts with temperature, with close encounters growing more important when hot. Distant weak pulls never contribute, they show.
arxiv-2506-23629:
Xin Liao, Bing Yang, and Cai Yu propose a neural method for filling gaps in water quality records. Their 2025 paper addresses monitoring data that arrive with many holes from sensor failures and transmission delays. The resulting records are wide and sparse, and older filling methods miss the dynamics hidden in them.

Their model pairs a low-rank view of the data with a convolutional network. The network mixes information across time slots to capture how readings depend on their neighbors. It also extracts nonlinear local patterns, joining features across many measured quantities. Tests on three real monitoring data sets beat leading imputation models on accuracy. Reliable filled records support the decisions that protect rivers and drinking water.
arxiv-2507-02229:
Sifatul Anindho and four co-authors explore the inner emotional states people experience while solving problems together in teams. Their paper came out in 2025. Collaborative problem solving mixes thinking, social interaction, and emotion, and it is common in schools and workplaces.

Teams of four first completed a new group task. Right afterward, each person sat alone and watched the video of their team, narrating what they had felt at each moment. The team analyzed that language for single words, word pairs, and emotion labels. Distinct patterns emerged, including characteristic phrases for different feelings and links between related emotion words. The results give a window into how emotion moves through group work.
arxiv-2507-02329:
Chang wrote in twenty twenty-five a review of nodal-line semimetals, a newer family of quantum materials. In these solids, electron bands cross along lines rather than at single points. Those lines sit inside the Brillouin zone, the map of allowed electron states. The lines can form links, knots, and chains. Special symmetries protect the patterns from easily breaking apart.

Chang sorts the materials by their line shapes and protecting symmetries. Flat states on the surface, called drumhead states, are a key sign. The review also covers responses to fields, charge flow, and light. Strong interactions between electrons can twist the basic phase. Magnetism and superconductivity can then intertwine in new ways, which the review traces for readers.
arxiv-2507-05429:
Dominic Thompson and co-authors wrote this photonics paper in 2025. Photonic crystal waveguides steer light on a chip and can slow it to boost light-matter effects. Their flaw is loss: tiny flaws in the build scatter light backward, a snag that has dogged the field for decades. The team set out to design guides that shrug off such flaws.

They joined a fast solver for light modes with formulas for how flaws scatter, then let inverse design search for better shapes. At the same slowing of light, the new shapes cut backward loss a great deal. Gains held for the standard guide shape and for guarded topological modes as well. Their method works in full three dimensions and can be retuned for other aims, from photon sources to on-chip buffers.
arxiv-2507-05629:
Yuan An and three co-authors test AI-generated practice questions in twenty twenty-five. Retrieval practice is a proven way to deepen learning and retention. Writing good practice questions, though, is time-consuming for instructors. Technical subjects that change fast make the burden worse. Language models could automate the writing.

The authors ran an empirical study in two college data science courses. About sixty students took part. One week, students received model-generated multiple-choice retrieval questions. Another week, they received none. Learning outcomes were compared between the two weeks. The design isolates the effect of the generated questions themselves. Readers in education get early classroom evidence on whether machine-written practice actually moves learning.
arxiv-2507-06929:
Sita Schönbauer and colleagues train machine-learned force fields at coupled-cluster accuracy for crystal vibrations. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Coupled-cluster theory is a gold standard, but far too slow for long simulations. Density functional theory is faster and less exact. The test solids are diamond and lithium hydride. Phonon patterns and vibrational spectra judge the results.

Delta learning bridges the two levels of theory. The learned field targets the gap between coupled-cluster and functional results. A charge-aware variant handles long-range effects and missing force data. Optical vibration frequencies rise toward the experimental values. Anharmonic effects in lithium hydride are estimated at the higher level too. The workflow brings top-tier accuracy within simulation reach.
arxiv-2507-07229:
Krithika Ramesh and co-authors present SynthTextEval, a toolkit for rating synthetic text, in this 2025 paper. Fake text from language models could replace sensitive records in health and law. That swap protects privacy only if the fake data stays useful and safe. Judging quality takes more than one score.

The toolkit measures downstream utility, fairness, and privacy leakage risk. It also compares distributions with the source text and gathers expert impressions. Users can upload data or generate it inside the toolkit. Demonstrations use healthcare and legal datasets. Standard, shared evaluation should make synthetic data claims comparable across teams. High stakes fields need that discipline before trusting artificial records.
arxiv-2507-08129:
Maryam Abbasi and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how to run parity-time symmetric systems on a quantum computer. Such systems lose and gain in balance, yet their spectra stay real. They tempt use in sensing and in making linked states. Standard quantum gates, though, are unitary and cannot copy that drift at face value.

Their trick maps the system to a Hermitian twin by a change of basis. Two algorithms run the twin near the points where states merge. One leans on a classical side loop; the other swaps that load for one extra qubit. A weak pair of such systems is handled by perturbation steps. Runs on real gear and noisy fakes check the plan.
arxiv-2507-09029:
Vaibhav Singh and co-authors introduce a new way to train large networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pre-training at scale strains memory and needs costly communication between machines. Their framework, Subnetwork Data Parallelism, splits a model into subnetworks trained on separate workers.

Workers never exchange activations, which cuts communication sharply. Two masking regimes are studied: one sparsifies only the backward pass, the other also thins the forward pass. Subnetworks can be built at neuron level or block level. Tests ranged from a billion-parameter language model to an image network. Memory per device fell by up to sixty percent while performance held or improved.
arxiv-2507-10229:
Netzer Moriya sets out a view of how wild phase faces with set whole count bias make spin of light round its path. The frame works out pick rules that say which spin modes can be made in tune. Mean spin through a group lives sole when the bias trait takes whole counts. Those counts must match the set spin space. That makes tiers that are let in and tiers that are shut out.

Math terms give the strength range of the spin made, with a scale law that holds for all in the let in set. Mock runs with chance picks back the pick rules. They show shut out tiers cut by more than ten to the fourth fold. The scale calls also matched with rare truth. The view links made up mess to builds of light with form.
arxiv-2507-10729:
Duong Nguyen and a team of co-authors test whether tools that flag risky code changes are judged fairly, in two thousand twenty-five. Such tools aim to catch a commit that introduces a security flaw, at the moment it lands. Most past tests used balanced data built only from flaw-linked commits, a setting unlike real projects.

The team built a public set of more than a million commits from two large projects, including neutral commits. Eight leading tools lost most of their skill on the real-style data. The cause was the rarity of flaw commits among all commits. Common fixes for skewed data did not help, so the authors call for methods built for this setting.
arxiv-2507-11329:
Hagar Shmuely, Michal Rivlin, and Or Perlman present, in twenty twenty-five, an AI-boosted MRI method to image several metabolites in Parkinson's disease at once. Classic molecular imaging for this disease needs radioactive tracers, long scans, or gives blurry maps. Their method pairs a rapid saturation transfer MRI scan with deep learning reconstruction. Saturation transfer is a trick that makes faint chemical signals visible. They quantify glutamate, mobile proteins, semisolid material, and mobile macromolecules in a mouse model of the disease.

The maps matched tissue histology and spectroscopy checks well. Three measures, tied to semisolid transfer, amide groups, and a relayed effect, may serve as disease biomarkers, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-14229:
Vanja Stojanović, Žiga Lesar, and Ciril Bohak teach a neural network to crack the affine cipher. That classical scheme shifts and stretches letter positions by a secret key. The team's hybrid network reads a ciphertext two ways at once. One branch is built for modular arithmetic, the cipher's native math.

The second branch studies letter frequency statistics, the classic codebreaker's clue. On English-derived data sets, the hybrid recovered keys with high accuracy for short and moderate texts. It beat purely statistical approaches on this cipher. Very long ciphertexts, oddly, degraded performance, exposing a generalization weakness. The authors frame the result as a step in neural cryptanalysis of classical schemes. Interpretable modular networks, borrowed from arithmetic research, give the attack its edge.
arxiv-2507-16829:
Giovanni De Toni and five co-authors set out a way to cut the unwanted picks that recommender systems push on users. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such systems shape what people read and watch. They are now faulted for picks that are off-topic, unwanted, or even harmful. That harms user trust and feeds ills such as false tales and drift to extremes. Sites give tools to block such picks, but they are weak and slow to learn. The new way uses a risk control method with firm odds. It is plain to grasp, fits any model, and needs no guess on how data spread. It aims to cap the rate of bad picks.
arxiv-2507-17929:
Brinthan Kanesalingam and co-authors build math tools in 2025 for a microscope that sees strain deep inside crystals. Dark-field X-ray microscopy can image bulk crystals at tiny scales over a wide field, which older methods cannot do at once. But turning its images into a full map of how the crystal lattice bends was an open problem.

The team derived the missing link between the angles the microscope records and the deformation tensor, a grid of numbers that captures stretch and rotation at each point. They also wrote code to run the math both ways, from strain to image and back. Their sensitivity analysis shows how errors in each angle flow into the final map, which helps plan better experiments.
arxiv-2507-21429:
Agnideep Aich, Ashit Aich, and Bruce Wade prove conditions under which training a neural network converges fast, at a steady geometric rate, rather than crawling. Their paper came out in 2025. Earlier work showed gradient descent can stay trapped in a well-behaved region near its starting point, but only promised slow progress there.

Their result needs the network's tangent kernel, a matrix describing how outputs respond to parameter nudges, to start positive and stay stable in that region. Then the training loss obeys a local inequality that forces geometric decay. Experiments on handwritten digit classification matched the theory, including a width test where a smaller step size rescued the fast regime. A check on images from a harder dataset also held up.
arxiv-2507-22129:
LaDuca and co-authors ask how well a substrate's crystal pattern can shape a film grown on top of a graphene sheet, in a 2025 perspective paper. In this growth method, called remote epitaxy, the film lines up with the base below the graphene, as if the sheet were see-through. The trick promises flexible devices and new ways to stack materials.

The authors argue that the base's pull through graphene is weak and hard to measure. They propose math tools that sort the pattern's parts by spacing, with no built-in bias. They also weigh rival accounts, such as growth seeded by tiny holes in the sheet. One reported case, they say, still resists those rival accounts, and they call for sharper tests of the core claim.
arxiv-2507-22329:
Erin Gatz, Yasmine Kotturi, Andrea Afua Kwamya, and Sarah Fox wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It studies feminist makerspaces, community workshops that offer an alternative to mainstream tech culture, and asks how they manage to last.

The authors interviewed eighteen founders and members across eight such spaces in the United States, and drew on their own experience inside them. The spaces center care, mutual aid, and shared knowledge rather than profit or growth. The study finds they endure not by expanding or formalizing, but through careful stewardship, alliances with local justice movements, and shared decision making. The authors call them counterspaces that live their values now instead of promising them later. The paper names the labor and coalition work that keep such alternative tech cultures alive.
arxiv-2507-22429:
Erwin de Gelder, Maren Buermann, and Olaf Op den Camp compare in 2025 two ways to estimate how often self-driving cars face each kind of traffic scene. Safety testing needs those frequencies to turn test results into a risk number. Guessing a simple curve shape can bias the answer, while flexible methods struggle as variables multiply.

They test normalizing flows, a learning method that warps a simple distribution into a complex one without shape assumptions. Against the classic kernel method, flows cost more computing but resist the blowup that comes with many variables. The flows gave tighter risk estimates with less uncertainty. The authors see them as a useful upgrade for scenario-based safety checks.
arxiv-2507-22929:
Xiaoyu Pan and co-authors build a benchmark for false answers in eye-care language models. Their 2025 paper notes that medical models can invent findings when their eye knowledge is thin or their image reading is weak. Existing tests do not sort these errors well or point to fixes.

Their benchmark sorts model errors into two broad classes, one about seeing and one about reasoning, each with sub-types. They also propose a three-stage agent workflow that pulls in knowledge, studies cases, and checks results. Tests show the workflow cut both kinds of error in a clear way. The work gives eye-care AI a sharper test, and a traced path from question to answer that staff can audit.
arxiv-2507-23329:
Luca Buiarelli, Turan Birol, Brian Andersen, and Morten Christensen read the traits of kagome layered shandites from first principles. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a crystal family where metal ions sit in kagome nets. Those layers stack in a slanted way, split by other ions and chalcogens. States near the Fermi level rest on the metal d orbitals. Saddle points in the band shape sit near key spots of the zone.

The team joins symmetry reads with quantum math to link those saddles to shakes in the lattice. All parent compounds read as stable at plain states. Yet set cases show how close the stack sits to a shift. Readers in quantum materials get a map of a hot lattice family.
arxiv-2507-23529:
Shohini Bhattacharya, Renaud Boussarie, Bernard Pire, and Lech Szymanowski point to a new window on meson structure in this two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. Generalized distribution amplitudes describe how a quark-antiquark pair turns into two mesons; they are nonperturbative objects encoding internal structure. The chiral-even versions are accessible in electron-positron annihilation through single-photon exchange. The chiral-odd versions, long missing experimentally, enter only through two-photon exchange.

The authors show that interference between the one-photon and two-photon amplitudes produces specific, measurable effects when annihilation creates two low-mass meson pairs. Facilities such as BES III or future tau-charm factories could observe them. That would open direct experimental access to the chiral-odd sector of meson structure. In physical terms, it probes the spin-orbit correlation inside a spin-zero meson, sometimes described as an anomalous tensorial magnetic moment.
arxiv-2508-00429:
Guo and co-authors present a 2025 framework that turns each node in a graph into a small agent. Graph networks pass notes between neighbor nodes by fixed rules. Fixed rules treat rich and sparse nodes alike and miss far-off but linked facts. In the new frame, each node plans its own next step from its own memory, so note passing adapts node by node.

A search tool lets nodes pull in content that matches in meaning, not just in links. That builds bridges across the whole graph. The system, called ReaGAN in the catalog title, runs on a frozen language model with no fine-tuning. It still scored well on few-shot tests. Agent-style nodes could help graph tools for fraud maps, citation webs, and other linked data.
arxiv-2508-01129:
Emily Sheetz and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on human and robot teams that red team each other's plans for safety. Robots in risky jobs must earn human trust by how they act, not just by what they can do. Red teaming means the pair hunts for hazards and weak spots in a plan before the work starts.

Their frame walks through hazard spotting, risk grading, risk cuts, and safety reports as a joint act. Tests span two worlds: a lunar habitat and a home. Robots with unlike bodies learned safe work in both, though the sense of safe shifted by place. The team says the drill makes safety a shared habit.
arxiv-2508-01729:
Talib and Ahsan compute the energy level patterns of trapped interacting bosons in this 2025 physics paper. They trap the particles in a harmonic well on a nearly flat plane. The bosons repel each other through a soft Gaussian force.

Using exact diagonalization, they study the lowest 100 energy levels for 12, 16, and 20 bosons. At moderate interaction the still system's level spacings look random in the orderly Poisson way, a sign of regular motion. At strong interaction the pattern switches to the chaotic form seen in random matrix theory. Rotating states with a single vortex show weak chaos at moderate strength. The authors track both short-range and long-range correlations to read these signatures.
arxiv-2508-01829:
Philippe Martin Wyder and co-authors published this robotics paper in 2025. Modular robots are built from repeating units that can rearrange into new shapes. For decades, research has focused inward on the modules themselves: their motors, connectors, controls, and manufacture. That focus has kept such robots mostly inside tidy laboratories. The authors argue the field has neglected a resource every real setting offers for free: the environment itself.

Their paper explores how a modular system might exploit floors, walls, gravity, and obstacles to help it reconfigure. Letting the surroundings do part of the work could ease the demands on each module. The newest generation of truss-style modular robots motivates the question, since long strut-like units interact strongly with terrain. The authors frame environment exploitation as a design philosophy rather than a single mechanism. It points modular robotics away from sterile benches and toward messy real-world deployment.
arxiv-2508-02029:
Zhilong Zhao and Yindi Liu wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on checking the work of language models that code text into categories. Such coding is now done at scale by AI, but human experts often disagree, so there is no clean answer key.

The pair studied more than five thousand coding calls made by eight top models across ten categories. A model's own stated confidence tracked how much the models agreed with each other. Adding a diversity measure, based on how spread out the answers were, made the pair of signals explain agreement almost fully. From this they build a three-tier flow: easy cases pass on their own, which cuts hand work by about two thirds. Tests in other fields showed the method travels well. The authors frame it as a base method, with harder tasks still to come.
arxiv-2508-03529:
Vukosi Marivate and eleven co-authors present Mafoko, an open resource of terms in many languages for South Africa, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Neatly ordered term data for the country's official languages is very scarce, and that holds back language technology.

Government and school word lists exist but sit in bits and pieces, in formats machines cannot read. Mafoko gathers, cleans, and puts them into one standard form, as data sets that tools can share, put out with Africa at its center. As a demonstration, the team plugged the term list into a search-aided making pipeline. English-to-Tshivenda machine translation by large language models got a lot better in accuracy and in how steady it was across domains, showing the resource's quick useful value.
arxiv-2508-04729:
Ivan Pereira-Sánchez and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five for sharpening satellite images. The Sentinel-2 mission records Earth in thirteen bands at mixed resolutions. Fine bands show crisp structure, while coarser bands carry richer color information. Joining them well can give images that are both sharp and rich.

Their model first builds a guide image rich in shape detail from the fine bands, using a cluster-based step. That guide feeds a back-projection network that borrows similar patches across the image through an attention mechanism. The authors built test sets covering urban, rural, and coastal scenes. Their method beat both classic and deep learning rivals on those tests.
arxiv-2508-05729:
Linus Thummel, Benjamin Bose, and Alkistis Pourtsidou explore, in twenty twenty-five, islands of weak gravity inside a broad family of modified gravity theories. Horndeski gravity extends Einstein's theory with extra fields. Some of its regimes weaken gravity versus general relativity, which would slow the growth of cosmic structure late in time. The letter introduces a method to generate such models on demand, with stability built in and no fixed parametrization. Starting from a stable basis, they evolve its functions with Gaussian processes that encode stability and target behavior.

They find a broad range of stable weak-gravity islands, including cases with a fifth force and cases where the modification vanishes today. Swapping in a recent best-fit expansion history from the DESI survey still yields stable islands.
arxiv-2508-07729:
Juliusz Banecki proves a theorem in algebraic geometry in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. He studies rational varieties, shapes whose points can be described by ratios of polynomials. A shape is called uniformly rational when each of its points has a neat local chart of a standard kind.

Banecki takes any smooth rational variety and forms its product with the complex plane. He proves the product is uniformly rational. A clean payoff follows: any smooth variety that turns rational after taking a product with flat space is also stably uniformly rational. The proof is short, yet it settles the product case in full.
arxiv-2508-08529:
Arshia Ilaty, Hossein Shirazi, and Hajar Homayouni present SynLLM for making synthetic medical data in this 2025 paper. Privacy rules restrict real patient data, which slows health research. Language models can invent realistic records, but prompting them well is unsystematic. Their framework tests that generation process in a structured way.

Twenty open source language models were compared under four prompt styles. Prompts ranged from example driven to rule based, encoding schema and medical knowledge without retraining. Output was scored on statistical fidelity, clinical consistency, and privacy protection. Three public medical datasets anchored the evaluation. The results show which models and prompts give usable synthetic tables. Such data can support research where real records cannot be shared.
arxiv-2508-10429:
Yi Dong, Yusuke Muraoka, Scott Shi, and Yi Zhang release a public data set of 100,000 food images with rich labels, in a 2025 paper. The set is a curated open tenth of a larger corpus of 1.2 million images gathered in six weeks from more than 87,000 contributors. Each entry records details such as dish name and region, and each submission links to a contributor wallet in a secure ledger, so its origin can be checked.

The team describes the data schema, the gathering pipeline, and the quality checks that mix community sourcing with AI screening. To prove the set is useful, they fine-tuned large vision-language models on it to predict nutrition from photos. The tuned models beat their out-of-box versions across standard metrics. The rest of the corpus stays reserved for paid access, with revenue shared to contributors.
arxiv-2508-10729:
Yanjun Li and seven co-authors present EgoCross, a benchmark for video question answering from a first-person view. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that past tests stick to daily life, like cooking and cleaning. Real use brings domain shift: new settings that look and mean quite different things.

EgoCross covers four hard domains: surgery, industry, extreme sports, and animal view. It holds about a thousand questions over hundreds of clips, across prediction, recognition, localization, and counting tasks, each in open and closed form. Top models, even those built for first-person video, struggled outside daily domains. The team also trials fine-tuning and reinforcement learning as fixes.
arxiv-2508-11429:
Shivam Dubey built a pipeline in 2025 to make AI humor feel less generic. Jokes from language models often land flat because humor depends on culture, mindset, and the moment, none of which a bare prompt captures. His HumorPlanSearch system plans before it jokes, in five cooperating stages that keep context in view throughout.

A search step drafts varied, topic-tailored strategies, and chain-of-thought templates encode cultural and stylistic reasoning. A knowledge graph recalls strategies that scored well before, an embedding filter cuts near-duplicates, and judges drive revision rounds. A new humor score blends direct ratings, persona feedback, win rates, and relevance. Across nine topics with human judges, the full pipeline beat a strong baseline clearly.
arxiv-2508-12329:
Schrettner studied families of algebraic curves in this mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. A family here means curves made by nudging the coefficients of their defining equations. Each curve has a reduction type, which describes its shape after reduction modulo a prime. The author works over a discretely valued field, the natural home of p-adic questions.

He proves the reduction type stays constant for small nudges, in the topology set by the valuation. Related invariants behave the same way. These include the Tamagawa number and a factor from the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer circle of ideas. The Galois representation attached to the curve is covered as well. The results give stability guarantees for invariants used across arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2508-13929:
David Fouhey and KD Leka recover the Sun's full surface magnetic field from its easiest measurement. Line-of-sight magnetograms need only intensity and circular polarization, so archives overflow with them. The perpendicular field component demands trickier linear polarization. Alone, the line-of-sight part is not physically meaningful, and the common fix, assuming a radial field, is nearly always false.

Their learning method builds on a recent inversion approach fed originally by full polarization data. It takes one or more line-of-sight maps plus metadata and returns the field in proper heliographic components, no disambiguation step needed. Tests on unseen data from two instruments succeed, including observations predating the current solar observatory. The authors are candid: learning cannot replace dedicated vector-field facilities. It can, though, unlock decades of archived data and beat the radial assumption soundly.
arxiv-2508-14529:
Kobak and co-authors use two kinds of stellar masers to pin down which fine transition dominates a methanol maser line, in a 2025 paper. Masers, nature's microwave lasers, trace magnetic fields where massive stars form. The hydroxyl maser's field readings are trusted, but the methanol line's tangled hyperfine structure muddies its Zeeman readings. The team observed both lines nearly at once toward two young massive objects with a European antenna network.

They measured fields in many hydroxyl spots and Zeeman splitting in a few methanol spots. The two emissions seem to sample the same field at different densities. Yet the splitting coefficient they derived matches none of the published table values. The dominant transition stays unidentified, though density arguments narrow the field. The authors report the puzzle openly.
arxiv-2508-15529:
Kaiyuan Tan and colleagues improved virtual test drives in 2025 by rendering what a car would see on roads it never quite drove. Simulators extrapolate new viewpoints from recorded driving logs, but drifting away from the recorded path exposes artifacts, and generative models used as stand-in ground truth tend to blur geometry. ExtraGS, their framework, insists on both geometric discipline and generative help, each where it belongs.

A hybrid representation marries Gaussian splatting to a signed distance function for the road surface, keeping the drivable plane exact, while far-field Gaussians with learnable scales handle distant scenery cheaply. A self-supervised uncertainty estimate, built from spherical harmonics, flags where extrapolation is actually breaking, and only there are generative priors invited in. Across several datasets and multi-camera rigs, the extrapolated views gained realism and geometric consistency while keeping the fidelity of the original recordings.
arxiv-2508-16429:
Schumacher and three colleagues show that how a wire mesh material is cut at its faces steers its trapped light modes in twenty twenty-five. The material is two metal nets woven through each other in three dimensions. Slabs of it can trap light for very long times in near bound states. Two face cuts were compared: a flat tennis net cut and a cut with posts sticking out.

The flat cut held light far longer than the post cut. Microwave tests and full wave models agreed on the gap. Bulk rules that ignore faces cannot explain the split. Adding fading bulk states to the math gave a clear picture. Face design is thus a real design lever.
arxiv-2508-16629:
Zeyu Zhang and five co-authors teach language model bots how to keep facts in mind. They do not hand design the bots' mind tools. Mind tools for bots in past work are set by hand by those skilled in the field. That costs work and gives scores less than best. They also snub the mind loop of store, fetch, and use of facts in joint acts.

The frame models that loop straight. A gate built as a mix of skilled parts backs fetch. A learn step to join parts lifts use of facts kept in mind. Thought on the task in hand shapes what gets stored. Train uses both off plan and on plan best fit so bots learn mind plans for one zone. Tests through more than one score set show the way works, and the code is put out.
arxiv-2508-16929:
Junxuan Wang and four co-authors find a hidden shape in transformer attention in a twenty twenty-five paper. Attention is the core of large language models, and its outputs are thought to fill a high-dimensional space. The team shows those outputs in fact sit in a low-dimensional subspace, about sixty percent of the full size.

Other parts of the model, the feed-forward outputs and the residual stream, stay near full rank at about ninety percent. The squeeze comes from the attention output projection matrix. It also explains a pest in sparse dictionary learning: dead features that never fire. Training dictionaries inside the active subspace cut dead features from most to near none.
arxiv-2508-17429:
Akanksha Chouhan, Abhishek Erram, and Ashwin Tulapurkar showed a new way in twenty twenty-five to gauge spin-orbit torques in magnetic bilayers. These torques let a current in a heavy metal layer twist the magnetization of a nearby ferromagnet. That trick is eyed for memory devices. The torque splits into damping-like and field-like parts. How strong each part is matters a lot.

Their way tilts the magnetization out of plane. It does so in second harmonic Hall tests on two stacks. One is platinum-cobalt. One is tantalum-cobalt-iron-boron. Both have perpendicular anisotropy. From the equation of magnetization dynamics in the low-frequency limit, they get both efficiencies. The tantalum stack showed an odd field-like torque that hangs on the direction of magnetization. They also show a resonance test based on the anomalous Hall effect. It cross-checks these perpendicular systems.
arxiv-2508-18429:
Warren Pickett asks why some hydrides superconduct so well in twenty twenty-five. Squeezed metal hydrides can superconduct near room temperature. The community picture says a candidate's stability and coupling can be computed from first principles. Those calculations give large electron-phonon coupling, mostly from high-frequency hydrogen vibrations. Predicted critical temperatures match measured ones in known cases.

That much was foreseen by Ashcroft two decades ago. Yet Pickett argues the deeper why is still not understood. His paper focuses on the sharper question of why hydrogen, of all elements, plays this role. He claims the full answer is missing but maps a pathway toward it. Readers get a candid stock-taking of a hot field's foundations.
arxiv-2508-18529:
Vignon Oussa attacks a special case of a famous open problem about time-frequency shifts of smooth functions, in a 2025 paper. The HRT conjecture limits how a function and its shifts can be linearly linked. Oussa studies very smooth Schwartz functions obeying one identity: a mix of translates equals a single frequency shift. On the Fourier side, the identity becomes a multiplying rule along a ladder of points.

He rewrites the growth of that product as an average over a compact group, using ergodic theory. If the key average is nonzero, or a recurrence condition holds, the transform must grow exponentially somewhere. Schwartz functions must instead decay fast, so the identity collapses. The result conditionally bars such identities for this configuration.
arxiv-2508-20429:
Dennis Salinel and Kristian Villegas study bosonization in models with R-paraparticles. Their twenty twenty-five physics paper uses a generalized Luttinger model. Parastatistics describes particles beyond the usual bosons and fermions. Recent work suggests such particles may appear as excitations in real materials.

The authors ask when density and flavor waves can be rewritten as bosons. Density waves always allow that rewriting in their model. Flavor waves allow it only for a smaller class of particles. The effect holds at low temperatures, based on the model spectrum. Turning on interactions then splits flavor and charge signals apart. That split could give experiments a way to spot these unusual particles.
arxiv-2508-20529:
Suprabha Bhattacharya, Vivek Sabale, and Atul Kumar study, in a 2025 paper, how chains of quantum spins could serve as quantum batteries. A quantum battery stores energy in quantum states and may charge in ways no ordinary battery can. The team tested spin networks in several configurations, including open chains, closed rings, and a supercube.

Charging is driven by spin interactions and a transverse magnetic field, with one added ingredient: the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, a twist in how spin pairs affect each other. That interaction raised the ergotropy, the stored energy, in the XXZ model, most of all in the supercube configuration. The team tried regular graphs, where each point has the same number of links, with 3 to 12 qubits. Highly symmetric shapes kept clean sinusoidal charging and discharging behavior when the interaction was tuned well. The authors name symmetry and link count as design rules for larger quantum batteries.
arxiv-2508-20829:
Zeyue Zhang and four co-authors build ATM-GAD, a network that spots fraud in money flows by the small time-stamped shapes those flows make. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Fraud costs vast sums, and its webs of linked accounts beat plain tools. Graph tools help, but they miss two time marks of fraud. One is the set shapes that recur as a scheme unfolds. The next is that each account's bad span is short and its own. The new net pulls the most telling shapes from each account's past. Twin focus blocks then read within and across those shapes. The aim is to catch fraud as it moves.
arxiv-2508-21529:
Ronan Docherty, Antonis Vamvakeros, and Samuel Cooper give a new way in place of U-Net to cut up shots of stuff under a scope. Sight base models make rich traits for shots, but their patch traits are too coarse for fine detail. They are also too coarse for the huge shots used in this work. Their fix is a net that lifts those low grade traits to a fine grade. It uses the first shot as a guide.

Used with no more train time, the lift tool backs cuts of plant cells, a lithium-ion cell part, and pure grown shapes. The traits split hard parts such as hair thin cracks. Cuts made by hand with these traits reach high grade far more fast. They need far fewer marks than train of a plain net from scratch.
arxiv-2508-21629:
Robert Corless, Mark Giesbrecht, Leili Rafiee Sevyeri, and David Saunders present a 2025 method for linear systems whose numbers carry symbols. In such systems the answer's shape can flip as the symbols take set values. Classic covers list a case per shape, but the case count can explode. The new method runs in time tied gently to the matrix size and term degrees, for up to three symbols.

The trick maps the system into a one-symbol world where two classic matrix forms expose the special points. Those points, where the algebra kinks, split the symbol space into a modest set of regimes. Worked cases hint the reach may stretch past three symbols. Symbolic solvers in physics and design tools stand to gain speed.
arxiv-2509-00529:
Eunjung Cho, with two co-authors, Alexander Hoyle and Yoan Hermstruwer, studies motivated reasoning in legal summaries made by large language models. Tailored summaries can frame a court decision to fit a reader's side, a risk when the reader is a judge, prosecutor, or attorney.

Cho and her co-authors prompt models with different legal roles and score summaries for which facts and reasoning steps are included and how favorable the tone is to each side. Even with balancing instructions, models show selective inclusion that matches the assigned role. The findings warn that role-aware testing is needed, since models may also infer a user's role from context without being told.
arxiv-2509-00729:
Raushan Kant, with three co-authors, Ananyo Maitra, A K Sood, and Sriram Ramaswamy, reports experiments on chiral active particles, vibrated granular rods that rotate with a handedness as they move. At hard boundaries, they find skipping orbits, paths that hug the edge and circulate opposite to the particles' own rotation.

These classical edge states cause stronger boundary accumulation than for achiral counterparts, and their directed motion gives a high-fidelity way to sort particles by chirality, even for solitary particles. Kant and his co-authors propose a unified theory where an outward radial force, proportional to motility and chirality, explains the hugging. Experiments also confirm a predicted pairing shift, from apolar spinners to polar circle walkers, as bead density rises.
arxiv-2509-01429:
Magnetars are neutron stars with immense magnetic fields, and at times their X-ray brightness surges by orders of magnitude before fading over months. D. De Grandis, with eight co-authors, simulates such outbursts as the result of heat deposited in a patch of the star's crust. A magnetothermal code, built for short-term events, follows the surface as it cools.

The code includes the star's outer layers, where heat moves faster, and uses thinner blanketing envelope models than earlier work. Those thinner envelopes can hold a higher surface temperature, though for less time, which matches the brightness of real outbursts even from hotspots only a few kilometers wide. The team varies several parameters tied to the heating. Their results test how crust heating and cooling together shape a magnetar's flare.
arxiv-2509-01529:
Community unionism takes labor organizing beyond the workplace, into coalitions and local social action, and its forms have changed over a century. Thomas Compton compares two cases: the National Boot and Shoe Union in the 1920s and Unite Community in the 2010s and 2020s. Topic modeling, with a method called BERTopic, maps the themes in each union's discourse.

Word frequency checks join the topic analysis, and the study weighs how far each union's talk matches community unionism traits such as coalition building and grassroots engagement. Unite Community aligned more strongly with outward, social justice themes. The earlier union's corpus stressed internal administration, industrial relations, and member services, a traditional servicing model. Compton also draws method lessons, showing how modern language tools can sharpen the study of historical labor archives.
arxiv-2509-02029:
Nikos Giakoumoglou, Andreas Floros, Kleanthis Marios Papadopoulos, and Tania Stathaki test fake photos and fake hard pairs for training image models that learn on their own. Such training needs vast real data and hard pairs picked with care. Their frame, called Syn2Co, fakes both sides of that need at once. Models that make images supply more training shots to widen the spread of scenes.

Fake hard pairs are built in the trait space to make tough tests for the learner. Two types of image model carry all of the tests in the study. Finds show hope for training with fake data, plus clear limits to that hope. Learned traits grow more strong and move to new tasks in some checks. The work shows when fake data can stand in for real sets.
arxiv-2509-02329:
Tim Schwägerl, Karl Jansen, and Stefan Kühn present a 2025 lattice physics study comparing three ways to place fermions, matter particles, on a discrete grid. Their test case is the two-flavour Schwinger model, a simpler cousin of quantum chromodynamics with two particle types.

Using tensor networks called matrix product states, the team checks staggered, Wilson, and twisted mass fermions. Twisted mass fermions, little studied here before, kept their expected accuracy gain once interactions were switched on. An electric-field method handled mass tuning well. The pion mass then settled quickly toward the continuum value, and volume effects stayed milder than for rivals. Isospin breaking also appeared, echoing patterns in real lattice work.
arxiv-2509-02729:
Marcus Michelen and Mehtaab Sawhney wrote a 2025 probability paper. It settles a question Erdős posed in 1961. The topic is random power series on the unit circle. Random signs multiply fixed coefficients. The issue is where the series converges on the circle.

Classic results show divergence almost everywhere when coefficients decay slowly. A stronger size condition gives divergence everywhere. Erdős asked if slower decay guarantees some convergence point. The authors prove a strong yes. When coefficients shrink faster than the threshold rate, the convergence set has Hausdorff dimension one. That is the largest possible size for a subset of the circle. So convergence points form a rich fractal set, not a few strays.
arxiv-2509-03129:
Priyavrat Deshpande, Aditya Karnataki, and Pratiksha Shingavekar used data science in 2025 to study congruent number elliptic curves. A congruent number is the area of a right triangle with rational sides, a classical problem tied to a family of elliptic curves. For each square-free whole number up to three million, they examined the matching curve.

They tracked several rank measures, which describe how many independent rational points a curve has, plus related Selmer ranks. Their statistics test predictions by Heath-Brown about rank patterns and check Goldfeld's conjecture on a fifty-fifty split between two rank values. They also study a group measuring hidden failures of local-to-global reasoning. Machine learning classifiers then try to predict which numbers are congruent from curve data. Frobenius traces, by contrast, averaged toward zero with no striking pattern.
arxiv-2509-03329:
Melissa Robles and 3 co-authors introduced SESGO in 2025, a benchmark for bias in Spanish-language AI outputs. Most bias testing of large language models centers on United States English, leaving harms in other languages and cultures largely unexamined. Their framework is grounded in Latin American Spanish and its everyday expressions.

Prompts adapt an underspecified question method from an English dataset, weaving in regional sayings that encode stereotypes. Four social categories are covered: gender, race, socioeconomic class, and national origin. A new metric joins accuracy with the direction of errors, across both ambiguous and clarified prompts. Leading commercial models showed varied bias patterns in their tests. Mitigations tuned for English did not transfer well to Spanish, and bias stayed stable across sampling temperatures.
arxiv-2509-04229:
Alexander Sandrock, writing alone, calculates a faint neutrino flux created when cosmic rays strike a sea of older neutrinos in a 2025 physics paper. Stars that exploded long ago across the universe left behind a diffuse background of neutrinos, particles that almost never interact. That background remains undetected directly. Fast cosmic rays can hit those slow neutrinos and boost some to much higher energies, a trick also proposed for hunting dark matter.

Both Milky Way and distant cosmic rays enter the calculation. The boosted flux comes out vastly smaller than several known or expected neutrino flows, including the IceCube observatory's measured astrophysical flux. Direct detection through this channel looks hopeless, the numbers imply.
arxiv-2509-04429:
Gregory H Jones and two co-authors propose cheap warning gauges for a workhorse quantum chemistry method in a 2025 research paper.
