Coupled cluster calculations predict molecular energies accurately, but static correlation, a strong mixing of electron arrangements, can quietly degrade them. Their two diagnostics compare a static-correlation measure between the standard CCSD level and its triples-corrected upgrade, CCSD(T). One gauge is the plain change; the other is that change as a share of the total correlation shift.

Small values signal the electron density has settled, so later energy changes come from dynamic correlation alone. Larger values flag leftover static correlation needing higher levels. The ratio also moderately predicts when post-CCSD(T) effects will matter. Chemists gain an affordable quality check.
arxiv-2509-04729:
Clouds hide the ground in satellite images, and spotting them takes both local texture and wide context. Tianxiang Xue, lead author with four co-authors, propose CD-Mamba for cloud detection in a 2025 remote sensing paper. Convolutional networks capture short-range detail well, while Mamba models long-range dependencies across an image.

Their hybrid network unifies convolution with Mamba state-space modelling. The design handles pixel-level texture and patch-level atmospheric similarity at the same time. Extensive experiments show stronger performance than existing methods across varied spatial scales. The authors aim for more reliable data from cloud-affected remote sensing images.
arxiv-2509-04929:
Setting the scale of a telescope instrument that maps ionised carbon emission needs a model that can replay its own observations. A. Lundgren, lead author with thirty-eight co-authors, present a forward model for the CONCERTO instrument in a 2025 astronomy paper. CONCERTO, a Fourier-transform spectrometer on the APEX telescope in Chile, observed a field in COSMOS to study early cosmic line changes.

Their model simulates the spectral response and raw interferograms for each scan under known inputs. A pipeline built for the task describes raw data across varied sky conditions. With the model, the team measure how scans line up and how strongly each part responds. That supports setting the true brightness scale of the spectra.
arxiv-2509-05029:
A space telescope built for distant objects also records solar flares bouncing off Earth's atmosphere. Hiromasa Suzuki, lead author with fifteen co-authors, report the first such results from the XRISM mission in a 2025 astronomy paper. About a year of data cover medium and very large flares.

Abundance measurements for several metals show an inverse first-ionisation-potential effect, matching earlier satellite results. Some elements decline with flare size while calcium rises, broadly matching a theoretical model. High-resolution iron spectra separate scattered line components. The team also trace abundance changes inside flare loops over hundreds of seconds.
arxiv-2509-05329:
Handwritten jazz lead sheets, which carry a melody plus chord symbols, defeat existing music reading software, and Juan Carlos Martinez-Sevilla with five co-authors tackle them in a 2025 paper. Variability and poor image quality in handwriting add to the difficulty.

The team releases a dataset of a few hundred handwritten lead sheets covering well over a hundred distinct pieces, with thousands of staves aligned to ground truth scores in two standard formats. Synthetic score images made from that ground truth support training. They also build a recognition model and discuss token choices suited to this data, plus gains from synthetic images and pre-trained models. All code, data, and models are public.
arxiv-2509-05429:
The overall shape of a training graph can leak out of a graph neural network, Jie Fu and three co-authors demonstrate in a 2025 privacy paper. Such networks learn from linked data like social or citation graphs, and earlier privacy work mostly guarded single edges rather than whole structure.

Their topology inference attacks rebuild a target graph's structure using only black-box access to a trained model. Existing edge-level privacy methods either fail against these attacks or wreck accuracy. Their defence, Private Graph Reconstruction, trains the network on a synthetic graph that is refined step by step alongside the model. In experiments it cut topology leakage sharply while barely affecting accuracy.
arxiv-2509-05729:
Word meanings that shift with context are encoded on quantum hardware by Charles M. Varmantchaonala and four co-authors in a 2025 paper on quantum natural language processing. Their model, QCSE, is a pre-trained quantum embedding that aims to use quantum expressiveness for linguistic structure.

Five methods for building context matrices are proposed and tested, using decay, sinusoidal modulation, phase shifts, and hash-based transforms to make each word's representation depend on its neighbours. Evaluation uses a small Fulani corpus, a low-resource African language, and a slightly larger English one. The model captured context sensitivity on both. The Fulani test highlights a hope that quantum language tools may help data-poor languages.
arxiv-2509-05829:
Finding racist restrictions buried in old property deeds is the work supported by a 2025 paper from Jiyoon Pyo and three co-authors. Racial covenants in twentieth-century deeds are unenforceable today, yet they still shape housing inequality. The Mapping Prejudice project uses volunteers to transcribe deeds and tie them to modern maps, a slow process that automation can speed but not replace.

The authors add two plug-and-play language tools: one flags restrictive wording with context, and one pulls location descriptions from deeds and resolves them to real places. On deeds from six counties in Minnesota and Wisconsin, false alarms dropped by about a quarter while recall stayed high, and locations were pinned within a square mile in most cases. Volunteers then spend their time verifying finds instead of hunting blindly.
arxiv-2509-06729:
A planet photographed directly around a double star is confirmed by Nathalie K. Jones and fifty-three co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The planet orbits the spectroscopic binary HD 143811 in the Scorpius-Centaurus star-forming region. It was spotted by the Gemini Planet Imager survey in 2016 and 2019, with a later look from the Keck telescope in 2022.

Watching the planet move with its host stars across the sky proved it is bound to them, not a background object. Its orbit is fairly wide and mildly eccentric. Spectra and brightness measurements fit planet atmosphere models better than star models, giving a temperature estimate and, through cooling models, a mass of several times Jupiter's. No directly imaged planet around a binary had previously been found on anything but an extremely wide orbit, making this system a test case for how planets form around pairs of stars.
arxiv-2509-06829:
Carbon-rich dwarf stars turn out to live mostly in the galaxy's halo, report Jay Farihi and four co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The sample covers about a thousand main-sequence carbon stars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, matched with Gaia data for full positions and velocities. Reliable distances for such a large sample are new.

Motions and orbital actions were compared with dynamical models of the Milky Way's three main components. Around sixty percent of the stars belong to the halo, and over thirty percent come from the thick disk. That makes dwarf carbon stars a metal-poor halo population and a fine resource for stellar archaeology, the study of the galaxy's past through its stars. The authors also urge better atmosphere models for these cool stars, whose strong molecular features challenge current tools.
arxiv-2509-06929:
Edges where telescope images join can bias measurements of galaxy shapes, and Erin Sheldon tests how badly in a solo 2025 astronomy paper. Weak gravitational lensing reads tiny shape distortions, so calibration must be extremely clean. Coadded images, stacks of many exposures, contain discontinuities in the point spread function and noise wherever input edges cross.

Sheldon uses the Metacalibration and Metadetection methods with a simple weighted-mean stack. He finds no meaningful bias for ordinary galaxy samples, at the edge rates surveys normally see, or in stacks built from tens to hundreds of exposures. Biases beyond survey requirements appear only in extremes: stacks of just two images, edges crossing a quarter of objects, very large point spread function size changes, or small galaxies. Even then, a simple statistic measuring point spread function size variation across each object can flag and remove the bad measurements.
arxiv-2509-07329:
Zhejun Yang proves an upper bound for a transport problem in a 2025 research paper. The problem links prime numbers and the zeros of the zeta function. The problem uses KL-regularized optimal transport, which measures the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another with a penalty term. Yang shows the distance stays below a bound that grows only slightly faster than the range itself.

The proof uses a band-limited test scheme with Fejér averaging, a smoothing method from Fourier analysis. Careful normalization keeps the error terms under control. A smoothed explicit formula then finishes the estimate. The bound needs no extra assumptions. It gives number theorists a clean baseline result for this prime-zero transport quantity, against which sharper future estimates can be measured.
arxiv-2509-07429:
Weimin Chen, in a solo 2025 paper, sets out a method for studying unions of symplectic surfaces in a class of four-dimensional spaces. The method is aided by computer work. Symplectic geometry is the branch of geometry built around area-type measures. It lies at the heart of much work on four-manifolds, spaces with four dimensions. The method grows out of Chen's past work on symplectic Calabi-Yau four-manifolds.

A key tool is a symplectic form of Cremona moves, borrowed from algebraic geometry. These moves reshuffle a surface layout in a controlled way. Chen also answers basic questions about the computer-aided side of the method. As a test case, he gives a new proof that a layout called Fano planes cannot exist in the symplectic class. The proof joins the Cremona tool with Gromov's theory of pseudoholomorphic curves. It stands apart from past algebraic and topological proofs.
arxiv-2509-07529:
Priyanka D. Bhoyar and 2 co-authors report an unusual phase transition in a coupled map lattice in a 2025 paper. A coupled map lattice is a grid of simple chaotic maps that influence their neighbors, a standard model of spatiotemporal systems. The system can fall into an absorbing phase, a quiet state it never leaves, and such transitions usually fall into a few universality classes with fixed critical exponents.

Quenched disorder, fixed randomness frozen into the couplings, is added as asymmetric links: stronger coupling to the right neighbor, weaker to the left. With no asymmetry, the system sits in the directed percolation class, as expected. With any asymmetry, the critical exponents change continuously and match no known universality class in any limit. The authors link the effect to changes in the eigenvalue spectrum of the connectivity matrix as disorder enters.
arxiv-2509-07729:
Jacopo Borga and 2 co-authors study random permutations drawn from the Luce model in a 2025 probability paper. In the Luce model, a permutation is built step by step. Items are sampled one by one, with no replacement. Each pick is weighted by a prescribed positive weight. Such permutations model rankings. They also appear in the Tsetlin library and in related Markov processes.

The authors assume very little about the weights. They prove a permuton limit theorem for the global shape of large Luce permutations. They give an explicit density for the limiting permuton, a continuous portrait of the permutation. They compute limiting pattern densities. They also measure how far exact permutations sit from the approximation. Local convergence results follow. They include a quenched Benjamini-Schramm limit and central limit theorems for pattern counts and for the number of inversions.
arxiv-2509-07829:
Literary translation between English and Romanian gets a full pipeline in a 2025 paper by Mihai Nadas and 3 co-authors. The team builds the TinyFabulist Translation Framework, a system for making data, training models, and scoring results. Romanian has few digital resources, so small open models often translate its literature poorly.

Starting from a large set of synthetic English fables, the pipeline uses a strong large model to create fifteen thousand Romanian reference translations. A twelve-billion-parameter open model is then tuned in two stages, first for story style and then for efficient use. Judging covers five dimensions of quality. The work shows how low-resource languages can gain literary translation tools without closed commercial models.
arxiv-2509-08129:
Multiple instance learning trains models from bags of examples when only the bag carries a label, a common bind in medical imaging. Francisco M. Castro-Macías and 3 co-authors release torchmil in a 2025 research paper. Torchmil is an open-source Python library built on PyTorch. The field had lacked shared tools, so groups rebuilt the same pieces and comparisons stayed shaky.

The library offers modular building blocks for multiple instance models in one framework. It standardizes the data format and bundles benchmark datasets and reference models. Documentation and tutorials support both practitioners and researchers. The authors aim to speed progress and make the field easier to enter for newcomers. Reproducibility is the deeper point: shared tooling lets results be checked, extended, and trusted across labs.
arxiv-2509-08429:
Yiran Xu and Changqing Xu build a unified calculus for matrix-valued functions in a 2025 maths paper. Such functions run through control theory, imaging, and model reduction. Their rates of change are often handled case by case. The pair set out to make the rules systematic, once and for all.

The derivative of one matrix with respect to another is a fourth-order tensor. With that in hand, whole systems of equations can be written in a compact tensor form. The solution mirrors the scalar case: an exponential of the system tensor, times a constant. A partial Tucker split then shrinks big tensor equations for fast use. Engineers with huge coupled systems need cuts that keep the structure. A tensor-native calculus makes those cuts routine.
arxiv-2509-08629:
Daryl R. DeFord and 2 co-authors introduce the Cycle Walk in a 2025 paper on sampling redistricting plans. Redistricting divides a map into balanced districts, and researchers sample many plans to judge fairness. Their method works on spanning forests, a set of trees covering the map.

Local cycle moves change districts from inside, while global moves trade population between neighbors. A Metropolis-Hastings step keeps the sampling correct at several scales at once. Tests on synthetic and real precinct data show better convergence for hard distributions. The method also handles compactness measures that match policy concerns more closely.
arxiv-2509-08729:
Hyunjun Kim and 3 co-authors present X-Teaming Evolutionary M2S in a 2025 paper on jailbreak testing. M2S compresses a multi-turn attack on a language model into one structured prompt. Earlier templates were few and written by hand.

Their framework discovers and improves templates through language model guided evolution. Smart sampling draws from twelve sources, and a judge model scores attempts with auditable logs. Five generations yield two new template families and notable success on GPT-4.1. A cross-model panel shows gains transfer unevenly, and longer prompts tend to score higher. The work stresses careful thresholds and testing across models for safety research.
arxiv-2509-08829:
Recommenders that know your personality feel personal, but they may quietly treat demographic groups unequally. Chandan Kumar Sah examines that tension in a 2025 research paper written alone. Sah proposes PerFairX, an evaluation framework for personality-based recommendations from large language models. It uses the OCEAN personality model, the standard five-trait scheme psychologists use.

The framework benchmarks two leading models on movie and music datasets. Prompts range from neutral to personality-sensitive, across varied user profiles. Personality-aware prompting improved the match with a person's traits. It also widened fairness gaps between demographic groups. One model fit personalities better but swung more with prompt wording. The other stayed steadier but less personal. PerFairX gives developers a principled way to weigh fit against demographic equity before shipping.
arxiv-2509-08929:
Embryos elongate along one axis early in development, and lab-grown stem cell clusters called gastruloids do the same trick. Richard D. J. G. Ho and 8 co-authors ask what aligns the cells to make that happen, in a 2025 research paper. Three-dimensional light sheet imaging watched the clusters grow. A pulse of a Wnt-activating drug triggered the elongation.

Cell nuclei stretched in both treated and untreated clusters. Only the treated ones aligned their nuclear axes coherently across the whole tissue. That polarity coherence tracked the tissue-scale remodeling. A minimal physical model, with cells that align and stick according to their polarity, reproduced the symmetry breaking and elongation. Local alignment alone, the authors conclude, can drive the flowing rearrangements that lengthen an embryo-like structure. The result links a molecular signal to a mechanical outcome.
arxiv-2509-09029:
One ultraviolet emission line dominates the spectra of small stars, and it bathes their planets in atmosphere-stripping light. Sarah Peacock and 6 co-authors measure that Lyman-alpha line directly in a 2025 research paper. Interstellar gas normally absorbs most of the profile, forcing uncertain reconstructions. The team chose stars moving fast toward or away from us, whose Doppler shift moves the line clear of the absorption.

Twelve such stars span the transition from K to M dwarfs. The team measured most of each line's flux directly. Self-reversal, a dip carved in the line's core, weakens as stars get cooler. Two stars watched over several days varied by about a fifth in the line core. Habitable-zone fluxes for these stars fell below the reconstructed values used for other stars. The results give exoplanet researchers firmer ground for modeling how starlight erodes planetary atmospheres.
arxiv-2509-09129:
Jung-Wan Ryu and 2 co-authors sort pairs of exceptional points in non-Hermitian systems in a 2025 paper. An exceptional point is where two energy values and their states merge into one. Such points occur in open systems that can gain or lose energy.

Pairs fall into four classes, set by how energies wind, what phase builds up on a loop, and how a state projects on a basis state. Simple two level models lay out each class. Computer work in optical microcavities, tiny light traps with three scatterers, backs the sort. Loops around pairs give braid and phase traits tied to the wind class. Chiral light modes offer a lab sign.
arxiv-2509-09329:
Vincent Delmas and 5 co-authors automate the choice of coordinates for photochemical dynamics in a 2025 paper. Simulations of light driven reactions scale badly with dimension, a hard cap on system size. Cutting dimensions can keep results true while slashing cost, if the right axes are kept.

Surface hopping runs on three photoreactive molecules are done at full size and in reduced spaces. Two selection methods, principal component analysis and normal mode variance, pick the axes. Both replay full results in far fewer dimensions for all three cases. The principal component method cuts more, with clear gains for electronic traits and ring opening steps. Automation removes human bias from the choice.
arxiv-2509-09429:
Peisong Wen and 4 co-authors tackle patch-level learning for images in a 2025 self-supervised learning paper. Methods trained on whole images have advanced quickly, yet dense features for small patches still scatter too widely within one object or category. That over-dispersion hurts later tasks that need fine spatial detail.

The team argues whole-image training quietly gathers meaning together, through loose spatial alignment and shared parts across similar images. Dense training cannot copy that directly, so they build the gathering in explicitly. Patch matches are distilled, a ranking loss tolerates noisy labels, and shared patterns are separated from cluttered scenes. The aim is features that stay semantically tight at patch scale.
arxiv-2509-09729:
Gerard Sant and 6 co-authors introduce MultimodalHugs in 2025, a toolkit that lets sign language experiments run inside the Hugging Face ecosystem. Sign language processing matters more each year, yet its code tends to be bespoke, which hurts repeatability and fair comparison between studies. Mainstream tools built for tidy experimentation were not flexible enough to hold sign data without strain, a view confirmed by the team's own survey of researchers.

Built on top of Hugging Face, their framework adds an abstraction layer for varied modalities and tasks while keeping the platform's conveniences. Worked examples show pose estimation data for signing and pixel data for characters flowing through the same harness. Although aimed at sign languages, the design welcomes other misfit use cases too.
arxiv-2509-10129:
Alessio Chen and 4 co-authors address a trust problem in document question answering in this 2025 paper. Vision-language models can pull answers out of complex documents, but they often cannot show exactly where the answer sits on the page. Without that location, users cannot check the answer, and real-world use suffers.

The team built DocExplainerV0, an add-on module that predicts the bounding box of an answer separately from the answer itself. Because it is separate, it can plug into existing models, even closed ones that cannot be retrained. Their tests measure the gap between getting the text right and pointing to the right place, and they offer the setup as a benchmark for more open, checkable document tools.
arxiv-2509-10329:
How large is the space of hyperbolic surfaces with short closed curves? Jinsong Liu and three co-authors study that growth question in this 2025 geometry paper. Their stage is the moduli space of genus-g hyperbolic surfaces, equipped with the Weil-Petersson metric, and they define a cutoff length that itself grows with the genus.

Curves shorter than that cutoff count as short geodesics, and the authors compute how the volume of surfaces possessing them grows. A striking special case emerges: when both genus and cutoff head to infinity, surfaces with short geodesics fill essentially the whole space, taking up volume equal to the total almost surely. The result sharpens the picture of what a typical high-genus hyperbolic surface looks like.
arxiv-2509-10529:
Teaching an image generator new tricks without erasing old ones is Aoi Otani's solo 2025 study of continual learning for text-to-image diffusion models. Networks that learn sequentially suffer catastrophic forgetting, and diffusion models also fall into mode collapse, repeating themselves. Otani borrows Latent Replay from neuroscience: like the hippocampus storing patterns rather than raw sensations, the method keeps compact internal features instead of full images.

Across five visual concepts learned in sequence, latent replay preserved versatility far better than rival methods. After all five, alignment on the very first concept stayed near seventy-eight percent, well above baselines, and outputs stayed diverse. Oddly, choosing which stored features to replay at random beat choosing by similarity. The findings point to personalized image models that can keep evolving with a user cheaply.
arxiv-2509-11429:
George P. Yanev wrote this 2025 probability paper with no co-authors. It treats branching processes where the swarm tends to shrink away. The processes are critical ones with migration. Emigration beats immigration here. A subordination step randomizes the clock through renewal events.

The findings tie long-run fate to two inputs. One is the size of the starting group. The other is the mean gap between renewal events. Both shape the chance of avoiding wipeout. Yaglom-type limit theorems describe the group when survival is given. An alternating version cycles between empty and filled states. The work pairs with past studies of the reverse regime. There, immigration prevails instead.
arxiv-2509-11529:
Rishab Parthasarathy builds a hardware accelerator for sparse linear equations on FPGA chips, in a 2025 engineering paper. Solving such systems sits under circuit design and traffic planning, with millions of constraints, yet standard iterative software solvers run poorly on current hardware.

Two bottlenecks explain the poor fit: weak short-term data reuse causing scattered memory access, and complex dependencies that limit parallelism. Parthasarathy builds Azul, a past accelerator design made only of fast on-chip memory, as a grid of tiles with processing units linked by a network on chip. Simple cores with custom instruction add-ons run a task-based model. Test cases checked the build and matched the speed of a simulation of the first design.
arxiv-2509-11929:
When a database query returns far too many answers, showing a varied handful beats dumping them all. Marcelo Arenas and three co-authors rethink how that variety should be measured in 2025, arguing that distance-based scores can behave in unintuitive ways.

The standard recipe adds up or minimizes pairwise distances between tuples, yet picking the best subset is generally intractable and approximations are known only for scattered special cases. The alternative proposed here scores a set by volume instead of distance. Within that framework, the authors prove a constant-factor approximation is always achievable for volume-based measures, and they link query evaluation to ranked enumeration of solutions. Under stated conditions, the approximation even runs in polynomial time in the combined complexity sense.
arxiv-2509-12129:
One navigation brain for quadrupeds, drones, wheeled robots, and cars alike is the ambition behind NavFoM, introduced by Jiazhao Zhang and nineteen co-authors in 2025. Vision-language models generalize broadly, yet their navigation skill has stayed locked inside narrow tasks and body-specific designs.

Training swallowed eight million navigation samples spanning vision-and-language navigation, object searching, target tracking, and autonomous driving. A unified architecture reads multimodal input from varied camera rigs, with identifier tokens telling it which camera view and time horizon it faces. A dynamic sampling strategy squeezes observations into a fixed token budget for real deployment. Across public benchmarks the model matches or leads specialized systems with no task-specific fine-tuning, and live robot trials back the claim.
arxiv-2509-12229:
MSR Avinash profiles fine-tuning a large language model on a consumer graphics card in a 2025 paper. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA and QLoRA adapt a model by training only a small part of it, making work possible on modest hardware. How efficient that training is under an eight-gigabyte memory limit had not been studied systematically.

Avinash tested the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct model on a single NVIDIA RTX 4060 across three configurations. Batch size, sequence length, optimizer choice, and numeric precision were varied, and speed, memory use, and energy estimates were recorded. A paged optimizer raised throughput by up to a quarter, while one precision format performed worse than the other. Sequences up to about two thousand tokens still fit within the tight memory budget.
arxiv-2509-12529:
Cluster states are webs of entanglement prized for measurement-based quantum computing, and building them from sound instead of light is the goal of A. Govindarajan and three co-authors in 2025. Their phononic network strings together phonon waveguides, mechanical resonators, and optical cavities.

The design is modular: pairs of mechanical modes form the units, linked only by local, tunable interactions with cavity modes. A pulsed protocol generates continuous-variable cluster states, graded by an average nullifier score. Moderate squeezing gives high-quality states, while stronger squeezing backfires under dissipation. Encouragingly, the score can improve as the network grows, and distant modes get entangled through local measurements.
arxiv-2509-12829:
Yorick Herrmann, Connor Hill and four co-authors build chains of integer sets in 2025. Each set holds the last. The sets flip between two kinds. One kind has more sums than gaps. The next has more gaps than sums. Such sum-rich sets are rare. They were first a surprise in counting.

They solve the hard form of a question from Samuel Allen Alexander. In that form, any gap inside a set range must stay a gap. It must stay a gap in all later sets. A partner paper solved the easier fill-in form. The strict rule makes growth much harder. The new chains show the flip can repeat forever. It repeats even under that strict ban.
arxiv-2509-12929:
Maria-Catalina Isfan and 4 co-authors develop quantum computing tools for fast gravitational wave detection in a 2025 paper. The work is framed by the planned LISA space mission, which will observe gravitational waves from space. Gravitational wave data are challenging because signals vary with their sources and complex noise is present throughout.

The team is building a low-latency detection pipeline based on quantum neural networks. Earlier work showed such networks can recognize simulated gravitational waves and distinguish noisy signals from pure noise in LISA Consortium data. Current evaluation uses the Sangria LISA Data Challenge dataset and compares against classical methods. The networks reliably distinguished signals embedded in noise with classification accuracy above ninety-eight percent in their tests, and identified most mergers in the dataset.
arxiv-2509-13329:
Jeroen Gardeyn, Greet Vanden Berghe and Tony Wauters release sparrow in 2025, an open heuristic for 2D irregular strip packing. Nesting ranks among the hardest cut tasks, yet progress stalled for a decade. Near-optimal claims masked real headroom in scores.

Sparrow splits the task into feasibility steps where collisions ease stepwise. It beats the prior best, at times by wide margins. Ten new real cases aid fair tests. Stagnation is blamed on entry bars and poor reproducibility, not true optimality. Open code aims to reboot the field culture for steady gains that others can verify and extend.
arxiv-2509-13429:
Anthony Arnold and Mark Marron present Catalpa, a garbage collector for a low-variance software stack, in a 2025 paper. Application performance is usually treated as a continuous function of memory and time used. In practice, users view performance more as a binary. Either the application responds fast enough, in under roughly a tenth of a second, or it leaves them waiting and potentially abandoning the task.

Industrial developers therefore focus on ninety-fifth and ninety-ninth percentile tail latencies as heavily as on averages. The authors' vision is a software stack that actively supports those needs through programming language and runtime design. Catalpa is a novel garbage collector design for the Bosque programming language and runtime, with an allocator designed to minimize latency and tail latency.
arxiv-2509-13929:
Lisa Orloff Clark and Malcolm Jones unify two constructions of groupoids in a 2025 mathematics paper. Higher-rank graphs are small categories generalizing both directed graphs and free monoids, and their path groupoids, algebraic objects encoding the graph's paths, are usually built either from filters or from graph morphisms. Whether the two routes agree in full generality was unsettled.

The authors generalize the morphism approach to finitely aligned P-graphs over weakly quasi-lattice ordered groups, a much broader class. They define conjugacy for partial monoid actions and show conjugate actions have isomorphic semidirect product groupoids, the bridge that makes the two constructions coincide. Combined with results elsewhere, they survey the many isomorphic presentations of these groupoids at different levels of generality.
arxiv-2509-14129:
Kit T. Rodolfa and eleven co-authors report a machine learning case study in public policy in a 2025 paper, a collaboration between Johnson County, Kansas, and Carnegie Mellon University. Many people cycle through jail with untreated mental illness, substance dependence, and homelessness, needs the justice system is poorly built to meet. The county tried targeted, proactive mental health outreach instead.

The team describe their data, predictive model, and a field trial testing both prediction and impact. The model proved highly predictive of new jail bookings: over half of the highest-risk group returned to jail within a year. Outreach helped most exactly there, shifting mental health service use, emergency dispatches, and justice involvement. The study weighs those gains against the racial disparities that frame the whole system.
arxiv-2509-14329:
Surajit Bera and three co-authors show in 2025 that local measurements alone can create large scale entanglement in a quantum system. Measurements usually break entanglement down. Recent work hinted that clever measurement only dynamics could still build strongly entangled states.

Their setup has no built in unitary evolution at all. A main chain of fermions sits beside an auxiliary chain, and detectors couple locally to the system. Measurements are local, fixed in pattern, yet fail to commute with each other. Over long times the system reaches states with volume law entanglement, where entanglement grows with system size. That result widens the toolkit for making entangled states, using measurement as the engine rather than the enemy.
arxiv-2509-14429:
Alireza Rahmani, Mohammad Javad Hajiahmadi and Reza Faraji-Dana design in 2025 a microwave system to heat deep brain tumours while sparing healthy tissue. Hyperthermia, controlled heating, can aid tumour treatment. Deep targets are hard to focus on without heating the path.

Their method uses time reversal, sending signals backwards from a target to learn a focusing pattern, delivered through a four layer metasurface array. A metasurface is a thin engineered sheet that steers waves. Simulations on realistic and simple head models guide the design. The team then built the array and a thermal head phantom for lab tests. They report a first experimental demonstration of metasurface time reversal focusing for deep brain heating, with localised warming.
arxiv-2509-14629:
Rupam Jyoti Borah and Umananda Dev Goswami study in 2025 how a Gauss-Bonnet trace anomaly shifts black hole quasi periodic oscillations. Those oscillations are flicker rhythms in X-ray light from black holes pulling in gas. The anomaly adds a quantum tinged fix to gravity, set by one size value.

From the paths of test masses, the pair track shifts in the force well, spin momentum, energy and the innermost stable round orbit. Base orbital rates follow from those values. They then test more than one standard oscillation model, linking upper and lower rates and their resonance radii. If the anomaly moves rate pairs by a gap timing can see, X-ray watches could bound a fix now held in theory.
arxiv-2509-14729:
Ali Sufyan and four co-authors screen materials at high speed in 2025 for altermagnetic band splitting. Altermagnetism is a new found class of magnetism with zero net pull, yet spin splitting that shifts with momentum. Light, common elements can host it, which suits next wave spintronics.

Finds have lagged, since magnetic symmetry checks are hard and past searches were slow. The team build a pipeline that gauges the splitting and run it across a large set of materials. Candidates are ranked by splitting size for lab follow up. High speed screening turns a boutique symmetry hunt into a catalogue task. A ranked list gives crystal growers and device teams a firm place to start.
arxiv-2509-15629:
Lester Phillip Violeta leads a team that reports on the 2025 Singing Voice Conversion Challenge. Entrants build systems that change a recorded singer into another singer. This year added a second task: change the singing style, not just the identity. The team ran the event and studied its results in depth.

They built a new data set for the event, set two tasks, and shared base systems. Thirty three systems were judged by crowd listening tests and by machine scores. Top systems matched real samples on identity scores. Style proved harder: breathy tones, slides, and vibrato still sound less natural. The team also note flaws in both test styles used for style.
arxiv-2509-15729:
L. F. B. Souza leads a team that studies how waves push particles out of a plasma's edge. They model the edge field as a sum of waves with set patterns and a phase shift between them. From that model they derive a step by step map for particle motion. They then cut the model down to two waves for a close study.

When both waves share a pattern, phase rules the outcome: opposite phases clash and hold particles in, while matched phases add up and drive wild transport. Mismatched pairs give richer maps, with extra resonances and sticky zones. A fractal measure shows their borders are rough, unlike the smooth borders of matched pairs. Phase and pattern jointly set the flow.
arxiv-2509-16029:
Finding valid setups for string theory means searching a vast space of flux choices, most of which fail. Moritz Walden and Magdalena Larfors apply models that generate new examples to this search for type IIB string vacua. One model, a flow network suited to discrete data, learns to propose flux vectors that form valid vacua.

A second model, a transformer, is steered to sample vacua with traits the user wants. Both models find good vacua at a strong rate in tests. The results show that generative tools can speed the study of the string landscape, where brute force search is far too slow.
arxiv-2509-16129:
Most processes forget their distant past, but real systems in social, brain, and finance data sometimes jump back to an old state. Sudharsan Senthil and Avhishek Chatterjee model such random resets to the past and ask how to learn the hidden influence graph behind the data. The graph shows which parts of the system drive which others.

Their stepwise greedy method rebuilds any graph of bounded links, as long as the jumps back stay rare compared with the sample count. The method needs no stored memory of past steps. That makes it suited to long data streams where storing all history is not an option.
arxiv-2509-16329:
Reading the mood of a whole crowd from sound is harder than reading one speaker, since voices blend into noise. Orchid Chetia Phukan and eight co-authors test whether speech models trained on many languages handle crowd emotion better than narrower models. Crowds mix accents and speech styles, so broad training may help a model cope.

Across tests on a benchmark crowd set, the many-language models won at every clip length tried. They led even on clips as short as a quarter second. The results set a new guide for building crowd emotion tools and may shape future benchmarks in the field.
arxiv-2509-16429:
Mapping the brain's white matter wiring from diffusion scans means tracing fibers through spots where they cross, merge, and fan out. Itzik Waizman and three co-authors treat each fiber as a sequence and let a transformer predict its next step, guided by the path so far and the local scan data. A convolutional network reads the tissue traits around each point to inform the step.

The combined method improved the precision and completeness of pathway maps over classic tractography. Standard scoring tools rated it level with leading methods. On a real-world data set it held up well, which suggests sound generalization.
arxiv-2509-16529:
O. P. Jyothilakshmi and V. Sreekanth study exotic stars in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The stars they model are made of dark energy and pull harder in some directions than others. The pair ask whether neat links between star traits, seen in normal stars, also hold here. Such links are called universal relations.

They model the stars with a modified gas law and a rule for uneven pressure. They compute mass, size, and vibration rates under slow spin. A shared pattern does hold for these odd stars. One gas parameter tracks the vibration rate closely. Uneven pressure can strengthen or weaken that link. Future wave detectors could test these claims.
arxiv-2509-16629:
Kaichen Xu and co-authors give transformers a new sense of order in a 2025 paper. Transformers need a tag that tells where each token sits. Standard tags assume a fixed line-up of features. Real data, though, can link features by cause rather than by place. The team build tags from those cause links instead.

Their method is called CAPE. Tests on made-up and real datasets check its theory and its gains. Models with CAPE tags did better on data with no natural order. Code is shared in public. Cause-based tags could help with medical, finance, and sensor data, where links matter more than raw order in a row.
arxiv-2509-16929:
Yongrui Chen and co-authors help models keep reasoning over structured knowledge in a 2025 paper. The task turns plain questions into formal queries over a knowledge base. New tasks arrive in sequence, and models must not forget old ones. Past continual methods generalize poorly here and grow bloated as tasks pile up.

Their system, K-DeCore, splits knowledge into parts that transfer cleanly. A memory step consolidates what each stage learned. Made-up practice data, guided by structure, sharpens generalization. Tests on four benchmarks beat prior continual methods across measures. The work used several large model backbones, showing the idea is not tied to one model.
arxiv-2509-17129:
Sarif Khan, Jongkuk Kim, and Hyun Min Lee propose a new particle physics model in a 2025 arXiv paper. The model tries to explain a single high-energy neutrino event recorded by the KM3NeT detector. It also links that event to dark matter and to gravitational waves from cosmic strings in the early universe.

In the model, an added force gives a new heavy particle that can serve as dark matter. Slow mixing with known forces lets it decay, which could produce the observed signal. A low reheating temperature after inflation, with extra entropy poured in, keeps the amount of this heavy dark matter at the right level. The authors also show that strings in this setup would give waves that planned detectors could pick up, though the signal fades at high frequencies.
arxiv-2509-17329:
Neham Jain, Andrew Jong, Sebastian Scherer, and Ioannis Gkioulekas present a way to see through smoke in three dimensions. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins scene rebuilding with smoke removal, working from video shot at several viewpoints. Older tools lean on learned priors that can invent detail, or they handle only still, thin smoke.

The method, SmokeSeer, pairs normal color video with thermal video, since heat cameras scatter far less in smoke. It builds the scene with 3D Gaussian splatting and splits the result into smoke and non-smoke parts. The system copes with smoke from thin to thick, and the smoke may drift and change as time passes. Tests cover both synthetic scenes and a new real-world data set with paired color and thermal footage. Code and data are posted on the project site.
arxiv-2509-17629:
Antonio Bucchiarone, Juri Di Rocco, Damiano Di Vincenzo, and Alfonso Pierantonio explore a new home for modeling constraints in web tools. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from the low-code boom: platforms built on Node.js and frameworks such as React let non-experts build software as cloud services. Model validation inside those platforms still leans on OCL, the Object Constraint Language.

A JavaScript version of OCL exists, but it covers only part of the standard, sees little use, and meshes poorly with modern front-end toolchains. The authors propose JSX, the declarative dialect of JavaScript used across the React world, as the constraint language instead. JSX is already where these tools draw their interfaces, so constraints written there live beside the components they guard. The paper weighs what that swap would take and what it could fix for SaaS-based modeling.
arxiv-2509-18029:
Abdellah Tounsi and 6 co-authors run a quantum solver on real hardware for a magnet puzzle on a kagome grid. Their 2025 paper deals with the lowest-energy state of a Heisenberg model, where nearby spins pull against each other. The kagome grid, a web of triangles, makes that state hard to pin down.

Their custom circuit is shallow and shaped by the grid itself. It recovers key traits of the ground state, such as spin-to-spin links, with no error fixes in the main runs. Those traits held up under hardware noise. A geometry-based design also made the search settle in fewer steps than a standard noisy method.
arxiv-2509-18129:
Yan Huang and 4 co-authors tune how often scattered workers compute and talk in shared training. Their 2025 paper deals with distributed stochastic optimization, where data at each node are not alike. More local steps save talk, while more talk keeps nodes in sync, so the best mix shifts by system.

Their method, FlexGT, lets each round set both counts freely, with a tracked snapshot gradient. A joint proof frame gives tight bounds for talk and compute cost. A sped-up variant, with graph facts known in advance, hits the best trade curve. In the non-convex case, its costs match known floors.
arxiv-2509-18229:
Anthony Patera and Rohan Abeyaratne tame the hit-or-miss nature of GPT on engineering sums. Their 2025 paper notes that one run can solve a basic mechanics task with no flaw, while the next run fails it. Such swings bar plain GPT from class or work use, they argue.

Their agency runs many solver copies on the same task, each on its own. A compare agent then weighs the set of answers and picks a best one, with bits from runners-up kept where fit. A classic jury result backs the plan: if each solver beats chance, a large set most often lands right.
arxiv-2509-18329:
Quantum sensors can measure tiny magnetic fields, but most are costly and closed to tinkering. Mark Carney and Victoria Kumaran present Uncut Gem, an open-source sensor anyone can build and modify. Their 2025 paper gives an overview of the full platform. It rests on small flaws in diamond, called NV centers, that react to magnetic fields.

The design uses cheap parts bought off the shelf, arranged in a new hardware layout. Its control software is open source and written with Arduino tools, so it is easy to move and change. The sensor is small and low cost by design. The authors aim it at teaching, lab research, and new quantum technology projects. They frame it as open science, built for a community to improve.
arxiv-2509-18529:
DNA reads the same forward and backward: a sequence and its reverse complement carry the same meaning. Mingqian Ma shows that top DNA language models often miss that symmetry in this 2025 paper. Their predictions can change when the same stretch is fed in flipped form. That inconsistency undercuts trust in the models for real biology work.

Ma proposes a fine-tuning rule that directly punishes any gap between a model's output on a sequence and on its flipped twin. The rule works with any model design. Tests spanned three model families and many task types, from sorting sequences to predicting profiles. The rule cut prediction flips and errors sharply. Accuracy held steady or improved versus fixes like flipped-data training or averaging at test time. The recipe leaves one single, robust model that is cheap to run.
arxiv-2509-18829:
Piecewise functions switch formulas from one interval to the next, and they appear across applied math. Christophe Berthod presents Piecewise, a Julia language module for working with them, in this 2025 paper. The user picks the rule for each interval freely. A fitting mechanism can also match a piecewise function, built from user formulas, to a target curve.

With the right formulas in place, many integral transforms of the function come out directly, with no numerical quadrature. The module ships seven formulas that yield the function's moments fast. A companion module adds a fast Hilbert transform on the same base. Another extends some formulas to a Lorentz transform, a variant the paper names. The work is a software paper: its value is speed and convenience for transform-heavy calculations. It targets Julia users in signal and physics work.
arxiv-2509-19029:
Training giant models across many machines in a pipeline wastes bandwidth shipping activations and gradients between stages. Boao Kong and five co-authors present Clapping, a compression scheme built for pipeline-parallel training. Older compression methods lean on shaky assumptions about gradients, or they store data per sample, a memory cost that grows with the dataset. Clapping instead reuses samples lazily across steps, breaking that per-sample memory barrier.

It works in few-epoch and even online training, where data may be seen only once. Two variants, called FC and FU, both converge without assuming unbiased gradients. They also keep compression errors from compounding across workers, a known failure mode in pipeline setups. Numerical experiments across several learning tasks confirm the performance gains. The method targets the communication bottleneck that slows the largest training runs.
arxiv-2509-19229:
Pavel Meshcheriakov, writing alone, solves pieces of a toy version of quantum chromodynamics: scalar QCD in two dimensions with many colors. The theory confines its scalar quarks, and its meson spectrum obeys an equation much like the famous 't Hooft equation. Meshcheriakov builds a nonperturbative analytic method around that likeness, based on integrability and on a technique devised by Fateev, Lukyanov, and Zamolodchikov for the original model.

Within that approach he finds spectral sums and a systematic large-level expansion for the meson masses. The formulas behave correctly in the near-critical and heavy-quark limits and agree well with numerical data. Continuing the quark mass into the complex plane reveals two endless families of points where single mesons become massless. The author suggests those singularities hint at a hidden link to nontrivial conformal field theories.
arxiv-2509-19629:
Farm irrigation must earn money while leaving enough water in rivers for nature. Nahid Sultana and three co-authors widen a planning framework for splitting irrigation water. They first solve two extreme goals: highest farm profit, and lowest shortfall in river flow. Those extremes mark the edges of what any plan can achieve.

Between the edges, they chart the full trade-off curve with combined goals and evolutionary search. Tests on the Muhuri Irrigation Project in Bangladesh show profits and flow shortfalls spanning wide ranges. The chart lets planners pick a balance with eyes open, rather than discovering costs later. Climate pressure and scarce water make such charts valuable. The study adds depth to a framework already in use by the project team.
arxiv-2509-19829:
Inner functions, analytic maps of the disc with unit boundary values, are pillars of function theory. Jiaxing He and three co-authors view them through persistence modules, the algebraic bookkeeping of topological data analysis. Level sets of an inner function generate the modules. The authors chart their basic properties.

For a wide class, the modules split into simple interval pieces, even without finiteness assumptions. The interleaving distance between modules varies smoothly with the function's supremum norm, at least for Blaschke products. An explicit distance formula is given for one example. That smoothness speaks about how the space of Blaschke products connects. The bridge runs both ways: data tools illuminate classical analysis, and classical objects stress-test the newer theory.
arxiv-2509-19929:
Engineers often must rebuild a full physical field from a handful of noisy sensors, an ill-posed guessing game. Arnaud Vadeboncoeur and three co-authors teach a generative model the shapes that fields can take. Their geometric autoencoders learn from many systems with varying geometry, with no need for the governing equations. The learned prior then guides Bayesian inversion on new systems.

Their slogan is learn first, observe later. Geometry-awareness is the hard part: standard methods assume one fixed shape. Lessons distilled across systems ease the ill-posedness that plagues single-system inference. Uncertainty estimates come with the reconstruction, as engineering decisions demand. Bridges, turbines, and medical phantoms all fit the pattern of sparse sensing on shifting geometry.
arxiv-2509-20129:
York Hay Ng, Phuong Hanh Hoang, and En-Shiun Annie Lee wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on language data. Typological databases record facts about how each language builds words and sentences. One such database, URIEL+, is rich but huge and sparse, above all for low-resource languages. That size and sparsity weaken distance measures between languages.

The authors build a pipeline that selects the most useful features and fills in missing values. The result is a compact set of features that stays readable and meaningful. They test these reduced sets on language distance tasks and on downstream language technology tasks. The smaller representations gave more informative distances between languages. They also improved performance in multilingual applications. The work shows that careful trimming can beat simply using every feature available.
arxiv-2509-20229:
Angelos Plastropoulos, Nicolas Avdelidis, and Argyrios Zolotas wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on aircraft maintenance. Robots that inspect aircraft inside hangars must know exactly where they are. Hangars block satellite positioning and bounce signals off metal walls, so localization is unusually hard. The paper compares three indoor positioning options on cost and accuracy.

The options are motion capture, ultra-wideband radio, and a network of ceiling cameras. They are scored across robot localization, asset tracking, and surface defect detection in one hangar bay. A two-layer optimizer picks camera models and positions that meet accuracy targets with minimal hardware. The study gives maintenance planners a concrete method for balancing accuracy, coverage, and budget. An optimized camera layout, the authors argue, can deliver robust sensing at fair cost.
arxiv-2509-20929:
Complex numbers enter physics whenever symmetries are studied, even though the underlying symmetry algebras are real. Tanguy Marsault and Laurent Schoeffel sort out that relationship in a 2025 paper on Lie algebra complexification. They define the concept precisely and prove a central identity step by step.

The proof shows that complexifying a real form recovers a product of an algebra with its conjugate. With that result in hand, the authors determine the irreducible representations of the proper Lorentz group. Those representations classify the physical objects allowed under Lorentz symmetry, such as particles of given spin. The paper is pedagogical in spirit, making a subtle point of representation theory fully explicit for physicists.
arxiv-2509-21229:
Approximating a growing function by the phase of an inner function is a delicate problem in function theory. It comes from Alex Bergman. An inner function is a bounded holomorphic function, flat in size on the real line. Its phase grows steadily along the line. Many problems need to approximate a given growing function by such a phase. The paper treats the case where the target function obeys a doubling condition.

Bergman gives a main result on such approximations from inside. He then gives two applications of the result. The first is a density condition for a set to be a zero set of a Toeplitz kernel. The second describes which majorants are allowed in Beurling Malliavin theory for model spaces. The scope covers most spaces built from one component inner functions.
arxiv-2509-21529:
Zero forcing is a graph process where coloured vertices can force neighbours to change colour under a rule. Ryan Moruzzi and 2 co-authors study a leaky variant on grid subgraphs in a 2025 paper. Leaky zero forcing allows some vertices to resist forcing. The setting is induced subgraphs of d dimensional grid graphs. Leaky forts, special blocking sets, drive the structural results.

For small leak counts, every nonempty leaky fort meets the graph boundary. That yields general bounds and, in some settings, exact forcing numbers. The authors also define Hopi rectangle graphs on an integer lattice. For that family, the zero forcing number equals the maximum nullity. The leaky forcing number is completely characterized for all leak values.
arxiv-2509-21629:
Loop invariants are the bottleneck of program verification: a prover needs them, but finding strong ones is hard. Anjiang Wei and 5 co-authors test language models as invariant generators in a 2025 paper. Their system, Quokka, validates each generated invariant directly. Prior work treated model output as noisy material needing heavy post processing. Quokka instead checks whether an invariant helps prove the target assertion.

Soundness guarantees accompany the simpler design. A benchmark of hundreds of scoring instances derives from the SV-COMP competition, with thousands of training instances. Nine language models from multiple families were evaluated. Supervised fine tuning and best of N sampling gave measurable improvements. Quokka consistently beat prior language model based verifiers in their tests.
arxiv-2509-21729:
Slobodan Mitrović, Theodore Pan, and two co-authors study a classic problem in graph algorithms: finding the densest part of a directed graph. Their 2025 paper works in two models built for very large data. One model splits the work across many machines. The other reads the graph in a single pass with small memory.

The team gives a parallel method that reaches a near-best density estimate in few rounds of computation. They also give the first one-pass streaming method for this problem that works without randomness. Tests on time-based data sets show the streaming method does far better than its worst-case promise. The parallel method also needs fewer rounds than earlier work.
arxiv-2509-21829:
Jianyu Gong, You Wang, and Ellis Ye Yuan build a systematic way to study Feynman integrals in this 2025 physics paper, submitted to JHEP. The integrals they study evaluate to a family of functions called multiple polylogarithms. Knowing a compact code for such an integral, called its symbol, reveals much of its structure. Their frame starts from the integral's form in projective space.

The authors classify the integral's logarithmic singularities through geometric setups they call touching configurations. These setups point to the first entries of the symbol. They also produce new, simpler integrals, called elementary discontinuities, through an operation named bi-projection. Real discontinuities of the original integral are sums of these simpler ones. By repeating the analysis on each new integral, the full symbol can be built. The paper works the method through two one-loop examples in detail.
arxiv-2509-22029:
Yuxi Hu and Reinhard Racke study a fluid model in which heat does not spread in the classical way. Their 2025 paper treats the three-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations, which govern moving fluids, with hyperbolic heat conduction. The classical Fourier law is replaced by the Cattaneo-Christov relation, which gives heat a finite travel speed and a wave-like character. The authors pose the system as an initial boundary value problem and focus on flows with spherical symmetry.

They establish that small solutions exist for all time and stay uniform in size. The proof rests on careful advance estimates that hold across the whole evolution. Building on those estimates, they rigorously justify two limits of the model. In the relaxation limit, the heat law returns to its classical form. In the vanishing viscosity limit, the fluid's internal friction fades out.
arxiv-2509-22129:
H. Kaur and Prince A. Ganai study the heat behavior of a simple black hole in a modified theory of gravity. The black hole is the BTZ solution, which lives in two space dimensions plus time. The theory, called bumblebee gravity, breaks the symmetry between space directions through a vector field with a nonzero vacuum value. Their 2025 paper also uses Barrow entropy, which adjusts the usual area law for entropy with corrections meant to reflect quantum gravity.

To define the thermodynamics cleanly, the authors place the black hole inside a finite heated cavity, following York's approach. They then work out the corrected temperature, the free energy, and the conditions for the black hole to be stable. The results show that the Lorentz-breaking dynamics and the Barrow corrections together reshape the phase structure of the system. Equilibrium configurations and thermal stability both shift in a marked way.
arxiv-2509-22229:
Jiaping Yu and four co-authors tackle the problem of adapting an image model to a new domain when the original training data cannot be shared. Privacy and cost often block access to source data, yet a model trained elsewhere may falter on new kinds of images. Their 2025 method, Experts Cooperative Learning, puts two experts on equal footing: a frozen model from the source domain, lightly extended, and a large pretrained vision-language model with a tunable text prompt.

The two experts mine the unlabeled target data for points they agree on. It first retrieves likely source-like samples and complex target samples together. It then fine-tunes each expert on its own retrieved set. Finally it forces the two experts' learning outcomes to stay consistent with each other. On four benchmark data sets, the approach matched the best reported performance for this source-free setting.
arxiv-2509-22629:
Lucas Aragão and 4 co-authors prove an exponential upper bound for induced Ramsey numbers. The induced Ramsey number of a graph is the smallest host size that forces a monochromatic induced copy under any edge coloring with a set number of colors. Induced copies must match the graph exactly, including missing edges, which makes these numbers hard to bound. Their main result gives a bound that grows like a power tower-free exponential form in colors and graph size.

For two colors, the bound resolves a conjecture of Erdős from 1975. For more colors, it answers a question of Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov in a strong form. The result caps a long search for the right growth rate.
arxiv-2509-22829:
Cyril Belardinelli finds the exact shape of a heavy spring hung between two supports. A spring suspended at both ends sags under its own weight, and its resting curve is a classic Elastica problem. The total energy depends on two unknown functions at once. One describes the shape of the hanging spring. The other describes how mass is distributed along the stretched spring.

Calculus of variations, Belardinelli shows, gives a rather short and elegant solution to the coupled problem. He notes that this route does not appear to be widely known in the literature. The result is an exact determination of the curve, not a numerical approximation.
arxiv-2509-23229:
Most separation logics hide the pointers inside containers, which blocks precise specs for APIs that lend those pointers out. Yawen Guan and Clément Pit-Claudel present logical pinning, a light borrowing model for sequential programs. Users can track selected internal pointers at the logical level. The model generalizes the magic-wand operator for partial data structures. Precise specs, including pointer-stability traits, become easier to write and prove.

Only the way predicates and specs are written changes. That keeps the approach compatible with most separation logic variants. The pair verify small pointer programs and sharpen common container specs. All results are mechanized in Rocq with the CFML library.
arxiv-2509-23329:
New sky data strain the classic Starobinsky inflation model, and a small deformation may relieve the tension. Jureeporn Yuennan, Farruh Atamurotov, and Phongpichit Channuie test a marginally deformed version. A tiny parameter shifts the potential away from the exact Starobinsky form, as quantum corrections might. Slow-roll formulas give the spectral index and tensor ratio. Planck, ACT, and DESI data supply the constraints.

Nonzero deformation raises both predicted quantities. That eases the mismatch with recent ACT and DESI readings. The model still matches the observed perturbation amplitude. It also softens the fine-tuning of the quartic coupling. A small parameter range stays viable and testable.
arxiv-2509-23429:
Toric domains in four dimensions gain a singular cousin whose boundary is a lens space, not a sphere. Jonathan Trejos extends the definition and computes an invariant for one family. The new domains carry a natural orbifold point, hence the name singular. He calculates their ECH capacities for a concave-like subfamily. The math runs through the orbifold setting directly.

The results adapt to embedding problems in smoother spaces built from these domains. Examples include the unitary cotangent bundles of the sphere and the projective plane. Capacities give sharp blocks for such embeddings. The work widens the reach of ECH methods to singular targets.
arxiv-2509-23529:
Hard contest problems in Russian form a new test for language models named DOoM. Ilya Kuleshov and 4 co-authors built the open-source benchmark from math and physics tasks. Problems range from school level to university olympiad and entrance exam items. The paper explains why the set was made, how it is structured, and how answers are scored.

Early runs across several models show a link between scores and the number of tokens a model uses. Results also split by subject, with math and physics performance differing in clear ways. The authors offer the set as a public yardstick for reasoning in Russian.
arxiv-2509-23829:
Teaching robot hands needs data that human teleoperation cannot supply at scale. Kefei Zhu and 10 co-authors built DexFlyWheel, a framework that grows its own dexterous manipulation data in a self-improving loop. Seed demonstrations start the cycle. Imitation learning extracts human-like behavior, residual reinforcement learning widens it, and rollouts in simulation are augmented across settings before feeding the next round.

Each pass enlarges the diversity of the data set, a flywheel effect. The system produced over two thousand demonstrations across four hard tasks. Policies trained on that data averaged about eighty-two percent success on challenge tests and transferred to a real dual-arm lift at a similar rate.
arxiv-2509-23929:
Ramsey theory asks when a large graph must hide a neat pattern in any red-blue coloring of its edges. Abhishek Girish Aher and Aparna Lakshmanan S study chains of graphs called Ramsey chains. In such a chain, each graph sits inside the next. Any coloring of a late graph forces a one-color copy of an early one.

One open problem asked for a chain with two traits. The color count of the graphs must grow without end, while the clique size must stay bounded. The pair show that general shift graphs form such a chain. They also give a fresh proof of the broad Ramsey claim for many colors.
arxiv-2509-24029:
Charges placed on a thin straight rod push each other away, yet the full pattern is not plain. Orion Ciftja and 2 co-authors study point charges on a conducting needle, starting from a bead model with a set count of charges. They prove that one balance state exists and that it is the only one.

The team also tracks charges that move under their own push. That moving system, they show, does not settle into the balance state. As the charge count grows, the spread of charges tends toward an even spread along the needle. This holds even though charges pile up near the ends at any fixed count. Pictures help make the odd limit clear.
arxiv-2509-24129:
Mashing, spreading, and slicing change what a thing is, not just where it sits. Priyanka Mandikal and 5 co-authors present SPARTA, a framework for this family of robot tasks. Most robot work targets moves such as picking, placing, or opening, which leave the object itself intact.

SPARTA's key idea is that these state-change tasks share a pattern: regions of the object shift from actionable to transformed, step by step. The system maps those regions to build both its observations and a dense reward for progress. Two policy styles use those signals, one learned by reinforcement and one greedy for fast setup. On a real robot across ten objects and three tasks, SPARTA trained faster and scored higher than standard baselines.
arxiv-2509-24529:
Matthias Allard and Sampad Lahiry study a family of two-dimensional Coulomb gas systems where a gap is about to be born. The equilibrium density vanishes on a ring strictly inside the droplet, a sign the gas is on the edge of splitting. They work at a fixed inverse temperature and use radial symmetry throughout.

The team expands the log of the partition function at large particle count, up to the constant term. A novel term appears at a fractional power of the count, between the known orders. A double scaling limit at that same scale yields a new correlation kernel in the bulk. It differs from the classic Ginibre kernel, marking the gap's birth.
arxiv-2509-24629:
Synthetic voices can sound happy or sad for a whole sentence, but shifting emotion word by word inside one sentence is far harder. Tianrui Wang and 12 co-authors built WeSCon, a self-training framework for word-level control of emotion and speaking rate in a pre-trained zero-shot speech model. No data set with in-sentence emotion transitions was needed, which has been the field's bottleneck.

A transition-smoothing strategy and a dynamic speed control guide the model through multi-round inference. Self-training then folds that skill into the model end to end, with a dynamic emotional attention bias to simplify use. Results reached the top level for word-level expressive control while keeping zero-shot quality.
arxiv-2509-24729:
Vyacheslav Kungurtsev formulates control of systems buffeted by season-like repeating noise, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Energy and farm systems face weather and demand patterns that cycle with the calendar. Steering them well calls for foresight and caution about risk, yet classic scenario methods grow too heavy over long horizons.

The formulation forces the system's state distribution to repeat with the same period as the noise. That single move lets solutions be built from periodic building blocks, avoiding growth that explodes with time span. The author shows the setup on several examples that fit the frame. The paper offers the method as a tractable route for long-run control under repeating uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-26429:
Emil Javurek and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-five for predicting how one patient would fare under different treatment sequences. In personalized medicine, doctors choose ordered doses over time. Each choice shapes later options. Learning the best sequence from past records is hard because errors compound over long horizons.

Their learner views the problem through causal inference. It is built to stay valid if one of its two helper models is wrong. It also ignores first-order errors in those helpers. In the long run it performs almost as well as if the true helpers were known. It works with both discrete and continuous patient states and can pair with any machine learning model. Simulations support the theory and beat prior methods.
arxiv-2509-26529:
Shangshu Qian, Lin Tan, and Yongle Zhang present CSnake, a testing tool that exposes self-sustaining failure chains in distributed systems. Their paper was published in 2025. In such a chain, one fault triggers the next, and the outage keeps itself going across many machines.

Normal fault testing misses these chains, because each step needs its own specific trigger. CSnake links single fault tests together by cause, comparing each test run with a clean run to see which new faults a fault sets off. A budget plan tests the most varied faults first, and a quick check avoids joining steps whose conditions clash. The tool found fifteen such bugs in five systems, and several were confirmed or fixed.
arxiv-2510-00229:
Rohan Kadekodi and colleagues at the University of Washington published this 2025 paper on running AI agents directly on user devices. On-device models protect privacy and cut costs, but small local models fumble tool calls. They pick the wrong tool from large sets and botch the arguments a tool needs. The team splits tool calling into those two distinct subtasks.

Their decoupled fine-tuning trains separate LoRA adapters for tool choice and for argument writing. The DualTune framework then loads whichever adapter the current step requires. A hierarchical scheme narrows the tool list before selection even begins. On the MCP-Bench benchmark, a seven-billion-parameter model improved its tool-calling accuracy by nearly half. It beat rival local models of its size in every comparison the authors ran. It also topped models twice its size in most cases.
arxiv-2510-00329:
Sarmad Mehrdad and three colleagues published this 2025 paper on learning the hidden rules behind human arm reaching. When people point at a target, their motion seems to optimize some mix of smoothness, effort, and accuracy. Inverse reinforcement learning can recover that mix from recorded movements. Their variant, MO-IRL, needs far fewer example movements than classical approaches.

The team used motion-capture data from a pointing task and a two-link arm model. Each reach was split into phases, and each phase learned its own mix of seven candidate costs. Time-varying weights cut joint-angle errors to roughly half the single-weight baseline. The learned mix stressed low joint acceleration at the start and end of each reach. That emphasis matches the smoothness seen in biological motion. The costs also transferred to an unseen person's trials with similar accuracy.
arxiv-2510-00429:
Jiaqi Li and five colleagues published this 2025 computational physics paper on Fe3GaTe2, a layered ferromagnet prized for spintronics. The material orders magnetically at high temperature and prefers its magnetization pointing out of plane. Experiments showed that squeezing it near ten gigapascals flips that preference into the plane. Nobody knew which atoms drive the flip, so the team ran detailed calculations.

Their calculations reproduce the switching pressure and dissect it site by site. Under pressure, iron magnetic moments shrink as spin bands broaden and drift apart. The outer iron layer's spin-orbit contribution, once the backer of out-of-plane order, fades and changes sign. Tellurium atoms add a steady push toward in-plane order as their contribution declines. The inner iron layer still favors out-of-plane, but it loses the tug of war. The study gives spintronic designers a microscopic recipe for tuning magnetic anisotropy with strain.
arxiv-2510-00529:
Anbi Guo and Mahfuza Farooque published this 2025 paper on hunting intruders in structured security logs with a small language model. Advanced attacks unfold in stages scattered across days of log lines. Fixed context windows chop that story into pieces no model can follow. Their framework, DM-RAG, gives a compact model two kinds of memory.

A short-term buffer holds summaries of recent activity for immediate context. A searchable long-term store keeps historical patterns ready for retrieval. Bayesian fusion decides which memories earn permanent persistence. On a standard network intrusion dataset, the system reached recall near ninety-nine percent, topping fine-tuned and retrieval baselines. Accuracy stayed modest, but catching nearly every attack suits a monitoring role. The design stays lightweight and interpretable, needing no giant model or outside corpus. Real-time deployment in tight environments is the goal.
arxiv-2510-00729:
Udhwani and five co-authors dissect an ultra-strong magnesium absorption system at redshift 1.13 in this 2025 arXiv paper on galaxy environments. A background quasar's spectrum, taken with the VLT's UVES instrument, shows absorption just eighteen kiloparsecs from a star-forming galaxy. The Mg II absorption is strong and spreads across roughly four hundred sixty kilometres per second in components. Lines from Mg I, Fe II, and Ca II appear as well.

Component-by-component ionization modelling found several clouds at solar or higher metallicity. The models predict a hydrogen column so large that the system qualifies as a sub-damped or damped Lyman-alpha absorber. The galaxy sits well inside its virial radius relative to the sightline, and the absorption lies along its major axis. The velocity spread exceeds the disk's rotation speed. The team concludes the gas mixes corotating structures with material moving outside the disk's rotation.
arxiv-2510-00929:
Sechaud, Scanvic, Barthélemy, Abry, and Tachella train image reconstruction networks without any ground truth in this 2025 arXiv paper on computational imaging. Inverse problems such as MRI and compressive sensing must recover images from too few, noisy measurements. Supervised networks win on accuracy but need clean reference images, which are often expensive or impossible to obtain. The harder setting here gives only a single incomplete observation model to learn from.

The authors define equivariance for reconstruction networks and pair it with self-supervised splitting losses. Their theorem shows the combination has, in expectation, the same minimizer as a supervised loss. Experiments covered image inpainting, accelerated MRI, and compressive sensing. The method reached state-of-the-art results among self-supervised approaches, especially with highly rank-deficient forward models. In MRI at eightfold acceleration it nearly matched supervised training. The work widens where learning-based imaging can be deployed at all.
arxiv-2510-01229:
Peshevski and co-authors train small, cheap search rerankers entirely on data that large language models manufacture. Big models rerank beautifully but cost too much to run on every query. Small specialists need labeled examples, which most domains never collect.

Their pipeline has a large model invent realistic queries from domain documents. The same kind of model then labels strong matches and tempting near-misses. Contrastive training on that synthetic diet sharpened a compact transformer considerably. Medical question data showed large in-domain gains, and the skill carried to unfamiliar domains too. Hard negatives do the teaching, since easy rejects fool nobody. Localized contrastive loss keeps comparisons focused on nearby rivals. Medical text supplied the domain where labels were scarcest. Supervision moves from humans to models, and cost follows it down. Small models stay deployable on ordinary hardware everywhere. Cheap search improves quietly.
arxiv-2510-01429:
