Khajouei and Azizi compute how bottom baryons carrying an omega configuration decay, using the sum-rule machinery of quantum chromodynamics. These heavy baryons decay weakly into charm partners, sometimes with leptons, sometimes with mesons. Measuring the transitions tests the standard model and exposes heavy-quark structure.

Three-point sum rules with operator expansions to dimension six yield the governing form factors. Those factors produce decay widths for three lepton channels and branching ratios. The same inputs then predict the nonleptonic modes with pion-like or vector emissions. Future experiments gain a complete scorecard to check against reality. Spin three-halves and spin one-half states both enter the analysis. Lepton-neutrino pairs carry the semileptonic signature. Pseudoscalar and vector mesons cover the nonleptonic emissions. Every reachable channel gets a width, not just the fashionable ones. Heavy baryons remain underexplored next to famous heavy mesons.
arxiv-2510-01529:
Fairoze and co-authors expose a structural weakness in the lightweight filters that guard commercial chatbots. Prompt guards screen incoming text for attacks, but they are kept small and cheap on purpose. The team's attack hides a jailbreak inside an encoding that the guard cannot afford to decode.

The full model downstream is strong enough to decode the payload and obey it. In tests, the method broke through the protected chat services of several major providers while keeping answer quality high. The same probing surfaced other issues, including leakage of training data and guarded text. The authors argue that defenses must police outputs, not only screen inputs. Resource asymmetry is the core insight, since guards must answer in milliseconds on every message. Upgrading guards alone cannot close a gap built into the architecture. Output checks aim at the harm itself.
arxiv-2510-01729:
Ene, Nguyen, and Vladu speed up a core fitting problem in this 2025 algorithms paper. The problem is l_p regression, which fits data while penalizing errors with a chosen power. A standard tool for it is iteratively reweighted least squares, a loop that solves weighted fits again and again. Prior fast methods were either practical but slower in theory, or fast in theory but complex.

The authors present a simpler scheme built on a primal-dual framework. Its update rule falls out of an invariant kept on the dual objective. The new method matches the best known iteration bounds from the complex theoretical algorithm. It also improves on the earlier practical method's guarantees. In experiments, their algorithms beat both that earlier method and standard MATLAB and CVX solvers by clear margins. The work closes a standing gap between practical and theoretical regression algorithms.
arxiv-2510-01929:
Gabrielli, Sestito, and Masi propose running language models in reverse to make them safer in this 2025 paper. Defenses for large language models remain fragmented compared with older classifier defenses. Their framework, Inverse Language Modeling, attacks two problems at once. It hardens models against perturbed inputs, and it grounds outputs by tracing them back to their triggers.

The idea is to invert a model's output and recover which input parts plausibly caused it. Suspicious or toxic triggers in the prompt then become visible for inspection. Experiments show the approach improves resilience against adversarial input perturbations. It also helps red teams probe models before deployment. The authors release their code publicly for other groups to build on. They frame the method as a step toward models that are controllable and trustworthy. Such grounding matters more as models graduate from chatbots into acting agents.
arxiv-2510-02129:
Reichenberg and Laue make a soccer-playing humanoid robot reliably stand itself up in this 2025 paper. In robot soccer, a fallen NAO that cannot rise is removed from play. Their stand-up routine, refined since 2019, tackles the main cause of failure: large errors between commanded and executed joint positions. Wear and tear makes those errors worse over a robot's life.

Two fixes carry the routine. Special motions free limbs that get stuck, such as trapped arms. Other joints then compensate for the errors that remain. The success rate of standing up rose significantly under this error-compensation approach. Other Standard Platform League teams adopted the same motions and saw similar gains in tournament play. Video analysis across multiple competitions backs the claim. The paper documents a rare case of a robotics trick proven in live competition rather than only in the lab.
arxiv-2510-02329:
Yoon and co-authors speed up language model replies by letting the model judge its own drafts. Their 2025 paper improves a method called speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes tokens quickly. A large target model then checks those tokens. Strict checking wastes the speedup, so judge methods relax it. Older judges needed human labels or tasks with known answers. SelfJudge trains its judge from the target model itself. It measures whether swapped tokens keep the original meaning. That score builds training data automatically for any task.

Experiments spanned a diverse set of language benchmarks. SelfJudge gave better speed and accuracy trade-offs than rival judges. Fidelity to the target model stayed high throughout. The verifier used here is a simple linear model. Stronger verifier designs remain open for later work. Faster inference with honest quality is the practical gain.
arxiv-2510-02629:
Sun and co-authors build the first gold standard test for explanations that highlight which context a model used. Their 2025 natural language processing paper targets a transparency gap. Language models answer from memory or from supplied context. Users cannot tell which source drove a given answer. Highlight explanations promise to point at the exact passages used. Nobody had checked whether those highlights are accurate. The new framework uses controlled cases with known ground truth. Four explanation methods faced four scenarios and four datasets. Five language models powered the comparisons.

One method, adapted from mechanistic interpretability work, won clearly. MechLight showed the highest utility in every scenario. Two popular methods gave no real transparency value at all. Long contexts degraded every method tested. Position bias appeared whenever two contexts competed. Explanation tools need the same rigor as the models they explain. This benchmark sets that bar for context attribution.
arxiv-2510-02729:
Wang and co-authors discover an accuracy law that bounds how well deep forecasters can ever do. Their 2025 machine learning paper studies time series forecasting. The field grows fast but lacks a finish line. Image recognition can dream of perfect accuracy. Forecasting faces a floor of irreducible error instead. Partial observability and uncertainty impose that floor. The authors trained over two thousand eight hundred forecasters. Statistical tests linked error to window level complexity. Classical predictability metrics showed no clear relationship. A clean exponential law emerged from the new analysis.

Intrinsic window complexity sets the minimum achievable error. The law exposes which benchmark tasks are already saturated. It also guides training of large time series models. Effort can flow toward tasks with headroom left. Knowing the ceiling changes research priorities field wide. Future work extends the law to multivariate settings.
arxiv-2510-03029:
Ghosh Paul, Zhu, and Bayley grade AI-written code for quality, not just correctness. Working code can still be messy and hard to maintain. Programmers call such flaws code smells. The team built an automatic test system for the job. It splits tasks by topic and difficulty into scenarios. Each scenario compares model output with pro-written reference code. Four leading models wrote Java for the tests.

Every model produced smellier code than the human baseline. The average rise in smells passed three fifths. Falcon fared least badly, and Codex fared worst. Implementation smells rose much faster than design smells. Harder tasks and advanced topics drew the worst code. Object-oriented tasks showed the gap most clearly. Model rankings also mirrored human rankings by scenario. The smell types worst in human code grew worst in model code too. Correct answers, the study warns, are not the same as good code.
arxiv-2510-03129:
Hwang and Zohren build a transformer that allocates money directly, not by forecast first. The usual pipeline predicts returns, then optimizes a portfolio. Forecast errors swell inside that second step. Worse, the forecaster never learns what the portfolio needs. Their Signature-Informed Transformer skips the split entirely. It trains on a risk-aware goal from the start. That goal is the portfolio's conditional value at risk.

Path signatures summarize each asset's recent price path. These summaries capture shape and lead-lag links between assets. A signature-aware attention block bakes those links into the model. Daily data for the S&P 100 stocks supplied the test. The model beat classic and deep rivals by a clear margin. Predict-then-optimize systems suffered most from the mismatch. Realistic trading costs did not erase the lead. End-to-end, risk-first learning is their central claim.
arxiv-2510-03229:
Chiu and co-authors test whether the equipartition shortcut for galactic magnetic fields can be trusted. The standard formula assumes equal magnetic and cosmic-ray energy. That equality rarely holds point by point in real galaxies. The team checked the formula inside a detailed simulation. The Arepo code modeled cosmic-ray transport and a multiphase medium. Synthetic synchrotron maps were compared with the true simulated fields.

The formula erred less than its broken assumption suggests. Its estimates overshot the true field by roughly a third on average. That offset held for face-on and edge-on views alike. The error depends only weakly on the local energy ratio. Edge-on views did hide a spatial bias, though. Fields in the disk were underestimated while halo fields were overestimated. Averaged profiles flipped the bias direction entirely. Face-on maps emerge as the formula's safest use case.
arxiv-2510-03429:
Ánh presents a 2025 arXiv paper in algebra on splitting free polynomials into factors. Free polynomials use variables that do not commute, so order matters in every product. The work links three tools: Cohn localizations of matrices, a Leavitt localization of a row of generators, and Jacobson quasi-inverses in rings with a topology. The object is the Fox algebra of a free group, built from Fox derivatives. Link modules, borrowed from topology, turn out to live over these algebras.

The main result builds a factorization theory for free polynomials with nonzero constant part over a field. Factorizations correspond one to one with chains of module compositions, which forces a uniqueness statement. The author calls it a first step toward a structure theory for matrices over free algebras. Such theory matters for noncommutative algebra and for the topology of links, where these modules appeared. Readers should expect dense proofs throughout.
arxiv-2510-03529:
Liang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on LapSurgie, the first system that lets a humanoid robot perform laparoscopic surgery under remote human control. Surgical robots cost millions and need special rooms, so rural and poor regions go without them. Humanoids can walk into ordinary operating rooms and use standard tools as they are. The team maps a surgeon's hand motions onto wristed laparoscopic instruments while respecting the fixed pivot point where tools enter the body.

A stereo vision console gives the operator live depth feedback during tasks. In a user study across platforms, the system matched the accuracy of the gold standard research robot kit. It also clearly beat unaided manual operation in those tests. Speed still trails the specialist platform, which the authors blame on hardware and control complexity. Cheaper, place anywhere surgical robots could narrow the care gap between rich hospitals and remote clinics.
arxiv-2510-03629:
Eris and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper introducing RawBench, a benchmarking framework for methods that analyze nanopore sequencing signals. Nanopore devices read DNA as raw electrical traces, and the conversion step, basecalling, needs neural networks and graphics processors. Raw signal analysis skips that cost but had no way to compare techniques. RawBench splits a pipeline into three parts: encoding the reference genome, segmenting the signal, and matching the representations. The authors ran comparisons across organisms of differing complexity.

Statistical segmentation methods beat the intermediate outputs of basecallers in their tests. Carefully designed context aware machine learning models surpassed those statistical methods. A pore model, Uncalled4, gave consistent quality gains across settings. Hash based matching proved the most robust choice as genome complexity grew. Portable sequencers on laptops and field kits stand to gain most from cheaper analysis. A benchmark lets new methods prove themselves against the best parts.
arxiv-2510-04429:
Schmidt and eleven coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a hidden galaxy core. A gamma ray source in the Fermi telescope catalog had no known match at other wavelengths. A candidate object sat behind the crowded center of the Milky Way, where dust blocks normal telescopes. The team used an infrared survey of that region to pick the candidate. They then took its infrared spectrum with the Gemini South telescope in Chile.

The spectrum showed emission lines from hydrogen and iron gas around the object. Those lines gave a redshift that places the source far beyond our galaxy. The line shapes and ratios match a type 1 active galactic nucleus, also called a Seyfert 1 galaxy. The find sits at low galactic latitude, deep in the zone that surveys usually avoid. The team argues that infrared work can census many more hidden active galaxies there.
arxiv-2510-04929:
Siddhartha Jain, Vishnu Iyer, Rolando D. Somma, Ning Bao, and Stephen Jordan add a new tool to quantum computing in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their tool is a quantum version of the Hermite transform. That transform rewrites data using Hermite functions, a family tied to the quantum harmonic oscillator. It can be seen as the Gaussian cousin of the Fourier transform.

The authors show the transform can run in time that grows only logarithmically with the problem size and the allowed error. The key step fast-forwards the motion of a quantum harmonic oscillator at exponential speed. With this tool, they prove quantum advantages for certain testing and learning tasks. One task checks whether a function stays close to a low-degree form under Gaussian inputs.
arxiv-2510-05029:
Rhiannon Udall and seven co-authors study a data-quality threat to gravitational-wave astronomy in this 2025 arXiv paper. Detectors such as LIGO record the faint ripples of merging black holes. Short noise bursts, called glitches, sometimes pollute those recordings. The team asks whether glitches can quietly distort measurements of black hole spin.

They inject simulated glitches and signals into the analysis pipeline. Even glitches too weak to flag left leftover power after subtraction, because the cleanup is never exact. Those leftovers, and the glitches themselves, biased spin estimates across many shapes and alignments. Bias appeared even when glitch and signal were not closely matched in phase. The authors argue for fitting glitch and signal together instead of subtracting first.
arxiv-2510-05829:
Gramaccioni and colleagues generate soundtracks for silent video with tighter semantic control. Video-to-audio models must match both timing and meaning of the footage. Separately trained encoders leave video, text, and audio embeddings misaligned. Their 2025 FoleyGRAM system aligns all three modalities jointly using GRAM.

GRAM aligns embeddings geometrically beyond pairwise cosine similarity. A diffusion model then synthesizes audio conditioned on those aligned embeddings. Waveform envelopes add precise temporal control through a ControlNet branch. The system outputs high-quality stereo audio at standard sampling rates. On the Greatest Hits benchmark, semantic accuracy advances the state of the art. Using several aligned modalities at once enriches the generated sound's semantics. Sound designers for film and games are the intended users. Accessibility tools and immersive media also benefit from automatic foley. Training stays lightweight, needing only a small dataset and modest compute.
arxiv-2510-05929:
Thejitha and colleagues prove new vanishing patterns in q-series coefficients. Certain infinite products expand into power series whose coefficients follow arithmetic patterns. Recent work found whole progressions of coefficients equal to zero. Their 2025 paper studies variants of those products modulo five and seven.

For one explicit product, every coefficient at positions five n plus three vanishes. Comparable vanishings hold across the families treated in six theorems. The proofs use q-series manipulations and the Jacobi triple product identity. Ramanujan's theta function identities supply the remaining machinery. Hirschhorn's and Tang's earlier vanishings are the direct predecessors generalized here. Vanishing progressions reveal hidden modular structure inside innocent-looking products. The results extend a research line several authors opened recently. Elementary identities, carefully combined, do all the heavy lifting. Periodicity of the coefficients is flagged as the natural next question.
arxiv-2510-06329:
Guillaume and eight co-authors simulate how a major galactic merger distorts stellar streams in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Streams are prized as dark matter tracers, yet many perturbers can dent them. What a major merger does to a whole stream population was unexplored.

The team ran collisionless N-body simulations of a Milky Way-like galaxy with thirty-six globular cluster streams. A perturber galaxy then merges with the host. They propose a metric comparing cumulative density profiles of leading and trailing tails. The merger imprints over- and under-densities depending strongly on each progenitor's orbit. Since the effect strikes streams at different times, population-averaged signatures stay detectable only about two and a half billion years. Individual wide-orbit streams, perturbed before coalescence, keep asymmetries far longer. They caution that reading dark matter from stream shapes is degenerate without the host's merger history.
arxiv-2510-06429:
Mao, Sui, Matthaiou, and Li design a hybrid detector for weak signals arriving over fading channels in a 2025 signal processing paper. Sensor networks must detect faint signals under additive and multiplicative Gaussian noise. Some sensors can send full-precision observations, while others send only quantized versions to save bandwidth.

The proposed detector fuses both observation types at a central fusion center. It is derived as a locally most powerful test from the composite distribution of the mixed data. The authors analyze its asymptotic detection performance in closed form. Sensor-side quantization thresholds are optimized for near-optimal local performance. Bandwidth allocation across sensors is then solved as a mixed-integer linear program. The formulation respects bandwidth limits and error-prone transmission channels. Simulations confirm the hybrid detector's superiority over single-format alternatives. The advantage grows in challenging, error-prone channel conditions, exactly where detection systems struggle most.
arxiv-2510-06529:
Chen and four co-authors give vision-language models image generation by reusing their understanding representations in a 2025 computer vision paper. Vision-language models understand images and text jointly, but generating images remains hard. Reconstruction-oriented autoencoders misalign the two representations. Complex bridging mechanisms add architectural bulk.

VUGEN first compresses the vision encoder's latent space. The reduced distribution stays tractable while preserving visual information. The model learns to sample in that reduced space, aligned with its understanding. A dedicated pixel decoder maps latents back into images. A VAE-free pixel diffusion decoder matched or beat complex latent diffusion decoders. Benchmarks confirm substantial generation gains. Prompt-following scores rose while COCO FID fell from about twelve to about nine. The model's original understanding capabilities remained fully preserved. Understanding-first generation avoids the trade where new skills erode old ones.
arxiv-2510-06729:
Fahimeh Khosh-Ahang Ghasr builds bridges between graph theory and commutative algebra. The 2025 paper studies simplicial complexes, which are structured families of sets drawn from a graph or similar object. Each complex carries an ideal, an algebraic object built from its facets. The question is when the ideal's generators form a tidy reduced Gröbner basis.

Ghasr characterizes the classes of complexes where that tidy basis exists. The result reproves a known fact about determinantal ideals in a special case. It also extends several results on binomial edge ideals and determinantal facet ideals. New generalizations of interval graphs and proper interval graphs support the classification. Those graph classes then power several applications. They yield examples of well-behaved Cohen-Macaulay normal rings. They also give Gröbner bases for edge ideals of proper interval graphs. Equivalent conditions for sorting certain independence complexes complete the picture.
arxiv-2510-07029:
Edward McCann, a single author, builds solvable models for exotic particles called Fock parafermions. The 2025 paper works in condensed matter theory, where parafermions generalize ordinary fermions. Each site can hold a parafermion in four possible states. Interacting versions resist exact analysis, so clean noninteracting models are valuable guides.

McCann maps moving spin-half fermions onto these four-state parafermions. The mapping yields tight-binding models whose energies stay real and readable. Total energy is a sum of single-particle levels, each weighted by an occupation number. Those levels match the levels of familiar fermion models exactly. He checks this on the Rice-Mele and Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models. The heat distribution of occupation numbers also agrees with the mapping. A parafermionic version of the Kitaev chain follows naturally. Its topological phase has a fourfold-degenerate ground state. Majorana-like edge modes carry the fourfold label, a signature experimenters could hunt.
arxiv-2510-07129:
Cechnicka and colleagues tackle a data problem in medical imaging in their 2025 paper. Doctors who study tissue samples under a microscope need many labeled images to train software. Real patient images are scarce and private. The team proposes a way to make realistic fake tissue images instead. Their method gives users close control over what each image contains.

The method first builds a simple graph for each image. Nodes in the graph stand for the main structures in the tissue. Lines between nodes show how those structures relate. A diffusion model then turns the graph into a full image. Tests used the fake images in place of real labeled patient data. Software trained on them segmented tissue about as well as software trained on real data. That result could ease data sharing in sensitive medical work.
arxiv-2510-07329:
Pestana and Brilhante borrow the logic of ant trails to watch over an industrial frying line. Their 2025 paper classifies a production system as in control or out of control. The test bed fries potato chips in two-minute cycles. Each cycle yields eight temperature readings. Each reading sequence acts as a digital ant. It lays down virtual pheromone that raises or lowers a base score for the system's health. Later sequences reinforce or erode that score.

Warning signs add a threat score on top. Extreme heat, wild swings, and detected change-points all raise the alarm level. The summed total drives real-time judgments. The case study found that costly stoppages followed stretches of moderately high heat that older rules missed. Many sequences also ran fully below the target heat, undercooking batches and hurting crispness and seasoning quality.
arxiv-2510-07429:
Wei and co-authors present BaRP, a router that learns which language model should answer each query by watching only its own choices pay off. Their 2025 paper frames routing as an online decision problem. Models differ in skill and price, and users weigh accuracy against cost differently. Offline routers cheat in training, peeking at every model's answer to every prompt. Deployment offers no such luxury: only the chosen model's outcome is ever seen. BaRP trains under that same partial feedback, using a contextual bandit over prompt features and a user preference vector.

A dial in the preference vector lets operators shift the performance-cost balance at test time without retraining. Experiments show BaRP beating strong offline routers by double-digit margins. It also edged out simply always calling the largest model. Performance held up on tasks never seen in training.
arxiv-2510-07729:
Gao and ten coauthors wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper on placing 3D objects into 3D scenes convincingly. Gaussian Splatting renders scenes fast, but objects carry their old lighting and shadows with them. Merged naively, an object clashes with its new surroundings. Fixing that needs relightable objects and good estimates of scene light. Earlier inverse rendering used slow ray tracing for the first task.

The team introduces surface octahedral probes that store lighting and occlusion around an object. Querying the probes by interpolation replaces ray tracing and at least doubles reconstruction speed. Shadows then compute in real time. For scene light, they capture a full panorama at the placement point and complete it with a tuned diffusion model. Their ComGS system renders at about twenty-eight frames per second, with vivid shadows. An edit takes well under a minute, which suits interactive design tools.
arxiv-2510-08329:
Muxi Diao and co-authors present AutoRed in a 2025 arXiv paper, a tool that invents attacks to test chatbot safety. Red teaming probes language models with crafted prompts that try to trigger harmful replies. Most methods start from seed instructions, which limits how varied the attacks can be. AutoRed needs no seeds and writes free-form adversarial prompts from scratch.

The framework works in two stages guided by invented personas. First it generates attack prompts in character, then a reflection loop polishes weak ones. A verifier scores prompt harmfulness without querying the target models, which saves time and cost. Using AutoRed, the team built two data sets, named Medium and Hard. Against eight leading models, AutoRed beat existing baselines in attack success rate. It also generalized better across models, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-08429:
Stella Dong and James Finlay build ClauseLens in a 2025 arXiv paper, a pricing system for reinsurance that cites the rules behind each quote. Reinsurance treaties shift big risks between insurers, and regulators demand auditable pricing. Current quoting is often opaque, with little record of why a price was set. ClauseLens grounds every decision in retrieved statutory and policy clauses.

The system frames quoting as a risk-aware constrained decision process, solved with reinforcement learning. Retrieved clauses enter the agent's observations, limit its allowed actions, and support written justifications. A verifier-style reward penalizes tail risk using CVaR, a measure of expected loss in the worst cases. In a multi-agent treaty simulator fitted to industry data, solvency violations fell by fifty-one percent. Tail-risk performance improved by 27.9 percent, and clause-grounded explanations reached 88.2 percent accuracy.
arxiv-2510-08529:
Xiangyuan Xue and co-authors let language model agents improve by debating each other in a 2025 arXiv paper called CoMAS. Self-evolution after pretraining is a central goal for capable agents. Recent reinforcement learning methods need dense external rewards or squeeze intrinsic rewards from a single model. Human intelligence instead grows through mutual discussion and collaboration, the authors note.

CoMAS generates intrinsic rewards from the dynamics of inter-agent discussion itself. A language-model judge turns those discussions into reward signals for each agent. Each agent's policy is then optimized by reinforcement learning, with no external supervision. Experiments showed CoMAS consistently beat untrained agents across evaluation settings. It reached state-of-the-art performance in most settings tested, the authors report. Ablations confirmed interaction-based rewards are necessary, and gains grew with more and more diverse agents.
arxiv-2510-08629:
Jort Vincenti, Metod Jazbec, and Guoxuan Xia add a dynamic expert router to visual autoregressive image generation in a 2025 arXiv paper. Visual Autoregressive Models generate images scale by scale, calling transformers repeatedly at growing resolutions. That repetition wastes compute on easy tokens and regions. Their dynamic Mixture-of-Experts router sends each token only to the experts it needs.

Scale-aware thresholding balances expert selection by token complexity and current resolution. The scheme needs no additional training of the underlying model, a practical advantage. The result is about twenty percent fewer floating-point operations than the dense baseline. Inference also ran about eleven percent faster in their measurements. Image quality matched the dense baseline despite the savings, they report. The design trades compute for quality in a controlled, adjustable way.
arxiv-2510-08729:
Sanchita Pramanik and Timir Karmakar solve for flow through a wavy channel filled with porous material in a 2025 arXiv paper. The channel walls ripple symmetrically, and an anisotropic porous medium fills the interior, so permeability differs by direction. Flow combines a steady push with a pulsatile, oscillating component. The governing model is the Darcy-Brinkman equation for flow in porous media.

Using perturbation methods for a channel narrow compared with its wavelength, they solve the problem to second order in the small parameter. Their focus is flow reversal near the wall's crests and troughs, and how the permeability ratio steers it. Under steady flow, separation near crests traps fluid in recirculating zones. Under pulsatile flow, short-lived vortices form at certain phases, bulge into the mainstream, and produce complete backflow.
arxiv-2510-08929:
Guan, Balasubramanian, and Ma adapt a popular image-generation method to work inside bounded shapes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Flow matching learns a smooth current that carries random noise into realistic samples. When samples must stay inside a convex domain, a dent-free region, mirror maps bend the flow to respect the walls. The standard bending, though, creates heavy-tailed targets, distributions where extreme values stay common, and the usual bell-curve starting noise matches them badly.

The authors fix both ends of the problem. A regularized mirror map tames the bent distribution's tails and keeps its averages finite. The starting noise is swapped for a Student-t distribution, a heavier-tailed cousin of the bell curve, which pairs better with such targets. They prove stability and convergence guarantees for the recipe. In synthetic tests on bounded domains it beat rival methods, and it stayed competitive on real constrained tasks.
arxiv-2510-09729:
Samuel Oleksak, Richard Gazdik, Martin Peresini, and Ivan Homoliak propose SNARKChain in a 2025 arXiv paper, a blockchain consensus design that does useful work. Proof of work secures permissionless blockchains but burns electricity on puzzles with no external value. Proof of useful work tries to fix that, yet many proposals fail to bind the puzzle solution to the chain and the miner's identity, leaving them insecure.

SNARKChain makes miners compute SNARK proofs, compact cryptographic proofs outsourced by clients, as the work that secures consensus. The same mechanism supports a decentralised marketplace where clients pay for proof generation. The authors say it is the first marketplace of its kind to operate at the consensus layer while meeting all the necessary properties of proof of work. Their design aims to keep the security of the original scheme while turning its energy expenditure into a service others value.
arxiv-2510-09829:
Kučera studies the wave equation on a compact interval in this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical physics. The setup adds a sharp, point-like damping term, modeled with a Dirac delta, and fixes the ends of the interval with Dirichlet boundary conditions, which pin the wave to zero there. The question is what vibration frequencies, called the spectrum, such a damped wave can have.

Kučera shows that the whole spectrum is fixed by the zeros of a single entire function, a smooth function defined on the whole complex plane. He also shows that the spectral behavior changes in a marked way at certain critical values of the damping strength. So a small change in damping near those values can reshape the allowed frequencies.
arxiv-2510-09929:
Hirsch, Jaime Fernández Fisac, and Sylvia Herbert bridge two safety frameworks in this 2025 arXiv paper on control theory. Control barrier functions keep a system inside a safe region by shaping its controller. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability instead computes which states can stay safe at all, giving conditions for safety.

The two views grew up apart, one centered on controller design and the other on analysis. The authors introduce viscosity control barrier functions, named for the viscosity solutions used to handle rough value functions in reachability theory. Their construction shows how a barrier function can carry the reachability guarantee with it. The bridge lets engineers design controllers with the stronger safety logic that reachability provides.
arxiv-2510-10029:
Yang introduces PPOPT in this 2025 arXiv paper on reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning agents usually need huge numbers of environment interactions to learn a policy. That cost blocks training in settings where each trial is slow or expensive, such as physics-based environments.

PPOPT, short for Proximal Policy Optimization using Pretraining, first pretrains the agent and then fine-tunes it with a standard policy method. The authors report strong efficiency and stability while training on very small samples. Pretraining gives the agent a head start, so fewer live interactions are wasted on basic competence. The work targets the sample efficiency problem that keeps deep reinforcement learning out of many practical domains.
arxiv-2510-10229:
Gottschling, David Iagaru, Jakob Gawlikowski, and Ioannis Sgouralis bound reconstruction accuracy in inverse problems in this 2025 arXiv paper on imaging mathematics. Inverse problems recover an unknown object from noisy measurements, as in medical imaging, radar scattering, and astronomy. They are often ill-posed, so small noise can cause large errors.

The authors derive average kernel sizes that give computable, sharp accuracy bounds for such reconstructions. Sharp means the bounds cannot be uniformly improved. Computable means a practitioner can evaluate them for a real setup, not just in theory. Knowing the best achievable accuracy before reconstructing tells users whether their measurements can answer the question at all, and how much noise matters.
arxiv-2510-10329:
Luu and Ondřej Bojar survey speech translation in this 2025 arXiv review paper. Speech translation converts spoken words in one language into text in another. Two designs compete: the traditional cascade, which transcribes speech and then translates the text, and the newer end-to-end design, which goes straight from speech to translated text.

The authors focus on how speech foundation models and large language models are being integrated into both designs. Foundation models supply strong speech representations, while language models bring fluent, knowledgeable translation. Joining them well is the current research frontier. The review organizes recent systems so builders can see where end-to-end models have caught up with cascades and where they still lag.
arxiv-2510-10429:
Sergio Da Silva and Aniya Stewart propose a new key exchange protocol built to resist quantum attacks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their tool is the universal Gröbner basis, a large structured set of polynomials tied to a mathematical object called an ideal. In their design, that basis serves as the private key. Encryption needs only a single, easier basis, while decryption needs the full universal one.

The security rests on a gap in difficulty. Building the universal basis requires computing the Gröbner fan of the ideal, which is far harder than the steps an attacker can easily perform. The authors analyze the protocol's security and the complexity of its parameters. They also give efficient recursive ways to generate the universal basis for toric ideals of graphs, a special family of ideals. Those generation methods, they note, are of interest to algebra researchers in their own right.
arxiv-2510-10529:
Vishal Subramanian, Bikash Kanungo, and Vikram Gavini present a software tool that works density functional theory backwards, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The theory, called DFT, is the most widely used method for computing material properties. It is exact in principle but relies on approximations to one key ingredient, the exchange correlation functional. Solving the inverse problem, finding the exact potential matching an accurate density, can reveal what that functional should look like.

Their open source framework, invDFT, computes these potentials from a target density alone. It uses a finite element basis that converges in a controlled way, plus corrections to the density's tail behavior. This tackles known troubles such as fake wiggles in the solution and failures to converge. The code runs in parallel on hybrid CPU and GPU machines. They show its accuracy and scaling on densities for systems up to 100 electrons, covering weakly and strongly correlated molecules.
arxiv-2510-10729:
Manas Zambre and Sarika Bobade propose a deep learning framework for detecting sarcasm in text, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Sarcasm is easy to miss in writing because tone and body language are absent. Their design is modular. It combines deep convolutional neural networks with contextual models such as BERT, and it analyzes linguistic, emotional, and contextual cues through a multi layer architecture that includes sentiment analysis and emotion detection.

The authors are candid about the stage of the work: the model remains conceptual. No trained system or benchmark results are reported. Instead, the paper argues the design is feasible. It points to uses such as chatbots and social media analysis, where misreading sarcasm can flip a message's meaning. The contribution is an architecture blueprint that joins several proven components, offered as a basis for later implementation and testing rather than as a validated detector.
arxiv-2510-11129:
Watching a video stream that runs for hours, at a steady frame rate, quickly overwhelms the fixed memory of today's video language models. Guangzhi Sun and co-authors present video-SALMONN S in this 2025 arXiv paper, a streaming audio-visual language model built for that problem. The model processes video continuously while keeping its memory budget fixed, instead of discarding or merging tokens and losing information.

The design adds a test-time-training memory module that keeps updating token representations to capture long-range links, plus a memory reader that retrieves only the stored content relevant to each prompt. The authors report the first system that handles videos longer than three hours at one frame per second and 360p resolution under fixed memory. Their 8-billion-parameter model scored 74.2 percent overall and 67.8 percent on the long split of Video-MME, beating both offline and streaming baselines on long-video benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-11229:
An insurer running several lines of business faces ruin if total claims overwhelm reserves, and heavy-tailed claim sizes make that probability hard to compute. Dimitrios G. Konstantinides studies a multivariate version of the problem in this 2025 arXiv risk theory paper. The lines share a common renewal arrival process, and the surplus is perturbed by Brownian motion, a random jitter modeling small fluctuations.

When the integrated tail of claims is multivariate subexponential, he derives an asymptotic formula for the infinite-time ruin probability. For regularly varying claims he gives a more explicit form. A notable conclusion is that the asymptotic behavior is insensitive to the Brownian perturbations: the heavy tails dominate. He also proves that a broad class of dominatedly varying, long-tailed distributions automatically has a subexponential integrated tail, which makes checking the theorem's conditions easier.
arxiv-2510-11329:
Quantum coherence, the ability of a state to sustain superposition, can depend on the basis chosen to describe it, which makes it hard to measure. Ming-Ming Du and co-authors study a basis-independent coherence measure for a free Dirac field in this 2025 arXiv quantum physics paper. They ask how that coherence between field modes behaves when the observers measuring it accelerate relative to each other through the Unruh effect.

Three results stand out. The coherence between one inertial mode and one accelerated mode decreases as acceleration grows, yet stays finite even in the limit of infinite acceleration. At zero acceleration, coherence with the second Rindler region is nonzero, unlike basis-dependent coherence, which typically vanishes there. And the coherence between the two accelerated regions stays constant whatever the acceleration, a freezing phenomenon. Together the results show basis-independent coherence is intrinsically robust under relativistic motion effects.
arxiv-2510-11629:
The first stars lit up inside small dark matter halos, and tracking them with full simulations is accurate but slow. Ryan Hazlett and co-authors extend a semi-analytic model, a fast calculation built on halo merger trees, in this 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The model follows Population III stars, the metal-free first generation, and their enriched descendants, including reionization feedback, calibrated against two hydrodynamical simulations.

The calibration uses Aeos, resolving individual early stars, and Renaissance, covering larger volumes. Matching both required raising the normalization of the critical halo mass for star formation, flattening its redshift dependence, and adding scatter to it. The model also treats the delay before enriched star formation carefully. Applied to bigger volumes, it predicts about ten Population III sources at redshift ten inside the sky area strongly lensed by the galaxy cluster MACS J0416.
arxiv-2510-11829:
Jin Ma, Ying Tan, and Renyuan Xu put a modern AI workhorse on firm ground. Generative AI models transport a simple distribution into a complex data distribution. A classical framework for such transport is the Schrödinger bridge problem, which steers random motion between two fixed endpoints. Its hard terminal constraint often destabilizes practical algorithms, especially in high dimensions. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyzes a softened version instead.

In the soft-constrained problem, missing the target exactly is allowed at a price set by a penalty function. Ma and colleagues prove that optimal solutions exist at every penalty level. As the penalty grows without bound, the soft solutions converge to the classical bridge's solutions, and they do so at a linear rate. Their tools include Doob's h-transform, Gamma-convergence, and a new fixed-point argument. These are the first convergence guarantees with hard numbers for soft-constrained bridges.
arxiv-2510-12029:
Jung-Woo Shim and three colleagues blame many AI hallucinations on the question, not the model. Users often write vague or badly structured prompts, and the model obediently answers the question it guesses was meant. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces Curative Prompt Refinement, a plug-and-play framework that treats the prompt before the big model ever sees it.

A fine-tuned small language model does the curing. It cleans the ill-formed prompt and appends an informative task description that pins down the user's true intention. No external knowledge is fetched; the fix is purely in the phrasing. In empirical studies, answers to refined prompts beat answers to the originals over ninety percent of the time. Generation quality rose while hallucination fell across the tested models. The authors pitch CPR as a cheap front door for any language model deployment, catching a whole class of errors at their source.
arxiv-2510-12229:
Raimondi and colleagues investigate whether a known human moral bias appears inside fine tuned language models, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Knobe effect is the tendency to judge harmful side effects as intentional more readily than helpful ones. The team asks whether models learn this bias during fine tuning and where inside the model it lives.

They ran a layer patching analysis on three open weights language models, swapping activations between the fine tuned and pretrained versions layer by layer. The bias did appear after fine tuning and was localized to a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, patching pretrained activations into just a few critical layers was enough to remove the effect entirely. The findings suggest that social biases in language models can be located and reduced through targeted changes, without retraining the whole model.
arxiv-2510-12329:
Mal and colleagues present DiffCrysGen, a diffusion model that designs new magnetic materials without rare earth elements, in a 2025 arXiv materials science paper. Searching chemical space for useful crystals is slow. Most design models run separate diffusion steps for atom types, positions, and the lattice, adding complexity and extra rules.

DiffCrysGen learns one diffusion process that builds complete crystal structures at once. This simpler design speeds sampling up by two to three orders of magnitude over existing methods, with no loss in the range of structures made. The team checked the new crystals with density functional theory, the standard quantum test of stability. Several rare earth free magnetic materials passed as stable and likely possible to make. They include ferromagnets with strong magnetism and large directional preference, plus metallic antiferromagnets.
arxiv-2510-12429:
Athanasiou, Mondal, and Yau prove that trapped surfaces, the hallmark of black hole formation, can form dynamically in Einstein's theory coupled to collisionless matter, in a 2025 arXiv paper. No symmetry is assumed. The system couples general relativity to a Vlasov field, describing matter as a spread of particles moving under gravity. Earlier work leaned on symmetry assumptions that real collapse does not obey.

Their large data, semi global existence theorem rests on a finely tuned hierarchy of bounds for the Weyl curvature, the connection coefficients, and the velocity moments of the matter distribution. The Vlasov field's weak integrability and smoothness are handled by rescaling key coefficients, cutting the elliptic bounds needed, and fitting a commutator calculus to the mass shell geometry. The authors call this the first symmetry free construction of dynamic black hole formation with kinetic matter. They expect the framework to simplify other stability problems.
arxiv-2510-12829:
Le Duc and Liberti report a theorem-proving experiment with large language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. During 2024 and 2025, models began solving hard contest problems, raising the question of whether they could also close open conjectures without inventing false steps. Their protocol splits the work between separate prover and verifier instances of the same frontier model.

The instances collaborate through an application interface with minimal human involvement, and every final proof is checked formally by the Lean proof assistant, software that verifies each logical step. A human confirms only that the formal statement matches its plain-language version. The protocol solved five of six problems from the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad and closed about a third of sixty-six number theory conjectures on cyclic numbers. The authors also report several newly discovered and proved theorems.
arxiv-2510-13129:
Teyssier's lecture notes survey numerical cosmology in this 2025 arXiv paper for SciPost Physics Lecture Notes. Computer simulations are central to preparing and interpreting large galaxy surveys. These notes teach the state of the art for simulating large-scale structure and galaxy formation, from dark matter scaffolding to gas and stars.

The course begins with collisionless N-body methods that solve the Vlasov-Poisson equations for dark matter. It then covers simple recipes for populating dark matter halos with galaxies, including abundance matching techniques and baryonification, which folds baryonic effects back onto the matter distribution. The final part models gas by solving the Euler-Poisson equations, examining local thermodynamic equilibrium assumptions and numerical diffusion errors. Examples show a Milky Way-like halo evolved without cooling, with cooling, and with star formation, followed by subgrid prescriptions for star formation and feedback from supernovae and black holes.
arxiv-2510-13229:
Zhang and colleagues teach recommender systems from language model demonstrations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models recommend flexibly and interpretably, but deploying one as the live policy means constant application programming interface calls with latency, hallucination, and bias problems. The authors instead extract the model's know-how offline and hand it to a reinforcement learning agent.

Inverse reinforcement learning recovers a reward model from trajectories the language model generated, with no fine-tuning of the big model itself. The reinforcement learning policy is then guided by cumulative rewards from that learned model, transferring the semantic insight in the demonstrations into a fast standalone policy. Experiments on two benchmark datasets showed the framework beating leading reinforcement learning based recommenders and in-context learning baselines. The authors release their code publicly.
arxiv-2510-13329:
Yuan, Shabani, and Liu rerank retrieved passages with cross-passage awareness in this 2025 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation splits long texts into passages for finer search. Answering may require inference across passages: resolving pronouns, telling entities apart, and gathering scattered evidence. Leading rerankers, despite using large pretrained models at high cost, still score each passage nearly in isolation.

Their reranker, EBCAR, works on passage embeddings, keeping it lightweight. It adds structure cues about how passages relate, plus a hybrid attention mechanism that captures both high-level interactions across texts and low-level links inside each passage. On the ConTEB benchmark, which stresses cross-passage links, EBCAR proved effective against leading rerankers while also winning on efficiency. The authors present embedding-level reranking as a cheaper path to evidence quality in retrieval systems.
arxiv-2510-14229:
Koki Yumoto and co-authors demonstrate that a spacecraft navigation camera with a lens aperture of only fifteen millimeters can detect planets crossing distant stars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Small satellites could reduce detection biases in exoplanet surveys, but no unambiguous exoplanet detection had been shown with optics smaller than sixty millimeters.

The team used the telescopic Optical Navigation Camera aboard Japan's Hayabusa2 asteroid spacecraft to observe transits of two hot Jupiters, WASP-189 b and MASCARA-1 b, across ten and four events respectively. Each event already showed the transit clearly, and stacking all events raised the detection strength. Transit mid-times were measured to six minutes precision and agreed with the TESS space telescope within two minutes, and the planet-to-star size ratio matched TESS closely. Combining the data updated both planets' schedules, and revealed a notable discrepancy in the previously reported orbital period of MASCARA-1 b.
arxiv-2510-14529:
Lefkir and colleagues, writing on arXiv in 2025, measure how the X-ray brightness of active galaxies flickers over time. These galaxies host feeding black holes that vary randomly from seconds to years. The pattern of the flicker, called its power spectrum, usually falls steeply at high frequencies. The point where it bends relates to the black hole's mass. Patchy observing schedules make them hard to estimate.

The team applied a method from their earlier work to fifty-six variable galaxies. The data came from the XMM-Newton and Swift space telescopes over two decades. They measured the bend in fifty sources, the largest such sample in soft X-rays. They updated the relation linking bend timescale, mass, and luminosity, using timescales from seven minutes to sixty-two days. They also found low-frequency bends in five galaxies, three of them, including Mkn 766 and Mkn 279, not published before.
arxiv-2510-14629:
Huang, Zou, Xia, and Li propose, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a recommendation assistant that remembers users and reasons about what it knows. Language model recommenders often forget earlier interactions, because their context window is limited. They also tend to reason in a single pass. Both limits weaken personalization, especially in interactive settings where tastes shift.

Their framework, MR.Rec, joins memory and reasoning in one system. A retrieval layer indexes outside information and fetches what is relevant to the current user. Unusually, the retrieval itself is guided by reasoning, not just by matching the latest query. A reinforcement learning stage then trains the model to use memory well and to refine its reasoning on its own. Across several measures, MR.Rec beat leading baselines by a clear margin in the reported experiments. The authors read this as evidence that memory and reasoning work best when each improves the other.
arxiv-2510-14729:
Talenti and a large team of co-authors demonstrate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way to sculpt how light of different colors travels through a chip-scale optical device. Controlling dispersion, the color dependence of propagation, over a broad band is a standing challenge. Their platform is aluminium gallium arsenide on insulator, a semiconductor pairing known for strong nonlinear behavior and high index contrast.

The device is a linear resonator built from distributed Bragg mirrors, layered structures that reflect chosen wavelengths. Because the effective cavity length depends strongly on wavelength, the mirrors become a dispersion engineering tool. The team applied a shape-constrained inverse design method: specify the dispersion profile wanted, then compute mirror shapes that produce it, under fabrication-friendly constraints. This is the first experimental demonstration of the technique for this purpose. Simulations and measurements agreed strongly, and the approach is presented as general for integrated optical circuits.
arxiv-2510-14829:
Hidalgo-Pineda, Gronke, and Grete simulate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how cold gas can survive being swept up by the hot winds that galaxies blow into space. Those winds shape galaxy evolution, but theory has struggled to explain why cold clouds are not simply shredded by the hot, fast flow. The team ran high-resolution three-dimensional simulations of hot outflows crossing a multiphase interstellar medium, varying how much cold gas it holds, its depth, and its clump sizes.

They identify a universal survival rule. Cold gas survives when its volume filling fraction, times the medium's depth, exceeds a critical length. The criterion generalizes the classic single-cloud condition and holds down to clumps a hundred times smaller. Surviving gas forgets its starting structure, settling into a self-similar Zipf clump spectrum. It gathers into extended plumes or confined cold shells, shaped by turbulent mixing and cooling.
arxiv-2510-14929:
Chen, Gnedin, Price-Whelan, and Holm-Hansen introduce StarStream in a 2025 arXiv paper. It is an automatic algorithm for finding the ribbons of stars that globular clusters shed as the Milky Way tears them apart. Gaia has revealed over a hundred streams, mostly spotted by eye. Traditional searches assume streams are thin and dynamically cold. Real streams vary widely with their parent cluster's mass and orbit, so visual methods find a biased subset with unmeasured reliability.

StarStream predicts where a stream's stars should sit in the space of observables, using a physics-inspired model with fewer free parameters for stream diversity. Tested on a mock stream catalog built for Gaia's third data release, the algorithm achieved purity and completeness of at least sixty-five percent for streams at high Galactic latitudes. They built it for the survey era: detection that scales in quality and quantity, with known error rates.
arxiv-2510-15129:
Lydia Brenner, Carsten Burgard, and Vincent Croft look at a data problem in particle physics in this 2025 arXiv paper. Detectors smear the events they record, and unfolding is the math that works backward to recover the true spread of the data. Known flaws in the instruments and models add uncertainty, and the team asks how best to track that uncertainty through the math.

Using the RooUnfold software toolkit, they test a new unfolding method against the standard ones. The new method puts a smoothing term, named for Tikhonov, right inside the likelihood, the core formula that scores how well a guess fits the data. A rival method applies the same term outside that formula instead. Tests on a sample problem, run with and without the flaws included, compare bias, spread, and coverage.
arxiv-2510-15429:
This 2025 doctoral thesis by Shashank Gupta at the University of Amsterdam asks how reinforcement learning can be safe, efficient, and robust when it learns only from logged user interactions. The applications are web search ranking and recommendation on one side, and text-to-image diffusion models on the other.

The first part derives a bound on ranking quality and turns it into a training objective provably no worse than the system that logged the data, even from few clicks. A robust extension keeps the guarantee under misspecified behavior models. The middle part unifies several standard estimators inside one baseline-correction framework and proves an optimal baseline choice. The final part compares two classic algorithms on diffusion models and proposes leave-one-out PPO, which matched the stronger method's quality with better text faithfulness. Gupta frames the whole as a path to reliable learning from logs.
arxiv-2510-15529:
Josh Cudby and Sergii Strelchuk launch the quantum study of a classic genomics problem: finding one string close to many others. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in parameterized complexity, where hard problems become tractable when some parameter, like the allowed distance, is small. The closest string problem and its substring variant matter for tasks like finding shared motifs in DNA sequences.

The authors present three quantum algorithms for closest string and one for closest substring. Each beats the best classical algorithm in some parameter regime, for instance when the alphabet or distance takes certain values. They also prove a conditional lower bound for the binary alphabet case. That bound matches their first algorithm's dominant scaling, showing it cannot be improved in that respect without breaking standard assumptions. Cudby and Strelchuk frame the work as a starting point for quantum parameterized algorithms, a field they argue genomics data growth makes timely.
arxiv-2510-16029:
Yasemin Kara, Stef Nomden, and Ekin Özman hunt for non-trivial solutions to a mixed-exponent Diophantine equation over number fields. The equation balances two p-th power terms against a cubic term, with fixed coefficients. Their tool is the modular method, the strategy that links such equations to modular forms and Galois representations.

Assuming standard modularity conjectures, the three authors first prove an asymptotic result for general number fields that meet an S-unit condition, and they verify that condition for several imaginary quadratic fields. They then prove an effective version for a specific family over four named imaginary quadratic fields. For each field they give an explicit bound, depending on the field, beyond which no solutions of the type studied can exist for larger prime exponents. The bounds turn an infinite search into a finite one.
arxiv-2510-16129:
Lauryn E Williams and three co-authors study Thorne-Żytkow objects. These are odd hybrid stars with a neutron star core wrapped in a huge, loose outer layer. They are still only a theory. One idea for how they form starts with a neutron star blasted sideways by its own supernova. If that kick sends it into its partner star, the two might merge into one body.

The team ran computer models of such crashes with a moving-mesh fluid code. They find the merged stars settle down and stay stable when the neutron star passes within one star radius of its partner. Past work had doubted these crashes could work at all. The result gives star modelers a sound starting point for tracking how these rare objects age and shine.
arxiv-2510-16229:
Vienna Li and four co-authors propose catching GPS spoofing by tilting the antenna. Spoofed satellite signals can mislead aircraft navigation, and simple detectors matter for general aviation and drones. Their proof of concept watches the carrier-to-noise density ratio, a signal-strength measure, while a receiver antenna is held flat, banked right, and banked left.

With a u-blox receiver and a satellite simulator, genuine signals fluctuate with orientation in ways reflecting true satellite geometry. Spoofed signals behave differently: the flat orientation facing the spoofer reads strongest, while both banked positions weaken, betraying the single ground-based source. The authors suggest brief banking maneuvers could give pilots an early spoofing cue from hardware already on board.
arxiv-2510-16329:
Jian-Jian Cheng, Jun-Ling Che, Lin Zhang, and Ming-Liang Hu give diffraction a particle-based origin story. Diffraction is the spreading pattern light makes when it slips through a narrow slit. A recent view of the double-slit experiment blames the pattern on bright states and dark states. Detectors can catch the bright ones but not the dark ones.

The team stretches that view from a few set paths to the endless modes of a single slit. They build a full detector-based basis and show the pattern comes from the photon landing in one bright mode. Spots where no light lands hold photons only in dark modes, which span an endless space. The picture unifies quantum and classical wave optics under one particle story. It also predicts fresh quantum marks in higher-order links between detections.
arxiv-2510-16529:
Kinjal Patel and Kaushal Thakkar compute a particle decay in their 2025 paper. One heavy baryon, a three-quark particle, turns into a lighter one plus an electron and a faint partner. The pair use a quark model that treats the three quarks in one shared frame. Form factors are numbers that shape how the decay rate spreads. They get baryon masses by solving a six-part wave equation on a computer.

Spin-linked terms and a mix of pull types feed that solve. Form factors come with fixes for the finite mass of the heavy quark. Those fixes go past the plain heavy-quark limit. The pair then find the decay width and branch share by spin sums. Their values are set side by side with rival model values.
arxiv-2510-16729:
Jianbiao Mei and six co-authors present IR-WM, a world model for vision-based driving that predicts only how a scene changes. Most driving world models rebuild the whole future scene, wasting effort on static background. Their model instead keeps a strong view of the present and forecasts the residual, meaning the change since the last step.

The model builds a bird's-eye view from camera input, then uses the prior view as a base for action-aware change prediction. An alignment module corrects meaning and motion drift over time. The team also tests ways to link forecasting with planning. On the nuScenes benchmark, the implicit future states improved planning accuracy.
arxiv-2510-16829:
Navreet Kaur and five co-authors ask who is really asking in a 2025 study. People often hide personal context inside their questions to chatbots. A question from a patient sounds different from one from a doctor. Most model tests ignore that hidden role entirely.

Their framework, called CoRUS, builds role-based questions from a real community. They studied posts from an online opioid recovery group. From those posts they sorted askers into patients, caregivers, and practitioners. The team then generated over fifteen thousand believable role-marked questions. Testing five models showed the same question drew different answers by role. Vulnerable askers got warmer replies but less hard knowledge. The method gives testers a fairer way to judge chatbots.
arxiv-2510-17029:
Jake Kettinger and Shahriyar Roshan-Zamir study a famous line-and-point pattern in a 2025 paper. The pattern is the Böröczky configuration of lines and multiple points. It shows extreme behavior in algebra and combinatorics. It appears in problems about powers of ideals and point-line incidences.

The authors compute a key constant for the pattern's defining ideal. That constant, the Waldschmidt constant, measures asymptotic containment behavior. They also bound the degrees of the ideal's minimal generators. Their bound comes from a weighted projective plane construction. Applying it to an elliptic curve yields a fresh counterexample. The example defeats a hoped-for containment between ideal powers. Such counterexamples guide algebraists about where general theorems must stop.
arxiv-2510-17129:
Wenbing Tang and three co-authors frame a smarter body-based agent in this 2025 paper. Large language models read and write well but lack a physical body. Agents with bodies must sense, move, and act in messy real rooms. Weak grasp of scene sense is a main block for such agents.

Their frame, called SIDE, stacks sense in layers like living minds do. Higher layers hold scene sense that guides each choice to act. The design aims for acts that fit the place and task at hand. It draws on how humans and beasts merge sense streams. The authors offer it as a step toward more able body-based agents.
arxiv-2510-17329:
Where a wandering walker first steps into positive ground is a basic question in the study of random walks. Claude Godrèche and Jean-Marc Luck give a detailed study of that first positive position for walks on a line of equally spaced points. The walker starts at the origin, moves symmetrically, and each step lands on one of finitely many whole number offsets.

Godrèche and Luck work out the full distribution of that first positive landing spot in closed analytical form. Their self contained account ties the result to the wider study of extremes and records in one dimensional walks. Readers get exact formulas rather than simulations, which makes the paper a reference for checking approximations in related problems.
arxiv-2510-17429:
Programming with tangled pointer structures is error prone, and Jin Sano, Naoki Yamamoto, and Kazunori Ueda work on a language that replaces pointers with graphs. Their language treats hypergraphs as the basic data, lets programmers operate on them declaratively by pattern matching, and uses its type system to keep those operations safe. Two gaps remained: the type system could not describe incomplete graphs, where parts of a structure are still missing, and it fell back on runtime checks during pattern matching.

Sano and his co-authors close both gaps by adding linear implication types to the language, with fresh constraints that keep the enlarged system sound. The change lets programmers write and check programs that build graphs piece by piece, a common pattern in real data structures. The paper lays out the new typing rules and the reasoning behind them.
arxiv-2510-17529:
Men with low or medium risk prostate cancer can often choose active surveillance, regular checks instead of immediate treatment, but tracking the gland across many scans is slow manual work. Yovin Yahathugoda and six co-authors build a system that outlines the prostate and its zones in each new MRI scan by leaning on the previous scan and its outline. Expert labels for these repeated scans are scarce, which limits ordinary training.

Their network, MambaX-Net, merges the new scan with the earlier outline through a cross attention module built for long range patterns, and a shape module that encodes the gland anatomy. A self training step uses outlines guessed by an existing tool, avoiding the need for expert labels. On a surveillance data set, it beat leading U-Net and transformer models.
arxiv-2510-17629:
Nicolai Gerber, with Rishabh S. Gvalani and three co-authors, studies clumping in weakly interacting particles in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their particles drift randomly on a ring while a short range attraction pulls nearby ones together. The group asks when the particles spread evenly and when they gather into clusters. The answer ties closely to sudden phase changes in a matching mean field equation, which describes the average density.

A new variant of a rearrangement inequality anchors their proofs. It shows the lowest energy states are either uniform or a single symmetric cluster. Particle clusters can merge and trade mass by diffusion. Mean field clusters cannot move, so they trade mass only. The authors model that trade and confirm it with careful simulations.
arxiv-2510-18029:
Aymane Hassini, as sole author, presents DynaQuery, a system for asking questions in plain language over mixed databases. Modern stores hold neat tables plus linked files like images and text, and questions often span both. Plain retrieval over loose text, the author argues, breaks badly when context is lost in such hybrid settings.

At the center sits an engine that reads the schema first and treats linking tables to content as a real planning step. Across several benchmarks, the structure-aware design beat the plain retrieval approach the study compares against. Database builders get a blueprint for unbound stores that keep meaning tied to structure.
arxiv-2510-18229:
Xinhao Cai, with Liulei Li and five co-authors, tackles bias in object detection in a 2025 paper. Object detection means teaching computers to find and label things in pictures. Detectors often do worse on rare or unusual objects, and adding fake training pictures can keep the same bias.

The team scores how well each group is represented, not just how often it appears. They then draw a clear visual blueprint, meaning a precise layout picture, to guide new image creation. Tests show the gap shrinks for underrepresented groups, with clear gains for large and rare objects. The approach offers a fairer way to train detectors.
arxiv-2510-18429:
Alexander Bentkamp works with Jasmin Blanchette, Matthias Hetzenberger, and Uwe Waldmann. They revise a proof method for higher-order logic. In that logic, claims can speak about functions. The old method is the lambda-superposition calculus. It proves such claims well. But two of its parts can explode in size. One part lists all ways terms can unify. The other says equal functions must act alike on all inputs.

Their new version is called optimistic. It delays the explosive unification work. It stores constraints next to the clauses instead. It solves them only when it must. The function rule is used in a narrower way. The authors prove the new calculus sound and complete. The proof uses the standard Henkin reading of the logic. No prover runs it yet. Worked examples still suggest real gains. It may beat the old calculus or usefully complete it.
arxiv-2510-18629:
Sam Kirkham and Patrycja Strycharczuk ask whether ultrasound images of the tongue can stand in for a more cumbersome speech measurement. Speech scientists model the tongue and jaw as a driven spring-like system moving toward targets, and they usually fit those models with electromagnetic sensors glued to the tongue, a setup called articulography. Ultrasound is easier to use, but its model parameters had not been checked against the sensor standard.

Recording both methods at the same time, the authors found that ultrasound produced dynamical parameters comparable to the sensor data, so the fitted spring constants and related values agreed across methods. A short-tendon tracking approach for the jaw also captured jaw motion adequately. The results support using ultrasound tongue imaging to test models of speech control, which could make such studies cheaper and more comfortable for participants.
arxiv-2510-18729:
Yhonatan Kvich and his four co-authors recover signals that were folded before recording. Modulo sampling wraps a signal into a fixed interval instead of clipping its peaks, so cheap hardware can capture huge dynamic range without losing information. Unfolding the result is hard, especially with noise and coarse quantization, and at low sampling rates.

Their network, mSQUID, unfolds a classical sparse-recovery solver into a learnable model, keeping the solver's interpretability while adding trained flexibility. A soft-quantization module teaches the model that the true signal must sit at whole multiples of the folding range away from the recorded values. Under Gaussian noise and low sampling rates, reconstruction beat rival methods, and the system separated two signals of vastly different strengths sharing the same recording. It also runs fast enough for real-time, resource-limited hardware.
arxiv-2510-19029:
Ayan Chakravorty and two co-authors use advanced first-principles calculations to decode how a family of antiperovskite materials behaves with light and electricity. These compounds are candidates for solar and light-based devices, yet their exciton and polaron behavior has been little studied because the calculations are expensive.

Across compounds built from calcium or strontium with iodine and a second element, all show direct band gaps in a range well suited to absorbing light with little loss. Exciton binding energies are moderate, favoring separation into free charges, which is what practical optoelectronic devices need.
arxiv-2510-19129:
Qiancheng Fu, Hongwei Xi, and Ankush Das present TLLC, a type theory that adds session-based concurrency to a dependent linear type system. Session types describe the shape of a conversation between concurrent processes, and adding dependency lets those protocols state properties of the messages themselves, not just their order.

With that power, programmers can relate a concurrent program to an ideal sequential version and lift correctness proofs from the simple version to the parallel one. The authors point to verified data structures such as queues and algorithms such as map-reduce. The goal is concurrent code whose correctness is built in, not tested afterward.
arxiv-2510-19229:
Juntang Wang and four co-authors present a brain-inspired clustering frame. They call it configurations. It is modeled on how infants form categories. Babies spot new things with no labels at all. They adapt as contexts change. Current machine learning finds both feats hard.

Configurations clusters data at a fixed resolution. One parameter sets that resolution. Attraction and repulsion dynamics shape the groups. The frame yields layered order and a sense for novelty. A new heatmap tool compares behavior fairly. Tests show strong novelty detection and much better stability as categories evolve.
arxiv-2510-19629:
Xavier Pritchard, Matthew Starbuck, and Wingfung Leung work out how physics beyond the Standard Model would change the early universe's equation of state, and what that means for primordial black holes. When new particles grow heavy and slow, or symmetry breaks, the primordial plasma softens. Black hole formation then jumps sharply. The team works through several supersymmetric and composite Higgs models.

Such models predict many extra degrees of freedom, and those feed straight into the equation of state. Put into abundance sums, some example black hole populations grow by up to twenty orders of magnitude. The work ties far-out particle theory to a concrete effect that telescopes might one day see.
arxiv-2510-19829:
Meghna Roy Chowdhury, Yi Ding, and Shreyas Sen present SSL-SE-EEG, a system for learning from unlabeled brain-wave (EEG) recordings. EEG is central to brain-computer interfaces and nerve diagnosis. But real-world signals are noisy and patchy, and labeling them costs a lot. Their system pairs self-supervised learning with squeeze-and-excitation networks. It turns the signals into structured two-dimensional images for deep learning.

Self-supervision pulls useful features out without labels. The excitation blocks sharpen the channels that matter and add robustness to noise. On four datasets, among them MindBigData and TUH-AB, the method reached top accuracy, scoring ninety-one and eighty-five percent on two of them. The authors pitch the approach for low-power, real-time brain-computer interfaces.
arxiv-2510-19929:
Yong-Kang Li, Yi-Ning Wang, and Jiang-Hao Yu develop a constructive heavy particle effective theory built from the nonlinear realization of broken Poincaré symmetry. Starting from a heavy one-particle state, they show that the nonlinear boost transformation reveals a shift symmetry in the coset construction. That shift corresponds to reparameterization invariance, a known guiding principle for heavy particle theories.

Using the Wigner rotation of the little group, they recover the Foldy-Wouthuysen transformation for the heavy field. At the operator level they propose a general parametrization of the boost based on symmetry alone, which links different Wilson coefficients and yields a bottom-up way to build independent operators. Extra constraints on the transformation and Lagrangian follow from the approach.
arxiv-2510-20029:
Shengyu Chen and four co-authors present BrainPuzzle, a method for imaging the brain with ultrasound sent through the skull. Bone distorts the sound badly, and full arrays of probes are hard to fit in clinical practice, so both physics-only and data-only methods struggle. Their system aims to recover an accurate map of sound speed in brain tissue.

BrainPuzzle works in two stages, first using time-reversal acoustics to form migration fragments that keep structure even with weak signals. A transformer network with a graph-based attention unit then fuses those fragments into one quantitative image.
