Tests on two synthetic datasets show better accuracy and completeness than rival approaches.
arxiv-2510-20429:
Biao Dong, Bin Cao, and Qinyu Zhang study coordination gains in integrated sensing and communication systems under a compress-and-estimate framework, where inference performance is the key metric. They characterize that performance through an error probability bound written as a monotonic function of a quantity called discriminant gain. The central question is whether designing for that gain beats the usual design that minimizes mean squared error.

Closed-form solutions for both design targets reveal water-filling structures and an explicit trade-off between sensing and communication. Numerical experiments confirm that the discriminant-gain design transmits more power efficiently, especially at low signal-to-noise ratio. It does so by sending power only to informative features and saving the rest of the power budget for sensing.
arxiv-2510-21029:
Kyle Matkovic leads eight co-authors on growing and characterizing thin solid neon films with a superconducting resonator array, work tied to a new qubit platform where electrons float above solid neon. Film uniformity is crucial, since rough or uneven neon degrades qubit quality in any scalable design.

Multiplexed microwave resonators watch the film grow, their frequency and quality factor shifts quantifying coverage across the chip. A pulsed gas deposition protocol near the neon freezing point gives controlled layer growth. The in place measurement turns a blind deposition step into a monitored process, helping labs reproduce the films these qubits need.
arxiv-2510-21629:
Lucas Rouhi and Christophe Droz tailor how waves travel through engineered lattices whose parts interact beyond their nearest neighbors. Such metamaterials can slow, stop, or reverse waves. Designing their dispersion is the hard part. Dispersion links wave frequency to wavelength. It usually needs heavy analytics, and it can demand impossible negative stiffness.

Their framework takes an interpolation approach. Instead of rebuilding entire dispersion curves, it pins down chosen frequency-wavelength points. It then solves for couplings that hit those points. Stiffness always stays positive, and the material stays passive. Demonstrations cover spring lattices and beam lattices. They create roton-like dips in the curve and tune how wave packets spread. They also sculpt decaying waves inside band gaps with chosen decay rates. The result is a practical, physically honest route to advanced sound and vibration devices.
arxiv-2510-21729:
Nathan Paull adapts small search models to specialized document collections without any human labeling. General embedding models turn text into searchable vectors. They lose their edge on niche corpora far from their training data. Company email and chat archives are exactly such corpora. Retrieval-augmented chatbots need those models most there.

His framework, CustomIR, has a large language model invent diverse queries rooted in the target corpus itself. It then verifies hard negative examples, documents that look relevant but are not. Those negatives sharpen the training signal. Fine-tuned on the synthetic pairs, small models gain up to about two points of recall at ten results. The tests use enterprise email and messaging data. The gains let small models rival far larger ones, so cheaper deployments follow.
arxiv-2510-21829:
Yi Yin and six co-authors, Yuntao Shou, Zao Dai, Yun Peng, Tao Meng, Wei Ai, and Keqin Li, tackle survival prediction when some of a patient's data is missing. Doctors increasingly combine tissue slide images with genomic profiles to estimate outcomes, but real records often lack one source or the other, and guessing the missing part can badly distort it.

Their framework pairs a compact low-rank Transformer with a flow-based generative model that reshapes one data type's distribution to match another, guided by outcome class. That produces a replacement whose statistics stay consistent with real data, while the small Transformer limits overfitting when the inputs are huge. Tests show leading accuracy both when all data is present and when parts are missing.
arxiv-2510-22829:
Will viewers remember a commercial brand later? Aleksandar Pramov, writing alone in 2025, predicts that memorability. The work is part of a MediaEval 2025 task. His system fuses visual and text features. A Gemma-3 language model forms the backbone.

Visual features come from a vision transformer. Text features come from an embedding model. Projections merge both feature types. Low rank adaptation tunes the model cheaply. Prompts add expert based rationale about memorability. A tuned tree ensemble serves as baseline. The language model system proved more robust. It also generalized better on the final test set.
arxiv-2510-23029:
Hamza Rehman, Saddam Hussain, G Abbas, and Tao Zhu ask how an accelerating black hole would change the flicker seen in X-ray binaries. Black holes in crowded places like globular clusters may be pulled by nearby mass, and that pull should shift quasi-periodic oscillations, the rhythmic X-ray signals from gas near the hole.

The team computes basic frequencies for test particles around a spinning, accelerating hole. They then apply precession, resonance, and forced models to link those frequencies to observed signals. Comparing the shifts with data offers a way to test whether real black holes carry measurable acceleration.
arxiv-2510-23229:
F D Amaro leads a collaboration of fifty one researchers characterizing parts of the CYGNO dark matter detector for low-radioactivity running. Dark matter makes up about twenty seven percent of the universe mass-energy, yet its makeup is unknown. CYGNO hunts low-energy nuclear recoils from dark matter in a gas time projection chamber with optical readout.

This report focuses on the field cage and cathode of the demonstrator now under construction. Both parts must add almost no background radioactivity, or faint signals drown. Careful material and design checks are essential before the full directional search for dark matter can begin.
arxiv-2510-23329:
Shreya Santra, Thomas Robbins, and Kazuya Yoshida test whether a navigation policy learned by deep reinforcement learning on farmland can transfer to the Moon. Robots in unstructured terrain must reach goals and avoid obstacles under uncertainty. Hand-tuned algorithms need extensive retuning for each new environment, limiting scale.

The authors train a data-driven policy through direct interaction and probe its generalization across visually and physically distinct domains. Success would mean one policy family serves farm robots and planetary rovers alike. Their feasibility study marks where cross-domain transfer holds and where it breaks.
arxiv-2510-23529:
Cláudia M. Araújo, Faustino A. Maciala, and Pedro Patrício study generalized inverses for matrices built from two families of directed graphs. These graphs are the double star and the D-linked star shapes. Generalized inverses act like partial undo buttons for matrices that cannot be inverted in the usual way, and each kind — group, Drazin, and Moore-Penrose — follows its own rules.

For double stars, the authors compute the Drazin index and give direct formulas for the Drazin inverse. They also state exactly when a Moore-Penrose inverse exists and write it out when it does. For D-linked stars, they do the same for the group inverse and handle a special singular case. The results tie the algebra of these inverses closely to the combinatorial shape of the graphs.
arxiv-2510-23729:
Ian P. A. Johnson and two co-authors simulate tidal disruption encores, a two-act version of a star being torn apart. The first act happens inside a nuclear star cluster, where a stellar-mass black hole shreds a passing star. The debris escapes that black hole but stays bound to the cluster's central massive black hole, so a delayed second flare follows.

Running hydrodynamic simulations with the moving-mesh code AREPO, the team finds outcomes hinge on the disruption geometry, the big black hole's mass, and the pair's separation. Two shapes recur: ring encores, where debris settles into a torus, and direct encores, where streams plunge straight in. Their brightness peaks on different clocks, matching freefall time in one case and an orbital period in the other. Each shape has its own brightness range, giving observers a way to probe cluster dynamics and hidden black hole populations.
arxiv-2510-23829:
Jingwang Diao and a co-author set upper limits on how much gravitational-wave energy exploding stars can emit, using LIGO and Virgo data from their third observing run. The target is the gravitational-wave background, a hum made of countless faint signals. Core-collapse supernovae are candidate sources alongside merging binaries, but the background itself is still undetected.

By cross-correlating detector outputs and accounting for the binary contribution, the authors cap one supernova's energy output. The cap is about one percent of a solar mass converted to waves, at ninety-five percent credibility. That bound is about a hundred times tighter than earlier limits from initial LIGO data. They also forecast third-generation detectors like the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer. Those machines will likely catch individual supernova events before the collective background emerges, reversing the usual order of discovery.
arxiv-2510-23929:
Emily Kim and three co-authors present TurboPortrait3D, a fast method for rendering a person's portrait from new viewpoints starting from one frontal photo. Image-to-3D avatar tools produce renderable heads but often leave artifacts, lose detail, or drift away from the person's identity. Image diffusion models make prettier pictures, yet they know nothing of 3D and cost too much time.

The pipeline runs a feedforward image-to-avatar step to get a rough 3D head and noisy renders from several angles. A single-step diffusion model then refines those renders together, conditioned on the input photo, keeping the views consistent with each other. Training first uses a large synthetic multi-view corpus, then fine-tunes on real high-quality images. The authors report their method beats the current state of the art in quality while running with low latency, a combination portrait applications have struggled to reach.
arxiv-2510-24229:
Surender Kumar and three co-authors study tiny flakes of a layered crystal and the magnetism that forms at their edges. The flakes are triangles made of molybdenum and sulfur, grown in liquid. Such small magnetic zones could one day serve in spin based devices. The team made the flakes in models with sulfur at the edges and hydrogen capping the rim. They then used first principles math to find the spin state for flakes of many sizes.

Flakes with edges below about one and a half nanometers show no magnetism. Larger flakes do turn magnetic, but more than one spin pattern has near the same energy. The magnetism is not spread out evenly. It sits in set zones near the edges. That detail will matter when engineers try to build spin devices from such flakes.
arxiv-2510-24629:
Christian Kremer and Marco Volpe move an old shape idea into a newer, more broad math frame. The old idea deals with maps that act almost like fiber maps, where each point has a neat local form. They set a fresh term for such maps that works for a broad class of spaces.

The pair give a few ways to tell when a map fits the term, and they link it to shape views. They also take a fresh look at cell like maps, a close kin of their main topic. Their proof stays in the new frame and widens a past result by Lurie.
arxiv-2510-25429: Malte Henkel and Stoimen Stoimenov predict scaling functions for systems in non-equilibrium critical dynamics, in a 2025 physics paper. Working with dynamical exponent z equal to two, they use a new time-dependent non-equilibrium representation of the Schroedinger algebra. From it they derive explicit forms for single-time and two-time correlators. They then test those predictions in the ageing of several exactly solvable models, and they report that the predictions are confirmed. The paper is a compact theoretical study for readers in statistical physics.
arxiv-2510-25629:
Dahvyd Wing and Alexandre Tkatchenko model molecular exchange-repulsion. Their 2025 paper presents a transferable force field part. It is needed in molecular force fields. Current models often need over twenty atom types. Chemical quality demands that many settings traditionally. Broadly transferable settings are hard to find.

It produces sub-kilocalorie quality for organic molecule dimers. Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and bromine also transfer well. Testing used nearly nineteen hundred unique molecular pairs. Pairs came from one hundred thirty-five molecules selected. Machine learning of electronic density is progressing recently. Their model offers a path toward accurate force fields. next-gen machine-learned force fields may incorporate it.
arxiv-2510-26029:
Michael Lau, Filippo Pecci, and Jesse D. Jenkins speed up a method that maps the range of good alternatives in large energy system models. Modelling to Generate Alternatives explores many near least cost solutions within a small cost slack, by varying investment choices while keeping operations feasible. Each variant needs a full model solve, and hundreds are typical, which makes detailed models with discrete build and retire choices far too slow by standard methods.

Lau and the team reformulate the problem with a tailored cutting plane method based on Benders decomposition, a split between a master problem and subproblems. Sharing cuts between variants and grouping objectives cut solve times in their tests, opening detailed alternative mapping to larger models.
arxiv-2510-26229:
Geert Brethouwer, working alone, studies the stability of two classic shear flows when the whole system rotates about the direction of flow. Plane Couette flow is driven by moving walls, and plane Poiseuille flow by a pressure gradient, both between parallel plates. Rotation about the streamwise axis can destabilize these flows at far lower speeds than usual, and the pattern depends on the rotation rate.

Linear stability analysis and direct numerical simulations reveal two regimes. At low rotation rate, the critical Reynolds number, the flow speed where instability starts, and the critical streamwise wavenumber grow in proportion to the rotation rate. At high rotation rate they approach fixed limits that Brethouwer reports for both flows, matching values known from spanwise rotation studies in a way he explains.
arxiv-2510-26329:
B. Bilata-Woldeyes, J. D. Perea, and J. M. Solanes run one hundred controlled simulations to trace how the brightest galaxies and diffuse light in small galaxy groups evolve under gravity alone. Galaxy groups of low mass hold a few dominant galaxies plus intragroup light, faint starlight spread between them. The simulations are cosmologically motivated N body runs, following gravity for many particles without gas or star formation physics.

Bilata-Woldeyes and the team track indicators of dynamical relaxation, the growth of diffuse light, and the mass histories of the four major galaxies and their progenitors. Early assembly is consistent with a steady Poisson merger process. Diagnostics such as galaxy separations, velocity dispersions, and the offset of the top galaxy from the group center are tested as age proxies.
arxiv-2510-26429:
Salvador Lucas studies computations that are defined by elementary inference systems, rule sets that build results step by step from basic facts. Such a system grows out of Smullyan's elementary formal systems, written in Gentzen's rule style, and its proof trees settle which claims hold. Lucas asks how to state and test broad traits of what these systems define.

He pairs each system with a first-order theory made of definite Horn clauses, and he treats traits as sentences that are true or false in a special canonical model of that theory. That model can be impossible to compute, so he shows how a trait can be proved or disproved in any other model of the theory instead. Uses include checking traits of programming languages and rewriting systems, whose runs such systems can describe.
arxiv-2510-26629:
Nir Sherf, Remi Goerlich, Barak Hirshberg, and Yael Roichman compare two ways for a wandering particle to settle down. A Brownian particle in a harmonic trap, a bowl-shaped pull, normally relaxes toward a thermal steady state. Stochastic resetting instead teleports the particle back to a chosen point at random times, a trick known to speed up searches.

Sherf and his three co-authors show resetting always settles faster than thermal relaxation, but to a different final state. One dimensionless number, built from the reset rate, the fluid's thickness, and the trap's stiffness, governs both the speed and the shape of that state. Faster settling trades against how widely the particle explores. Resetting stays faster even when the return point sits far from the trap's bottom.
arxiv-2510-26729:
Alberto Accardi and Matteo Cerutti report updates from a global analysis of parton distribution functions, the maps of how a proton's momentum is shared among its parts. Their CTEQ-JLab work focuses on deep inelastic scattering at large x, where a parton carries most of the proton's momentum. There, power corrections and nuclear effects matter most, and pulling them apart cleanly is the challenge.

Accardi and Cerutti describe how higher-twist and off-shell corrections are built into the analysis, and they show early results from the next round, CJ25. That round adds the full Jefferson Lab six giga-electronvolt data sets, gathered in a broad DIS database, plus a first look at twelve giga-electronvolt measures. They close with thoughts on how future data may untangle nuclear and partonic dynamics in light nuclei.
arxiv-2510-27029:
Morrison Rickard and M. Houssem Kasbaoui work on simulating fast turbulent flows over complex walls. Large eddy simulation resolves big swirls and models small ones, while immersed boundaries let a fixed grid handle curved walls. Blending both ideas by volume filtering the flow equations creates extra stress terms and a body force that must be modeled well to stay accurate.

The key unknown is wall-slip velocity, the apparent sliding of fluid at the wall. Two models are offered, one from a filtered classic velocity profile and one based on slip length. Checked against filtered direct simulation data for channel flow, both match well on average. Slip varies across the wall and carries marks of flow structures, while residual stress proves too large to ignore.
arxiv-2510-27229:
Ali Nour Eldin, Benjamin Dalmas, and Walid Gaaloul present BPMN-ProX, a low-code testing framework for business processes that depend on data. Business process models are widely used yet lack formal meaning, which blocks rigorous verification. Since data drive how process steps actually execute, the framework injects data handling directly into an executable form of the BPMN modeling language.

The platform couples advanced data handling with verification through state-of-the-art model checkers, giving formal guarantees while staying usable by non-technical experts. By marrying theory with practical modeling, it aims for more agile, reliable, and user-centered process management. The work shows how formal execution semantics can be packaged so domain experts and professionals can test data-aware processes together.
arxiv-2510-27529:
Valentin Fonck, Mohammadali Razeghi, and six other co-authors map heat flow inside layered computer chips in this 2025 paper. The chips are cryogenic CMOS circuits, electronics run near absolute zero for quantum machines. Stray local heat can spoil device behavior and blur qubit states. The hot spots sit buried under layers, hard to probe.

Their tool extends scanning thermal microscopy with a sideband trick: it reads the phase of traveling heat waves. Phase reveals how heat spreads from buried heaters through the stack. The maps are spatially resolved, spot by spot. With them, engineers can judge cooling designs in numbers, not guesses. The work also sets up heat checks done in place, under real cryogenic running conditions.
arxiv-2510-27629:
Boyi Wei and twelve co-authors set out best practices in 2025 for testing biorisk in open-weight models trained on life science data. Such models can speed drug and lab research, yet they could also aid harm. A common guard is to filter risky data from training. Whether that guard holds is unclear, since users can fine-tune open models, which means retraining them on new data.

Their framework, BioRiskEval, checks virus sense in three ways: sequence modeling, mutation effect forecasts, and virulence forecasts. Filtered knowledge can in some cases return fast with fine-tuning, and it can spread in sequence tasks. Dual-use clues may also sit in shared model parts. Tests like these help judge if guards truly cut risk.
arxiv-2511-00229:
Rajsekhar Mohapatra, Alankar Dutta, and Prateek Sharma simulate the diffuse gas that wraps around galaxies, known as the circumgalactic medium. A key puzzle is how much of that gas stays cold and dense instead of hot and thin. The team runs detailed turbulence simulations of small patches, guided by quasar light observations, and resolves the cooling length that sets cold gas behavior.

Density makes the difference. Thin gas cannot hold cold clouds for long, because mixing destroys them faster than they cool. Denser patches settle into a steady mix where up to half the mass is cold but fills only about one percent of the volume. Cutting a small box out of a big simulation, they warn, distorts the mixing and gives wrong answers.
arxiv-2511-00329:
Masoud Makrehchi argues that ethics goes wrong when it judges acts one-to-one. On platforms, a single public act spreads: each share exposes new people, and small harms or goods can multiply across a network. He builds a minimal message-passing model where an act's tone spreads hop by hop, shaped by exposure, salience, compliance, and how long the spread runs.

The model yields a simple multiplier that compares network impact with the one-to-one baseline. A threshold separates three regimes: spreading that fades, spreading that grows in a straight line, and spreading that explodes. Platform design choices, from reach to friction on sharing, move that threshold. Uses range from vaccine campaigns to curbing harmful norms, wherever downstream responsibility needs a number.
arxiv-2511-00629:
Alexander Abanov and Boris Khesin tour infinite-dimensional systems with nonholonomic constraints, the rolling-without-slipping rules that make dynamics subtle. In finite size, the two kinds of dynamics, nonholonomic and vakonomic, both arise as limits of ordinary systems with friction-like loss. A skate gliding on an inclined plane makes the split plain in a classical, concrete way.

The endless-dimensional menagerie includes subriemannian and Euler-Poincaré-Suslov systems on Lie groups, the Heisenberg chain, and the Camassa-Holm equation of shallow water fame. Also featured are a nonholonomic Moser theorem, fluid approximations, parity-breaking fluids, and transport-born solutions of Burgers-type equations. The tour ends with a car pulling endlessly many trailers, whose limit becomes a Chaplygin sleigh dragging a string, governed by an endless-dimensional distribution.
arxiv-2511-00829:
Olivier Geoffroy and David Saint-Martin document the second version of ARP-GEM, a global atmospheric model able to run at kilometer scale resolution, as fine as about one kilometre per grid cell. Their focus is how the model behaves over several years at slightly coarser resolution, with and without parameterized convection.

Parameterized convection is a stand in for storms too small for the grid to resolve directly. Simulations without it resembled runs with very strong entrainment, the mixing of outside air into rising plumes. Results suggest the stand in still shapes the average climate at kilometer scale, while finer grids help capture variability. The authors conclude a trade off remains, and still finer resolution may be needed for clear added value.
arxiv-2511-01229:
Yuanhao Feng and colleagues make the Shapley value practical for power systems. The Shapley value divides costs or responsibilities fairly among participants by averaging each one's marginal contribution, but computing it exactly explodes combinatorially, which kept it to small systems. Their test case is allocating carbon emission responsibility across a power network.

Their framework, SurroShap, pairs efficient coalition sampling with deep learning surrogate models that cheaply evaluate what each coalition would emit. They prove time averaged allocations converge to within a stated tolerance of the exact values. On nine systems, up to nearly two thousand entities, the method finished inside real time operational windows. It ran ten thousand to one hundred thousand times faster than other sampling methods. Year long simulations on a Texas sized grid confirmed real world use.
arxiv-2511-01529:
Murali Sridharan and five colleagues study self-admitted technical debt, the notes programmers leave in code comments confessing to shortcuts and known flaws. Earlier research mostly hunted and ranked these confessions; this team asks a different question: what kind of code surrounds them?

Working from the PENTACET dataset, with comments drawn from more than 9,000 open-source Java projects, they linked over 225,000 debt comments to the statements around them. Debt clustered in inline code near definitions, conditionals, and exception handling, exactly where developers face uncertainty and trade-offs. The authors read this as a deliberate signal of awareness during change, not simple neglect, which changes how maintenance teams might use the comments.
arxiv-2511-01629:
Tristan Millet and Erwan Liberge simulate fluids flowing around rigid bodies with the lattice Boltzmann method, a scheme that moves particle distributions across a grid. The hard part is forcing the fluid inside a solid region to move exactly with the body, without tracking the interface with extra machinery.

Their constraint penalization method extends the fictitious domain idea: a penalty term applied directly to the fluid velocity field enforces rigid-body motion, so no Lagrange multipliers or explicit interface forces are needed. The lattice Boltzmann algorithm keeps its locality and simplicity, and the fluid-solid coupling becomes implicit. Numerical experiments reproduce rigid-body motion and hydrodynamic interactions accurately at minimal extra cost, demonstrated on particle sedimentation from a simple case upward in complexity.
arxiv-2511-01729:
G. Fichet de Clairfontaine, M. Perucho, and J. M. Martí chase the source of an extraordinary neutrino, event KM3-230213A, detected by the KM3NeT telescope at energies near 220 PeV. Where astrophysical neutrinos are made remains unsettled, but evidence increasingly points at relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei.

Assuming protons are accelerated at shocks, the authors work out the proton distribution and the energy budget the event demands. Three flaring candidate galaxies sat inside the error region at the time; the results favor PMN J0606-0724, which showed a strong radio flare matching the neutrino's arrival. In their picture, a red giant star crossing the jet injects the baryons. Infrared photons from the dusty torus then set the extreme energy scale. The star's own light would yield neutrinos of only about 1 to 10 PeV.
arxiv-2511-01829:
Joshua Barrow and six colleagues compare the two ways to hunt one of the rarest hypothetical events in physics. It is a neutron turning into an antineutron. That change would violate baryon number. One approach watches free neutrons in a beam; the other watches enormous detectors for the annihilation that follows a conversion inside a nucleus, a sign of matter instability.

Translating the strong intranuclear limits into free-neutron terms traditionally relies on nucleus-specific estimates. Those estimates say how the medium suppresses conversion. They are computed in mean-field theory, under a single-operator assumption. The authors warn that this suppression can be scenario-dependent, shifting the translation by several orders of magnitude and blinding searches that trust it blindly. They call for a broader phenomenology program for the transition, akin to those built for electric dipole moments, before next-generation searches commit.
arxiv-2511-01929:
Qingyue Long, Can Rong, Tong Li, and Yong Li tackle a data problem in city science: how to create fake human travel records that still behave like real ones. Real trajectory data, the paths people take through a city, serve planning, traffic, and health work. Yet real records raise privacy risks, cost much to gather, and often have quality flaws.

Earlier generators mostly copy single person movement patterns. They miss how the spread of a whole population, shifting across districts over time, shapes each person's trip. The team's diffusion model adds that missing piece. A spatial graph strengthens links between places. A denoising network built to sense population spread learns the patterns of movement in space and time. In tests, the fake trips matched real ones on key statistical measures, beating the best prior methods by more than half.
arxiv-2511-02029:
Duc Tran, Dung Truong, and Duy Le defend a federated optimization task against its own participants. Submodular maximization picks a small subset that best represents a huge dataset, a workhorse for summarization and data selection. In the federated version, clients hold the data locally. Each has its own view of a fair sample. The server repeatedly aggregates their local computations. The arrangement respects privacy. But it invites sabotage, from malicious clients feeding fake information.

Their solution, RobustFSM, is built to withstand a range of practical client attacks, which differ from ordinary federated learning backdoors because of submodular maximization's structure. Tests on real-world datasets show a clear pattern. Under severe attacks, RobustFSM's solution quality far exceeds the standard federated algorithm's. The improvements depend on dataset and attack scenario. They reach as high as about 200 percent.
arxiv-2511-02229:
Aditi Sengupta, Santosh Kumar, and Sanjeev Kumar map how air or fluid flows past a spinning cylinder as the flow speed rises. The problem is tied to the Magnus effect that curves spinning balls and can drive ships. Holding the rotation rate fixed and high, they varied the Reynolds number from one thousand to six thousand in fine steps. They solved the compressible flow equations with high-fidelity numerical methods across 101 cases and a million core-hours of computing.

For moderate speeds, rotation-driven circulation cuts pressure drag, but at higher speeds the boundary layer thins, separation is suppressed, and the benefit saturates. A critical Reynolds number near 5,650 marks a change in the global behaviour of the Magnus effect, beyond which the wake turns dynamically unstable and forces fluctuate sharply. A neural network trained on the simulation data reproduces lift, drag, and instability onset in a fraction of the time.
arxiv-2511-02329:
Shaohan Li, Yunpeng Shi, and Gilad Lerman estimate where every camera was when a set of photographs was taken, a core step in three-dimensional reconstruction. Doing this globally and robustly is hard because mismatched image pairs act as outliers. Their method, Cycle-Sync, builds its location solver from message-passing least squares, a technique borrowed from group synchronisation, and reworks it to emphasise cycle consistency: information that agrees around loops of cameras.

Cycle consistency is redefined using distance estimates from earlier rounds, and a robust loss function damps the outliers. The authors prove the strongest known deterministic guarantee for exact recovery of camera locations, showing cycle consistency alone reaches the lowest known sampling requirements. An outlier rejection module borrowed from robust subspace recovery plugs in for extra protection, and experiments on synthetic and real data beat leading estimators, including full pipelines that use bundle adjustment.
arxiv-2511-02529:
Masataka Watanabe, a theoretical physicist, points out an unexpected identity between two-dimensional quantum gravity and the statistics of a growing interface. Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity is the workhorse toy model of quantum gravity, and the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation describes how rough surfaces grow. Watanabe connects them through two better-known systems: the double-scaled SYK model, whose Schwarzian limit captures the gravity side, and the weakly asymmetric exclusion process, whose fluctuations obey the growth equation.

The claim is precise. The path-integral measure that defines the Euclidean evolution between two end-of-the-world branes in the gravity theory is exactly the stationary measure of the KPZ equation on an interval with Neumann boundary conditions. Correlation functions match as well. Correspondences of this kind matter because each side's hard questions can sometimes be answered with the other side's tools.
arxiv-2511-02829:
Alex Takeda proves a structural property of a certain dioperad, an algebraic object that encodes operations with several inputs and outputs. The dioperad in question encodes bialgebras with a product, a coproduct of a shifted degree, and a rank three cyclic tensor, all obeying a deformed form of the balanced infinitesimal bialgebra rule. His 2025 paper shows this dioperad is Koszul, a strong duality property.

The proof studies special subcomplexes of the assocoipahedra built by Poirier and Tradler. Those parts match a class of special differentials on the complex projective line, which Takeda calls cloven Strebel differentials. The geometric picture controls the shape of these parts. That control forces key cohomology groups to vanish, which is what the Koszul property requires.
arxiv-2511-03029:
Kajol Kulkarni and seven colleagues report how a European exascale project learned to measure the energy its simulations burn. Supercomputing faces rising power bills as machines grow. Their 2025 paper shares the CEEC project's experience across major European systems, reviewing ways to measure energy and the metrics worth reporting, then testing real fluid flow codes.

Four programs ran on machines including LUMI, MareNostrum5, MeluXina, and JUWELS Booster, on both standard and graphics hardware. The team compared the energy a job used against the time it took. Graphics hardware and mixed precision math cut energy use while keeping results accurate. The authors urge centers to make energy data easy to gather, so users can act on it rather than guess.
arxiv-2511-03229:
Yong Huang and co-authors present U-Print, a method that can identify smartphone users just by watching encrypted Wi-Fi traffic. Earlier attacks could tell which app was open, but they could not tell who held the phone. U-Print works passively, reading frames in the air without joining the network at all.

People favor different apps and tap through them in different ways, and those habits leave distinct traffic patterns. U-Print reads those patterns with tailored neural networks, then groups behavior traces to name the user. In tests across three real settings, it reached high accuracy for user guesses and also named most apps and actions correctly. The result shows how much private habit can leak from traffic that looks locked.
arxiv-2511-03929:
NVIDIA, credited as the collaboration name in the arXiv record, introduces Nemotron Nano V2 VL, a vision-language model aimed at document understanding, long video comprehension, and reasoning. It succeeds an earlier eight-billion-parameter Nemotron vision-language release and claims gains across vision and text domains.

The model builds on a hybrid Mamba-Transformer language model and adds token reduction methods that raise throughput on long documents and video. Architecture, datasets, and training recipes all changed from the prior version. Checkpoints are released in three numeric formats, and large parts of the datasets, recipes, and training code are shared, making the release unusually open for a corporate model report.
arxiv-2511-04329:
Jonas Berx, writing alone, studies optimal lossy compression of a fluctuating stochastic signal into a few discrete readout states. The signal drives transition rates of a two-state system. The encoder must trade retained mutual information about the system's state against a fixed encoding cost, tracing a Pareto frontier between the two.

Genetic algorithms map those optimal trade-offs numerically. Fronts are concave in places and show convex intrusions split by first-order transitions in the best protocol elsewhere. A high-rate expansion finds a universal cube-root law for optimal threshold density, mixing the prior with Fisher information. Non-Gaussian signals can beat Gaussian stand-ins outright, needing fewer states for the same information.
arxiv-2511-04429:
Pablo Gómez and three colleagues built Cutana, a tool for cutting small images from huge sky surveys. The Euclid mission's first quick release holds thirty million sources over about sixty-three square degrees. Later releases will reach petabyte scale, and older tools cut one source at a time.

Cutana pulls batches of cutouts at once using fast array operations. It schedules work to fit the memory at hand and runs locally or in the cloud. Output can be saved as FITS or Zarr files, with several common ways to scale brightness. In tests on the Euclid data, it beat the standard Astropy tool in every case.
arxiv-2511-04529:
Kalyan Banerjee and two colleagues construct imaginary biquadratic fields with large class groups. Class groups measure how far a number field sits from unique factorization. Finding whole families where that failure is large is a delicate task.

The team builds two distinct families, each with infinitely many members. Elliptic curves and their quadratic twists produce the first family. The second mixes elliptic and hyperelliptic curves in its construction. Key inputs come from results by Soleng and by Banerjee and Hoque. Infinite families like these give number theorists firm ground for testing claims about class group growth.
arxiv-2511-04629:
Saswata Mandal and his co-author propose pair mixing as the source of time-reversal breaking in a layered superconductor. Experiments on 4Hb-TaS2 and related hybrids show spontaneous breaking, hinting at chiral superconductivity. Yet its transition temperature matches plain forms that show no such signal.

Their state mixes a dominant conventional s-wave pairing channel with a weaker chiral p-wave one. A finite Cooper-pair momentum couples the two channels together. Symmetry analysis, statistical mechanics, and quasiclassical theory support the picture. Pair mixing could explain exotic signals appearing without any change in the basic transition temperature.
arxiv-2511-04729:
Rucha Deshpande leads nine authors hunting shape artifacts in synthetic medical images. Synthetic data can ease data scarcity for training clinical models. Unexamined fakes, though, may carry distortions that hurt performance and real-world use.

Their knowledge-based detector works in two stages. A new feature extractor studies angle gradients along anatomical boundaries in each image. An isolation forest then flags images whose shape features look abnormal. Tests on two synthetic image sets show the method catches network-made shape flaws. Screening synthetic data this way could stop quiet artifacts from reaching clinical model training.
arxiv-2511-05029:
Sakiko Obuchi and co-authors report ID830, a radio-loud quasar at redshift 3.4 that shines bright in X-rays. It is the most X-ray bright radio-loud quasar found in the eROSITA final survey field of the equator.

Data from radio, infrared, and optical bands show a dust-red quasar with a steep X-ray slope. From a magnesium line width, the team weighs its black hole at a few hundred million solar masses. Its glow hints at an Eddington rate above the norm, which may mark a short shift phase in how such black holes feed.
arxiv-2511-05829:
Somnath Dutta leads a large team using the ALMA observatory to rank three very young protostars by age. Jets from protostars reveal how far star formation has run in each core. The team picked the three sources with the shortest jet timescales, marking them among the youngest known.

They mapped several molecules and dust emission at two resolutions, tracing where molecules freeze out or boil off the dust. One source shows a warm envelope and signs of a more advanced stage. Another has no dense central structures, suggesting it is younger. The third, with a cool envelope and compact emission, looks youngest of all. Comparing the three orders the earliest steps of star birth.
arxiv-2511-05929:
Jiaxuan Li and co-authors speed up masked autoencoders, a self-teaching method where an image model hides part of an image and learns to rebuild it. Random hiding works well but takes many training rounds, and the vision transformer inside uses its parameters poorly because every layer keeps one fixed resolution.

Their system, CoMA, hides image parts in a complementary pattern so every pixel gets sampled evenly across rounds. A new hierarchical transformer varies its attention windows dynamically, cutting parameters and compute while learning finer detail. Pretrained on a standard image set, their model matched the usual approach using only a small share of the training rounds. Each round also ran faster, which the authors cite as proof of better learning per step.
arxiv-2511-06329:
Fei Li and Junjie Cao compare three supersymmetric models to see which can naturally host light dark matter. The candidates are the minimal model, its Z3-symmetric next-to-minimal extension, and the general next-to-minimal model. All must satisfy limits from dark matter abundance, the LUX-ZEPLIN 2024 experiment, Higgs data, and collider searches.

Only the general model naturally fits dark matter lighter than one hundred giga-electronvolts, with a mainly singlino-like candidate. Its advantage is separating the interactions that set the relic abundance from those governing direct detection. Two mass orderings are studied; one allows a light higgsino scale with little tuning, while the other needs a much heavier scale and more fine-tuning.
arxiv-2511-06529:
Hongnan Ma and co-authors generate counterfactual explanations for decisions made on multivariate time series. A counterfactual shows what minimal change would flip a model's verdict, but time series explanations built by swapping in chunks from other examples often look unrealistic. Generative alternatives fix realism yet hug the decision boundary, so a small model change can void the explanation.

TriShGAN works inside a generative adversarial framework with triplet loss added for distance learning. Explanations stay close to the original series, resemble the desired outcome class, and keep a safer margin from the boundary. A shapelet extractor picks the most telling segments of the series, keeping the suggested changes sparse and readable.
arxiv-2511-06629:
Changfeng Gui and co-authors prove that fully localized solitary waves of the three-dimensional capillary-gravity water wave problem are conditionally stable. These waves sit in finite depth under strong surface tension and were built by a non-variational reduction method, so they are not energy minimizers. Standard stability machinery, which leans on minimization, cannot be applied directly.

The proof adapts the Grillakis-Shatah-Strauss framework through Mielke's approach to bridge the gap between the well-posedness space and the energy space. Spectral analysis of the linearized dynamics does the core work, supported by careful handling of the Hamiltonian structure set by the energy and momentum functionals. Orbital stability follows under the stated conditions.
arxiv-2511-06829:
Zhun-Yong Ong studies how sound-like vibrations, called phonons, travel through a chain of atoms whose masses vary randomly because of isotopic defects. In such a disordered chain, repeated scattering normally makes transmission fall off exponentially with distance. Ong asks whether the placement of the defects, rather than their number, can change that fate.

Using the static structure factor as a guide, he gives a systematic recipe for arranging defects to suppress or enhance scattering inside a chosen frequency window. Numerical tests show transmission rising toward transparency or dropping toward opacity in that window, confirmed by changes in how localized the vibrations are. The idea may extend to layered substances built to pass or block heat-carrying vibrations.
arxiv-2511-07129:
Seungeon Lee, Soumi Das, Manish Gupta, and Krishna P Gummadi make collections of LoRA adapters usable on inputs whose domain is unknown in advance. LoRA fine-tunes large language models cheaply, but each adapter is trained for one task, while real traffic spans many domains. Current ways to combine adapters at inference time need labeled data or extra task-certain training, which is expensive at scale.

Their system, LoGo, is training-free: it selects and merges adapters per input instance. It uses signals from a single forward pass through the adapters to judge relevance and set each adapter's contribution on the fly. Across five NLP benchmarks, twenty-seven data sets, and three model classes, LoGo beat training-based baselines on some tasks by up to 3.6 points and stayed competitive elsewhere, without sacrificing inference throughput.
arxiv-2511-07329:
Yash Mittal, Dmitry Ignatov, and Radu Timofte generate neural network designs from fractal templates instead of searching for them expensively. Neural design search is powerful but computationally heavy. Their FractalNet system defines a structured space of convolutional networks through recursive fractal patterns, systematically varying fractal depth, column width. Layer configurations, with a generator producing candidates, a template module enforcing the recursive multi-path structure, and a runner handling training and logging.

Over twelve hundred distinct designs were generated and tested automatically on the CIFAR-10 image benchmark, trained in PyTorch with mixed precision and gradient checkpointing. Fractal designs trained stably and performed competitively, averaging sixty to seventy percent validation accuracy with a peak above eighty percent after only five epochs. The authors pitch recursive structure as an interpretable, resource-efficient route to design exploration.
arxiv-2511-07529:
Subhash Bose and colleagues report a rare supernova with no visible home galaxy. Supernova 2021hem is a Type Ia event, the kind used as cosmic distance markers. Its peak brightness and missing second infrared hump match the overluminous 2003fg-like subclass, which breaks standard patterns.

Slow light curves and early carbon absorption lines support that label. A fireball fit dates first light about sixteen days before peak, yet a detection came even earlier than the fireball rise. That early glow does not fit companion or surrounding gas interaction. Shallow or hidden hosts remain possible. Odd cases like this test explosion models.
arxiv-2511-07729:
Neil Sehgal, Hita Kambhamettu, and Sai Preethi Matam design mental-health chatbots with Indian teenagers, not just for them. Stigma and scarce professional help shape how adolescents seek support. A survey of three hundred sixty two teens plus fourteen interviews map their habits and wishes.

Teens report low shame about themselves but high social stigma around them. They prefer typing to voice, carry smartphones widely, yet rarely use mental health apps. Privacy, emotional warmth, and local content matter, while current bots lack personalization. A design-tensions framework names the trade-offs builders must balance, offering guidance grounded in lived teen experience.
arxiv-2511-07829:
Manu Sebastian, Sreenath Balakrishnan, and Safvan Palathingal engineer culture dishes whose stiffness cells can feel changing live. Cells respond strongly to substrate mechanics, but standard tunable dishes cannot change traits mid-experiment. Compliant parts offer a switch instead.

A compliant switch flips the substrate between positive and negative Poisson response, with size of effect that can be set. Stiffness between two points can switch from near zero toward set limits. Living cultures could then experience varied mechanics in one run. Dynamic substrates open experiments on how cells react when their world changes under them.
arxiv-2511-07929:
Yihang Wu and Ahmad Chaddad federate a vision-language model across hospitals without pooling patient scans. Medical image models need diverse data, but privacy law and ethics bar central collection. Federated learning trains locally and shares updates, though hospital data differ and vision-language models are heavy.

FedMedCLIP adapts CLIP for federated medical classification with a masked feature adaptation module that trims communication and compute. Heterogeneous scanners and populations are the explicit target. Resource-efficient federation matters because many hospitals run modest hardware. A shared model that respects both privacy and budgets could bring advanced image classification to smaller clinics.
arxiv-2511-08029:
Aarush Sinha, Pavan Kumar S, Roshan Balaji, and Nirav Bhatt improve biomedical search by mining hard negative examples from citations. Retrieval models learn best when near miss documents are clearly marked as wrong answers. In medicine those near misses are hard to spot by similarity alone, since related papers look alike.

Cited papers share context with a source paper without being duplicates, so they make natural hard negatives. Using citation links from twenty thousand PubMed articles, the team fine tunes small GTE retrievers. The models gain on in domain and out of domain tests, including long tailed topics, with little extra training.
arxiv-2511-08129:
Giovanni Romano and Raffaele Barretta offer a critical review of basic ideas in continuum mechanics, the theory of soft materials. Landmark mid century volumes by Truesdell and his partners set the field language, and their depth earned wide respect. The authors argue that this respect shielded several delicate basic notions from the careful checking they needed.

Followers, they contend, spread unsatisfactory formulations through the later literature. A missing engineering viewpoint made the problem worse. Using a geometric approach in four dimensional Euclidean spacetime, Romano and Barretta aim for clarity in notions, methods, and results that the usual approach cannot reach, and they catalogue errors they find.
arxiv-2511-08329:
D-M Mei and co-authors design a germanium based detector that could sense low mass dark matter through tiny phonon signals. Their phonon to charge transducer joins a slow phonon crystal region with radio frequency quantum point contact readout, cooled to four kelvin. A calibrated collection model folds together guiding, survival, and detection of primary phonons to give corrected energy thresholds in a very low range.

Background estimates use nanosecond timing gates and frequency band power windows. A one hundred gram module, under standard halo assumptions, projects sensitivity to dark matter scattering on electrons and nuclei below cross sections reached before. Heavy and light mediator cases are both covered, with systematic uncertainties and a staged path to larger exposures.
arxiv-2511-08529: Andrew Li and Hua Wang count colored compositions in which only some parts may receive colors, with the allowed colors depending on where a part sits in the composition. A composition is an ordered way of splitting a number into parts, and coloring adds a further layer of counting choices. The authors obtain the counting sequences through generating functions. They also discuss connections to many other combinatorial objects, supplying combinatorial arguments for those observations and generalizing them beyond the cases first noticed.
arxiv-2511-08629:
Jian Guo and four co-authors study online learning for systems that report only binary outcomes, where an attacker may tamper with the data stream. Offline methods cannot keep up with live control loops, so the team builds recursive estimators that update with each new observation.

A first-order gradient method handles the basic case, and a second-order quasi-Newton method converges faster without needing persistent excitation, a condition feedback systems rarely meet. Versions cover both known and unknown tampering strategies, and the estimates are proven to converge almost surely. The second-order method extends to adaptive control with a stated tracking error bound. Simulations and a vehicle emission control test confirm the methods resist tampering and sharpen detection of excess-emission events.
arxiv-2511-08929:
Q. Qian and five co-authors write simulation code for next-generation laser-plasma work. Their particle-in-cell algorithm tracks the spin of particles and the polarization of light inside strong-field quantum electrodynamics. The newest laser facilities accelerate particles to near light speed within microns and push fields toward the quantum critical limit.

The extension, built into the OSIRIS framework, resolves QED emission processes by spin and polarization. It does not average over them. That matters because the coming experiments aim to measure exactly those traits. The authors lay out the theory, then describe how the code was built and checked. Only ab-initio modeling this complete can capture the coupled electromagnetic, relativistic, and quantum processes at once.
arxiv-2511-09029:
Leonie Böhlke and two co-authors map how listeners perceive concert room acoustics without asking them for words. Instead of rating scales, music is convolved with measured binaural room impulse responses, and listeners judge similarities between the results, letting multidimensional scaling reveal the hidden axes of perception.

Five perceptual dimensions emerge from the scaling. Each one lines up with a measurable acoustic quantity: echo density, fractal correlation dimension, roughness, loudness, and early decay time. The method sidesteps two older habits, matching measures to experts' memories of halls and hunting correlates for bipolar rating scales. Because the dimensions come from the listeners' own similarity judgments, the authors present the approach as a cleaner route to what audiences actually hear in a room.
arxiv-2511-09129:
Jordan Moncrieff and four co-authors ask whether the gas discs around feeding black holes in galactic centers can marry two black holes of wildly unequal mass. The gravitational wave event GW190814 paired a twenty-three solar mass black hole with a companion under three solar masses, a ratio isolated binary evolution struggles to produce.

Suites of N-body simulations, coupling a self-consistent disc torque model with a regularized code carrying post-Newtonian terms, map the outcomes of encounters inside active galactic nucleus discs: captures, mergers, and resonant dances. Analytic models then tie capture and merger rates to local disc properties across all mass ratios. Capture probability follows a log-Gaussian law in a single governing parameter, the ratio of libration time to resonance crossing time. A low-luminosity galactic nucleus turns out to be a plausible birthplace for GW190814 itself.
arxiv-2511-09229:
Valery V. Ryzhikov studies weighted averages along flows in ergodic theory, the mathematics of systems that mix over time. He considers homothetic averages and more general weighted ones for dynamical flows. The work sharpens a result of Kozlov and Treshchev on nonuniform averages for ergodic flows.

Ryzhikov allows absolutely continuous convolutions of singular weights, widening the averaging schemes covered. From these convergence results he defines a notion called almost mixing, stated through homothetic weighted averages. He gives an example of a flow that is almost mixing without actually mixing. He also proves that rigid flows, which periodically return near their start, are never almost mixing.
arxiv-2511-09329:
Andreas Konstantin Kruff and four co-authors release Sim4IA-Bench, a benchmark suite for judging how well user simulators imitate real searchers. Simulation promises cheaper evaluation of search systems, but the field lacked shared measures and data. The suite grows out of a shared task at the Sim4IA workshop held with SIGIR 2025.

The dataset holds 160 real search sessions from the CORE search engine. For 70 sessions, up to 62 simulator runs predict the user's next query or utterance, split across two tasks. The suite also introduces a new measure for scoring next-query predictions. Beyond benchmarking, it supports studies of query reformulation, intent drift, and interaction-aware retrieval evaluation.
arxiv-2511-09729:
Qian-Ze Zhu, Paul Raccuglia, and Michael P. Brenner teach one neural model to emulate many partial differential equations, including equations it never saw in training. Numeric PDE solving is costly, and learned surrogates usually specialize in one equation with fixed settings. Their approach instead conditions the model on a vector encoding the equation's terms and coefficients.

Four modeling methods are compared as baselines, trained on a family of 1D equations from the APEBench suite. The approach performs strongly on held-out parameter values. It stays stable beyond the training time window and extends to an entirely unseen equation, they report. Data and code are public, supporting a broader push toward automated scientific software.
arxiv-2511-10029:
Jiangshu Du, Wenpeng Yin, and Philip Yu propose ScaleFormer, a plug-and-play way to give pre-trained encoder-decoder transformers a long memory. Standard self-attention grows quadratically with length, which blocks long documents, and efficient variants usually demand new architectures plus costly retraining. ScaleFormer instead cuts a long input into overlapping chunks and builds a compressed, context-aware representation for the decoder.

Its fusion trick is parameter-free: each chunk's boundary representations are enriched with cumulative context vectors gathered from every chunk before and after it. That gives the model a sense of the document's overall flow while keeping complexity linear. On long-document summarization the method proved highly competitive with, and often better than, state-of-the-art systems, without architectural changes or external retrieval.
arxiv-2511-10329:
Sunil Chandra, Pankaj Kushwaha, Pranjupriya Goswami, and Michael Zacharias dissect more than a decade of multi-wavelength data on the blazar CGRaBS J0211+1051. They hunt the origin of its high-energy emission. Two major gamma-ray flares, in 2011 and 2019, came with brightness in other bands, yet some optical outbursts had no gamma-ray counterpart. The source's X-ray spectrum is unusually soft for its class, and its ultraviolet and optical spectrum does not extrapolate cleanly into X-rays.

Modeling four broadband spectral energy distributions in quiet and flaring states, purely leptonic scenarios struggled against the steep optical-ultraviolet shape. Lepto-hadronic models fit better. The hadronic reading makes the blazar a candidate neutrino emitter and potentially bright above ten TeV, a test bed for multi-messenger jet physics.
arxiv-2511-10429:
Wouter Jongeneel writes on attractors in dynamical systems, the sets toward which a system's motion settles over time. When attractors are compact, several rival definitions agree and the theory is fairly complete. Without compactness the picture blurs, and basic structural questions about closed attractors have stayed open.

Jongeneel characterizes when a closed, asymptotically stable attractor is a strong deformation retract of its domain of attraction. In plain terms, the whole basin can be continuously shrunk onto the attractor without tearing. The result works on locally compact metric spaces and needs no compactness of the attractor itself. It is meant to support a deeper structural study of feedback stabilization problems, where such attractors arise naturally.
arxiv-2511-10529:
H. Thankful Cromartie and seven co-authors report fifteen years of radio timing of the millisecond pulsar PSR J1231-1411, gathered with the Nançay and Green Bank telescopes. The pulsar is a prime target for the NICER X-ray telescope, and weighing it precisely would help reveal what neutron star interiors are made of.

The team targeted specific orbital phases to catch the Shapiro delay, a relativistic slowdown of pulses passing near the companion star. Both frequentist and Bayesian analyses give relatively weak mass constraints, around 1.9 solar masses for the pulsar with wide uncertainty, though the orbital inclination is pinned down much more tightly. Capping the allowed pulsar mass lowers the estimate somewhat, and the authors draw lessons for future high-precision mass campaigns.
arxiv-2511-10829:
Mikhail Masliaev, Dmitry Gusarov, Ilya Markov, and Alexander Hvatov test whether neural operators, models that learn to solve whole families of partial differential equations, can be pretrained once and transferred widely. Training these models is expensive, and transformer-based versions had previously been applied only to specific problems.

The team studies a general transfer learning setting: pretrain on simpler or mixed problems, then fine-tune elsewhere. Their experiments cover extrapolation to unseen physical parameters, absorbing new variables into a problem, and transfer from datasets containing several equations at once. The results show advanced neural operator designs can indeed carry knowledge across different PDE problems effectively, a step toward all-purpose operators that do not start from scratch for every new physics task.
arxiv-2511-11029:
Özgür Akgün, Mun See Chang, and their colleagues tackle wasted search in solvers that work with abstract structures such as nested sets. Modelers write problems in high-level languages, but solvers need those structures recast in simpler forms first. Many problems also contain symmetries, and breaking them early can speed the search by a vast amount.

Standard symmetry breaking adds order rules that pick one member from each symmetric set. For abstract types, that route creates a huge number of complex rules that run poorly. The authors show a new partial method that breaks such symmetries in a better way. Their aim is faster solving without losing the gains symmetry breaking brings.
arxiv-2511-11529:
Luisa Mao and three co-authors introduce SPACER, a method that builds terrain costmaps telling off-road robots which ground is cheap or costly to cross. Good costmaps must handle new terrain types and also let operators re-rank surfaces quickly when a mission changes, two strengths earlier methods rarely combined.

SPACER trains on synthetic data to generalize to unseen ground, then adapts at test time through a scaled preference context that a user supplies. Tests on large aerial maps show it can reweight terrain costs on demand without retraining. For field robots in farming, rescue, or exploration, that mix of flexibility and reach could matter a great deal.
arxiv-2511-11929:
Ghani Imadouchene builds a symmetric bimetric cosmology, a universe described by two metrics at once, one leaning anti-de Sitter and one de Sitter, coupled through a scalar field. Bimetric gravity doubles geometry to enrich cosmic dynamics while hoping to keep the standard model's successes.

Starting from Einstein-Hilbert terms for both metrics plus an inter-metric potential, modified Friedmann and Klein-Gordon equations govern the pair. In the symmetric effective-fluid limit, the model reproduces the standard cosmology's main behavior with one small dynamical correction that fades with redshift, and Vainshtein screening keeps local gravity tests satisfied. The construction is offered as a minimal extension worth calibrating against data.
arxiv-2511-12029:
Nicholas Tetteh Ofoe, Weilun Wang, and Lei Wu determine how short a forecast horizon a battery operator can get away with. Model predictive control of energy storage re-plans constantly under volatile prices, and the plan is only as good as the price forecast, yet longer horizons cost computation and compound forecast error.

A trajectory-alignment definition sharpens the question: the minimum horizon is where every rolling decision matches the full-horizon global optimum. Their algorithm finds it exactly, where earlier methods gave only sufficient conditions and could ignore inconsistencies between successive control actions. Tests use real price data from a bidding zone. Storage assets earn money on timing, and knowing the shortest sufficient lookahead is money.
arxiv-2511-12329:
Arman Pourghorban and Dipankar Maity study a target defense game where intruders arrive one after another and a single defender must stop as many as possible. Both sides move with Dubins dynamics, meaning they turn like a vehicle with a minimum turning radius. Each intruder tries to breach the target perimeter, and the next appears at a random point on a circle once the last is caught or breaks through.

The defender's ending spot in one round becomes its start in the next, linking the rounds. The authors split each round into partial and full information phases. They use Dubins paths and guarding arcs to judge capturability. They then estimate capture rates for finite and endless sequences. Random trials check those rates.
arxiv-2511-12529:
Sanchaita Hazra, Doeun Lee, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder and Sachin Kumar run a randomized trial. It tests the value of AI help in scientific writing. That task demands precision, synthesis across modes and domain skill. The test focuses on writing abstracts. Experts are split into author and reviewer pools in a mock conference setup, with incentives that push authors to edit drafts to publishable quality.

The design varies two factors: whether the draft abstract was written by a human or a model, and whether that source is disclosed. Authors edit human drafts most, compared with undisclosed model drafts, guided in part by the higher perceived readability of model text. Once the source is revealed, editing effort converges across conditions.
arxiv-2511-12629:
Shiyun Lin studies learning in housing markets, the classic matching model where each agent starts owning a house and holds private preferences over all houses. The goal is an allocation in the core, where no group can all do better by trading among themselves. The model is widely studied, but usually preferences are assumed known.

Lin places the market in a multi-player bandit framework, where agents learn their preferences from random rewards over repeated rounds. A new measure, core regret, captures the market objective for each player. Both centralized and decentralized learning approaches are analyzed, with logarithmic regret bounds proved for each, and a matching lower bound for the decentralized case showing the rate cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2511-12729:
Amirhossein Hassanzadeh and four co-authors build an uncertainty workflow for land surface temperature maps from the Landsat satellites. Current Landsat temperature products use a single-channel method, and their stated uncertainty is often too large because it leans on a cloud mask that flags clear pixels as cloudy. From Collection 3, a split-window method will produce the temperatures instead. That change needs its own uncertainty estimates, and this paper supplies them for Landsat 8 and 9.

Their workflow ties uncertainty to total precipitable water, the moisture in the air column. Since Landsat cannot measure that quantity directly, they train an XGBoost model to infer it from Landsat's thermal bands, using a MODIS product as reference, and reach high accuracy. Standard error propagation then turns the moisture estimate into per-product uncertainty. The result is a dedicated uncertainty chain matched to the new split-window temperatures.
arxiv-2511-12829:
Michael Chen and five co-authors run a controlled comparison of how particle physics foundation models should learn. Rival training objectives compete in the field, but they are usually tested inside rival systems, so wins are hard to attribute. Here one transformer encoder for particle clouds, one preprocessing pipeline, and one jet classification dataset are held fixed. Contrastive objectives, both supervised and self-supervised, masked particle modeling, and generative reconstruction are then trained under the same regimen and judged by one evaluation protocol.

The study separates what the objective contributes from what the surrounding machinery contributes, and it reports each method's strengths and limits. Targeted supervised changes to the architecture reached state-of-the-art benchmark scores. The authors offer the setup as a reference point with reproducible baselines, so future base-model work in particle physics can show cleaner progress.
arxiv-2511-12929:
Z.-H. Peng and twenty-eight co-authors present observations of supernova 2016iog, one of the fastest-declining Type II-L supernovae known. Their photometry and spectroscopy track the explosion from near peak, about fourteen days after it blew, through late phases. The supernova faded unusually steeply after a bright peak, and its early spectrum was a nearly featureless continuum, a sign that the blast was already crashing into material around the star. Broad hydrogen lines persisted throughout.

A late spectrum showed a double-peaked hydrogen feature, pointing either to dust forming in a cool dense shell or to unevenly distributed circumstellar material. The team argues the whole picture fits a red supergiant star wearing a low-mass hydrogen envelope, wrapped in thin surrounding gas that the supernova kept hitting. The study adds a well-documented extreme case to the small family of fast-declining hydrogen-rich supernovae.
arxiv-2511-13029:
Declan Jackson and three co-authors grade frontier language models on knowing, and on knowing that they do not know. AA-Omniscience asks six thousand questions drawn from authoritative academic and industry sources across forty-two economically relevant topics in six domains. Its Omniscience Index runs from minus one hundred to one hundred, jointly penalizing hallucination and rewarding abstention when uncertain, so a model that guesses wildly scores worse than one that stays silent. Zero means a model is right as often as it is wrong.

The results are humbling. Claude 4.1 Opus topped the ranking at four point eight, and only three models scored above zero at all. Leadership also changed by domain, with three different labs' models leading the six areas. For knowledge-critical work, choose models by domain performance and calibration, not reputation. .
arxiv-2511-13129:
Julien Marché and Seokbeom Yoon connect two invariants that knot theory and quantum topology each compute in their own language. Their objects are two-bridge knots, a tractable family labeled by two integers, and the adjoint Reidemeister torsion of such a knot, evaluated at parabolic representations. The authors establish an explicit formula relating that torsion to the Frobenius algebra. That algebra governs the signatures of the vector spaces produced by SU(2) topological quantum field theory at a root of unity.

Two applications follow. First, the sum of the inverse torsions is constant for every two-bridge knot. Second, along sequences of roots of unity of a certain form, the TQFT signatures behave asymptotically exactly as the Verlinde formula predicts. Such bridges let results proved on one side be spent on the other.
arxiv-2511-13229:
Mary Chriselda Antony Oliver and 3 co-authors extend Laplace learning, a graph-based method for learning from few labels, to the Wasserstein space of distributions. The move takes a tool built for flat finite spaces into an endless-dimensional setting. Their work rests on the view that high-dimensional data often lie near much lower-dimensional shapes.

The authors prove that a discrete graph energy tends to its continuum form as data grow dense. They also describe the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a submanifold of the Wasserstein space in clear terms. Tests on benchmark data show steady classification results in high dimensions, which supports the theory behind the extension.
arxiv-2511-13329:
Shufan Yang and 7 co-authors present RegionMarker, a watermarking scheme that protects text embedding services from theft. Such services sell access to embeddings for language tasks, but attackers can copy the model by querying it. Older watermarks blocked only some attacks and left providers exposed on other fronts.

RegionMarker hides marks inside trigger regions of a low-dimensional space reached through a secret projection. Because the mark fills the whole region and uses the embedding itself, paraphrase and dimension attacks struggle to erase it. Broad tests on several datasets showed the scheme resisted varied removal attacks while still flagging copied services, guarding provider income.
arxiv-2511-13529:
Máté Gedeon and 5 co-authors release two Hungarian speech datasets built for spontaneous and conversational recognition. Speech technology thrives on large corpora in major languages, while Hungarian lacked natural talk and dialogue data. Both sets come from unprocessed parts of the existing BEA Hungarian corpus.

BEA-Large adds hundreds of hours of spontaneous speech from hundreds of speakers with rich segment labels. BEA-Dialogue holds tens of hours of real conversations split so speakers never cross between training and test parts. Baselines with public models reach their best word error rates on repeated speech, while true conversation stays much harder. Diarization baselines are also reported for future work.
arxiv-2511-13629:
F. Acerbi and 296 co-authors sharpen the search for low-mass dark matter particles with liquid argon in the DarkSide program. Argon detectors read dark matter recoils through ionization, and the response at low energies sets how light a particle they can catch. Their analysis joins new ReD setup measurements with calibration data from DarkSide-50, ARIS, and SCENE.

The combined data pin down atomic screening effects inside the Thomas-Imel recombination model far better than before. Feeding the improved response back into the DarkSide-50 analysis produced stronger exclusion limits, now world-leading for particle masses in the low giga-electronvolt range. Updated projections for the coming DarkSide-20k detector show a much stronger discovery reach.
arxiv-2511-13829:
Yi-Neng Zhou, Robin Löwenberg, and Julian Sonner describe a simpler way to make a quantum system act truly random. Their method lets a system evolve under one random Hamiltonian, then switches it once, at a chosen time, to a second random one. That single switch breaks leftover patterns that stop steady chaotic motion from reaching full randomness.

The resulting set of operations closely matches the ideal random benchmark known as a unitary design, yet needs only one control step. The authors also show the switch time gives a practical way to measure the Thouless time, a marker of chaos. Possible uses include randomized measurements, benchmarking of quantum devices, and tomography.
arxiv-2511-14029:
Kristoffer Eggestad, Marc Vila, Sverre M. Selbach, and one co-author show that crystal twin boundaries can switch on a spintronic effect that symmetry normally forbids. The effect, nonrelativistic spin splitting, is prized for next-generation devices but usually appears only in specially constrained magnets. Using density functional theory and transport calculations, the team studies two oxide materials with natural domain walls.

In both a perovskite oxide with ninety-degree walls and a layered delafossite oxide with several wall angles, twin boundaries paired with ferromagnetic walls produced spin splitting like that of d-wave altermagnets. Tight-binding models show how the effect scales with domain size and density. The authors pitch twin boundary engineering as a broad design route.
arxiv-2511-14229:
Jim Broadbent, Felix Cohen, Frederik Hvilshøj, and two co-authors present EBind, a lean way to bind the embedding spaces of different senses into one. Their recipe uses a single encoder per modality and leans hard on data quality, training a competitive joint model on one GPU in hours instead of days. The model spans image, text, video, audio, and 3D at under two billion parameters.

Training mixes three sources: millions of automatically assembled five-way matched sets, a million human-judged triples marked negative, partial, or positive, and millions of pre-existing captioned items. Across thirteen evaluations the small model beat rivals several times its size. Code, weights, and data are open-sourced, along with a new audio-to-3D classification benchmark.
arxiv-2511-14729:
Antonio Alarcón and Franc Forstnerič prove that the flaws of a conformal minimal surface can be smoothed away without tearing the surface. A minimal surface behaves like a soap film, and its flaws here are branch points, where the surface folds on itself, and certain complete ends of finite total curvature. The surface starts from any open Riemann surface and lands in ordinary space.

Their theorem says an isotopy, a gradual deformation through surfaces of the same kind, removes all such points and ends. The same result holds for null holomorphic curves into complex space. Removing flaws by deformation is a strong flexibility statement, useful wherever minimal surfaces are built to order.
arxiv-2511-14829:
Takatoshi Ko, Ryosuke Hirai, Taiga Sasaoka, and Toshikazu Shigeyama explain a puzzle in Pa 30, the leftover cloud of a supernova seen in the year 1181. A fast wind blows from the central white dwarf and slams into surrounding material, lighting a shock front. The size of that shocked region says the wind began centuries after the explosion, not right away.

The team proposes that fallen-back carbon-rich debris slowly gathered on the dwarf and ignited late, switching the wind on. Matching a delay of several centuries requires a fairly hot core left over from the blast. The result supports the picture of Pa 30 as a rare Type Iax remnant with a surviving star.
arxiv-2511-15029:
Zekun Wang and Sashank Varma ask whether computer vision models develop geometric and numerical concepts in a child like sequence. Vision models trained only to classify images still form internal concepts similar to adult human concepts. The new question is developmental: does improvement during training mirror how children progress? A detailed case study centers on a standard deep network.

For geometry and topology, training stages align with child development for some concept classes. Numerical concepts are examined in the same developmental frame. Alignment is partial, not universal, which itself is informative. The work links machine learning curves to cognitive development data. It suggests training dynamics can serve as a model for studying concept growth.
arxiv-2511-15129:
