Kimikazu Taniguchi settles a derivation dispute inside boson expansion theory, a method that rewrites nuclear motion in terms of boson-like phonon excitations. Practical calculations keep only some phonons and map the physics into that smaller subspace. Whether that subspace map truly follows from the full-space map was muddled by older treatments that simply dropped the ignored phonons' effects.

Using the recent norm operator formulation, which accounts for the ignored phonons properly, Taniguchi shows the subspace map does follow once their contribution is correctly renormalized. A long-standing confusion is also corrected: when the ignored phonons contribute nothing at all, the subspace map is just the full map with those modes discarded, nothing more.
arxiv-2511-15529:
Yifei Gao and three co-authors solve decentralized classification for teams of autonomous underwater vehicles that must map communication success. Underwater acoustic links suffer short range, multipath, and low bandwidth. Vehicles need a shared map of where communication will work, built in real time. Each vehicle only sees its own success and failure events.

The main contribution is a rigorously derived policy for which readings to share. Sharing a chosen subset balances map quality against scarce bandwidth. Real acoustic data from Virginia Tech vehicle teams validate the policy experimentally. The approach lets a robot team learn its communication environment cooperatively. Better maps support planning for subsea missions where surfacing to communicate is impossible.
arxiv-2511-15729:
Alexander Povolotsky derives recurrence relations for k-fold nested sums of integer powers. Nested sums again and again apply partial adding up to classic Faulhaber polynomials. The final functions generalize well studied power sums. Povolotsky gives an direct recurrence linking one nested sum to sums of lower power and higher nesting level.

The identity flows from a core algebraic relation among binomial weights in the sum form. Links are drawn to a 2010 paper on nested sums by Butler and Karasik. Equivalence to a related recurrence for hypersums by Cereceda is also discussed. Such recurrences let nested sums be worked out and analyzed recursively. The note tidies connections between several strands of combinatorics literature on power sums.
arxiv-2511-16329:
Mélanie Bertelson, Pranav Chakravarthy, and Sheila Sandon prove global rigidity results in locally conformal symplectic geometry, a loosening of symplectic geometry where the defining form may rescale from place to place. Their tools are generating functions for Lagrangian submanifolds of twisted cotangent bundles, used to define spectral selectors.

From those selectors the authors build a bi-invariant partial order and an integer-valued metric on groups of locally conformal symplectic Hamiltonian maps. They also define an integer-valued capacity for domains. The capacity yields a non-squeezing theorem in the spirit of the contact result of Eliashberg, Kim, and Polterovich: certain domains cannot be squeezed into narrower ones. The paper also introduces essential Lee chords and translated points, and proves such points always exist for the maps studied.
arxiv-2511-16529:
Xuemei Gu, Carlos Ruiz-Gonzalez, and Mario Krenn derive an exact formula for two-mode squeezing, a core operation that creates entangled photons, in the photon-number basis. Standard low-gain approximations and Gaussian methods can hide how individual photon-number amplitudes interfere, especially inside nonlinear interferometers run at high gain.

Their closed-form expression gives the action of the squeezing operator on any pair of number states, so interference can be analyzed directly at arbitrary squeezing strength. Within that framework they give physical readings of several known interference effects. They also predict a new multi-photon interference phenomenon in a four-crystal geometry that should be easy to observe in the lab. The result is a compact toolkit for designing quantum sensing and state generation setups.
arxiv-2511-16629:
Shihab Ahmed, El Houcine Bergou, Aritra Dutta, and Yue Wang propose reward profiling, a plug-in fix for the instability of policy gradient reinforcement learning. Gradient estimates in these methods are noisy, so returns improve unreliably and convergence crawls.

Profiling wraps any policy gradient algorithm and updates the policy only when a high-confidence estimate says the new policy is genuinely better. Theory shows the wrapper does not slow the baseline method's convergence, and with high probability it delivers stable, monotonic improvement instead. Profiling was tested on eight continuous-control benchmarks from Box2D and MuJoCo/PyBullet suites. It reached near-optimal returns up to one and a half times faster. It also cut return variance by up to a factor of about one and three quarters on some setups.
arxiv-2511-16729:
Vijay Balasubramanian, Hanzhi Jiang, and Simon F. Ross track how multiparty entanglement evolves in time in chaotic quantum systems, using the membrane theory of entanglement dynamics. Single-region entanglement measures miss the richer patterns that scrambling creates among several regions at once.

Different multiparty signals behave in qualitatively different ways, reflecting distinct kinds of entanglement pattern. The dynamics show discontinuities that mark phase transitions in the entanglement structure itself, stretches of transient and non-monotonic behavior. There are also periods when a region's extensive entanglement is entirely multipartite, shared among all parties rather than held pairwise. The results, aimed at chaotic systems and holographic conformal field theories, give a sharper picture of how quantum information spreads and hides during scrambling.
arxiv-2511-17729:
Yang Zhou, Mingyu Zhao, Zhenting Wang, and six co-authors introduce a benchmark for multimodal agents that use tools through the Model Context Protocol. Real tasks often need many steps, linked tools, and both images and text, with results carried from one step to the next.

Their M3-Bench spans many servers and more than two hundred tools, with checked task paths built by an executor and judge process. A matching method lines up tool calls one to one so scores stay auditable. Tests of leading models show clear gaps in argument accuracy and workflow consistency.
arxiv-2511-18029:
Dylan M Paré and thirty-five co-authors study magnetic fields inside large gas filaments near the centre of our galaxy. The galactic centre is an extreme zone holding dense gas and dust in a region called the Central Molecular Zone. Using data from the ACES survey with the ALMA telescope array, the team picks out filaments traced by a specific molecule. They compare the direction of the magnetic field with the direction each filament runs.

Field readings come from two other observatories working at longer wavelengths. The measured angles span a wide range, which points to varied local conditions shaping the filaments rather than one ruling process. The team also compares the real data with synthetic views from a magnetic simulation of the region, to judge which formation stories the observations support.
arxiv-2511-18329:
Shohei Tanaka, Atsushi Hashimoto, and Yoshitaka Ushiku map the layout of science posters. A poster sums up a study in one sheet, and tools that read its order and parent child links can present it well on screen. Papers have drawn most layout work so far, while posters, with freer designs, have drawn little.

The team build SciPostLayoutTree, a set of about eight thousand posters marked with read order and layout links. It holds more hard cases than past sets, like up ward, side ways, and long range links. Their reader model joins image cues with box place and type, and picks the best tree by beam search. The set and model push poster reading toward paper grade tools.
arxiv-2511-18829:
Kanav Arora, Girish Narayanswamy, Shwetak Patel, and Richard Li study how to shrink heart rate models for wearables without losing their skill. Watches and trackers estimate heart rate from optical pulse signals, and deep models do this well, but the devices impose strict memory and speed limits. The team explores knowledge distillation, training a small student model to copy a large teacher, across four strategies from hard and soft copying to feature-based teaching.

They sweep teacher and student sizes in a grid and chart the scaling laws that link model size to accuracy for each strategy. The characterisation shows where shrinking is nearly free and where it starts to cost. For health device makers, such maps guide how small a model can go before heart rate estimates degrade in daily use.
arxiv-2511-19229:
Selena Song and six co-authors give video generation models a memory of how the world behaves. Diffusion transformer models now make sharp, coherent video, yet they often break basic physics and common sense. Experiments here show these models can be steered through their hidden states, and simple filters split low-level appearance from high-level physical and semantic cues.

Their encoder, DiT-Mem, turns reference videos into a compact set of memory tokens using stacked 3D convolutions, filters, and self-attention. Only the encoder is trained, on a modest data set, while the video model stays frozen. At use time the memory plugs into new models and guides generation toward more plausible motion.
arxiv-2511-19829:
Ke Chen, Yifeng Wang, Hassan Almosapeeh, and Haohan Wang tackle a weak point in prompt engineering for large language models. Good prompts are often judged and improved in separate steps, so the scores rarely guide the edits well. Their work links the two steps at the level of each single query, or user request.

They combine several prompt quality measures into one evaluation framework and train an evaluator that scores a prompt from its text alone, with no need to run the model. Those scores then steer targeted, readable prompt edits. The evaluator predicts prompt performance with high accuracy, and the full method beats earlier approaches on eight benchmark datasets with three different language models.
arxiv-2511-19929:
Oleg Viro studies complex slices, a special kind of real algebraic variety. Start with a real variety and its complex points; a complex slice is where the real points meet a complex subvariety in a transverse way. Such slices carry a natural orientation and represent an integer cohomology class, so they sit at a crossroads of geometry and topology.

Viro gives a test for when a codimension-two projective variety is a slice: exactly when it is the base of a pencil of real algebraic hypersurfaces. He also proves an upper bound for the linking number of a real projective curve that bounds inside its complexification together with such a slice. The results pin down the structure of these special varieties.
arxiv-2511-20229:
Ruffing, Petrov, Zillien, and Wendzel fingerprint malware hiding inside DNS traffic. Their 2025 paper applies locality sensitive hashing to covert channels. Malware abuses DNS lookups to chat with control servers. The hidden data rides inside subdomain names. Spotting traffic is easier than naming the culprit.

Subdomain sequences are hashed into similarity features. Similar inputs land in similar buckets by design. A random forest classifier reads those features. It separates malware families from benign traffic. It also infers what the malware is doing. Uploading, downloading, and idling leave distinct patterns. Accuracy beat prior approaches across several datasets. False positive rates dropped markedly at the same time. Modified and unseen malware samples were still caught. That robustness matters as malware mutates constantly. Idle traffic with low variance stays hard, they admit. Extra timing or meaning features may close that gap. Forensic attribution gains a practical new tool.
arxiv-2511-20329:
Haqq-Misra, Kopparapu, and Profitiliotis plan how to spot alien industry using Earth's own futures. Their 2025 paper maps technosignature searches onto ten Earth scenarios. The scenarios project our tech future a thousand years ahead. Each is self-consistent, spanning different development paths. Future telescopes need concrete targets to design against.

The Habitable Worlds Observatory opens the stepwise strategy. It could catch a carbon dioxide plus nitrogen dioxide pair. That pair signals burning and heavy industry. Up to eight of ten scenarios show it detectably. Radio follow-up could find directed narrow-band beacons. Two scenarios include such transmissions. The LIFE interferometer would probe mid-infrared fingerprints. CFC features appear in four scenarios there. One adds a fluorinated gas triple marker. Farm gases form a detectable triple in two scenarios. A solar gravitational lens mission could image surfaces. Flying a probe out remains the conclusive option.
arxiv-2511-20729:
Sean Bin Yang and five colleagues present in 2025 a tutorial survey of trajectory foundation models, a young field adapting the foundation-model idea to movement data. A trajectory is a timed sequence of positions, the digital trail left by a person, vehicle, or animal. Researchers now want the same train-once flexibility for trajectory tasks like travel-time estimation and path ranking.

The tutorial runs as a 90-minute lecture in four parts, from basic definitions through data types and learning methods to open problems. It sorts methods by data type: raw GPS points, map-matched road segments, grid-based paths, and mixes adding text or images. Learning approaches range from contrastive methods, which teach models by comparing similar and dissimilar paths, to augmentation schemes that manufacture extra training views. The authors close with challenges around building models that are robust, responsible, and transferable, the systematic map the field lacked.
arxiv-2511-20929:
Anton Baychkov, Markus Brill, and Jannik Peters ask in 2025 how much total welfare a famously fair budget rule must sacrifice. In participatory budgeting, citizens vote on projects and the Method of Equal Shares splits the budget evenly among voters, letting groups pool their shares to buy projects they approve. Fairness can cost efficiency: the chosen bundle may please fewer people overall than a greedy pick. The authors derive minimum welfare guarantees for the rule.

The guarantees cover DNS satisfaction functions, including the two standard utility measures: total cost of approved projects funded, and their count. Bounds depend on the cheapest and priciest projects, and collapse to the known multiwinner guarantee when all costs are equal. The bounds are asymptotically tight among rules meeting a strong proportionality axiom, so no fairer-style rule can promise more welfare. With wildly varying costs, they also show, no meaningful guarantee exists for any rule.
arxiv-2511-21029:
Kaixing Yang and colleagues present in 2025 FlowerDance, a music-to-dance generator built for speed as much as beauty. Diffusion-style dance models need many sampling steps, leaving no compute headroom for high-fidelity 3D rendering in live applications. FlowerDance uses MeanFlow, learning the average velocity of the motion trajectory so a dance can be sampled in only a few steps. Physical consistency constraints pull each step back toward plausible human motion, with reconstruction, velocity, and joint-position losses.

The backbone is BiMamba, a sequence model whose cost grows linearly with length rather than quadratically like attention, fused with music through channel-level cross-modal mixing. Generation is non-autoregressive, and users can edit motion interactively. On the AIST++ and FineDance benchmarks, FlowerDance topped prior methods on motion quality and on efficiency alike, including inference speed and memory use. The target is real-time virtual performers and choreography tools.
arxiv-2511-21329:
Chien-Hua Chen extends a classical counting tool into higher rank in a 2025 paper on Drinfeld modules, the function-field cousins of elliptic curves. Modular polynomials encode when two such objects are linked by an isogeny, a structure-preserving map, and for rank two they are well understood. For rank three and above, even writing down the right bivariate polynomial was unclear, a gap earlier work by Breuer and Rück framed but did not close computationally.

Chen gives an explicit procedure to construct the self-isogenous modular polynomial for Drinfeld modules of rank at least three with complex multiplication. For the prime ideal generated by T, he provides a computing algorithm. For the ideal generated by T squared plus T plus 1, he proves an explicit degree bound. He also formulates a generalized volcano structure for the isogeny graph, layered like a crater, and proves it appears for these modules.
arxiv-2511-21529:
Jasper De Witte and twelve coauthors stamp quantum light sources onto a photonic chip with factory-grade reliability, in 2025. Scalable quantum photonics needs single-photon emitters inside low-loss circuits. The best emitters, indium gallium arsenide quantum dots, live in gallium arsenide, not in the silicon nitride platform favored for circuits. Their solution is micro-transfer printing, a pick-and-place tool that prints emitter waveguides onto the nitride chip.

De Witte and his coauthors report a processing yield of about 95 percent using a commercial printer, the reliability large circuits demand. Each emitter sits in a p-i-n diode, which quiets charge noise for near blinking-free output. The diode also tunes the emitter's wavelength with ordinary CMOS-level voltages, letting many dots be brought into mutual resonance despite fabrication scatter. The result is a credible route to chips carrying many quantum building blocks at once.
arxiv-2511-21629:
Anna Marklová, Ondřej Vinš, Martina Vokáčová, and Jiří Milička ask whether readers can tell machine-written Czech poetry from human work, in 2025. Most such studies use English, which dominates AI training data. Czech is a morphologically complex, low-resource Slavic language, a harder test of generative fluency. Native speakers judged poems and guessed each one's origin.

They guessed at chance: 45.8 percent correct on average, no better than coin flips, and neither poetry familiarity nor literary training helped. The twist is bias. Readers who believed a poem was AI-generated rated it worse, even though AI poems actually scored equal or better than human ones when judged blind. The more a reader liked a poem, the less accurately they assigned its authorship. Beliefs about who wrote a poem, the study shows, steer aesthetic judgment itself.
arxiv-2511-21729:
Single author Jithin Krishnan reports that in retrieval-augmented generation, how components combine matters more than how strong each one is, in 2025. RAG systems fetch documents before answering, and builders keep adding hybrid search, multi-model checking, and adaptive confidence thresholds. Krishnan tested each upgrade alone and together in a multi-agent setup.

The ablation study ran 50 queries: 15 answerable, 10 edge cases, and 25 adversarial. Deployed alone, adaptive thresholding, ensemble verification, and hybrid retrieval each gave zero improvement. Integrated properly, they cut abstention from 40 percent to 2 percent, a 95 percent reduction. The paper also unmasks a measurement trap: inconsistent verdict labels made safe behavior look like a 40 percent hallucination rate. Ensemble confidence ran very high at 0.988, so query-adaptive thresholds were needed to stop over-answering. Retrieval alone engaged in 40 percent of queries yet helped only when paired with stronger verification.
arxiv-2511-22229:
Wang, Cheng, Wu, and colleagues dub silent videos with a speech language model. Video dubbing must synthesize speech that matches the script, clones a reference speaker's voice. Lands syllables on the actor's lip movements; earlier systems stitched together lightweight specialist modules and sounded mediocre, while modern speech large language models sound excellent but ignore the video's timing. Their VSpeechLM bridges the two by teaching a speech LLM to take orders from the picture.

A text-video aligner first learns fine-grained correspondence between phonemes and lip movements, then emits an expanded phoneme sequence carrying explicit lip-synchronization cues, which the speech decoders consume as their prompt. In experiments VSpeechLM significantly outperforms previous visual text-to-speech methods on overall quality, speaker similarity, and synchronization metrics. The authors flag harder conditions, partially invisible lips and low-quality video, as the next frontier for the approach.
arxiv-2511-22329:
Beauville, a leading algebraic geometer in Nice, surveys when a family of geometric shapes varies as richly as it possibly can. A linear system is a family of hypersurfaces cut out by sections of one line bundle. It has maximal variation when a general member has the maximum possible number of moduli, meaning almost no two members are isomorphic. So the family genuinely explores the whole moduli space rather than tracing a thin slice of it. A simple differential criterion exists, but checking it in practice proves surprisingly hard.

Four expected settings get detailed treatment: hypersurfaces, double coverings of projective space, K3 surfaces, and abelian varieties. Beauville proves maximal variation outright for abelian varieties; the first three yield only partial results, and closing sections collect counterexamples marking the phenomenon's boundary. The survey maps what is known versus merely expected.
arxiv-2511-22729:
Labate and colleagues solve a practical blocker for AI agents using tools: answers too big to read. When a tool returns a huge output, it can overflow the model's context window and kill the task, while truncation or summarisation lose information scientific workflows genuinely need in full. Their method changes what the model handles: instead of raw data flowing through the context, tool results are stored in memory and the model manipulates pointers to them.

Tools are redefined to accept and return these memory references, so bulky payloads never enter the context and responses of any length stay usable without information loss. The method is validated on a real materials science application conventional workflows cannot execute. In a comparative experiment where both approaches succeed, the pointer workflow used roughly seven times fewer tokens than the traditional one, with faster execution.
arxiv-2511-22829:
Tian and Lin build a lane-changing planner treating safety as a guarantee rather than a hope. Their pipeline starts with dynamic risk fields, maps scoring collision risk from surrounding vehicles, capturing static obstacles and velocity-dependent danger. It then generates time-varying convex feasible spaces, regions certified to satisfy kinematic limits and stay collision-free as traffic moves.

Inside them, a constrained iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator optimises smoothness, control effort, and risk exposure over a finite horizon while keeping strict feasibility. In simulations it beat traditional approaches on safety and efficiency together: collision-free lane changes over 28.59 metres in 2.84 seconds, cutting distance and time by 32.4 and 61.0 percent against artificial-potential-field and model-predictive-control baselines in the reported comparison. In dense roundabouts it kept larger margins, a minimum distance of 4.23 metres, lower jerk, smoother curvature, a 99.2 percent success rate, and 12.3 millisecond computation.
arxiv-2511-22929:
Padó and Thomas test how far vision-language models get at reading paintings as art historians do: emotionally. Emotion is central to art but is realised abstractly, changes historically, and leans on symbols whose reading takes expertise. They presented 38 artworks to three models, a LLaVA-Llama system and two Qwen models, with four question sets: content, emotional content, how emotions are expressed, and emotion symbols.

The models recognised content well and identified which emotions a work depicts and how they are expressed, independent of period and style. The Qwen models showed more detailed art historical knowledge than LLaVA-Llama. Performance was best on concrete images and failed on abstract or symbolic ones: recognising emotion symbols remained fundamentally difficult, demanding long inference chains, and the models gave inconsistent answers to related questions. The authors see cataloguing and accessibility description as uses, with experts still reviewing the output.
arxiv-2511-23029:
Inui and colleagues build a text-guided generator that paints realistic textures onto digital terrain, the surface coloring used in games and film previsualization. The hard part is fidelity: the painted ridges, valleys, and land cover must follow a supplied elevation map, called a DEM, rather than inventing their own hills. And hand-painting such maps is slow, labor-intensive work.

Their pipeline, Geodiffussr, uses flow matching, a generative method related to diffusion, and injects elevation features into its network at several resolutions, a step they call multi-scale content aggregation. Against a version without that step, image quality scores improved sharply, with FID falling by 49.16 percent and LPIPS by 32.33 percent in their tests, while the height-appearance mismatch dropped close to zero. They also release a worldwide training set pairing elevation maps with Sentinel-2 satellite images and written captions of the visible land cover.
arxiv-2511-23129:
Mamonova and colleagues built a model of flares on young M dwarfs, the magnetically violent stars that host many Earth-sized planets. Flare ultraviolet light can erode a planet's atmosphere or help start prebiotic chemistry. Their Young M Dwarfs Flare model combines radiative-hydrodynamic simulations of the stellar atmosphere with beams of high- and low-energy electrons, the energy-deposition picture.

The model reproduces the brightening of the continuum in the TESS telescope's band and in the far-ultraviolet A range across flares of many sizes. It misses the blue continuum rise in the far-ultraviolet B segment, a gap for future work. It also matches the energy released in optical and ultraviolet light. The team finds that flare frequency distributions for young M dwarfs follow a statistical law, a two-coefficient broken power law. The module uses it to generate synthetic flare populations.
arxiv-2511-23329:
Palma-Amestoy and Provenzi recast color enhancement algorithms, the filters that fix contrast and color casts in photographs. As an optimization problem guided by how human vision actually works. Rather than hand-designing another algorithm, they write down basic requirements that any perceptually inspired energy functional should satisfy. Exhibit an explicit class of functionals meeting all of them, and single out three members of basic interest for detailed study.

Minimizing such a functional turns out to balance two opponent mechanisms. A local nonlinear contrast boost and a control keeping pixel values dispersed sensibly around middle gray and around the original image. The family also reunites famous models, since one member reproduces the ACE algorithm and another amounts to a symmetrized Retinex. And the authors cut the computation from quadratic in the pixel count to nearly linear, proving stability and existence of minima along the way.
arxiv-2511-23429:
Tang and colleagues introduce Hunyuan-GameCraft-2, a generative world model that lets players steer a generated video game world with free-form natural language instructions instead of only fixed keyboard actions. Built on a 14 billion parameter image-to-video mixture-of-experts foundation model, it also accepts keyboard and mouse signals. And a text-driven injection mechanism gives fine-grained control over camera motion. Character behavior, and environment dynamics in real time.

To train it, the team defines the concept of interactive video data and builds an automated pipeline converting large-scale unstructured text-video pairs into causally aligned training sets. Then evaluates on a new benchmark called InterBench. Instructions like open the door, draw a torch, or trigger an explosion produce temporally coherent, causally grounded video responses. And the model outperforms prior state-of-the-art systems across interaction fidelity, visual quality, and temporal coherence in their reported experiments.
arxiv-2512-00029:
Connected devices now run urgent tasks across small edge units, local hubs, and distant cloud servers. Andreas Kouloumpris and three co-authors present an optimization framework, in a 2025 study, for deciding where each task should run. The setting differs from standard edge computing because it often uses one sensing edge device paired with one hub.

The framework aims to assign work across these layers in a clean, streamlined way so demanding applications run well. Such applications need fast responses and careful use of limited local hardware. For system designers, the study offers a structured way to split tasks among edge, hub, and cloud rather than sending everything to one place.
arxiv-2512-00129:
Deep learning systems can flag breast cancer in mammograms, but they often fail on images unlike their training data. Jayan Adhikari, Prativa Joshi, and Susish Baral tackle that reliability problem in a 2025 study. Scans from other modalities or different equipment can lead to wrong detections and misdiagnosis.

Their approach filters out-of-distribution inputs with a ResNet50-based stage, then detects cancer with YOLO models. Explainability methods and domain adaptation are part of the design. The goal is a screening tool that stays dependable when hospital equipment and imaging conditions change, instead of performing well only in the lab. Reliability under changed conditions is the theme that runs through the whole design.
arxiv-2512-00229:
Neural networks often fail silently when given inputs unlike anything in their training data. Suhail, Afroz, and Sethi present TIE in 2025, a framework for detecting such out-of-distribution inputs. The name stands for training, inversion, and exclusion, its three main stages.

Dependable systems need to estimate uncertainty and flag unfamiliar samples in a unified way, because overconfident predictions can be dangerous. TIE is designed to stay visually interpretable while it decides. The work matters for medical, driving, and security systems, where recognizing the unknown is as important as classifying the known. Interpretability is built into the framework's name and design, not added afterward. Uncertainty estimates give downstream systems a principled way to abstain.
arxiv-2512-00829:
Md Mehrab Hossain Opi, Sumaiya Khan, and Moshammad Farzana Rahman study faster training for Bangla language models in a 2025 paper. Training such models takes heavy computing power and long hours. In Bangla natural language processing, access to high-end hardware is often limited, so costs bite harder.

The team tests automatic mixed precision training. That method does much of the math in a lighter numeric format, while keeping key steps precise. Done right, it speeds training and saves memory without hurting model quality. Their work checks whether those savings hold for Bangla tasks, which would help local researchers do more with modest machines.
arxiv-2512-01029:
Vladimir Dragović and David Kalaj construct minimal surfaces over special quadrilaterals in a 2025 math paper. A Pitot quadrilateral has two pairs of opposite sides with the same total length, a property first tied to tangent circles. Minimal surfaces are shapes that locally minimize area, like soap films.

The authors build Scherk-type minimal graphs over any Pitot quadrilateral, with a fully explicit framework. First they produce a harmonic map from the unit disk onto the quadrilateral. Its stretching is the square of a Möbius map fixed directly by the quadrilateral's vertices. Explicit formulas make these surfaces computable, not just provable.
arxiv-2512-01629:
Yumeng He and co-authors rebuild articulated objects from a single photo for simulation. Objects with moving parts fill homes and workplaces. Robots need sim-ready models of them, with part trees and joints. Hand modeling those assets is slow expert work.

Their frame, SPARK, uses vision-language knowledge to infer parts. It outputs physically consistent, kinematic part models. Each part gets a place in a hierarchy with motion limits. One-photo assets could stock training worlds for robots far faster than hand modeling allows. Vision-language priors supply part names and joint guesses, which cuts the need for motion capture rigs in building each new asset.
arxiv-2512-02329:
Software engineering may be heading toward teams where autonomous AI agents do the core building, guided by human-set norms. Hoa Khanh Dam and four co-authors sketch in 2025 a new class of software engineering agents powered by large language models and equipped with beliefs, desires, intentions, and memory.

Such agents would reason about their work in a human-like way rather than merely completing tickets. The paper envisions autonomous normative multi-agent systems, teams of agents that also follow shared rules of conduct. It is a position paper, mapping how human-AI development teams could be reorganized around agents as primary drivers.
arxiv-2512-02429:
Algebraic geometers simplify complicated shapes by running the minimal model program, a sequence of surgeries toward a canonical form. Donghyeon Kim and Dae-Won Lee study in 2025 how that program behaves on the generic fiber of a fibration whose fibers are mostly of log Calabi-Yau type.

The setting assumes that over a dense set of the base, each fiber is a mildly singular log Calabi-Yau space. What the program does on the typical fiber governs the geometry of the whole family. Results here feed the classification of higher-dimensional varieties, where fibrations are the main tool for taking shapes apart.
arxiv-2512-02629:
C. Ramos Almeida and a large team study dust around feeding black holes using the James Webb telescope. Type-2 quasars hide their central black hole and inner gas behind thick dust and gas. Mid infrared spectra can still probe the dusty torus, the donut shaped cloud doing the hiding.

Webb's MIRI instrument recorded spectra from the centers of five nearby quasars of this type. Silicate emission in those spectra constrains the torus shape and how radiation pushes back on it. Better torus models sharpen our picture of how black holes grow inside their dusty cocoons. Dust that glows in this way tells on the shape of the cloud that hides the hole at its heart.
arxiv-2512-03229:
A combined galaxy catalog can tighten cosmic growth measures. H. Zou presents such a measure in this 2025 work, using the maximum likelihood fields method. The work joins three DESI first-release sources into one analysis.

The combined catalog holds hundreds of thousands of galaxy redshifts. It also holds tens of thousands of peculiar velocity measures from two distance methods. Blending both kinds of data gives a fuller picture of how matter moves. The resulting growth rate constraint helps test models of gravity and dark energy. Blending catalogs also cross-checks distance methods against each other in one frame.
arxiv-2512-03729:
In May 2025, a small free-flying robot aboard the International Space Station was steered by a reinforcement learning policy. Samantha Chapin and colleagues from the US Naval Research Laboratory describe that experiment, named APIARY, in a 2025 robotics preprint. Their goal is autonomous assembly work in orbit, where robots must act without a human hand on the controls.

The team trained a control policy for the NASA Astrobee robot inside a physics simulator, using an actor-critic method called Proximal Policy Optimization. Training randomised target poses and mass distributions so the policy would cope with surprises. The paper walks through simulation tests, ground tests, and the flight run itself. The authors argue the flight run shows learned control can work in orbit. That is a step toward robots handling exploration and logistics tasks with less human guidance.
arxiv-2512-03829:
High-power proton cyclotrons feed applications such as accelerator driven systems, but tuning their beams by hand is slow and rarely optimal. M. Haj Tahar and a large team at the Paul Scherrer Institute report a first in a 2025 accelerator physics preprint. They deployed a reinforcement learning system to tune the Injector 2 cyclotron, a testbed for high-power operation.

Their framework pairs a tailored learning algorithm with live diagnostics and control. One physics-inspired trick, an overshoot strategy, cut magnetic field settling times nearly sixfold. Across a twelve-day campaign, the agent learned stable tuning policies within hours for each operating point, then ran overnight evaluations with low beam losses. Policies trained at low current still worked at far higher currents. The authors call it the first such demonstration on a high-power cyclotron, with lessons for future driver machines.
arxiv-2512-03929:
Quantum measurement is usually told as a story of an apparatus that must itself be treated quantum mechanically, spawning an endless chain of couplings. Dagomir Kaszlikowski and Pawel Kurzynski cut that chain in a 2025 quantum physics preprint. In their framework, a single qubit couples directly to a classical measurement bit, with no quantum apparatus in between.

The trick lies in how states and interactions are written. The qubit becomes a positive probability distribution spread over a pair of classical bits. The apparatus is one more classical bit. The interaction between them is a map that may use negative transition probabilities, even though every state stays positive. When this process acts, it produces a collapsed state and an outcome with exactly the probabilities quantum mechanics predicts. The nonclassical character of measurement, the authors argue, lives in the interaction itself.
arxiv-2512-04129:
Multi-agent systems let language models hand work to each other. Whatever an upstream agent says, downstream agents tend to trust and execute. Ruichao Liang and colleagues show how an attacker can ride that trust in a 2025 security preprint. Their topology-guided attack plants contamination at exposed edge agents. The system's own wiring carries it, hop by hop, to high-privilege agents.

The scheme combines reconnaissance of the agent topology, a model of how contamination propagates, and payloads wrapped in layers so they survive reinterpretation along the way. Success rates across three frameworks and five layouts ranged widely, and two real-world applications fell in most tested scenarios. The authors propose a defence, a topology-trust mitigation that blocked nearly ninety-five percent of these attacks in their tests. Their broader warning is that multi-agent security cannot be assessed one agent at a time.
arxiv-2512-04229:
Dark matter may have been made in the reheating era after inflation, cooked through a heavy mediator particle called a Z-prime. Stephen E. Henrich, Yann Mambrini, and Keith A. Olive map that production in a 2025 particle physics preprint. Three regimes, freeze-out, freeze-in, and ultra-relativistic freeze-out, shade smoothly into one another, and no study had covered all three for this portal.

The authors find much of the available parameter space sits in the ultra-relativistic regime. That holds for dark matter masses from keV to TeV, when the mediator weighs between about a TeV and a PeV. When the mediator outweighs both the dark matter and the reheating temperature, the mechanism robustly yields cold dark matter. Particles born hot cool down if freeze-out happens during reheating. Compared with standard freeze-in, the regime also tolerates stronger couplings and lighter mediators.
arxiv-2512-04529:
Xin Liang, Zhilin Zhang, Xiang Zhang, and co-authors present SlideGen, a team of AI agents that turns a research paper into a clean slide deck. Making slides is not just cutting text down. A presenter must pick a story, choose which figures and formulas to show, and lay pages out without crowding. Prior tools mostly picked text, leaving decks unbalanced and hard to follow. Their 2025 arXiv paper splits the job among specialist agents.

One agent plans the narrative outline. Others ground each claim in the paper's figures, tables, and formulas. A layout agent then composes pages with visual balance in mind. The agents pass drafts back and forth, much like a human team. The result aims for decks with a clear arc and tidy pages. Such a tool could save researchers hours before talks, while keeping the slides faithful to the source.
arxiv-2512-05029:
Amin Mosallanezhad and six co-authors show that lumpiness may be the missing ingredient in winds blown off accretion discs. Around white dwarfs and the black holes in galactic centers, gas spiraling inward can be pushed back out by starlight pressing on its spectral lines. In simulations, though, the light over-strips the gas of electrons, the push fades, and the wind dies — at odds with what telescopes see.

Using a standard shortcut, the team's new simulations treat the gas as clumped into small dense knots. They find that even modest clumping lowers the stripping, strengthens the push, and raises the outflow sharply. The clumpy winds produce the ultraviolet fingerprints missing from smooth models and can reprocess a large share of the disc's light. Since real winds are expected to be patchy anyway, clumping gives a physical way to square the theory with observation for both kinds of system.
arxiv-2512-05329:
Anqi Feng and eight co-authors present CATNUS, a tool for carving the thalamus into its component nuclei on brain scans. The thalamus is a relay hub whose individual nuclei serve distinct functions and are hit differently by neurological and psychiatric disease. Yet drawing their borders is hard. Many nuclei are tiny, contrast inside the thalamus is faint, and anatomy varies between people. CATNUS attacks the problem with a three-dimensional neural network given a sense of position.

Coordinate-aware layers help the network localize large and small nuclei across thirteen nuclei or groups. Pretrained versions accept the clinical scan types as well as quantitative maps, widening where the tool can run. Benchmarked against methods, CATNUS segments accurately, repeats reliably on rescans, and holds up on travelling-subject data gathered across scanners, field strengths, and vendors. The authors aim it at large-scale brain studies and clinical assessment alike.
arxiv-2512-06129:
Alexandros Efstratiou, Kayla Duskin, Kate Starbird, and Emma Spiro dissect a famous claim about Twitter's algorithm in the window after the ownership change but before the rebrand to X. Earlier work reported right leaning gains in the algorithmic feed. The boost replicates. The harder question is what traveled with it. The advantage, they find, was not necessarily politics itself. Those accounts posted more agitating content, and drew the owner's attention.

Legacy verified accounts actually lost exposure. The algorithm may run a behavior market, where outrage converts to reach. Reform should target incentives, not viewpoints. Platforms shape discourse by reward schedule.
arxiv-2512-06229:
Lucas Colucci and Marco D'Emidio prove a bound in Ramsey theory, the branch of math that looks for order hidden in large networks. Take a huge set of points joined by every possible link, and paint each link with a label from a prime sized cycle of numbers. Their question asks how big the set must be before some fixed tree like shape is forced to appear with labels that add to zero.

The authors show that, for any forest shape meeting a few plain conditions, the needed size grows in a straight line with the shape, not faster. Their bound links the count of points, the prime, and the edge count in one clean formula. Results like this sharpen what math knows about when neat patterns must show up inside large, wildly labeled structures.
arxiv-2512-06429:
Jaeyong Hwang, Ana Maria Rey, and their co authors turn the shaking of two atoms into a hybrid quantum device. The atoms sit in a laser trap, an optical tweezer, and interact with each other. Their motion can play the part of an oscillator, a quantum swing, while an internal state plays a qubit. By pulsing the trap in a steady rhythm and tuning how uneven its pull is, the team enacts a full set of operations on the swing, plus versions steered by the qubit.

That control can sense the faint magnetic pull between the atoms, reaching very small frequency shifts in seconds and finer ones in minutes across a grid of traps. The scheme gives labs a flexible handle on the motion of atom pairs. It suits studies where spins meet oscillators, and precise probes of the forces and traps around the atoms.
arxiv-2512-06529:
Md Abdullah Al Kafi, Walayat Hussain, and Raka Moni study why computing students often shrug off the non computing courses their degree requires. Required courses in other fields can fill seats without being seen as real computing knowledge. The authors call that gap a curricular legitimacy gap, and model two responses apart: devaluation, judging such courses needless, and integrative intention, the will to reuse what they teach later.

They surveyed computing undergraduates in Bangladesh and fitted their model with careful statistical checks, including thousands of resampled fits. Feeling burdened by the extra courses fed devaluation, and devaluation in turn cut the will to reuse the learning. Feeling the courses were useful worked the other way, both directly and by lowering devaluation. The model captured a large share of the spread in both responses. Degrees, they suggest, win students by cutting burden and showing clear use.
arxiv-2512-06729:
Priyankush Ghosh and five co authors release XODIAC, a fast model of the chemistry of exoplanet atmospheres, built for the Webb telescope era. Rich new spectra keep arriving, and reading them means simulating how starlight drives chemistry in a planet's air. Slow models bottleneck that work. XODIAC runs on graphics processors, solves one dimensional photochemistry, and carries a built in equilibrium solver plus an updated database of reaction data.

Three chemical networks ship with it, including a new house network linking hundreds of species through thousands of reactions. The team benchmarked the model on the well studied hot Jupiter HD 189733 b against two established codes. Agreement was excellent, and when the same network and starting state were used, the solving scheme itself barely mattered. The authors then revisited that planet's chemistry across all three networks, showing how the choice of network colors what telescopes should see.
arxiv-2512-06929:
MinCheol Jeon designs a forecasting model for time series that refuse to sit still. Real data drift, shift their averages, and carry patterns at several time scales at once, all of which break ordinary models. His architecture, AdaMamba, opens by cleaning each series: an adaptive block pulls out trends at multiple scales and rescales each channel, steadying what remains.

The cleaned sequence then passes through an encoder that chops it into patches and reads it with a Mamba-enhanced transformer. A mixture-of-experts layer lets different parts of the network specialize, catching both long-range links and quick local moves. A light head issues forecasts for several horizons ahead, and the removed trends are folded back in at the end. Tests against transformer baselines show steadier, more accurate predictions across varied data sets. The modular design also leaves room for versions that report uncertainty, not just single best guesses.
arxiv-2512-07029:
Yuan-Zhe Dai and co-authors assemble the largest catalog yet of planets in star clusters, places where stars are born together and share a known age. Cluster planets are precious because their ages are pinned down, letting astronomers watch planetary systems grow up. The team separates true open clusters from looser moving groups using a size criterion, then asks whether their planets differ.

Cross-matching the newest cluster lists with transit surveys yields a catalog of confirmed planets plus a larger set of candidates inside both kinds of group. The authors refit each group's structure and hunt for substructures with two clustering algorithms. Moving groups consistently host a higher share of planets than open clusters, especially giant hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2512-07429:
Nina Effenberger, Maxim Samarin, Maybritt Schillinger, and Reto Knutti wrote this 2025 climate science paper. It deals with Central Europe and the planning of wind and solar power. Planners need fine local climate detail, yet full regional models are costly and slow to run.

The team trains a machine learning emulator on older global and regional simulations. The emulator learns how coarse global fields map onto fine regional ones. Tested on newer global runs it had never seen, it still gives realistic local detail. With it, they study days when weak wind and dim sun strike together. Such energy drought days, their results suggest, are likely to grow less common in the future. The method offers a fast partner to full regional climate modeling efforts.
arxiv-2512-07529: Patrick Cabau wrote this 2025 mathematics paper, published in Italian, on a new geometric structure. He introduces the notion of a partial Jacobi manifold. The work sits inside the convenient smooth framework built by Frölicher, Kriegl, and Michor. Cabau gives explicit examples in both finite and infinite dimensions. He also analyses the characteristic distribution that comes with the structure. The paper closes by pointing to research directions that deserve further study.
arxiv-2512-07729:
Aidas Aglinskas and Stefano Anzellotti wrote this 2025 paper on how machines and people recognize actions. A video of an action carries two kinds of clues. The body's pose and motion form one stream; the background scene forms the other.

Networks trained on a large action dataset lean strangely on the second stream. Remove the body, and their accuracy barely drops at all. Remove the background instead, and they fall to chance level. Human viewers behave in the opposite, more balanced way. People read actions well from body alone and scene alone alike. Their body-only scores beat their scene-only scores by a clear margin. The brain, after all, keeps separate regions for bodies and for scenes. The authors copy that layout into a new network design. Separate streams process body and background before their results combine. Accuracy rises, and the pattern across test versions turns human-like.
arxiv-2512-07929:
Sotirios Karamitsos and Benjamin Muntz wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on an ambiguity in gravity. Effective theories of gravity can be rewritten in many equivalent frames. Weyl transformations connect those descriptions, but they also reshape the field space metric.

Swampland conjectures lean on that metric to bound how far fields may travel. If the metric is frame-dependent, the conjectures' meaning becomes unclear. The authors resolve the puzzle with a fully frame-covariant framework. All conformal frames appear as slices of one higher-dimensional geometry. That auxiliary space is singular, and its slicing explains the frame freedom. Viewed through that geometry, Weyl and unit changes become transparent. They revisit the species scale and sharpened distance conjectures within it. The bounds emerge from universal features of how frames transform. Quantum gravity may not be imposing those limits from outside after all.
arxiv-2512-08029:
Tianxingjian Ding, Yuanhao Zou, Chen Chen, Mubarak Shah, and Yu Tian, researchers in medical imaging and machine learning, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, called CLARITY, tackles a hard problem in cancer care. Doctors must forecast how a tumor will change under treatment, yet most artificial intelligence tools only make static predictions from one moment in time.

CLARITY is a medical world model that simulates disease paths under different treatments. It combines imaging based latent states, the uneven timing of follow up visits, and patient specific clinical context. A planning method then tests long term treatment strategies inside those simulated paths, refining choices with survival aware feedback. The system reached top results on three cancer datasets, covering brain tumors and breast cancer, beating earlier generative methods and medical language models.
arxiv-2512-08229:
Tony Salloom, Dandi Zhou, and Xinhai Sun, robotics researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about depth completion for industrial robots. Robots that grasp, inspect, and navigate need solid three dimensional maps, but depth sensors return patchy data. Completion methods fill in a dense map from a color image plus sparse depth, yet they usually train on sparse points picked at random, unlike real sensor patterns.

The authors propose sampling sparse depth in a way that respects surface geometry. They estimate surface normals from the point cloud and score each pixel for depth reliability, then draw samples following that score. Plugged into a diffusion based completion model, the sampling improved accuracy on a standard indoor dataset. It also cut artifacts near edges and depth jumps. Training under such realistic conditions, they argue, better prepares models for the messy depth real robots receive.
arxiv-2512-08529:
Yunzhu Zhang, Zeyu Pan, Zhengwen Zeng, and colleagues, computer scientists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their method improves GUI grounding, the step where an agent turns a spoken instruction into exact screen coordinates. They noticed a fragility: cropping an image by a few pixels can flip a prediction from right to badly wrong, which is worst on high resolution screens with tiny elements.

Their framework, Multi View Prediction, needs no training. First, attention between the instruction and the image proposes several sensible cropped views of the screen. The grounding model predicts coordinates in each view. Then a clustering step gathers all predictions and picks the center of the densest cluster, treating lone predictions as outliers. Across models and benchmarks, the trick lifted accuracy substantially. The lesson is simple: ask the model the same question from several angles, and trust the consensus.
arxiv-2512-09029:
Jeanne Colbois and coauthors argue that extreme values of simple local measures can locate a quantum phase transition. The transition studied is between a superfluid phase and a Bose glass phase, of the Berezinskii Kosterlitz Thouless type. Rare chain breaking events favor localization.

The model is a random field spin chain at zero temperature, equivalent to bosons that interact in a random potential, with attractive forces between them. In the strong disorder regime, localization is driven by weak links that act as chain breaking events. Those events show up in the extreme values of on site density or local magnetization,. High precision numerical simulations show those extremes capture the transition accurately, even for fairly short chains. The weak disorder regime is harder due to finite size effects.
arxiv-2512-09329:
Amin Tavakoli leads a team improving protein language models, artificial intelligence systems trained on amino acid sequences the way chatbots are trained on text. Fine-tuning such models for protein design is usually improvised, because labeled protein data are scarce and costly. Their recipe aims to make that fine-tuning fast, simple, and general.

The trick is self-distillation: the model itself generates candidate sequences, and a light curation pipeline with domain filters picks the good ones to train on. The same filters can also screen model output directly and nominate candidates for lab testing. The authors demonstrate the recipe with a genome-scale model on the tryptophan synthase enzyme family. After fine-tuning, the model produced sequences that were more novel than natural ones yet more stable and functional by their measures, reaching beyond the variants evolution has already tried.
arxiv-2512-09429:
Zehong Liao and colleagues build a fast emulator for fusion reactions between heavy atomic nuclei at energies near the Coulomb barrier, the energy hill two nuclei must cross to fuse. The accurate calculations, called coupled-channels, are slow, which makes it hard to scan many nuclear shapes. Their emulator uses eigenvector continuation, a reduced basis method that rebuilds full solutions from a small set of examples.

They apply the emulator to oxygen nuclei fusing with samarium and tungsten targets. The test question is whether nuclear deformation, how stretched or squashed the target nucleus is, can be extracted from fusion data using the emulator. The emulator not only speeds the calculations up greatly, it also recovers the deformation parameters accurately. The authors present it as a powerful tool for systematically exploring the intrinsic shapes of atomic nuclei and sharpening understanding of basic nuclear properties.
arxiv-2512-09529:
Wei-An Chen, Seamus D. Clarke, and Ya-Wen Tang ask whether a gas clump's properties can predict how the dense cores inside it, the direct progenitors of stars, will be arranged. Clumps span about a parsec; cores are smaller fragments inside them. Observers see core distributions in millimeter surveys, and it was unclear how much of that pattern the clump controls.

Using magnetohydrodynamic simulations of converging flows, the team generated a sample of clumps and measured their properties with techniques. Alignment parameters quantified how the cores are distributed, while energy terms weighed the influence of gravity, magnetic fields, and turbulence. Core distributions correlated only weakly with clump properties overall. Inside a clump, turbulence seems to drive much of the pattern by causing uneven collapse and fragmentation. Across the population, gravity dominates, making core distributions more compact. The authors conclude clump properties alone cannot determine where cores end up.
arxiv-2512-09929:
Rohun Agrawal and colleagues close a mismatch in how world models for robot planning are trained and used. At planning time, though, a world model is used to choose a whole sequence of actions. Gradient based planning exploits this efficiently, but it has lagged behind slower search methods. The authors argue the training objective is the culprit: next state prediction does not prepare the model for action selection. They propose train time data synthesis techniques that narrow this gap.

With their training changes, existing world models plan far better by gradient descent. At test time, the approach matches or beats the classical cross entropy method, a strong gradient free baseline, across manipulation and navigation tasks. It does so using only a tenth of the time budget. Better training, not a new planner, unlocks the speed gradient methods promised.
arxiv-2512-10729:
Si-Ren Xiao and co-authors sharpen the cosmic tape measure used by pulsar timing arrays. These arrays hunt nanohertz gravitational waves by watching clock-like pulsars, but pinning down a continuous wave's source is limited by how poorly the pulsars' distances are known. The phase of the wave's pulsar term, the part recorded when the wave passed each pulsar, encodes that distance.

Their method reads phase information from several continuous-wave sources at once and infers each pulsar's position in two dimensions, not along one line. The team ran simulations of a Square Kilometre Array era array with realistic parallax-based priors. Pulsars about a kiloparsec away reached distance precision finer than a parsec. They needed only a few sources. In some cases the gain was an order of magnitude. Better distances mean a chance of naming the host galaxy of a gravitational wave source and coordinating telescopes.
arxiv-2512-10829:
Vitor Curtarelli compares microphone beamformers that must be two things at once. A beamformer blends several microphone signals to listen in one direction. Two quality measures pull against each other: the directivity factor, how sharply the array focuses, and white-noise gain, how robust the result is to sensor noise and small errors. Practical designs strike a compromise between them, and several recipes claim to do it well.

Curtarelli sets purpose-built compromise designs against beamformers assembled by combining single-task designs, and runs the comparison in simulation. The robust superdirective beamformer and the tunable beamformer came out best among those studied. Remarkably, the two produced nearly identical output on every metric evaluated. Both are also the more practical options, since each lets the user slide continuously between the two objectives rather than jumping between fixed designs.
arxiv-2512-11029:
Martin Carrascal and colleagues ask how much information it takes to describe an effective field theory, the simplified theories physicists use at accessible energies. A consistent theory, they argue, should admit a finite description. They measure that descriptive complexity using a framework from tame geometry, applied to a classic supersymmetric gauge theory.

The test case is pure supersymmetric Yang Mills theory, whose quantum behaviour is captured by Seiberg Witten elliptic curves. Near the edges of its parameter space, extra light states appear and need their own local descriptions, each in a suitable duality frame. Using several frames keeps the total complexity finite, while insisting on one frame makes it blow up. The study shows how dualities help tame geometry give finite descriptions of effective theories.
arxiv-2512-11529:
Qingxiao Sun and a large team build xGR, a serving system that makes generative recommender models fast enough for production use. Generative recommendation borrows language model machinery to read long histories of user behaviour and predict what to show next. Its workload differs sharply from chat serving: prompts are long, outputs short and fixed in length, but searching a vast item catalogue with wide beams is expensive.

xGR unifies the reading and generation phases through staged computation with a separated memory cache. Sorting of candidate items can stop early, and mask based filtering reuses data structures to prune the catalogue cheaply. The whole pipeline is rebuilt to overlap stages and run parallel streams. On real world datasets, throughput rose to nearly three times the best baseline while respecting strict latency limits under heavy concurrency. The system targets the economics of large scale personalised recommendation.
arxiv-2512-11629:
Anish Nair and co-authors design a small partner craft that beams power to a host spacecraft. Called PaddleSat, it would sit near the host and send energy by a tight laser beam. Extra power could shrink the host own power gear or stretch its working life.

The team weighs the main design trades. A narrow beam wastes less power but needs exact pointing as both craft drift. A wide beam is forgiving but weak. They work through link budgets, light gear choices, and orbit control needs. The study maps what it would take for laser charging in space to pay off, a step toward craft that refuel on light instead of docked plugs.
arxiv-2512-11729:
Diego Tancara and co-authors test a quantum algorithm on states with heavy entanglement. Variational algorithms are a leading hope for near term quantum machines, but flat training zones, called barren plateaus, block many. ADAPT-VQE builds its circuit step by step and resists that trap, yet it was mostly tried on low entanglement chemistry states.

The team studies the qubit version on four qubit spin systems. They sort ground states into entanglement classes with an algebraic scheme, then start the algorithm from one member of each class. In every class it found the true ground state with care. The result broadens trust in ADAPT style methods beyond easy, weakly linked states.
arxiv-2512-11829:
Jacob Poschl proposes a compact way for agents to switch strategies as situations change. In shifting environments, an agent may need different tastes and habits in each hidden context. Giving every context its own full parameter set quickly becomes unworkable.

His answer is value profiles: a small kit of reusable bundles, each holding outcome tastes, action biases, and confidence levels. As beliefs about the hidden state shift, the active control settings blend from the kit by belief weights. In a reversal learning task, the profile model beat simpler rivals by about 100 AIC points. Recovery tests show its parts can be identified from noisy data. Analysis suggests action biases, not confidence, do the adapting.
arxiv-2512-12029:
Asmaa Abada, Antonio Enrique Cárcamo Hernández, and Salvador Urrea build a model where two seesaw mechanisms grow on their own. Seesaws explain why neutrinos are so light: linear and inverse versions use different heavy partners. Most models insert the needed terms by hand.

Here a local U(1) symmetry plus two discrete symmetries do the work. After symmetry breaking, both seesaws switch on at two loops, by the symmetry rules alone. The same rules protect two dark matter candidates, one scalar born at tree level, one fermion born at one loop. The model fits neutrino data, dark matter searches, and collider limits. It also explains why the atmospheric mass split exceeds the solar one.
arxiv-2512-12129:
Protima Nomo Sudro, Anton Ragni, and Thomas Hain compare four generative models at turning adult voices into child voices. Voice conversion for dubbing child speech is a niche with no room for uncanny results. Generative models lead adult conversion, but child targets had never been tested.

Diffusion, flow based, variational, and adversarial models all produced plausible speech. None matched the target child speaker closely enough on their own. A cheap frequency warping step applied to the output cut the adult child mismatch sharply for every model. Scores mix machine measures with listener judgments, on a purpose built dubbing corpus with specific speaker pairs. Warping, the authors argue, should be a standard add on.
arxiv-2512-12529:
Designers of the upgraded prototype Schwarzschild-Couder Telescope camera report its test results in a 2025 paper. The telescope is a dual mirror design proposed for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory, which will sharpen gamma ray astronomy. Its prototype, in Arizona since 2019, saw Crab Nebula gamma rays with a partly filled camera.

The upgrade fills the focal plane with 11,328 silicon photomultiplier pixels across 177 modules, plus electronics that cut crosstalk and noise. A calibration routine was built and checked on a test module. The module showed low noise, minimal crosstalk, and excellent charge resolution. After tuning, all 177 modules will be installed for commissioning and sky checks.
arxiv-2512-12729:
Andre Cirne, Patricia R Sousa, Joao S Resende, and Luis Antunes present RunPBA, a runtime attestation system for microcontrollers, in a 2025 paper. Embedded devices now run in critical settings, making them targets for attack. Their tight energy and computing budgets leave little room for heavy defenses against control flow attacks, which hijack a program's execution path.

RunPBA uses PACBTI, a processor extension for the Arm Cortex M family that checks pointers and branch targets, to attest runtime behavior in hardware. Unlike similar systems, it needs no hardware modifications. A proof of concept ran two benchmark suites with a geometric mean overhead of only 1 percent and 4.7 percent. That low cost suits real world deployment under strict power limits.
arxiv-2512-13229:
Mischa Huisman and co-authors present a controller design method that makes cyber-physical systems harder to attack. Such systems, from water plants to vehicles, depend on networks that attackers can feed false sensor data into. Stealthy attacks that dodge standard detectors are the main threat here.

Their idea is a plant equivalent controller realization: a controller that behaves exactly like a given one in normal use but reacts very differently under attack. Reachable set analysis measures the worst harm an attack can do. Matrix inequality tools then synthesize the realization that shrinks that harm most. Tests on a four-tank process under stealthy sensor attacks showed the benefit.
arxiv-2512-13429:
Kanat Abdukhalikov and Gyanendra Verma construct two new families of linear codes by modifying generalized Reed-Solomon codes, a classic family built from polynomial evaluation. Their goal is codes with the MDS property, the best possible error tolerance for a given size, that are provably not of Reed-Solomon type.

For both families they derive parity-check matrices in explicit form. They give necessary and sufficient conditions for the MDS property to hold. Inside these families they isolate subfamilies that are non-GRS MDS codes, a sought after class. They further characterize self-orthogonal and self-dual members and present concrete examples of the constructions.
arxiv-2512-13629:
Adrien Orué and co-authors compare two methods for clinical trial endpoints that mix repeated events with a terminal event. Trials in oncology and cardiology often track events that recur, plus death. A time-to-first-event view can hide much of what matters to patients and doctors.

They compare a joint frailty model with a last-event win ratio method. The frailty model gives adjusted, component-specific hazard ratios, while the win ratio gives one summary of treatment benefit that respects a set order of death over recurrences. Simulations varied frailty spread and event rates. The joint frailty model gave higher power and looked most reliable for inference and sample size planning, in both cancer and heart examples.
arxiv-2512-13829:
Nicolas Monod develops a general form of conditional probability for arbitrary ordered vector spaces. Classical probability assigns numbers to events, but in a vector space setting the basic objects are vectors, not events. A related problem is how to assign a numerical value to one vector relative to another.

Monod describes the groups for which these generalized probabilities can be stationary, or invariant, under group action. The answers depart from the classical probability setting in useful ways. They lead to a new criterion for amenability, a property of groups tied to invariant means. They also give a new criterion for fixed points in cones, linking probability-like structures to geometry and group theory.
arxiv-2512-14229:
Alexandr Malijevsky, Martin Pospisil, Miriam Magociova, and Jiri Janek study complete wetting and drying at wavy walls in a 2025 paper. The walls are sinusoidally corrugated, like a smooth wave, and the authors ask how wall shape and force range change the fluid layer that coats them.

They use two models: short ranged forces for drying, and long ranged van der Waals forces for wetting. For each they derive scaling relations for the width and shape of the adsorbed layer near two phase coexistence. Unlike wall shapes give unlike scaling regimes. Numeric results from classical density functional theory confirm the predictions, and the contrast between short and long range forces is a central finding.
arxiv-2512-14629:
Yash Vishe and co-authors study how well current methods edit music while keeping its context intact. Music editing matters across film, broadcasting, and game development, and new generation models can now transfer timbre, swap instruments, or transform genre.

Their benchmark, MuseCPBench, tests editing methods through the lens of music context preservation: does the edit change what it should and leave the rest of the music alone? An empirical comparison gives producers and researchers a shared yardstick instead of scattered claims. The work helps clarify which editing tools are ready for real production use and which still damage the music around an edit.
arxiv-2512-14929:
Paul J. Weiser leads a team that uses deep learning to read brain scans which keep the water signal most scans throw away. Magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging maps the chemistry of the brain, but the huge water signal is normally suppressed. Keeping it allows water and metabolites to be imaged together, yet water sidebands corrupt the fits.

Their pipeline scans at 7 tesla with fast, non grid sampling and a very short echo time. A network called WALINET+ strips out lipids, water, and sidebands, and other networks rebuild the image and fit the chemistry. The water signal then gives absolute metabolite levels, magnetic susceptibility maps, and myelin water fractions at once. In tests the method matched standard scans closely, giving three kinds of brain maps in 12 minutes at 2 millimeter resolution.
arxiv-2512-15029:
Xiangdi Huang and two coauthors present a claimed resolution of a long standing open problem in fluid mathematics. The problem asks whether the two dimensional viscous shallow water equations, introduced by Saint-Venant in 1871, admit smooth solutions for all time from arbitrarily large starting data. Under radial symmetry, the authors claim an affirmative answer.

Their argument treats the viscous Saint-Venant system as the endpoint case of the BD entropy condition for compressible Navier-Stokes equations. A second hurdle is a critical embedding that currently works only in two dimensions. The same framework is claimed to give global smooth solutions for the two and three dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations under general BD entropy conditions, away from the endpoint case. Because the shallow water result has stood open for so long, the claim is one for specialists to scrutinize closely.
arxiv-2512-15329:
Juliane Krautz studies weak notions of curvature on metric graphs in a 2025 math paper. A metric graph is a network of edges with lengths, and curvature bounds help describe how heat and motion behave on it. The paper asks whether three weak ways of stating a lower curvature bound all mean the same thing.

Krautz proves that the three forms are in fact equivalent. One comes from the Bakry Emery condition, one from a variational inequality, and one from convexity along shortest paths. The proof uses careful smoothing of curves and an explicit form for the Cheeger energy. A short final part discusses links to the Schrodinger bridge problem.
arxiv-2512-15529:
Erik Broman and Johan Tykesson study the Poisson stick model in two dimensional hyperbolic space in a 2025 paper. Random sticks of fixed length L are scattered by a Poisson process, and overlapping sticks form clusters. Percolation models in hyperbolic space usually show two transitions as density rises: clusters merge, and later the giant cluster becomes unique.

The authors find how the two critical densities scale for large L. The percolation threshold scales like L to the power minus two, matching Euclidean space. The uniqueness threshold scales like L to the power minus one, which differs from the Euclidean case. The contrast highlights how negative curvature changes large scale connectivity.
arxiv-2512-15629:
Maryna Kachanovska and Adrian Savchuk ask what it means for a 3D star shaped scatterer to be small in the time domain in a 2025 paper. In frequency domain scattering, an obstacle can be replaced by a point scatterer once the wavelength far exceeds its size. In the time domain, recent work suggested an extra temporal scale also controls that smallness.

The authors argue this extra scale is not always needed. For a sound soft scattering problem with a star shaped obstacle in three dimensions, they construct asymptotic models whose error does not grow over time. The result sharpens when point scatterer approximations can be trusted for wave problems that evolve in time.
arxiv-2512-16129:
Tran Quoc Viet and four co-authors release a software tool in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. Nuclear pairing, the tendency of protons and neutrons to form pairs, shapes how atomic nuclei behave. Solving the pairing problem exactly for large systems is costly, so approximations are common.

Their program, EP version 1.0, computes exact pairing energies and states at zero temperature for odd and even nuclei. It exploits the sparsity and symmetry of the pairing matrix, uses standard solver libraries, and applies a trick to locate the ground state block in odd systems quickly. On a desktop it handles 26 deformed levels and 26 nucleons in about 100 seconds, and up to 63 levels with more resources. Future versions aim at finite temperatures and parallel running.
arxiv-2512-16229:
Chenkai Xu and ten co-authors speed up a new kind of language model in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025. Diffusion language models write text by filling in many tokens at once, promising fast output. In practice they manage only one to three tokens per forward pass, because the order in which blanks are filled limits how many can be settled together.

Their algorithm, LoPA, tries several filling orders in parallel branches and keeps the order whose confidence promises the most future parallelism. It needs no training and plugs into existing models. Applied to the D2F model, LoPA raised output to 10.1 tokens per pass on the GSM8K math benchmark while beating the base model's quality. A multi-device system built around branch parallelism reached 1,073.9 tokens per second for a single sample.
arxiv-2512-16429:
Tsuyoshi Miyatsu and three co-authors pin down dense matter physics in this short conference paper. It comes from the 2025 International Nuclear Physics Conference in Korea. The nuclear equation of state says how nuclear matter resists squeezing. It also decides how large neutron stars can be. The authors test a new family of mean-field models, called OMEG.

The models were tuned to match lab nuclear data. They also match sky data from the NICER telescope and the wave event GW170817. A mixing term softens the symmetry energy near twice normal density. That gives smaller star radii and less tidal stretching. The matter stays stiff enough at high density to support stars of two solar masses. The data favor a small or negative curvature value for the symmetry energy. That is a concrete clue for model builders.
arxiv-2512-16529:
Julien Gachadoat and Guillaume Lagarde build a tool for artists in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. Generative art algorithms expose dozens of knobs, and the beautiful settings hide in small, scattered pockets of a huge parameter space. Artists find them by tedious trial and error, leaving much of the space unexplored.

Their framework, ParamExplorer, borrows from reinforcement learning to guide the search. It is interactive and modular, accepts feedback from the artist or from automated measures, and plugs into existing p5.js projects, a popular creative coding library. Inside the framework the authors implement several exploration strategies, called agents, and evaluate how well each hunts down interesting regions. The aim is to turn blind knob-twiddling into a guided partnership between artist and algorithm.
arxiv-2512-16629:
