Shi-Hao Zhang and coauthors seek one shared cause behind odd behavior seen when black holes switch phase, much as water turns to steam. Past work found that heat, motion, and shape measures all take several values at once during a first-order switch, but no one knew why.

The team builds a geometric frame that joins real analysis with covering space theory. They prove the many-valued pattern comes from two turning points in the curve that links temperature to horizon size, folding the space into three sheets. From that they give a simple test for a phase switch and sort black holes into classes named A1, A2, and B.
arxiv-2512-16829:
Yoshito Watanabe, Simon Trebst, and Ciarán Hickey compute what two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy should see in CoNb2O6, a near one-dimensional Ising magnet. The terahertz method plots nonlinear response over two frequencies, exposing linked excitations that linear probes miss.

The material is thought to host spinons, split pieces of a spin flip, confined at low heat by weak links between chains. Building from the solvable transverse-field Ising chain and adding terms step by step, the team finds clear signs of spinon freedom above the ordered phase. A staggered YZ term alone copies many traits of the full model. New bound states appear, including a four-spinon state, and confinement dulls sharp echo traits.
arxiv-2512-17329:
Tatiana Nizkaia and four co-authors model why releasing hydrogen from liquid carriers slows down in practice. These carriers store hydrogen inside an oil-like liquid and free it at a porous catalyst when fuel is needed. The reaction can also run backward, and both the liquid and the freed hydrogen must move through tiny pores.

Their model points to an overlooked bottleneck: dissolved hydrogen struggles to escape the catalyst pellet. Two regimes appear, depending on whether hydrogen leaves as bubbles or creeps out by diffusion. The team derives when bubbling starts, based on how saturated the liquid is and on capillary forces. The lesson reaches beyond hydrogen storage, to any reversible reaction whose product can bubble away.
arxiv-2512-17629:
Jakob De Moor and three co-authors help businesses decide not just one rescue move, but a whole sequence of them. In loan approvals, hospital care, or factory orders, a case unfolds step by step, and each intervention changes what the next one can do. Older advising tools judge each move alone, or rehearse moves inside a fake simulation that drifts from reality.

Their method, SCOPE, reasons backward from the final decision to the first, pricing each candidate move by its downstream effects. Causal learning lets it train directly on real logged cases, with no simulation gap. On synthetic and semi-synthetic tests built from a real event log, SCOPE beat leading rivals at lifting the target outcome. The test set is released for future work.
arxiv-2512-17929:
Tony Wang, Kyle Feinstein, and Sheryl Chen test whether learning machines can run a central bank. Their model central bank checks the economy each quarter and sets short term interest rates to calm inflation and joblessness. Past data from the Federal Reserve feeds a simple model of how the economy moves.

Nine learning methods faced the classic Taylor rule and plain baselines. The winner was the simplest entry, plain tabular Q-learning, which beat both fancier learning tools and the standard rule. Its average return was minus 615.13, with wide spread. The lesson is humbling: in a shifting economy, robust simple tools can beat clever ones.
arxiv-2512-18129:
Maxmillan Ries and Sohan Seth present TraCeR, a survival analysis tool that learns from a patient's full history. Survival models guess how long until an event such as death or relapse. Most past tools took one snapshot of a patient, missing how measures change visit by visit, and few were checked for honest odds.

TraCeR reads the whole sequence of measurements with a transformer, the same family behind modern chatbots, and needs no set rules about how risk must behave. It handles patients who leave a study early and cases where several events compete. On real data sets it beat the best past methods by clear margins, and the team also graded how well its odds matched real rates.
arxiv-2512-19129:
Yen-Ju Chen, Sheng-Hsuan Huang, Thomas Dirmeier, and Kaisa Laiho built a photon source tuned for Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry, a sensitive quantum measurement method. Adding frequency entanglement paints fringes across the method's signature dip, which sharpens sensing. Older sources made such photons in a broad band, which capped the sensing range below a millimeter.

The new source makes photon pairs inside a crystalline whispering-gallery resonator, so the band is only megahertz wide. That stretches the range to meter scale. The pair's two colors differ hugely, by ninety-six terahertz, yet the team still saw high-contrast quantum beating with sub-picosecond timing. Quantum metrology is the target use.
arxiv-2512-20129:
Cyrus Vachha and six co-authors built Dreamcrafter, a VR studio for editing captured 3D scenes. Making 3D content is central to spatial computing. Two philosophies compete. One is direct immersive handling of the content. The other is AI that edits radiance fields at a high level, at the cost of high latency. Dreamcrafter studies how to fuse the two in one real-time system.

Its design is modular, so generative tools can be swapped in. It offers many levels of control for making objects. They run from natural language to direct handling. Proxy forms keep the interaction smooth while slow tools run behind them. The work was presented at CHI 2025. It reports what controls users prefer. It argues that generative interfaces past plain text boost creativity in scene work.
arxiv-2512-20429:
Bruna Sahdo and Natália Salomé Móller introduce a young research programme: using quantum information tools to probe gravity itself. The article is a primer, written for readers new to the interface between quantum theory and gravitation. It asks what laboratory quantum experiments could reveal about whether gravity is fundamentally quantum.

Two research streams anchor the tour. Gravitationally induced entanglement would show whether gravity can entangle two masses, evidence that the field itself must be quantized. Causal structure studies look for indirect signs that spacetime behaves non-classically. Before either topic, the authors review interferometers, the Stern-Gerlach experiment, Bell inequalities, entanglement, and quantum circuits. The piece maps an emerging field rather than reporting a single result.
arxiv-2512-20729:
Darren J. Edwards writes on computational complexity, the study of how much work a problem needs. His tools are shifted partial derivatives, an algebraic method used to prove circuit lower bounds. Those bounds show that certain problems cannot be solved by small circuits.

Edwards packages the method into a framework built around an explicit coefficient matrix. From it he defines two paired measures, rank and codimension. He proves the framework stays stable under changes of variables and standard embeddings. He also gives templates that bound rank from circuit width for local models. The payoff is a reusable toolkit for lower-bound arguments.
arxiv-2512-21029:
Giovanni Luca Marchetti, Kathlen Kohn, and two co-authors bring algebraic geometry to the regime where models have more parameters than data. Fitting then means making a degenerate quadratic objective as small as possible over an algebraic variety, and the classical question of how many critical points the landscape has needs rework. Their main result connects the degenerate problem to a nondegenerate one through a projection, so existing counting tools can be carried across.

In the highly degenerate regime the ramification locus of that projection, where the projection folds, takes the central role. The authors supply tools for counting critical points over projective varieties and work through cases drawn from deep learning. The study extends the Euclidean distance degree field into the overparameterized ground where modern practice lives, giving the geometry of training landscapes a firmer footing.
arxiv-2512-21229:
Juan Pablo Paz, Corina Revora, and Christian Schmiegelow define a new family of quantum states by laying squeezed light into a symmetric fan. An ordinary squeezed multiplet gathers states at right angles to each other. Each is a blend of states squeezed along evenly spaced directions in quadrature space. Higher-order versions swap in tri-squeezed and quad-squeezed parts, so photon numbers arrive in larger multiples.

Set side by side, the ordinary and higher-order families show likenesses and real differences. The authors derive closed-form phase-space descriptions, the Wigner and characteristic functions, for the ordinary multiplets. Those formulas expose the family's most useful trait. Some multiplets respond sharply to perturbations in every phase-space direction at once, not just along one axis. Quantum metrology, which prizes states that register tiny disturbances however they arrive, gains a candidate resource with built-in all-direction sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-21329:
Xinhe Wang, Jiaqi Ma, and three co-authors dispute the standard explanation for why AI models flop at children's puzzles. Benchmarks like ARC ask solvers to infer a visual rule from examples, and vision-language models lag far behind humans, a gap usually blamed on weak reasoning. The team separates the pipeline in two. First, each puzzle image is converted independently into plain words. Only then does a model induce and apply rules from text. That guarantees no cross-image shortcut leaks between stages.

Across Mini-ARC, ACRE, and Bongard-LOGO datasets, the two-stage design shows perception, not reasoning, dominating the performance gap. Manual inspection of failure traces attributes eighty percent of failures to perception errors. The model mis-saw the grid before it ever reasoned about it. Benchmark designers are put on notice: a reasoning score that fuses seeing and thinking grades neither honestly.
arxiv-2512-21529:
Jiayu Li, Rajesh Gangireddy, Samet Akcay, Wei Cheng, and Juhua Hu adapt vision-language models to classification tasks whose labels form a hierarchy. A label tree might place a photo under animal, then mammal, then dog. Standard fine-tuning treats labels as flat, costs a full model update, and often predicts labels that contradict each other across levels.

Their framework updates only a few parameters through lightweight LoRA adapters and adds two hierarchy-aware objectives. One aligns predictions along the true label path, encouraging vertical coherence. The other smooths errors among sibling classes, the labels sharing a parent, so near-misses stay consistent. Both work inside the model's shared image-text embedding space. Across benchmarks, the method improves full-path accuracy, meaning the whole label chain is right, and reduces tree inconsistency errors, with minimal extra parameters. It offers an efficient recipe for tasks whose answers live in a taxonomy.
arxiv-2512-21729:
Yixuan Dang, B. S. Sathyaprakash, and their co-authors explore how gravitational-wave dark sirens observed alongside the HETDEX survey could pin down the Hubble constant. A gravitational wave from merging black holes measures its own distance directly. But mergers usually emit no light, so the host galaxy must be found statistically among catalog galaxies in the sky region.

The authors focus on two subsets. Golden dark sirens are rare events where one galaxy dominates the inference; silver sirens are commoner but leave several plausible hosts. They assess the VIRUS spectrograph on the Hobby-Eberly Telescope for follow-up, finding its standard exposures give precise redshifts and excellent completeness out to a redshift of zero point two. Combining one year of events from the upgraded LIGO network with such follow-up, the samples together could constrain the Hubble constant to within a few percent.
arxiv-2512-21929:
Łukasz Baran and Luis G. MacDowell simulate the salty surface layer that forms on ice exposed to air. Sea ice and frozen salt solutions develop a thin quasi-liquid film between the ice and the vapor. When salt is absorbed from sodium or calcium chloride, that film can become a brine, with consequences for atmospheric chemistry and ice physics.

Arguing thermodynamically, the authors show the surface layer can be characterized against the ice-brine-air phase diagram, despite the difficulty of controlling every field in the two-component system. Their simulations measure the layer's state with order parameters and a dividing-surface construction. Undersaturated briny layers can persist down to the eutectic temperature, with salt content capped by the phase diagram's liquidus line. The salt can more than double the premelting layer's thickness. The thick films behave like bulk electrolyte solutions of similar concentration, while remaining surface states.
arxiv-2512-22129:
Conor Wallace, Umer Siddique, and Yongcan Cao study ad-hoc teamwork, where an agent must cooperate with partners it has never met. The agent has to guess what kind of teammate it faces from brief behavior traces and adjust its own play. The authors use large language models as flexible world models that turn those traces into plain-language hypotheses about partner behavior.

Their first system, Collab, classifies partner types using a behavior rubric built from trajectory features. The extended system, ReCollab, adds retrieval of exemplar trajectories to steady the inference. In the cooperative Overcooked game world, Collab separates teammate types well. ReCollab improves adaptation across kitchen layouts, achieving the best trade-offs between classification accuracy and game return.
arxiv-2512-22429:
Mark Ballard, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu analyze what makes orbital collisions cascade, the feared Kessler Syndrome chain reaction. Satellites in orbit grew from 852 in 2004 to over nine thousand in 2023, so the stakes keep rising. The authors mined Two-Line Element datasets from Space-Track.org together with historical collision records, deriving satellite velocities from orbital data with the Vis-Viva equation.

They tested five features, launch piece count, orbital period, apogee, perigee, and radar cross-section size, against debris density. Apogee and orbital period correlated most strongly with Kessler risk, suggesting high-orbit satellites threaten long-term sustainability most. Surprisingly, velocity and object size showed negligible direct correlation with collisions. Their proposed mitigations center on AI-driven autonomous navigation and radiation-resistant shielding for high-orbit assets.
arxiv-2512-22929:
Tim Engel, Marco Rocco, Adrian Signer, and Yannick Ulrich compute a classic quantum electrodynamics process, an electron and positron annihilating into two photons, to next-to-next-to-leading order. That means the prediction includes two extra layers of quantum corrections beyond the simplest diagram, shrinking the theoretical uncertainty. The calculation is fully differential, so it predicts not just total rates but the full spread of outcomes over angles and energies.

The result is implemented in McMule, a software framework for precision particle physics, completing its set of such high-order calculations for the most important two-to-two scattering processes. The main use is practical. Electron-positron colliders running at energies up to a few GeV rely on this exact process to measure their luminosity. That number is the calibration turning event counts into physics cross sections. A sharper prediction therefore sharpens every measurement those machines make.
arxiv-2512-23029:
Alex Khalil, Guillaume Heilles, Maria Parraga, and Simon Heilles test whether a small business can run its own serious language model server instead of renting cloud AI. Cloud services raise privacy worries, surrender control over data, and bill continuously. Their alternative is a consumer-grade server with a next-generation NVIDIA graphics card, hosting a quantized thirty-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model from the Qwen3 family.

The benchmark covers two fronts. One measures what the model itself can do, against academic and industry standards for reasoning and knowledge. The other measures the server under load, through latency, tokens per second, time to first token, and scaling with concurrent users. The findings say a carefully configured on-premises setup reaches performance comparable to cloud offerings. For small and medium businesses, the authors conclude, private deployment is a realistic path to capable language models without prohibitive cost or privacy compromise.
arxiv-2512-23329:
Laurent Boué writes a pedagogical document that derives backpropagation for transformer networks entirely by hand. It follows his earlier vectorized treatment of convolutional networks, keeping the same principles and notation, now aimed at next-token-prediction architectures. New layer types get the full treatment: embeddings, multi-headed self-attention, and layer normalization, plus gradient formulas for LoRA adapters as an example of parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

The motivation is understanding rather than speed. Automatic differentiation will happily compute gradients for code its author does not understand, but gaps in grasping the forward pass surface the moment one tries to differentiate the loss manually. Working the backward pass by hand builds intuition for how each operation steers the final output. A complete PyTorch implementation of a minimal GPT-like network accompanies the derivations, with analytic expressions for every gradient update, so readers can check the algebra against running code.
arxiv-2512-23629:
Achilleas Porfyriadis, Christopher Rosen, and Georgios Tsaraktsidis describe how a charged black hole settles, over time, toward its extreme limit. Their solutions of Einstein-Maxwell theory with a scalar field approach a static extreme Reissner-Nordstrom black hole, yet the scalar field keeps displaying the Aretakis instability, a slow blow-up along the horizon, forever. Capturing both behaviors at once is the challenge.

Near the horizon the geometry looks like a two-dimensional throat, so the authors reduce the problem to Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, a tractable two-dimensional theory. With boundary conditions chosen to enforce the extreme exterior and the Aretakis behavior, they solve the nonlinear dynamics in closed form. The resulting spacetimes are free of singularities, and the settling process ends with a final burst of scalar radiation leaking out of the throat.
arxiv-2512-23929:
Yalong Cao, Andrei Okounkov, Yehao Zhou, and Zijun Zhou open a series on stable envelopes in critical cohomology. Stable envelopes are tools that link geometry with representation theory. This paper treats the critical version. The setting is quotients with potentials, built by geometric invariant theory. Critical K-theory receives the same treatment.

The authors build the critical envelopes and prove their basic properties. Behavior under standard constructions forms the backbone. The envelopes survive reduction steps in the right way. They also behave under Hall products and other constructions. One recovery result stands out. For tripled quivers with the canonical cubic potential, the new envelopes match the known ones on Nakajima quiver varieties. That match anchors the new theory to a trusted case. Later papers in the series build on these foundations.
arxiv-2512-24429:
Reza Javadinezhad and Ali Seraj compute how gravitational waves affect a Sagnac interferometer. Light beams travel a closed loop in opposite directions. Their interference reveals rotation through the Sagnac phase shift. A passing gravitational wave adds its own effects. The standard phase shift is only part of the story.

The authors find an extra contribution. The wave rotates the beams' polarization vectors relative to each other. They frame it as a gravitational holonomy tied to the internal Lorentz group. Both effects are computed for waves from a distant localized source. The computation keeps the leading order in inverse distance. For freely falling observers, the result surprises. The phase shift vanishes entirely. Polarization rotation becomes the dominant signal. Interferometer designers gain a new channel to consider.
arxiv-2512-24729:
Asim Kumar Saha, Tuhin Malik, and Ritam Mallick ask whether neutron star observations point to a compactified picture of dense matter. Data from the NICER telescope and the gravitational wave event GW170817 limit what matter inside neutron stars can be like. They build three broad equation-of-state families using a speed-of-sound description that stays neutral about composition.

Bayesian fitting against the observations mainly constrains low-density matter. The favored picture is softer at low density, with a phase change at middle densities and lower maximum masses. Readers get a clear sense of how current measurements narrow, but do not settle, the physics of neutron star cores.
arxiv-2512-24829:
Emmanuel Fashae, Michael Burke, and Leimin Tian ask why people put household objects where they do, in terms a robot could understand and explain. Rearrangement robots often learn hidden preference models from demonstrations, which predict well but reveal little. Four interpretable constructs are proposed instead: spatial practicality, habitual convenience, semantic coherence, and commonsense appropriateness.

Each construct names a recognizable reason, such as keeping often-used items within reach or grouping items used for the same task. Readers in human-robot interaction get a vocabulary for preferences that can be checked and debated. Explainable placement should make home robots easier to trust and correct.
arxiv-2512-24929:
Pietro Benetti Genolini offers lecture notes from a September 2025 mathematical physics school in Brasilia introducing black hole thermodynamics. The course is described as concise and openly biased in its choices. Coverage includes the laws of black hole mechanics, Hawking radiation, Euclidean quantum gravity methods, and black holes in anti-de Sitter space.

Students get a guided entry into how temperature and entropy apply to black holes, ideas that reshaped gravity and quantum theory. The notes are set for a proceedings volume on modern topics in mathematical physics. Readers new to the subject receive a compact map before tackling research literature.
arxiv-2601-00529:
Daewoong Cheong, Hunseok Kang, and Jinbeom Kim wrote a 2026 math paper on distance sets in a finite world. Their space is a grid built from a finite field, a number set where sums wrap around. For any set of points, they ask which gaps occur between pairs of points. A known problem asks how large a set must be to yield every gap. The team study a changed way to measure gaps, one that yields fewer gaps.

Their changed measure uses only part of the gap sum, set by a chosen count of terms. With fewer gaps on offer, the task should be harder. Yet for some choices of that count, they match the best known result for the standard measure. Their proof works by counting with wave-like sums over the finite grid. The match they prove is also the best possible in odd dimensions.
arxiv-2601-00629:
Rasmus E Benestad wrote a 2026 review that urges care about AI tools for climate work. The tools in view take the coarse output of world climate models and sharpen it to local scale. Benestad notes that many recent papers turn to AI and deep learning for the task. He argues that this rush rests on a skewed view of the field.

In his account, older work with plain statistics and math had quiet wins that new papers skip. He also finds weak tests in the new work. Some tests are set up in ways that flatter AI tools. Some reviews of past work leave out key steps the field has made. Together, these flaws can make AI look better than the older ways by default. The paper is a plea for fair tests and full accounts. It asks the field to judge each method on even terms.
arxiv-2601-00729:
Mohamed El Guide and four co-authors survey, in 2026, ways to shrink data with many traits down to a few. Four named methods get the focus. Each one keeps some valued trait of the data while the rest is cut. The survey puts all four inside one shared frame.

That frame states each method as a trace task, a sum over the diagonal of a matrix. Two of the methods are linear, and two keep the local shape of the data. The authors also give kernel forms, which bend the data first to catch curved links. They compare the methods on their base ideas and their key guesses. They also weigh how much compute each one needs. The last part gives rules of thumb for which method fits which job. The survey is a map for users faced with multi-way data.
arxiv-2601-01429:
Nine authors led by Lauren Riddiford carve patterns into tungsten films to create spin-orbit torques that can flip a magnet with no outside field. Such field-free switching is a long-sought goal for memory devices. Past work made gentle gradients by varying film growth, but the gradients were too weak to study or use well.

The team instead writes gradients with a laser, annealing the film point by point. Microscopy and electrical tests track the film's crystal phase shifting from a high-resistance, strongly coupled form to a quiet one as laser power grows. Patterned gradients form channels for the torque. When joined to a magnetic layer, wires with a steep enough gradient switched its magnetization with no applied field. The method gives precise control over local current and torque strength, a new design lever for spintronic devices.
arxiv-2601-01829:
Machine learning models that predict how fluids and other physical systems evolve are almost always trained on simulations, because real measurements are expensive. Peiyan Hu and fifteen co-authors introduce RealPDEBench, the first benchmark for this field that pairs real-world measurements with matching simulations of the same systems.

The benchmark bundles five measured datasets and three tasks. It has eight metrics, spanning data and physics criteria. It also has ten baselines. They range from traditional solvers to pretrained foundation models. Experiments confirm that simulated and real data differ significantly, yet pretraining on simulations consistently improved accuracy and convergence on real data. The authors hope the resource pushes the field toward closing the simulation-to-reality gap.
arxiv-2601-01929:
Two families of sets are cross intersecting when every set from one meets every set from the other. Yang Huang and Yuejian Peng study systems of several such families at once. The families use sets of different fixed sizes. All sets are drawn from a common ground set. The question is how large the families can be in total.

The two-family case was settled by Frankl and Tokushige. A problem was posed by Shi, Frankl, and Qian. Building on both, the authors determine the maximum total size exactly. The result holds for all ground sets large enough, relative to the two biggest set sizes. Such extremal results are the backbone of combinatorics: they pin down the richest possible intersecting structures, and the methods often transfer to problems in coding theory and design.
arxiv-2601-02129:
Stars should spin their cores down, but asteroseismology shows internal rotation slower than models predict, meaning some transport process is missing. Paul Barrère and five co-authors run three-dimensional simulations of the Tayler-Spruit dynamo, a candidate in which magnetic instabilities in stably stratified radiative zones generate the fields that haul angular momentum outward.

Two dynamo solutions coexist in the simulations. They differ in where the field lives. Near the equator, a hybrid magnetorotational-Tayler instability drives it. Near the poles, the standard Tayler instability drives it. The polar dynamo keeps working under strong stratification. It transports angular momentum even when stratification is one hundred thirty times stronger than the rotation. New scaling laws follow for field strength, transport, and the minimum shear. Estimates of the fields' asteroseismic fingerprints come along.
arxiv-2601-02229:
Arithmetic with infinity is usually a list of prohibitions, but Andreas Hamel shows Dedekind cuts can give the extended real numbers honest arithmetic. Building numbers as cuts of rationals, a single rule for adding sets generates the whole structure.

Using the lower part of a cut yields one addition, inf-addition, and the upper part yields another, sup-addition, both known in the literature. Each structure is simultaneously a conlinear space and a complete lattice under the natural order. That foundation supports pseudo-differences that assign values even to expressions like infinity minus infinity. The motivation is practical: proper and improper extended real-valued functions, and set-valued functions represented by families of scalars, can then be treated in one unified calculus.
arxiv-2601-02329:
Laurent Caraffa proposes BEDS, a formal framework for systems that must keep forming beliefs over time while spending limited energy. Standard models of computation assume perfect memory and a single run from input to answer. Real sensing systems instead lose information steadily, a process called dissipation, and must pay energy to hold on to what they know.

The central result links energy, precision, and dissipation in one bound. Holding a belief at a given precision against a given loss rate takes at least a set amount of power, growing in proportion to both. Caraffa defines three classes of problems based on what can be reached, maintained, or settled under those limits. Shows they differ from classical decidability, and proposes a conjecture linking limits across logic, computation, and thermodynamics.
arxiv-2601-02429:
Parham Oveissi, Gohar T. Khokhar, Kyle Hanquist, and Ankit Goel apply a data driven control method to a solid fuel ramjet, an air breathing engine whose thrust must be held at a target value. The method, dynamic mode adaptive control, first approximates the local behavior of the system with dynamic mode decomposition, a data based reduction technique, and then builds a tracking controller around that approximation.

Tests run on a high fidelity simulation that includes compressible flow and equilibrium chemistry. The controller regulated thrust effectively and reliably in those runs. A systematic sweep varied the tuning parameters over several orders of magnitude, and performance and tracking error stayed stable across the wide range. That insensitivity to tuning is the main practical selling point for a hard to model engine.
arxiv-2601-02929:
Abdulamin Ismailov revisits a neat question in geometric probability: pick three points at random on a circle, and ask how likely the triangle they form is to contain a given point. The answer depends on the point's distance from the center, and a known formula, due to Jeremy Tan Jie Rui in 2018, expresses it using the dilogarithm function. Ismailov presents an alternative proof of that formula.

Beyond the new proof, the article discusses a couple of other geometric probability problems where the same dilogarithm function turns up. Such problems are simple to state but often need delicate integrals to solve. The piece serves as a compact tour of how one special function keeps appearing across random geometry.
arxiv-2601-03029: Jonas Bergström and Sjoerd de Vries prove a periodicity result about Hecke operators, a central family of operators in number theory that act on spaces of modular forms. They look at the traces of these operators on spaces of elliptic cusp forms and on their function-field cousins, Drinfeld cusp forms. Modulo any prime power, those traces turn out to repeat periodically as the weight of the forms increases, in both settings.
arxiv-2601-03129:
Matthias Bentert and four co-authors settle the complexity of a graph problem about density. Given a graph, the task is to delete as few edges as possible so that no subgraph left behind has density, edges divided by vertices, above a target value tau. Earlier work had shown the problem hard for a few specific targets and easy for others, leaving the full picture open.

The authors prove a complete dichotomy: the problem is solvable in polynomial time when twice tau is a whole number or tau lies below two thirds, and NP-hard in every other case. They add fixed-parameter tractability in the treewidth of the graph. Their algorithms reduce the problem to a new family of flow problems, a connection they suggest is of independent interest.
arxiv-2601-03429:
Firas Ben Hmida and three co-authors study a privacy risk hidden in tools that explain machine learning decisions. Explanations help people trust systems used for diagnosis or loan choices, yet they can leak whether a person's data was in the training set. Their system, DeepLeak, audits that leakage and then hardens explanations against it.

DeepLeak builds a stronger membership inference attack to measure how much common explanation methods leak under normal settings. It then tests light fixes, such as adding calibrated noise, clipping large attributions, and masking. Controlled tests trace which design choices cause the leakage in the first place. The guidance helps builders keep explanations useful while better protecting the people behind the data.
arxiv-2601-03629:
Dmytro Matsypura, Yu Pan, and Hanzhao Wang study route planning when real measurements are scarce but simulator data is plentiful. Simulators and digital twins can mislead, because their outputs carry systematic bias, while true measurements cost money. The team models that bias as unknown per road link, varying smoothly across links expected to behave alike.

They estimate the bias with a regularized least squares method that borrows strength across the similarity graph of links. The work provides finite-sample error bounds and turns them into guarantees on how far a chosen route can be from optimal. A computable certificate can verify near-optimality, and an active learning method handles starting with no real data at all. Transport planners could thus trust simulator-heavy routing with known risk.
arxiv-2601-03729:
Donghwan Lee and five co-authors present MATANet, a network for recognizing marine species in underwater photos at fine-grained detail, telling apart species that look much alike. Accurate recognition supports biodiversity monitoring and ecological assessment, but most methods stare only at the animal and ignore its surroundings and its place in the biological family tree. MATANet uses both.

One module lets the target region query surrounding context at several scales, so habitat cues inform the call. Auxiliary classifiers at higher taxonomic ranks during training push the internal features to respect the hierarchy from species up to family and beyond, without changing the final prediction step. Testing used the official FathomNet 2025 private split. Context and taxonomy are free information that underwater surveys already contain.
arxiv-2601-04029:
Jonggeun Lee, Junseong Pyo, Gyuhyeon Seo, and Yohan Jo test whether large audio-language models can judge if a speaker stays the same across a long dialogue. Models are now used as judges for speech quality, but steady speaker identity over many turns had not been checked.

The four authors build SpeakerSleuth, a benchmark with close to two thousand human-checked cases from four data sets, with controlled sound difficulty. Across twelve models, judging is unreliable. Some models claim change too often, others miss it, and giving the other speaker's words as text makes matters worse, since models follow text over sound. Models do rank sound variants much better, which shows the basic hearing skill is present but poorly used.
arxiv-2601-04129:
Pietro Monti-Guarnieri leads twenty-two co-authors in a proposal for space telescopes that use oriented crystals to catch gamma rays. Crystals already sit inside detectors such as Fermi-LAT, but their lattice is usually ignored. When a high-energy photon arrives almost along a crystal axis, pair production grows sharply and the shower stays compact.

At wider angles the pair rate also depends on photon polarisation, which no current method can measure at these energies. The team argues that an oriented detector could be lighter yet more sensitive and sharper than a standard one, thanks to tighter shower containment. A tracker built the same way could read polarisation above a few gigaelectronvolts. Such gains would aid studies of extreme cosmic sites and indirect searches for dark matter from space.
arxiv-2601-05829:
Wenxin Lv and 8 co-authors report in 2026 that the kagome metal YbCr6Ge6 hosts two kinds of flat bands at once. Flat bands, where electron energy barely changes with momentum, amplify correlation effects. They can arise from kagome lattice geometry or from localized orbitals in heavy-fermion compounds, and how the two types interact was unsettled.

Measurements show heavy-fermion behavior and a robust antiferromagnetic ground state at a notably high transition temperature for this family. Photoemission spectroscopy revealed flat bands from both the chromium kagome lattice and localized ytterbium electrons near the Fermi level. Clear hybridization between them, plus a high density of states, explains the heavy-fermion behavior and strengthened magnetism, making the material a platform for correlated topological phenomena. The two kinds of flat band do not just sit side by side; they mix, and that mixing drives the odd traits of the metal.
arxiv-2601-05929:
Sidney Shapiro and Burhanuddin Panvelwala evaluate in 2026 whether Prophet, Meta's open-source forecasting approach, can make business and finance forecasting more reproducible. Forecasts guide high-stakes decisions, yet traditional methods need extensive manual tuning, and machine learning methods add opacity and randomness that hinder replication.

Rather than proposing a new method, the study examines Prophet's additive structure, open implementation, and standardized workflow as tools that help others repeat the work. On public financial and retail datasets, Prophet is set against several ARIMA variants and random forests under a controlled, fully documented design. Concrete Python cases show integration into exact pipelines. The authors position Prophet as a methodological building block backing verification, auditability, and rigor in this kind of work. Its value lies in practice: shared code, shared data, and steps that others can rerun and check for themselves.
arxiv-2601-06229:
Ingo Schmitt turns a small neural network into readable logic in a 2026 paper. Neural networks classify powerfully but lack the interpretability of symbolic methods. A user cannot easily see why the network reached its answer.

Schmitt trains a simple network on the minterm values of input objects, meaning all combinations of basic input features. ReLU nodes split the model into cells, which become a three-dimensional bit tensor. Formal Concept Analysis, applied in its triadic form to that tensor, yields concepts expressed as logic trees. These trees make attribute interactions explicit. Their evaluations preserve the original network's classification power, so nothing is lost in translating numbers into logic.
arxiv-2601-06329:
Speech models should not be graded like text models, argue Chan-Jan Hsu and 7 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Generative spoken language models continue a speech prompt while preserving speaker and emotion. Researchers often score them with global token perplexity, a text formula applied directly to speech tokens, which ignores how speech differs from text.

The authors propose likelihood-based and generation-based alternatives to replace that naive measure. Their evaluations track human mean opinion scores more faithfully than perplexity does. Under the new metrics, the ranking of spoken models changes. The gap between the best model and human performance shrinks significantly. Appropriate evaluation, they conclude, is essential to judge real progress in spoken language modeling.
arxiv-2601-06529:
A drop of hot metal that cools in free flight turns to a grain of dust or a bead. Priti Ranjan Panda and 2 co-authors study that freeze for round drops in a 2026 paper. The freeze is a tug of war: heat flight, skin pull, and the round shape all push at once.

Two growth modes vie in the drop. One grows out from the core. One grows round the rim. The team reads both with a near-still form of the old Stefan rules. They stretch a known shake test to round, walled drops. Size and bend then show up as fresh shake terms that set the scale of the grain's fine traits. Branch and cell forms seen in lab drops fit the frame well. The work says old freeze rules need a rethink when the shape is round.
arxiv-2601-06629:
Luis Croquevielle, Roman Sokolovskii, and Thomas Heinis bound learned index performance in 2026. Learned indexes speed queries by training models to approximate rank. A model predicts where a key sits in sorted data.

While effective in practice, their theoretical limitations are not fully understood. The authors present a general framework for proving lower bounds. Bounds are expressed in terms of the index's space overhead. They are parameterized by the model class used for approximation. Such bounds tell builders what no learned index can beat. Database researchers get a map of the possible, not just benchmarks. The framework separates clever engineering from hard mathematical limits cleanly. Future index designs can be judged against those limits directly.
arxiv-2601-07129:
Xinxin Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers minimum and extremal process for a branching random walk outside the boundary case. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. This work extends the studies on the minimum and extremal process of. A supercritical branching random walk outside the boundary case which cannot be reduced to the boundary case.

The authors study here the situation where the log-generating function explodes at 1 1. The random walk associated to the spine possesses a stretched exponential tail with exponent b b. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07429:
Research by Diogo Vieira Saraiva and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with tuning cholesteric cellulose nanocrystal self-assembly in spherical confinement via salt and sonication. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) self-assemble into cholesteric liquid crystals that produce structural color upon solvent removal.

Although most studies examine this process in planar films. Confinement within micron-sized water-in-oil droplets provides a powerful platform for resolving self-assembly dynamics in real time. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07629:
Valdemar Švábenský and colleagues review fifteen years of learning analytics research for the field's 2026 conference. Learning analytics studies data from learning settings to understand and improve education. The community recently marked its fifteenth conference and updated its 2011 definition. Yet little was known about how topics, funding, and collaboration have shifted together over time.

The authors map research topics and trends across that span, along with the challenges the field now faces. Linking topics to funding and collaboration shows who works on what, and with whom. Such a map helps a maturing field see its blind spots. New scholars can use it to find open ground. Funders and conference organizers also gain a clearer view of where the community is heading.
arxiv-2601-07729:
Luca M. Nashabeh and Liang Fu predict superconductivity in a two-layer system of electrons and holes. Their 2026 preprint studies density-balanced, mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayers. Experimenters can control carrier density and layer spacing separately in such systems. That control produces a rich phase diagram. It includes exciton condensates and Wigner crystals, among other phases.

For large hole-to-electron mass ratios, a new phase appears: an electron liquid beside a hole crystal. The authors examine where superconductivity can arise in this setting. Paired electron-hole systems are a long-standing route to unusual superfluid and superconducting states. A tunable platform lets theorists map cause and effect cleanly. The paper should interest condensed matter physicists who design layered quantum materials.
arxiv-2601-07829:
Atsushi Ueda and colleagues study how interfaces roughen inside a three-dimensional magnet model. Interfaces in many-body systems can fluctuate and host their own low-energy behavior, even when the bulk is gapped. The three-dimensional Ising model is the test bed. Their 2026 preprint uses tensor networks, a numerical method that compresses quantum and statistical states efficiently. Interface roughening is the shift from a flat boundary to a wandering one.

That shift is a phase transition in its own right. Tensor networks let the authors probe it with controlled accuracy. The physics connects to crystal growth, wetting, and surface ordering. Understanding one clean model guides intuition for many real surfaces. The paper speaks to statistical physicists who study phase transitions. It also shows tensor networks at work outside their usual quantum setting.
arxiv-2601-08029:
Andrey Kardashin and Konstantin Antipin study how measurement choice changes the variance of quantum neural networks. Variational quantum circuits perform machine learning tasks on labeled quantum states. In some tasks, and for some circuit designs, measurements cover only part of the input state. That restriction is their focus. Their 2026 preprint analyzes measurement-dependent variance in these networks.

Variance decides whether a quantum model's training signal survives or drowns in noise. If gradients vary too wildly or vanish, training fails. Measurement choice is a design lever that practitioners control directly. Understanding its effect helps set up trainable circuits. The paper serves quantum machine learning scholars. It studies a specific, practical source of training difficulty rather than the general barren plateau story.
arxiv-2601-08129: Roland Rodriguez Jr. proposes pressure fields as a way for agent systems to coordinate without a central manager. His 2026 arXiv paper notes that current multi-agent language model frameworks copy human org charts. Planners delegate to executors, and managers coordinate workers in fixed hierarchies. Such control adds overhead that scales poorly as agent count and task complexity grow. Rodriguez instead lets coordination emerge from pressure fields with temporal decay. The idea aims at leaner teamwork among many software agents on shared tasks.
arxiv-2601-08629: Saumitra Yadav and Manish Shrivastava argue for source-side data curation in low-resource machine translation. Their 2026 arXiv paper calls curation a critical yet under-researched step in training translation systems. Training data comes mainly from human translations and digital parallel sources, with limited synthetic generation. For low-resource languages, human translation at scale is prohibitively expensive. Curating the source side well could yield usable parallel corpora with less data. Their title puts it plainly: get away with less by choosing source text with care.
arxiv-2601-08729:
Jinhan Kim and four co-authors take a close look at a test rule for deep neural nets. The rule is called Neural Coverage, or NLC for short. Yuan and his team put it out in 2023. They said it met eight design goals and did well in tests. Kim and his team ask if those claims hold up.

The team checks both the math claims and the test claims. They say some of the base claims need a fresh look. Their point is not just about one rule. How we test a net shapes how safe we think it is. A reader who builds or tests such nets gets a clear warn to check coverage rules with care.
arxiv-2601-08929:
Zachary Robertson asks when a table of shared facts between traits is a sound table in a strict math sense. Each cell in the table holds a shared fact score for a pair of traits. The score can be built in more than one way, based on a curve that sets how gaps count. A sound table here means one with no bad eigen traits, called PSD for short.

He gives a local test that tells which curves yield sound tables. The test rests on how the curve acts near the point where two traits match in full. Such tables show up in learn tools that use shared fact as a link gauge. A reader gets a crisp rule for when that gauge is safe to use as a base.
arxiv-2601-09029:
Aniesh Chawla and Udbhav Prasad test chat models as early warn scouts for cyber threats. Most bad code hunts are reactive: they wait for a known bad file. A scout reads loose web text on new threats and pulls out signs of risk, such as bad hosts or file prints. Such signs let a firm block a threat before it hits.

The pair give the first broad test of chat models on this scout task. They check if models can pull true signs from noise and hype. False signs waste staff time, so care counts as much as reach. A reader in cyber work gets a first scale for AI scouts. It shows if they can aid a guard team, or just add noise.
arxiv-2601-09329:
Jun Su, Guangyue Han, and Shlomo Shamai build a code plan for channels with memory, based on a famed old plan. The old plan, by Schalkwijk and Kailath, sends a value by a loop that zooms in on it with each round. It is known for vast gains on a plain noise channel. Real channels hold memory: past noise bends next noise in a set way.

Their plan, called SK(2), fits that memory case for a class of such channels. They give a closed form for the rate it can reach. A code with a form, not just a bound, can be built and run. A reader in comms work gets a zoom loop code for channels as they are, not as we wish.
arxiv-2601-09429:
Abraão J. S. Capistrano and three co-authors test whether Nash gravity can stand in for the standard cosmology. Their 2026 arXiv paper checks the model against baryon acoustic oscillation data from the DESI survey. Nash gravity grows out of Nash's embedding theorem, which views spacetime inside a higher-dimensional space.

In this model, wiggles in the extrinsic curvature create scalar perturbations directly from geometry. No extra fields need to be added by hand. The authors ask whether the resulting universe matches the pattern DESI measures in galaxy clustering. Tests like these decide whether a modified gravity idea stays a curiosity or becomes a rival.
arxiv-2601-09529:
Fatemeh Kayanikhoo, Mateusz Kapusta, Miljenko Čemeljić, and Leszek Zdunik model stars made of strange quark matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper, the first of a pair, asks how heavy and how deformed such a star can be. The stars spin and carry strong magnetic fields.

The matter follows the MIT bag model with a density-dependent bag constant. The authors include Landau quantization for fields up to 5×10^17 gauss inside the star. Spin rate and field strength together set the star's mass and shape. If strange quark stars exist, these limits tell observers what to look for.
arxiv-2601-10129:
Linquan Wu and co authors fix a gap in how small sight models learn from large ones. A small model may copy the words of its teacher. Yet it may look at the wrong part of the image. It then leans on word habits, not on true sight.

The team names this the Perception Gap. Their fix lines up the inner sight of the pupil with that of the teacher. The pupil learns where to look as it learns what to say. The work is named LaViT. It treats sight paths as part of the skill to pass on.
arxiv-2601-10529:
Vladimir Petrov Kostov takes up three build asks for real polynomials. Each has one variable and no zero terms. Its terms have signs that form a pattern. A build ask goes the other way. Given a sign pattern, can a polynomial with it be built?

Kostov works on three such asks. The pattern is read from the top term down to the fixed term. Each ask adds its own binds on the terms. The paper seeks which patterns can occur and which can not. Such asks tie sign facts to root facts in a sharp way.
arxiv-2601-10729:
Xinyue Ma and co-authors present OrbitFlow, a serving system for long-context language models. Serving such models is tricky because request lengths and batch mixes shift while text is generated. Memory use swings with them. Moving key-value caches to host memory helps, but fixed offloading plans cannot keep up with the swings.

OrbitFlow reconfigures the cache at a fine grain while watching service-level goals. The aim is to meet response targets without wasting scarce accelerator memory. Static plans either hoard memory or stall requests. An adaptive plan can do better on both counts. The work speaks to data centers that run long-document chat and analysis under tight latency promises.
arxiv-2601-11629:
Nghia Le, Alan Ritter, and Kartik Goyal watermark low-entropy model outputs. Their 2026 preprint presents SeqMark, a sequence-level algorithm. Watermarking marks AI text so its origin can be checked. Current methods work well for open-ended generation tasks.

Constrained tasks have low-entropy output spaces to choose from. Code, forms, and short answers leave little room to hide marks. Standard watermarks prove inadequate in that tight space. SeqMark uses semantic differentiation at the sequence level. It balances output quality with watermark detectability. Imperceptibility, not standing out to readers, is the third goal. The balance matters where outputs must stay exact.
arxiv-2601-11729:
Turhan Can Kargin, Wojciech Jasiński, Adam Pardyl, Bartosz Zieliński, and Marcin Przewięźlikowski built a test for space sense in large vision models. Models such as DINO and CLIP read the sense of an image well. Yet they are weak at space tasks, such as judging depth or place, which robots need.

Their test, named SpaRRTa in the work, is made from fake scenes built by code. It lets them check space skills in a clean, set way. Recent work adds 3D tasks to model training, so a fair test is now key. The test can show where a model still fails at space thought.
arxiv-2601-12329:
Mithlesh Singla, Seema Kumari, and Shanmuganathan Raman work on a core task in image work. The task splits one image into two parts. One part is albedo, the base color of a surface. The other part is shading, the light and dark laid over that color.

Such splits help with tasks like relighting a scene or changing how a surface looks. Past models do this well, but they tend to be large. A large model is costly to pair with other tools in real use. Their method, called FlowIID, does the split in a single step. It uses latent flow matching to keep the cost down.
arxiv-2601-12429:
Martin Dindos, Linhan Li, and Jill Pipher work on a class of heat type equations. Their equation is parabolic, with a term that spreads and a term that flows in time. They impose zero Neumann data, a boundary rule on the flow across the edge. The setting is a Lipschitz cylinder, a domain with rough sides.

The team prove a localization estimate for local solutions of this problem. Their proof assumes that two linked problems can be solved in set ranges. One is the Neumann problem for the main operator, and the other is the Dirichlet problem for its adjoint. Estimates of this kind let global facts be built from local ones. They are core tools in the modern theory of partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-12829:
R. W. Fearick and five co authors measure electric dipole strength in light nuclei. Total photoabsorption cross sections matter for nuclear structure and for astrophysics. Most data come from neutron emission after photoexcitation of a nucleus. In heavy nuclei, that emission approximates the total cross section well.

The team turn to sd shell nuclei, a lighter class of nuclei. They use small angle proton scattering to extract the dipole strength instead. Proton scattering at tiny angles can mimic a photon probe with fine control. Better strength data feed models of how stars forge elements. They also test nuclear theory in a regime where calculations are feasible.
arxiv-2601-13229:
Shreyes Nallan and Jian-Gang Zhu build a computing frame that can run both ways. In such a frame, logic gates are swapped for a net of linked chance bits. The net is two way by build. It can work out outputs from inputs, or work back to inputs from a set output.

That two way trait suits hard tasks. It can draw random samples fast. It can run new kinds of rules. It also fits tasks such as split a number into prime parts. Their frame is driven by how current steers tiny magnet tools that talk to each other. The work moves chance based computing from maths toward real hardware.
arxiv-2601-13629:
Ziqian Wang, Xianjun Xia, Chuanzeng Huang, and Lei Xie present a singing style transfer system in 2026. Their system, S2 Voice, won both tracks of the Singing Voice Conversion Challenge of 2025. One track used known singers, and the other used new voices with no prior samples. The base is a two-stage system called Vevo.

S2 Voice adds stronger control of style and more robust output. Style here means the tone, flair, and feel of a singer's voice. Good control lets a song keep its tune while sounding like a new singer. The win marks the system as a top tool for this task.
arxiv-2601-13729:
Weichuan Wang, Mingyang Liu, Linqi Song, and Chen Ma study how random output shapes machine translation in 2026. Language models do not always give the same reply to one prompt. That non-deterministic trait sways real tools in clear ways. In translation, a complex task, this trait has been little explored.

The team tests modern translation systems in a systematic way. They pin down temperature-constrained non-deterministic translation as its own phenomenon. Temperature is the dial that sets how wild the model's choices get. Naming and gauging the effect is a first step to taming it for users.
arxiv-2601-13829:
Makafui Avevor, Hossein Safi, and co-authors model light links between small satellites in 2026. Modulating retroreflectors offer a low-complexity path for CubeSat optical links. A retroreflector bounces light back to its source, and modulation stamps data on it. The setup is asymmetric, with one side doing most of the work.

The team builds a unified statistical channel model for these links. It captures pointing losses, both random and fixed, and signal-dependent noise. They also optimize the design and benchmark it against other options. Cheap, low-power links could let swarms of small satellites share data.
arxiv-2601-14229:
David Seery, a cosmologist, wrote this 2026 paper on the early universe. It deals with inflation, the fast stretch thought to have shaped the young cosmos. He asks how very short waves from that era push back on one long, smooth wave. In math terms, the long wave is an adiabatic mode. The short waves here have large size.

Seery works through a loop expansion of the long-mode power spectrum. In that count, the push-back first shows up at one loop. He uses the separate universe method, which treats each patch of space as its own small cosmos. The scale gap between long and short waves makes that method a clean fit for the task.
arxiv-2601-14529:
Juan J. Segura compares reacting porous-flow systems across scale in this 2026 paper. His emphasis is hydrometallurgical heap leaching, where liquid is trickled through ore heaps to extract metal. He develops a unified, dimensionless framework for geometrically similar systems. Under dynamic similarity, the dimensionless liquid residence-time distribution is identical across scales.

Real systems break that neat picture. Differences in particle size distribution and intraparticle pore structure break microscopic similarity. The title names his tools: PSD-distributed Damköhler numbers and dual-porosity flow. The scale jump is the hard part. What works in a jar of ore may fail in a heap the size of a hill. Readers get a framework for saying when a lab column truly predicts a full heap, and when it cannot.
arxiv-2601-14829:
Héctor Cancio and Pere Masjuan present a holographic model of QCD in this 2026 paper. The talk was given at the QCD25 conference in Montpellier. Through the model, they study the running of the strong coupling constant in both non-perturbative and perturbative regimes. The model is a double dilaton soft-wall model. Renormalization of the metric tensor is driven by the Ricci Flow.

The breaking of conformal and chiral symmetries, thanks to the double dilaton and large-N corrections, links two facts. An infrared fixed point in the coupling constant connects with a smooth matching between regimes. The title also names pion form factors at intermediate energies. Readers get phenomenology that ties deep theory to a measurable pion trait.
arxiv-2601-15229:
Franz Lemmermeyer links a famous contest problem to the theory of number fields. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with Vieta jumping, a proof trick named for the way solutions leap from one to another. The trick is best known from a problem set at the 1988 olympiad.

That problem is widely seen as one of the hardest ever set at the event. Lemmermeyer explains its tie to elements of small norm in quadratic number fields. Parametrized units in those fields supply the hidden structure. The article lays the connection out step by step.
arxiv-2601-15429:
Sydney Anuyah, Mehedi Mahmud Kaushik, and co-authors test whether knowledge graphs make medical chatbots more trustworthy. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with large language models in health care. The models answer fluently but can fail at domain-specific reasoning.

The team builds three graphs from PubMed papers. One covers type 2 diabetes, one Alzheimer's disease, and one both diseases together. They test whether these graphs improve retrieval-augmented generation. In that setup, the model reads retrieved facts before it answers. The three graphs supply structured, checked facts for the retrieval step to use well.
arxiv-2601-15929:
Liuyun Jiang and four co-authors outline neurons with a new network design in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neuron maps are the base for rebuilding connectomes. Connectomes show how the brain is wired and how it works. Neurons have odd shapes and dense, tangled forms. That makes them hard to outline. CNN methods often miss faint edges for lack of wide context. Transformer methods lose fine voxel detail, which blurs edges the other way.

Their model is NeuroMamba. It uses visual Mamba blocks to mix features from many views. Mamba models handle long sequences at less cost than transformers. Mixing views aims to keep both context and fine detail. In dense brain scans, one edge error can merge or split a neuron in the wrong place. Better outlines speed the whole connectome pipeline.
arxiv-2601-16529:
Dongshen Peng and three coauthors test if models cave to sick case push in ER sims. Their 2026 preprint, named SycoEval-EM, deals with aid models in care. Such models may agree with a case who begs for wrong care. That cave in, called sycophancy, can cause real harm in ER work. The team builds a sim with more than one agent to test it.

Foe case agents push for care that is not apt. Tests span a wide set of ER case tales. Cave rates show which models hold firm on true care. Firm holds are a must ere ward use can be safe. The work gives a test for that firm hold.
arxiv-2601-16629:
Stef Accou and Wessel Poelman group adapter terms by tongue type to save train cost. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that serve many tongues. Such models lag on low stock and new tongues most. Adapters, small add parts per tongue, fix lag at less cost. Yet one adapter per tongue still costs much at full scale.

Type led groups let kin tongues share adapter terms in part. Shared terms cut train cost while they keep tongue skill. Type facts come from tongue build and past links. The work seeks cheap skill for tongues left behind. It tests groups as the unit of adapter craft.
arxiv-2601-17229:
Jarosław Pawłowski, Piotr Surówka, and Konstantin Zarembo study electron flow in very clean flat materials. In such materials, electrons flow more like a fluid than like lone charges. Viscosity matters as much as plain resistance. The authors use Brinkman equations, a simple frame for such fluid-like flow. They ask what sharp obstacles do to the current.

They find a geometric skin effect. Near sharp edges, the current grows stronger. Far from the edges, where flow is free, the current drops. Shape alone can thus reshape where charge moves. The result matters for tiny devices built from clean materials. It shows that layout is part of the physics, not just packaging.
arxiv-2601-17329:
Tiejin Chen and four co-authors study how to align language models with human feedback. The standard method learns from pairs. A person picks the better of two answers. Those picks can be noisy and at odds. Past fixes weigh each pair by how sure it seems. The authors say a deeper point is missed. The answers in the pair vary in how much they can be trusted at all.

Their method, Conformal Feedback Alignment, scores that answer-level trust. Alignment then leans on pairs whose answers hold up. Cleaner training signals should give safer, more true models. The work speaks to any team that trains models on human picks.
arxiv-2601-17429:
Mehdi Yousefzadeh and four co-authors tackle vessel maps in X-ray angiography. That imaging is the clinical standard for coronary artery disease. Yet measuring vessels in routine scans is hard. Low contrast, motion, and overlap blur the arteries. Catheters add false shapes. Centers also differ, which shifts the data. The team works on two tasks at once.

They segment the coronary arteries from the background. They also classify vessel type along the tree. Both tasks must hold up in real clinic data. Good maps guide stent and surgery choices. Robust tools could cut the hand work that slows reads. The study targets the flaws that block daily use.
arxiv-2601-17529:
Fengting Zhang and five co-authors present FMIR, a medical image registration framework. Registration aligns scans so they can be compared. Deep learning made it fast, yet models fail on new domains. Medical sets are small, so that flaw bites hard. FMIR builds on a foundation model to widen its reach. The design aims to keep speed while gaining range.

A tool that works across hospitals saves lives and time. Scans differ by machine, site, and patient group. Broad registration supports surgery plans and disease tracking. Foundation models bring broad prior knowledge to the task. FMIR tests if that breadth solves the domain gap. The clinic, not the benchmark, is the real judge.
arxiv-2601-17629:
Meysam Babapour and Ehsan Taheri design robust low-thrust spacecraft trajectories. Low-thrust engines push gently for long spans. Plans must hold up under random disturbances. The authors use chance-constrained covariance steering. One key point is spacecraft mass change. Mass shifts affect thrust acceleration. They also affect how strong disturbances feel.

Both levels of mass effect enter the design. A covariance form keeps the math efficient. Robust paths save fuel and cut mission risk. Deep-space missions cannot be re-flown if plans fail. The method gives planners a systematic path. It treats doubt as part of the route, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-17729:
Zihan Pengmei presents cuGUGA, a new solver for a hard task in quantum chemistry. The 2026 preprint deals with configuration interaction, a method that builds the state of a system from many simpler states. The solver works in a basis that keeps spin symmetry built in from the start. It runs on graphics hardware through CUDA, the platform for such chips.

Two design choices keep the solver fast. Counts of paths through a graph are precomputed, so ranking states takes a fixed, short time. Segment factors are also stored in tables ahead of time. That makes the coupling terms quick to evaluate as well. The result is a tool aimed at larger and harder chemistry problems.
arxiv-2601-17829:
Dan Greenstein, Zohar Karnin, Chen Amiraz, and Oren Somekh study how to make training data for tool-using AI agents more varied. Their 2026 preprint is about function-calling agents, systems that pick and fill software functions to get tasks done. Good training data is a main bottleneck for such agents. Past work varied the functions, the call patterns, and the turns of talk.

Two gaps got less care: how requests are worded, and which argument values appear. A request can name a city or a stock code in many ways. If training data is too samey, agents stumble on real user phrasing. The authors target that language and argument spread head-on. Wider spread should make agents hardier in live use.
arxiv-2601-17929: Tarik Aougab, Hikaru Jitsukawa, and Kim Ruane write an elementary primer on the quasi-isometric rigidity of the integers. Their 2026 preprint sits in geometric group theory. The text also serves as a tribute to Chatawate (Flame) Ruethaimetapat, a young scholar in the field who died in August 2024. The primer keeps the tools basic so new readers can follow the proof ideas.
arxiv-2601-18029:
Kengo Deguchi, Haider Munawar, and Runjie Song derive simple tests for when a swirling flow stays calm. Their 2026 preprint studies inviscid shear instability in axisymmetric flows. The base flows run in annuli and pipes. The authors seek plain criteria that say whether such a flow is stable or will break into disturbance. They treat both symmetric and non-symmetric disturbance types.

Their sufficient condition for stability sharpens a classical result. It builds on the second Kelvin-Arnold stability theorem. Simple, sound tests save heavy computation in design work. Flows in pipes and rings sit inside engines, reactors, and lab rigs, so the tests have wide reach.
arxiv-2601-18129:
Kunat Pipatanakul and Pittawat Taveekitworachai present Typhoon-S, an open effort to give smaller language communities their own large models. Their 2026 preprint notes a skew in the field. Top models are trained and tested mostly in high-resource languages like English and Chinese. They are also built by a few groups with huge compute and data. Sovereign models aim to break that dependence for other nations and tongues.

The authors describe a minimal, open post-training recipe. Minimal means the steps are kept few and clear, so others can copy them. Open means the results can be checked and reused. The work serves countries that want AI in their own language, on their own terms.
arxiv-2601-18429:
Corentin Barloy and three colleagues study how small logic rules can keep track of sets of words as they change. The frame is a live one: a word list is kept up to date while bits flip one by one. A rule set counts as fit if it can state, after each flip, which words still pass a fixed test. Past work showed the full set of plain word tests can be kept in this way.

The team sort the word tests into finer ranks. For each rank they ask what kind of maths the rules must hold to stay in step. Their ranks use forms from algebra, the study of sets with rules for join and swap. The work ties two fields that seem far apart: the shape of words and the shape of change. That tie may help in checks on live data streams.
arxiv-2601-19029:
An unnamed author argues that piano playing should be judged from sound, not just from note data. Scores in MIDI form list which notes were hit and when, but they miss the tone and touch that make playing expressive. The author instead uses audio foundation models, large models trained on sound itself.

Two such models, MuQ and MERT, feed a system that scores many sides of performance quality. The target list spans a wide set of traits that listeners hear. If sound based scores beat note based ones, teachers and exam tools gain a judge that hears what an audience hears.
arxiv-2601-19129:
Puzhen Wu and eight co-authors fix badly exposed photos with help from a vision language model. Poor exposure wipes out detail, shifts colors, and flattens contrast. Fixes face two snags. They ignore what each object in the scene is, which causes odd color shifts. And real photos rarely come with a corrected twin to learn from.

Their method is unsupervised and aware of scene meaning, guided by CLIP. Object aware fixes can treat sky, skin, and shadow in ways that suit each one. Work that needs no hand made ground truth can scale to the messy photos people truly take.
arxiv-2601-19229:
Benling Li and Wei Zhao report analytic facts on Finsler manifolds that break Riemannian habits. Finsler geometry lets distance depend on direction, a looser frame than the Riemannian one. In the Riemannian world, every flat Cartan-Hadamard manifold is just Euclidean space in disguise.

That sameness underlies the sharpness of key inequalities, like Hardy's and the uncertainty principle. On Finsler manifolds, the pair find phenomena with no Riemannian twin. Such surprises warn analysts about tools built for the classic setting. Those tools may fail, or change meaning, when direction starts to matter. The pair mark the exact spots where the old intuition gives way.
arxiv-2601-19729:
Aldo Gardini and Lorenzo Mori work on a measurement problem in public health. Health surveys sample few people in each small area, so direct estimates for those areas are noisy. Small area estimation borrows strength across areas to sharpen the numbers. The authors apply these methods to mapping smoking behaviour.

Their outcome data come from self-reports, which suffer from coarsening. People round answers and favour certain digits, blurring the true values. Ignoring that blur can bias the maps. The authors build a Bayesian two-part model that handles coarsened data directly. Better local estimates help target anti-smoking programs where they are needed most. The method suits other self-reported health measures too.
arxiv-2601-19829:
M. Khodas, Libor Šmejkal, and I. I. Mazin explore superconductivity in a newly recognised kind of magnet. P-wave magnets have no net magnetisation, yet their electron bands split by spin in a non-relativistic way. That combination resembles altermagnets, another recent class of magnetic materials. The spin polarisation in these systems points in a fixed direction across momentum space.

The authors discuss whether such magnets can host superconductivity, and of what kind. They call the possibility nonrelativistic-Ising superconductivity. Pairing in a spin-split band structure should differ sharply from ordinary superconductors. If realised, it could yield devices that marry magnetism with zero-resistance current. The paper maps the theoretical ground for experimentalists to test.
arxiv-2601-20029:
Enhyeok Jang and six colleagues cut the training cost of a quantum optimization algorithm. QAOA tackles combinatorial problems by alternating quantum operations tuned by classical parameters. Its multi-angle variant gives every Hamiltonian term its own parameter. That freedom improves answers with fewer layers, but the parameter count inflates classical training cost.

Their cyclic layerwise training scheme organises the optimization to tame that cost. Training proceeds layer by layer in a repeating cycle. The scheme aims to keep multi-angle quality while restoring practicality. Optimization problems from logistics to finance motivate the algorithm. Cheaper training decides whether such quantum methods ever leave the lab. The cost is paid in plain cash and time.
arxiv-2601-20329:
A. Rahmatinejad, T. M. Shneidman, and N. Jovancevic calculate level densities for two plutonium isotopes, split by parity. Level density counts how many quantum states a nucleus has at a given energy. The authors track the ratio between positive and negative parity across a broad range of shapes, from spherical to strongly deformed.

Their range covers both the ground-state shape and the second minimum, the fission isomer. They compare the energy at which the two parities reach equilibrium between these shapes. Such densities feed into models of fission and neutron capture, where the nucleus passes through its deformed states.
arxiv-2601-20429:
Junseo Lee and four colleagues present GRTX, an efficient ray tracing method for rendering scenes built from 3D Gaussians. Gaussian splatting renders scenes fast and with high quality, but most systems use rasterization, which projects shapes onto the screen. Rasterization has fundamental limits, such as trouble with reflections and complex light paths.

Ray tracing can handle those effects but is costly on Gaussian scenes. GRTX aims to make it practical. Efficient ray tracing would let Gaussian scenes gain realistic lighting and shadows while keeping their speed edge, a gain for games, simulation, and virtual production.
arxiv-2601-20529:
Julia Richter and a large team set out a practical framework of key performance indicators for multi-robot field tests on the Moon and other planets. Robots will prospect for resources such as ilmenite, rare earth elements, and water ice. Analog field trials pursue these goals, but their results are hard to compare because platforms and setups differ so much.

The authors propose shared indicators so trials can be measured on common ground. Common measures would let space agencies and teams learn from each other's tests instead of starting over. That speeds the path to robots that can scout the Moon reliably.
arxiv-2601-20829:
Minwu Kim, Safal Shrestha, and Keith Ross tackle a stall in training reasoning models. Their 2026 paper studies reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. That method has greatly improved the reasoning of large language models. But training stalls once problems become saturated. Saturated problems are ones the model now almost always solves. They stop teaching it anything new.

The authors name the core issue: informative failures are hard to reach. The learning signal lives in failed attempts, yet standard rollouts rarely produce them. Their fix is failure-prefix conditioning. Training starts the model from the front part of a failed attempt. From there, useful failures become common again. The method aims to keep hard training sets useful for longer.
arxiv-2601-20929:
Wendy Sun, Rohan Naidu, and a large team argue that the centers of Little Red Dots are a new kind of object. Their 2026 paper studies these compact red sources, seen by JWST in the early universe. Their central engines may be black hole stars. Such a star is an early stage of black hole growth wrapped in dense gas. The best evidence comes from a few sources.

In those sources, the host galaxy is fully outshone. Their spectra show steep Balmer breaks, a mark of dense gas. The title's sums state the claim: take away the host, and a black hole star remains. The authors propose one at the center of each Little Red Dot. If right, this rewrites how the first black holes grew.
arxiv-2601-21029:
Samuel Stanek and four co-authors study a flaw that dims a fast laser scanner. Their 2026 paper concerns electro-optical deflectors made from KTN crystals. These deflectors steer laser beams with unmatched speed. They serve laser-scanning microscopy and other applications. Their weakness is a limited deflection range.
