Detecting up to three photons from squeezed-light sources with a photon-number-resolving detector, they continuously control the balance between wave-like and particle-like traits. The method builds a spectral family of quantum states with high making rates, tuned to the required fault-tolerance threshold. It establishes generalized photon subtraction as a versatile toolbox for tailoring non-Gaussian tools, opening a path to efficient Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubit making and tackling a central bottleneck in optical quantum compute.
arxiv-2602-21929:
JiaKui Hu and nine co-authors propose a new way to generate videos that wander through a three-dimensional scene without losing track of its layout. Older methods lean on outside memory banks or rebuild the scene step by step, and small errors early on pile up into drift. Their 2026 arXiv paper instead treats scene geometry itself as context for the video model.

The model works in turns: it estimates the geometry of the current view, then renders and repairs fresh views from that scene, guided by camera poses through a special attention module. During training, geometry hints are sometimes withheld so the model can also run on plain text and images alone. Tests on forward and return camera paths show steadier scenes and tighter camera control than prior methods.
arxiv-2602-22029:
One-click song generators are handy for casual users, but professional songwriters want to keep control of the core melody. Fang-Duo Tsai and six co-authors build a score-to-song pipeline that takes its roadmap from vocal MIDI, with its timing and chord data. Older score-to-song tools handle only short clips and lose coherence in long songs, especially in silent stretches like intros and bridges.

Their system, called MIDI-SAG, plans the song's structure first, marking time boundaries and labels for vocal and non-vocal sections alike. That plan keeps generation steady across a whole song, and the design trains on a single graphics card by reusing specialized pretrained parts. Tests suggest the approach can carry long-form songs without losing the thread.
arxiv-2602-22229:
Fully homomorphic encryption lets computers work on encrypted data, but at enormous cost, often orders of magnitude slower than plain computation. Lohit Daksha and twelve co-authors argue GPUs, not custom chips, are the pragmatic platform: they are scalable, programmable, and widely available. The snag is that modern GPUs optimize for low-precision machine-learning math, a poor match for the wide-precision modular arithmetic encryption needs.

The paper proposes rethinking GPU design around that gap, showing how encryption primitives can exploit GPU parallelism despite it. For privacy-preserving computing, it sketches a path to encrypted computation on hardware everyone already has. The work is grounded in the mismatch between tensor cores built for narrow math and the wide-integer arithmetic of schemes like CKKS.
arxiv-2602-22329:
TOI-260 b sits in the radius valley, the sparsely populated gap between rocky super-Earths and gassy sub-Neptunes, making its atmosphere a telling test case. Annabella Meech and eighteen co-authors present its JWST transmission spectrum, combining two transit observations from the COMPASS program. Careful binning yields high-precision spectra from both visits and their combination.

The spectrum is mostly featureless, with a possible feature near three microns and an offset between the two detector segments, both checked with non-parametric models. Retrieval analyses detect no clear molecular signatures. The result constrains the planet's atmosphere to muted possibilities, and shows how far current precision can push on small, cool worlds.
arxiv-2602-22529:
Saber Zerhoudi and one co-author built Agent4DL, a simulator that plays the part of a digital library user. Real search logs are scarce because of privacy, which has long slowed research on library search. Agent4DL creates realistic user profiles and full search sessions, copying how people query, click, and decide when to stop, tuned to each profile.

Checked against real user data, the simulator matched actual interaction patterns well. It also stood up against SimIIR 2.0, an existing search simulator, with an edge in producing varied, context-aware behaviour. For library researchers, it offers a privacy-safe stand-in for real users when testing search tools and interfaces.
arxiv-2602-23329:
Chen Bo Calvin Zhang and 18 co-authors test whether large language models lift novices on dual-use biology tasks done in silico. Models score ever better on biology benchmarks, but it is unclear whether they help novices beat what internet-only resources allow. That question matters both for speeding science and for dual-use risk.

In a multi-model, multi-benchmark human study across eight biosecurity-relevant task sets, with up to 13 hours per hard task, novices with language models were 4.16 times more accurate than internet-only controls. On four benchmarks with expert baselines, model-assisted novices beat experts on three. Standalone models often beat assisted novices, suggesting users did not draw out the models' best work, and 89.6 percent of participants found dual-use information easy to obtain despite safeguards. The authors call for sustained, interactive uplift testing beside standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-23429:
Nicolas Esser and two co-authors estimate the gravitational wave signals from planetary-mass primordial black holes passing near or through neutron stars, with an eye on the Galactic center. Prior work focused mainly on detailed waveforms, but this paper estimates event rates from the Galactic center and the chance of detection over ten years of LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observations.

Bound black holes on eccentric orbits produce repeated gravitational wave bursts in correlated series, one burst per periastron passage. Despite the boost from many bursts per pair, bound-pair signals remain subdominant to random unbound encounters between primordial black holes and neutron stars. Both signal types carry a very small detection probability, at most about one in one hundred million over a ten-year period. That sobering outlook nonetheless quantifies the search space for these exotic encounters.
arxiv-2602-23529:
Martin Černý and three co-authors study how to learn an unknown subadditive set function with few value queries, minimizing additive error. Such functions matter in combinatorial auctions, optimization, and interpretable machine learning. But specifying one means assigning values to exponentially many subsets, often requiring costly retraining.

Omitting values creates ambiguity that grows when the incomplete function is later optimized. Known work shows multiplicative error is inapproximable with deterministic queries. The authors instead target additive error: closing the gap between minimal and maximal completions. Their work maps minimal and maximal completions across set-function classes, analyzes the resulting gaps, and develops methods that shrink the gap by disclosing values of extra subsets under a known prior.
arxiv-2602-23729:
Seungdong Yoa and six co-authors move from static benchmarks to a dynamic plan for agent-centric anomaly spotting. LLM testing has relied on static data sets, giving limited scaling and failing to capture shifting thinking powers.

The new agent-centric model adds a dynamic plan in which self-run agents make, check, and solve problems. A teacher agent makes trial problems, a checker agent checks soundness and guards against attacks, and a student agent attempts checked problems. An invalid problem is revised by the teacher until it passes checks. If the student solves right, the checker prompts the teacher to make harder variants. The benchmark scales in hardness on its own as capable agents are swapped into any role, giving stepwise testing without hand-made sets. Using text anomaly spotting as the format, needing cross-sentence thinking and blocking pattern-matching shortcuts, the plan exposes corner-case errors.
arxiv-2602-23829:
Yahir Mio and Miguel Alcubierre study the dynamical stability of electrically charged Proca stars, compact objects built from a massive vector field. The 2026 paper follows earlier stationary solutions, where charge has a critical value at which electric repulsion exactly cancels gravitational pull. Only a limited range above it allows solutions.

Perturbing each stationary star and evolving it in spherical symmetry, the authors split the parameter space into three regions: bound and stable, bound but unstable, and unbound and unstable. Unstable cases end in one of three ways, set by binding energy and perturbation shape: collapse to a charged black hole, migration to a stable branch, or dispersal to infinity. The map clarifies which charged Proca stars could persist in nature and which must transform or vanish.
arxiv-2602-23929:
Mara Meyer zum Alten Borgloh and six co-authors show, in ultracold mixtures, control of atom-molecule Feshbach resonances with electric fields. The 2026 paper works with ground-state sodium-potassium molecules mixed with potassium atoms, a system where magnetic fields already tune interactions through resonances that can form dimers and trimers.

Electric fields shift resonance positions in a systematic way, and the trimer bound states they reveal carry field-dependent energies. Compared with isolated dimers, the response differs markedly, showing that the molecular partner rotates only with difficulty when an atom sits nearby. Electric fields thus add an independent control knob for atom-molecule resonances and open spectroscopic access to triatomic quantum states. Put plainly, the fields give the team a new way to steer these pairs. The team can then read the small states that the pairs form when they bind.
arxiv-2602-24129:
Omar Alterkait and four co-authors present the first end-to-end differentiable simulator for optical particle detectors, unifying simulation, calibration, and tracking in one gradient-based framework. The 2026 paper addresses large homogeneous detectors with optical readout, such as Cherenkov and scintillator neutrino detectors.

Accurate calibration aligns simulation with real detector data, while tracking infers particle properties from optical signals; traditionally those tasks are handled separately. The differentiable simulator yields smooth, physically meaningful gradients across light generation, propagation, and detection. Modularity lets the framework adapt to varied detector geometries and materials, offering a flexible foundation for experimental physics.
arxiv-2602-24229:
Włodzimierz Lewoniewski and three co-authors study how to identify Wikipedia articles on science fiction, fantasy, or hybrids of the two, a task complicated by porous genre boundaries. The 2026 paper notes that Wikipedia offers machine-readable structure beyond article text, including categories, internal links, and Wikidata statements.

Each of those signals can be biased or incomplete and reflects community conventions, so no single signal suffices. The study examines structural and semantic features that can mark science fiction and fantasy content. The work offers a grounded account of genre identification in a collaborative encyclopedia, where genre is negotiated by editors rather than fixed by publishers. Structural cues must be read with their biases in mind.
arxiv-2603-00029: Roh, Cho and Kim argue that massive activations in large language models are not mere glitches but interpretable functional units from domain specialisation. A few feature axes dwarf the rest, and a simple size-based rule picks out domain-critical axes with no training. Analysis shows they act as semantic sensors for symbolic, quantitative or own-domain patterns. Steering only those axes, named Critical Dimension Steering, beats whole-axis steering in domain adaptation and jailbreaking tests.
arxiv-2603-00529: Parekh presents CaptionFool, a universal adversarial attack that fools transformer captioning models into writing attacker chosen captions, including offensive text. Changing only seven of 577 image patches, about one percent of the image, the attack succeeds in nearly all trials. It can also plant slang terms crafted to slip past content moderation filters. The work exposes serious flaws in deployed vision language systems and presses the case for stronger defences.
arxiv-2603-00829: Storf and three colleagues study constitutional black-box monitors for detecting scheming in LLM agents, where agents covertly pursue misaligned goals. Their monitors are prompted classifiers using only outside inputs and outputs, tuned on synthetic data from plain behaviour notes. Two pipelines, STRIDE and Gloom, generate 1,000 samples each, and monitors tuned on them are tested on 7,500 held-out runs from ControlArena. Monitors chosen on synthetic data work in realistic settings, but performance levels off quickly, simple prompt sweeps match heavier tuning, and pushing further leads to overfitting.
arxiv-2603-01029: He and three co-authors improve road anomaly segmentation for safe driving, where pixel stats cry wolf on sky and plants while missing true unknown blocks. Their VL-Anomaly plan lines visual traits up with CLIP text vectors of known kinds, cutting false alarms in normal backdrops. A multi-source check at run time blends text-led scores, image-text scores, and sensor trust, reaching top results on RoadAnomaly, SMIYC, and Fishyscapes.
arxiv-2603-01129: Lombardo and Villar connect phase shifts of a dephasing qubit to ergotropy, the usable energy. The dynamic phase tracks only the incoherent part, its purely energetic root, while the geometric phase mixes wave order, loss, and extraction. In the weak-coupling, long-time limit the geometric phase follows the incoherent part alone, hinting ergotropy could be read from phase tests via standard tomography.
arxiv-2603-01329: Hu and four colleagues build a Landau theory for tilted achiral magnets, a novel magnetic family with no net pull but spin-polarized band structures. They show the crystal's achiral symmetry appears in the inverse-space spin texture, which presents only spatial-even poles. Those poles, set apart from straight magnet poles by high-order secondary order parameters, couple to effects such as the spin Hall effect and pressure-magnetic effect. The theory is shown by the tilted achiral magnet NiS2, a model linked Mott non-conductor showing both effects.
arxiv-2603-01429:
Xiaoxuan Lin, Qian Wu, Wei Kou, and Xurong Chen test a bold claim about a new force in this 2026 study. Odd results from nuclear tests hinted at a light new particle, often called X17. If it exists, it should shift energy levels in atoms where a muon orbits the nucleus.

The team computes those shifts for muonic atoms with light stable nuclei, using one shared model. Shifts that ignore spin grow fast for heavier nuclei, while spin-based shifts favor odd nuclei in two distinct ways. A score that weighs signal size against test precision picks the best near-term targets. Light helium and hydrogen-like systems lead for one channel, while heavier cases lead for raw signal size.
arxiv-2603-01729:
Geoffrey Lacour, Nicolae Cindea, and Julien Aniort estimate how fast calcium and citrate cross dialysis membranes. Their 2026 work models hollow-fiber hemodialysis, the treatment that cleans blood when kidneys fail. Flow rates differ by patient, so one shared estimate may fit no one well.

Their frame couples fluid flow with multi-species transport and reaction inside the fiber device. A search with no need for gradients fits membrane traits to outlet concentration readings. Patient inputs come from clinical data, with a per-patient flow calibration to keep physics consistent. Pooling residuals across many patients turns the fit into one global least-squares task. Tests on synthetic data show the traits can be recovered, and noise checks probe how errors grow. The method then runs on real clinic data from a named dialysis system.
arxiv-2603-01829:
Alberto Bassanoni and Omer Hamdi refine the Big Jump Principle for sums with stretched-exponential tails. Their 2026 work studies sums of independent random variables whose rare large values follow a softened exponential law. Past theory shows a phase split: typical sums act Gaussian, while extreme sums hinge on one huge jump.

Their expansion adds systematic corrections that reach past the far-tail limit into moderate deviations. That bridges the zone between everyday Gaussian wiggles and single-jump dominance. The approach mirrors the classic Edgeworth expansion, but corrects the big jump regime instead of the Gaussian core. Leading terms expose the scaling that governs the crossover between the two regimes. Extensions cover continuous-time random walks, where random wait times mix with jump sizes to shape transport, and simulations back every prediction.
arxiv-2603-01929:
L. Gordeev and E. H. Haeusler comment on a claimed refutation of their earlier complexity results in this 2026 note. The note responds to a paper by Jerabek on a simplified lower bound for implicational logic. Implicational logic is a stripped-down logic that keeps only implication between statements.

In earlier sketches, the authors argued for striking equalities among major complexity classes. Those classes sort problems by the time and memory they need to solve or verify. Jerabek claimed to refute those results with exponential lower bounds for implicational minimal logic. This note sets out the authors' comments on that claimed refutation and its approach. Readers should treat the exchange as an open dispute between specialists, since each side contests the other proofs.
arxiv-2603-02029:
Felipe Maia Polo, Aida Nematzadeh, Virginia Aglietti, and colleagues extract fine-grained model evaluations from cheap automated scores. Their 2026 work moves past leaderboard averages that hide how a model does on each prompt type. Human gold labels are too costly at that scale, while raw automated ratings drift from human taste.

Their statistical model, based on tensor factorization, merges cheap autorater data with a small human set. Autorater scores pre-train latent representations of prompts and of the models being judged. A small calibration set then aligns those representations to human preferences. The method proves robust to autorater quality and predicts per-prompt human views better than standard baselines. Tight confidence intervals come along, and granular leaderboards can be built from autorater scores alone.
arxiv-2603-02329:
Lei Yao, Yong Chen, Yuejiao Su, and colleagues ground robot intentions in 3D objects in this 2026 paper. An affordance is what an object lets you do, like grasp or pour. Humans read affordances from watching interactions in images and video. Their system, HAMMER, uses large multimodal models to do the same for new objects.

Instead of describing attributes or borrowing flat image segmenters, HAMMER condenses the interaction's intent. That intent becomes a contact-aware embedding that guides the model to name affordance labels. A layered fusion step refines 3D features with the model's broader knowledge. A geometry module adds spatial detail at several scales for precise location. Tests on public data and a new corrupted benchmark show strong, robust gains over prior methods.
arxiv-2603-02429:
Shiyuan Zhang, Qiwei Di, Xuheng Li, and Quanquan Gu prove dimension-free sampling bounds in this 2026 paper. Langevin samplers draw from probability distributions defined by an energy function. The underdamped version adds momentum and works well in high dimensions in practice. Past guarantees, though, grew with dimension and became useless when dimension was huge.

Their result is the first KL divergence bound for discretized underdamped sampling with no dimension factor. The bound depends instead on the trace of a curvature bound for the energy. When that trace is far below the dimension, iteration costs improve sharply. The proof refines a local error framework into a dimension-free form. Overdamped methods look worse in exactly those favorable regimes. An open theoretical gap is now closed.
arxiv-2603-02829:
Huanlei Guo, Hongxin Wei, and Bingyi Jing cut the wasted work in text-to-image generation. Their 2026 paper addresses the common generate-then-select routine, where many candidate images are drawn and only a few are kept. Each candidate costs dozens of costly cleanup steps, and quality scores usually arrive only at the end.

Their plug-in, Probe-Select, reads early internal signals from the generator itself. Even at one fifth of the way through, those signals show the layout and structure that predict final quality. Weak seeds can be stopped early, saving over sixty percent of sampling cost while raising the quality of what survives. The trick works across both diffusion and flow-matching generators without changing the base model.
arxiv-2603-02929:
Xiangzhao Hao, Shijie Wang, Tianyu Yang, and colleagues teach a retrieval model to think before it searches. Universal multimodal retrieval must handle intents from plain keywords to layered instructions mixing images and text. Most models compress the query into a fixed vector at once, which fails when the intent needs actual deduction.

Their system, TRACE, first writes a short chain of reasoning about the query, then squeezes that reasoning into the search vector through a special token. Training data with graded difficulty teaches it when reasoning is worth the cost. On a major benchmark it set a new best score, while learning to skip reasoning for simple queries. The internalized reasoning also transferred well to unseen domains and new constraint types.
arxiv-2603-03129:
José María Arroyo-Polonio, Giuseppina Battaglia, and Guillaume Thomas correct the weights of the faintest galaxies for an invisible bias. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies show tiny stellar velocity spreads, implying they are the most dark-matter-dominated systems known. But undetected double stars add their orbital motion to those measurements, inflating the apparent spread.

The authors build the expected velocity distribution of binary stars from modern population models, then blend it with a galaxy component in a mixture model where the binary share is free. Applied to observed dwarfs, dynamical masses fell by a factor of about one and a half to three. The method extends to multi-epoch data, where repeated observations catch some binaries directly. The corrections matter for using these galaxies to test dark matter models.
arxiv-2603-03229:
Adam Watts, Andrew Jeon, Destry Newton, and Ryan Bowering rebuild a shock's time history from its fingerprint. Engineers describe a shock by its response spectrum, which records how simple oscillators of many frequencies would react. Many different shocks share one spectrum, so reversing the map is ill-posed, and classical searches are slow and rigid.

Their conditional variational autoencoder learns the inverse map from data instead. Once trained, it generates acceleration signals matching a target spectrum with no iterative optimization. Experiments show better spectral fidelity than classical techniques and strong generalization to unseen spectra. Inference runs three to six orders of magnitude faster. The Los Alamos team presents generative modeling as a scalable route to shock reconstruction.
arxiv-2603-03329:
Xinghua Lou, Miguel Lázaro-Gredilla, and Antoine Dedieu let a language model write its own safety harness. As agents, models often attempt actions the environment flatly forbids; in one chess competition, most losses by a leading model came from illegal moves. People usually hand-write code around the model to block such moves. Their 2026 paper shows the harness itself can be synthesized automatically.

Given feedback from the game environment over a few refinement rounds, the smaller Gemini model produced harness code that prevented every illegal move across a large suite of text games. That let it beat a much larger sibling model. Pushed further, the model generated the entire playing policy as code, needing no model calls during play, and outscored two flagship models on single-player games. Automatic harnesses proved cheaper as well as stronger.
arxiv-2603-03629:
Immanuel Ben-Porat, José A Carrillo, and Alexandra Holzinger put interacting particle systems with changing weights on firm mathematical ground. Each particle moves under the influence of the others, and each carries a time-evolving weight that scales its influence, a setup used for opinion dynamics and neuroscience models. Their 2026 paper follows the system from finitely many particles to its mean-field limit, the single formula describing the crowd.

Three results interlock. The limit formula has exactly one solution, with controlled growth of its logarithmic gradient. The companion Kolmogorov formula admits weak solutions obeying an entropy inequality. Those estimates then feed the relative entropy method, which rigorously derives the mean-field equation from the particle system. Both the interaction and influence kernels need only mild regularity, widening the class of models the theory certifies.
arxiv-2603-04029: Domberg and Schildbach present self-adapting robotic agents through online continual reinforcement learning with world model feedback. Learning-based robotic controllers are usually trained offline with fixed settings, limiting adaptation to unforeseen changes. Building on DreamerV3, their method uses world-model forecast errors to spot out-of-distribution events and trigger finetuning. Adaptation progress is monitored through task signals plus internal training metrics, letting convergence be judged without external supervision. Validation spans steady control problems including a simulated quadruped and a real model vehicle, sketching a path beyond static training.
arxiv-2603-04729: Rathnayake, Shahin, and Abaei evaluate three LLMs for automated Behaviour-Driven Development scenario generation. They build a dataset of 500 user stories and matching BDD scenarios from four proprietary products. Quality is judged with similarity metrics, LLM-based checks, and human expert assessment. GPT-4 leads on similarity metrics, while Claude 3 rates highest with human experts and LLM-based evaluators. DeepSeek-based evaluators track human judgment more closely than similarity metrics do. Prompting success is model-specific: GPT-4 favors zero-shot, Claude 3 gains from chain-of-thought, and Gemini favors few-shot.
arxiv-2603-05029: Johannes Buerger and Mark Cannon offer a lean nonlinear Model Predictive Control algorithm for safe, learning-based control, building the system as basis functions with unknown settings under added set-bounded shakes. One after one line-fitting around nominal guessed paths accounts for doubts from line-fitting, model errors, and shakes via oval sets, keeping control-input and state constraints met. Toughness comes from bounds on line-fitting errors plus a step-back line search. The method locks in looping feasibility and real balance in the input-to-state sense.
arxiv-2603-05329: Qi-Sha Ran and colleagues investigate J/ψ production in Higgs decay to J/ψ plus a photon in nonrelativistic QCD, a Higgs charm-quark Yukawa probe. Maximum Conformality removes scheme and scale ambiguities from the next-to-next-to-leading-order series. From the measured J/ψ leptonic width, they extract long-distance matrix elements. With the short-distance coefficient, they obtain a scale-invariant decay width. Their fixed-order result beats earlier predictions, with good convergence. They find a decay width of 6.4574 x 10^-11 GeV.
arxiv-2603-05629: Tapli and team rethink concept bottleneck models, which ground predictions in concepts but face deep limits. No metric judges concept relevance in advance, a straight-line problem lets models bypass the neck, and rightness lags behind. They present CBM-Suite, a framework tackling these problems. A spread-based metric sizes concept-set fitness. A non-linear layer after concept firings ties rightness to concept relevance. A boil-down loss steered by a linear teacher probe narrows the rightness gap. Wide tests show CBM-Suite yields righter models.
arxiv-2603-05829: Upasani and team study many-shot prompting as test-time tuning, where in-context samples update model ways without setting changes. Scores often improve with more demos, but trust and limits remain poorly known for open-source models. The authors analyze score shifts with update size, order, and picking policy, plus Dynamic and Reinforced in-context learning as other paths. Many-shot prompting suits structured tasks with high information gain, yet proves touchy about picking plan and limited for open-ended making. The study maps when tuning helps versus harms.
arxiv-2603-06229: Janoš and his team look into how varied laser pulses build excited molecular states. The Born-Huang expansion and exact factorization serve as two ways to write the molecular wave function. They probe two edge cases: a stationary molecular state from a long pulse and an electronic wave packet from an ultrashort attosecond pulse. Old ideas of population transfer, resonance rule, and sudden vertical excitation, tied to the Born-Huang view, look new under exact factorization.
arxiv-2603-06829: Gupta and colleagues turn joint gravity and magnetic inversion into a rectified flow problem for finding ore underground. Shallow minerals are running out, so surface readings must reveal hidden densities, yet that reconstruction is ill-posed and non-unique. Fixed deterministic methods need hand-made priors, land on one answer, and miss the spread of possible answers. Their system trains on Noddyverse, the biggest physics-based inversion collection, with a Ginzburg-Landau regularizer that borrows the Ising model to help spot ore.
arxiv-2603-06929: Iacocca proposes a non-equilibrium heat field for ultrafast magnet motion, with features tied to atomic spin flip odds. Femtosecond bursts from lasers or currents drive far-from-equilibrium motion, modeled usually by atomistic spin models, while micromagnetic models fail to reproduce ultrafast demagnetization on any grid. Treating each spin flip as one quantum of angular momentum gives matching temperatures in the thousands of Kelvin. Demagnetization is reproduced in numbers for several cell sizes, and the approach can be refined toward grid-independent multiscale work.
arxiv-2603-07029: Das and colleagues read Swift and NuSTAR views of NGC 4278, a dim active galaxy core, with dim inflow flows. They report the first NuSTAR hard X-ray views, seen beyond 10 keV with a hard power-law spectrum and no high-energy cutoff. Flux is low versus the active state in 2021 but varies over a month. A dim flow model with a variable inflow rate explains both states. TeV gamma rays cannot escape the disk, so high-energy gamma rays seen by LHAASO likely come from outer jets and winds.
arxiv-2603-07129: Bilotto and colleagues study the long-run states of non-rotating, nearly two-dimensional viscous flows over bumpy ground. They build a framework by reducing the 3D Navier-Stokes equations in the limit of infinite Rossby number, then compute attractors at fixed kinetic energy across Reynolds numbers. Under turbulence, the attractor spreads across the lowest excited states rather than staying unique. In every steady state, large vortices settle in topographic valleys, unlike the rotating case.
arxiv-2603-07529: Akbari, Afshari and Boddeti introduce Obliviator, a post-hoc erasure method that guards attributes against nonlinear adversaries. Existing erasure leaves curved stat links between representations and unwanted traits intact. It frames erasure with composed kernels and morphs the feature space step by step instead of solving it in one shot. The gradual path prices the cost of nonlinear guarding and yields trade-off curves beating rivals, above all on well-separated models.
arxiv-2603-07629: You and Zhou test sim-trained exoskeleton controllers that reduce biological joint moments. Data-driven models replace lab math, and physics-guided learning trains assistance rules without extensive human trials. Their framework learns hip and knee help from short histories of gait motion and checks predictions against an open gait dataset. Match runs strongest at the hip, weakening at higher speeds and steeper inclines, especially for joint power.
arxiv-2603-08429: Jiang argues that the usual two-model setup for agent retrieval wastes work. A language model agent first writes a search query as text. A separate embedding model then turns it into a vector, though the agent's hidden states already hold the full context. Jiang adds a light projection head mapping those hidden states straight into the embedding space, trained with alignment, contrastive and rank distillation losses. Tests on the QReCC conversational search benchmark claim it keeps 97% of baseline retrieval quality with no second model.
arxiv-2603-08529: Bethlehem and colleagues model the gas chemistry just inside where dust burns away around a young Herbig star. The dust-free inner zone proves rich in molecules, with hydrogen, water, and silicon monoxide beside carbon monoxide. Gas there runs hot and thick enough to glow in overtone lines, and the inner zone supplies most of the carbon monoxide and water line light.
arxiv-2603-08729: Seine Shintani builds a self-hosted pipeline that turns lecture PDFs into multiple-choice quizzes with no outside service. A local model drafts questions, but the shipped banks are plain text with a full quality trace and need no model at run time. In a seed sweep over three short dummy lectures, all 120 accepted items pass hard checks, while a warning layer flags eight items for softer risks like doubled distractors.
arxiv-2603-08929: Benjamín Guzmán presents bsort, a sorting method that avoids comparisons for integers and floats. The method unifies signed and unsigned integers with floats through a binary-quicksort approach, running in time proportional to word size times input size with word-size extra space. It works best for small word sizes, where tests show it rivals tuned hybrid sorts from popular libraries.
arxiv-2603-09329: Arttu Paju and colleagues measure what Tor users actually try to reach by planting honeypot onion websites and seeding neutral-looking links. Links went out through the Ahmia search engine, a paste service, and pastebin.com during March and April 2025. Nearly all human visitors arrived from Ahmia, and traffic collapsed once the links left its results. The honeypots posed as forums on varied illicit themes, letting the team compare engagement across categories.
arxiv-2603-09429: Eigil Fjeldgren Rischel approaches convex duality through category theory, defining a category whose objects are optimization problems. Convex minimization holds a wealth of theorems because convexity is specific enough to be powerful yet general enough to cover many cases. Applied category theory has largely skipped the field, apart from work decomposing problems categorically. As illustrations, Rischel rederives a minimax-type theorem and the fact that the Legendre dual of a convex function's dual returns the function itself.
arxiv-2603-09829: Lucas Davron, Pierre Lissy and Swann Marx study linked systems where control flows one way, from a heat part to a wave part. The heat side takes a boundary control, and its state passes through a second boundary to drive the wave side. Working in an abstract linear frame, they prove the system is well posed. They also show joint exact and near control, plus polynomial settling under feedback.
arxiv-2603-09929: Eduardo Abreu and coauthors study how wave character changes in radially symmetric flow of a compressible isentropic gas. They track rarefactive and compressive traits across outward supersonic, subsonic and inward supersonic setups. For each case they find limits on which changes can occur and sign domains that stay invariant for set starting data. New asymmetric change paths appear in the slower regimes, with conditions for blow up in finite time.
arxiv-2603-10029: Mateo Pechon-Elkins and Jon Chun audit a game theoretic framework that claims to measure strategic reasoning in language models. Rechecking raw transcripts from many model interactions, they find a token limit made some models return empty answers that parsers quietly replaced with fixed moves. That flaw voids one model's reported profile and taints every game type. After correction, fitted personal propensities predict choices better than equilibrium based candidates.
arxiv-2603-10429: Thanasis Karakasis, Emmanuel N Saridakis, and Zi-Yu Tang study the heat side of the Simpson-Visser black hole. This smooth hole is built with nonlinear electrodynamics and a scalar field of negative kinetic energy. They re-derive the solution so its constants can vary in the analysis. The mass term cancels, so the hole has zero thermodynamic mass. It still has charge, one horizon, finite heat, and entropy, and the first law holds. In a shared heat bath it loses to the singular, scalar-free rival.
arxiv-2603-10529: Giulio Turrisi and co-authors present BinWalker, a four-legged robot with an arm, built to pick up litter in hard outdoor places. Litter gathers on rough ground, coasts, parks, and roadsides, and manual cleanup is slow, costly work that leaves much behind. The robot pairs legged mobility with a manipulator arm and an onboard bin, so it can spot, grasp, and store items while crossing uneven terrain. Field tests outdoors showed the approach works, a step toward helping large cleanup efforts where wheeled machines struggle.
arxiv-2603-11229: Elizabeth Cucuzzella, Rafael Izbicki, and Ann Lee build a live fix for machine learning forecasts. Their forecast distributions go wrong exactly where it matters most, at rare tail events. Local miscalibration thrives where training data hold few extreme cases. Their semiparametric work models a diagnostic transport map. The map depends on covariates parametrically while being fitted nonparametrically. The maps yield live local checks plus a reshaped distribution. A use on tropical cyclone intensity forecasts exposes error modes. It makes severe-weather forecasts better.
arxiv-2603-11329: Srijan Bharati Das and coauthors map where hammerhead-shaped proton velocity distributions occur in the solar wind. These anisotropic structures may feed the wind's non-adiabatic heating with their free energy. Parker Solar Probe first spotted these diffused beams, with a pinched gap between core and beam. Simulations have reproduced their look without matching their prevalence or extremes. Across twenty encounters, the structures cluster around the heliospheric current sheet. They concentrate into windows near crossings, as the sheet tilts over the rising solar cycle.
arxiv-2603-11429: Ha and co-authors compute Gamow-Teller strength in the light carbon isotopes carbon-12, carbon-14, and carbon-16. Their method is the deformed quasiparticle random-phase approximation, with deformation built in from the start. Mean fields come from Skyrme Hartree-Fock work, and key interactions draw on Brückner G-matrix results. Deformation matters most for carbon-12, where it helps explain the measured strength spread. Carbon-14 in the spherical limit matches charge-exchange data well, and carbon-16 gains extra high-lying strength from mixing.
arxiv-2603-11629: Gangopadhyay and Kumar study warm inflation once the noise behind it gains a memory. Standard work treats the stochastic force on the inflaton as Markovian, with no correlation time. The pair asks how a finite correlation time reshapes the primordial scalar power spectrum. Memory effects, they show, suppress the spectrum against the white-noise result. A simple formula ties the correction to background thermal dynamics. The size of the effect scales with the ratio of bath temperature to Hubble scale.
arxiv-2603-12229: Mieczkowski, Collins, Sucholutsky, Vélez, and Griffiths frame teams of language models as distributed systems. LLM teams now deploy at scale, but basic design questions lack a firm base. When does a team help, how many agents should it hold, and when does one agent win? Distributed computing faced these same trade-offs for decades of study. Many core gains and pains from that field show up again in LLM teams. The authors mine that cross-talk for practical rules on team design and testing.
arxiv-2603-13129: Zhiping Li and co-authors solve chance constrained programs with penalty-based difference of convex algorithms. Chance constraints resist direct handling, so a rank-based split of the constraint comes first. Their primal algorithm needs no feasible starting point to begin. A lifted form with complementary constraints then improves stability for nonlinear cases. That form yields a tractable dual structure over a simple polyhedron, with finite termination. Tests beat state-of-the-art benchmarks in speed and results.
arxiv-2603-13229: Azaz Ahmad and Takami Tohyama study magnetotransport in a Weyl semimetal with two kinds of topology. Momentum-space Berry curvature acts with skyrmion-induced emergent magnetic fields. Their semiclassical Boltzmann approach adds Berry-curvature terms and intervalley scattering. Stronger scattering between valleys can flip the sign of the longitudinal magnetoconductivity. An emergent field shifts the field curve and makes a weaker sign-reversal regime. It also drives a planar Hall response that can signal real-space topology on its own.
arxiv-2603-13329: Minkyung Cha and co-authors propose LUMINA, a graph model for fMRI-based diagnosis of brain disorders in youth. Graph Convolutional Networks treat brain regions as linked nodes, which fits how the brain works as a whole. Yet their smoothing can blur the contrast that marks some disorders. LUMINA uses a Quad-Stream GCN with a bipolar RELU and dual-spectrum Laplacian filtering. That design keeps more of the varied dynamics in each fMRI scan. Cross-validation on ADHD200 and ABIDE data beat prior models on ADHD and ASD accuracy.
arxiv-2603-13429: Matteo Rossi and Pony Matt propose MSD-DETR for visual inspection of locomotive coil springs. Defects vary in shape and scale, and industrial backgrounds are complex, so checks are hard. Their detection transformer uses structural re-parameterization to split training-time branches from fast inference. A deformable attention mechanism samples space in a content-adaptive way, focusing on defect zones. Cross-scale feature fusion with GSConv and VoVGSCSP blocks merges multi-resolution data. On a real dataset it reached 92.4 percent mAP at 98 FPS, beating YOLOv8 and RT-DETR.
arxiv-2603-13529: Kunal Garg and Xi Yu propose hybrid topology control for multi-robot systems. Teams must keep communication links to meet goals, but holding links restricts mobility and hurts performance. Most prior methods use consensus frameworks whose decision time scales with the number of nodes and needs many communication rounds. Their leader-based algorithm uses a central node for real-time reconfiguration in one information round. Decision time then depends on graph diameter, not node count. Position estimates account for unknown disturbances and communication delays, and simulations show the method works.
arxiv-2603-13629: Dionysios P. Theodosopoulos and co-authors project how well paleo-detectors could sense dark matter that interacts with nuclei. Paleo-detectors read recoil tracks left in natural minerals over geological time, in place of a huge lab detector mass. The team works in a Non-Relativistic Effective Field Theory frame, for both elastic and inelastic scattering. They project upper limits on isoscalar coupling constants at 90 percent confidence, with cosmogenic and radiogenic backgrounds counted. For dark matter masses of 1 to 10 GeV, paleo-detectors beat current lab experiments.
arxiv-2603-14229: D B and co-authors present A.DOT, a planner that answers questions over hybrid data lakes with tables and documents side by side. Plain retrieval searches each store by brute force and merges later, which wastes effort and misses multi-hop chains. A.DOT compiles each question into a directed acyclic graph plan. Sub-queries run in parallel across stores, with schema-aware reasoning and checks before execution. Smart caching with paraphrase matching speeds repeat work.
arxiv-2603-14429: Rojo computes the self-force of a Dirac string in direct, elementary terms. A Dirac string acts as a half-endless solenoid that carries a fixed magnetic flux. Dirac noted the string should feel a nonzero force that grows without bound, but worked examples are rare. Rojo stacks the string as current loops and sums the pull from the radial field of the rest. The force scales with flux squared over radius squared, so it blows up as the radius shrinks to zero.
arxiv-2603-14529: Geger, Briechle and Rausch present Bots and Blocks, a project course for robotics teaching. Classic degree courses lean on lectures and leave students short on hands-on skill. Their course runs one agile project across a full semester. Students build robot software with the Robot Operating System. Short schools mix lectures with drills to set base skills. Team work on a real robot grows as the term advances. One class project built a disassembly software system for hardware robots.
arxiv-2603-15129: Chen and co-authors present NeFIC, a method for image compression at ultra-low bitrates that borrows from video diffusion. Decoding starts from a compact anchor frame that keeps scene layout and meaning but drops fine detail. A pretrained video diffusion model then predicts the step from that anchor to the full image. Starting from a visible, faithful anchor improves both realism and fidelity. On the CLIC2020 test set, the method saved over half the bitrate versus DiffC on several quality metrics, with decoding up to five times faster.
arxiv-2603-15229: Nambi and Qureshi study squarefree powers of closed neighborhood ideals of trees. They pin down exactly which trees have a highest non-vanishing squarefree power that is componentwise linear. They also examine the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of these powers. That regularity can grow much larger than the degree of the ideal itself. For caterpillar graphs, a special family of trees, they give an exact formula for the regularity.
arxiv-2603-15729: Viitanen and co-authors present AGILE, a simulator for the Rubin LSST sky survey. Finding active galactic nuclei from light alone is hard at survey scale. AGILE builds mock skies of AGNs, galaxies, and stars from end to end. Galaxy samples gain AGNs by observed accretion rates. Each AGN gets a spectrum and a damped random walk light curve. The first release covers one square degree in COSMOS. The team checks pipeline flux recovery and Type 1 AGN selection. The dataset is shared as a test bench.
arxiv-2603-15829: Roshan and Saha compute twin-peaked wave signals from a Z2 phase change. A scalar singlet gains a vacuum value and breaks the symmetry. A second-order change yields waves only from domain wall decay. A first-order change adds the transition burst itself. Two peaks then mark the combined spectrum. An extra scalar doublet keeps the singlet in thermal contact early on. The same doublet feeds fermionic dark matter by freeze-in. The setup matches the observed dark matter density.
arxiv-2603-16129: Zhang and co-authors sharpen zero-shot object counting with quantity-aware prompts. Text-named counting without sample images fools coarse retrieval habits. Their QICA frame pairs quantity perception with spatial aggregation. Numerically tuned prompts adapt both vision and language encoders. A cost aggregation decoder works straight on similarity maps. Spatial cleanup fights feature warping during adaptation. A multi-level quantity loss enforces numeric consistency end to end. FSC-147 scores stay competitive with top methods. CARPK and ShanghaiTech-A tests show strong unseen-domain reach.
arxiv-2603-16429: Rui and co-authors release LenghuSky-8, eight years of all-sky images from the Lenghu site. Observatories need minute-by-minute cloud awareness at their own site. Older sets are short, daylight-heavy, or lack calibration. This set holds 429,620 frames, mostly at night. Star-aware masks mark clouds, and each pixel carries altitude-azimuth values. A probe on DINOv3 features reached about 93% segmentation accuracy. Calibration error stays near 0.37 degrees at zenith and 1.34 degrees low in the sky.
arxiv-2603-16529: Muñoz adds transaction costs to a mean field game model of liquidity pools. Traders in a constant product market maker were modeled as a mean field game before. Pool fees change how traders hold inventory. Traders now act at a mid-price shifted by those costs. The DAI inventory follows a new dynamic. Muñoz proves that equilibria exist for the new game. He also works out trader strategies and the conditions for existence.
arxiv-2603-17129: Zelazo and Theran study when a network of unlike control affine agents can be made to synchronize. They split the design into two steps. First, an edge space step fixes a stabilizing evolution for the relative outputs. Second, a lift step realizes that edge motion through each agent's allowed input directions. They introduce an admissibility notion that captures when this plan is feasible. They derive checkable combinatorial certificates that tie graph topology and actuation limits to admissibility. The results are illustrated on synchronization of nonlinear oscillators.
arxiv-2603-17429: Willingham and co-authors recalibrate dust corrections for H-alpha luminosity functions with radio data. They match obscured H-alpha rates against unobscured radio rates from the EMU and GAMA surveys. A local calibration overstates the cosmic star formation rate density by over a hundredfold at high redshift, they find. Letting the dust trend fade with redshift fixes the match across cosmic time. Early galaxies likely hold dust in a different form or layout.
arxiv-2603-17629: Adithya and co-authors study postselection in continuous-time quantum walks on networks. Picking out chosen paths adds an effective nonlinearity to open-system dynamics. With Haken-Strobl noise, that extra term cancels and the walk settles uniformly, they find. With quantum stochastic walk noise, balance breaks on uneven networks instead. Walkers then pile up at low-degree edge nodes while keeping quantum coherence. The same trick steadies spin excitations in many-body systems.
arxiv-2603-17829: Sutawika and co-authors train CodeScout, an agent that finds code in large repositories. Rival agents lean on heavy extras like static-analysis graphs. Their agent works with nothing but a plain Unix terminal. A tuned reinforcement learning recipe does the heavy lifting instead. On three SWE-Bench variants, the models match or beat systems built on far larger bases, they report. Some runs even near top closed models with special scaffolds.
arxiv-2603-17929: Katsukawa and co-authors describe SCIP, a new spectro-polarimeter aboard the Sunrise III balloon observatory. The tool reads near-infrared light near 770 and 850 nanometers. Those bands hold lines that sense solar magnetic fields and flows in two layers of the Sun. A rotating waveplate modulates the signal for twin cameras behind polarizing splitters. Polarimetric sensitivity reaches 0.03 percent at ten-second steps, they report. SCIP flew with two sister tools in 2024.
arxiv-2603-18329: Ding and co-authors present FaithSteer-BENCH, a stress test for inference-time steering of language models. Past steering claims rest on relaxed tests that skip deployment limits and trade-offs. The bench grades methods at one fixed operating point on control, utility, and robustness. It finds illusory control, a cognitive tax on unrelated skills, and brittleness under mild prompt changes. Diagnostics suggest many methods give prompt-conditional alignment, not stable latent shifts.
arxiv-2603-18429: Shi and co-authors present AndroTMem, a diagnostic framework for anchored memory in long-horizon Android GUI agents. Full replay is redundant and noisy; summaries erase key dependency details. Their bench holds 1,069 tasks with 34,473 steps built on strong step-to-step causal links. Longer tasks fail mostly from memory lapses, not perception or single action errors, they find. Anchored State Memory stores linked intermediate states and lifts task completion by 5 to 30%.
arxiv-2603-18729: Ullasci and co-authors test whether language models tie stereotypes to dialect, and what reduces the effect. Inputs in Standard American English and African-American English draw different suggested names, jobs, and adjectives. Eight prompt templates probe how the bias shows up. An LLM judge scores the outputs. Gaps appear in every category, strongest for adjectives and job assignments. The gap is largest for Claude Haiku and smallest for Phi-4 Mini. Chain-of-thought prompting helps Haiku, while a generate-critique-revise agent setup cuts bias across all models tested.
arxiv-2603-18829: Fernandez presents ACP, a protocol that judges agent actions by history, not one request at a time. Harmless-looking requests can stack into harmful patterns. ACP scores risk over full execution traces, mixing static scores with anomaly buildup and cooldown signals. In a 500-request test where each request passes alone, a stateless engine approves all 500. ACP allows only 2 to run on their own, escalates after 3, and denies after 11. Version 3.0 scopes anomaly signals per agent and resource. Formal checks in TLA+ found no violations across billions of states.
arxiv-2603-19129: Knudstrup and co-authors measure how the hot Jupiter TOI-1333Ab lines up with the spin of its host star. They watch the planet cross the star and model the dip in starlight from that transit. The orbit turns out to be well aligned, with a tilt of about minus five degrees. The star is hot, a class where such planets are often skewed. The team weighs two paths for how the planet moved in close. Both disk drift and a later tidal fix remain in play.
arxiv-2603-19329: Li and co-authors teach a model to prove that code meets its specs in Lean 4. Their Goedel-Code-Prover first splits a hard goal into simpler subgoals, then proves each piece. A single score grades each split by sound logic and structural gain. That score serves as both training reward and test-time ranker. One policy learns both splitting and proving, tuned by supervised steps and hybrid reinforcement learning. On 427 tasks, the model proves 62 percent of cases. That is 2.6 times the best baseline rate.
arxiv-2603-19429: Filipe and Behnke seek a middle path between lifted and grounded encodings for planning tasks. Full grounding can blow up in size, while pure lifted forms are hard to solve. Their SAT encodings keep actions lifted but ground predicates in part. Size grows in a straight line with plan length, not with its square. That edge helps most on long plans in hard-to-ground fields. Their best encoding beats the prior state of the art on such tasks. The work is an extended version with full detail.
arxiv-2603-19529: Xu and co-authors present SurfaceXR, which fuses smartwatch motion sensors with headset hand tracking. Mid-air gestures in extended reality tire users and lack precision. Tapping on real surfaces is more accurate, but vision alone tracks hands poorly and misreads surface planes. The watch inertial unit adds high-frequency motion data that vision lacks. In a 21-person study, the fused system improved touch tracking and eight-class gesture recognition. It beat each single-sensor approach by a clear margin.
arxiv-2603-19629: Siahkoohi and Sabeddu ask what memorization does to learned priors for seismic inverse problems. Good training sets of subsurface models are scarce in geoscience. A generative prior may then just memorize its training examples. The authors show the posterior then acts as a weighted lookup over those stored examples. For diffusion models, the prior takes a closed Gaussian mixture form. A local linear step gives a matching mixture for the posterior. Tests on a toy problem and on full waveform inversion bear this out.
arxiv-2603-19929: Jia and co-authors present RAM, a system that recovers 3D human motion from hard real-world video. Crowds, occlusion, and fast interaction often break motion capture tools. RAM pairs a motion-aware tracker with adaptive Kalman filtering to keep identities straight. A memory-augmented module adds space-time priors for smoother, more consistent motion. A small predictor module forecasts future poses to bridge gaps. A gated combiner then mixes rebuilt and predicted features. On PoseTrack and 3DPW tests, RAM beat prior methods in tracking stability and 3D accuracy.
arxiv-2603-20229: Gong, Sanders, and Schneier test if language models can predict how Americans answer opinion polls, as a distribution. Polling grows costly and suffers rising non response and thin demographic coverage. Their framework prompts a model once to output a full response distribution. They score it against the large Cooperative Election Study survey. The distribution method beat repeated single respondent simulation on accuracy. It also cost far less to run. Performance varied in systematic ways across demographics and questions.
arxiv-2603-20329: Mis and de Hoop study how to recover a moving probability law from few moving sensors. They work in Bayes Hilbert spaces, where laws become paths via log-ratio coordinates. For smooth paths, they build a minimum-energy transport picture of the motion. They then pose recovery as an inverse problem on path space. Mobile sensors can identify the path, yet no stable bound holds in full generality. In finite dimensions, recovery reduces to explicit matrix conditions. Even one well-placed moving sensor can recover the reduced path.
arxiv-2603-20429: Iorio and co-authors ask whether predicted RR Lyrae binaries hide within Gaia data. Theory says most metal-rich disc RR Lyrae should sit in wide binaries. Yet no genuine case has been robustly confirmed so far. They study 100 Gaia DR3 stars chosen for metal-rich disc motion. Realistic mock observations include astrometric bias from the stars' variability. Bayesian checks then bound the hidden binary fraction. Current errors prevent a firm rejection of a high hidden fraction. The hunt continues into Gaia DR4 data.
arxiv-2603-20529: Canale and co-authors study low degree points on singular plane curves. Their results extend known work by Debarre and Klassen. The curves carry finitely many ordinary nodes or cusps. That singularity count is bounded by a quadratic in the curve degree. Within those bounds, they prove analogues of the earlier theorems. The work clarifies which low degree points such curves can host. It ties the geometry of singularities to arithmetic point behavior.
arxiv-2603-20729: Silva presents a weakly supervised method to segment acoustic borehole images with help from well logs. Dense expert labels for these wall images are rare. The method starts from threshold based pseudo labels, as classic tools do. Learned stages then denoise and refine those rough labels. Fusion with depth aligned logs can go several ways. Depth aware cross attention with confidence gating worked best. Plain joining of the two inputs gave only small gains. The top model beat image only and threshold baselines across wells.
arxiv-2603-20929: Pati compares sequential and parallel coordinate ascent variational inference. Both forms are in wide use, yet they act in ways that do not match. He studies a linear model with many traits. The sequential form tends to run more slowly. Still, its proof of convergence holds under weaker rules than the parallel form. The parallel form is liked because blocks of work can run at once, which can cut the time a job takes.
arxiv-2603-21329: Li and co-authors introduce COIN-Bench, a benchmark for collective intent understanding in language models. Models follow single instructions well, but distilling shared intent from noisy public discussion is untested. Their live updating benchmark works in the consumer domain. It treats intent as a layered structure, from plain scenarios to deep causal reasoning. Scoring mixes rule based checks with a model judge, plus hierarchical structuring and retrieval based verification. Twenty leading models handle surface aggregation well. They still struggle with the depth that complex intent synthesis needs.
arxiv-2603-21529: Kang and co-authors build SynSym, a framework that generates synthetic training data for spotting psychiatric symptoms in social media posts. Expert labeling is slow and lacks standard guidelines, so real datasets stay small. SynSym expands each symptom into sub-concepts, then writes expressions in varied linguistic styles. It also composes multi-symptom posts guided by clinical co-occurrence patterns. Models trained only on the synthetic data matched models trained on real data across three benchmarks. Adding real data for fine-tuning helped further, they report.
arxiv-2603-21629: Guo and co-authors adapt multi-object tracking to new test conditions while the tracker runs. Appearance and motion shifts between training and test data usually drag performance down. Frame-level adaptation alone misses identity links across time. Their TCEI framework pairs two systems modeled on human judgment. An intuitive system recalls recent objects for fast predictions. An experiential system uses lessons from earlier test videos to calibrate those calls. Confident and uncertain objects become priors and reflective cases for later frames. Benchmark tests show steady gains under distribution shift.
arxiv-2603-21829: Yuan and Zeng segment coronary arteries in CT angiography scans with a two-stage network. These vessels are thin, branching, and tiny next to background tissue, hard to trace. Plain CNNs miss long-range links, while Transformers cost too much for clinical use. Their model pairs a deformable convolution that adapts along three anatomical planes with a Mamba decoder. Mamba keeps long-range modeling at linear cost. A coarse pass locates the vessels, and a fine pass works block by block to recover detail and cut false alarms.
arxiv-2603-21929: Schmidt classifies the simple supermodules over the special linear Lie superalgebra sl(m|n) that can carry a unitary structure. The full set is pinned down, in both finite and infinite dimensions. The proof leans on the algebraic Dirac operator built by Huang and Pandžić. Inequalities tied to that operator filter which supermodules can be unitarizable. One uniform argument covers all cases at once. Notably, the proof needs no explicit constructions of the modules and no complete branching rules, which are the usual heavy tools in this area.
arxiv-2603-22729: Elayan and Kontar model driver differences with a quantum-inspired representation. Driver traits are often squeezed into labels or fixed regimes. Their approach treats each driver as a changing latent state, written as a density matrix. Driving data are embedded with random Fourier features. State updates blend steady habits with context-driven profile shifts. The authors test the method on the TGSIM driving dataset. They show how driving profiles can be drawn out and analyzed from the states.
arxiv-2603-23029: Zhou and Komsa fine-tune universal machine-learning potentials for two-dimensional high-entropy alloys. These mixed-metal materials are costly to model with density functional theory. Universal potentials offer a starting point, but training data are hard to build. The team generates and selects training structures with care. Raw universal models give poor mixing energies, they find. Fine-tuned models reach near-DFT accuracy on the target alloy system. They also enable Monte Carlo runs and random structure sampling at scales DFT cannot reach.
arxiv-2603-23229: Zhou and three co-authors test how well multimodal language models read figurative meaning in memes. Memes blend text and images to carry layered, often nonliteral messages. The team runs eight leading generative models on three datasets. The models must spot and explain six types of figurative meaning. Human raters then check whether each explanation backs its label and stays true to the meme. All models lean toward seeing figurative meaning even when none is there. Right labels also often come with unfaithful explanations.
arxiv-2603-23329: Taylor, Chandrasekar, and Kale present a diffusion-based load balancer for apps with chatty, long-lived objects. Uneven, shifting workloads leave parallel programs unbalanced across nodes. Classic balancing moves work but can ignore how much objects talk to each other. Their method spreads load along the communication graph itself. That cuts cross-node traffic while evening out the work. A variant covers cases where the traffic pattern is not known up front. Tests include simulation and a particle-in-cell run on up to 8 Perlmutter nodes.
arxiv-2603-23529: Fernandes and Patkar build tools for Konkani, a low-resource Indian language. Language models stumble on Konkani for two reasons: scarce training text and three writing scripts. The pair create Konkani-Instruct-100k, a synthetic teaching set made with Gemini 3. They benchmark open models like Llama 3.1 and Gemma 3 against closed rivals. Their fine-tuned Konkani LLM lifts machine translation over its base models. In several settings it matches or beats the closed systems. A multi-script benchmark is also in the works.
arxiv-2603-23629: Rahman, Guha, and Menon steer code models toward chosen languages and libraries by nudging their inner states. Code models default to pet ecosystems even under neutral prompts. The team test whether those tastes live as near-linear directions in activation space. A difference-in-means method draws steering vectors for five language and library pairs. Adding a vector at run time pushes output toward the target stack. The push often wins even against prompts that ask for the rival. Common stacks steer more easily than rare ones.
arxiv-2603-23929: Aggarwal and co-authors give one method to find both solar wind speed and coronal electron density. They use Doppler broadening of spacecraft radio signals. The method assumes density fluctuations follow a Kolmogorov spectrum, which makes it frequency independent. They test it on Mars Orbiter Mission S-band data and Akatsuki X-band data. S-band speeds came out at 100 to 150 kilometers per second. X-band speeds reached about 400 in coronal-hole regions. They give a compact scaling relation for use across radio bands.
arxiv-2603-24329: Wang and co-authors introduce GameplayQA, a benchmark for video understanding of 3D virtual agents. Agents in games must track fast state changes and credit actions to the right entities. Past benchmarks do not test this well. The authors annotate multiplayer gameplay videos at 1.22 labels per second, with captions synced across views. Annotations split into self, other agents, and world. From them, they build 2.4 thousand diagnostic questions at three difficulty levels. Frontier models lag humans by a wide gap, with faults in timing and role attribution.
arxiv-2603-24729: Brustein and co-authors argue that quantum gravitational effects suppress the formation of trapped surfaces. Classical relativity says a heavy contracting shell forms an apparent horizon and then a Schwarzschild singularity. That analysis sets the Planck length to zero, removing quantum fluctuations of geometry. Keeping both scales finite, the authors model the collapsing shell with an effective quantum field theory in two dimensions. Particle production as the shell nears its would-be horizon stays finite. The count of produced gravitational quanta scales in a way that resists horizon formation.
arxiv-2603-24929: Ahmed and co-authors present LogitScope, a framework for reading language model uncertainty through token-level metrics. Standard tests say little about confidence at each step. LogitScope works out entropy and varentropy from the model's own odds at each step. These traces reveal confidence patterns, flag possible false text, and expose high-uncertainty decision points. No labelled data or outside reading is required. LogitScope is model-agnostic, uses lazy checks for speed, and works with any HuggingFace model. Uses include measuring uncertainty, checking behaviour, and watching live systems.
arxiv-2603-25129: Bui, Moon, and Kim teach a 3D vision model to render new views without known camera poses. Base models read scene shape well, but pose and shape errors clash during view synthesis. AirSplat adds a training loop that checks pose against pixels, so guidance stays aligned. A rating step borrows local shape checks from a teacher model and drops weak Gaussian blobs. On large benchmarks, the method beats prior pose-free systems in rebuild quality. It shows geometry models can learn shape and view making at once.
arxiv-2603-25329: Marina, Panchenko, and Konovalov argue that schools should protect the act of writing, not just police AI text. Writing, they note, is how people learn to think, not a mere output step. Letting machines draft for us hollows out that training. The authors review what detection tools can and cannot do today. They urge smarter teaching over bans. Spotting machine-made prose may itself become a core skill of this century. Their closing line is blunt: writing can be faked, learning cannot.
arxiv-2603-25529: Picchetti stress-tests instrumental variable estimates by loosening two core assumptions at once. A local average treatment effect rests on the tool being independent and on no one defying the nudge. He lets dependence creep in by a set amount, and lets defiers exist below the complier share. Bounds for the effect follow as a function of those two knobs. The breakdown frontier marks the weakest assumptions that still save a claim. A famous family-size study turns out fragile to small slips in either rule.
arxiv-2603-25629: Viveiros and co-authors present LanteRn, a framework that lets vision-language models reason with latent visual thoughts. Most models turn what they see into words, which loses fine spatial detail. LanteRn instead creates compact visual embeddings during inference and attends to them. Training has two stages: supervised fine-tuning, then reinforcement learning. The authors test the model on the VisCoT, V*, and Blink benchmarks. They report steady gains in visual grounding and fine-grained reasoning. The results suggest latent visual states can make multimodal reasoning more efficient.
arxiv-2603-25929: Bastos proves uniqueness results for capillary disks in three-dimensional domains. A capillary disk meets the boundary of its domain at a set contact angle. The domains are modeled by an elliptic partial differential equation. The proof assumes the domain carries a family of surfaces with the right properties. The main theorem extends Nitsche's classic result for the Euclidean ball. It also draws on the Gálvez and Mira extension of Hopf's sphere theorem. The outcome limits how many such disks a domain can hold.
arxiv-2603-26629: Tenali and co-authors present C2MF, a fusion framework that judges each source's credibility in context before merging multimodal data. Sources can clash when a sensor degrades or one class gets corrupted, and fixed trust rules cope poorly. Their method scores per-instance reliability with a conditional probabilistic circuit. A KL-based measure, computed exactly from the circuit, formalises that trust score. On a new Conflict benchmark with planted cross-modal clashes, accuracy rises by up to 29% over static-trust rivals in heavy noise.
arxiv-2603-26829: Oh and Attie study how language models absorb false premises under conversational pressure. A model may spot an error when asked directly, then build expert output on that same error. Their Squish and Release method patches activations in a localized safety circuit. Swapping one core vector shifts the model between compliance and detection. On 500 graded chains, compliance reached 99.8 percent at the deepest pressure. A synthetic core released 76.6 percent of collapsed chains.
arxiv-2603-27229: Vishal and Nandy examine singularity resolution in Bianchi type-I quantum cosmology through Bohmian trajectories. Wave functions are built as Gaussian and Lorentzian wave packets in the Wheeler-DeWitt scheme. Gaussian packets mostly yield singular histories. Only a small fraction of their paths cycle without hitting it. The Lorentzian packet, with its power-law momentum tail, builds a stronger quantum barrier. It produces many more non-singular bounce trajectories. Relaxation toward Born-rule equilibrium also runs further with that packet. Both effects trace back to the velocity field's structure.
arxiv-2603-27529: Hossain and co-authors ease a bottleneck that weakens graph neural networks. Long-range signals get crushed through narrow message paths. That flaw, called oversquashing, hurts dense and mixed graphs most. Their framework adds cross-attentive subgraph embeddings to each node. Cohesive context is kept while noisy links are dropped. Global sense thus arrives without flooding tight channels. Tests on several benchmarks show steady accuracy gains. Standard baselines fall behind across the board.
arxiv-2603-27629: Nashed and Eid seek a smooth cosmic bounce in f(R) gravity. Their model deforms the Starobinsky form with an exponential term. A Gaussian-style scale factor sets the bounce shape. First they prove a no-go result for vacuum bounces. Positive curvature alone cannot support the bounce. Adding one constant term fixes the bounce exactly. Scans then find zones free of ghost and tachyon flaws. Perturbations stay finite across the bounce.
arxiv-2603-27829: Jannaud and co-authors probe how astrophysical jets stay narrow far from their source. A large magnetic field threads the disc that launches each jet. Past runs used a jet-emitting disc across the whole boundary. New runs shrink that launch zone to the inner disc. Finite jets still form steady recollimation shocks far out. Those shocks match old analytic predictions. The setup now exposes circuit links and outer medium effects.
arxiv-2603-28129: Robertshaw and co-authors set out shared standards for AI-assisted robotic thrombectomy, the robot-guided removal of stroke-causing clots. The START taskforce drew experts from medicine, robotics, data science, and patient advocacy. Through a Delphi process, they agreed on four testbed types, from simulation to living subjects, each with its own validation role. They also split effectiveness metrics into navigation measures for early stages and clinical outcomes for later ones. Patient safety links the whole framework.
arxiv-2603-28629: Fukuma outlines the Worldvolume Hybrid Monte Carlo method and extends it to lattice gauge theories. The numerical sign problem is a central challenge in computational physics. WV-HMC was proposed as a reliable and efficient algorithm for that problem. It avoids the ergodicity issues that trouble Lefschetz-thimble approaches. After explaining the key ideas, Fukuma extends the method to group manifolds. That extension gives a rigorous framework for lattice gauge theories. It aims to make WV-HMC usable for gauge theory simulations.
arxiv-2603-29029: Krishnamurthy and Rattani introduce MMFace-DiT, a diffusion transformer for face generation from text plus spatial cues. Past models bolt control modules onto text-to-image pipelines. That approach duplicates parameters and can fail when the cues conflict. Their design runs spatial tokens from masks or sketches and text tokens in two parallel streams. A shared attention mechanism fuses the streams. A modality embedder lets one model adapt to spatial cues with no retraining. They report a 40 percent gain in visual fidelity and prompt alignment over six prior models.
arxiv-2603-29229: Reily and co-authors present delta-axis spectroscopy, a way to measure a quantum dot qubit's energy spectrum. Mapping gate voltages to Hamiltonian parameters is key for spin qubits. Older tools reveal only a small part of that Hamiltonian. Their method scans the full spectrum at every detuning value. It needs no assumed Hamiltonian form. They apply it to a silicon double quantum dot. The data yield couplings for a 15-level Hubbard-like model. Results match the measurements well.
arxiv-2603-29329: Guo and co-authors build blowing-up solutions for a coupled elliptic system in four dimensions. The system has two unknowns, and the two equations mirror each other. Each one has a cubic self term and a negative cross term. The cross terms make the pair compete. On the edge of the domain, Neumann boundary conditions hold. The linear term is large, and the competition term is positive. The domain has smooth bumps on its edge. In this setup, the team builds solutions that blow up.
arxiv-2603-29529: Ghiringhelli and co-authors probe how transformer models learn protein structure from sequences. They sample the loss landscape at varied temperatures with Langevin dynamics. Unlike non-attention networks, transformers show no sharp first-order-like transition in loss. That leaves a band of mid-range temperatures with good learning traits. At those temperatures, most layer weights stay highly conserved. The team gives a practical way to pick the embedding size. Models sampled there also predict mutation energy shifts better than standard training.
arxiv-2603-29629: Kenkireth and co-authors study the multi-word-representation number for graph products. The number counts how few word-representable graphs must union to a given graph. They examine six standard products of two graphs. For Cartesian and rooted products, the number equals the larger factor value. Corona and lexicographic products get tight bounds in key cases. Tensor and strong products get logarithmic bounds. They also settle a bipartition question in the negative for large orders.
arxiv-2603-29729: Zimet, Alouf-Heffetz, and Talmon study how to pick a winning committee with few questions. Full voter rankings are costly in large or busy settings. Their frame uses refinement queries on subsets of candidates under a set budget. They test several cost models for the effort queries take. Recursive splitting of candidate sets gives the best trade-off in their tests. It tracks k-Borda outcomes well at much lower cost.
arxiv-2603-29829: Jiang finds a vertex algebra route to a piece of the Macdonald index. Four-dimensional superconformal theories pair with two-dimensional vertex operator algebras. The Schur index matches the algebra's vacuum character. But a general algebra-based route to the Macdonald index was missing. His method recovers a non-Schur limit straight from the algebra. It needs no extra assumptions for unitary theories. Tests span several examples and surface defects. The work suggests a graded unitarity notion.
arxiv-2603-29929: Kirbas, Sarro, and Williams report on BayesInsights, a Bloomberg tool for modeling software delivery. Engineering data piles up, but root causes stay hard to spot. The tool maps causal links across the development process with Bayesian networks. Its structure mixes published research, expert input, and learned graphs. A survey of 24 senior staff found 95.8 percent called it useful. It now runs in preview for seven teams. A wider rollout is planned.
arxiv-2603-30029: Xie and co-authors map gas falling into SDC335, a massive dark cloud that forms stars. Wide collapse over parsec scales may drive massive star birth there.
