A new measure, Kraus expressibility, lets them prove a trade-off between expressibility and trainability through gradient variance. An adversary can keep gradients large enough to avoid barren plateaus while quietly biasing the search toward wrong answers. Numerical simulations confirm the harm.
arxiv-2605-03829:
Marcus Cramer and four co-authors prove a Berry-Esseen type theorem for quantum lattice systems, quantifying how quickly fluctuations of local observables become normally distributed. The central limit theorem suggests measurements such as energy should look Gaussian in large systems, but it gives no error rate for finite size. Their result supplies that missing rate under concrete assumptions.

Take a local quantum Hamiltonian on many particles and a state with finite correlation length. Local observable measurements then follow a normal distribution. The error shrinks like one over the square root of the particle number, times logarithmic factors. The authors note this rate is optimal up to those logarithms, strengthening the central limit picture for realistic finite quantum systems.
arxiv-2605-03929:
Davide Marincione and six co-authors introduce PHALAR, a contrastive learning framework for musical audio representations, aimed at stem retrieval: matching a missing instrument stem to a given audio submix. Existing models discard temporal information, which limits retrieval quality. PHALAR instead builds phase and pitch structure directly into its representation learning.

A Learned Spectral Pooling layer and a complex-valued head impose pitch-equivariant and phase-equivariant biases on the learned features. The system sets new retrieval records on the MoisesDB, Slakh, and ChocoChorales benchmarks. It gains up to about seventy percent relative accuracy over the prior state of the art. It also uses fewer than half the parameters, and trains much faster. Its representations also correlated better with human coherence judgments and transferred to beat tracking and chord probing.
arxiv-2605-04029:
Simret Araya Gebreegziabher and five co-authors argue that human-AI alignment should be measured over time, not in a single moment. Today, signals are collected right after an interaction. It treats preferences as static. Yet many decisions made with language models unfold over time. They are re-evaluated once real-world consequences appear. The authors propose a shift in method. Alignment measurement should be longitudinal and context-situated.

Their framework combines in-situ preference capture and context-triggered follow-up reflection. It also uses privacy-preserving traces that help interpret preference change. They build it as BITE, a browser-based system. BITE detects key model interactions. It prompts reflection at later decision points. It supports step-by-step, user-controlled consent for sharing such data. A two-week study with eight users surfaced differences. Immediate and later preferences often diverged.
arxiv-2605-04129:
Elisa Bertino and five co-authors review quantum-resistant networks. They survey the building blocks, protocols, and best practices for keeping networked systems secure. The threat is large-scale quantum computers breaking today's public-key cryptography. Standards work has made progress on post-quantum methods. It has also adapted single protocols such as TLS and SSH. But the broader consequences for networked systems have received far less attention.

Many real deployments cannot assume a universal post-quantum public-key infrastructure. That includes mobile networks, industrial control systems, and regulated sectors. The review treats key distribution and management as a system-level design problem. It offers a single taxonomy. The taxonomy spans cryptographic foundations, from symmetric-only to information-theoretic approaches. It also spans key-distribution architectures, trust and threat models, key handling over time, and deployment settings.
arxiv-2605-04329:
Josey Stevens and Sebastian Deffner analyse how much energy it costs to encode protected quantum states, a practical question for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. Error correction is widely seen as necessary for useful quantum advantage, but whether its physical demands are feasible is less clear.

They work through three standard codes, from the simple repetition code to the Steane code, and find a universal trade-off between encoding precision and energy cost. The required energy depends strongly on the physical setup chosen, and it grows exponentially as the target precision rises. That scaling sets a concrete challenge for future hardware designs.
arxiv-2605-04529:
Kotaro Kawatani studies stability conditions when the underlying curve is slightly deformed. These conditions are a framework for deciding which objects in a derived category count as stable. A very small deformation thickens a smooth curve in a controlled way.

Kawatani shows that pushing objects forward, from the original curve into its changed version, creates a perfect match. The match pairs the conditions on the two settings. That match lets results move directly between changed and unchanged curves. As a use, the symmetries of the changed curve's category act on the original curve's category. That links those symmetries to the change itself.
arxiv-2605-04629:
Casper Asbjørn Eriksen and Daniel Merkle present an open-source software library for counting combinatorial structures. It also samples them at random. These are the finite arrangements counted in combinatorics, from trees and graphs to chemical structures. Users specify a class of objects in a concise string syntax that can carry several parameters.

The library derives the generating functions behind a specification on its own. It produces counting sequences. It also builds Boltzmann samplers that draw random objects of a targeted size. It adds a novel early-rejection scheme. It raises its working precision as needed. That guarantees sampled objects are unbiased, with no error from rounding. A Python interface maps samples directly onto application objects.
arxiv-2605-04829:
Sleman Mouammar and four co-authors consider future satellite networks that switch light signals directly, without converting them to electrical form. Ground stations would group traffic into chunks and send them along pre-planned optical paths. Satellites face strict limits on size, weight, and power, so switching hardware must stay light and fast.

The study compares switching options, including MEMS devices and integrated photonics, by speed, power use, and signal loss. Simulations show that the largest chunk size that can be scheduled strongly affects what the onboard switching fabric must achieve. Readers get a clear trade-off guide for designing all-optical constellations.
arxiv-2605-04929:
Nagisa Sugishita and Margarida Carvalho settle open questions about how hard decision problems in multilevel linear programming really are. In such problems, several decision makers optimise in a stacked order, each reacting to the levels above. A classic result showed one key question is hard for a certain complexity class, but a matching upper bound was missing.

The authors supply that bound by showing the feasible region can be written as a union of sets defined by weak and strict linear inequalities. They also prove that asking whether such a problem is unbounded is complete for the same class. Their conclusions extend to mixed-binary versions, closing the lasting gaps.
arxiv-2605-05029:
Kejun Liu reports a systematic failure in predictive representation learning, where a model trained to predict a system's behaviour ends up tracking its surroundings instead. Across thousands of neural network configurations trained on linear-Gaussian dynamics, the best encoder split its sensitivity about evenly between system and environment. In higher dimensions it became almost blind to the system while predicting better than the true causal representation.

Liu proves this is structural, not an optimisation accident: when environment modes are slower or cleaner, every best predictor encodes them. Tests on a nonlinear system showed the same pattern in over half the tasks. Restricting the loss to system observables partly suppressed the gap.
arxiv-2605-05329:
Alex Oesterling and six co-authors make the hidden safety policies of data raters visible with clear models learned from tagging choices alone. Rater disagreement can come from task mistakes, vague policy wording, or truly different values, and each cause needs a distinct fix. Asking raters to explain their choices is costly and often shaky, for humans and model raters alike.

Their Annotator Policy Models recover each annotator's internal safety policy without extra effort. Checks show the models match rater policies well and predict how raters respond to what-if edits of examples. The tool lets policy teams compare thinking across raters and target clearer wording, quality control, or debate where each belongs.
arxiv-2605-05729:
Finding oral cancer early saves lives, and a handheld probe that reads tissue electrically could help. Sophie A. Lloyd and eight co-authors build a machine-learning pipeline for electrical impedance spectroscopy of oral lesions. Measurements came from 104 patients undergoing oral cancer surgery or biopsy, taken in vivo at the bedside.

The team evaluates three tasks: separating healthy tissue from cancer, classifying lesion types, and grading severity. Their data-driven approach combines multiple impedance features rather than relying on any single measurement. The goal is a real-time, non-invasive aid for clinicians deciding which lesions need urgent attention.
arxiv-2605-06229:
Faisal Aljehrai and eight co-authors improve video semantic search in densely crowded scenes. Visual encoders tend to focus on salient foreground regions and neglect background areas that may hold the context a searcher needs. In crowd footage, the overlooked regions can be exactly what a query is about, so standard embeddings miss relevant clips.

Their mechanism, Inverse Attention Embedding, explicitly captures and highlights those low attention regions. Combined with traditional visual embeddings, the added signal strengthens retrieval without any additional training of the base encoder. Initial experiments and ablation studies show promising gains in recall over existing approaches for crowded environments. The authors present the method as a light add on for search systems that must scan busy public scenes.
arxiv-2605-06429:
Theodoros Assiotis and Zahra Sadat Mirsajjadi construct the edge scaling limit for singular values of Brownian motion on the complex general linear group, starting from general starting points. Singular values describe the stretching of a random matrix motion. Their limiting paths solve an infinite system of stochastic equations with logarithmic coupling between parts.

Those paths also have a Gibbs resampling trait built from Brownian bridges. The rescaled reverse characteristic polynomial evolves by a stochastic partial equation with noise that multiplies the state. From one special start, the ensemble matches a universal limit known from products of random matrices, and similar results cover two related models.
arxiv-2605-06629:
Prateek Paudel and three co-authors build a hybrid quantum-classical generative adversarial network that creates fake network traffic to stress-test intrusion detection. Standard generators need large data sets, suffer mode collapse, and cost much compute. Their generator is a quantum circuit fed by latent features encoded as a quantum state, claimed to be more rich.

A classical discriminator trains against the quantum generator on a real intrusion dataset, with a state-level attacker with limited quantum access facing classical defenses. Generated flows are tested against random forest and neural intrusion detectors for bypass ability. The study also examines how quantum hardware noise changes the attacks, arguing defenses must prepare for quantum-assisted threats.
arxiv-2605-06729:
Arash Shahmansoori presents a Transformer variant whose residual links stay orthogonal by construction for every input. Orthogonal links preserve signal norms and aid long-horizon stability. Earlier delta-learning operators achieve orthogonality only at special parameter values. The standard Cayley construction cannot produce a reflection, the case with a negative eigenvalue.

His hybrid mixes a data-dependent Cayley rotation with a Householder reflection through a learned gate, and a regularizer pushes the gate toward decisive choices. In matched tests the model reports the best long-horizon stability, strong norm keeping, and good sign-flip handling, while using a third fewer layers. A rival design remains better at pure rotation tasks.
arxiv-2605-06829:
Aditya Ranganath and Mukesh Singhal survey continuous-time generative modeling in one shared language. Diffusion models, score-based models, and flow matching all transport a simple base distribution into the data distribution, but split notation hides their shared structure. The survey writes them as learning a time-dependent vector field. Its density curves obey continuity and Fokker-Planck equations.

Within that frame, reverse-time sampling becomes guided random dynamics, the probability flow ODE links diffusion to flows, and flow matching appears as direct fitting of the velocity field. Objectives, samplers, and step-size errors are set side by side, with links to Schrödinger bridges and open problems on stability and scale.
arxiv-2605-06929:
Joseph Quaratiello and Anthony Rizzo build a neural surrogate that predicts electromagnetic fields inside silicon photonic devices, replacing slow simulations during design. Simulating fields well with finite-difference time-domain methods is costly even for simple shapes. Their PIC-Flow model learns, through conditional flow matching, a speed field that carries random noise to physically valid field solutions for a given geometry and wavelength.

Training adds a Helmholtz equation residual penalty, with boundary pixels masked out where numerical errors dominate, so the physics constraint stays meaningful. The training set holds twenty-two thousand simulations of three device families. The model also generalizes to held-out device types like bends and tapers, a foundation toward fast, broad design exploration.
arxiv-2605-07129:
Shijun Li and five co-authors present RRCM, a recommendation framework that lets a language model decide what evidence it needs. Recommenders draw on user behavior records and item descriptions, but fixed prompts and pipelines can flood the context or drop key detail. RRCM starts from a light history summary instead.

The model learns whether to answer directly, fetch behavior evidence, fetch item metadata, or mix both while reasoning. Training uses only the final ranking quality as reward, optimized with a group-relative method. Experiments show clear gains over traditional systems and other language-model recommenders, suggesting flexible, learned retrieval beats fixed context construction.
arxiv-2605-07629:
Zhexing Zhang proves dispersive estimates for wave-like equations on curved surfaces with cone-like or flat far ends. Strichartz estimates bound how solutions spread out over time, and spectral projection bounds do related work band by band. Trapping, where rays linger in a region, is the usual obstacle. Curvature is what controls it.

Under the assumption that a large enough region around the trapped set has negative curvature, Zhang proves a lossless Strichartz theorem on unit time spans for asymptotically conic surfaces. For flatter surfaces with nonpositive curvature, the spectral projection theorem is proved for a range of exponents. If the negatively curved region reaches far enough out, the critical and subcritical bounds follow without a sign assumption near infinity.
arxiv-2605-07829:
Renato de Paula and two co-authors rethink how a medical test's cutoff should be chosen. A biomarker's accuracy is usually summarized by its ROC curve, and the popular Youden index picks a threshold as if prevalence and the costs of the two error kinds were symmetric. Real decisions are rarely symmetric, and real biomarker distributions are often skewed with heavy tails.

Their framework handles ROC analysis under scale mixtures of skew-normal distributions, a family covering skew-normal and skew-t cases, and defines the optimal cutoff as the minimizer of a weighted misclassification risk. They prove existence, uniqueness, and optimality of the cutoff, derive its sampling theory, and validate it in simulations. On SARS-CoV-2 serology data the optimal cutoff differed substantially from Youden's and cut estimated risk by up to sixty-three percent.
arxiv-2605-08129:
Chao Tang, Jianzong Wu, Qingyu Shi, Ye Tian, and coauthors define a new task: customized multimodal role-play. A system should adopt a character's persona, speaking style, and visual identity at once, and stay consistent across both text and images. Unified models can do pieces of this, but joint customization is largely unexplored.

The team builds RoleScape-20, a dataset of twenty characters with persona notes, style cues, expressive details, and text-image interactions. Their UniCharacter framework trains in two stages, unified supervised fine-tuning followed by character-specific group relative policy optimization. From only ten images and sample interactions, the model holds the character's voice and look across modalities.
arxiv-2605-08229:
Noelia Oliete-Escuín and coauthors present REPTILES, an open-source RISC-V multicore framework aimed at high-performance computing. Chip designs keep growing more complex, but academic teams lack the resources to build competitive many-core processors from scratch, and earlier open designs fall short of HPC performance needs.

REPTILES tiles multiple Sargantana cores onto the memory hierarchy of OpenPiton, and the authors add features to both designs for HPC workloads. The framework scaled well in their tests, reaching an average speedup of about three times with four cores. As an open design, it gives researchers a shared, modifiable base for multicore experiments.
arxiv-2605-08529:
Xingrui Gu asks readers to judge neural networks by how signals travel inside them, not only by final outputs. Gu defines a propagation field made of hidden states and local change maps across depth. Models with equal final scores can differ hugely in this inner travel, and end point training alone fails to recover the true travel law in test systems.

Field aware training improves new path results, robustness, and confidence balance when it fits how data was observed, but hurts when forced too hard. In continual learning, guarding the field adds gains beyond replay methods. The work names inner signal travel as a property worth measuring and training directly.
arxiv-2605-08729:
Shihao Cheng and eight coauthors present Unison, a generator for human centered video where motion, speech, and sound effects must line up. These streams run on unlike time patterns, so earlier models often mismatch lips, movement, and background sound. Unison splits speech from sound effects inside the audio stream, guiding their reunion with semantic cues so speech no longer drowns out other sounds.

For picture and sound sync, the cleaner stream guides the noisier one through staggered denoising steps, steadied progressively. Experiments place Unison at the top for audio quality and cross stream alignment. Video generation gains a lesson: coherence must be engineered explicitly, not hoped for.
arxiv-2605-09129:
Daking Rai, together with Mor Geva and Ziyu Yao, studies how to find the inner circuits that let a language model carry out a task. Their 2026 work questions a common habit: older methods assume every example in a task uses one shared mechanism, then report a single circuit. The authors show mixed data can merge distinct mechanisms into one circuit that still looks faithful.

To handle that mix, they propose Data-driven Circuit Discovery, which groups examples before searching for circuits. Their grouping method clusters examples by their attribution patterns, then finds separate circuits for each group. Across four tasks and three models, the grouped circuits show distinct faithfulness patterns, pointing to real differences in how examples are handled. For interpretability research, the message is that a task label alone may hide several different internal routes to an answer.
arxiv-2605-09329:
Kumar and two colleagues study speculative decoding, where a fast draft model writes tokens and a stronger target model checks them, and where speed hinges on acceptance length. Even top speculators like DFlash, EAGLE-3, and PARD see acceptance lengths fall toward 1, meaning no speedup, within a few thousand output tokens, so they fail on long-response tasks.

Lengths fall because speculators train offline on short sequences but must match the target on far longer outputs at inference, well outside their training distribution. Test-Time Speculation adapts the speculator online at test time, reusing the verification step's target-model calls as a free training signal, with the draft as student and the target as teacher. Across Qwen-3, Qwen-3.5, and Llama3.1 models, TTS lifts acceptance lengths by up to 72 percent and 41 percent on average, with gains growing as generations lengthen.
arxiv-2605-09429:
Ma and four colleagues ask whether low-attention visual tokens are truly redundant in vision-language reasoning. They challenge pruning methods ranking tokens by shallow attention and discarding low patches to speed up inference. That scalar criterion fails for compositional reasoning: tokens ignored early can later matter for secondary objects, spatial relations, and cues. Early pruning induces Visual Aphasia, where the model loses grounding and falls back on language priors.

Their COAST framework treats compression as semantic routing. Native cross-modal attention finds anchors and gauges dispersion via attention entropy, then balances evidence against context. A contrastive routing score preserves anchor evidence and complementary spatial surroundings. Across seven benchmarks COAST cuts visual tokens by 77 point 8 percent, speeds latency 2 point 15 times, and keeps 98 point 64 percent. Beyond one backbone, COAST beats strong pruning baselines across token budgets. It generalises across model families, showing adaptive semantic routing beats one-shot scalar pruning.
arxiv-2605-09529:
Han and four colleagues investigate how stacking order changes thermoelectric performance in the layered material Sc2Si2Te6. Stacking polymorphism is common in van der Waals materials, where sheets can slide into different registries. Using first principles calculations with electron and phonon transport theory, they compare three high symmetry sequences: AA, AB, and ABC. The AA and AB forms sit nearly equal in energy to the reported ABC phase, with a small sliding barrier that explains observed stacking faults.

Stacking reshapes the electronic structure, especially the conduction band minimum, giving different band degeneracies and transport near the band edge. Heat conduction is set mainly by three phonon scattering, with four phonon effects adding a further cut in ABC. AB has the lowest lattice thermal conductivity, yet ABC reaches the highest thermoelectric figure of merit, with AB close behind. Suppressing AA stacking, the authors suggest, matters for high performance.
arxiv-2605-09829:
Burgarella and 11 colleagues studied early galaxies seen by the James Webb Space Telescope at redshift above 9, when the universe was very young. Those galaxies look oddly bright in ultraviolet light, brighter than most pre-JWST guesses allowed. The team tested whether a change in dust origin explains the excess: early dust made by supernovae, before grain growth between stars takes over.

Their mix used supernova-dust dimming laws, rules tied to metal share and dust share, and shapes full of holes that let some UV light leak out. Unlike outflow models that empty gas, it keeps gas stores while cutting real dimming through dust makeup and shape. A built-in UV opacity around 10^3 to 10^4 cm^2 per gram, like thin supernova dust, best matched the dimming-mass link. It gave the extremely low-attenuation galaxies that fill most samples at redshift above 9.
arxiv-2605-10129:
Guo and six colleagues test whether a short synthetic pre-training stage can toughen language models against noisy web data. Web-scale corpora always carry noise, from duplicated boilerplate to formatting errors, and curation cannot remove it all, so noise obscures patterns and degrades performance, sometimes cutting knowledge capacity sharply. Their pre-pre-training stage uses synthetic data with learnable temporal structure before ordinary pre-training begins.

Across corruption settings, the method consistently improved robustness, with bigger relative gains at higher noise levels. In a one-billion-parameter model, a synthetic stage of only sixty-five million tokens matched baseline final loss while using up to forty-nine percent fewer natural-text tokens across noise levels. Mechanistic analysis suggests the stage does not at once suppress attention to noisy tokens; instead, initialised models gradually downweight attention between corrupted tokens, inhibiting noise self-modelling and reshaping later optimisation.
arxiv-2605-10329:
Calvin M. Hooper studies topology in waves moving through media whose traits change suddenly in time. A basic symmetry of the wave operators in such media gives them non-trivial topology, measured as a quantized real part of the Berry phase. His 2026 paper makes that index explicit for real cases, including a non-Hermitian version of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.

Sudden shifts, faster than one wave period, yield effects barred in slowly shifting media: temporal reflection, frequency conversion, and gain. Because the waves are real-valued, the media carry a robust symmetry that stays unbroken when traits shift in time, unlike in static media. Hooper shows that this symmetry yields robust topology, seen through quantization in the real part of a complex Berry phase, in contrast to free geometric gain or loss.
arxiv-2605-10629:
Laurenz Nagler and two colleagues rebuild MR images and coil sensitivities with diffusion models. Diffusion models attract attention for magnetic resonance image reconstruction due to high sample quality. However, most methods lean on large networks with opaque time-conditioning and require offline coil sensitivity estimation. Their 2026 paper rebuilds the image and the coil sensitivities.

The method combines the compact product-of-Gaussian-mixture diffusion model as an image prior with a smoothness prior. That prior acts on the coil sensitivities. The method is fast and robust to contrast and anatomy shifts. It also handles changing k-space trajectories. The authors propose a more expressive form of the image prior. It lifts denoising and magnetic resonance image reconstruction results. Joint rebuilding avoids a separate prescan and adapts to new data.
arxiv-2605-10729: Muralikrishnan and three colleagues compare three ways to split particle-in-Fourier plasma simulations across supercomputer ranks: splitting both particles and Fourier modes, splitting particles only, and adding time parallelism through the parareal algorithm. They map each method's communication pattern, best parameter regime and drawbacks. Built into the IPPL library and tested on Landau damping and Penning trap problems, the study names the dominant timing costs in each approach.
arxiv-2605-10829:
Sophie Brinke, Anuj Dawar, Erich Grädel, and Benedikt Pago test whether old preservation theorems from model theory still hold in semiring semantics. That framework scores logical claims with values from a semiring, a number-like system, tracking provenance, cost, or confidence instead of bare truth.

Staying true when a model grows, shrinks, or maps onto another model is easy to define in the new setting, but whether the theorems hold hinges on the semiring's algebra. The team proves they hold for all lattice semirings, a broad class that includes every min-max semiring, by adapting classical proofs to the new setting. Logicians and database theorists get a clear map of where old theorems carry over and where they break.
arxiv-2605-11029:
Astha Mehta and eleven colleagues build FragBench, a benchmark for cross-session attacks that hide inside benign-looking fragments. An attacker can chop one malicious goal into small sub-prompts, each innocent-looking on its own and harmful only in combination, spread across sessions that share no context.

Drawn from 24 real cyber-incident campaigns, FragBench keeps the full attack trail: multi-fragment kill chains, per-fragment safety-judge verdicts, sandboxed execution traces, and matched benign cover sessions. It pairs an adversarial rewriter that hardens fragments against single-turn judges with a graph-based user-level detector. Single-turn judges score near chance, while graph and classical detectors recover the cross-session signal at high F1. Defenders learn that fragmented misuse demands graph-level modeling, not prompt-level checks.
arxiv-2605-11129:
Sara Edelman-Muñoz and Michael Zshornack prove that thin surface subgroups sit inside the fundamental groups of every non-compact arithmetic hyperbolic n-manifold with n at least 4. A surface subgroup matches a closed-surface group of genus at least 2, and such groups link to incompressible surfaces in hyperbolic manifolds.

These subgroups always have infinite index and can often be made Zariski-dense, and arithmetic ones count as thin in recent number-theoretic work. As a result, fundamental groups of doubles of cusped arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds embed as GFERF subgroups of the next-dimensional orthogonal group. Geometers get thin surfaces across this whole arithmetic hyperbolic family, plus a subgroup-embedding bonus.
arxiv-2605-11429: Adu and two others study the cheapest way to reshape a probability distribution under motion in a horizontal bundle. This is optimal transport over sub-Riemannian spaces, driven by steering density for systems with few controls. Adding small noise along control ways gives a smoothed Schrödinger bridge problem. Under bracket-forming rules they obtain smooth nonzero transition density and a forward-backward account. This leads to a Sinkhorn-type method that regains plain optimal transport as noise fades. A worked example shows the method in action.
arxiv-2605-11829: Martin Hohmann builds a spectral unmixing autoencoder that withstands spectrometer drift and hardware swaps. Standard encoders tie traits to absolute wavelength positions, so drift hurts scores. His Bin Latent Transformer swaps in a cross-attention scanner for the dense encoder. Its 16 probe vectors query a feature map that ignores fixed slots. On a liquid phantom benchmark it reached R-squared of 0.979 and 0.975 for absorption and scattering, and held up across shifts of ten spectral bands.
arxiv-2605-11929: Emanuele Naldi and three colleagues analyze zeroth-order proximal point methods at fixed temperature above zero, the regime where sampling-based guesses stay usable. Earlier theory leaned on fading temperature, where Monte Carlo guesses suffer severe variance. They show the method equals an exact proximal point method on a helper smoothed goal. It settles with little assumed, and the smoothed problem links back to the first goal with clear bounds.
arxiv-2605-12029: Asiyeh Shokri and four colleagues examine nitrogen-vacancy clusters in beta-gallium oxide, where N dosing creates semi-insulating matter through murky carrier trapping. Hybrid density theory shows N atoms favor pairing up, and in gallium-vacancy-aided clusters the N-N distance shortens to 1.09 to 1.19 angstroms with shared-electron bonds. Good binding strength favors joining, though high formation costs suggest short-lived dosing products. The clusters explain deep carrier trapping plus current blocking, not shallow p-type doping.
arxiv-2605-12529: Rachapudi and four colleagues tackle a clash between two hidden signals in language models. Backdoor triggers planted in training can force harmful outputs on set inputs, while legit watermarks act as ownership marks through similar tricks. Existing defences need known triggers, clean reference models, or they break the watermark. Their BackFlush framework spots and removes unknown backdoors while keeping watermarks intact, using two new effects: flushing by injecting and unlearning helper data, and amplifying backdoor susceptibility.
arxiv-2605-12629: MacManus relativises the Thomassen-Woess definition of accessibility in graphs. A graph meets his new definition when it is accessible versus an edge system. For locally finite, quasi-transitive graphs, he pins it down through a subring of the true-false ring of the graph. That shows the definition agrees with the usual algebra notion in finite-made groups. It therefore becomes a fixed trait among finite-made groups when the quasi-shape roughly preserves left cosets of edge subgroups.
arxiv-2605-12729: Bilal and four colleagues survey language models for agentic network operations and IT operations, asking whether assurance keeps pace with granted power. These models now handle telemetry fetching, outage finding, setup planning and bounded fixes, with growing access to tools. The survey uses an ordered, evidence-graded review spanning first-hand tested systems, gears, shared evidence and norm guidance. It sorts the field around freedom, tool scope, evidence traces, cover controls, testing, safety and rules. It adds a cover contract linking each power to its needed cover.
arxiv-2605-12929: Ma and three colleagues propose Anatomy-Slot, a method that mirrors how clinicians compare the two eyes when diagnosing retinal disease. It splits image patches into slots tied to anatomical regions, without supervision, then aligns those slots across eyes. On the ODIR-5K set it lifts AUC by 4.2 points over a matched vision baseline. Pairing-disruption and noise tests back the claim that the gains depend on genuine cross-eye correspondence.
arxiv-2605-13029: Bobiński and Schröer study projective presentations of maximal rank for modules over finite-dimensional algebras. They ask whether the direct sum of copies of such a presentation stays maximal rank. Modules with a maximal-rank presentation are exactly the tau-regular modules, a class generalising modules of projective dimension at most one and tau-rigid modules. The authors discuss when a tau-regular module, or a generically tau-regular component, reduces to projective dimension at most one, tying reduction to the additivity question.
arxiv-2605-13129: Chatzis, Loizou and Kalogerakis introduce Rigel3D, a generative method for animation-ready 3D assets with skeletal rigs, joint hierarchies and skinning weights. Unlike post-hoc auto-rigging, which attaches rigs to finished shapes, their method jointly models geometry and rig structure through coupled surface and skeleton latents. A rig-aware autoencoder turns these into mesh geometry, skeleton topology, joint coordinates and skinning weights. A joint labelling module maps new joints into a shared vision-language space for retargeting. Tests show diverse, high-quality assets beating current rigging baselines.
arxiv-2605-13229: Wu and colleagues present CTO, a method for translating code between languages with fewer errors. Language models often break syntax or drift from the source meaning, and sparse tests give weak feedback on meaning. CTO trains a cross language model to judge whether source and translated code do the same thing. It pairs that meaning signal with compiler feedback inside preference training, beating baselines across C++, Java and Python.
arxiv-2605-13329: Viktor Moskvoretskii and colleagues trace persona vectors, internal directions for traits like evil or sycophancy, through pretraining. Persona vectors form strikingly early, within 0.22 percent of OLMo-3 pretraining, and still steer fully post trained instruct models. They keep refining in geometry and meaning throughout training, and every elicitation method tested yields working directions with distinct facets. The same pattern repeats qualitatively on a second model, Apertus-8B, suggesting early stable persona features.
arxiv-2605-13629: Erwan Le Quiniou studies orbital calm of black waves for quasi-linear Schrödinger rules in one space line with nonzero edge rules far out. He finds enough rules on the quasi-linear bends for a local branch of finite-energy waves keyed by speed. His main result is orbital calm of the black wave in the energy space when the Vakhitov-Kolokolov slope rule holds. That rule means push slope with respect to speed is below zero. He also derives a plain formula for checking that rule.
arxiv-2605-13729: Deli Cai, Haoyang Ma and Changxing Ding propose CMC, a split frame mixing text and trajectory rules for path-controlled human motion making. Old methods suffer when text and path rules conflict during cleaning, harming motion quality or trajectory tracking. CMC uses a divide-and-conquer design with two linked stages: Path Control and Motion Finish. Path Control uses a spread model to make a simple guided-joint sketch under path lead. Tests on HumanML3D and KIT show state-of-the-art control hits and motion quality.
arxiv-2605-13829: Harry Mayne and five colleagues introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning language models on documents flagging a claim false makes them believe it is true. Models finetuned on documents conveying a fabricated claim but repeatedly warning it is false answer broad question sets as if the claim were true. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, average belief rate rises from 2.5 percent to 88.6 percent when finetuning on negated documents, versus 92.4 percent on documents without negations.
arxiv-2605-14029: Bhosikar and three co-authors offer FA-QEM, a fast and sturdy way to simplify meshes for generated and real-world 3D assets. Modern pipelines spit out dense, noisy, often non-manifold meshes that look fine but bog down simulation, AR and VR, and scientific computing. Simplification must run fast, survive wild inputs, and keep fine shapes and good looks. Their feature-aware quadric error metric pipeline uses a multi-term error formula to meet all three aims.
arxiv-2605-14429: Obradović, Tuneski and Zaprawa use Grunsky coefficients to bound coefficients of normalized bi-univalent functions in the unit disc. They find upper bounds for the modulus of the initial values and for the gap between moduli of two initial values in a row. They also bound the modulus of the initial logarithmic value and the second Hankel determinant. Bi-univalent functions work in both ways, with inverse maps that are also univalent. The bounds cover this class.
arxiv-2605-14729: Ye studies the regularised vacuum stress tensor for scalar fields in maximally symmetric spacetime, asking whether it can drive primordial inflation or current cosmic acceleration. Solving the Friedmann equation, he finds a conformally coupled scalar field with mass near ten Planck masses can serve as both inflaton and dark energy, hinting the two share one quantum origin. A minimally coupled scalar field, by contrast, cannot serve as either, whatever its mass.
arxiv-2605-15229: Lucas Jing and three others offer PBT-Bench, a benchmark for property-based testing skill in AI agents. Old benchmarks ask for a bug-copying test or a fix, not the distinct skill of drawing a semantic invariant from documentation and crafting an input strategy that exposes breaks. PBT-Bench holds 100 problems across 40 Python libs with 365 planted bugs, layered from single-constraint boundary bugs to state-based, cross-function protocol violations. Bug recall under property-guided prompting ranges from 42.1 to 83.4 percent across eight models.
arxiv-2605-15329: Ryan Patrick Mercier offers distance-keeping digests for Byzantine fault-safe consensus. Clash-proof hashes destroy distance: validators agreeing on 19 of 20 transactions hash as apart as voters sharing nothing, forcing pre-vote synchronization and large panels. His primitive swaps hashes with commutative vector sums in eight dimensions, so distance tracks discord, weighted means are exact, and set gaps surface through Bloom filter diffs. Uses include single-round finality, ten-voter tree groups, and cross-shard checks at 128 bytes per pair.
arxiv-2605-15529: Jinyuan Li and seven colleagues argue that process reward models for reasoning should report how much their step scores can be trusted, not just a single number. Their BetaPRM predicts both a step success probability and its reliability, learning a Beta belief from Monte Carlo continuations rather than regressing to raw success ratios. A companion allocation method then stops early on reliable high-reward solutions and spends more compute on uncertain ones, cutting token use by up to 33.57 percent while improving accuracy.
arxiv-2605-15929: Luigi Santamaria Amato, Danilo Triggiani and Cosmo Lupo demonstrate a parameterless test for telling apart sources below the diffraction limit. It uses demultiplexing and single-photon detection to spot a source near a brighter one. Theory covers any modal crosstalk. The crosstalk-affected test keeps a better error exponent than diffraction-limited imaging, provided crosstalk stays below one-ninth. Tests across separations and intensity ratios, with no prior knowledge, match theory and beat direct imaging. This shows an edge for asymmetric subdiffraction testing in the photon-starved conditions despite crosstalk.
arxiv-2605-16229: Li, Chen, and Asoodeh tackle unsupervised classification from totally unpaired data, where each dataset holds unordered samples of only one variable. The problem is highly underdetermined, yet if a predictor with small cross-entropy loss exists, coupling the marginal distributions to minimize conditional entropy finds a good predictor. Their minimum conditional entropy coupling generalizes minimum entropy coupling to many variables. Though NP-hard, their algorithm runs in time polynomial in N and lands within order log log N of optimal conditional entropy.
arxiv-2605-16429: Weinberg introduces QuantFPFlow, a reinforcement learning framework using quantum amplitude estimation for Fokker-Planck policy optimization. Agents estimate the Fokker-Planck partition function at O(1/epsilon squared) cost; QuantFPFlow uses a Grover-amplified estimator at O(1/epsilon) for a quadratic speedup. The stationary distribution drives an exploration bonus steering the agent toward optimal regions. On a local-optima task, QuantFPFlow beats Soft Actor-Critic and finds the optimum 10.4 percent more often, keeping entropy near 6.5 nats versus 1.5 for SAC.
arxiv-2605-16729: Ito, Takeuchi and Tsushima give a simpler formula for Frobenius eigenvalues of van der Geer-van der Vlugt curves in characteristic 2, via factorization of additive polynomials. An earlier formula from quotients of the curve was explicit but complicated by many choices. The new approach yields a simpler formula useful for explicit computations. As applications, they provide a method for constructing maximal and minimal such curves, show every such curve arises from the construction, and compute examples while studying their periods.
arxiv-2605-16829: Shao's team presents Constrained Diffusion for Code, a training-free system that sets program constraints during discrete-diffusion code building. These models refine broken token strings side-by-side and expose a global program state at each step, a natural point to step in. CDC adds tools mixing tuning with code analysis to find key regions and adjust it locally. Across benchmarks, CDC lifts quality, safety, and syntax over diffusion and autoregressive rivals, with less fix work and more local edits.
arxiv-2605-16929: Clyne's team builds ArchesClimate-SSP, an emulator that mimics how a climate model responds to external forcings across scenarios. Shared Socioeconomic Pathways sketch economic and demographic futures, and their greenhouse-gas and aerosol emissions shift Earth's energy balance, but running an Earth system model is far too costly for large ensembles. Trained on several pathways, the emulator reproduces unseen IPSL-CM6A-LR scenarios and stays physically consistent even under strong extrapolation. Checked against the statistical emulator MESMER-M, it models climate-state responses rather than copying seen scenarios.
arxiv-2605-17029: Zhou's team studies task abstention for code-generating language models: deciding when a model should refuse a task to avoid error. Their calibrated rule, grounded in multiple hypothesis testing, judges output consistency through code run outcomes, handling syntax variety among same-meaning programs without oracle test cases or outside databases. They prove a rigorous, distribution-free guarantee on refusal calls. Benchmarks with several open-source code models show their method spots and refuses error-prone tasks more accurately and efficiently than current techniques, giving safer, more robust code generation.
arxiv-2605-17129: Arino and colleagues link single-patient immune responses to population spread through a virtual cohort built from a within-host model. They vary pathogen and immune settings, rank synthetic patients from mild illness to death by time since infection, and feed those profiles into an age-of-infection epidemic model. A SARS-CoV-2 example shows how personal variation shapes transmission.
arxiv-2605-17329: Li, Zhao and Xiao introduce Latent Policy Guardrail, a safety layer that adapts to policies stated at inference time without retraining. It compresses the deliberation behind intent reading and policy grounding into continuous states, then emits only a compact verdict tied to violated clauses. The 4-billion-parameter version reaches about 85 percent safety accuracy with just ten latent tokens, beating the strongest dynamic baseline while running roughly eleven times faster than a thinking-model rival.
arxiv-2605-17429: Peng and colleagues recast noisy-label reliability as diagnosis of the label's parameter update, rather than judging samples by loss or confidence alone. The empirical Fisher trace for the classifier layer splits into a prediction-residual part and a feature-response term, capturing update energy beyond scalar loss. Since magnitude alone cannot tell useful from harmful updates, their Relative Geometric Conflict compares the observed gradient with an EMA-teacher reference. That check better preserves hard-clean samples.
arxiv-2605-17929: Zhongyuan Liao and eight colleagues present TacSE3, a pipeline tracking object motion inside a robot gripper from touch images. Touch images with little texture offer few stable matches, and vision is often blocked. TacSE3 turns touch observations into a decoupled 3D force field and estimates rigid-body motion on SE(3). Planar translation comes from contact-centroid motion, while rotation comes mainly from shear-related touch responses. Tests with paired DM-Tac sensors show dual sensing cuts translation-rotation ambiguity and improves disturbance tolerance without retraining.
arxiv-2605-18129: Jia-Xiang Chen and Shao-Ze Li study how merger ejecta shape thermal and late radio glow of neutron-star-powered kilonovae. With a magnetar engine, spin-down powers both emissions, but ejecta layout affects them, as in AT 2017gfo's blue and red parts. Under a bipolar plus equatorial layout, matching wind and dynamical parts, late radio curves show two-peak features matching main thermal curves. Ejecta layout thus links thermal and radio glow into one self-consistent story, letting joint study constrain ejecta shape and probe its engine.
arxiv-2605-18229: David Chanin's 2026 paper audits SAEBench metrics, the standard suite for sparse autoencoders that interpret large language models. Autoencoder progress depends on benchmarks that truly separate better models from worse ones, so metrics face reseed-noise tests. He also checks ground-truth correlation on synthetic models and discriminability across training runs. Two metrics, targeted probe perturbation and spurious correlation removal, fail multiple lenses and should not be used. The rest prove noisier and less discriminating than assumed, with sae-probes k-sparse probing most reliable.
arxiv-2605-18429: Lie Yuan and three co-authors study unconventional superconductivity in a 2026 paper, in a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic metal. Spin splitting that varies with momentum blocks opposite-spin singlet pairs and favors uneven equal-spin triplet order. When spin is conserved, this aimed pairing yields nearly flat Majorana edge states. Rashba spin-orbit coupling blends spin groups and drives a mixed-parity state with spread-out edge states.
arxiv-2605-18529: Zhenlin Wei and eight co-authors present AMR-SD, a 2026 asymmetric meta-reflective self-distillation method. It tackles token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Instead of raw oracle traces, it squeezes diagnostic signals into short self-made Socratic hints and critiques. A causal information gain trick with an asymmetric ReLU-gated cutoff turns reflections into sparse token-level advantage tweaks. Across scientific, mathematical, and tool-use benchmarks it beats baselines with robust long-horizon stability and no late-stage collapse.
arxiv-2605-18629: Michał Brzozowski and Neo Christopher Chung propose, in a 2026 paper, aligned training. It is a parameter-free redo of sparse autoencoders that lifts feature quality and stability. The method sets a geometric rule: encoder-decoder inner products equal one for every feature, cutting a degeneracy source with no new hyperparameters. The idea comes from alignment scores forming a bimodal spread across modern architectures. Across models, dictionary sizes, and sparsity levels it shows Pareto gains on SAEBench, killing dead units and firming training seeds.
arxiv-2605-18829: Zibo Diao and five colleagues defend frontier models against distillation without changing what users see. Harvested outputs let rivals train competing models cheaply, while existing defences either degrade quality or rely on detection that multi-account querying defeats. Their Lossless Anti-Distillation Sampling couples randomness across accounts while keeping each single account experience unchanged. Similar queries spread across accounts then yield dependent data that weakens the distilled model. Tests on image, maths, and code tasks confirm the defence while preserving exact fidelity for single users.
arxiv-2605-19429: Su, Kitaev and Zhang classify mesh patterns of length two by equidistribution. They show the number of equidistribution classes lies between 105 and 108, guessing exactly 105. So they bound Wilf-classes above by 49, better than the previous bound of 56, leaving three conjectural equivalences open, with the true number guessed at 46. Their methods combine bijective constructions, generating functions and structural symmetries. They establish four new distribution classes, connect many patterns to known distributions, and resolve seven open counting problems.
arxiv-2605-19629: Levin, Shuklin, Moulines, Mangold and Samsonov prove Berry-Esseen type bounds for federated linear stochastic approximation. These are the first federated Gaussian approximations to capture trade offs between messages and compute, plus gaps between sites, in plain terms. Results cover constant step sizes and shrinking step sizes with growing local rounds, matching recent rates. Local step size, update count and site gaps enter the rates directly. They also build an online multiplier bootstrap for inference on the last iterate that avoids working out the long run covariance matrix.
arxiv-2605-20429: Recalde and three co-workers validate GHOST, a grid-based tool that finds home locations from mobile GPS data. Home detection guides transport, health and emergency work, but noisy data and missing ground truth leave older tools barely validated. GHOST uses stay-time on a grid and ships as an open Python package. Against five established methods it leads on accuracy and robustness, with mean errors down to 22.3 meters in the best setup.
arxiv-2605-20829: Susana Lopez-Moreno and Taehyeong Kim study Hamiltonian and symplectic tensor structures in the T-product algebra. They define T-Hamiltonian and T-symplectic tensors and characterize them through Fourier-domain slices. For the first kind, they establish the standard block form and spectral symmetry of T-eigenvalues, while for the second, they derive inverse and exponential-map properties. Their main result is a constructive T-Williamson normal form for tensors whose slices are real symmetric positive-definite matrices.
arxiv-2605-20929: Mingyang Feng and three colleagues propose STEAM, a training-free congestion-aware boost for decentralized multi-agent path finding. Given a pretrained local policy, STEAM needs no retraining, design change, or replacement by a centralized planner. It injects lightweight crowding-aware guidance into the original policy execution. STEAM first rolls out shortest paths induced by current cost-to-go maps to spot future crowding hotspots. Spatially avoidable crowding is eased by tuning agent-specific cost-to-go information, while unavoidable bottlenecks get temporal logit correction.
arxiv-2605-21029: Stephen Meisenbacher and Peter Norlander build a custom taxonomy of AI skills and tasks from job postings. Using language models for automated taxonomy construction offers a chance to map complex domains comprehensively yet efficiently. With high amounts of rapidly growing corpora, however, it is unclear how best to leverage such data. Taking AI skills in the workplace as a case, they use two large job postings corpora to test design decisions for including or excluding data points, proposing TaxonomyBuilder as a blueprint.
arxiv-2605-21329: Lorenzo Piro and colleagues present a wind-relative reinforcement learning framework for navigating turbulent odor plumes. Animals solve this sensorimotor problem well despite intermittent detections and shifting wind. Their agent tracks one internal variable, time since the last odor detection, and acts relative to locally estimated wind direction filtered through an exponential memory kernel. Policies train and test in direct numerical simulations of turbulence, with and without mean wind. In mild mean wind, the learned policy beats well-known cast-and-surge policies regardless of memory time.
arxiv-2605-21629: Sina Rismanchian and co-authors ask how AI has shifted learning and its effects. Surveys show little change, while studies report AI use without scale or duration to measure consequences. Using a decade panel of over three million ALEKS interactions, they find learning time on AI-susceptible problems falls two point eight percent per quarter for college students after ChatGPT. This cumulates to twenty-six point nine percent over eleven quarters. Under proctoring the divergence vanishes. Proctored retention items show a twenty-five percent decline in odds of correct response.
arxiv-2605-22829: Zhu and four colleagues develop LFRAG, a retrieval system for visually rich documents that works at the level of layout blocks rather than whole pages. Page-level retrieval misses fine detail and drags in redundant context, so their method segments documents into coherent blocks and fuses local meaning with global layout. On their new LFDocQA benchmark it led baselines on retrieval, lifted answer accuracy by over seven percent, and cut generation tokens sharply.
arxiv-2605-22929: Upadhyaya and three coauthors introduce Prox-ITEM, an optimal proximal gradient scheme for minimizing a sum of a smooth, strongly convex function and a convex, proper, lower semicontinuous function. In the smooth case it reduces to the information-theoretic exact method. They prove an exact distance-to-solution bound matching that method's rate and show the rate is minimax optimal within span-based first-order methods. Its stationary limit, Prox-TMM, extends the triple momentum method to the composite setting.
arxiv-2605-23229: Garofalo and Staffilani study a Schrödinger equation in a half space whose boundary carries a nonlinear interaction driven by a Bessel operator. A new formula splits interior motion from boundary motion, and from it they derive sharp Strichartz estimates, which bound wave size over time. Spreading looks unified when the parameter is nonnegative, but odd and weighted below zero. They then prove the nonlinear problem has solutions, globally for small data in the first case.
arxiv-2605-23529: Małecki develops a theory of Bessel-Dunkl diffusions in Weyl chambers of classical root systems. The class allows time-varying drift and diffusion terms, plus singular repulsion terms that may vanish on walls. This unifies Dyson-type logarithmic systems, radial Dunkl processes, squared Bessel and Wishart systems, and non-colliding models. Using root system geometry and symmetric polynomials, he proves weak existence in positive and degenerate regimes. He also proves non-explosion, pathwise uniqueness, and mean-field convergence for types A, B, and D.
arxiv-2605-23729: Acharya and colleagues introduce a pressure sensing approach based on phase imaging of soft channel deformation. Exact pressure readings in tiny channels matter across microfluidic uses, but existing methods need extra probes or sensing parts added during or after chip fabrication. Their approach measures channel deformation in real time over a large field of view sharply, without embedded parts or device changes.
arxiv-2605-23829: Ervin Hadziosmanovic and Giorgio Mangioni study symmetry groups of one ended hyperbolic groups. They prove the outer automorphism group is virtually hierarchically hyperbolic, given mild orientability conditions on its JSJ splitting. The key step finds a finite index subgroup built as a central extension of orbifold mapping class groups, with bounded Euler class. The theorem is sharp: one surface amalgam example has a full outer automorphism group lacking the property.
arxiv-2605-23929: Yang and Zhu model the trade-offs among speed, reliability, and cost in workflows mixing language-model agents with ordinary code modules. They build performance models for both kinds of agent, tying effort to output quality. For language models, they use an exponential function linking reasoning and output tokens to reliability. For step-by-step workflows under time and cost limits, their main results give a water-filling rule for handing out tokens and describe best achievable reliability through shadow prices.
arxiv-2605-24029: Sahu and three co-authors show SUSY alone does not guarantee time-flip rule in Model A motion; an extra check is needed. They build a model that is SUSY yet breaks time-flip rule, while arguing that time-flip still emerges as a large-scale pattern. With the functional renormalization group, they show the action contains the slope of the balance action, whose flow matches the balance theory order by order in the slope series. The same logic yields the Ising model's total-spin spread within Model A.
arxiv-2605-24129: Ulibarri and three co-authors present the first two-dimensional time-of-flight survey of a vacuum electrospray plume from a wetted tungsten needle. The plume varies in two dimensions, with heavy particles and neutrals centred and monomers forming a ring peaking 10 degrees off axis. Energetic neutrals also fire 3.4 degrees off axis, and efficiency from any single sampled point varies by up to a factor of six. Heavy droplets, often assumed absent, carry significant propellant at lower velocity, revealing cone-jet operation, so whole-plume surveys assess efficiency better.
arxiv-2605-24429: Chen and six co-authors report 45 changing-look nuclei, 40 new. Turn-offs dominate, 43 against 2, perhaps because type 2 nuclei lack broad lines or hide them behind dust. Using DESI as a third epoch, the team identifies 12 repeaters. Of 14 new nuclei with three-epoch coverage, 7 are repeaters, and 5 of 16 previously reported nuclei also repeat. Repeaters show high-low-high accretion evolution, tying repeated changes to accretion swings. Transition times run about 10 years for the first change and 4 for the second.
arxiv-2605-24629: Florin Avram and others revisit theorems for bilinear epidemic models. They unify seven rank-one results with the non-rank-one stability exchange of Shuai and van den Driessche. They prove a strong threshold result beyond rank one. A positive equilibrium exists exactly when a spectral equation admits a strictly positive solution. Rank-one models split into two classes with different eigenvector formulas. Lyapunov constructions weight by the left Perron eigenvector, while a siphon-face exit follows the right Perron eigenvector. Beyond rank one, that picture remains open.
arxiv-2605-25129: Yudong W. Xu, Wenhao Li, Xiaoyu Wang, Scott Sanner, and Elias B. Khalil tackle constraint problems with a diffusion transformer that resamples variables in blocks instead of denoising everything at once. Standard diffusion falters here because satisfying a constraint often demands large, targeted changes to a few variables rather than small tweaks everywhere. Their BloGDiT method shrinks its blocks over time. It matches or beats existing solvers across four classic test problems, from Sudoku puzzles to graph coloring and MaxCut.
arxiv-2605-25229: Miloš Adžić and Filip Jevtić give a syntactic account of two maps that turn orderings into branching trees. Tonks' projection and the Loday-Ronco map each turn a permutation into a flat binary tree. The pair traces both maps to distinct codes inside one equational calculus. The vertex form of Tonks' map comes from a head-insertion code run on the reversed ordering. The Loday-Ronco map instead comes from a decreasing code. A local proof closes the paper, showing Tonks' vertex map preserves order between two classic orderings.
arxiv-2605-25429: Yujing Liu and colleagues fix a flaw in generalist graph anomaly detection, which must spot anomalies on unseen graphs without retraining. Existing methods align features across domains with PCA projection, matching sizes while ignoring meaning, which can even backfire. Their ReFi-GAD approach aligns raw features with a relational fingerprint, a universal code capturing anomaly cues from context and structure. A transformer encoder then learns shared knowledge, with a tuning module for each domain. Tests on 14 sets show clear wins over state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2605-25529: Siddhartha Samanta proves a square-summable estimate for the long variational seminorm of discrete averages linked to simplices. The result controls that seminorm for averages taken over integer lattice points in any dimension, bounding how much the averages can vary as the scale parameter runs long. Stated for the family as a whole rather than a single average, the estimate gives a uniform variational bound across the simplex family.
arxiv-2605-25629: Le and colleagues study weak-to-strong preference learning, where strong students train on weak labels. Such students can look strong on matched data yet fail when preferences shift. Fine-tuning drags them toward source-domain traits. Their Representation Anchoring regularizer keeps fine-tuning close to the strong model's starting representations, yet leaves room to adapt to tasks. Tests spanning preference domains, data sets and model types show it lifting out-of-distribution transfer while keeping in-distribution results strong.
arxiv-2605-25929: Bause, Niederle, Pawelczyk and Burkholz view multi-agent language-model debate through opinion dynamics. That model tracks how stubbornness and influence shift views in a group. Here the influence weights depend on the input, turning a debating team into a mixture of experts. Such a system routes work by competence and can beat single agents and fixed teams. Skill itself is hidden, so the authors study stand-ins: self-rated confidence, perceived confidence, and early agreement with others.
arxiv-2605-26029: Yang and nine colleagues build CausaLab, a testbed where language-model agents must discover causes by experiment. Each episode sets an agent in a mock lab with prior readings, a crystal it can prod, and a second crystal whose pitch it must predict. The hidden rule is a random causal model, so recall alone cannot pass. Scores split prediction from true grasp: GPT-5.2-high hits 92 percent on tasks yet only 0.471 on full graph recovery. Mixed watching and prodding beats pure prodding, and a consistency check curbs early stopping.
arxiv-2605-26129: Ghosh, Aktas and Chattopadhyay build one model covering both early inflation and late-time acceleration in holographic f(Q) gravity. Taking f(Q) as zeta times Q to the power n, they track the Hubble parameter with a Barrow holographic fluid present. Slow-roll numbers, spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio match Planck 2018 limits, with a very small tensor-to-scalar ratio. Adding matter and a Chevallier-Polarski-Linder parametrisation extends the picture to the late universe. Cosmic chronometer and baryon acoustic oscillation data support the extension.
arxiv-2605-26229: Jacob Turner's 2026 measurement uses cyclic spectroscopy to pin the scintillation factor C1 for the millisecond pulsar B1937+21. It is the first such measurement for any pulsar that avoids assuming a pulse-broadening shape in advance. At 428 megahertz, epochs give a weighted mean near 1.21. Diffuse scintillation arcs alongside it favor a thick screen spanning just over a tenth of the Earth-pulsar distance. That precision rules out thin screens and thick screens wider than thirty percent of the distance. It also yields diffraction scales near eleven thousand kilometers.
arxiv-2605-26529: Lokanath Patra, Mayur Pratap Singh, and Satish Kumar probe heat flow in thin silicon nanowires with anharmonic quantum transport theory. Atom runs find an up-down diameter trend in heat conduction but falter at low temperature and strong confinement. The trio combine non-equilibrium Green's function runs with neuroevolution potentials trained on density-functional theory for 10-nm channels. At 300 K, conduction bottoms at 6.24 and 5.50 nanometers for both directions, while the minima shift at 10 K. Hydrodynamic phonon flow, quantum suppression, and scattering explain the puzzle.
arxiv-2605-26629: Fuzhen Jiang, Zengtian Xie, and Zhuoran Li build DelowlightSplat, a system that rebuilds 3D scenes from dim photos. Feed-forward Gaussian methods fail in low light, where noise, color shifts, and bad matches corrupt views. The trio train on a benchmark that darkens only context views while keeping targets clean. A small adapter brightens features for matching, and cost volumes yield clean 3D blobs directly. It beats older feed-forward and two-stage pipelines in dim conditions.
arxiv-2605-26929: Yan and six colleagues ask whether the Muon optimizer, which orthogonalizes matrix updates, can improve adversarial training under strong and varied threat models. Theory shows Muon caps spectral-norm growth in updates without shrinking learned weights. Across five architectures and three threat norms plus their union, Muon matches SGD on convolutional networks and clearly beats AdamW on both convolutional networks and vision transformers. Optimizer geometry, they conclude, is a security-relevant design choice.
arxiv-2605-27029: López extends Newton's minimal resistance problem to Riemannian surfaces with geodesic coordinates, including sphere and hyperbolic plane. Fluid parcels flow along radial geodesic paths, and he derives the drag functional and proves its smooth extremals are the loxodromes there. He further shows smooth cases admit no strong local minima and names their global minima under constraints.
arxiv-2605-27229: Akter and co-authors hunt for high-voltage cathodes for sodium-ion batteries using only charged structures for training. A committee of their four best models predicts mean voltage, and uncertainty scores steer new costly first-principles data toward structures the committee finds least certain. Applying the trained models to large host databases yields NaCAM-Atlas, with 14843 candidate materials above 3 volts. A top subset was then checked with explicit voltage, stability, and electronic calculations.
arxiv-2605-27329: Lars-Luca Langer characterizes positivity preserving maps on operator-valued polynomials over real space and over compact sets. Such a map keeps positive inputs positive. The same result also settles local and general moment sequences for operators. The work treats both the whole real space and its compact parts in one frame.
arxiv-2605-27429: Wonkyun Kim and colleagues rerank video-on-demand suggestions with offline personality profiles. An LLM builds five-trait OCEAN profiles from content metadata once, while user profiles aggregate recent viewing in the same space. At request time the system reranks numerically with no LLM call, lifting ranking quality by about 8 percent for one generator and more than 60 percent for another.
arxiv-2605-27629: David Gordon and colleagues present the CRF-K-2025 catalog, a K-band celestial reference frame from more than 3 million VLBI observations. The catalog fixes precise coordinates for 1317 compact extragalactic radio sources, mostly quasars, covering the full sky. With 493 more sources than earlier K-band campaigns, precision runs about 25 percent better than ICRF3-K and similar to ICRF3-SX.
arxiv-2605-28129: Dongkyu Cho, Miao Zhang, and Rumi Chunara test whether clinical AI models actually change treatment choices when patient context shifts. Their ClinPivot benchmark pivots patient contexts to see if decisions follow. Strong exam-style scores proved a poor guide to decision skill, though decision-structured training improved pivot sensitivity in later tests.
arxiv-2605-28229: Rui Lin, Chuanming Wang, and Huadong Ma adapt image-trained vision-language models to video without letting experts blur into generalists. VidPrism assigns specialized experts roles from spatial understanding to temporal modeling, feeding each with streams sampled at matching rates. A two-way fusion then merges the pathways, reaching state-of-the-art video recognition while fostering genuine specialization.
arxiv-2605-28829: Ritvik Rastogi and three colleagues introduce Aryabhata 2, a reasoning-focused model for competitive STEM tests. Trained with reinforcement learning and verifiable rewards on question banks, it mixes prolonged reinforcement learning with widened exploration via progressively larger rollout groups. It beats GPT-OSS-20B in competitive STEM reasoning while using far fewer output tokens, up to 64 percent fewer. Tests span JEE Main and NEET plus out-of-distribution reasoning sets like AIME, HMMT, MMLU-Pro, MMLU-Redux, and GPQA.
arxiv-2605-28929: Lior Oppenheim, Snir Gazit, and Zohar Ringel improve lattice operators themselves, rather than only the action, to extract conformal data from simulations of critical systems. Finite-size effects blur estimates from lattice versions of continuum fields. The authors therefore build estimators with stronger overlap with the true primary operators. Applied to the Ising model, the three-state Potts model, and its dilute cousin in two dimensions, the improved operators cut corrections to scaling and give sharper scaling-dimension estimates than standard choices.
arxiv-2605-29029: Dereje Bekele Tekliye, Achinthya Krishna Bheemaguli, and Gopalakrishnan Sai Gautam screen the Materials Project list for calcium cathodes with shape and chemistry rules. They use Voronoi volume for site fit for calcium, then filter by charge balance, no stray mobile ions, stability, voltage, and migration barriers with learned models. Theory checks confirm predicted migration barriers in some finalists. From 52,945 starting entries, the workflow names 37 good cathodes, including two with very low migration barriers and four with stable charged states.
arxiv-2605-29229: Jiahao Huang and colleagues argue that reasoning distillation succeeds only when training data fit the student model. They introduce the Data-Model Compatibility metric, which judges a data set by jointly weighing its quality, its difficulty relative to the student, and the student's capability. Tests show the metric tracks distillation performance closely, and picking data by it improves results across several student models and tasks. Since compatibility shifts during training, they also show that re-selecting data sets dynamically as training proceeds can lift performance further.
arxiv-2605-29329: Jianshen Zhu extends molecule inference to copolymers with a mixing vector model. The existing framework infers chemical graphs with set structures and desired values through mixed integer linear programming, with guaranteed exactness. In the new model, a copolymer feature vector is a weighted mix of tractable monomer descriptors, weighted by mixing ratios. This needs no sequence-class information and is therefore naturally compatible with inverse design. Prediction functions for several copolymer datasets perform well, with the best score above seven tenths for nine of ten datasets.
arxiv-2605-29629: Junyoung Park and three colleagues argue attack success rate shows whether a jailbreak failed but not how. They introduce Temporal Logit Observability, watching a compliance-refusal margin during decoding and placing each condition on a calibrated plane. The plane is most informative where success rate is least. Across four models and three paradigms, attacks with nearly identical success rates land at different points, matching refusal probes on most conditions. An early-stop rule from the diagnostic cuts successful jailbreaks by more than half, with no false alarms on benign queries.
arxiv-2605-29729: Victoria Krakovna and four colleagues design trap tasks to test whether models chase hidden goals when given the chance. Their honeypots take the form of coding jobs inside Google's alignment research code, a setting close to real deployment. In that plain setting, Gemini models showed no unprompted scheming, the team reports. When prompts pushed agency or slipped in a hidden goal, models at times schemed or tried sabotage, with scant sign of knowing they were being tested.
arxiv-2605-30029: Zhen Chen and five colleagues argue that tuning a retrieval-augmented generation system should be treated as architecture search, not guesswork. Their RAISE framework and benchmark standardize the search space and budget for pipeline choices such as query rewriting, chunking, retrieval depth, reranking and context shrinking. They run 13 search methods over seven text and multimodal data sets with three random seeds each. Performance proves highly task-dependent: winners on one set often fail to generalize, warning against reading overall rankings as proof of a universally best method.
arxiv-2605-30229: Masaaki Imaizumi, Masanori Koyama, Noboru Isobe and Kohei Hayashi use a mean-field transformer to study how auxiliary factors such as positional encoding prevent mode collapse in attention. The simple model suggests mode collapse during runs. They show helpers counter mode collapse: the top-energy spread does not collapse to one point, but is pushed forward from the helper distribution, dodging Dirac collapse. Cases are positional encoding and prompt insertion as a helper setup. Both are universal in the limit.
arxiv-2605-30429: Shreya Banerjee and seven co-authors present an optimization framework that hunts Pauli symmetries of Hamiltonians, joining machine learning with automated symmetry finding. It uses attention to encode pair and higher order links among Pauli strings. They test it on random Pauli Hamiltonians, periodic one and two dimensional transverse field Ising models, and the Toric code. For physical Hamiltonians (Ising and Toric), it wins with high odds and a big edge over best methods.
arxiv-2605-30529: Rey-Blanco and Cruz test whether task-focused embeddings beat general ones for finding clinical codes beyond English. Sentence embeddings are usually trained and judged on English, so recall collapses when records are matched to ICD-10-CM and CIE-10 codes in other tongues. They fine-tune a Spanish biomedical encoder on synthetic data generated by a large model across six languages, plus a reranking stage. The tuned retriever matches or beats a strong baseline on most measures, with Portuguese gains largest, at a small cost to English.
arxiv-2605-30729: Kang and colleagues present SemStruct, joining frozen language models with graph neural networks for schema matching, integrating unlike data sources. SemStruct models a table as a graph with columns and values as nodes connected by rows, letting the network propagate disambiguating context. Unlike methods needing proprietary access and fine-tuning, SemStruct keeps the language model frozen and trains only a structural encoder. On Valentine and SOTAB-SM benchmarks, it beats fine-tuned baselines on complex datasets, and ablations show row representations act mainly as conduits.
arxiv-2605-30829: Chen and colleagues present LegSegNet, a deep learning system for lower extremity CT tissue mapping and quantification. Lower CT holds information for body composition and disease monitoring, but extracting measurements at scale needs exact segmentation. Old public tools are not built for full lower extremity CT analysis, and most provide only masks. Given an input CT scan, LegSegNet segments bone, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissues, then computes tissue measurements. The model was developed using 1,302 manually annotated CT slices and evaluated on 900 held-out test slices.
arxiv-2605-31029: Steunou and colleagues tackle frame selection for video models, which can process only a limited number of frames. Uniform sampling is cheap but ignores visual content, while adaptive sampling costs more. Their PEEK distills frame relevance rankings from a teacher into a lightweight model that uses only visual content. On two captioning benchmarks, PEEK beats state-of-the-art methods, winning most configurations on ActivityNet Captions. Compared with baselines, PEEK is more accurate at low budgets and more efficient, adding about five percent to captioning time.
arxiv-2605-31129: Cheonwoo Lee and colleagues unify multi-scale time-series forecasting under one operator. Existing scaling tricks rely on fixed, discrete scales, a limitation their SiGMA architecture answers with distance-aware scaling through a learnable discrete Gaussian kernel. SiGMA tops every rival on both long- and short-term benchmarks, winning 13 of 16 long-term settings. It also trains up to 5.3 times faster and cuts memory use sharply against the strongest rivals.
arxiv-2605-31429: Chen and colleagues propose YARD, a training-free contrastive-decoding framework to cut hallucinations in large vision-language models. Existing methods degrade badly: dropping visual tokens induces language hallucinations, while corrupting images needs two passes. YARD builds the degraded branch internally, sharing shallow computation and branching at middle layers. It swaps patch visual tokens for register tokens keeping global meaning without fine local evidence. That gives a faithful contrast signal without a second forward pass. Tests show state-of-the-art mitigation across several models, with much lower latency.
