Some separation-based matches are rejected as chance coincidences, about half of the disputed set. The catalog gives X-ray astronomy cleaner optical identifications at scale.
arxiv-2606-19529:
Manuel Hernández and Eduardo Sánchez-Soto argue in 2026 that plain graphs cannot capture modern distributed sensing networks. A simple graph links nodes with single edges and scalar weights. Real sensor webs mix unlike agents, rich multi-modal streams, and context-bound ties that one weight cannot express.

Sheaf theory supplies the richer language the pair call for. A sheaf attaches data spaces to each node and edge, with rules for how local records must agree. The sheaf Laplacian, built from those agreement rules, then drives data fusion across the network. Repeated local averaging under this operator pulls the network toward consensus. Unlike a graph Laplacian, it can flag records that clash rather than merely differ. Fusion and agreement thus share one operator with a clear mathematical meaning. The framework suits sensor webs where units differ in kind, not just in place.
arxiv-2606-19629:
Dareen Alharthi, Bhuvan Koduru, Rita Singh, and Bhiksha Raj make voice attribute editing sturdier against bad labels in 2026. Voice editing tools change traits like age and gender while keeping speaker identity intact. Large speech datasets carry noisy, inconsistent attribute labels that destabilise such tools.

Their framework, RIVET, leans on idempotency: applying an operation twice changes nothing the second time. Forcing edits to be idempotent acts as a built-in regulariser. Models then lean less on mislabelled examples during training. Tests use controlled label noise plus the GLOBE dataset, whose annotations are naturally noisy. RIVET improves editing success over standard training in both settings. Speaker identity also survives edits better under the new objective. A simple algebraic property thus buys robustness that data cleaning alone struggles to give.
arxiv-2606-19929:
Motor-speed data, rather than the vibration-prone inertial unit, drives a new state estimator for multirotor drones in a 2026 paper by Matěj Petrlík, Filip Novák, Robert Pěnička, and Martin Saska. Spinning propellers shake the onboard inertial sensor and blur its readings, yet tight control near obstacles demands a precise position estimate. The team preintegrates accelerations derived from motor angular speeds and folds them, with lidar data, into a factor graph, forming the open-source MASLO algorithm.

Against a leading inertial method, MASLO cuts position error by about a quarter and velocity error by about two thirds, with lower measurement lag. The motor-speed factors work on their own for propagation and stay robust when parameters are set wrong, which matters for agile flight. Removing the shaky sensor from the loop offers drone builders a cleaner route to precise flight near obstacles.
arxiv-2606-20129:
Niels Doorn, Bart Knaack, Tanja Vos, and Beatriz Marín report lessons from thirteen workshops that teach software testing through puzzles. Their 2026 experience report builds on a framework called P4TEST for puzzle-based learning in critical testing literacy. That term names the habits of mind that make a tester probe a system rather than trust it. Testing is vital yet hard to teach, so the team turned testing ideas into hands-on puzzles for students, professionals, teachers, and pupils.

The first eleven workshops varied puzzles, materials, and timing. Later sessions added workbooks and think-aloud protocols to gather richer evidence. Participants consistently felt they were experimenting as they solved. Students tended to converge on one answer, while professionals kept exploring the solution space. Feelings showed in behavior but surfaced poorly in written reflection, whereas think-aloud speech exposed reasoning in the moment.
arxiv-2606-20229:
Somayeh Chopoghloo, David Fernández-Duque, Joost Joosten, and Sofía Santiago-Fernández settle when the standard axioms completely describe a family of two-dimensional modal logics. Their 2026 paper studies expanding products, bimodal logics blending a horizontal and a vertical logic between a fusion and a full Cartesian product. Earlier work showed such products are often decidable, but by semantic methods that produce no complete axiom system.

The authors fix the vertical component as Gödel-Löb logic, the logic of provability, and vary the horizontal one. The standard axiomatization proves complete when the horizontal logic is K4 or GL itself. It proves incomplete for Grz and for logics between K4.3 and Grz.3. That mixed verdict partially answers a question Gabelaia and colleagues posed over two decades ago, mapping how proof systems strain when two dimensions of reasoning interact.
arxiv-2606-20429:
Sheldon Dantas, Helena del Río, and Tomáš Raunig generalize the Daugavet property to Banach spaces carrying a group action. Their 2026 paper introduces the G-Daugavet property for spaces where a group G acts by surjective linear isometries. The new notion unifies the classical Daugavet property and its alternative variant.

The classical case corresponds to the trivial action, and the alternative property to the scalar action of the unit circle. The authors describe the G-property through G-slices and closed convex G-invariant hulls, recovering the usual slice picture as special cases. Group actions also produce genuinely new behavior: the property can hold on classical reflexive spaces where the classical theory forbids it. Daugavet theory gains a symmetry knob it never had.
arxiv-2606-20529:
Md Nayem Uddin and three colleagues give tool-calling agents an explicit ledger of task state. Their 2026 paper targets customer-service agents that must track facts, identifiers, and constraints across turns while obeying domain policies. Standard agents keep none of this separately: everything sits in the prompt, to be reconstructed at every decision.

That implicit design breeds two failure modes: decisions grounded in stale, missing, or incorrect facts, and syntactically valid calls that violate policy. LedgerAgent maintains structured state outside the prompt, so the agent reads its obligations from a ledger rather than from memory of the transcript. Policy adherence becomes a check against explicit state. Customer-service automation, where a wrong fact can mean a wrong refund, needs exactly that discipline.
arxiv-2606-20629:
Yinsicheng Jiang and eight colleagues introduce AgentCARD in 2026, a benchmark for teams of large language model agents split into roles such as planner, executor, and verifier. In such teams, cost and accuracy depend on which model fills each role and where it runs, through an application programming interface, on local hardware, or in a hybrid mix. Older benchmarks fix the model or setup, so they give little guidance for choosing a cheap yet accurate deployment.

AgentCARD combines a role-by-role test harness, a shared cost model, Pareto frontier analysis, and a Shapley diagnostic that credits each role for its share of success. Mixed teams reach the cost and accuracy frontier more often than uniform teams. They raise accuracy by up to 44 percent at equal cost. They can also match the best uniform team at twelve times lower cost.
arxiv-2606-20829:
G Congedo and the Euclid Consortium present a LensMC shear catalogue in 2026 from Euclid Quick Release 1 images, released in March 2025. Weak lensing slightly distorts galaxy shapes. Measuring those shapes lets astronomers map dark matter around galaxy clusters. The catalogue gives shapes, positions, weights, and morphology for galaxies over 63 square degrees of Euclid visible-light images.

Galaxy density reaches high values at the stated magnitude limits. No spatial pattern is found in additive biases within the scope of the work. An empirical correction based on galaxy size and brightness is applied across the area. Two-point statistics and cluster profiles validate the measurements. Results are cross-checked with external cluster catalogues. As the first LensMC shear catalogue ahead of Euclid Data Release 1, it prepares cluster lensing science and tests the pipeline that later, larger releases will depend on for precision cosmology.
arxiv-2606-21029:
Guansheng He, the only author named in the hosted text, presents an open-source tool in 2026 for rational orbits and gravitational radiation in static round spacetimes. Timelike orbits probe the intrinsic properties of curved spacetime. Their gravitational radiation offers a direct window on strong-field gravity. The tool is built on Mathematica with parallel computing support.

A user supplies only the metric of the spacetime. The tool then computes rational orbits across many configurations. It also gives gravitational wave polarization states and characteristic strains for those orbits. The Schwarzschild spacetime serves as the test case. Several functions of the code are illustrated there. A one-stop package lowers the barrier for testing exotic spacetimes, without rebuilding the machinery for each new metric.
arxiv-2606-21129:
Zhen Zhao and six colleagues propose AgenticOS in 2026, an intent-oriented secure operating system architecture for autonomous AI agents. Agents now plan, call tools, access networks, run code, and work across applications. Classic system security exposes low-level resources and checks permissions. A compromised agent can combine those primitives into actions far beyond the user's task. Prompt injection and poisoned tool outputs are real entry points.

AgenticOS rebuilds the system as an intent filter. Agents no longer request files or network access directly. They submit structured intent declarations in a manifest. The system then synthesizes a least-privilege environment for that intent. Resource exposure shrinks to what the declared task needs. Intent-first design could contain agent incidents at the system layer, instead of trusting every tool and prompt the agent encounters during a long autonomous run.
arxiv-2606-21329:
Mingzhi Chen, Yiyu Gui, and Guibo Luo present MedTS-TTT in 2026, a classifier for medical time series such as brain and heart signals that adapts to each new patient at test time. People differ enough that a fixed model often degrades on unseen subjects. Test-time training adjusts the model on unlabeled incoming data, but many versions loop through slow inner optimization steps for every sample.

MedTS-TTT pairs a closed-loop self-alignment method, which builds a token-level self-supervised target and updates fast weights in a single step, with a gated convolutional backbone that models local dynamics. Across four public EEG and ECG datasets with subject-independent splits, it takes eleven of twelve top rankings against nine baselines. Fast, per-sample adaptation suits sequential clinical monitoring, where patients arrive one by one.
arxiv-2606-21429:
Md Millat Hosen and Md Nazmus Sakib surveyed Bangladeshi students in 2026 about why they chose private universities in India's National Capital Region, a little-studied study-abroad corridor. Their study surveyed students at Sharda, Noida International, and Galgotias universities, keeping fifty-six valid responses from sixty-three. Push-pull theory frames the analysis: home-country pressures push students out, while destination traits pull them in.

Disruptions to Bangladesh's academic calendar, from political and official causes, scored as the top push factor. Geographic and cultural proximity was the strongest pull, closely tied with visa accessibility, hinting at a combined access advantage for short regional moves. Advisory networks shaped most students' choices of university and course. Clustering split respondents into three decision profiles, from broadly motivated students to low-salience enrollers.
arxiv-2606-21529:
Smith, McClure, Kamp, and Cazaux examine in 2026 how the optical constants of water ice, the numbers that say how ice absorbs and refracts light, affect models of planet-forming disks. Ice spectra shift with temperature and thermal history, yet disk models usually pick one fixed set of constants. The team built temperature and history dependent optical constant composites from laboratory data spanning 0.1 to 10,000 micrometers, deriving matching refractive indices through Kramers-Kronig integration.

Four radiative transfer models of the edge-on disk HH 48 NE compare the standard single-temperature sets against the new multi-temperature ones, for ices deposited cold or deposited then cooled. The 3-micrometer absorption band and the far-infrared emission features shift measurably with the choice. Self-consistent ice optics, they argue, are required to read ice distributions from disk spectra correctly.
arxiv-2606-21629:
Bo Xiong and four colleagues test in 2026 whether language models can spot the salient classes in a code commit, the primarily changed classes that drive the rest of a multi-class change. Reviewers use those classes as an entry point into tangled commits, and prior tools find them with heavy program analysis: syntax parsing, relation extraction, and handcrafted features. The team asks whether a model can read the commit directly, with no feature engineering, graphs, or training.

They built ApacheJavaCM, 7,911 commits with 25,914 labeled classes, and evaluated two large models and one small model under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting. All beat the strongest reproducible baseline, and a nine-billion-parameter open model with few-shot prompts matched a much larger closed model. Lightweight local models, they conclude, suffice for this industrial task.
arxiv-2606-21829:
Garay-López, Luviano-Flores, and Valencia-Negrete use tropical mathematics in 2026 to study power series solutions of nonlinear differential equations. Tropical algebra swaps the usual operations for minimum and addition. Hard questions of analysis then become counting problems a computer can handle. Their aim is a clear basis for describing all formal solutions near a point, plus the orders at which those solutions vanish.

Garay-López, Luviano-Flores, and Valencia-Negrete first study tropical equations on their own. It compares two sets of solutions, the elementary ones and the minimal ones, and shows the sets are closely alike across three widening classes of series. The authors then turn to an algebraic equation with meromorphic coefficients. They prove that the orders of its true Hahn-series solutions always lie inside the orders computed from its tropical shadow. Tropicalization thus gives a computable outer bound on real solution behaviour.
arxiv-2606-22129:
Wang redesigns the Jansen linkage in 2026, adding joint wear to a leg mechanism long optimized for gait alone. The linkage is the eleven-bar walking mechanism behind Theo Jansen's strandbeests, driven by a single crank. Wang couples a kinematic model, an inverse-dynamic model, and an Archard wear model to score any link lengths for both gait quality and per-cycle sliding wear.

A bi-objective optimization with NSGA-II then trades composite gait error against total joint wear, under step-length, clearance, and duty constraints. The classical Jansen design turns out to be Pareto-dominated. One adjusted design, with link lengths changed by up to twenty-nine percent, flattens the stance by twenty-eight percent. It also smooths stance velocity by fifty-eight percent and cuts total joint wear by about fifty-six percent. Sensitivity analysis names the two link lengths that dominate wear.
arxiv-2606-22329:
KC introduces BabelJudge in 2026, an open-source benchmark and audit framework for measuring the reliability of language models used as judges. Judge models carry built-in biases that raw accuracy hides: they favour the response in the first slot, prefer longer answers regardless of quality, and degrade sharply in lower-resource languages. BabelJudge measures position bias, verbosity bias, order inconsistency, and cross-lingual decline without needing human preference labels.

Its key device is gold-labelling by controlled damage: a controlled perturbation of a high-quality reference creates a pair whose correct winner is known by construction. Evaluating a quantized Qwen model across English, Hindi, Arabic, and Swahili, reliability falls from 0.714 in Hindi to 0.550 in Swahili, a gap raw accuracy understates. Nine trajectory-level perturbations extend the audit to agentic settings.
arxiv-2606-22629:
Soumyadip Ghosh and five colleagues tackle triangle counting in huge graphs in this 2026 paper. Triangles underpin clustering measures and help detect communities, predict links, and flag anomalies. The standard route uses the trace of the cubed adjacency matrix, but forming that cube is infeasible at scale.

Hutchinson's randomized estimator approximates the trace from matrix-vector products alone. On split machines, though, gathering every entry costs dearly, thanks to communication overhead and stragglers. The team propose a variant that works under partial observation, where both the number and the identity of observed entries are random. They prove the estimator stays unbiased and bound its variance and sample complexity. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show accurate triangle counts with reduced synchronization costs. The work adapts these methods to modern clusters and points toward counting larger motifs.
arxiv-2606-22929:
Johannes Buchner uncovers a failure mode of nested sampling in this 2026 paper. Nested sampling is a Monte Carlo algorithm for estimating posteriors and comparing Bayesian models, prized for handling multi-modal posteriors. It keeps a population of live points spread over the whole prior, advancing them past rising likelihood thresholds, so modes survive until data rule them out.

Buchner shows the same Monte Carlo replenishment can accidentally discard a mode. He connects the process to the neutral Moran process in genetics, where random drift eliminates variants, and models live point occupancy as a simple symmetric random walk. From that model he derives the probability of mode die-out. The analysis yields a simple rule for setting the minimum number of live points so that losing a mode becomes unlikely. The result gives practitioners a principled way to size their sampling runs.
arxiv-2606-23029:
Henri Prade and Gilles Richard extend analogical proportions to probabilities in a 2026 paper. An analogical proportion says that one item is to a second as a third is to a fourth. The four items can be numbers, truth values, or whole profiles of attributes. Work by the authors and others showed such proportions can drive accurate classification. This paper moves the idea into the probabilistic setting. The items become probability values, or full distributions over the values of some attribute.

Prade and Richard study definitions built from arithmetic proportion, geometric proportion, and blends of the two. For distributions, the definitions must also preserve normalization, so the values still sum correctly. They discuss the formal properties each definition keeps or loses. Experiments then test whether profiles whose distributions form such proportions tend to share the same class, extending the earlier classification idea.
arxiv-2606-23129:
Alex Costanzino and colleagues gate the frequencies inside implicit neural representations in a 2026 paper. Such networks store a signal, like an image or a sound, as a continuous function fitted to coordinates. They face a spectral dilemma. Wavy activations capture fine detail but also memorize noise. Compact activations smooth noise away yet miss high-frequency detail. The team models each neuron's activation as the steady response of a damped harmonic oscillator pushed by a sine wave. The oscillator's amplitude then acts as a natural frequency gate.

Costanzino and colleagues tune the oscillator settings jointly with the network weights during training. Starting in the blocked band, the network learns broad structure first. Its gate then widens step by step, admitting fine detail only when the fit demands it. Across experiments, the method matched or beat established representations with no task-specific tuning of any settings.
arxiv-2606-23329:
Stefano Palombo and colleagues release CodeXHug, a dataset linking pretrained models to real code that uses them in a 2026 paper. Pretrained models spread through repositories like Hugging Face, where model cards describe them. Most cards lack worked code patterns, leaving newcomers to guess how a model is actually called. Whether models get used in real projects, or only in toy demos, was also unclear. The team mines the GitHub ecosystem for genuine usage of models that carry a tag and a model card.

Palombo and colleagues curate over seven thousand distinct models tied to hundreds of thousands of Python files. To show a concrete use, they extract representative usage patterns for specific models by statistically analyzing and clustering relevant code snippets. Such patterns can enrich model cards directly. The authors also discuss the research opportunities the dataset opens for studying model adoption.
arxiv-2606-23429:
P. S. Houdayer and M. Rieutord model surface convection in cool stars with a phase-space closure in a 2026 paper. Surface convection sets the entropy jump between a star's atmosphere and its deep convective envelope. That jump shapes the radius and structure of stellar models in one dimension. Standard treatments control it through an effective efficiency, a tuning knob. The authors build a closure that ties the mean stratification to the local spread of entropy and velocity among convective elements.

Houdayer and Rieutord first build a maximum-entropy model of the convective bulk. Its predicted entropy distribution matches the deep parts of three-dimensional simulations. Near the surface, radiative cooling splits the distribution into two components: an optimal bulk and a cooled plume population. Their two-population closure matches the mean entropy stratification in four reference simulations over most of the range.
arxiv-2606-23629:
Tseng, Akgun, and Liu examine why language models misjudge the quality of pretest questions, in a 2026 paper on education technology. Pretesting asks students questions before teaching the material, and the attempt itself improves later learning. Good pretest questions need the right openness, cognitive depth, and fit to learning goals, but writing and grading them by hand is slow. The authors build an AI assisted workflow that generates questions, scores them with a rubric, and keeps the best.

Because machine scores do the filtering, the study tests how well machine and human judgments align. A two by two design varies the rubric wording and the scoring mode. Disagreements turn out to be systematic, not random noise. Revising the rubric to state quality criteria more explicitly helps alignment more than asking the model to reason first. The two fixes also stack, each adding gains the other misses.
arxiv-2606-23729:
Calvat and colleagues introduce a framework that learns directly from the spatial structure of materials, in a 2026 paper on materials data science. How a metal behaves depends on its microstructure, the layout of crystals, phases, and defects across scales from atoms to parts. Machine learning usually predicts that behavior from hand built descriptors, which throw away the spatial organization that governs performance.

Materials Spatial Intelligence compresses data on microstructure and deformation, at high resolution, into shared latent codes that keep spatial relationships intact. One learned space serves prediction, reading of results, and design tuning at once. Applied to structural alloys, the framework identifies the features that govern mechanical behavior and property tradeoffs. It also supports feature driven design of microstructures. The authors present it as a base for systems that explain their reasoning while speeding up discovery.
arxiv-2606-23829:
Sarauer and colleagues run decade long climate simulations with a machine learned treatment of cloud droplet physics inside a major Earth system model, in a 2026 paper on climate modelling. Cloud microphysics, the birth and growth of droplets and ice crystals, is a stubborn source of error in climate models. The team trains a neural scheme on a global simulation fine enough to resolve convection directly, then couples it into the ICON model at coarse resolution.

The scheme uses a classifier to find active cells and a regressor to predict the changes. Physical guardrails, such as never letting cloud mass go negative, prove essential. The coupled model runs stably for a decade and matches the observed climate about as well as the classical scheme. It also removes two tuning knobs.
arxiv-2606-23929:
Gorda, Komoltsev, Kurkela, and Schaffner-Bielich show that neutron star matter models can be judged by what they would demand at densities no star ever reaches. Their 2026 paper treats dense matter physics. An equation of state links pressure and density inside a neutron star. Microscopic models supply one up to the highest densities in stable stars; beyond lies an unstable branch modelers ignore. Any model must still extend to the very high density regime where perturbative quantum chromodynamics applies, staying causal and consistent.

Those demands tightly constrain the unreachable densities. The authors make the constraints explicit and provide a tool for building valid extensions. Purely hadronic models often need radically different high density behavior than their own assumptions suggest. Models with extra degrees of freedom fare better. The analysis disfavors purely nucleonic models and supports extra degrees of freedom in the heaviest stars.
arxiv-2606-24129:
Hossain and colleagues audit wheelchair accessibility by sending a software agent along footpaths before any traveller risks the trip. Map platforms show where a path exists but not how it feels: steep running slopes, tilted cross slopes, and sudden level changes can make a mapped route unusable. Their 2026 framework, OmniPath, fuses OpenStreetMap's network with high-density aerial LiDAR from the USGS 3DEP programme to build a detailed three-dimensional model of the walking environment.

The agent traverses the network virtually, examining the surface in half-metre increments and scoring each friction point against ADA compliance standards. A weighted severity scale sorts hazards from mild to critical. Validation against two hundred physical field surveys around the National Mall in Washington shows strong reliability for the worst hazards, with the best detection scores on severe and critical barriers. Hossain's team aims to replace the map's broken promise with audited, trustworthy routing information.
arxiv-2606-24429:
Khosravani and Mockus count how much open-source code AI agents are actually writing, and find the usual yardstick misses most of it. Generative coding agents leave often hidden traces across repositories. Their multi-layered detection framework scans configuration files, commit messages, author-identity patterns, and bot signatures. It runs across the World of Code infrastructure, spanning 180 million Git repositories.

No single method captures more than a fraction of the activity. Multi-method detection finds hundreds of thousands of Claude Code commits in one snapshot. Bot account lookup, the signal adoption studies lean on most, recovers only a thirtieth of them, a thirtyfold recall gap. Every pattern is hand-validated. Tracking snapshots from late 2024 into spring 2026, such agents generate hundreds of thousands of commits monthly, led by Claude Code across tens of thousands of projects. Single-signal prevalence estimates, the authors warn, are biased badly low.
arxiv-2606-24629:
Ibrahim and colleagues make a teleoperated robot arm move the way a human hand would, without overriding its operator. Human like motion eases human robot interaction. Teleoperation systems distort the natural motion of hand movements, though. Their 2026 framework reshapes end effector paths in real time, according to the two thirds power law, the regularity linking speed and curvature in voluntary human movement. The operator's intended control inputs are preserved.

Experiments on a six degree of freedom Dobot CR10 arm confirm the shared control approach. Generated paths adhere more strongly to human like motion profiles than conventional control. The estimated power law coefficient moves much closer to its theory value. The operator stays in command of where the arm goes. The framework only humanises how it gets there. Ibrahim's team frames the gain as contact quality: a robot that moves like a person is easier to predict, trust, and work beside.
arxiv-2606-24929:
Evgeny Nikulchev proposes reconstructing chaotic systems in jet space rather than in the usual delay coordinates. Takens' theorem is the gold standard for rebuilding an attractor from a time series. It promises only a shape level equivalence, though, so metric features and symmetries can be lost. Jet space instead tracks the signal together with its derivatives. Nikulchev proves that this switch preserves the system's symmetry group exactly. A theorem on Lie algebras under jet prolongation justifies this.

Tests on the Lorenz and Rössler systems back the claim: the jet rebuild keeps the geometry that Takens embedding distorts. Two metrics quantify the gap: an elastic energy score and the correlation dimension. In some cases its invariant estimates beat even projections of the true system. Nikulchev offers a coordinate free way to classify strange attractors.
arxiv-2606-25029:
Quantum simulation at fixed particle number can be written in two equivalent ways: a particle picture and an occupation number picture. Jack S. Baker, Gaurav Saxena, and Thi Ha Kyaw build explicit quantum circuits that convert coherently between the two, since their resource costs differ sharply by task.

Their conversion unitary takes a state in the particle picture to its occupation number form while reading off the input's exchange symmetry. It works uniformly for bosons, fermions, and parastatistical sectors: symmetry blind on the way in, fully resolved on the way out. The Schur transform sits at the centre, identified as the non abelian Fourier transform of a commuting pair of symmetry groups. Occupations are computed by reversible arithmetic from the pattern labels, giving gate counts polynomial in particle number, dimension, and the log of the inverse precision.
arxiv-2606-25129:
Direct detection of light dark matter usually assumes a standard model of how dark matter moves through the galaxy. Muping Chen and three colleagues remove that assumption for a new class of detectors: quantum sensors with energy thresholds below an electron volt. These can register slow, light dark matter particles that conventional experiments miss.

Their framework splits the scattering rate into a response function, fixed by the detector and particle model. A second piece, one universal halo function shared by all experiments, is to be read off from data. Two sensor types, aluminium transition edge sensors and titanium nitride kinetic inductance detectors, respond to different parts of the velocity distribution, so they complement each other. On mock data built from several benchmark halo models, the team shows the halo function can be reconstructed, mapping how local dark matter actually moves.
arxiv-2606-25229:
Philippe Baron and Athanassios Panagiotopoulos tackle a slow step in molecular simulation: computing chemical potential, the energy cost of adding one more molecule to a liquid. Their 2026 paper introduces minimal normalizing flows, which are deliberately simple learned mappings between two states of a system. Instead of a large flexible network, the mapping makes one or two physically chosen changes, such as shifting particles radially. A new training score based on the Bhattacharyya distance helps keep training near one minute of graphics processor time.

Simple test liquids saw speedups of at least ten times for chemical potential estimates. For sodium and chloride ions dissolving in water, the method multiplied the effective sample size by up to three for charging calculations and up to eight when comparing force fields. The authors argue that small, physics guided mappings can stay cheap to train for each new problem.
arxiv-2606-25929:
Emiliano Puddu rethinks where the Klein-Gordon equation, the basic wave equation for relativistic particles, comes from. Textbooks obtain it by forcing the Schrödinger equation to fit Einstein's energy-momentum relation, which treats the formula as an algebraic starting point. Puddu begins with a physical picture instead. Every localized particle carries an inner oscillation. Its phase repeats with a fixed proper frequency in its rest frame.

That single assumption yields a mass-frequency relation directly, with mass acting as an intrinsic frequency scale rather than an independent input. Puddu then shows the Klein-Gordon equation is the simplest wave equation that fits. It is local, linear, and respects relativity. Kinematics falls out of phase coherence. Particle motion reads as the group velocity of wave packets. One account covers free motion, dispersion, and tunneling.
arxiv-2606-26129:
Karl Kreder builds a single algebraic calculus for the geometry of complex hyperbolic two-space. That space can be seen as a ball with a special metric, a symmetric space, or a projective domain of negative lines. Its boundary carries a contact structure rather than an ordinary sphere. Real projective geometry has a tidy invariant language, built on quadrance and spread. The Hermitian setting refuses to collapse into one such pair.

Invariants multiply instead, and Kreder catalogs them. Hermitian pair moduli, determinant quadrance, polar spread, and triple-product phase each capture part of the picture. Cross-ratio laws, boundary contact formulas, and kernel identities on the normalized ball join the list. Everything grows from one datum: a complex space with a Hermitian form of signature two-one. The calculus gives workers in this geometry one toolkit instead of scattered formulas.
arxiv-2606-26329:
Sujan Vijayaraj and Mauro Paternostro strengthen device-independent quantum key distribution with routed Bell tests. Device-independent security trusts almost nothing about the hardware, only the observed statistics. Distance is its weak point: practical links demand near-perfect local Bell violations. Routed tests, where a distant measurement unit swaps entanglement, offer a way out. Their protocol multiplies the sources and detectors instead of perfecting one pair.

Each round picks local devices at random for routed tests. Crucially, local Bell tests are still checked even when the distant swap succeeds. Consistency between the conditional local results and the overall test is demanded. Critical detection efficiencies improve by several percentage points at high visibility. Long-distance device-independent keys come within reach of efficient, loophole-free routing hardware. A dimension-witness variant extends the routing idea to a semi-device-independent setting.
arxiv-2606-26429:
Aaron J. Li and eight colleagues at Berkeley propose DualEval, a way to grade large language models that joins two signals usually kept apart. Fixed benchmarks give right-or-wrong labels but can go stale or leak into training data, while arena contests, where people pick between two anonymous answers, capture open-ended quality but resist diagnosis. DualEval places models and test items in one shared space.

The framework estimates each model's ability together with each item's difficulty and sharpness, meaning how well an item separates strong models from weak ones. The team applied it across coding, mathematics, general knowledge, and everyday user questions, using eighteen leading models. Rankings came out reliable and balanced, and the learned item profiles supported practical uses such as shrinking benchmarks for cheaper testing and flagging contaminated or odd items that distort scores.
arxiv-2606-26529:
Kwan Soo Shin names a failure mode he calls the Inattentional Gap. Safety tests grade a model on finding the hazards it was told to find. Accidents, though, often come from the hazard nobody mentioned. Shin shows that giving a language or vision model a narrow task suppresses its reporting of other dangers sitting in plain view. The models can report those signals when asked directly.

Tests covered radiology and driving scenarios in text, plus chest X-ray tasks for vision models. Suppression appeared in every model tested. It did not shrink as models grew larger. It persisted in a reasoning model, and family mattered more than size. Shin argues this gap splits measured safety from real safety. A system can ace specified hazards while staying blind to unspecified ones.
arxiv-2606-26629:
Evan Ning, Wei Xue, Dong Lou, and Yike Guo fight catastrophic forgetting in language models differently. Continual learning teaches a model new tasks without erasing old ones. Standard methods protect important weights, the model's internal settings. On large language models those methods disappoint. The authors blame polysemanticity: single units mix many meanings, so weight importance cannot isolate knowledge worth protecting.

Their method protects activations instead, the signals flowing through the model. A sparse autoencoder supplies a dictionary of single-meaning features. A compact mask of important features is built from current-task data, and only the mask is kept. Training then balances stability against flexibility in feature space. The authors show the classic weight method is a special case of their formulation. On two continual learning benchmarks, their method achieved the strongest results reported in the study.
arxiv-2606-26829:
Philipp Allgeuer, Jan-Gerrit Habekost, and Stefan Wermter present AnomNOVIC, a system that lets robots recognise objects they have never been told about. Open-vocabulary detectors usually need a text prompt or a candidate list. Continuous robot deployment cannot stop to write prompts. Their two-stage framework works in a known workspace without any prompt.

An anomaly detector, trained as a masked autoencoder, first proposes boxes around anything object-like. A fast open-vocabulary classifier then names the contents of each box. No candidate class list is needed. Tests used a tabletop setup with the NICOL humanoid robot. The system beat strong open-vocabulary baselines by wide margins. On a wild test set with forty-eight objects, prompt-free detection and naming reached high accuracy.
arxiv-2606-27029:
Choudhary and colleagues work on teaching neural networks the hidden energy rule behind a moving system. Such rules are called Hamiltonians, and they govern how position and momentum change over time. Learning one from noisy records is hard, because small errors can break energy saving over long runs. The team builds its network around a structure-keeping solver, called a symplectic integrator, which respects the geometry of the motion. 

Training uses a neat shortcut based on the adjoint system, a companion set of equations for error signals. Its structure-keeping steps give the same error signals as direct back-calculation through the solver. A predictor and corrector scheme with repeated fixed-point steps cuts the cost of each hidden solver step. Tests on tangled, non-separable, and chaotic systems show better system recovery and energy keeping. Extra polishing with backward error analysis sharpens the learned energy rule further.
arxiv-2606-27229:
Dutta introduces CARVE, a recurrent language model design that lets the model peek at its own memory before forgetting. Recurrent models squeeze everything that came before into one fixed-size state matrix. Leading delta-rule models gate that state using only the incoming token, so erasure decisions are memory-blind. In 2026, value-axis coupling blocks the fast triangular chunk solver that makes recurrent training efficient.

Restricting all gating to the key axis restores that single fast solve unchanged. Content-aware erasing reuses the output tensor the kernel already writes, taking its chunk mean as a cheap memory glimpse. A zero-start projection feeds that glimpse to the erase gate, so training begins identical to the baseline. Selectivity grows as training proceeds. Value efficiency trims the write gate to a lean per-head form. Speed and memory awareness improve together.
arxiv-2606-27529:
Diaz, Beyer, and Hesse model chronic stress as a wiring change inside recurrent neural networks trained on a working memory task. In the brain, chronic stress shifts prefrontal pyramidal neurons toward inhibitory dominance, but the mechanism is unknown. Eight stress operators are compared against three signatures drawn from experiments: inhibitory dominance, excitatory hypofunction, and weak task performance. In the 2026 neuroscience paper, one mechanism recovers all three marks.

Stronger inhibitory-to-excitatory synapses alone reproduce the full stress profile. Networks then trained under it become robust: performance survives stress, and the network stays in the same regime with or without it. The protection costs generality, since the protected networks handle longer memory demands worse than naive ones. The trade-off persists across stress levels and network sizes. Rigid, habit-like behaviour after chronic stress gains a model analogue.
arxiv-2606-27829:
Drafting tokens ahead of time can speed up model generation. This trick, speculative decoding, works poorly for image generation, though. Drafts are accepted too rarely. Loosening the checks directly harms image quality instead. Mingcheng Wang and ten colleagues propose CSD in 2026, a content-aware method for autoregressive image generation. Entropy, a measure of uncertainty, guides how checks adapt to content.

Different image regions carry different uncertainty. CSD adjusts each candidate token's acceptance odds to match. Low-detail areas accept more drafts, which speeds generation. A resampling strategy keeps the odds principled. A filter then aligns the output distribution with the target model's own. Quality is protected while speed rises. Experiments ran on Lumina-mGPT and Janus-Pro, two image generation models. CSD beat existing methods of this kind on both. The authors release the source code publicly.
arxiv-2606-27929:
Robots are becoming agentic, able to deliberate and learn during a task. Robot teams, meanwhile, still share mostly maps and assignments. Yuxuan Yan, Yuanyuan Jia, and Qianqian Yang argue in 2026 that teams should share more. Their paradigm is Embodied Collective Intelligence. A team would accumulate world context, task progress, and skill experience, all as shared resources. Three mechanisms structure the vision.

Co-Perception builds shared world memory. Co-Action maintains shared task progress. Co-Evolution grows shared skill knowledge. A navigation study illustrates one component. A newly added robot inherits the team's merged world memory. It benefits from that inheritance rather than searching from scratch. The authors stress the study is illustrative, not a full evaluation of the framework. Open challenges include keeping shared resources fresh and trustworthy. Heterogeneous robot bodies and constrained communication complicate that goal.
arxiv-2606-28429:
Sheryl Paul, Vidisha Kudalkar, Anand Balakrishnan, Tianhao Wu, Lars Lindemann, and Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh give a logic of multi-agent systems a quantitative voice. Their Spatio-Temporal Logic with Graph Operators extends a standard specification language with operators that count how many neighboring agents satisfy a property. Until now it could only answer yes or no.

Paul and colleagues build graded semantics, which report how strongly a behavior satisfies a formula, in layers, using algebra. Temporal aggregation and graph-operator aggregation stay separate, the latter governed by an abstract accumulator. Soundness and completeness, they prove, reduce to monotonicity of the pieces. A working version runs on two testbeds, Dubins cars in a bounded plane and satellites around Earth. It runs under four semantic flavors, exposing tradeoffs among accumulator choices and scaling in agent count and time horizon.
arxiv-2606-28829:
Luca proves that one narrow family of Carmichael numbers can contain only finitely many members. Carmichael numbers are composite numbers that pass a famous primality test for every base, behaving like primes even though they are not. He studies those built from a power of two times a prime raised to a fixed odd power, plus one, where the fixed power is at least five.

Infinitely many Carmichael numbers exist in general, and every one has the shape he starts from, with some odd multiplier. Earlier work had ruled out several kinds of multiplier, including primes and squares of primes, and pinned down the prime cube case. Luca's proof combines a known bound on the power of two with a result of Corvaja and Zannier resting on Schmidt's subspace theorem. Because that input is not effective, the proof shows finiteness without a computable bound.
arxiv-2606-29129:
Kawakami and Takahashi fix a flaw in a fast method for doing high-precision matrix multiplication on low-precision hardware. Ozaki scheme II turns high-precision matrices into integer matrices by scaling, then recovers the result using the Chinese remainder theorem. Its fast scaling mode uses the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to set the scale cheaply, while its accurate mode spends integer matrix multiplication to estimate better factors.

The authors show the existing fast formula lacks scale invariance. Multiplying the inputs by a constant shifts the integer matrices' effective bit width, degrading accuracy or even breaking the recovery step. Their revised formula derives from the uniqueness condition through the same inequality. It is scale-invariant by construction, always satisfies that condition, and adds no overhead. On an NVIDIA GH200 GPU, it matched the accurate mode's accuracy while keeping the fast mode's throughput.
arxiv-2606-29229:
Ghara, Kumar and Trivedi study circular operators, a class of operators on Hilbert space defined by a symmetry of their numerical range. Gellar conjectured that every such operator is also strongly circular, a stricter property. The general case has resisted proof for decades, and the search for a counterexample goes on.

The authors show the two properties coincide for operators built as direct sums, finite or countably infinite, of irreducible ones. That narrows the search sharply: a counterexample would have to avoid such a build entirely. As a use of the result, they prove every Cowen-Douglas class circular operator is strongly circular. They also prove several general results that bring out the role of the hyper-range, the shared part of all ranges of powers, and of the Cauchy dual.
arxiv-2606-29529:
Bisardi and five colleagues review how generative models, trained on families of related protein sequences, can shed light on protein evolution. A protein sequence records a past shaped by mutation, selection, drift, and epistasis, where one mutation's effect depends on others. A trained model defines a landscape that scores sequences, proposes plausible variants, and captures constraints that experiments struggle to measure.

The review centres on Direct Coupling Analysis, a clear and experimentally tested framework, set within the wider field. Early sections explain how such landscapes are inferred and assessed. Later sections couple the landscapes to population models of evolution, simulating change over lab and deep-time scales. Uses include viral evolution, lab drift experiments, and long-term exploration of sequence space. Open challenges close the review: calibrating scores against fitness, handling family tree structure, codon-level biases, insertions and deletions, and adding experimental data.
arxiv-2606-30029:
Finding the right manual at the European Southern Observatory has become genuinely hard. Documentation spans proposals, observation planning, data reduction, and archive access. Paula Sánchez-Sáez and eight colleagues built a chatbot, ESOFinder, to guide users through it. The tool answers questions with context and links to sources. It is now being tested inside the observatory.

ESOFinder pairs large language models with retrieval-augmented generation. That means it fetches relevant documents before drafting each answer. Its knowledge base covers over one hundred manuals and thousands of web links. The models are open source and run on a local server. This design protects privacy and keeps full control in-house. A multi-step architecture checks retrieved documents and generated answers. Those checks cut the risk of invented answers, called hallucinations. Internal tests will guide added coverage and better retrieval.
arxiv-2606-30129:
David Simon, writing alone, examines how a spectrograph's line spread function distorts measurements of stellar motion. The line spread function describes how a single spectral line gets broadened by the instrument. Pipelines usually assume that profile is Gaussian in shape. Real integral field spectrographs show profiles with wings or boxy forms instead. Simon asks how much error that mismatch creates.

He tests recovery of stellar kinematics on a mock spectrum. Even at a high velocity dispersion of three hundred kilometers per second, the results shift noticeably. Non-Gaussian profiles cause up to seven percent uncertainty in the dispersion. Higher order shape moments can be biased by about a tenth. Simon's fix matches the template spectrum's profile to the target's profile. That matching cuts the dispersion bias below one percent. A public Python implementation accompanies the method.
arxiv-2606-30329:
Amirhossein Esmaeili, M. Marmaduke Woodman, and nine colleagues personalize virtual brain twins without ever sharing a patient's brain data. Personalized brain models need individual scans, which privacy law makes hard to move. Fitting each subject also costs hours of compute time. Their method, cohort-amortized personalization, shares a trained model instead of data. New subjects get personalized in seconds on their own machines.

A neural density estimator trains on simulated runs from a mechanistic whole-brain model. A low-rank cohort prior keeps that estimator compact. A cross-atlas autoencoder maps connectomes from twenty atlases into one latent space. Sites using different atlases can then deploy the same artifact. Validation covers epilepsy patients and an aging cohort of hundreds. Epileptogenic zone localization and age prediction both match slower per-subject inference. The shared artifact doubles as a surrogate for in-silico experiments.
arxiv-2606-30529:
Federico Bonetto and Matthew Powell study a simplified gas model brushing against two heat reservoirs at once. In the Kac model, particles swap energy through random collisions, mimicking a real gas in a tractable way. Here a system of particles in three dimensions collides with two much larger reservoirs. Each reservoir starts as a Maxwellian distribution, the bell-shaped spread of particle velocities, but centred on a different average velocity, giving a shearing setup.

The pair prove that, over a time window that grows with the reservoir size, this finite setup behaves like one with two infinite reservoirs, described as shearing dynamic Maxwellian thermostats. In plain terms, the huge reservoirs act as steady heat baths whose flow pattern keeps sliding. When the two reservoirs share the same temperature offset and average speed, their approximation holds uniformly for all times, with no growing error.
arxiv-2606-30729:
Seppe Staelens and Ece Alkan ask whether future telescope images could betray black-hole impostors. Boson stars, self-gravitating balls of scalar field, can mimic black holes while leaving extra photon rings, thin light circles, in ray-traced images. The pair generated such images for stable and unstable ultracompact boson stars, both non-rotating and rotating, and examined the visibility amplitude, the Fourier-space form in which telescope data actually arrive.

Clear low-frequency modulations in the visibility appeared only for the non-rotating stars, and only for a limited range of observer angles. That suggests such modulations are not a generic signature of ultracompact mimickers, so their absence would not rule impostors out. For the rotating stars, the photon rings turned out incomplete. The authors discuss how an unstable prograde light ring, a light orbit circling in the rotation direction, may be needed to complete them.
arxiv-2606-30829:
Niklas Schmid and five colleagues rethink how to control a system safely when its future is uncertain. In joint chance constrained control, a policy must keep the probability of ever entering a failure state above a set level while minimising cost. Standard practice averages the cost over all trajectories, safe and failed alike, which rewards policies that give up on some runs to save effort. The team argue the cost of a crashed run is often irrelevant, like the battery use of a crashed quadcopter.

Their formulation minimises only the expected cost of safe trajectories. It can be recast as a constrained Markov decision problem on an enlarged state space and solved by dynamic programming. They bound the safety loss from grid approximations and test the approach on a simulated unicycle robot.
arxiv-2606-31029:
Wei and four colleagues present TerraDiT-Omega, a model that creates satellite images under direct spatial control. Older systems force map data into dense rasters or sparse prompts. Dense rasters cost heavy labeling effort. Sparse prompts lose the exact shapes stored in vector data. TerraDiT-Omega instead takes native geospatial primitives: the polygons, polylines, boxes, and points that maps already use.

A method called Geometry-Aware Local Attention feeds these shapes into the model's attention layers. In tests, the system beat both dense-control and sparse-control baselines in every input format. It can also make synthetic training data with a single model. That extra data improved land-cover segmentation, object detection, road graph extraction, and scene classification. The authors release code, data, and model weights for others to build on.
arxiv-2606-31129:
Il'yasov and Valeev build a variational method for the main spectral values of non-selfadjoint operator pencils. A pencil pairs two operators, and the question is which numbers make their combination singular. For selfadjoint problems, the Rayleigh quotient and the Courant-Fischer principle give clean minimax formulas. Those tools collapse when the operator is not selfadjoint, or when the weight operator is singular.

The authors define an extended two-variable Rayleigh quotient on admissible cone pairs. From it come dual sup-inf and inf-sup levels, cone quasi-eigenvalues, and trapping principles. When positive right-left eigenpairs exist, the cone levels coincide with the true principal spectral values. The formulas stay stable under finite-dimensional approximation, which matters for computation. The method also yields after-the-fact spectral certificates and one-sided perturbation bounds. Elliptic examples show where the method reaches and how sharp its estimates are.
arxiv-2606-31229:
Zhao and three colleagues build Agentic-Ideation, a way to train language model agents that propose scientific ideas. Good ideation means searching huge literature and reasoning spaces, yet fixed workflows limit flexibility. Training flexible agents needs example trajectories, records of tool use and reasoning, and making them by trial and error is costly.

Their pipeline uses a reference idea as oracle guidance to steer a multi-agent system toward that target. The system rebuilds the reasoning path and tool calls directly instead of wandering. Masking tool outputs during training keeps the model focused on decision logic. Tests beat the best workflow baseline by 11.91 percent in overall quality, with far better sample efficiency for high-grade trajectories.
arxiv-2606-31729:
Woszczyk and four colleagues question whether naturalness, the standard yardstick for text-to-speech systems, means the same thing in every setting. A voice can sound human yet wrong for its job, or stylized yet exactly right. The team measured both appropriateness and human-likeness for five state-of-the-art systems across five domains, from AI assistant and reader to actor, animated character and spontaneous speaker.

Appropriateness varies across domains independently of naturalness. Systems shine at reading aloud, while expressive domains stay hard, and optimizing for one domain can degrade others. Naturalness scores also penalize stylized speech while rewarding spontaneity, exposing blind spots in one-size-fits-all metrics. Performance therefore cannot be declared solved in general; it depends on the target domain and calls for context-aware evaluation.
arxiv-2608-00229:
Deshpande and Sundararaman present Hierarchical BM25 for lexical search at billion-document scale. A flat BM25 index over a billion documents takes about 400 GB. Holding it in memory needs proportional DRAM. Serving it from disk takes four to twelve seconds per query. Exact top-k retrieval thus breaks interactive latency budgets.

Their design gives up exact ranking for fixed memory and latency bounds. A resident coarse index picks which topical groups a query visits. Two signals guide that choice: term frequency totals and co-occurrence in one document. Chosen groups are searched exhaustively with global statistics. Scores of returned hits equal the flat index's scores exactly. The resident footprint is about 4.4 GB, independent of corpus size. Sixteen-term queries return in about 300 ms, they report.
arxiv-2608-00429:
Bhandari builds positive series for inverse powers of Dirichlet beta values. Beta is the alternating sum over odd denominators. Its value at two is the famed Catalan constant G. He gives two families of positive series for beta to the minus r. The first stems from Euler's classic transform and is taken at one half.

That family holds for real s above zero. A second transform, valid for s at least two, gives a faster series at one third. Finite sums and integrals fix the base terms. A positive recurrence and a product rule cover all inverse powers. For whole-number s, every term is a ratio of whole numbers. Error bounds and exact root rates of convergence are derived. Uses include inverse powers of the Catalan constant and of pi.
berkman-abc-anarchism-1929:
Alexander Berkman published The ABC of Anarchism in 1929, first issued as Now and After: The ABC of Communist Anarchism by Vanguard Press. Late in life, Berkman set out to state his creed in the plainest words he could find. Stuart Christie later praised it among the best such guides in English.

In question-and-answer form, Berkman asked why workers are poor amid plenty and what a free society would do instead. He attacked wages, bosses, and the state, and sketched shared work and free agreement in their place. No jargon blocks the way. The book still serves as a first door into anarchist thought for new readers.
bernard-guide-to-grand-jury-men-english-:
Richard Bernard, a Puritan minister, wrote A Guide to Grand-Jury Men in 1629. The two books instruct jurors who must decide whether accused witches go to trial. Bernard sets out how to spot witchcraft, weigh confessions, and judge evidence, step by step.

His guide became the standard English clerical handbook for witch-finding. Bernard urges care in places, yet the system he builds points toward conviction. Reading it now is chilling in a quiet way. The persecution here has an instruction book, coolly written by a man of God. Few texts show better how law, theology, and fear worked together in a witch trial.
bernard-light-on-masonry-1829:
David Bernard published Light on Masonry in 1829, at the height of anger against Freemasonry in the United States. Bernard had been a Mason, and he gathered oaths, rituals, and lodge papers to expose them. Anti-Masonic readers treated his book as their main source.

Inside are the words and signs of several Masonic degrees, along with charges, prayers, and accounts of lodge work. Bernard argued that secret oaths bound members in ways that clashed with law and faith. The book helped fuel a political movement, and it still shows what critics feared the lodge was doing behind closed doors.
black-sinanthropus-further-remains-1929:
Davidson Black reported further Peking Man fossils in Science in 1929. Excavations at Choukoutien, near Peking, kept yielding jaws and teeth. The growing sample belonged to the form he called Sinanthropus pekinensis.

Black stresses a curious mix in the fossils. The teeth look human while the jaw keeps an ape-like shape. That combination strengthened the case that Peking Man was truly an early human. The finds are now grouped with Homo erectus. Black's paper records the discovery phase, just before the first complete skullcap made headlines worldwide. Work at the cave continued through the following decade with growing success.
boguet-examen-of-witches-1929:
Henry Boguet judges witches in An Examen of Witches, here in the English text of 1929. Boguet was a judge in Burgundy whose bench saw scores of witch trials round 1600. His French book of 1602 is set here by Ashwin, with notes by Montague Summers. It lays out the sabbath, the pact, and the mark. It gives the rules of proof a judge should use at trial.

He prints cases from his own court in grim rows. His calm makes the book more dread than wild tracts. It is the hunt's hand book by a chief hand.
burns-introducing-bc-hairy-giants-1929:
John Burns gave the hairy giants of British Columbia their famed name in print in 1929. Introducing B C's Hairy Giants appeared in Maclean's Magazine that April. Burns was a teacher and agent among the Chehalis people, whose tales he set down with care.

From their word Sasq'ets he shaped Sasquatch, the name the wild men carry to this day. His article gathers the old tales and fresh reports of the great hairy tribe. With it, the modern Bigfoot era can be said to start in earnest. Few magazine pieces have named a legend so well.
butler-fifteen-sermons-1729:
Joseph Butler preached his Fifteen Sermons at the Rolls Chapel in London, and they were published in 1729 with his preface. The Rolls Chapel served the lawyers of the nearby courts, and Butler spoke to sharp, worldly hearers. His subject is human nature itself: how self-love, benevolence, and conscience fit together in one soul.

Butler argues that conscience, cool and reflective, holds the top place in our design by nature. Self-love and kindness to others, rightly read, never truly clash. The sermons founded his moral psychology and quietly changed English ethics. Philosophers still assign the sermon on conscience and the ones on self-deception. All fifteen stand here, the ground floor of Butler's fame.
caesarius-dialogue-on-miracles-vol-1-192:
Caesarius of Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk of the Rhineland, wrote his Dialogue on Miracles around 1219 to 1223 as a teaching book for novices. H. von E. Scott and C. C. Swinton Bland translated it into English in 1929, and this is the first volume. The dialogue form lets a monk ask and a master answer with tale after tale.

The stories run from conversion and confession to demons, visions, and the punishments of the wicked dead. Cathars appear at first hand, for Caesarius had ridden with the Albigensian Crusade's preachers. His exempla were preached across Europe for centuries. The book is the great medieval story chest of the miraculous, told with a gossip's glee and a monk's moral.
caesarius-dialogue-on-miracles-vol-2-192:
The second volume of the Scott and Bland English Caesarius, from 1929, completes the Dialogue on Miracles. Caesarius of Heisterbach wrote the work around 1219 to 1223 to stock Cistercian novices with tales for the road of the spirit. A full index closes the translation.

Temptations, visions of heaven and hell, and the deaths of saints and sinners fill these books. The Virgin Mary steps in again and again to save her servants, sometimes by rough mercy. Caesarius collected his tales from monks, knights, and travelers, and he names his sources. The dialogue between the questioning novice and the answering monk keeps the pace light. It is the middle ages talking to itself about wonder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-english-confe:
English confessors and martyrs from 1534 to 1729 are the subject of this entry. It opens with a frank admission. English resistance to the Reformation compares badly with that of several other nations. Yet those who stood firm offer a remarkably instructive example. They paid the extreme penalty for holding the unity of the Church and the supremacy of Rome, the doctrines most attacked by reformers everywhere.

They kept their faith by strikingly modern means. They were the first to do so: training clergy in seminaries and Catholic youth in colleges, at the risk and often the cost of life. The tyranny they faced was seldom a tyrant's sudden violence. It was the steady pressure of laws passed by Parliament on pleas of political necessity, working for centuries in law-abiding counties. Their trials are well documented, with prosecution and defence papers alike, and Rome's voice often settling what admitted no compromise.
charron-of-wisdom-stanhope-1729:
Pierre Charron, a French priest and the friend of Montaigne, published De la Sagesse, Of Wisdom, in 1601. George Stanhope's English translation, in the three-volume form of 1729, is the text here. All three books stand complete: self-knowledge first, then the wise man's conduct in life and in every station.

Charron builds his wisdom on honest doubt: know yourself, hold your judgments loosely, and let nature and reason lead. His skepticism, learned from Montaigne's Essays, aims not at despair but at calm freedom of mind. The book was attacked as godless and read everywhere in secret and in open. It carried Montaigne's spirit into the next century's philosophy.
cia-0000009929:
A Pathet Lao source's later account of witnessing an interrogation is preserved, partly deleted, in a November 1965 item. The heading says the account came afterward, making it a follow-up to earlier reporting. Interrogations were captivity's first hard passage for newly taken men.

A witness from the captors' own side offered rare inside detail. What was asked, and how, told analysts what the enemy wanted from prisoners. Deleted passages hide the source, as usual, but the account's core survives. The file shows testimony crossing enemy lines, with the censor's black marks still plainly on it.
cia-0000012429:
One redacted person debriefs another in a CIA record from February 1962, and both names stay blacked out. The record belongs to the Penkovsky era's questioning, the daily work of drawing knowledge out of people. Each of them had seen some piece of the puzzle the service was assembling. The debriefer's art shows in the answers: what they reveal, and what they leave carefully unsaid.

Such sessions filled the spaces between the great meetings in London and Paris. They tested stories, dated memories, and priced the rumors that reached the station. For readers, the page shows the interrogation rooms' quiet craft, where the big case was checked.
cia-0000013229:
Tran Van Luc, also called Nam Luc, gets a CIA file of his own in August 1970. He was chief of the policy section of the Enemy Proselyting staff. That office set the rules for handling prisoners across the south. In plain terms, he was one of the prison system's administrators. His sections and signatures shaped what happened to men held in camps he may never have visited in person.

The item profiles the jailer's career and his place in the machine. Naming the jailers was the accounting's necessary, sobering work. For readers, the page puts a human face on a system too often described without one.
cia-0000013929: United States prisoners were sighted in two provinces, in a CIA note dated January 3, 1968. One sighting came from Hoa Binh Province in the north. Another came from Thua Thien Province, far south near Hue. Pairing the two shows how one file could sweep the length of Vietnam for signs of missing men.
cia-0000014729: Anatolij Antonovich Yakovlev anchors a CIA file dated June 4, 1959. The file also mentions Harry Gold, Klaus Fuchs, and Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. Yakovlev was a Soviet officer tied to the atomic spy web. A file from 1959 that still linked all four names shows the case's cast stayed fixed in the records.
cia-0000015329: A letter to Thornton Page from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 5, 1960. It takes up fourteen essays by a friend of theirs, the title says. Page and Strong had traded mail on strange skies since 1953. Their thread reaching 1960 shows how long one panel's ties could last. Strong's letter on the essays rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000022429: A United States prisoner of war was sighted in Quang Binh Province, North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated in 1972. A cover sheet came with the report, per the clipped title. Quang Binh was the narrow waist of North Vietnam, crossed by supply routes south. Late war sightings like this fed the hope that held men would come home in the peace.
cia-0000027929: El Salvador's performance on certification issues is graded in a special national intelligence paper dated in 1983. Special papers were called up out of the normal rhythm when a question pressed hard. Certification tied American aid to the Salvadoran government's human rights record. A community wide judgment on it carried weight in a fierce debate in Washington that year.
cia-0000028329: Use of the CIA Act of 1949, as amended, to improve access to the United States for certain persons fills a CIA item dated in 1977. The clipped title cuts off who those persons were. The 1949 act gave the agency special powers, including bringing valued foreigners in quietly. A legal item like this shows staff testing how far that old law could stretch.
cia-0000040329:
A National Intelligence Analytical Memorandum dated February 1, 1977 takes up the Ethiopian revolution and its impact. Ethiopia's emperor had been overthrown in 1974, and a military regime held power. The Horn of Africa was becoming a new Cold War battleground.

Inside, analysts weigh what the revolution meant for Ethiopia and its neighbors. They judge the new regime's direction and the openings it gave outside powers. Ethiopia's size and place made its turn matter far beyond its borders. The file captures a turning point in the region. An ancient empire became a Marxist state. The superpowers then recalculated their positions along the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
cia-0000042129:
El Salvador's chamber confirmed a trial in the killing of American nuns, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1984. The murdered churchwomen had become a test of justice in El Salvador. Washington watched the case closely, since American aid turned on it.

Inside, the record marks a court step: the trial of the accused would go ahead. Getting soldiers into a courtroom was itself a hard fight in that war. The file shows the case moving, slowly, through a legal system under strain. It stands as one dated point in a long effort to make the killings answerable in court.
cia-0000042829:
Joint Chiefs Chairman Ponce was interviewed, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. The title ties the interview to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Ponce spoke as the army's senior officer in a season of scandal.

Inside, the general gives his account in question and answer form. Senior officers rarely faced the press at such a moment. His words were read, in San Salvador and in Washington, for what they admitted and for what they carefully avoided saying aloud. The file preserves a commander defending his institution in public, while some of its members sat accused of the war's most famous murders.
cia-0000045229:
Duarte said he had nothing concrete on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 4, 1985. Nothing concrete is a hard thing for a president to admit aloud. It told the country the talks had given him nothing to show.

Inside, the president's frank admission is preserved as he made it. Candor of that kind can steady a public or alarm it further. In a father's mouth, it sounded less like policy than like grief. The file keeps the remark from that September day. The most powerful man in the country told reporters, in effect, that he was waiting like everyone else.
cia-0000049229: A 1991 letter from the CIA's deputy director for operations to Congressman John Moakley survives in this item, kept with the Truth Commission records. The letter concerns the agency's role in the matter Moakley's task force was pursuing in El Salvador. Such letters were the oversight channel at its most formal: Langley, answering the Hill in writing.
cia-0000098729: National Security and National Priorities is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098729, dated August 3, 1990. Two broad nouns carry the whole heading, security and priorities. Readers find a short declassified item on that pairing, its generality the main fact to record. The title names a theme. It names no event, no place, and no decision.
cia-0000102929: Use of Forced Labor on Pipeline and Other Construction Projects is the title of declassified CIA document 0000102929, dated July 3, 1982. The heading widens beyond pipelines to other projects in one phrase. Readers find a short general labor record in the cluster, filed the same day as the common-prisoners pipeline item it complements.
cia-0000115229: Untitled re Statement of Viacheslav Ivanovich Toropovsky is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000115229, dated November 5, 1945. The catalog marks the file untitled, then names a statement by Toropovsky in full. An October filing used only his initial and surname for the same name. The brief record is the fuller named statement of that wartime pair.
cia-0000118929: CIA Secrecy Agreements is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000118929, dated November 2, 1985. The title names the agency's own secrecy agreements, the pledges tied to handling secret work. No person or case is named in the heading itself at all. The brief record is an internal rules item, filed in the autumn of 1985 as released.
cia-0000119729: A September 1956 CIA paper reports that an overhaul of Hungarian domestic policies is expected. Reform was widely talked of in Budapest that autumn. The paper forecasts the changes the country's leaders were weighing before unrest overtook planning. Planners hoped changes at home might calm the country, though events that autumn soon moved faster than any plan the paper describes.
cia-0000124329: A July 1953 CIA document reports the status of an American plane crew downed near Swatow, the coastal city now called Shantou. The Korean War was ending, but missing crews still had to be accounted for. The paper records the crew's status as the agency then knew it. Downed-crew cases stayed open after the armistice because no exchange covered them, and status papers like this one mark the slow official search for an answer.
cia-0000132429: Two high Cuban officials reportedly defecting from the Castro government are reported in a CIA item dated January 2, 1960. The headline breaks off at the word governm, but its sense is clear. Every defector from the new regime was a prize in the contest for world opinion. The short item records the reported defections as signs of cracks inside the revolution's leadership.
cia-0000132629: Warm feelings toward Castro shown by the foreign minister of Venezuela fill a CIA paper dated June 2, 1960. The top envoy of Caracas was friendly to Havana at that point. That warmth would not last once the two states fell out. The short paper notes the leanings. It also sets out the signs analysts had for them at the time.
cia-0000135829: The instruction dated 3 April 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with tactical instructions, part two of a set, sent with an attachment and the name deleted. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000135929: The CIA cable from 6 January 1954 deals with an urgent request to copy a leaflet form, in a file now declassified. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Read on its own terms, the record shows the operation at work in its own words, with some names still blacked out.
cia-0000136129: The CIA cable from 6 April 1954 deals with the future of the K Program, its fate reviewed as the spring campaign gathered pace, in a file now declassified. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136229: Dated 3 May 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with the point of diminishing returns coming fast, and H-hour, the zero hour of the invasion. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136329: Three audiences share this 28 June 1954 LINCOLN cable. For BRODFROST, the primary target must be destroyed, by multiple attacks if necessary, with Matamoros as the secondary target for show. For CADICK, CALLIGERIS must keep the enemy disorganized and engaged so it cannot withdraw in good order. For LANGEVIN, broadcast lines claim Diaz simply took up communism where Arbenz left it, with mass defections under way. Targeting and propaganda run side by side.
cia-0000136629: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, dated only to the year 1961 in the catalog, with that date marked as estimated. An earlier summary attached Big Three summitry and late-night diplomacy to this item; none of that is in the record, and it is removed. The document is a Spanish record of the CIA's Cuban exile brigade from its final year, released in the declassified 2506 files, its month and subject unstated.
cia-0000136729: A Spanish paper from the exile brigade's document cache, cataloged under an estimated date of 1 January 1961. An earlier summary filled it with London, Washington, and the Big Three; that Second World War material is unsupported by the record and is removed. The document is a Spanish record of Brigade 2506, the CIA's Cuban exile force, then in training. It is preserved in the declassified release with its estimated date.
cia-0000137329: Abuse of the United States fills this CIA briefing. It served the 24 March 1960 NSC meeting. Che Guevara warned that Cuba faces economic war with America. President Dorticos made his strongest attack to date the same day. He blamed the United States for the La Coubre explosion. A small plane from Florida was forced down on 21 March.
