Government radios took up a new theme within hours. Another aggression, they shouted. Opposition is growing more outspoken, the briefing notes. Castro remains strongly in control, though.
cia-0000139029: A captured Russian soldier talks in this July 1946 interview report. Mihail Strikunoff is 21 years old. Nationalists captured him at Liaoyang. They took the town from the Eighth Route Army. He had been held sixty days at interview. He claims no knowledge of aid to the Communists. He admits machinery was removed from Manchuria. That was an official order from higher up, probably Stalin. Private looting was not supposed to be allowed. Nobody paid attention to the rule, he says. Long-fighting soldiers simply took what they could.
cia-06479729:
Recruiting overview titled CIA Target Segment Overview - Women sets out how women in the target group look for jobs. The internet is named as the first resource used, through company sites and job boards such as Monster and CareerBuilder. Social and professional networking sites, friends, and colleagues are also listed. Younger women are said to rely often on college career counselors and career fairs.

Salary is named as the most cited factor in a rewarding job. Health care, leave, and education benefits also matter, along with flexible hours, work-life balance, and a supportive setting. The overview advises the CIA to stress flexible work and good benefits. It also reports that few in the target felt the CIA website urged women to apply, and it calls for more visuals of female staff on the site.
cia-06486329:
Additional views of Senator Richard C. Shelby, dated December 10, 2002, are titled September 11 and the Imperative of Reform in the U.S. Intelligence Community. Shelby wrote as Vice Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. A DCI Action Center routing slip at the front dates receipt in DAC to 19 December 2002 and gives document number DAC 07991-02.

The statement opens by tracing the intelligence community's birth to the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. It argues that a crisis, not steady review, is what forces deep reform of the system. Shelby, a former committee chairman quoted in the text, presses for new and bolder thinking after an attack that killed about 3,000 people. A long middle section discusses the proposed Total Information Awareness program and limits that policymakers could place on its use.
cia-06527529:
Memorandum marked Secret, addressed to the Director of the Office of Research and Development, sets a scenario for trained birds. The memo asks that the contractor design the bird training program to fit the attached step-by-step plan. The plan covers one possible photographic mission in the USSR.

Two weak points are singled out, at steps 6c and 7b of the scenario. The first is handing the birds over from a case officer's car, in view of at least one observation post. Birds had to tolerate a closed, possibly light-tight hiding device until release. The second weak point is the launch itself, watched by hostile surveillance. Launch ideas tested include a moving car window at up to 50 miles per hour, a skier's knapsack, and a picnicker's lunch basket. Testing in the United States had to mirror the Moscow plan.
cia-06628029:
Short Top Secret paper dated 11 October 1984, in a contents listing of sanitized papers, is titled Argentina: Political Problems. It assesses President Alfonsin, spelled Aliansin and Alfonsin in the scan, after he acted on several charged issues. The economy is named as his lasting point of weakness.

The paper states that, with Alfonsin's approval, trials of former junta members charged over 1970s human rights violations moved the week before to civilian courts. Senior commanders reportedly expected him to limit the number of officers affected. Lower ranking officers who feared inquiry were voicing discontent. A comment assesses that Alfonsin would probably mute criticism over the trials and the Beagle Channel accord. It judges convictions would be harder to win in civilian courts.
class-of-29:
Class of '29, by Orrie Lashin and Milo Hastings, is a stage play handled by the Dramatists Play Service of New York for nonprofessional production. The service's own catalog pages open the volume, listing plays it leased to college, university, and little theatres. Class of '29 stands in that list beside works by Maxwell Anderson and Robert E. Sherwood.

The play itself speaks in tight, worried dialogue. Kate and Martin spar over a man who cannot find work and may starve. Shoddy goods are scorned: it has to be Rolls Royces and polo ponies or nothing. Kate ends the scene with sudden resolve. If he wants a job, she will get him one, by asking for it herself.
crowley-moonchild-1929:
Crowley turned his magic into a novel in Moonchild, printed in 1929. A secret war is fought over an unborn child, by two camps of magicians in London and Paris. The book is a roman à clef of the Golden Dawn and O T O circles he knew well.

Friends and foes of Crowley's real life walk its pages in thin masks. The plot turns on a plan to draw a soul of power into a child yet to be born. As fiction it moves fast; as a document it maps his world from inside. It is his major work of prose fiction.
dewey-quest-certainty-1929:
The Quest for Certainty, published in 1929 from Dewey's Gifford Lectures, carries his subtitle: a study of the relation of knowledge and action. It attacks the spectator theory of knowledge, the idea that knowing is a mind passively viewing a fixed world.

Dewey traces the quest for absolute certainty to man's fear of a perilous world, and shows how it split theory from practice. Modern science, he argues, replaced that quest with controlled inquiry and warranted belief. Knowing is a kind of doing, tested by results. The book is the fullest statement of his instrumentalism, and a landmark of pragmatism.
europmc-pmc10242329:
Wang and co-authors review the role of the tumor microenvironment in cancer progression and treatment strategy, in a 2023 paper. Cancer is now seen as a disease of the whole tumor neighborhood, not just of rogue cells. Over twenty years, research has shown how the cells, vessels, and signals around a tumor shape its growth and its response to drugs.

The review explains how that neighborhood helps tumors spread and resist care. It surveys treatments that target the surroundings, from vessel blockers to immune activators. The paper frames the neighborhood as a treatment frontier.
europmc-pmc10335929:
Hofmeister and colleagues gave a 2023 method, SHAPEIT5, for sorting DNA by parent. Each person holds two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. Phasing means telling which DNA changes sit on which copy. The team ran the method on UK Biobank data, a huge UK health data set.

SHAPEIT5 phased rare DNA changes with an error rate below 5%. That held even for changes seen in just 1 sample out of 100,000. The team also found a way to phase changes seen in a single person. With the sorted data, they found 549 genes where both copies were knocked out. Such finds help show which genes people can live without.
europmc-pmc10679229:
Guo and co-authors reviewed psoriasis in 2023, a chronic skin disease driven by immune faults. Scales and red patches mark the skin, and the burden on patients and health systems runs high. New drugs have changed care in the past years. Rarer forms of the disease are still poorly grasped.

The review maps signals that pass between cells and inside them, Guo reports. It also weighs fuel use and gene control shifts that may drive the disease. Links to other ills, such as joint and heart disease, get a close look. Two flaws of current care stand out: harsh side effects and return of disease when drugs stop. Targeted drugs and fresh plans fill the last part.
europmc-pmc10850029:
Welsh and many colleagues present updated field guidance on tiny cell sacs in this 2024 document. Extracellular vesicles are small sacs cells release, and their cargo can show the state of the cell that made them. Interest in their use as disease markers and treatments grows each year. Yet the field still lacks shared names and clean ways to sort sacs from other particles.

The guidance, called MISEV2023, comes from the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles, the field's main society. It updates two earlier versions from 2014 and 2018. It surveys methods to make, sort, and describe sacs from cell cultures, body fluids, and solid tissues. Pros and cons of each method are laid out. The authors also cover newer tools that stretch what labs can measure.
europmc-pmc11077829:
Lin and colleagues explain why brain tumours resist immune attack in this 2024 review. Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour in adults. Standard care pairs surgery, radiation, and a drug called temozolomide, yet outcomes stay poor. A key reason is the suppressive immune climate inside the tumour.

The review details three cell groups that enforce that climate. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells make up only 4 to 8 percent of immune cells in the tumour, yet play a central role, the authors note. They help the tumour evade immunity, grow vessels, invade, and spread. Tumour-linked macrophages and regulatory T cells add further suppression. The authors survey new immune and targeted strategies built on this map. They argue that breaking this suppression is the pivotal step for better therapy.
europmc-pmc11184729:
Song and colleagues review a growth signal path in cancer formation and therapy in this 2024 paper. The Wnt and beta-catenin pathway steers development, tissue upkeep, and cell growth. In healthy tissue it is meticulously regulated. Mutations in its parts, chemical tags on DNA, and crosstalk with other pathways can switch it on wrongly.

Such faulty activation drives tumour initiation and progression, the review says. Drugs targeting the pathway's signal chain have shown promising prospects in studies. More such medications are being developed and validated each year. The authors summarise the latest advances in how the pathway drives carcinogenesis, the process of cancer formation. They also map the targeted therapies now in play. Current opportunities and challenges in aiming drugs at this pathway are weighed in closing.
europmc-pmc11485229:
Vakaniaki and a large team describe a sustained outbreak of a new mpox lineage in eastern Congo in this 2024 study. Mpox is caused by monkeypox virus. Historically, outbreaks in Central Africa came from animal spillover of the clade I virus. In 2022 a different subclade caused a global epidemic linked to sexual contact. This outbreak, in a mining region, was caused by clade I.

Surveillance from September 2023 to January 2024 identified 241 suspected cases. Genome analysis showed a distinct clade I lineage, divergent from strains previously circulating in the country. Of 108 confirmed cases, the median age was 22 years, 51.9 percent were female, and 29 percent were sex workers. Mutation patterns and an estimated emergence in mid-September 2023 point to recent, sustained spread between humans. The authors flag a potential role for sexual transmission.
europmc-pmc12280729:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed changeable risk factors for Alzheimer disease in 2021. Alzheimer disease is the top cause of dementia. It accounts for about half to seven in ten cases. No cure can reverse its course.

Genes set part of the risk, but life factors matter too. The disease likely starts decades before symptoms show. That long lead time opens a window for prevention. Acting in midlife or early old age may delay onset. Zhang surveys population evidence on risks people can change. The goal is fewer cases through earlier action.
europmc-pmc1240129:
Swan, Elkin, and Fenster revisited claims of falling sperm counts in 2000. A 1992 report claimed a global decline over fifty years. Later checks found declines in some regions but not others. Debate over methods and bias ran hot.

The team pooled 101 studies published from 1934 to 1996. They adjusted for age, abstinence time, and collection method. Declines appeared in the United States and Europe or Australia. Data from non-Western countries were sparse and showed no decline. Swan urges care in reading global claims from uneven data. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2000.
europmc-pmc1250929:
Pfeiffer and Kirkegaard tested a high-accuracy poliovirus in mice in 2005. RNA viruses copy with many errors, forming mixed swarms. Theory held that error swarms help viruses survive pressure. A mutant polymerase made this virus copy with fewer errors.

The accurate virus grew almost normally in cell culture. In mice it proved far less able to cause disease. Under a set genetic pressure, it lost a growth race badly. Even a tenfold head start could not save it against normal virus. Pfeiffer shows copying errors themselves aid viral fitness. It appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2005.
europmc-pmc1260029:
Oberdörster and a large working group set screening principles for nanomaterials in 2005. Engineered materials under 100 nanometers were multiplying fast. Regulators lacked a hazard identification playbook. An international expert group drafted one from the limited data then available.

The strategy covers mouth, skin, lung, and injection exposure routes. It lays out broad data gathering rather than a fixed test protocol. Three key elements anchor the screening approach. The group stresses use patterns decide which routes matter. Oberdörster frames screening as the first stage of full risk assessment. The three elements start with material traits, then cell tests, then animal tests. Each stage adds data for later risk review.
europmc-pmc1310929:
Åkesson and colleagues studied kidney effects of low cadmium exposure in Swedish women in 2005. Cadmium harms kidneys, but the critical level for the public was undefined. The survey covered 820 women aged 53 to 64 in southern Sweden. Median cadmium was 0.38 micrograms per liter in blood.

Urine cadmium averaged 0.52 micrograms per liter. Higher cadmium tied to markers of tubule damage in the kidney. Links held even in women who had never smoked. Glomerular function markers also showed associations. Åkesson finds kidney effects at ordinary environmental exposure levels. About 71 percent of invited women took part, in a survey run from 1999 to 2000.
europmc-pmc1513329:
Autism likely grows from a mix of genes and surroundings. Hertz-Picciotto and co-authors launched the CHARGE study in 2006 to sort those causes. Past links to chemicals and viruses rested on weak methods. Twin and family studies support inherited risk, yet early life conditions may switch that risk on or off.

CHARGE compares children with autism to others, gathering deep detail. It collects development tests, medical records, surveys, and body samples. Labs linked to the study probe immune function, chemical loads, and gene activity. The design also covers children with developmental delay. Hertz-Picciotto aims to test how exposures and genes interact, not just each alone.
europmc-pmc1868929:
Vastrik, Stein and colleagues described Reactome in 2007, a curated online knowledge base of human biological pathways. A pathway is a chain of molecular events, such as the steps that burn sugar or copy DNA. The finished human genome listed the parts, but not how the parts work together.

Reactome's expert-curated entries record those chains reaction by reaction. The resource can project human pathways onto other species to infer their matching reactions. It also serves as a lens for high-throughput data: gene activity lists from microarrays gain meaning when mapped onto known pathways. The authors compare a parts list to an aircraft's components spread on a hangar floor. Knowing the parts alone does not explain flight, so a verified wiring diagram is the real prize.
europmc-pmc1955829:
van Dulmen, Bensing and co-authors reviewed other reviews in 2007 to find what actually helps patients stick to medical treatment. Non-adherence is a stubborn, widespread problem, and many programs built to fix it fail. The field lacked a sound theory of what works, so the team looked across the review literature itself.

They gathered 38 systematic reviews, published from 1990 to 2005, of interventions meant to improve adherence, drawn from four major databases under explicit selection rules. In 23 of the reviews, interventions differed clearly in how well they worked. Working interventions appeared under all four theory families: technical, behavioral, educational, and multi-part programs. Simplifying the regimen, a technical fix, often worked, though not for every therapy. No single approach won outright, so the authors argue for better theory to match tactics to situations.
europmc-pmc2124929:
Alexis Carrel reported in 1912 the long-term fate of two artery grafts sewn onto the aorta. In the first, a segment of leg artery taken from a young man was kept in cold storage for twenty-four days. It was then grafted onto the abdominal aorta of a small female dog.

That dog lived four years and two months in excellent health, bore litters several times, and died in labor. Her aorta was normal; the human segment was slightly widened, its wall plain connective tissue. The dog stayed well for two years and two months before an epidemic disease killed it. The vein graft matched the aorta's caliber, and its wall, too, had become connective tissue without muscle or elastic fibers. Yet it held blood pressure without marked widening. Readers get patience rewarded: proof that stored vessel grafts can serve for years.
europmc-pmc2125229:
W. G. MacCallum, R. A. Lambert, and Karl M. Vogel used dialysis in 1914 to test whether tetany is, at bottom, a lack of calcium in the blood. They built a dialyzing fluid with all the blood's diffusible salts except calcium. Normal blood washed against it loses a large part of its calcium.

Perfused through an isolated limb, that calcium-poor blood makes the nerves extremely excitable, exactly the state seen in tetany. Blood dialyzed identically, but against a fluid with normal calcium, causes no such excitability, pinning the effect on the missing calcium. Swapping a whole animal's blood works only slightly, since the tissues will not give up their calcium fast enough. The parathyroid secretion, they judge, is probably not removed by the dialysis. Readers get a mineral, not a hormone, put at the center of a spasm disease.
europmc-pmc2126329:
Marguerite M. Thomas, Herbert D. Taylor, and William D. Witherbee tested whether a mild X-ray dose can raise, rather than destroy, circulating lymphocytes. Their 1919 Journal of Experimental Medicine paper is the second in the X-ray effects series. It reports blood counts on nine rabbits given one set exposure of twenty minutes under fixed machine settings.

Seven of the nine rabbits showed an increase in circulating lymphocytes; in five the increase was marked, and in two it was definite but smaller. One animal's counts swung widely before and after alike, and one barely changed. A second, harder-penetrating dose tried on two animals produced no clear stimulation at all. Set beside the series' first paper, where large doses cut lymphocytes down, the result suggests the rays' effect turns on dose. Gentle exposure stirs the lymphocyte supply up; heavy exposure tears it down.
europmc-pmc2128129:
Frederick T. Lord and Robert N. Nye measured how pneumococci dissolve at different acidities, in the second paper of their pneumococcus studies. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. They suspended living germs in balanced solutions and in broth across a wide acidity scale, at incubator, room, and icebox temperatures, and compared living, heat-killed, and grown-out organisms.

Living pneumococci dissolved in solutions less acid than a fixed point, most strongly in a critical middle range. Some dissolving also occurred toward the alkaline end, and none at the most acid end. Cold weakened the effect but did not stop it. Germs killed by brief strong heat would not dissolve at all, and germs killed by longer gentle heat dissolved less than living ones. Fresh human serum added to the suspensions prevented dissolving altogether.
europmc-pmc2128329:
F. S. Jones asked where the germs in the lungs of healthy animals come from, culturing lung borders from calves, rabbits, guinea pigs, rats, and mice. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922, from the Rockefeller Institute's animal pathology department at Princeton. The normal lung was often assumed sterile; his cultures said otherwise.

The lungs of all these animals proved readily invaded by organisms. The commonest finds were streptothrix, molds, and bacteria of the Bacillus subtilis group. These forms originate in dry feedstuffs, hay and straw above all. Withholding those materials, or moistening them, cut the number of organisms in the lungs. Mice given dry feed in place of their usual scant supply soon matched the larger animals' lung counts. The bronchial lymph glands of guinea pigs grew the same organisms in two-thirds of tubes. Breathing dusty feed, Jones shows, seeds the healthy lung.
europmc-pmc2128529:
Carl A. L. Binger and George R. Brow measured the air left in the lungs at the end of a normal breath out, in healthy people and in ten lobar pneumonia patients. Their respiratory study appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. Breathing rate, depth, and volume were recorded by a graphic method, and arterial blood oxygen was measured where blueness showed.

One constant relation held through the disease. While symptoms persisted, fever, racing heart, rapid shallow breathing, and blueness, the leftover air volume shrank. As the symptoms cleared, soon after the crisis, the volume rose back toward normal. X-ray shadows and chest signs moved in parallel with the volume as well. Lung volume at rest thus tracks the clinical course closely enough to read the disease's turn from the measure. The study gives pneumonia a simple physical gauge beside the thermometer and the eye.
europmc-pmc2131329:
Harold Abramson opened a series on the mechanism of inflammation in 1927, working at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute in Berlin-Dahlem, Germany. Part one measures how horse blood cells move in an electric field, a motion called cataphoresis. His interest was why white cells travel to a point of injury, a core event in inflammation.

Red cells, white cells of several kinds, and lymphocytes all moved at speeds that rose in direct proportion to the voltage applied. Abramson set their electric charge values beside the voltage gaps thought to exist in injured tissue. The match suggests that electric forces in the tissue itself help pull white cells toward the injury, alongside any other guides at work.
europmc-pmc2131629:
Gilbert Dalldorf, at New York Hospital and Cornell University Medical College, reported muscle lesions in experimental scurvy in 1929. Guinea pigs deprived of the food factor that prevents scurvy, scorbutus, were examined for damage beyond the known signs. Earlier writers had barely mentioned the skeletal muscles. Dalldorf mapped where muscle damage sits and what brings it out.

Muscle degeneration turned up constantly in the rib muscles of scorbutic guinea pigs. The jaw muscle and the diaphragm showed it as well. Exercise produced the identical lesion in other skeletal muscles of scorbutic animals. The damage seems an inborn part of the scurvy process itself. Dalldorf suggests the muscle tenderness of scurvy in man may come from this same muscle disease.
europmc-pmc2140329:
Selig Hecht studied dark adaptation in Mya arenaria, the soft-shell clam, in a 1919 paper. Mya answers light after a reaction time made of two parts. Hecht timed both parts and modeled how the clam's sensitivity rebuilds in darkness, in terms of a photosensitive substance formed and broken down in balance.

The first part, sensitization, is extremely short, on the scale of photographic processes. The second, a latent period of a little over a second, runs without further light. Dark adaptation proceeds in an orderly way that fits a two-molecule reaction forming the sensitive substance. Hecht's equilibrium picture made two testable forecasts: reaction time at a set light should fall as temperature rises, and dark adaptation should speed with temperature. Experiments bore out both.
europmc-pmc2140429:
Philip Mitchell and Walter Wilson, at Brown University, opened a study of selective potassium absorption by animal cells in 1921. Part one uses frog muscle and asks what controls how much potassium the cells take up and hold. Potassium is the chief mineral inside living cells, and muscles were perfused, washed, with salt solutions to test their grip on it.

Potassium content varied notably from frog to frog, and ran higher in fresh summer frogs than in winter frogs kept in captivity. Washed with potassium-free solution, muscles lost only a small share of their potassium and held the rest tenaciously. Working muscles lost no more than resting ones. Rubidium and cesium, chemical kin of potassium, were taken up and kept by contracting muscle but not by resting muscle.
europmc-pmc2141029:
Halicystis, a marine alga with very large cells, lets L. R. Blinks push fine glass tubes into living cells and read the voltage across their surface layer. His 1929 study, from the Rockefeller Institute, borrows a technique built for the related alga Valonia and applies it to this Bermuda organism.

Impaled cells settle at a steady voltage of 60 to 80 millivolts between cell sap and sea water, with the outer surface positive. Contact with sap or balanced salt mixes lowers the voltage, and several single-salt solutions wipe it out fully. Sea water restores it promptly. Blinks notes Halicystis differs from Valonia in sap makeup and cell build, making the comparison between the two algae instructive for early cell physiology.
europmc-pmc2360029:
Baeuerle and Gires took stock of EpCAM in 2007, a protein found on the surface of many cancer cells. EpCAM, also called CD326, helps epithelial cells stick together, and epithelial cells line organs and skin. It was among the first tumor markers ever found, in the late 1970s, yet its role in causing cancer stayed unclear for decades.

The authors reported on the first international meeting devoted to this protein. Talks covered how often EpCAM appears on cancers such as breast, colon, and lung tumors, and whether its level predicts patient outcomes. Evidence showed EpCAM actively sends growth signals inside cancer cells, not just marking them. At least seven EpCAM-targeted immune therapies were then in clinical trials, some already in mid-stage testing.
europmc-pmc2360429:
Osterlund and co-authors ran a randomised trial of a probiotic during colon cancer chemotherapy in 2007. Probiotics are live bacteria taken for gut health. The drug 5-fluorouracil, a mainstay after colon cancer surgery, often causes severe diarrhoea that forces dose cuts.

The trial enrolled 150 patients on two versions of the drug plan for 24 weeks. Half also got daily Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, a probiotic strain, plus fibre. Severe diarrhoea struck 22% of the probiotic group versus 37% of the others, and they needed less hospital care. Added fibre alone changed nothing. One drug schedule, the simplified de Gramont plan, caused far fewer severe side effects overall, at 45% versus 89% for the monthly Mayo plan.
europmc-pmc2363129:
Sheard and Maguire combined trials of psychological help for cancer patients in 1999. Most trials offered counselling or therapy to all patients with a diagnosis, not just those in distress. The authors ran two meta-analyses, one for anxiety and one for depression.

For anxiety, 19 trials with 1,023 patients scored the treated groups 0.42 standard deviations better than controls. A stricter estimate held at 0.36, a moderate benefit. For depression, 20 trials with 1,101 patients gave 0.36 at first, but the robust estimate fell to 0.19, which they called weak to negligible. Group therapy worked at least as well as one-to-one help. Only four trials targeted distressed patients, and those showed much stronger effects, suggesting help should aim at those who need it most.
europmc-pmc2430329:
Dennehy and a large team showed how two germ sensors cooperate in macrophages in 2008. Macrophages are immune cells that detect microbe parts through pattern receptors. One sensor, Dectin-1, spots fungal sugars. It was known to team up with a second family, the Toll-like receptors, to trigger strong cytokine release, but the wiring was unknown.

The team found the link runs through a relay enzyme called Syk. Without Syk, or without the Toll-side adaptor protein MyD88, the joint response collapsed. The teamwork also held when Dectin-1 paired with Toll-like receptors 4, 5, 7, and 9, not just receptor 2. Together the two paths kept an inhibitor protein, IkB, broken down for longer, letting the inflammation switch NFkB stay in the cell nucleus. Outputs such as TNF rose to levels matching the strongest known receptor pairings.
europmc-pmc2533029:
Than, Ruths, and Nakhleh presented a software package called PhyloNet in this 2008 paper. Biologists chart how species are related using family trees, but some history does not fit a tree: genes jump between species, and species hybridise. Such events make networks of relationships instead, and earlier tools for handling them were scattered.

PhyloNet gathers the needed tools in one suite. It reads and writes evolutionary networks in a compact format the authors devised, called eNewick. It can take networks apart into trees and clusters, compare two networks for how much they differ, and rebuild a network from a species tree plus gene trees. The authors argue the package makes network analysis practical on large data sets.
europmc-pmc2573929:
Hogan, Riordan, Gerber, Herschlag, and Brown surveyed in 2008 which RNAs are bound by 40 RNA-binding proteins in yeast. These proteins steer what happens to RNA messages after they are made, but most had never been studied systematically. The team pulled down each protein with its attached RNAs from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and identified the catch.

At least 33 of the 40 proteins held specific sets of RNAs. The sets ranged from a few to several hundred. Strikingly, each protein's targets tended to make proteins sharing a job or a location in the cell. For 16 proteins the authors found enriched sequence or shape motifs marking the targets. Seventy percent of all yeast messages bound at least one of the proteins tested, and each message averaged three protein partners, implying a rich regulatory web.
europmc-pmc2628729:
Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi deleted the worm's antioxidant defence genes in 2009 and got a result that defies the oxidative stress theory of ageing. That theory blames ageing on damage from reactive oxygen species, the byproducts of metabolism, which superoxide dismutase enzymes detoxify. Removing such enzymes shortens life in yeast, flies, and mice, so the team deleted each of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans's five sod genes expecting the same.

No deletion shortened lifespan, even in worms missing two or three sod genes, despite clear sensitivity to chemical oxidative stress. Deleting sod-2, the mitochondrial enzyme, actually extended life, even while oxidatively damaged proteins rose. The mutants breathed less oxygen and showed slow development like other long-lived mitochondrial mutants. The authors conclude sod-2 loss lengthens life by altering mitochondrial function.
europmc-pmc2646729:
Cookson reviewed in 2009 what is known about alpha-synuclein, a small protein tied to Parkinson disease and the death of brain cells. The protein collects in clumps called Lewy bodies inside the brains of patients. Faults in its gene cause a rare inherited form of the disease, and extra copies of the normal gene raise risk too.

The review gathers lab evidence on how this protein may kill nerve cells. Both the faulty forms and plain overload of the normal protein speed cell death in experiments. The cells lost include the dopamine-making cells of a deep brain region, the very cells whose loss drives Parkinson symptoms. Cookson weighs the proposed harm pathways, marks where proof is still thin, and asks what blocking this toxicity could mean for future treatment.
europmc-pmc2694429:
Mashima, Seimiya, and Tsuruo reviewed in 2009 the idea of starving cancers by blocking the fat-making machinery they depend on. Fast-growing tumor cells build their own fatty acids from scratch to supply membranes, fuel, and protein decoration. Most healthy adult tissues skip this work and simply take fats from food, keeping the machinery idled.

Two enzymes run the pathway. The first, ACC, converts a basic building block into malonyl-CoA. The second, FASN, stitches those units into long fatty acid chains. Cancer flips both on hard, and tumors lean on the flow for survival. That contrast, a busy pathway in tumors and a quiet one in normal tissue, is exactly what drug hunters want. The review surveys blockers of these enzymes and related steps, and weighs how selectively they might kill tumor cells.
europmc-pmc2704929:
Bochner reviewed in 2009 a global way to describe bacteria by how they grow, not just by their genes. Growth traits show if a microbe can use a food source or survive heat, salt, or poison. Such traits have long helped scientists tell bacterial species apart and test computer models of how a cell should act.

The review centers on Phenotype MicroArrays, plates that test hundreds of growth traits at once for one strain. Results can fill gaps in gene data, check model forecasts, and guide work in basic and applied microbiology, the study of tiny living things. Bochner frames this phenomics layer as the partner to gene, protein, and chemical data.
europmc-pmc2774229:
Ernst and co-authors dissected in 2009 how MprF, a bacterial membrane protein, defends Staphylococcus aureus against defensin-like antimicrobial peptides. MprF attaches the amino acid lysine to a membrane lipid, which lowers the cell's pull on these positively charged killers. It also matters for virulence and for resistance to the antibiotic daptomycin, making it a drug target, yet its inner workings were unclear.

They showed the protein splits into two separable domains. One domain makes the lysine-tagged lipid, needing only part of the protein plus a few conserved amino acids. The other domain flips that lipid to the membrane's outer face. Making the lipid alone gave little resistance. Only when both domains worked together, even as separate proteins, did full resistance and peptide repulsion appear. MprF is thus a two-part enzyme: maker and flipper.
europmc-pmc2788129:
Neyrolles and Quintana-Murci reviewed in 2009 the sexual inequality in tuberculosis, asking why case notifications run about twice as high in men as in women in most countries. Tuberculosis kills over one point seven million people a year. Barriers to care clearly hide some female cases, especially in developing countries, where women face more obstacles reaching clinics.

But they argue biology likely explains a significant part of the gap. Sex hormones, sex-linked genetic background, and metabolism all shape immunity, yet their roles in tuberculosis are barely studied. The male excess appears in nearly every region and adult age group, but not in children, a pattern that hints at biology rather than reporting alone. They call for research on hormones and sex-related genes in this disease. Answers would sharpen intervention strategies built for whole communities.
europmc-pmc2821929:
Maggini and colleagues showed in 2010 that mouse bone marrow stromal cells can flip activated macrophages into a calming, regulatory state. Macrophages are immune eater cells that normally pour out inflammatory signals when triggered. Stromal cells are already known to quiet immune responses, one reason they interest doctors as therapy.

Placed with triggered macrophages, stromal cells cut output of four inflammatory signals and raised a calming one, IL-10. A fat-like messenger the stromal cells release constantly, called PGE2, drove much of the effect, since aspirin blocked it. The flipped macrophages also ate dead cells better and presented far fewer flags to T cells. One downside stood out: they became far easier for a parasite to infect.
europmc-pmc2855329:
Ranganathan, Suthers, and Maranas introduced OptForce in 2010, a computational method that finds every genetic change needed to force a microbe to overproduce a chosen chemical. Earlier design tools leaned on stand-in goals like maximizing growth and ignored real measurements of the starting strain. OptForce instead classifies each reaction in a metabolic model by whether its flow must rise, fall, or stop to hit the production target, checking singles, pairs, triples, and beyond.

From that full map it extracts the smallest set of flows engineers must actively force through genetic edits. Demonstrated on succinate production in E. coli, the method recovered known winning strategies and surfaced non-obvious ones, coordinating changes in pathways far from the final production steps.
europmc-pmc2871929:
Phillips, Gassei, and Orwig reviewed in 2010 the stem cells that keep sperm production running for life. These spermatogonial stem cells sit in the testes and balance self-renewal with making cells that mature into sperm. Keeping that balance is what allows fertility to last for decades in males.

Transplanting the cells into sterile testes, growing them in dishes, and tracking their marker proteins are the main tools the field uses. Work with those tools has revealed the signals from surrounding support cells that tell stem cells when to copy themselves and when to advance. The authors close with future routes, from restoring fertility after childhood cancer treatment to preserving sperm production in valued farm and endangered animals.
europmc-pmc2882429:
MacPherson and the STRICTA Revision Group issued in 2010 an updated checklist for reporting acupuncture trials. The original standards, published in 2001 and 2002, helped readers judge and repeat trials by demanding full detail on the needling itself. Reviews since then showed real value and clear room to improve, so an expert panel of forty-seven people revised the draft by email and at a meeting in Freiburg.

The new checklist has six items covering the reasoning behind the treatment style, exact needling details, the treatment schedule, other care given, the practitioner's background, and the control treatment. It now stands as an official extension of the main trial reporting standard, CONSORT. Journals adopting it should make acupuncture evidence easier to trust and reuse.
europmc-pmc2893129:
Chou and Shen built in 2010 Plant-mPLoc, a predictor that guesses where in a plant cell a protein works. A protein's compartment hints strongly at its job, and knowing locations across a proteome maps how a cell organizes its labor. Earlier plant predictors covered only three or four sites and none could place multiplex proteins, those found at several sites at once.

Their predictor covers twelve locations, from chloroplast and mitochondrion to cell wall and nucleus. It fuses three evidence streams: the protein's gene ontology terms, its functional domain fingerprints, and its evolutionary profile, each compressed into a numeric signature. A top-down strategy settles broad placement before finer calls. Multiplex placement matters, the authors note, because proteins that shuttle between compartments often hold special regulatory roles.
europmc-pmc2904929:
Ooi and Liong reviewed in 2010 whether probiotics and prebiotics, live gut-friendly bacteria and the fibers that feed them, can lower blood cholesterol. Animal and human studies often reported drops in total and LDL cholesterol and blood fats, or rises in protective HDL cholesterol, after supplementation. Yet other studies found no meaningful change, so the claim remained disputed when they wrote.

The authors weigh the proposed mechanisms, including bacteria breaking down bile salts so the body burns cholesterol to replace them, and direct uptake of cholesterol by bacterial cells. Two gaps stand out: nobody knows the effective dose, and clinical proof is still thin. Safety also needs care, since rare bloodstream infections from probiotic strains have occurred, mostly in vulnerable patients.
europmc-pmc2909929:
Teede, Deeks, and Moran reviewed in 2010 polycystic ovary syndrome, a hormone state that affects as many as one in five women in their reproductive years. Its reach goes well past fertility: excess male-type hormones cause acne and hair growth, and insulin resistance raises diabetes and heart risk. Anxiety and low mood are also common. The mix shifts with life stage, ancestry, genes, and lifestyle.

Body weight interacts strongly with the state, since obesity-driven insulin resistance makes each feature worse. Close relatives also carry higher metabolic risk. Care must therefore span fertility, metabolic, and mental health across the lifespan, not stop at fertility treatment. The authors call for lifestyle therapy as the base, with drugs aimed at the feature that dominates for each woman.
europmc-pmc2916829:
Glaser and Meola demonstrated in 2010 that Wolbachia, a bacterium living inside insect cells, protects its native hosts against West Nile virus. Wolbachia had boosted virus resistance in transplanted hosts, but whether it defends the fruit flies and mosquitoes that carry it naturally was untested. The team compared infected and uninfected Drosophila flies and Culex mosquitoes, a real West Nile vector, against the virus.

Infected flies needed a five hundred times larger dose to become infected and carried one hundred thousand times less virus than clean flies. The protection passed through mothers as a cytoplasmic trait and vanished in flies cured with antibiotics. It barely extended to two unrelated viruses, suggesting real specificity. Culex mosquitoes also resisted better with Wolbachia aboard, keeping alive hopes of deploying the bacterium against mosquito-borne disease.
europmc-pmc2936529:
Hildebrand, Meyer, Eyre-Walker, and Nachman tested whether natural selection shapes the base makeup of bacterial genomes, in a study published in PLoS Genetics. Bacterial genomes differ hugely in how much of their DNA uses the bases G and C, a spread usually blamed on mutation habits.

Looking at silent DNA variants across well over a hundred species, they found changes eroding G and C far outnumbered changes building them up. Mutation bias alone would then imply most GC-rich species are steadily losing GC, which cannot hold. They conclude selection favours higher GC content in many bacteria.
europmc-pmc2940729:
Rask and co-authors reclassified the building blocks of PfEMP1, a highly varied surface protein of the malaria parasite, in a 2010 genome study. The protein anchors infected red blood cells to vessel walls, and antibodies against it help protect people in malaria regions.

Working through hundreds of PfEMP1 sequences from seven parasite genomes, they defined several new domain classes and found strong order in how domains combine. A new method picked out hundreds of small conserved blocks covering most of each sequence. Some domain subclasses proved to be hybrids, with a hotspot for swapping parts. Their VarDom server shares the catalogue.
europmc-pmc3036629:
Geva reviewed in 2011 how heart scans guide care for patients whose severe birth defect of the heart was repaired in childhood. The defect, called tetralogy of Fallot, leaves most repaired patients with a leaky lung valve. The leak overloads the right side of the heart with blood volume for years. The heart copes for a long time, but damage can become permanent if the valve is not replaced in time.

Magnetic resonance scanning has become the reference method for measuring heart size, function, and leak severity in these patients. The review explains the slow harm from chronic volume overload and weighs the gains and risks of valve replacement surgery. Scan measures help doctors pick the moment when surgery protects the heart without operating too early. The paper gathers the evidence clinicians use for that judgment.
europmc-pmc3046429:
Roth and coauthors tested in 2010 whether tiny regulatory RNAs floating in blood could flag breast cancer and its spread. These molecules, called microRNAs in full, help control gene activity and leak from tumors into the bloodstream. Blood was drawn from women with early breast cancer, women whose cancer had spread, and healthy women, and four cancer linked microRNAs were measured.

Total blood RNA and one microRNA separated early patients from healthy women clearly. Three microRNAs separated the spread group from healthy controls. Within patients, higher levels of several markers tracked with the presence of distant spread and with larger, later stage tumors. The authors call this a pilot study, the first of its kind for these markers. They propose blood microRNAs as a low burden way to detect progression that deserves larger trials.
europmc-pmc3078329:
Ahern and colleagues pinned down in 2010 which cells a gut inflammation signal must act on to cause bowel disease. The signal, called IL-23 in short, is tied by human genetics to inflammatory bowel disease, and blocking it calms gut inflammation in animal models. It was not known whether it works through T cells or through other immune cells. The team used T cells unable to sense the signal.

Without sensing in T cells, the intestine stayed healthy even though body wide inflammation could still occur. Sensing drove gut T cells to multiply, gather in the intestine, and turn into aggressive types that make two attack signals at once. It also held back the calming regulatory cells and their soothing output. Cells lacking the sensor divided poorly and failed to settle in the gut. The paper names T cells as the signal's key target in the bowel.
europmc-pmc3148429:
Jane Green and colleagues linked adult height to cancer in more than a million British women in a 2011 paper in The Lancet Oncology. Taller people had shown higher cancer rates in earlier studies, but whether the link varied by cancer type or lifestyle was unclear. Women were measured at entry and followed for roughly a decade.

Nearly a hundred thousand cancers appeared during follow-up. Total cancer risk rose steadily with each extra span of height. Risk rose for fifteen of the seventeen cancer sites studied, strongly for ten, including colon, breast, kidney, and blood cancers. The pattern barely changed with wealth or other personal traits, though it ran weaker in current smokers. Pooling with other studies found the same pattern across continents.
europmc-pmc3172229:
Rochelle Arvizo and colleagues showed how surface charge steers medical nanoparticles through the body in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Tiny engineered particles promise better cancer detection and drug delivery, but their travel behaviour was poorly mapped. The team made a matched family of gold particles differing only in surface coating: neutral, balanced-charge, negative, or positive, and injected them into mice by vein or belly.

Neutral and balanced particles circulated far longer than charged ones, whose blood levels fell quickly. The long travellers also entered tumours more, apparently by leaking passively through tumour vessels, while charged particles were cleared into organs sooner. The results give designers a simple rule: keep the surface uncharged to buy time and tumour access.
europmc-pmc3195729:
David Adams, Dorit Ron, and Patrick Kiely reviewed a versatile scaffolding protein in a 2011 paper in Cell Communication and Signaling. The protein folds into a seven-bladed propeller that grips many partners, letting it ferry proteins around the cell, anchor them in place, and stabilise their activity. It touches the protein-making machinery, surface receptors, and even nuclear proteins.

That reach makes it a crossroads for many signalling pathways. Chemical tags added after production steer where it sits and when it moves, fine-tuning its jobs. The review gathers its roles in development, cell migration, brain function, and daily rhythms, plus its appearances in disease. Few single proteins, the authors note, sit at so many control points at once.
europmc-pmc3225829:
Peter Ertl and Ansgar Schuffenhauer described a scoring method that predicts how hard a molecule is to synthesize, in this 2009 paper in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Drug discovery teams constantly rank candidate molecules, and a compound nobody can make is useless. Their score runs from one, easy to make, to ten, very difficult.

The method combines two parts. Fragment contributions, learned from a million real molecules in the PubChem database, capture the accumulated record of what chemists have actually made. A complexity penalty then accounts for awkward features such as large rings, unusual ring fusions, stereochemistry, and sheer size. Tested against the judgments of experienced medicinal chemists on forty molecules, the scores agreed very well. The authors offer the score for screening purchases, hit selection, and computer-designed molecules.
europmc-pmc3270029:
Li Liu and colleagues showed that tau pathology spreads between connected brain cells in living mice, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. In Alzheimer's disease, tau clumps begin in the entorhinal cortex and advance in a stereotyped pattern. The team engineered mice that produce pathological human tau only in that starting region, then watched where the pathology appeared over the animals' lives.

In young mice the human tau sat mainly in entorhinal cells and their axons. In old mice it filled neurons downstream along the known wiring, in the hippocampus and beyond. Those are exactly the regions Alzheimer's affects next. The tau now resembled mature tangles, while the axonal signal faded. The pattern supports spread across synapses along anatomical networks, rather than independent failure of each region, and the mouse models the disease's early march.
europmc-pmc3319429:
Lorenz and colleagues announced a major upgrade to a long running software package for predicting RNA shapes, in a 2011 paper. RNA molecules fold back on themselves, and that folded shape explains much of their behavior. For nearly twenty years, the ViennaRNA Package has let researchers compute likely shapes from measured energy values.

Version two rebuilds the underlying library and tools around an updated energy model and modern multi core computers. New features include tools for judging how two RNA molecules interact, summary shapes drawn from pairing probabilities, and scores that flag locally stable stretches. The programs accept common sequence file formats and run several calculations at once, yet keep the speed and compatibility users of earlier versions expected.
europmc-pmc3331829:
Sandberg and Ji reviewed why men run higher blood pressure than women for much of life, in a 2012 article. The gap appears across races, ethnic groups, and even species, from dogs and rats to chickens, which marks it as deeply biological. Both sex hormones and the sex chromosomes themselves seem to contribute.

The review moves through human population studies and animal experiments, including engineered models of high blood pressure in both sexes. It maps where knowledge is solid and where it thins out, especially on how chromosome differences act apart from hormones. Understanding these mechanisms, the authors argue, could lead to blood pressure drugs tailored to a patient's sex. Better tailoring would matter because high blood pressure drives strokes, heart failure, and kidney damage worldwide.
europmc-pmc3386629:
Eisenberg and co-authors reviewed in 2012 how herpesviruses fuse with and enter human cells. Every herpesvirus carries versions of the same three surface proteins, gB and the pair gH and gL. Extra helper proteins grab cell receptors or wake the core machinery, deciding which cells get infected.

Structural studies have largely sorted out what each part does. Protein gB does the actual merging, but only when gH and gL boost it, and in herpes simplex a fourth protein, gD, starts the chain by binding its receptor. The review lays out this stepwise model, mostly from the family's three prototype viruses. It also marks the steps still unexplained, giving entry research a shared map.
europmc-pmc3407129:
Massudi and co-authors measured aging chemistry in human skin in 2012, testing whether a repair process drains a vital molecule as years pass. The molecule NAD+ powers energy production and serves the DNA repair enzyme PARP. Skin samples came from patients aged from infancy to the late seventies.

DNA damage rose with age in both sexes, and fat oxidation rose with age in men. PARP activity climbed steeply with age in men while NAD+ levels fell, the two tracking each other closely. A related enzyme that depends on NAD+ also faded with age in men. The pattern backs the idea that overworked repair slowly starves aging tissue of NAD+.
europmc-pmc3419229:
Willing, Dreyer, and van Oosterhout asked in 2012 whether many genetic markers can make up for few sampled individuals when measuring how populations differ. The standard measure, FST, is widely used in ecology and evolution, and folklore held that large samples were essential for precision. Next-generation sequencing now supplies thousands of markers even for obscure species.

Simulating populations, the team tested three common estimators across sample sizes and marker counts. With a suitable estimator and more than a thousand markers, samples as small as four to six individuals gave sound estimates. Checking how markers were chosen mattered too, since selection bias can skew results. Conservation studies, they conclude, can now match the power once reserved for laboratory model species.
europmc-pmc3476529:
Haniffa and a large team identified a rare immune cell in human tissues that primes killer T cells, in a 2012 Immunity paper. Dendritic cells collect material from tissues and present it to T cells, a step that starts immune attacks on viruses and tumors. Mice have a champion presenting cell in their tissues, but no human match had been isolated.

The team found cells marked by high levels of a surface protein, CD141, in skin, liver, and lung. Those cells beat other tissue dendritic cells at the key presenting task. Their gene patterns matched the mouse champion closely, showing the cell types are conserved across species. Haniffa's findings help vaccine and therapy designers aim at the right cell in people.
europmc-pmc3574029:
Leif Jönsson, Björn Alriksson, and Nils-Olof Nilvebrant reviewed a bottleneck in biofuel making in Biotechnology for Biofuels in 2013. Turning plant matter, lignocellulose, into fuel starts with a hot acid treatment that frees the sugars for enzymes and microbes. That same treatment brews compounds that poison both steps, slowing sugar release and fermentation. Their review covers where the inhibitors come from and how producers clean them up.

Detox methods range from washing and treating the slurry to newer tricks described here. These include adding reducing chemicals inside the process itself, and breeding or adapting the enzymes and microbes to shrug the poisons off. Residues from farms, forests, and pulp mills could supply huge feedstock without taking food land, if the chemistry cooperates. The survey maps options for making plant-based fuels and chemicals at workable cost.
europmc-pmc3626529:
Ruibang Luo and a large team of collaborators released an improved genome assembler, SOAPdenovo2, in GigaScience in 2012. Assemblers stitch millions of short sequencing reads into a genome without a template. The original SOAPdenovo had assembled many published genomes, but it stumbled in repeat regions, drank memory, and left gaps. The successor redesigns the graph-building step to use roughly a third of the peak memory, resolves more repeats while building contigs, and lengthens and covers more in the scaffolding and gap-closing stages.

On the shared Assemblathon1 and GAGE benchmark sets, the new tool beat its predecessor clearly and matched rival assemblers on length and accuracy. As a showpiece, the team reassembled the first personal Asian genome, published in 2008: continuous pieces grew three fold, scaffolds fifty fold, and coverage rose from 81.16 to 93.91 percent. Large-genome projects on ordinary hardware are the intended winners.
europmc-pmc3689529:
Winter describes the decision making built into xia2, a program that automates X-ray crystallography data processing. Raw diffraction images must be indexed, integrated, and scaled before any structure can be solved, and each step involves choices that once demanded an expert watching the numbers.

Xia2 wraps established processing packages in a framework that makes those choices itself, following set protocols while logging why each route was taken, and it can also be driven interactively. Winter presents the design so that beamline users get expert-grade processing by default. The reasoning behind each automated decision stays open to inspection. That transparency matters when a structure later depends on choices made in the first minutes after data collection.
europmc-pmc3760829:
José Manjón and co-authors presented an image-cleaning method in PLoS ONE in 2013 for diffusion weighted imaging, a brain scan type that tracks water movement in tissue. Such images carry a low signal-to-noise ratio, and the noise skews the numbers researchers draw from them, such as fiber direction maps.

Their filter treats the multi-direction data as one set. In each small patch it keeps the strong principal components and shrinks the weak ones, using an overcomplete version of the analysis to catch fine structure. The team compared the method with leading alternatives on made-up and real clinical scans. It cleaned the images better and gave cleaner estimates of diffusion values. The authors argue the gain matters for automated processing, where noise can mislead.
europmc-pmc3793129:
Hao Du, Hongbo Liu, and Lizhong Xiong reported a rice study in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2013 on how stress changes two plant hormones. Drought, salt, and temperature extremes limit plant growth, and the stress hormone abscisic acid is well studied in the response. Whether the same stresses change other hormones, such as auxin and jasmonic acid, was largely unknown.

Measuring hormone levels and gene activity in rice, the team found that auxin, measured as IAA, fell after drought but rose under cold and heat. Cold also blocked auxin's effect on root bending. Jasmonic acid rose markedly under drought and cold but fell under heat, and the genes for making and sensing each hormone moved in matching directions. The authors conclude the two hormones play distinct roles in stress responses.
europmc-pmc3827429:
Josephine Y. Chau and a team of co-authors pool studies on sitting and death risk in PLoS One in 2013. Long daily sitting has been linked to poor health, but the shape of the risk was unclear. Their meta-analysis merges cohort studies that tracked adults over time.

Six studies fed the pool, with data on large adult groups from rich countries. Risk did not rise in a straight line with sitting hours. Modest sitting showed little added risk, while the highest sitting levels carried clear extra risk. Staying active softened but did not erase the link. The findings support cutting very long sitting time, even for people who exercise, though the exact safe limit needs more work.
europmc-pmc3916729:
Richard L. Doty and Vidyulata Kamath review how aging affects the sense of smell in Frontiers in Psychology in 2014. Smell loss is very common late in life, present in over half of people aged 65 to 80 and in more than three quarters of those over 80. It shapes nutrition, enjoyment of food, quality of life, and safety at home.

The review lists many causes: nasal changes, repeated damage to the smell-sensing tissue from viruses and the environment, bone growth closing small skull openings, and shifts in brain chemicals. Smell loss can also be an early sign of Alzheimer's disease or Parkinson's disease. The authors survey the anatomy of the aging smell system and how doctors test it in the clinic.
europmc-pmc3928029:
Julian H. Elliott and colleagues argue in PLoS Medicine in 2014 that systematic reviews of medical evidence should be kept alive rather than published once and left to age. A review can go stale fast as new trials appear, and stale reviews mislead doctors and policymakers. Small improvements to the usual updating process, the authors say, will not fix that currency problem.

Their proposal, the living systematic review, is a high-quality online summary that is revised as soon as new research arrives. It depends on faster production methods and on shared standards for publishing updates. Paired with better reporting of new trials and better use of evidence in health systems, living reviews aim to narrow the gap between what research shows and what care actually does.
europmc-pmc3933429:
Anda R. Gliga, Sara Skoglund, Inger Odnevall Wallinder, Bengt Fadeel, and Hanna L. Karlsson probe how the size of silver nanoparticles affects human lung cells, in Particle and Fibre Toxicology in 2014. Silver nanoparticles are among the most manufactured nanomaterials, yet published toxicity results vary wildly, often because the particles were poorly described. This study characterized its particles carefully before exposing lung cells grown in the lab.

Particles of 10, 40, and 75 nanometers with a citrate coating were tested, plus coated and uncoated variants. Only the smallest, 10-nanometer particles killed cells, regardless of coating. All particles raised overall DNA damage in a comet test, but without the breaks marked by a standard damage signal and without raising reactive oxygen. Uptake patterns did not explain the small particles' extra harm.
europmc-pmc3967529:
Reza Bavarsad Shahripour and two colleagues review N-acetylcysteine for brain disorders. Their paper appeared in Brain and Behavior in 2014. The compound is best known as an antidote. It treats overdose of the pain drug paracetamol. It also feeds the making of glutathione, a key antioxidant. It touches glutamate signaling as well. Growth-factor paths and inflammation feel its effects too.

Most proof so far comes from animal models. Few human studies in neurology are complete. The authors work through candidate uses one by one. Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease appear. So do multiple sclerosis and ALS. Inherited ataxias and some movement disorders join the list. The review closes with recovery after brain trauma. Stroke recovery gets a look as well. The tone stays careful: promise is not proof.
europmc-pmc4036129:
Daniela Bellincampi, Felice Cervone, and Vincenzo Lionetti review the plant cell wall as a battleground in infection, in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. Every attacker, be it fungus, bacterium, or worm, must breach the wall to feed on the plant. How much of the wall it breaks depends on its way of life.

Fungi that kill cells wreck the wall widely with cutting enzymes. Fungi that keep host cells alive cut in a tight, local way and feed through special structures. Plants sense both microbe traits and wall damage itself, then rebuild and toughen the wall in answer. Attackers can also bend the plant's wall system to ease their own entry, turning host tools into weak points. The review sets out the moves on both sides, from wall sensing to wall remodelling.
europmc-pmc4061029:
Romeo Cecchelli and colleagues described a lab model of the human blood-brain barrier built from blood-forming stem cells. Their method appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. The real barrier uses brain vessel cells to protect the central nervous system while letting needed substances through, and drug research needs faithful human models of it.

Starting from cord blood stem cells, the team first made vessel-lining cells. Growing them with pericytes, support cells from brain vessels, then gave them barrier traits such as tight junctions and transport proteins. The model kept most of these traits for at least twenty days and could be remade from different donors in different labs. It may help predict how compounds reach the human brain.
europmc-pmc4071229:
David C. Mohr, Stephen M. Schueller, Enid Montague, Michelle Nicole Burns, and Parisa Rashidi proposed a model for designing health programs delivered through phones, the web, and sensors. Their framework paper appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2014. Such behavioural intervention technologies lacked shared models to guide their design.

Their BIT model spells out both the clinical logic and the technical build of a program. Designers must state why it exists, what elements it contains, how it changes behaviour in concept and in code, and when each part reaches the user. Strategies such as education, goal setting, and monitoring become concrete features with set traits and workflow. The model extends earlier frameworks with finer detail.
europmc-pmc4104929:
Paul M. Lehrer and Richard Gevirtz reviewed how heart rate variability biofeedback might work. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Psychology in 2014. Training people to breathe in rhythm with feedback from their own heart signal has support as a treatment for varied conditions, from asthma to depression, and for performance gains.

The best-supported explanation is that the training strengthens the baroreflex, the blood pressure control loop, improving the body's self-balancing. Breathing near a personal resonance frequency makes heart and pressure waves reinforce each other. A newer proposal adds stimulation of the vagal pathway running from the body up to frontal brain areas. The authors weigh these and other candidate mechanisms, treating a stronger baroreflex as a marker of healthier autonomic balance.
europmc-pmc4181929:
Paula I. Johnson, Tracey J. Woodruff, and seven co-authors applied a new review method to a chemical called PFOA in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. PFOA was used in non-stick and stain-resistant goods and builds up in human blood. The question was whether exposure before birth slows fetal growth.

Following the Navigation Guide steps, the team found 18 human studies and pooled nine of them. Each added unit of PFOA in a mother's blood went with birth weight lower by about 19 grams. Bias risk across the studies was rated low, and the body of evidence earned a moderate quality grade. On that basis the authors judged the human evidence sufficient to say that developmental PFOA exposure reduces fetal growth. It was the method's first full test case.
europmc-pmc4196729:
Karel G. M. Moons, Gary S. Collins, and six co-authors wrote a checklist for reviewing prediction model studies in PLoS Medicine in 2014. Doctors use risk models to forecast who will get a disease or how a patient will fare. Studies of such models multiply fast, and reviewers lacked a shared way to judge them.

Their checklist, called CHARMS, starts with seven items for framing a sharp review question: who the model is for, what it predicts, and when. It then lists eleven domains for pulling data from each study and probing its weak points, from how participants were chosen to how missing data were handled. The items were drawn from existing reporting guides and methods work. The authors intend the list to raise the quality of evidence summaries behind clinical risk tools.
europmc-pmc4298229:
Oleg Varlamov, Cynthia L Bethea, and Charles T Roberts review how males and females handle fats and sugars differently. Their minireview appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology in 2014. Female metabolism is shaped by the demands of pregnancy and nursing, while male metabolism follows a different default, and sex hormones drive much of the contrast.

Women tend to store more fat and respond more strongly to insulin across the whole body, while men burn more fat as fuel. Patterns shift with the menstrual cycle, food intake, and exercise load. The review gathers the mechanisms behind these differences, since ignoring sex in metabolism research can blur results for both groups.
europmc-pmc4303229:
Hatem A Azim and Ann H Partridge review breast cancer that strikes women at a young age. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2014. Such cases are uncommon in rich countries, yet they tend to run a harsher course than the same disease in older women, with worse outcomes.

Young patients' tumors differ in hormone receptors, HER2 status, and growth markers, and inherited risk genes are more common among them. The breast tissue itself differs at young ages, and pregnancy and breastfeeding leave changes that may shape later tumors. Treatment still follows the same plans as for older women, and the authors argue the biology deserves study of its own to sharpen prognosis and care.
europmc-pmc4306929:
Moacir Fernandes Queiroz and five co-authors tested whether chitosan, a shellfish derived material used in medicine, could help form kidney stones. Their study appeared in Marine Drugs in 2014. Chitosan gathers in kidney tissue and raises calcium output in urine, both reasons to check its effect on calcium oxalate crystals, the main stuff of kidney stones.

In lab tests the commercial chitosan showed little antioxidant power but bound copper strongly. More to the point, it encouraged formation of the monohydrate form of calcium oxalate, the type most common in stone patients, and changed the crystals' size and shape. The findings advise caution in how freely chitosan supplements are used.
europmc-pmc4315529:
Ronald Boellaard and eleven co-authors issue version 2.0 of the European guidelines for FDG PET/CT tumor imaging. Their guideline paper appeared in the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging in 2015. PET scanning measures tissue activity in numbers, so numbers must mean the same thing at every site if they are to guide care or trials.

The document sets shared procedures for recommending, performing, reading, and reporting these scans in adults with cancer. It stresses quality control so that a value measured twice in one patient, or at two hospitals, stays comparable within known limits. Multicenter trials and treatment response checks both depend on that consistency. The update reflects newer scanners and accumulated practice since the first version.
europmc-pmc4319729:
Chad A. Lerner and eight co-authors tested flavored e-cigarette vapors on lung cells and on mouse lungs. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Use of electronic cigarettes and flavored juices was climbing fast, while the harm those aerosols might do to airways had barely been studied.

The vapor carried oxidant reactivity, traced to the heating element and stronger with some flavors; unvaporized juices also showed oxidative power tied to their flavor additives. Lung epithelial cells exposed to the aerosols suffered cell damage, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signals, and mouse lungs showed the same pattern. The work treats flavorings as active ingredients in the health question, not as harmless extras.
europmc-pmc4326529:
Doori Park and eleven co-authors report the first whole genome sequence of the Asian honey bee, Apis cerana. Their study appeared in BMC Genomics in 2015. The western honey bee's genome was already known and served as the model, but the Asian species has been kept by beekeepers for thousands of years and differs in many traits.

The draft genome spans about two hundred and thirty eight million bases and holds over ten thousand genes. Comparing the two bees highlighted genes unique to the Asian species, tied to its divergent biology and its role in the ecology of eastern and southern Asia. The sequence gives researchers a base for studying disease resistance, behavior, and breeding in this economically important bee.
europmc-pmc4365529:
Thomas Jacobs, Peter LaFayette, Robert Schmitz, and Wayne Parrott showed that the CRISPR/Cas9 editing system works in soybean, in BMC Biotechnology in 2015. CRISPR/Cas9 can cut DNA at chosen spots to make targeted changes in living things. The team aimed it at a glowing marker gene and at nine of the plant's own gene sites, in hairy-root cultures and in embryo cultures that can grow into full plants.

Targeted mutations appeared in 95 percent of the 88 hairy-root events checked. Small deletions were the most common change, with single-letter swaps and short insertions also seen. Related gene copies could be hit one at a time or together, which matters in soybean's duplicated genome. Changes in embryo cultures grew more common over time, opening a path to plants that pass edits to their offspring.
europmc-pmc4380029:
David Jones and Domenico Cozzetto presented DISOPRED3, a program that predicts floppy regions in proteins, in Bioinformatics in 2015. Many proteins contain stretches that never fold into a fixed shape, called intrinsically disordered regions. These stretches do real work, often by binding other proteins while staying flexible. Earlier predictors found them fairly well; the open task was saying what they do. DISOPRED3 extends the group's prior tool with modules for both tasks.

Tests place DISOPRED3 at the top of its field for spotting disordered regions, with gains in precision and in catching regions longer than 20 amino acids. A new classifier then marks which disordered stretches are likely to bind proteins, using sequence profiles and related features. Careful cross-checked tests show the binding calls are precise. The tool is free online for other researchers.
europmc-pmc4381529:
Stefan Schoenfelder and a large team mapped long-range gene control in stem cells, in Genome Research in 2015. The genome holds up to a million regulatory elements, many sitting far from the genes they control. They act by physically looping to gene promoters, but linking each element to its gene genome-wide was blocked by blurry methods. The team enriched interaction maps for more than 22,000 mouse promoters, in embryonic stem cells and fetal liver cells, to pin contacts at fine resolution.

Distal sites touching active genes carried active marks and bound control proteins, while inactive genes touched sites with repressive marks. Genes regulated together clustered in three-dimensional networks more than chance allows, matching their function and activity. The strongest clustering joined genes for transcription factors that steer early development. The catalog gives a first genome-wide wiring diagram for these cells.
europmc-pmc4383229:
Dmitry Andreev and co-authors studied how stressed cells keep making select proteins, in eLife in 2015. Under stress, cells shut down most protein synthesis by disabling a key starter factor, eIF2, which saves energy. Yet some messages must still be read to mount a defense. Using ribosome profiling in human cells stressed with arsenite, the team found overall translation fell more than fivefold, while certain messages resisted the shutdown.

Nearly all resistant messages carried at least one small upstream reading frame in their leader region, which normally holds the main gene back. Changing a single such frame in two test genes was enough to give the stress pattern, proving the mechanism in those cases. Family-tree analysis suggests some of these small frames even make working mini-proteins. Leaders, long treated as spacers, emerge as control panels.
europmc-pmc4417329:
Bruce Guthrie, Boikanyo Makubate, Virginia Hernandez-Santiago, and Tobias Dreischulte charted the rise of polypharmacy in Scotland, in BMC Medicine in 2015. Taking many drugs at once raises the risk of harmful interactions, and prescribing had climbed for years. The team analyzed dispensing records for all 310,000 adults in the Tayside region in 1995 and again in 2010, counting drug classes and potentially serious drug-drug interactions in the prior 84 days.

The share of adults dispensed five or more drugs doubled, to 20.8 percent, and the share on ten or more tripled, to 5.8 percent. Heavy use rose steeply with age and was also more common in deprived areas and care homes. Potentially serious interactions more than doubled, reaching 13 percent of adults in 2010. Drug count itself was the chief driver of interaction risk.
europmc-pmc4558529:
Bram Piersma, Ruud A. Bank, and Miriam Boersema review the signal pathways that drive fibrosis, in Frontiers in Medicine in 2015. Fibrosis is scarring inside organs: after chronic injury, cells called myofibroblasts pour out matrix until the organ stiffens and fails. Any cure needs to know which signals switch those cells on and keep them on.

Three pathways take center stage. TGF-β activates the SMAD complex, WNT frees β-catenin to enter the nucleus, and YAP/TAZ, from the Hippo pathway, also act by moving into the nucleus. The systems look nothing alike chemically, yet they converge on the same trick: shifting their messengers between cell body and nucleus. The review maps their overlaps as drug targets.
europmc-pmc4569729:
Xin Jing leads a ten-author team testing how variety above and below ground powers ecosystems, on China's Tibetan Plateau, in Nature Communications in 2015. Plant diversity often tracks with how well ecosystems work, but soil life below ground is usually left out of the account. The team measured both together, along with climate, across plateau grassland.

Combined factors explained up to 86% of the variation in multifunctionality, a bundle score of many ecosystem jobs at once. Above- and belowground biodiversity together accounted for 45% of that variation, more than either alone. Climate steered the strength of the biodiversity effect. The message for a warming world: soil diversity counts, and climate sets the terms.
europmc-pmc4585829:
Chelsea M. Rochman leads a nine-author team finding human-made debris in market seafood, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Plastic and textile fibers now litter the oceans and hundreds of wild species carry them. Whether the seafood people buy carries the same load was untested. The team bought fish and shellfish at markets in Makassar, Indonesia, and in California.

Debris was dissolved out of fish guts and whole shellfish and counted under a microscope. In Indonesia, 28% of individual fish and 55% of species carried debris; in the United States, 25% of fish and 67% of species did. A third of shellfish carried it too. Indonesian fish held only plastic, while American fish held mostly fibers.
europmc-pmc4598729:
In 2015, Zhong Wei and colleagues published a study on how root germ networks decide if a plant pathogen can invade. Diverse germ groups often resist invasion, but the cause was unclear. Their test pathogen was Ralstonia solanacearum, which wilts tomato plants. The work used lab microcosms and greenhouse tomato trials.

Networks built on rivalry for food predicted invasion success better than simple species counts. Groups with stable network shapes, and strong overlap with the food needs of the pathogen, blocked its growth. Plants with those groups stayed healthier. The results suggest that the protective power of a soil group can be judged from its food rivalry network, not just from how many species it holds.
europmc-pmc4718929:
A. L. Durham and I. M. Adcock reviewed the relationship between COPD and lung cancer in Lung Cancer in 2015.
