The two diseases share smoking as a cause, but the authors argue the link runs deeper than the shared habit. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease itself raises lung cancer risk beyond what smoking history explains. Both diseases are progressive, both worsen with age, and both concentrate in the same patients, which makes their overlap a major burden.

Shared engines fill the review: oxidative stress damaging tissue, cells aging early with shortened telomeres, inherited susceptibility, and scrambled chemical control of genes. The same exposures drive both, yet the damaged, inflamed lung of COPD seems to offer cancer fertile ground. Understanding the overlap matters for screening, since COPD patients are exactly the group where catching lung cancer early could pay most. The review assembles the mechanistic threads into one picture for clinicians and researchers.
europmc-pmc4743929:
Betrán, Ye, Moller, and four co-workers track how often births take place by caesarean section round the world. The surgery saves lives when birth goes wrong. But rates far past need add risk and cost with no clear gain. The team pull national data from 150 lands for the years 1990 to 2014.

By the last count, 18.6 percent of all births are by caesarean. Latin America and the Caribbean top the list at 40.5 percent. Africa is lowest at 7.3 percent. The world rate rose from 6.7 percent in 1990 to 19.1 percent in 2014. The team urge plans that curb overuse where rates are high and widen access where they are too low.
europmc-pmc4799429:
Nancy P. Gordon and four co-authors study the digital divide among older patients in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2016. Health plans push patients toward online portals for results, messages, and refills. Yet seniors, above all black and Latino seniors, use the internet less, and the team asked whether portal gaps reflect access, skill, or preference.

They paired plan records for over two hundred thousand members aged 65 to 79 with a mailed survey of a sampled group. Older bands registered and used the portal less than the youngest band. White and Chinese seniors led in registration, with black, Latino, and Filipino seniors behind at every age. Lack of access or of internet skill explained much, but not all, of the gap, and many non-users voiced interest if given support.
europmc-pmc4834629:
Lynne Turnbull leads a team of many co-authors in Nature Communications in 2016 showing that some bacteria build their biofilms by blowing up. Bacteria shed membrane vesicles, bubbles of their outer skin, and biofilms are laced with them plus loose DNA, yet where those parts came from was murky. Filming a Pseudomonas biofilm at fine scale caught the answer: a share of cells burst explosively.

The shattered skin fragments curl at once into vesicles, and the cell's insides, DNA included, spill into the shared matrix. A dormant virus gene inside the bacteria makes the bursting enzyme; mutants without it burst less, made fewer vesicles, and built poorer biofilms. Explosive lysis, the authors conclude, is a main supply line for the biofilm's shared goods.
europmc-pmc4862129:
Nadja B. Kristensen and co-authors reviewed trials of probiotic supplements in healthy adults in Genome Medicine in 2016, asking whether they truly change stool microbe makeup. Probiotics are live bacteria sold for gut health. The review gathered randomized trials that used modern DNA methods to track fecal microbes before and after dosing.

Across trials, clear shifts in the whole community were weak or absent in healthy adults. Dose, length of use, and delivery form varied widely, which blurs any pooled verdict. The review sets out what proof would settle the question. For now, claims that probiotics reshape a healthy gut rest on thin ground, whatever they may do in illness.
europmc-pmc4868329:
Gemma Vilagut and co-authors pooled studies in 2016 on how well a common mood questionnaire, the CES-D, screens for depression in the general public. Clinics need a cheap first pass to catch hidden depression. The review gathered validation studies from community and primary care samples where scores were checked against full diagnostic interviews, the gold standard.

Pooled results give hit and miss rates at several score cutoffs, plus an overall accuracy curve. Study quality and mixed results across settings get close review. At common cutoffs the scale catches most true cases while flagging some healthy people. The numbers help clinics pick a cutoff that fits their time and follow-up capacity.
europmc-pmc4876429:
Amy L. Whitehead and co-authors tackled pilot trial sizing in 2016: how large a pilot must be to keep a whole trial program small. Trials need a sound guess of outcome spread, and pilots supply it. But small pilots guess spread poorly, which can bloat or shrink the main trial. The team sought the pilot size that trims the combined total of pilot plus main trial.

Their method gives a best pilot size when the target effect for the main trial is known, for a continuous outcome. When the effect is unsure, tables guide a safe choice. Right-sizing the pilot saves recruits overall, a real gain when patients are scarce and each slot costs money and time.
europmc-pmc4892929:
Joseph G. Allen and co-authors tested 51 flavored e-cigarette products in 2016 for three flavor chemicals of concern. Over 7,000 flavors were on sale. One chemical, diacetyl, gained fame in the early 2000s when breathing it in factories caused a lung disease dubbed popcorn lung. The team picked flavors likely to appeal to youth, drained each product, and measured the captured vapor.

At least one target chemical appeared in 47 of 51 flavors. Diacetyl showed above lab detection in most of those, often with its cousins 2,3-pentanedione and acetoin beside it. Sweet flavors carried hidden lung risks, the data warn. Labels that list taste but not chemicals leave users blind to what they inhale.
europmc-pmc4994029:
Agua Sobrino and nine co-authors grow vascularized microtumors in a chip as a test bed for cancer drugs. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. Organ-on-chip systems aim to copy human tissue in miniature. Their tumor-on-chip grows human tumor and stromal cells in a three dimensional matrix, fed by living, perfused microvessels that form inside the device. Colorectal and breast cancer cells grew vigorously in the system and answered standard therapies with slowed growth or regression.

Vessel targeting drugs could be told apart by mechanism. Drugs hitting only VEGF receptors failed, while broader drugs that also hit PDGF receptors and Tie2 collapsed the vessels. Imaging showed strong metabolic variety inside the tumors, much like real cancers. The authors argue perfused microtumors give drug developers a human, vessel bearing model that flat cell cultures cannot match.
europmc-pmc5011129:
Martin Ingelsson reviews the toxic forms of alpha-synuclein in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2016, writing as sole author. Alpha-synuclein is a small protein that normally helps nerve cells release their chemical signals. In Parkinson's disease and related Lewy body disorders, it clumps inside cells, and those clumps mark the diseased brain at autopsy.

The review argues that the harm comes less from the large deposits than from smaller clumps, called oligomers, formed on the way there. These clumps can block protein cleanup, strain the cell's power units and other parts, disturb synapses, and pass between cells, seeding new clumps in connected brain areas. That picture makes the small clumps a prime drug target. Ingelsson gives special weight to antibody treatments designed to clear them early, before damage spreads through the brain.
europmc-pmc5015229:
Carol Cancelliere and six co-authors gather the best proof on return to work after injury or illness, in Chiropractic & Manual Therapies in 2016. Time off work carries heavy costs for the worker, the employer, and the health system, so knowing what helps or blocks a return matters. The team searched major databases and kept only systematic reviews judged at low risk of bias.

Fifty-six reviews passed, more than half on muscle and bone disorders, above all neck and back pain. Some factors helped across nearly all conditions: more schooling, higher income, strong self-belief, and hopeful views of recovery. Others hurt: older age, worse pain or disability, depression, heavy physical demands, and past sick leave. Care that joined the workplace and several kinds of support also raised success. The authors turn these shared lessons into updated principles for employers and clinicians.
europmc-pmc5045529:
Richard Strasser reviews protein glycosylation in plants in Glycobiology in 2016, writing as sole author. Glycosylation attaches sugar chains to proteins, and for proteins entering the cell's export pathway it is the most common finishing change of all. The early building steps are shared across plants, mammals, and yeast. What plants do with the chains later, in the Golgi apparatus, sets them apart.

Plant sugar chains end with marks animals lack, including a xylose and a fucose in set positions and Lewis A structures, and they never reach animal levels of branching. The review gives weight to the quality control system in the endoplasmic reticulum, where sugar tags decide whether a protein folds, ships, or is destroyed. Evidence from Arabidopsis and rice ties the mature plant patterns to sound growth under stress. Open gaps include full sugar maps for separate organs and species.
europmc-pmc5177329:
V. B. Green-Armytage described an operation for inoperable womb cancer in The Indian Medical Gazette in July 1913. Green-Armytage, resident surgeon at the Eden Hospital in Calcutta, notes a hard fact. Very few Indian patients arrive while cervical cancer can still be cut out. So most care is palliative: scraping and burning the growth, with rising drug doses for pain.

Following Charles Ryall of the London Cancer Hospital, he reports tying the internal iliac and ovarian arteries to starve the growth of blood, combined with curettage and cautery. Nine cases were done in eighteen months by three surgeons at the hospital. The operation was reserved for women in fair general condition where pain or bleeding was severe; weaker patients received the scraping and cautery alone.
europmc-pmc5385629:
Wenjun Ding and his co-authors use computer physics to predict a new family of ultra-thin materials in a 2017 Nature Communications paper. The materials are built from indium selenide and like compounds, in sheets one layer thick. The team looked for a trait called ferroelectricity, a lasting electric charge split that can be flipped, which is prized for memory chips and sensors.

Their sums say these sheets keep that trait at room heat, with the split running both across and along the sheet. Pairing one sheet with graphene gave a contact whose barrier could be tuned. Pairing it with another sheet shrank the energy gap of the pair. The authors say this widens the design choices for tiny devices.
europmc-pmc5403029:
Fuqiang Cui and eleven co-authors report on China's fight against hepatitis B in a paper in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Hepatitis B can settle into a chronic infection that leads to liver scarring and cancer. China once carried a huge share of the world's cases, with about one in ten people showing the virus marker in early surveys. The report weighs three national blood surveys against three decades of rising vaccine policy.

The marker rate fell by about half between the 1992 survey, taken before the modern vaccine era, and a 2014 survey. Among children under five, the fall was near total. Free infant shots and steps to block spread from mother to child drove the gain. The authors warn the work must hold for decades, with stronger steps to end spread.
europmc-pmc5422929:
Edwards and co-authors rethink how DNA methylation patterns are shaped and kept. Their review appeared in Epigenetics and Chromatin. Old views of methylation formed when the genome was poorly known. Whole-genome profiling now gives a sharper picture. Methyl marks sit on CpG sites across the genome. Most compartments carry dense marks. Promoter-linked CpG islands form the main bare zone.

The authors sort methylation levels by genome compartment. Repeat-derived sequences prove heavily methylated. Many marks that shift in germ cells sit in non-regulatory DNA. That finding questions their purpose. The review then explains how cells copy marks with high fidelity. It asks what cues send marks to be added or removed in early embryos. It closes with human disorders caused by faults in methyltransferase genes. Each disorder differs sharply from the others. The piece updates a classic topic with modern genome data.
europmc-pmc5433529:
Thursby and Juge introduce the human gut microbiota, the microbe community of the digestive tract. Their review surveyed what sequencing has revealed. Culture methods once missed most gut species. In one early study, 76 percent of sequences were novel. Gene catalogs now list 2,172 species isolated from humans. They fall into 12 phyla. Four phyla hold 93.5 percent of them. A combined catalog counts nearly 9.9 million microbial genes.

Colonization begins at birth, the authors explain. Delivery mode shapes the first community. Vaginal birth seeds many lactobacilli early. Cesarean birth delays Bacteroides colonization instead. Early life brings low diversity. Two phyla dominate the infant gut. Diversity climbs through the first year. By about age two and a half, the profile looks adult-like. Diet and environment leave country-level signatures. Different species mixes can still share functions. That redundancy matters for therapy design.
europmc-pmc5440529:
Mu and co-authors argue that a leaky gut lining can act as a danger signal for autoimmune disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. One layer of cells seals the gut from its contents. Tight junction proteins link those cells. Mucus and immune factors back them up. When the seal fails, toxins and bacteria slip into the blood. In people with the wrong genes, that leak may spark autoimmunity.

The review links leakiness to several diseases. They include celiac disease, type 1 diabetes, and lupus. Diet, alcohol, and disturbed gut microbes can all loosen the seal. Gut microbes also help maintain the barrier. Probiotics have reversed leakiness in some studies. They boosted tight junction protein output. Antibiotics helped in other cases by clearing harmful bacteria. The authors propose tuning gut microbes as therapy. Longer studies are still needed to prove the route.
europmc-pmc5467329:
Bolha, Ravnik-Glavač, and Glavač review long noncoding RNAs as markers for detecting and forecasting cancer. Their review appeared in Disease Markers. These RNAs do not code for proteins. They still regulate key cell processes. They help control gene activity, transport inside cells, and chromosome shape. When their levels go wrong, cancer can develop and progress. That link makes them promising signs of disease.

The review focuses on markers found in body fluids. Tumor tissue biopsies are the classic test, but they are invasive. RNAs circulating in blood and other fluids can be sampled far more gently. The authors survey studies that measured these RNAs in cancer patients. They weigh how well the profiles separate patients from healthy people. They also weigh links to patient outcomes. The authors see strong potential for routine clinical use once the tests are standardized.
europmc-pmc5476429:
Xu and co-authors present a methods paper in eLife on 3D imaging with electron microscopes. Their system, FIB-SEM, shaves thin layers from a sample and scans each new surface. It gives sharp depth detail, but slow speed and weak stability limited its volume. The team set out to make it faster and far more reliable.

Their upgrades let the system run for months without stopping. It can now image volumes large enough for mapping brain wiring. Example data cover mammal nerve tissue, a fruit fly brain, and a single-celled alga. Fine nerve fibers are easier to trace in such data. The authors say proofreading work should also speed up.
europmc-pmc5487729:
Yin and co-authors report a resistance gene discovery in mBio. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic against tough Gram-negative infections. Mobile resistance genes called mcr-1 and mcr-2 already alarmed health officials. Surveillance of farm animals in Shandong, China found a pig E. coli strain resisting colistin. It carried neither known gene, yet passed resistance onward.

A third mobile gene, mcr-3, explains the trait, they report. It rode a 261-kilobase plasmid packed with 18 other resistance genes. Similar elements turned up in isolates from Malaysia, Thailand, and the United States. Aeromonas species may serve as its hidden reservoir, they warn.
europmc-pmc5489929:
Bulbake and co-authors present an updated review in Pharmaceutics on liposomal drug products in clinical use. Liposomes are tiny spheres of fat-like membrane that carry drugs inside. Wrapping a drug in them changes where it travels in the body. That shift can raise benefit and cut side effects. Liposomes were the first nano delivery system to reach patients.

The review details the platform methods behind approved products. Stealth coatings and DepoFoam slow-release systems both feature. Marketed items such as Doxil and Ambisome are described in turn. Cancer drugs dominate the list, with fungal drugs and vaccines also covered. Ongoing clinical trials close the survey.
europmc-pmc5492929:
Gordon and Plüddemann present a review in BMC Biology on tissue macrophages. Macrophages live in nearly all tissues of vertebrate animals. They clear dead cells and microbes and help repair tissue. Far from being one uniform cell type, they vary by the organ they inhabit. The authors describe that variety and its organ-specific jobs.

Some macrophages arrive before birth and maintain themselves for life. Others stream in from blood monocytes after injury or infection. Each tissue shapes its resident cells with distinct receptors and tasks. The review treats the whole network as a dispersed organ system. Tumor growth and chronic inflammation show its dark side too.
europmc-pmc5506029:
Cabral and co-authors report a brain imaging study in Scientific Reports. At rest, the brain drifts through shifting patterns of network activity. Whether that drift relates to thinking skills was unclear. The team scanned 98 healthy older adults at rest. The volunteers came from a cohort of over 1,000 people with full cognitive testing. Best and worst performers were compared.

A new method tracked the dominant connectivity pattern moment by moment. Poorer performers showed weaker pattern stability over time, they report. Their brains also switched between states in altered ways. The findings tie resting brain dynamics to mental fitness in later life. Rest activity may thus support sharp cognition.
europmc-pmc5515629:
Kosiborod and the CVD-REAL investigators report a six-country outcomes study in Circulation on diabetes drugs called SGLT-2 inhibitors. One earlier trial found a drug of this class cut heart failure admissions and deaths. Whether the benefit covers the whole class in everyday care was unknown. The team matched over 300,000 new users against patients starting other diabetes drugs.

Starting an SGLT-2 inhibitor came with 39 percent fewer heart failure admissions, they report. Deaths ran 51 percent lower than with other drugs. The combined endpoint fell 46 percent. Results held across all six countries and all three drugs. Most patients had no heart disease at entry.
europmc-pmc5533829:
Wood and Goulson present a review in Environmental Science and Pollution Research on the environmental risks of neonicotinoid pesticides. These chemicals are the world's most used insecticides. Most applications coat seeds before planting. Crops absorb only about 5 percent of the dose. The rest disperses into soil, water, and wild plants. Bee harm findings led the European Union to a partial ban in 2013.

Evidence since then widens the concern, they report. Persistent low doses harm many free-living species, not just bees. Aquatic insects, birds, and soil life all show effects. The review gathers the post-ban literature for regulators weighing the moratorium.
europmc-pmc5551129:
Rappazzo, Coffman, and Hines present a systematic review on chemicals called PFAS. These substances make products resist stains and sticking. They persist in the body and in nature. The authors ask what exposure before birth or in childhood does to child health.

The team found 64 studies and rated their risk of bias as low to moderate. Health outcomes fell into six groups, from immunity to thyroid and kidney function. Evidence links PFAS to blood fat problems, weaker vaccine response, and asthma. Links also appear for kidney function and age at first period. Few studies treat PFAS as the mixtures they are. Readers get a careful summary of a still thin field.
europmc-pmc5626029:
Gomes and co-authors study a risky drug pairing in PLoS Medicine. Gabapentin and opioids are both prescribed for pain. They often land in the same medicine cabinet. Each can slow breathing on its own.

The team used Ontario health records spanning 1997 to 2013. They matched 1,256 opioid users who died of opioid causes. Their controls were 4,619 living opioid users. Gabapentin use in the prior 120 days was the exposure. After adjustment, co-prescription raised the odds of death by about half. Moderate and high gabapentin doses carried the added risk. A comparison drug class, NSAIDs, showed no such link. Nearly half of gabapentin users also held an opioid prescription. Readers get hard numbers behind a warning to prescribers and patients.
europmc-pmc5673929:
Barupal and Fiehn present a methods paper in Scientific Reports. It introduces ChemRICH for analyzing metabolomics data. Such datasets can hold over 800 identified metabolites. Reading their biology through pathway maps has known flaws. Pathway sets overlap, and many compounds lack clear assignments. ChemRICH instead groups molecules by chemical similarity. It uses structure data and chemical ontologies to name modules.

The resulting sets are study-specific and non-overlapping. Every identified metabolite gets placed exactly once. Set sizes are self-contained, so test values stay stable. Those values do not hinge on background database size. The authors show the method on a diabetes mouse dataset. It separated groups tied to disease development there.
europmc-pmc5749029:
Groß and co-authors compare three strains of Clostridioides difficile taken from one patient. This spore forming bacterium causes hospital gut infections, from mild diarrhea to severe colitis. Finding three strains in one person hints at a mixed infection. The team sequenced all three genomes and tested their traits.

Their account sets the strains against known epidemic types, such as ribotype 027. The species holds a wide pan-genome shaped by gene transfer between strains. Toxin genes sit on a mobile island in the genome. Comparing close strains in one host can show how fast the pathogen adapts, the authors note.
europmc-pmc5764329:
Smith and co-authors review how common patellofemoral pain is across groups. This form of knee pain hits adults, teens, and active people often. Reports of its rate have varied a lot. The team searched studies to June 2017 and kept 23.

Yearly prevalence was 22.7% in the general population, they find. In teens it was 28.9% by the same yearly measure. Point prevalence in teens pooled at 7.2%. Rates in military recruits swung widely by study. Teen girl athletes showed a point rate of 22.7%. Given poor long term outlook, the authors call this pain a research priority.
europmc-pmc5766829:
Hauser and co-authors map genetic variation in G-protein-coupled receptors, a large family of drug targets. These receptors are hit by about a third of approved drugs. Yet how often their genes vary in binding sites was unknown. The team read genome data from close to seventy thousand people.

They find that drug targeted receptors carry many variants in key functional regions. Tests on two receptors show that some variants change or worsen drug response. The team also links variants to British prescription and sales data. Sorting these variants could make prescribing more precise, they argue, and cut harm from uneven drug response.
europmc-pmc5797629:
Kametani and Hasegawa re-examine two rival accounts of Alzheimer's disease. The amyloid account blames amyloid beta build-up as the first cause. The tau account gives that role to tau protein tangles. Failed amyloid drugs motivate the fresh look.

The authors argue that tau fits the disease course better. They review family gene mutations and risk factors like APOE4. They also explain how tau damage may spread through the brain. Readers get a clear challenge to a long-held view and the case for a tau-first account. Both proteins form the plaques and tangles seen in affected brains.
europmc-pmc5833729:
Wu and co-authors show how nicotine speeds artery clogging through a fiery form of cell death. Their study appeared in Cell Death & Disease. Smoking is a known driver of atherosclerosis. The path from nicotine to plaque stayed murky.

In mice fed a fatty diet, nicotine grew larger plaques and raised inflammatory signals. In human artery-lining cells, it switched on the NLRP3 inflammasome. That trigger set off pyroptosis, a bursting death that spills cell contents. Blocking caspase-1, silencing NLRP3, or mopping up reactive oxygen species stopped the death. The chain runs from smoke chemistry to vessel damage.
europmc-pmc5834629:
Wu and co-authors link DNA methylation to gene activity and disease using summary data alone. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Genome scans find trait-linked variants but rarely name the gene at fault. The team asked whether methylation carries the signal from variant to gene.

Their method joins data across omics layers through shared genetic effects. It tied 7,858 methylation sites to 2,733 genes. Many sites sat in enhancers and promoters, far from their genes. For 12 complex traits, 149 sites and 66 genes formed plausible chains. Each chain hints how a variant may act through methylation and transcription.
europmc-pmc5841829:
Ghaffarizadeh and co-authors release PhysiCell, free software that simulates crowds of cells in three dimensions. Their paper appeared in PLoS Computational Biology. Tissue behavior emerges from many cells moving, dividing, and dying together. Lab work alone cannot follow each cell.

PhysiCell models each cell as an agent with physics. Built-in rules cover cycling, death, motion, and squeezing. A partner solver tracks oxygen, drugs, and signals diffusing between cells. Runs reach a million cells on a desktop workstation. Demo worlds include tumor spheroids and breast duct cancers. The code is open source under the BSD license.
europmc-pmc5845129:
Chen and co-authors review the layered defense the body mounts against influenza A. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Flu kills hundreds of thousands in a normal year. The immune system meets it in waves.

Mucus, interferons, and hungry phagocytes form the first wall. Antibodies then tag the virus for destruction. Killer T cells clear the cells it has infected. The airway's own local immunity guards the entry point. The virus counters with disguise and sabotage of alarms. The authors map each clash, from first detection to memory.
europmc-pmc5858529:
Poh and Ernst review how macrophages shape cancer and how drugs might target them. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. Macrophages fill much of the tissue around tumours. They can switch states in response to local signals. In most solid cancers, heavy macrophage presence links to poor outlook. These cells can help tumours grow, spread, and resist treatment.

The review explains how tumours programme macrophages to support them. It surveys therapies that block that support or turn the cells against cancer. Some approaches have shown promise in early trials with mice. Others are now in human trials. The authors discuss how such drugs might join standard cancer care. Challenges for real patient benefit are also weighed.
europmc-pmc5890129:
Franceschi and co-authors argue that ageing and age-related diseases form one continuum. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Medicine. A new field, geroscience, links ageing to chronic disease. Ageing is the top risk factor for such diseases. Both may share a small set of basic mechanisms. The authors propose that diseases can be seen as sped-up ageing. Frailty, muscle loss, lung disease, and cancer serve as cases.

At one extreme, centenarians age slowly and dodge disease. At the other, patients in their sixties show fast ageing. Between them lies a grey zone of mixed paths. Genes, environment, and lifestyle set each person's path. The authors urge markers that split biological from calendar age.
europmc-pmc5890329:
Fernández and co-authors review advances in targeting the folate receptor. Their article appeared in Chemical Science. Many tumours carry extra copies of this receptor on their surface. That excess can guide drugs straight to cancer cells. Healthy tissue, with far less receptor, is largely spared. Targeted delivery thus cuts toxic side effects of chemotherapy. The review centres on the alpha form of the receptor.

The authors set out what makes a good target receptor. Fast recycling to the cell surface is one plus. They survey recent drug delivery systems built on folate. Imaging agents that light up tumours are also covered. Progress in therapy and diagnosis is weighed together.
europmc-pmc5952429:
Crusell and co-authors link diabetes in pregnancy with shifts in gut microbes. Their study was published in Microbiome. The team checked gut microbes late in pregnancy. They checked again about eight months after birth. The groups held 50 women with this diabetes and 157 healthy women. Gene tests named the microbes in each stool sample.

Women with the diabetes held a changed gut mix, they report. Some germ groups were more common in them. A few kinds stayed distinct even when body weight was factored in. The range of gut microbes fell after birth in both groups. Eight months on, the diabetes group's mix was still off track.
europmc-pmc5967329:
Han and co-authors review the paracrine and endocrine actions of proteins secreted by bone cells. Their review appeared in Bone Research. The skeleton is remade without pause through life. Osteoblasts, osteocytes, and osteoclasts release proteins that steer that work. These signals guide bone formation, bone breakdown, and blood vessel growth. Osteocytes make sclerostin, which holds back bone formation. Osteoclasts send factors that act back on bone builders.

Some bone proteins act as hormones across the whole body. FGF23 regulates phosphate balance, the authors note. Osteocalcin shapes glucose use, reproduction, and cognition. Lipocalin-2 can suppress appetite through the brain. The review ties the skeleton to many other organs.
europmc-pmc6020529:
Gupta and co-authors report a dysprosium complex that works as a single-ion magnet. Their chemistry study appeared in Chemical Science. The complex joins one dysprosium ion with five water molecules. Two phosphonic diamide ligands complete the structure. Single-ion magnets hold their magnetization below a set blocking temperature. They mark the smallest size limit for future spin-based devices.

Most such magnets are fragile in air and moisture. This one stays stable in normal air. It also pairs a high energy barrier with a high blocking temperature. The team links this strength to the shape set around the metal ion. That shape limits quantum tunneling, which drains magnetization. Readers get a design route toward magnets that can survive real-world handling.
europmc-pmc6057429:
Jiang and co-authors review zinc oxide nanoparticles for biomedical use. Their article appeared in Bioinorganic Chemistry and Applications. These particles already serve in rubber, paint, and cosmetics. They are cheap, compatible with tissue, and low in toxicity. That profile draws strong medical interest.

The particles can trigger reactive oxygen species in cells. They also release zinc ions and prompt cell death. Those traits suit anticancer and antibacterial uses. Zinc supports insulin structure, which aids diabetes work. The particles glow, making them good for bioimaging. The review covers how the particles are made. It then surveys recent progress field by field. Readers get a compact guide to a versatile material.
europmc-pmc6060529:
Bombard and co-authors review how patients help design and judge health services. Their systematic review appeared in Implementation Science. The team searched nine databases for studies from 1990 to 2016. Forty-eight studies of active patient engagement qualified.

Working methods fell into design, recruitment, involvement, and leadership themes. Outcomes ranged from teaching tools to changed governance. Light consultation tended to yield documents and products. Deep partnership reshaped care processes themselves. Most patients felt stronger after taking part. Some still felt their role was token rather than real. Readers get evidence on what genuine engagement takes. The authors call for better study of patient experience.
europmc-pmc6073929:
Farzaei and co-authors review curcumin for oxidative liver disease. Their systematic review appeared in Nutrients. Curcumin is the main active part of turmeric. Oxidative stress drives much liver injury. Causes range from alcohol and drugs to viruses and diet.

The team searched four databases for the evidence. Curcumin calmed inflammatory signals in study after study. It lowered lipid peroxidation products. It raised the liver's own antioxidant defenses. It also curbed the stellate cells behind scarring. The molecule itself scavenges free radicals directly. Clinical evidence gets a separate look. Readers get mechanisms plus a call for stronger human trials.
europmc-pmc6115829:
Kim and Kim wrote a review in Nutrients on natural products that kill cancer cells through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum. The endoplasmic reticulum folds proteins inside cells. Tumor conditions can strain it and pile up unfolded proteins. Cells first try to adapt to that stress. If it lasts, they can be pushed to die.

The review explains how this stress leads to cell death. It then surveys plant and other natural compounds that use this route. The survey covers six major cancers, from lung to liver. Blocking the adaptive response is one proposed tactic. Pushing the death response is another.
europmc-pmc6191929:
Smirnoff wrote a review in Free Radical Biology and Medicine comparing ascorbic acid in plants and mammals. Ascorbic acid, or vitamin C, is made by most eukaryotes. Primates and a few other animal groups lost the final enzyme and must eat it instead. Bacteria neither make it nor need it.

Its power comes from donating electrons. That lets it scavenge free radicals and keep iron in its reactive form. At least three separate pathways for making it evolved, a sign of its value. In plants it also removes hydrogen peroxide formed during photosynthesis. Smirnoff compares its jobs across the two kingdoms, from defense against stress to enzyme support and possible signaling.
europmc-pmc6224529:
Chakravarthy and co-authors found a gene pattern that links stroma to immune escape. The matrix around tumours shapes cancer course. Support cells called fibroblasts build much of that matrix. The study ran a large pan-cancer analysis. It appeared in Nature Communications.

The team defined a set of matrix genes switched on in cancer. High levels linked to worse prognosis. The pattern tied to TGF-b signalling in fibroblasts. Tumours with it suppressed immune activity. They also carried distinct mutations, such as BRAF and TP53. The pattern predicted failure of PD-1 blockade therapy. It beat earlier proposed markers at that task. The authors suggest TGF-b blockade could help. That idea still needs preclinical testing.
europmc-pmc6295629:
Lushchak and co-authors review how pesticides poison living things, step by step. Their review appeared in the EXCLI Journal. Pesticides linger in soil, water, and food chains. The authors sort them by source, use, and body effect. Most kill weeds, fungi, or insects.

Herbicides block plant growth, light capture, or building of key compounds. Fungicides stop fungi from making cell parts or energy. Insecticides attack nerves, muscle, growth, or energy supply. The review tracks how these chemicals build up in bodies. It links exposure to many diseases, from nerve injury to metabolic problems. The authors call for safer, more targeted products. They also want more study of long-term low doses.
europmc-pmc6323929:
Athar and co-authors update ArrayExpress, an archive for functional genomics data. Their report appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The archive stores data from many assay types. These include gene activity and promoter binding studies. Sequencing-based experiments have grown fast in recent years. Single-cell RNA studies have grown fast too.

A rebuilt submission tool, Annotare, now captures richer study details. It handles raw and processed data for these new designs. Chosen datasets are reprocessed for a sister resource, Expression Atlas. That step also tests data quality. Multi-omics studies that mix assay types are rising as well. A newer archive, BioStudies, will in time take over. All existing records and access numbers will carry across.
europmc-pmc6365929:
Reichenbach and co-authors present a research article in EMBO Molecular Medicine on astrocyte reactions in Alzheimer's disease. Astrocytes near amyloid plaques become reactive, a change driven by the transcription factor Stat3. The team deleted Stat3 only in astrocytes of APP/PS1 mice, a standard Alzheimer's model.

Mice without astrocyte Stat3 had lower amyloid levels and fewer plaques. Nearby microglia cleared more amyloid, and inflammatory signals dropped. Brain network imbalance and memory decline were largely prevented. A Stat3-blocking drug given to the whole body produced the same protection. The authors present Stat3-driven astrogliosis as a promising treatment target.
europmc-pmc6371029:
Romano and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Immunology on regulatory T cell therapy. These cells keep the immune system tolerant of the body's own tissues. Giving patients extra regulatory cells could prevent graft rejection and calm autoimmune disease without heavy immune suppression.

The review covers how the cells develop, how they suppress other immune cells, and how clinics isolate and grow them. Early phase I trials in transplant and autoimmune settings showed the therapy is safe and feasible. Phase II trials are now enrolling. The authors close with strategies to make cell products purer, more stable, and more effective.
europmc-pmc6381229:
Evans and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis in The Lancet. They asked how long knee replacements last, using case series and national registry reports with at least 15 years of follow-up. The registries alone covered nearly 300,000 total knee replacements.

Pooled registry data suggest about 82 percent of total knee replacements last 25 years. Partial unicondylar replacements fared worse, at about 70 percent over the same span. Case series gave similar but less reliable figures. No long-term series covered kneecap-only replacements. The authors offer the estimates to help patients, surgeons, and planners judge when revision surgery may be needed.
europmc-pmc6416629:
Dulinska-Litewka and co-authors review iron oxide nanoparticles in Materials. Superparamagnetic particles respond to a magnet but lose their magnetism when the field is off. That trait gives doctors remote control over them inside the body.

Uses already include sharper MRI scans and heat treatment of tumors. The particles can also carry drugs to a chosen site. They are easy to make and fit well with living tissue, the authors note. Their main drawback is quick uptake by immune cells. Coatings and design tweaks aim to fix that flaw.
europmc-pmc6424229:
Giesel and co-authors report early human data on two gallium-68 FAPI tracers used in PET/CT scans of cancer patients, published in 2019. The tracers target fibroblast activation protein, which appears at high levels in the support cells around many tumors. Earlier lab work and a few clinical cases had raised hopes for sharper imaging.

Dosimetry from two patients suggested a 200 MBq scan gives roughly 3 to 4 mSv, close to standard tracers. Scans in 25 patients per tracer showed low uptake in healthy organs after fast kidney clearance. FAPI-4 held in tumors longer than FAPI-2, and both matched FDG on tumor uptake with lower background in brain and liver.
europmc-pmc6517429:
Hong and co-authors design a glue-like gel that seals severe bleeding, writing in Nature Communications. Uncontrolled bleeding from torn arteries or heart wounds is a top killer in trauma and surgery, and today's agents stick poorly to wet, moving tissue. The new material mimics the makeup of the body's own connective tissue.

A flash of UV light sets the gel in under a second and bonds it to the wound. Seals held against pressures up to 290 mmHg, well above normal blood pressure. In pigs, the gel stopped high-pressure bleeding from cut carotid arteries and from holes punched in the heart wall, and the animals survived. The authors offer it as a fast sealant for wounds that sutures cannot reach in time.
europmc-pmc6522529:
Li and co-authors test metal-organic frameworks that kill bacteria under light. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Most air purifiers use dense fibre filters. Those filters trap particles well but kill few germs. Trapped microbes can grow and spread again.

The team screened a series of frameworks for light-driven killing. A zinc-based one, ZIF-8, stood out. It inactivated over 99.9999% of E. coli in saline within two hours. The dose was simulated sunlight. Trapped photoelectrons at zinc centres drive reactive oxygen species. Those species do the killing. Filters made from ZIF-8 killed over 99.99% of airborne bacteria in 30 minutes. They also removed 97% of particles.
europmc-pmc6539529:
Batista and co-authors review the use of lipopolysaccharide, or LPS, to model brain inflammation in degenerative disease, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. LPS is a toxin from the coat of Gram-negative bacteria. Injected or added to cells, it fires the receptor TLR4 and sets off a wave of inflammatory signals.

Researchers use that wave to mimic the inflammation seen in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS and Huntington's disease. Results shift with the LPS strain, the route given and the number of doses, so the review compares protocols across animal and cell models. It also weighs what these models can and cannot prove about how inflammation drives neuron loss.
europmc-pmc6560329:
Marra and co-authors critically compare the two workhorse methods for measuring body composition, writing in Contrast Media and Molecular Imaging. Knowing a patient's fat mass and fat-free mass guides nutrition and care, but neither tool is flawless. The review lays out how each works and where each misleads.

Bioelectrical impedance passes a weak current through the body and infers water and tissue from its resistance. It is cheap, portable and safe, yet its accuracy hinges on the right prediction equations and strict measurement routines. DXA scanning is the reference method, splitting bone, fat and lean tissue in one pass. Its costs are price, expertise, and radiation that limits repeat scans. The authors map which patients suit which method, from clinics to hospital beds.
europmc-pmc6572829:
Menden and co-authors report a community contest to predict which cancer drug pairs work better together, writing in Nature Communications. Single targeted drugs usually fail as tumors resist, but the space of possible pairs is far too large to test by hand. AstraZeneca released 11,576 experiments covering 910 combinations across 85 cancer cell lines, and 160 teams competed to forecast synergy from the data.

The best methods leaned on prior knowledge of drug targets. For over 60% of combinations they predicted synergy as accurately as repeating the experiment itself. Yet a stubborn fifth of pairs defeated every method. The analysis also surfaced genetic logic behind some results, giving modelers both a benchmark dataset and a map of where prediction still breaks down.
europmc-pmc6604129:
Jia and co-authors pool trial evidence on exercise and Alzheimer disease. Their meta-analysis appears in BMC Geriatrics. Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of dementia. It burdens patients, families, and health systems heavily. Physical activity is a cheap, low-risk candidate therapy.

The authors searched five databases for trials published through late 2018. They included 13 randomized trials with 673 patients. Exercise groups scored better on the MMSE than control groups. The pooled gain was clear and significant. Subgroup checks compared different amounts of activity. High-frequency programs did not beat low-frequency ones by much. A dose threshold, the authors say, still needs settling. They call for more trials with rigorous designs.
europmc-pmc6629629:
Alsahafi and co-authors update the molecular biology and treatment challenges of head and neck cancer. Their review appears in Cell Death and Disease. These squamous cell cancers are aggressive and hard to treat. Surgery and radiotherapy remain the main options. Both carry heavy costs to quality of life. Resistance and relapse are common. The only approved targeted drugs block EGFR. Their benefit is limited, and resistance mechanisms stay murky.

The update stresses the tumour's surroundings as well. Immune cells, low oxygen, and oral microbes shape behaviour. HPV-positive tumours form a subgroup with better outlook. For them, gentler treatment is an open question. The authors call for biomarkers to guide personalised care.
europmc-pmc6651129:
Alves-Fernandes and Jasiulionis review the role of SIRT1 in DNA damage responses and cancer. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. SIRT1 is an enzyme that removes acetyl groups from proteins. It needs NAD+ to work. Its targets include histones and many other proteins. Through them it steers gene activity and genome stability. It also touches ageing, cell death, and growth. Studies paint the enzyme as double-edged in cancer.

Some tumours raise SIRT1, and others lower it. The pattern depends on cell type and location. The review examines its interplay with oxidative stress. It also covers links to the DNA repair machinery. Pinning down context is the authors' main plea.
europmc-pmc6688129:
Yonekura-Sakakibara, Higashi, and Nakabayashi trace the origin and evolution of plant flavonoid chemistry. Their review appears in Frontiers in Plant Science. Flavonoids spread across the whole plant kingdom. Over nine thousand compounds share the scaffold. Their genes offer a window on pathway evolution. Scaffold enzymes were recruited from primary metabolism. Chalcone synthase and isomerase came first. Both descend from lipid pathway ancestors. Later enzymes diversified the structures. Dioxygenases, P450s, and reductases did that work. Gene duplication supplied the raw material.

New profiling now maps flavonoids in fine detail. Merged genomic data reveal surprise gene functions. Spread patterns suggest stepwise pathway assembly. UV protection may be the ancestral role. Pigments and signals evolved later.
europmc-pmc6692429:
Albensi asks what nuclear factor kappa B is doing in and to the mitochondrion. His review appears in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. NF-κB signalling is famous for immunity and inflammation. Its mitochondrial life is far less charted. Subunits were first reported inside mitochondria in 2001. Pathway kinases were found there too. Follow-up work has stayed scattered since. Inside, the factor may regulate oxidative phosphorylation genes. It may switch cells between glycolysis and respiration. Apoptotic signalling also seems involved.

Influence flows from outside as well. Nuclear NF-κB shapes mitochondrial gene expression indirectly. Import mechanisms remain genuinely unclear, though. No defined targeting sequence explains the localisation. The author flags the speculation openly. More proof is the field's need.
europmc-pmc6747329:
Chen and Chang review why cancers resist cisplatin, a mainstay chemotherapy drug. Cisplatin kills tumor cells by damaging their DNA. Resistance is a major clinical barrier. Older research focused on defenses inside the tumor cell, such as pumping the drug out, detoxifying it, or repairing DNA faster.

New work shows the tumor's surroundings matter just as much. Support cells, matrix, blood flow, and immune cells all help tumors withstand the drug. Some combination treatments that target these surroundings have succeeded in trials. The review gathers this evidence, cell by cell and component by component. It highlights where new drugs might break resistance.
europmc-pmc6853829:
Chandra and co-authors review ovarian cancer in Cancer Medicine. Of cancers of the female reproductive system, it is the deadliest. Most cases are found late, when survival is poor. No good screening test exists for early disease. Standard care mixes major surgery to remove tumour bulk with chemotherapy.

Relapse is common, on average about every two years, and each round of treatment grows harsher. The review covers where care stands and what might improve it. Immune-based treatments draw growing interest, including engineered T cells aimed at ovarian tumour markers. Combining immune drugs with those cells is one proposed path. The authors also flag cost and quality of life as burdens that rise with each relapse.
europmc-pmc6855329:
DeFilippis and co-authors clarify a confusing corner of heart care, in Circulation. A heart attack means heart muscle died from lack of oxygen. The classic cause is a clot over a torn plaque. Type 2 infarction is different: supply and demand fall out of balance for other reasons, such as very low blood pressure or fast heart rhythms. Muscle can also be injured with no oxygen shortage at all.

Each year more than 8 million Americans reach hospital with possible heart attack signs, and about 700,000 receive that diagnosis. The authors set out how to tell these groups apart with blood tests and imaging. Treatment differs sharply by cause, so the sorting matters.
europmc-pmc6858629:
Das and Johnson review a hopeful side effect of cancer immunotherapy, in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. Checkpoint inhibitors have transformed care for many advanced cancers. Still, only 15 to 60 percent of patients respond. Doctors need signs that show early who is benefiting. One candidate is the immune side effects these drugs cause.

Such side effects arise when freed T cells also attack healthy tissue. The review gathers studies asking whether patients who develop them fare better. Several found longer survival in that group, across skin, gut, and hormone organs affected. The authors weigh the strength of that link and its traps, such as patients staying on treatment longer simply because it works.
europmc-pmc6859529:
Zhang and co-authors review stress inside the cell's protein factory, in Redox Biology. The endoplasmic reticulum folds most membrane and secreted proteins. Folding needs chemical bridges whose making also produces reactive oxygen. When misfolded proteins pile up, the organelle falls into ER stress. A rescue programme, the unfolded protein response, switches on.

That programme first tries to restore order by boosting folding help and antioxidant defences. One branch works through the factors PERK and NRF2. If stress drags on, the same programme turns toward cell death instead. The review traces how redox signals and the rescue response together decide a cell's fate.
europmc-pmc6882729:
Edger and co-authors report the genome of the cultivated strawberry, in Nature Genetics. The garden strawberry is an octoploid: its cells carry eight sets of chromosomes. It arose when two wild octoploid species crossed, themselves built from four diploid ancestors merged more than 1 million years ago. Untangling that layered ancestry was the challenge.

The team produced a near-complete, chromosome-scale assembly. They identified living relatives of each of the four diploid progenitors and found support for a North American origin. Among the four subgenomes, one dominates, holding more genes and higher activity. Its grip extends to flavour traits, including much of the sweetness chemistry.
europmc-pmc6882829:
Kobak and Berens offer a practical guide to a popular plotting method, in Nature Communications. Single-cell studies measure thousands of genes in up to millions of cells. To see the data, analysts squash it into two dimensions with t-SNE. The method reveals local groupings beautifully. Used naively, it also distorts the big picture, inventing gaps and hiding real distances.

The authors show how to avoid the worst traps. Starting the layout from a principal component map, using a high learning rate, and mixing similarity scales all help. For very large datasets they add exaggeration and a downsampled start. Worked examples on published data show the same cells forming far more faithful maps.
europmc-pmc7025029:
The WHO CVD Risk Chart Working Group presents revised heart disease risk charts in The Lancet Global Health. The charts estimate a person's 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke. Older charts fitted wealthy countries poorly matched low-income and middle-income settings, so the World Health Organization convened this effort to rebuild them for 21 global regions.

The models use age, smoking, systolic blood pressure, diabetes history, and total cholesterol. They were derived from 376,177 people in 85 cohorts, all aged 40 to 80 with no known cardiovascular disease at entry. The team then recalibrated each model with regional incidence and risk factor data, and tested it on separate studies. The charts let clinics judge risk where laboratory testing may be limited.
europmc-pmc7046529:
Sahai and a large group of co-authors present a consensus statement in Nature Reviews Cancer. Their subject is cancer-associated fibroblasts, support cells inside tumours. These cells build and reshape the matrix around cancer cells. They also swap signals with cancer cells and immune cells.

The statement grew out of an expert meeting held in March 2019. The authors sum up what is known about where these fibroblasts come from. They stress how varied the cells are. Some subtypes help tumours, while others restrain them. That mix makes them a tempting but tricky drug target. The statement sets out shared terms and research priorities. Its aim is to move the field toward safer ways to use these cells in therapy.
europmc-pmc7048229:
Zhang and co-authors investigate how infected patients shed the new coronavirus in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Diagnosis rested on oral swabs, and patients were released after two negative oral tests. Yet related coronaviruses also infect the gut and spread by the oral-faecal route. The team checked whether this virus also appears in other body sites.

Testing patients at a local hospital, they found viral RNA in anal swabs and in blood as well as in the mouth. Later in infection, anal swabs turned positive more often than oral swabs. That pattern suggests the virus is shed through the gut and could spread by the oral-faecal route even when throat tests clear. Blood antibody tests raised the overall detection rate, so the authors recommend adding serology to future surveys. Their caution: discharge rules based on oral swabs alone may free patients who still shed virus.
europmc-pmc7078829:
Mizumoto and co-authors estimate silent COVID-19 infections aboard a cruise ship in Eurosurveillance. The Diamond Princess, carrying 3,711 people, was quarantined at Yokohama from 5 February 2020 after a former passenger tested positive. By 20 February, 634 people on board had tested positive. A ship under quarantine offered rare data: nearly everyone was tested, whether or not they felt ill.

Simple case counts understate silent infection, because some people counted as asymptomatic would develop symptoms later. The authors model that delay, and the censoring caused by testing dates, to correct the figure. Their adjusted estimate puts the truly asymptomatic share of infections at 17.9 percent, with a credible interval from 15.5 to 20.2 percent. Most infections, the timeline shows, happened before quarantine began. The estimate informed early debate about how much spread comes from people who never feel sick.
europmc-pmc7100629:
Zhou and Bao built FerrDb, a hand-curated database of ferroptosis regulators and markers. Their paper appeared in Database, the journal of biological databases and curation. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death that depends on iron. Cells die as harmful lipid compounds build up inside them.

The pair mined 784 papers from PubMed by hand. They recorded 253 regulators, split into drivers, suppressors, inducers, and inhibitors. They also logged 111 markers and 95 links between ferroptosis and diseases. The database has a simple web interface, and the authors plan updates every six months. Readers get the first organized map of a fast-growing field, ready for cancer and degenerative disease research.
europmc-pmc7193629:
Hwang and co-authors test whether polystyrene microplastic particles can harm human cells. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Tiny plastic particles are now common in water, food, and daily products. Many people assume they cause little or no harm. Direct contact at the cell level is less well tested. The team focused on primary polystyrene particles. They varied both particle size and dose.

The authors report that the particles acted as immune stimulants in their tests. Exposed cells produced more cytokines and chemokines. The effect grew with higher doses. It also varied with particle size. These results point to possible harm from direct cell contact. The study does not test whole-body effects in people. Readers get a careful lab-based warning sign. It adds to wider concern about plastic waste in the environment.
europmc-pmc7199529:
Zhang and co-authors model how changed contact patterns shaped the COVID-19 outbreak in China. Their study appeared in Science. Restrictions in early 2020 cut daily life down sharply. Contact surveys in Wuhan and Shanghai measured mixing by age. The team fed those patterns into a transmission model.

Average daily contacts fell from roughly 14 to 20 down to 2. At that level, transmission dropped below the epidemic threshold. Preemptive school closures also reduced spread in the model. The results separate which measures did the heavy lifting. Contact reduction itself, not only case management, drove the fall. The study gave policymakers early evidence for distancing rules. It also showed the value of measuring social contact during a crisis.
europmc-pmc7228129:
Gaballah and co-authors test how GenX and other replacement PFAS chemicals affect young zebrafish. Their study appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives. PFAS are man-made chemicals that spread through water and soil and break down very slowly. The older, long-chain kinds were tied to harm in young animals. Makers swapped them for shorter kinds meant to be safer, but proof of that safety is thin.

The team raised zebrafish embryos in water dosed with several of these chemicals. They watched for body defects, odd swimming, and how much of each dose reached the fish's tissues. One older chemical made the young fish far too active at low doses. A newer relative caused much the same restless pattern. Each chemical left its own mark. Grouping the chemicals by shared effects is the aim, and the results feed the debate over whether replacements are truly safer.
europmc-pmc7285829:
Zang and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 can productively infect the human small intestine. Their study appeared in Science Immunology. Gut symptoms and viral RNA in feces are common in COVID-19 patients, but whether the virus actually replicates in the intestine, and could spread by a fecal-oral route, was unclear.

Working with human intestinal mini-tissues called enteroids, the team infected mature gut-lining cells that carry ACE2. Two proteases found in gut tissue, TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4, boosted the spike protein's ability to fuse with cells and let the virus in. However, fluid simulating the colon inactivated virus released into the gut, and no infectious virus was recovered from patient stool. The intestine may still help drive local and whole-body illness.
europmc-pmc7352229:
Hahad and co-authors review air pollution and brain health in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Air pollution is already the leading environmental cause of disease and early death worldwide. Beyond heart and lung harm, evidence now ties dirty air to stroke, dementia, Parkinson's disease, and depression.

Fine particles draw the closest attention, since they can affect the central nervous system. The molecular route is still partly unclear, but inflammation and oxidative stress look central, driven by overactive immune signaling in blood vessels and brain. The authors gather the evidence for each disorder and mark what remains unknown. Readers get a case that clean air is also brain protection.
europmc-pmc7356229:
Dompe and co-authors review photobiomodulation in the Journal of Clinical Medicine, the use of low-level laser light to steer cell behavior. Interest in laser therapy across medicine and dentistry has grown sharply in a decade. Effects depend on settings such as wavelength, energy density, power, and exposure time.

At the right dose, light can speed cell growth, guide stem cells to mature, ease pain, and calm inflammation while tissues repair. The authors trace the underlying mechanisms inside cells, with special attention to stem cells and healing. Because the method is non-invasive, clinics are testing it widely. Readers get a map of where light therapy is used and what must be pinned down before claims harden.
europmc-pmc7387429:
Mercatelli and Giorgi chart the mutations of SARS-CoV-2 across the world in Frontiers in Microbiology. They gathered 48,635 complete viral genomes shared through the GISAID consortium and compared each with the original Wuhan reference. Geography-specific patterns could, in principle, shape how the disease behaves in different places.

Each sample carried an average of 7.23 mutations. Single-letter transitions were the dominant change type everywhere. The genomes formed at least three clades with geographic signatures. Clade G, prevalent in Europe, carries the spike change D614G that later defined the pandemic's course. Mapping mutations this way, the authors argue, can guide tailored antiviral strategies. Readers get a world atlas of a virus in motion.
europmc-pmc7405629:
Özdin and Bayrak Özdin measure anxiety and depression in Turkish society during the COVID-19 pandemic, in the International Journal of Social Psychiatry. An online questionnaire gathered sociodemographic details plus standard scales for anxiety, depression, and health anxiety. The authors tested which life circumstances pushed scores up.

Above the clinical cut-off sat 23.6 percent of respondents for depression and 45.1 percent for anxiety. Female gender and living in urban areas were among the factors tied to worse scores in their analysis. Living with someone over 60, knowing an infected person, and prior psychiatric illness also entered the picture. Gender, the authors stress in their title and findings, shapes the pandemic's mental burden unevenly.
europmc-pmc7410829:
Vierstra and co-authors build a global reference map of transcription factor footprints in Nature. Transcription factors bind regulatory DNA in combinations to run genes, and disease-linked variants often sit in those regions. Footprinting with the enzyme DNase I can mark occupied sites at single-letter resolution, but only a small fraction had been resolved.

The team made dense cleavage maps from 243 human cell and tissue types. Integrated, they delineate about 4.5 million compact elements holding factor binding, inside roughly 1.6 million hypersensitive sites. Most sites host well-spaced single factor contacts. Cell type changes the pattern, showing regulation in context. The map helps judge which genetic variants actually disturb gene control.
europmc-pmc7463929:
Tottoli and co-authors review skin wound healing and new care technologies for wounds. Healing joins many cells, growth factors, and cytokines in a rare natural process. Normal healing restores tissue, but many wounds stall at plain repair.

The review traces how wound care has evolved over the years. It covers the main problems that block healing and how chronic wounds are managed in clinics. New strategies aim for true skin regeneration, not just closure. Scaffolds loaded with growth factors or living, altered cells lead the push. Cell and tissue engineering methods add more options. The goal is lower hospital costs, lasting relief, and better scars. Personal therapy design is a theme across the new methods.
europmc-pmc7466429:
Dai and co-authors review how chronic stress promotes cancer development. Stress is part of life, but long stress from hardship, depression, or loneliness can endanger health. Recent studies tie it to tumor growth.

Chronic stress switches on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the sympathetic nervous system. Stress hormones from both can feed tumor formation through many routes. Long stress also weakens immune watch and keeps inflammation simmering. Both shifts help tumors start and grow. Brain regions such as the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus lose function under strain. The authors ask if drugs that block stress signal paths could slow these cancers. Stress care, they argue, matters for patients and healthy people alike.
europmc-pmc7573629:
Schuster and co-authors build an automated microfluidic platform for drug screening in tumor organoids. Organoids model patient tumors better than flat cell cultures. Standard microfluidics could not yet handle organoids well.

Their system cultures and tests hundreds of organoids at once. It delivers drug mixes and changing doses over time. Real-time analysis tracks how organoids respond to treatment. Human pancreatic tumor organoids were used for validation. Responses differed between organoids from separate patients. Timed drug sequences beat constant single-drug dosing in tests. Timed plans also beat fixed combination dosing in vitro. The platform may help mirror real patient treatment courses for personal therapy.
europmc-pmc7615029:
Mill, Christensen and Pedersen review primary cilia as signaling hubs in development and disease. Cilia are tiny antenna-like parts on most vertebrate cells. They help control signals that guide growth and balance.

Faults in cilia genes cause over 30 human diseases. These ciliopathies overlap and vary in severity. Cilia hold receptors and channels for key pathways. Hedgehog and GPCR signals depend on that placement. Without the antenna, those pathways misfire in cells. New tools are speeding study of cilia diversity. Structure and function differ across cell types. Control shifts with cell state and growth stage. The review tackles how gene faults map to patient traits.
europmc-pmc7756029:
Bernardo-Castro and co-authors review how the blood-brain barrier leaks across the stages of ischemic stroke. The barrier shields the brain and keeps its inner state steady. After a stroke, its leak follows a multi-phase pattern. Each phase has unlike causes and unlike risks for patients.

Early on, oxygen loss damages the barrier and swells tissue. Next, inflammation deepens the leak and raises the risk of bleeding into the brain. In weeks 1 to 3, new vessel growth aids repair, though the young vessels leak. Past 6 weeks the barrier partly reseals. The authors say care choices should match the phase a patient is in.
europmc-pmc7784929:
Chen and co-authors map the immune landscape of nasopharyngeal carcinoma at single-cell level. This cancer shows strong ethnic and geographic skews. Its tumor microenvironment is a promising treatment target. The team profiled 7,581 malignant cells and 40,285 immune cells. Samples came from fifteen primary tumors and one normal sample.

The profiles exposed wide variation inside the tumors. Certain gene patterns marked more aggressive malignant cells. Many immune subtypes appeared, including a new CLEC9A+ dendritic cell type. The authors found regulators that drive immune cell diversity. Interaction maps pointed to possible immunotherapy targets. Signatures for five immune cell types tied to better survival. The dataset is offered as a base for precision therapy in this cancer.
europmc-pmc7801729:
van Kampen and co-authors measure how long hospitalized COVID-19 patients shed infectious virus. They cultured virus from samples of 129 patients. Only live virus in culture counts as infectious here.

Infectious virus was found in 23 of the 129 patients, or 17.8%. The median shedding time was 8 days after symptoms began. The chance of shedding fell below 5% after 15.2 days. High viral load raised the odds of infectious shedding a lot. A viral load above 7 log10 RNA copies per mL mattered most. A serum antibody level of at least 1:20 pointed the other way. It marked patients who were not infectious. The authors suggest lab tests could guide when isolation can end.
europmc-pmc7843029:
Thomson and co-authors study a spike change, N439K, that helps SARS-CoV-2 dodge antibodies. The virus can mutate to escape immunity. That puts vaccines and antibody drugs at risk. The team focused on the spike's receptor-binding motif. This zone is the main antibody target.

The motif proved to be a highly changeable region. N439K arose and spread widely in the population. The changed spike grips its human receptor more tightly. Lab growth and illness looked much like the wild type. Yet several lab-made antibodies lost their grip on it. One had US emergency approval. Blood from some recovered patients also worked less well. The authors urge steady tracking of such changes.
europmc-pmc7854729:
Osipiuk and co-authors map the shape of a key SARS-CoV-2 enzyme and its blockers. The papain-like protease, PLpro, is one of two viral proteases open to drug attack. It cuts viral proteins into working parts. It also helps build the copying machine and dulls host defenses.

The team solved the enzyme's structure at high detail. Shapes of a muted form were solved too. Bound forms with several blockers complete the set. Every compound stopped the enzyme in lab tests. Some also blocked virus growth in cells. The pictures show how each blocker grips the enzyme. That detail should speed design of strong PLpro drugs.
europmc-pmc7862229:
Dang and co-authors review ubiquitin signaling in cell cycle control and cancer growth. The cell cycle must run on a tight schedule. Cyclin-driven kinases push it forward step by step. Ubiquitin tags mark their partner proteins for timely removal.

Two ligase families do most of that tagging. The APC/C and the SCF complex share the work. Their faults let cells divide without control. Such loss of control ends in tumors. The authors map the diversity of this signaling web. Blocking the ligases is a live drug strategy. A clearer map should guide new cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc7921129:
Krook and co-authors present a review of fibroblast growth factor receptors in cancer. These receptors are switched on wrongly in 5–10% of all human cancers. Faults include single-letter changes, gene fusions, and extra gene copies. In bladder and bile duct cancers, the share rises to 10–30%. The review maps this landscape and the fight against it.

The authors first cover the hard task of testing for these faults in tissue and blood. They then survey the drugs built to block the receptors. Two drugs, erdafitinib and pemigatinib, already hold approval for defined cancer types. Most patients who first respond later grow resistant. The review sets out how that resistance arises, inside the tumour and beyond it. It closes with the next wave of blockers and fresh treatment plans.
europmc-pmc7925329:
Marco and co-authors present a consensus statement on fermented foods from an expert panel. The panel was convened in September 2019 by the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics. Fermented foods have been eaten for thousands of years. Fresh interest from scientists and shoppers made a clear definition urgent, since the term was used loosely.

The panel defines fermented foods and beverages as foods made through desired microbial growth and the enzyme-driven change of food parts. The statement sets fermented foods apart from probiotics, a point often blurred. It weighs the safety, risks, and health gains of these foods. Their nutrient traits and the ways they may aid gut and general health are reviewed. The panel also covers how such foods are regulated. It backs listing them as their own group in national dietary guides.
europmc-pmc7940029:
Buchanan presents a biographical study of Jean Guillaume Auguste Lugol and the solution that bears his name. A doctor's name often sticks to a drug or treatment while the life behind it fades. Lugol is such a case. He was born on August tenth, 1788, at Montauban in France. The town had a strong stock of schools and libraries for his early years.

Little is known of his parents or boyhood interests, Buchanan notes. Lugol studied medicine in Paris and served a hospital internship there. He took his doctorate in 1812. The paper then follows his work and the iodine solution linked to his name. It sets both against the medical world of his day. The study aims to restore the man behind a label still found in pharmacies. Buchanan writes for readers of medical history.
europmc-pmc7996329:
Alengebawy and co-authors present a review of heavy metals and pesticides as poisons in farm soil and plants. Pollution by such toxicants threatens both farm output and human health. Heavy metals such as cadmium, lead, copper, and zinc head the list. Pesticides for insects, weeds, and fungi stand beside them. The review covers how both build up in soil and crops and what harm follows.

The authors explain how the poisons move and act once inside plants and people. Soil traits and plant uptake set how much reaches food. The two poison classes can also team up or cancel out, changing the total harm. Diseases tied to exposure are listed in turn. Plant stress signs from contaminated soil get their own account. The review aims to give a full picture for those who guard food safety.
europmc-pmc8069529:
Kathayat and co-authors overview avian pathogenic E. coli, the bacterium behind colibacillosis in poultry. The disease strikes chickens, turkeys, and ducks with local and body-wide infections. It ranks among the top killers in poultry flocks. Meat and egg output fall, and many carcasses are condemned at slaughter. Losses run to hundreds of millions of dollars worldwide.

The review catalogs the tools the bacterium uses to cause disease. Classic virulence factors share the stage with newer ones. Quorum sensing, secretion systems, and gene regulators all play parts. Some bird strains closely match human strains that cause urine infections and meningitis. That overlap gives the bird pathogen real zoonotic weight. Resistance now spans nearly all antibiotic classes, carbapenems included. Vaccines and virulence blockers close the survey of controls.
europmc-pmc8192829:
Menon and co-authors report long-term results from a United Kingdom trial of ovarian cancer screening. Most women with this cancer are found late, and outcomes stay poor. The trial asked whether population screening can cut deaths.

Postmenopausal women aged 50–74 joined from 13 National Health Service centres. Women with prior ovarian surgery or raised family risk were excluded. Participants were assigned at random to screening or control paths. This report follows deaths after long-term follow-up. The scale of the trial gives its verdict unusual weight. It speaks to whether screening all women at set ages is worthwhile.
europmc-pmc8357629:
Alter and co-authors measure immune responses to the Ad26.COV2.S vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 variants. The vaccine had shown clinical effect against symptomatic disease, even against the Beta variant, which partly resists neutralising antibodies. How its immune response handled the variants of concern in humans stayed unclear.

The team studied 20 vaccinated people from an early phase trial. They tested blood and cell responses against the original strain of the virus. The Alpha, Gamma, and Beta variants were included, among others. Neutralising titres fell 5.0-fold against the Beta variant and 3.3-fold against the Gamma variant. Cell responses held up better across the variants. The data frame what a single dose of this vaccine can promise.
europmc-pmc8489229:
Yamashita and co-authors present Servalcat, a program for refining atomic models in cryo-EM studies. Cryo-electron microscopy builds maps of single particles in fine detail. Fitting an atomic model into such a map takes care and sound math. Servalcat was built to ease that task.

The program runs a refinement pipeline built on REFMAC5. It also computes difference maps that show where model and data disagree. The paper sets out the notation and theory behind the method. Scale factors and noise handling get exact treatment. The authors aim to give structural biologists a clear, shared tool. Better fits mean more trustworthy molecular structures for all users.
europmc-pmc8533829:
Mikulska and co-authors review the HPA axis in depression and schizophrenia, and new treatments based on it. This hormone axis links brain, pituitary, and adrenal glands in the stress response. Its overactivity shows up in chronic stress and major depression. There it drags down mood and thinking.

Gut microbes also talk with the axis and shape its tone. In schizophrenia, axis activity swings with illness severity. Many patients fail to answer standard antidepressants at first try. New drug ideas aim straight at the axis. They include blockers of hormone receptors in the stress path. The review sums up these fresh strategies and their promise.
europmc-pmc8541629:
Vaou and co-authors review antimicrobial activity in medicinal plants, the challenges and the outlook. Resistant germs spread fast, which drives a hunt for new bioactive compounds. Plant-derived compounds could give fresh, direct routes against bacteria. Sound modern methods are needed to find and test them.

Extraction choices shape which compounds come out and how strong they are. Tests of plant extracts can give varied results between labs. The review covers how plant compounds may kill or stop bacteria. It treats their chemical promise and their interplay with other substances. The authors also map what blocks new plant-based drugs. Efforts to boost compound strength close the survey.
europmc-pmc8616929:
