Büttner and co-authors present scCODA, a Bayesian model for changes in cell type mix in single-cell data. Shifts in cell types drive many body processes. Finding real shifts is hard. The data are shares that sum to a whole, and sample sizes are often small.

The model was built to handle both problems at once. In tests, it found real changes with strong accuracy. It also kept false finds under firm control. The model caught cell changes that the first studies had missed, and lab checks backed those finds. The tool is shared as open code. It gives labs a safer way to read cell mix data.
europmc-pmc8674129:
Pouwels and co-authors measure vaccine protection against new SARS-CoV-2 infections as the delta variant spread in the United Kingdom. The study used a large survey of randomly chosen households. It tracked new positive tests by variant and vaccine type. Both the Pfizer and Oxford vaccines were assessed.

Protection against illness or high viral load fell with delta. The drop was 10 to 13 percent for the Pfizer vaccine. It was 16 percent for the Oxford vaccine. Two doses still matched or beat protection from past infection. The vaccines also aged in distinct ways over time. People with past infection plus vaccine had the strongest cover, and younger adults fared better.
europmc-pmc8788129:
Verma, Lizama, and Chu review a triad of excitotoxicity, calcium, and mitochondria in synaptic nerve degeneration. Glutamate is the main excitatory signal in the mammalian brain. Too much of it can kill neurons after stroke or trauma. Its role in slow, chronic degeneration is more debated.

Mild excitatory injury now looks key in several diseases. Parkinson, Alzheimer, ALS, and Huntington diseases all show this pattern. Faulty handling of calcium inside mitochondria sits at the center. The review covers the pumps and channels that move that calcium. It also traces how disease proteins disrupt them. Restoring normal calcium flow is the proposed fix.
europmc-pmc8820829:
Wen and co-authors pool trial results for three oral antiviral drugs against COVID-19. The drugs are molnupiravir, fluvoxamine, and Paxlovid. Their meta-analysis asks whether these pills cut deaths or hospital stays. It also asks whether they raise side effects. The search covered major medical databases. Eight studies met the criteria for pooling.

The drug groups held 2,440 patients, and the control groups held 2,348. Death or hospital admission struck 54 patients on the drugs and 118 on control care. The pooled odds ratio was 0.33, a cut of about 67%. Side effects did not rise on the drugs. The authors read this as good safety. They call the three drugs a hopeful path for COVID-19 care.
europmc-pmc8878429:
Baliyan and co-authors test the antioxidant strength of Ficus religiosa, a plant long used in herbal medicine. Every part of the tree is credited with healing properties. The team used the DPPH assay, a standard free-radical test. In that test, antioxidants turn a purple radical solution pale. The depth of color loss gauges scavenging power. The authors also ran a quantitative phytochemical analysis.

Their results support real antioxidant activity in the plant. They link that activity to compounds that donate hydrogen atoms. Such action could help in disorders driven by free radicals. The paper also discusses making magnesium oxide nanoparticles with the plant. It explains how the assay logic applies there. The authors present the tree as a candidate source. New drug design is the hoped-for use.
europmc-pmc8986529:
Zhang and co-authors report a reconstruction trick that yields tough, highly ordered covalent organic frameworks. These porous crystals suit storage, electronics, and catalysis. Making them both crystalline and stable is hard. Reversible chemistry orders them but weakens them. The team's method pre-organizes the building blocks. A removable tether holds monomers in line. Polymerization then runs inside that confinement. The tether leaves, and order stays. No vacuum sealing is needed.

Reconstructed frameworks beat standard ones on order. Porosity rose sharply as well. Better order improved charge movement through the material. Light-driven hydrogen production reached 27.98 millimoles per hour per gram. That rate uses a sacrificial setup. The authors call the route general and scalable. Programming function through atomic order is the vision. Organic materials are the wider canvas.
europmc-pmc8995029:
Pulliam and co-authors test whether Omicron raised the risk of catching SARS-CoV-2 a second time in South Africa. The country had logged over 3.6 million confirmed cases by early 2022. Four waves had swept through. The team built two ways to spot reinfection trends in routine data. They then asked whether each variant era changed the risk. Beta and Delta eras showed no rise in reinfection risk. Omicron's arrival told a different story.

Reinfections rose once Omicron took hold. People from all three earlier waves caught it again. The risk of a third infection climbed from mid-November 2021. The pattern points to immune evasion by the variant. Prior infection alone protected less than before. The authors call this population-level evidence. Their monitoring methods can watch future variants too. Surveillance data, used well, flags escape early.
europmc-pmc9605829:
De Almeida and co-authors set out the basics of reactive oxygen species and their part in ageing. These molecules form as byproducts of cell metabolism. They were long cast as pure agents of damage. Their signaling role is now clear as well.

The review covers the chemistry of the main species first. Superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals are named. It then maps where cells make them, inside and out. The antioxidant system that holds them in check follows. As signals, the species steer inflammation and cell growth. They also help decide cell death calls. Balance of sources and defenses sets cell fate, they stress. The last part weighs their dual effect on ageing. Early on they may trigger repair responses that aid survival. Past a point, they pile on damage instead.
europmc-pmc9935929:
Ding and co-authors survey signaling pathways in rheumatoid arthritis as guides to targeted therapy. Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease with no cure. Its course deforms joints, cuts function, and lowers quality of life. Abnormal signaling sits at the core of its pathology.

The review opens with disease history, spread, risk factors, and disease course. It then covers genetic and epigenetic factors in depth. Primary pathways and molecular routes are set out one by one. New pathways and fresh inhibitors get special attention. Approved, clinical, and pre-clinical drugs are all reviewed. The authors hope this map speeds new targeted options. Readers gain both disease grounding and a therapy pipeline view.
faulkner-sartoris-1929:
Sartoris, published in 1929, was the first of William Faulkner's novels set in Yoknapatawpha County. The county and its town of Jefferson, Mississippi, would anchor most of his later work. At the center stands the Sartoris family, proud, brave, and haunted by its own past.

Old Bayard Sartoris and his grandson, young Bayard, carry the family name into a changed age. Young Bayard, back from the war, courts danger with fast cars and planes. Legends of a dashing Civil War ancestor hang over them both. Faulkner here began his great theme: a South unable to escape its history, told in rich, layered prose.
faulkner-sound-and-fury-1929:
William Faulkner published The Sound and the Fury in 1929, a novel about the fall of the Compson family in Mississippi. Four sections give four views of the same troubled house. Benjy, who has severe mental disabilities, opens the book with memories in no set order. Quentin, a Harvard student, tells the second part.

Jason, bitter and cruel, narrates the third part with biting clarity. The last part follows Dilsey, the family's Black servant, whose faith endures. At the center stands Caddy, the sister all three brothers loved and lost. Faulkner's bold method broke new ground in fiction. The novel is now a peak of American modernism.
formation-of-the-union-1750-1829:
Albert Bushnell Hart's Formation of the Union, 1750-1829, is the second volume of the Epochs of American History series. Hart studies causes rather than events, tracing how scattered and inharmonious colonies grew into an American nation.

The volume follows the break from English control, the move beyond narrow colonial politics, resistance to foreign rule, and the spread of popular government. Maps carry much of the matter into graphic form, and suggestions for readers and teachers head each chapter. Hart notes that although the book includes three serious wars, it contains no military history. Students of American origins will find it a compact, thoughtful survey.
fortune-sane-occultism-1929:
Clear thought and occult study belong together: that is Dion Fortune's case in Sane Occultism, printed in 1929. The book defends a rational path through a field full of fraud and fog. Fortune writes against credulity as much as against cold denial.

She tells how to test teachers, weigh claims, and keep one's feet while studying strange things. Her rules grow from her work as nurse, student, and lodge head over many years. The book is the manifesto of her no-nonsense school of study. It still reads as a sane friend in a field that needs one.
frus-1861-d129:
A letter dated 8 June 1861 went from William H. Seward to William Dayton in Paris. The letter is document 129 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's June orders to Paris dealt with the terms of French neutrality as it took form. Every clause on trade and ships could help or hurt the South. The letter armed Dayton to contest the details, not just the headline, of the French stand. Details of trade and ships filled most of the case the Union made in Paris. Contest the details he did, in note after note through the French file.
frus-1861-d229:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Fogg on 6 August 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 229 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d29:
A letter dated 8 July 1861 went from William H. Seward to Henry Sanford in Brussels. It is document 29 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid July found the Union army about to march on Richmond, with high hopes at home. Seward's letters abroad in those weeks spoke with bold faith in a short war. This note to Brussels belongs to that brief season of hope before Bull Run changed the mood. Hopes of a ninety day war still lived in Washington when this letter went out. The bold tone of July reads now as the last glow of a brief hope.
frus-1862-d129:
A State Department letter of 15 August 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 129 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d229:
F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State. He wrote to William Stuart on 1 September 1862, in a letter printed as Document 229 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was then acting head of the British legation in Washington.

The note came two days after the Union defeat at Bull Run, when Washington braced for an attack that never came. That the Department's work ran on, signed by the assistant secretary, shows the machine-like pace of the file. Small notes like this one kept formal business moving while the government absorbed a major loss. Lyons also reported home on each note, so most of these papers exist in two archives.
frus-1862-d29:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Charles Francis Adams, dated 1 March 1862. Congress received it as Document 29 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d329:
On 23 September 1862 William L. Dayton reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Paris, in a letter printed as Document 329 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Dayton wrote the day after Lincoln announced emancipation, though the news had not yet reached France. His report thus closes the Paris file's old era: within days. The proclamation's text would give him a new argument and French workers a new sympathy for the Union. The letter's date makes it a marker between two phases of the war abroad. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d429:
Gabriel García Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington, received this reply from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 June 1862. The note is Document 429 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

A secretary's answer to a resident minister was diplomacy at its most direct: one government speaking to another across a Washington desk. The Spanish exchange of 1862 touched Cuba, Mexico, and the rights of ships and trade in wartime. Seward's manner in these notes was studied calm, meant to keep Spain correct and neutral. Read after Tassara's note of late May, the reply shows the give and take of that careful relationship.
frus-1862-d529:
On 7 June 1862 Roest van Limburg sent a further note to Secretary of State William H. Seward from the Netherlands legation in Washington. It is Document 529 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Three Dutch notes in three days mark the June exchange as a matter handled in pieces. Each letter took up its own paper or point. Diplomatic practice required nothing less. The Netherlands guarded its carrying trade and its colonial ports with care. Van Limburg's task was to see Dutch rights respected. The power he faced was a blockading one. Seward, for his part, needed Dutch goodwill. The note is one turn in a formal conversation whose speed shows how seriously both sides took it.
frus-1862-d629:
On 25 October 1861 Edward Joy Morris reported from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 629 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Morris's autumn report covered the state of American interests at the sultan's court in the months before the Trent crisis broke. The Ottoman Empire, courted by Britain, France, and Russia alike, heard of the American war as a distant thunder. His letters kept Washington informed of the small real business of the post. They also gave Seward a reading, however refracted, of the great-power struggle in the Near East. That struggle touched American trade in the Mediterranean at every point.
frus-1863p1-d129:
On a day the pens crossed at sea, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 26 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London, and Adams letters of the same date sit right after this one in the volume. The letter is document 129 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote on a day when the pens would cross on the sea once more. His letter fed Adams the line for the points then live: the ships, the claims, the tone to hold with Lord Russell. It opens a same-date cluster in the file. Read with the Adams sheets that share its date, it shows the exchange running at full speed in late March.
frus-1863p1-d229:
The State Department's mail for London dated 6 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 229 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d29:
On 14 January 1863, William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 29 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward wrote on back-to-back days in this stretch of the file.

Close-spaced letters from the secretary often meant fresh news to pass on or a point to press harder. For London, the standing points were Britain's fair dealing and the warships being built in its yards for Southern buyers. This letter kept that pressure on. Read in line, it is one more turn of the screw in a file that never let up.
frus-1863p1-d329:
A note dated 27 November 1862 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 329 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Lyons reported each exchange to Lord John Russell in London. What he wrote to Seward, and what Seward answered, shaped British choices about the war. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d429:
On 28 March 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d529:
On 22 May 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d629:
Document 629 in the volume is a letter of 9 October 1863 from William H. Seward to William Stuart. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. With Lyons away from Washington, Stuart kept the British side of the correspondence going through the autumn of 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d129: Stephen Early, the President's secretary, wrote on November 15, 1943 to Secretaries Hull, Stimson, and Knox and to the head of the Secret Service. The letter is Document 129 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Early ran the White House's paper and press work, and letters in his name often carried the orders that moved whole departments. The record names the five men and the date. Its errand is in the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d229:
Paper C.C.S. 300/3, issued by the United States Chiefs of Staff aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943. It is a long estimate of the enemy situation in Europe for 1944, based on the picture as of 1 November. At some thirty-nine thousand characters, it is one of the longest papers in this part of the volume.

Its verdict is mixed. Germany is strained, on the defensive everywhere, short of fit manpower, and unable to shield her industry or her land fronts from Allied bombing. Yet her forces remain strong, skilled, and able to recover if pressure eases. The forecast sees Berlin standing on the defensive, seeking a split among her enemies, and suing for peace only when stalemate and a bargained peace both fail.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d29: Roosevelt opened September with a letter to Stalin on September 4, 1943, preserved as Document 29 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The autumn would bring the foreign ministers to Moscow and then the leaders to Cairo and Tehran, and this correspondence laid the track. The record states the date and the two names only. The letter's text, printed in the Foreign Relations volume, must supply its own subject.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d329:
President Roosevelt telegraphed Secretary of State Cordell Hull from Cairo on 26 November 1943 about civil affairs planning for France. Answering Hull's message of 24 November, he states flatly that this is not the time for final decisions or plans on that subject.

The North African situation is complicated, Roosevelt writes. De Gaulle's conduct in the Lebanon affair shows the Committee's temper. De Gaulle now claims the right to speak for all France. He talks openly of setting up his government there once the Allies land. Roosevelt leans instead toward a wholly military occupation of France. He sees no need for further discussion now, doubts the Russians will press for action, and hopes to hold the whole matter up with Churchill's help until the picture clears.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d429: Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Averell Harriman, still at Tehran, a secret telegram of triple priority from Cairo on 2 December 1943. The President has wired Steinhardt that day, Hopkins reports. Steinhardt is to assure President Inönü that he is invited to Cairo for a free discussion as between equals. Transport planes will be waiting at Adana on 4 December. Harriman is to see Molotov at once to make certain the Russian representatives are in Cairo that morning, and to advise Cairo of the answer.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d529:
Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek wrote to President Roosevelt on December 23, 1943. A month earlier Chiang had met Roosevelt and Churchill at Cairo, and the Cairo Declaration had promised China the return of lands seized by Japan. Since then, plans for joint operations in Burma had been cut back. The State Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Chiang's letters to Roosevelt often pressed China's needs with a sense of grievance, and December 1943 gave him cause: promises made at Cairo were already being trimmed by decisions taken at Tehran. For readers, the message shows the fourth ally's voice, less heard than the Big Three but impossible to ignore.
frus-1944-quebec-d129:
Polish Prime Minister Stanisław Mikołajczyk wrote directly to Roosevelt on September 10, 1944, in a letter also sent to Churchill. Reports from Warsaw, he said, showed the situation was desperate. The fight against overwhelming German power might end at any moment unless help came from outside, and London still had not decided on a large relief operation.

Mikołajczyk begged for a bold, immediate decision: bomb German concentrations and drop supplies to the Home Army together. A favorable decision delayed might come too late. He warned that if the rising were crushed without a last attempt at rescue, the tragedy would cast a deep, lasting shadow over Polish trust in its Western allies.
frus-1944-quebec-d229:
The Joint Chiefs answered Hull's Norway letter on September 12, 1944, enclosing the instructions already sent to General Deane. The enclosed Combined Chiefs telegram of August 30 ordered early military conversations with the Soviet General Staff about occupying Norway when German forces withdrew. The object was restoring the legal Norwegian government in full control as early as possible.

The plans distinguished two cases. Under Rankin B, an organized German withdrawal, forces would first occupy points such as Finnmark, Tromsø or Narvik, and Trondheim. Under Rankin C, a German surrender, southern Norway came first. The Soviets were invited to concert their plans, and to accept the Norwegian military attaché in the talks. A background enclosure admits no agreement made Norway a British-American sphere.
frus-1944-quebec-d29:
Harry Hopkins sent a message to Churchill on August 23, 1944. It was one of several staff-level exchanges that week. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Hopkins did much of the alliance's quiet work. He confirmed plans and tested ideas. He also prepared the leaders' meeting. He did so without committing either government. His August messages to Churchill cluster around the Quebec Conference. For readers, this one shows a summit being assembled. The work fell to a man both leaders trusted. He spoke plainly and kept confidences completely. The alliance was then passing from liberation to endgame.
frus-1945-50-intel-d129:
Vandenberg wrote to Braden, assistant secretary for American republic affairs, on 9 October 1946. The letter returns to Latin America, the field the summer's fight had divided. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

After rulings come arrangements: stations handed over, files shared, and men reassigned. Vandenberg writing to the State Department's Latin American chief shows the CIG settling into the hemisphere under the new terms. Readers should pair this letter with Hoover's July approach to Braden. Both chiefs courted the same regional secretary, before the ruling and after it. His bureau's favor could ease or sour the division on the ground.
frus-1945-50-intel-d229: On 22 October 1947 a memorandum went forward for Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. It stands as document 229 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work. A record memo speaks to the future reader more than to any chief: it exists so the file tells the truth later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d29:
General Magruder of the Strategic Services Unit wrote to Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy on 20 October 1945. McCloy was the War Department's senior civilian for such questions and Magruder's chief patron there. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The SSU lived on borrowed time and borrowed money, and its chief had to keep the War Department persuaded that it deserved both. Letters to McCloy were Magruder's lifeline. Readers can hear in them the tone of a man defending a remnant: proud of its wartime record, frank about its needs. The unit's survival through 1946, against the odds, is one of the volume's quiet stories, and papers like this one explain it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d329:
A memorandum dated 12 November 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Global Survey Group, Central Intelligence Agency (Montague). The reader was the Assistant Director for Reports and Estimates (Babbit). Readers meet it as document 329 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d429:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 10 was issued on 18 January 1949. It stands as document 429 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Reaching double numbers shows how far the rule book had grown in just over a year. Each added directive dealt with a task the founders had not fully foreseen. For readers tracing the growth of the CIA, these short orders mark the points where practice forced the rules to change. New tasks in the series ranged from shared reports to the guarding of secret sources. The growth in numbers shows a state learning how wide its secret needs had grown.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d129:
Severe, but run as one economy: that sums up the State Department's line in this 22 November 1944 summary for the President. Stettinius forwarded the paper, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, for use when Roosevelt redrafted his own memorandum on Germany's economic treatment.

The Department holds that the German economy should be run as nearly one unit as possible during the occupation. Policy should still be severe. Germans would live at a rock-bottom standard and furnish labor to rebuild the devastated parts of Europe. Factory gear and stockpiles would go to freed countries, as far as a minimum German economy allows. Men tied closely to the Nazi regime would be cleared from control of industry and finance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d229:
Iran has shelved all oil concession talks until the war ends, Ambassador Morris cabled from Tehran on 10 October 1944. His short secret telegram, number 749, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It is one line of news with a long shadow.

The Iranian prime minister, Morris reports, confirmed the postponement to him the night before. He was at once informing the Soviet representatives in Tehran of the decision. The representatives of the American and British oil companies then in the capital heard the same word. The freeze hit three rival hunts for Iranian oil at one stroke. It also set up the quarrel with Moscow that runs through the papers which follow.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d29: One day later, on 15 December 1944, Harriman sent Roosevelt a second report from Moscow. Filed as document 29 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, it continues his December reporting from the Soviet capital. Two reports on consecutive days suggest fast-moving business, and together they show the flow of information reaching the president just before the German Ardennes attack.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d329:
At 5 p.m. on February 4, 1945, the Yalta Conference opened in full session, and Charles Bohlen's minutes record it. Stalin asked Roosevelt to open the meeting. The President replied that his doing so, as at Tehran, rested on chance, not law or custom. He thanked his hosts for their care and splendid arrangements.

Roosevelt said the people he spoke for wanted peace above all, and the war ended as soon as it could be. He added that the three powers understood each other better now than in the past, month by month. The subject for the session was the military situation. Bohlen gives readers the ceremony and the substance together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d429:
Three powers, not four, proclaim the Declaration on Liberated Europe in this American text of February 9, 1945. The Soviet Premier, the British Prime Minister, and the American President declare their mutual agreement. During the temporary period of instability in liberated Europe, they will concert the policies of their three governments.

The aim is to help peoples freed from Nazi domination, and peoples of the former Axis satellite states, solve their pressing problems by democratic means. Order in Europe and the rebuilding of economic life stand as the stated goals. This text became the conference's most quoted promise — and, in time, its most argued-over one.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d129:
Robert Murphy accepted his invitation to the conference in a telegram from Hoechst on July 7, 1945. The brief message is document 129 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Secretary Byrnes had invited him two days earlier and asked him to arrange housing for the State Department party of thirty-six, due in Berlin on July 13.

Murphy thanks the Secretary for the invitation to attend the meeting of the three heads of government. He reports that he and General Clay are leaving for Berlin that morning. They will do everything possible to make sure the delegation's arrangements are satisfactory. He hopes to telegraph an account of the situation the next day. The reply set the advance work in Berlin in motion under the two Americans closest to the ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d229:
Naval aide George Elsey reminded the President's staff of Stalin's peace conference talk in a memorandum submitted July 1, 1945. The short note is document 229 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It was sent to Admiral Leahy and forwarded to Truman.

On two occasions during Harry Hopkins's recent visit to Moscow, Elsey writes, Stalin stressed the importance of planning at once for the peace conference on Europe. Stalin was apparently thinking of a formal conference. He referred to Versailles, where he said the Allies had not been properly prepared, and called that a mistake that should not be made again. Hopkins reported that Stalin would discuss arrangements for a peace conference at the Berlin meeting. The note set up a contrast with Washington's own plan for a council of foreign ministers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d29:
Hopkins took his leave of the Far East file at the sixth Kremlin conversation, on June 6, 1945, in Bohlen's memorandum. He asked whether Stalin had further comments for the President on the Far East, or whether all aspects had been covered. Stalin replied that the Soviet government intended to carry out the Crimea decision. It was not their habit, he said, to fail in commitments without special necessity.

Poland, voting procedure in the world body, Red Cross representatives for Poland, Hitler, a heads-of-state meeting, and General Eisenhower fill the subject list. The extract breaks off as Stalin asked whether a date had been set. The mission ended with the Pacific promise renewed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d329:
Lasting economic and industrial limits on Germany are weighed in an undated briefing book paper. It restates firm American pledges first: complete military disarmament, a ban on making arms, ammunition, and aircraft, and the destruction or removal of plants built for war work. Washington also favored wide removal of factory equipment as reparations.

Beyond that, the paper counsels care. The United States should accept no lasting or open-ended limits on the German economy at this stage. Studies of the problem were still under way, and the government did not want to prejudge their findings. The paper marks the line between disarming Germany and crippling her for good.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d429:
Berlin's four-power government takes shape in Murphy's cable from Hoechst of July 7, 1945. A second meeting of the Berlin Kommandatura had been held that afternoon at Marshal Zhukov's headquarters. Zhukov presided, with his staff; General Clay and General Weeks represented the American and British control groups, and Murphy attended.

The meeting discussed practical aspects of occupying Berlin and organizing the Kommandatura. Its agenda covered the status of each nationality in its own sector, and joint, common policies for military government across greater Berlin. It also set coordination at three levels, from regular meetings of the sector commanders down through their chief military government officers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d529:
Russian observations on the local surrender in Italy are handled in a Combined Civil Affairs Committee report dated July 8, 1945. The report considers an enclosure from the Supreme Allied Commander, Mediterranean, and frames recommendations to the Combined Chiefs of Staff. The enclosure carried a letter from the Soviet representative on the Allied Commission in Italy.

That letter referred to the surrender orders given to the German commander in chief in the southwest. The Soviet representative requested the return of all Soviet citizens who had fallen into German hands, and of all war material of Soviet origin. A partial reply by the supreme commander accompanied it. The Combined Chiefs, a later note records, approved the committee's recommendation and dispatched its message to Alexander.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d629:
State Department staff wrote a top secret briefing paper on Anglo-Soviet rivalry in Iran, filed June 17, 1945. It is document 629 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It urges that the United States itself open debate on the problem at Potsdam.

The paper warns that pulling Allied troops out of Iran would help, but would not solve the whole problem. British and Russian rivalry there, largely covert, is splitting the country fast. The Russians back leftist, socialist, and labor groups, it says. The British back the conservative landowners and old elites. That split is wrecking Iran's government and economy in turn. Left unchecked, the paper warns, Iran could disturb world peace as the Dardanelles did in the last century.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1029: Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Winant in London on July 18, 1945, about the French sector of Berlin. American and British military authorities in Germany agree, he reports. The French area will be formed from the existing British and American areas of the city. As soon as the British member of the European Advisory Commission gets like instructions, Winant may act. He is authorized to accept a Soviet proposal for the final sentence of the report that accompanies the French zone agreement, and to conclude that agreement.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1129:
Experts from the three teams made up the Subcommittee on Poland, and its report is dated 21 July 1945. Poland was among the hardest questions at Potsdam. The summit had to fix where the country's western border would run and what sort of state it would be.

A working group like this one thrashed out the details so the foreign ministers, and then the leaders, could decide. Its report fed straight into the choices the Big Three made on Poland. Those choices shaped the map of Europe for decades. The report is the staff paper behind one of the summit's most fateful bargains.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1229:
Togo wrote to Sato on 21 July 1945, steering the Moscow errand from Tokyo. The foreign minister's instructions kept the bid alive: press the Soviets, seek a hearing, hold out for terms that spared the throne. Tokyo's ruling circle was split, and Togo spoke for those seeking an end.

His cables show a government trying to bargain its way out of a lost war. The Allies, reading the traffic in secret, could watch the split in Tokyo's mind as it formed. This message is the home end of the exchange. It carries the hopes that Sato's cold reports kept failing to feed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1329:
A second Murray dispatch from Iran bears the date 20 July 1945. Two reports in a day from Tehran show a post with much to tell. The ambassador split his subjects across the pair as the occupation's frictions demanded.

Iran's north, held by Soviet troops, was the sore point. When those troops would leave, and what they would leave behind, worried every Western post in the region. Murray's twin cables belong to that watching brief. This one is the day's companion piece. Read together, they give the summit-week picture of a land that would soon test the peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1429:
The British delegation tabled a text on 30 July 1945, answering the pace set by Soviet submissions in the same days. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Summit drafting was a contest of paper, and late July saw all three sides feeding texts into the mill. A British text at this stage shows London still shaping the bargain's wording, where a phrase could ease or harden the peace. Readers can set it between the Soviet run nearby and the closing protocol. The three together show the settlement being written in real time, by rival hands, in the conference's final forty-eight hours.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-129: Printed without a number after document 710, this editorial note is part of the second Potsdam volume's editorial frame. The Foreign Relations historians wrote such notes to keep readers from losing the thread. They point to sources, name linked papers, and note where the file runs out. The note supports the record around it rather than adding a new voice.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-29:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the July 19, 1945 plenary session open with the Greek frontier incident. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen's compressed record runs parallel to Thompson's fuller minutes of the same session.

Churchill reports his inquiries into the trouble Stalin had raised. No fighting had been heard of, but sniping there was, and the peoples disliked each other. No Greek field division stood in the north, while far more troops lined the far side of the frontier. Small states, he insists, must be told that marauding across frontiers will not be tolerated. Frontiers will be settled by the peace conference. Truman backs the point in one line: such matters are for the conference, not for direct action. Stalin then distances himself from the topic. He raised it privately, he says, not at this meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d729:
A subcommittee on admission to the United Nations considered this text at Potsdam on July 20, 1945. Document 729 comes from the conference's work on the new world body. The United Nations charter had been signed weeks earlier in San Francisco. Which states would join, and on what terms, was now a live question.

Admission questions mixed law with politics. Each applicant raised the balance between the great powers. Readers see the conference acting as midwife to the new order, not only judge of the old. The text shows Potsdam's reach: the same men dividing Germany also framed the club that would outlast them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d829:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal on July 31, 1945, as document 829. It came on the last full day of the Potsdam Conference. Soviet drafters pressed their claims to the final hour. The text joined the closing papers of the second Potsdam volume.

A last-day Soviet text shows what Moscow refused to drop. Readers can read the final protocol against it, line by line. The matches show its wins; the gaps show its limits. The document balances the American last-day draft in this run. Together they frame the settlement's final trades, each side's ask preserved in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d929:
Edwin Pauley sent President Truman a staff report on Russian machinery removals from Berlin, with his letter of July 25, 1945. Two of his aides, Luther Gulick and J. Howard Marshall, drove through the city on July 22 and 23. Their report describes what they saw at rail yards, docks, and factory districts.

Yards serving the south stood nearly bare, while lines to the east ran four to eight tracks and bustled. Warehouses along the Spree were packed with machine tools, motors, and printing presses awaiting shipment. Work crews in Russian uniform loaded flat cars around the clock. Crating advanced visibly in a single day between the two visits.
frus-1969-76v29:
Volume XXIX of the 1969-1976 series joins Eastern Europe with the Eastern Mediterranean, for 1969-1972. Chapters open with general policy and the radios, Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty. Country chapters follow for Austria, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Finland, Hungary, Poland, Romania, and Yugoslavia. The second half treats Greece, Cyprus, and Turkey. Greece takes the largest share of that half.

The papers show small steps toward trade and travel with the East. Romania and Yugoslavia again draw the most interest. In the Mediterranean chapters, the Greek junta and the Cyprus question dominate. The volume links two regions where the Cold War ran at low heat.
gao-gaoreports-b-296029:
Poly-Pacific Technologies protested a change to an Air Force contract in GAO decision B-296029, dated June 1, 2005. The deal was held by U.S. Technology Corporation. It covered the lease and reuse of acrylic plastic media. The firm said the change eased the work past what the first contest had set.

GAO sustained the protest. The change did shift the scope of work. It went past what bidders could have seen in the first call for bids. That made the change improper. The ruling helps readers spot when a contract change is so large that a fresh contest was due.
gao-gaoreports-b-299929:
AlliedBarton Security Services protested a Federal Emergency Management Agency task order in New Orleans, Louisiana. The order went to Inner Parish Security Corporation for armed guard services. The guards watch FEMA housing sites. GAO ruled in the B-299929 series on October 9, 2007.

Eligibility turned on the Stafford Act. That law favors firms that reside or do business chiefly in the set area. The agency found the firm did not meet that test for Louisiana. GAO found that call fair. A second claim hit the winner's own eligibility. The firm lacked standing for that point. A third vendor stood next in line in any case. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-304829:
Claims about a writer who reused White House press releases fill this GAO decision, B-304829, dated June 6, 2005. James D. Guckert was said to have copied long parts of the releases. He put them in his own news work with no credit to the source. The claim was that this broke the ban on funds for publicity or propaganda.

GAO held that the claims, even if true, show no breach of the ban. Guckert acted alone as a private citizen. The ban binds agencies that spend public funds. It does not reach a private writer who copies public releases. The ruling marks a limit of the propaganda ban. It helps readers sort agency acts from private acts.
gao-gaoreports-b-307529:
Who may forgive bad pay to a Capitol Police worker is answered in this GAO opinion, B-307529, dated March 28, 2006. The force seems to have paid a worker in breach of the anti-nepotism law. A past law moved many pay tasks to the police Chief. The Senate Rules Committee asked if the power to forgive such pay moved too.

GAO held that it did not. The power to forgive bad pay is not part of a disbursing officer's tasks. Such power must be spelled out in law. It stays with the Speaker of the House and the Secretary of the Senate, who share it. GAO urged Congress to fix the shared setup to cut clash and waste.
gao-gaoreports-b-310329:
Blane International Group, Inc. lost its protest. GAO ruled in B-310329 on December 13, 2007. The Army sought nonstandard ammunition for Afghan and Iraqi forces. The award went to GSS, Inc. on a low-price, fit-to-serve basis. Three work plans drove the fit test. One was the ship and delivery plan. Blane said talks on its plan were not frank.

GAO denied the protest. The agency told Blane its plan was hard to read and hard to track. That word put the firm on fair notice of the flaw. Talks need not spell out each fix. A clear flag of the weak spot can be frank enough.
gao-gaoreports-b-311329:
Alliance Technical Services, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-311329, dated May 30, 2008. The firm said talks on its past work were not frank. It said the agency failed to weigh bids side by side for best value. The win bids in the race held the top tech marks. They held the low prices in the race as well. Alliance bid high in price and low in score.

GAO denied the protest. A top mark on the weak point would not lift the bid to a win. No harm can flow from talks that could not change the end. Top score at low price is a sound best-value pick.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-229:
Contract Management, GAO-05-229 of February 11, 2005, looks for slack in how the government strikes prices on a vast buy list. Agencies can buy over 8 million goods and services off General Services Administration schedule deals. Sales on those deals leapt from $4 billion to $32 billion in ten years. The list should turn bulk buy power into low prices.

Past probes found weak price tools and thin checks at the agency. GAO walks through how it haggles for best-customer prices now. It checks fresh steps to lift the craft of those talks. Chances to sharpen pricing sit in plain view, the title says.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-329:
Cooperative Threat Reduction, GAO-05-329 of June 30, 2005, grades how the Pentagon runs a plan to shrink the arms threat from the old Soviet stock. Law for fiscal year 2004 told GAO to test the plan's inner checks and their mark on the work. GAO used the federal rule book for such checks as its yard. It weighed work since 2003.

Six fields drew the close look: team shape, risk checks, feat marks, plan reviews, talk flow, and site watch. The verdict splits. Grip and checks have grown firm, the title grants. Hard tests stay, from work in far lands to proof that each gain will hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-429:
Aligning VA hospitals and clinics with the care veterans will need is the topic of GAO-05-429, a report GAO issued on August 5, 2005. The Department of Veterans Affairs runs one of the largest health systems in the country. Its CARES process set where inpatient services would be offered through fiscal year 2022. GAO examined three hard problems VA still faced in finishing and carrying out that plan.

VA lacked the data needed to settle alignment choices for long-term care and mental health care. It also lacked that data for inpatient services at 12 facilities. Its demand models were not yet able to forecast need well. VA also held 8.5 million square feet of vacant space, and disposal rules made excess property hard to shed. A third problem was setting priorities for buying care from outside providers. The report shows where the realignment effort stood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-829:
Great Lakes water standards are the focus of GAO-05-829, issued July 27, 2005. The United States and Canada share a goal: near-zero toxic pollution in the lakes. Levels remain too high. A joint initiative sets strict discharge standards for many pollutants. States run the permit programs that carry them out. GAO checked the initiative's reach, state uptake, and federal steps to ensure full and even use.

Section headings tell the story. The initiative has limited power to lift overall water quality. States have mostly adopted its standards into their rules. But measuring some pollutants at such low levels is a real challenge. The environmental agency has not ensured even use across states, GAO found. It also has not taken fit steps to measure progress toward the goals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-929:
Concierge medical care and Medicare is the subject of GAO-05-929, a report from August 12, 2005. In this model, doctors charge patients a membership fee for extra services and perks. A 2003 law told GAO to study the model and its Medicare links. Fears include fees that charge twice for care Medicare already pays for. Access for Medicare patients is the other fear. GAO found 146 concierge doctors nationwide.

GAO surveyed those doctors in fall 2004 and analyzed replies from 112. The report lays out the model's traits: the features offered, the size of practices, and how many old patients joined. It records what doctors did to help patients who did not join find new care. It also records doctors' views on the guidance they get about Medicare rules. Readers can judge how far the model might press on beneficiary access.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1029:
Nuclear plant safety oversight is refined in GAO-06-1029, a report issued September 27, 2006. The regulator watches 103 commercial plants. A new oversight process began in 2000 to fix weaknesses in the old one. GAO reviewed how oversight works now. It studied 5 years of results under the new process. It also checked the status of efforts to improve the process further, using a sample of 11 plants.

Headings state the findings. The regulator takes a risk-informed, graded approach. It gathers inspection results and measures reported by plant owners. An action matrix sorts plants and scales oversight to performance. Low-risk problems have still triggered added oversight for varying spans. The regulator is fixing weaknesses in several areas, GAO found. More effort is needed, it said. A first major step tackles a known weakness: safety culture at plants.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-429:
The insurer behind private pensions must show its own finances clearly. Dated March 27, 2006, GAO-06-429 reviews the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation. Its single-employer program insures benefits for over 34 million participants. They sit in almost 29,000 private defined benefit plans. A rise in probable claims raised questions about the agency's monitoring and disclosures.

GAO checked steps the agency takes to track probable claims and ensure their accuracy. It compared the agency's liability reporting with that of public companies. It also reviewed steps to improve openness and whether more is needed. GAO found chances to improve transparency further. Readers get claim and reporting detail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-629:
Geothermal energy and its growth prospects are studied in GAO report GAO-06-629, dated May 24, 2006. Geothermal resources use heat from the earth to make power and to warm buildings directly. In 2004, they produced about 0.3 percent of the nation's electricity. They also supplied heat to about 2,300 businesses and groups, from greenhouses to spas. An industry group estimated that 1 million geothermal heat pumps were installed across the 50 states.

GAO found that growth would depend on beating many hurdles. High upfront drilling costs and the risk of dry wells held back new projects. Access to federal land, permits, and power lines also shaped the pace. The report weighs the promise of a clean, steady energy source against those barriers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-829:
Shared support services at embassies are the subject of GAO-06-829, the GAO report of September 8, 2006. The State Department keeps embassies in about 180 countries. The Agency for International Development runs missions in about 90 of them. At many posts, the two sit on separate compounds and run duplicate warehouses, motor pools, and other support shops. New embassy construction offered a chance to merge those operations. GAO judged the consolidation effort.

GAO found that the two agencies had merged some services and planned more mergers. Yet they faced real challenges in widening the effort. Old habits, cost-sharing disputes, and security rules all slowed progress. GAO said both agencies should adopt a comprehensive plan to improve consolidation. Shared services, done well, could free funds for diplomacy and aid work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-929:
Credit card rates and fees, and how well cardholders grasp them, are studied in GAO report GAO-06-929, dated September 12, 2006. Penalty rates and fees had grown common and more complex. The Federal Reserve had begun to revise the notices cardholders get.

GAO traced how fees and terms changed, and how holders felt the change. It tested how clearly firms state their pricing. It weighed how far penalty charges feed into bankruptcies, and it checked issuer income and profit. The work drew on six large issuers, cardholder talks, and user tests of notices. The report links fine print to real household cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1129:
New reactor licensing gears up at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, GAO reports in GAO-07-1129, dated September 21, 2007. Nearly three decades after the last new reactor order, power firms plan 20 bids in the next 18 months. Since 1989 the agency has built a joint license path, one grant to build and run, tied to standard designs.

GAO judged the agency's readiness for that wave. It checked workforce plans and work load care. It read the rule frame and review steps for new reactors. It spoke with agency chiefs and near all bidders, and sat in on public meets. Staff and steps are largely in place, GAO found, but doubts remain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-29:
Credit unions pay no federal income tax, yet their members skew richer than bank customers. GAO probed that tension in GAO-07-29, a report dated November 30, 2006. A 1998 law widened who can join a credit union. GAO studied membership trends and regulator outreach to poorer households. It compared rates at like-sized banks and credit unions. It also checked how openly top pay is disclosed.

Only 31 percent of credit union customers were of modest means, GAO found. Banks served 41 percent in that class. Credit union customers' median income hit $50,000 in 2004. Bank customers' median was $43,000. The upper-income share of credit union customers rose from 43 percent to 49 percent between 2001 and 2004. The regulator's push to serve poorer members showed mixed reach. Pay for credit union chiefs stays far less visible than bank pay. GAO urged fuller public reporting on both fronts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-629:
Old audit advice to the tax agency is scored in GAO-07-629, a GAO report issued June 7, 2007. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) collects over $2 trillion in taxes each year. It handles hundreds of millions of returns. GAO has audited its books since fiscal year 1992. Each audit year brings fresh findings and a check on the old ones.

This volume is the scorecard. It lists each past recommendation and the state of the fix. It ties each item to the control habits the agency needs for its core work. GAO adds no new advice here. The point is tracking: managers can see at a glance what is done, what lags, and what each lag risks. For Congress, the report turns a pile of past audits into one map of a giant agency's slow repair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-729:
Checks on foreign airports and airlines fill GAO-07-729, a report GAO issued on May 11, 2007. The Transportation Security Administration grades security at airports abroad. It also inspects airlines that fly to the United States. The alleged August 2006 liquid explosives plot showed why the work matters. GAO reviewed the results of the checks. It tracked what the agency did when it found flaws. It also judged the agency's own oversight of the program.

Of 128 foreign airports checked in fiscal year 2005, 46 met all world security standards. The other 82 missed at least one standard. Quality control was the most common gap. Access control and screening of passengers and bags were key weak points. When needed, the Homeland Security chief took action against those that fell short. GAO told the agency to track its data better. It also urged measures based on results, not just activity counts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-29:
Ground safety at airports is graded in GAO report GAO-08-29, issued November 20, 2007. Runway incursions peaked in fiscal year 2001, then eased as the aviation agency pushed a safety plan. Early data for fiscal year 2007 show the rate near that peak again. About 30 serious incursions, where a crash was barely averted, still occur each year. Ramp areas, where planes are loaded and serviced, add their own toll.

The agency had finished or started 34 of 39 steps in its 2002 plan. Weak leadership, data gaps, and slow technology blunt further gains. Ramp safety lacks even basic standards, GAO found. Sustained effort is the title's demand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-529:
Death reviews in Medicaid home care are examined in GAO report GAO-08-529, dated May 23, 2008. Media reports have tied deaths of people with developmental disabilities to poor care under state waiver programs. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services approves and watches these waivers.

All 14 states GAO interviewed treat such deaths as critical incidents that providers must report. All but one state use most of six basic review parts named by experts, though some review only sudden deaths and others review all deaths. Reviews run locally and drive fixes such as targeted training. Thirteen of the 14 states roll death data together; one region spotted more choking deaths and taught families prevention. GAO urged the agency to push reviews in all states. The health department partly answered.
givry-musee-des-sorciers-1929:
Émile-Jules Grillot de Givry published Le Musée des sorciers, mages et alchimistes in French in 1929. The title calls the book a museum of sorcerers, mages, and alchemists, and the word museum fits. Givry gathered images and records the way a keeper gathers objects for display.

The result is a visual and written history of the grimoire tradition, the spell books passed down from the Middle Ages. Plates and documents fill the pages alongside Givry's accounts of the men who made and used them. The survey runs from medieval times toward the 1700s. Few single books show the look of the old magic world so fully.
guazzo-compendium-maleficarum-1929:
Francesco Maria Guazzo, a Milanese friar, first published the Compendium Maleficarum in 1608 as a handbook on witchcraft. The English text here is Montague Summers's translation of 1929. Guazzo gathered what courts and church writers of his day believed about witches, pacts with the Devil, and how such crimes should be proved and punished.

Pages sort witches into kinds, describe night gatherings and harmful spells, and list signs judges might use at trial. Cures, prayers, and exorcism close the work. Few books show the logic of the witch trials so fully, which makes it grim but key reading for that era of fear.
hegel-science-logic-johnston-vol-1-1929:
G. W. F. Hegel published his Science of Logic between 1812 and 1816, his most rigorous work. Volume 1 appears here in the 1929 translation by W. H. Johnston and L. G. Struthers. The Logic studies pure thought itself, starting from being and nothing. Categories unfold by dialectic, each giving rise to the next.

Volume 1 covers the Doctrine of Being and the start of the Doctrine of Essence. Quality, quantity, and measure receive long and careful treatment. Hegel meant the work to replace the formal logic of his day. Later dialectical theories all answer to it in some way. It is the hardest core of his system.
hegel-science-logic-johnston-vol-2-1929:
G. W. F. Hegel's Science of Logic reaches completion in Volume 2, given here in the same 1929 translation. This volume finishes the Doctrine of Essence and adds the Doctrine of the Notion. Essence deals with ground, appearance, and actuality. The Notion deals with concepts, judgments, and the Idea itself.

Hegel argues that logic and reality share one deep structure. Thought, fully developed, arrives at the Absolute Idea. The prose is abstract to a degree few books match. Readers need patience and, ideally, help from guides. With Volume 1, the work states his system in its purest form. Philosophers still wrestle with its claims.
heindel-rosicrucian-cosmo-conception-192:
Max Heindel founded the American Rosicrucian movement on the scheme set out in The Rosicrucian Cosmo-Conception. First printed in 1909, the book is given here in its 1929 form. Heindel called his teaching mystic Christianity, a path of growth for the soul.

He maps the worlds seen and unseen, man's bodies, death, rebirth, and the long road of the spirit. Christ stands at the center of his scheme as the guide of the coming age. The book trains the student in a full system, step by step. It remains the founding text of Heindel's fellowship to this day.
hemingway-farewell-to-arms-1929:
Ernest Hemingway published A Farewell to Arms in 1929, his novel of the Italian front. An ambulance driver's desertion and doomed love with a British nurse give the war novel's classic its human center. Hemingway had served and been wounded on that front, and the book burns with firsthand knowledge of its world.

Frederic Henry, an American in Italy's ambulance service, loves Catherine Barkley, a nurse, amid hospitals and mountain drives in wartime. The Caporetto retreat, rendered in famous plain prose, scatters the army and nearly costs Henry his life by firing squad. He deserts, rows to Switzerland with Catherine, and their idyll ends in a childbirth death in the rain. The close, he walks back to the hotel in the rain, is American prose's most imitated shrug at fate. Its anti-war feeling and spare style fixed Hemingway's world reputation.
history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-babylonia:
Gaston Maspero's ninth volume tells of the Iranian conquest of the ancient east. Zoroaster's legends, laws, and the Avesta open the account. Cyrus then moves on Lydia and Babylon in turn. Cambyses carries Persian rule into Egypt itself.

Darius and the making of the empire close the arc. Satraps gather taxes and forward them to the royal treasury. Maspero retails the old saying on the three kings: Cyrus a father, Cambyses a master, Darius a pedlar. Sayce edited and McClure translated the set. Readers see Persia turn conquest into a working world empire.
hubble-distance-radial-velocity-1929:
Edwin Hubble, an American astronomer at Mount Wilson, published this short paper in 1929. He had already shown that fuzzy 'nebulae' are in fact galaxies far beyond our own. Now he compared their distances with the speeds at which they move away.

Hubble found a clear pattern: the farther a galaxy sits, the faster it recedes. That simple rule, now called Hubble's law, meant the universe is expanding. It gave Lemaître's theory hard proof from the sky. Modern measures of the age and size of the cosmos all start from this page. The paper is brief, but its graph changed astronomy for good.
husserl-formale-und-transzendentale-logi:
Edmund Husserl published Formal and Transcendental Logic in German in 1929. Husserl, teaching at Freiburg, had founded phenomenology, the study of how things appear to consciousness. Late in his career he returned to a question that had driven him from the start: what grounds logic itself?

The book distinguishes formal logic, the theory of consistent statements, from the deeper inquiry into how meaning arises in the mind that uses it. Husserl argues that logic cannot rest on symbols alone; it must be traced back to the acts of judgment that give symbols sense. The argument is dense and exacting, the capstone of a lifetime's thought. Scholars read it as phenomenology's mature statement on the foundations of reason, with meaning itself put under the microscope.
jeans-universe-around-us-1929:
James Jeans published The Universe Around Us in 1929, a popular account of modern astronomy. Jeans was a noted physicist and astronomer with a gift for clear prose. The book surveys the solar system, stars, nebulae, and the expanding universe. New findings on the size and age of the cosmos fill its pages.

Jeans writes for readers with no training in mathematics. He explains how light and spectra reveal the lives of stars. The final chapters ask what the new cosmos means for human life. The book sold science to millions in Britain and America. It helped define popular cosmology between the wars.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-29:
Antoine Daniel dies at St. Joseph in Volume 29, from 1898. Thwaites covers Iroquois attacks and French lands across 1647 and 1648 here. The great Iroquois assault on Huronia begins in earnest in these years.

Survivors record Daniel's death while the event is still fresh and raw. He stayed with his flock as the town burned around him. More attacks follow, and the reports read like a passion story. Grief and faith share the page as town after town falls to attack. The end of a world is near, and all can feel it. The mission's long Calvary opens in this grim, moving volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-b-bizna-12: Abba ben Bizna was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. The whole entry runs to two lines. He is mentioned now and then as a haggadist, that is, a teacher of the non-legal, story side of tradition. He also handed down certain halakic, or legal, opinions. One such line of his is cited from the Jerusalem Talmud, on Baba Kamma. No dates, place, teacher, or work of his is named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abeles-simon-22: Simon Abeles is named as a supposed martyr of the Roman Catholic Church in Prague. By the report of the Jesuit John Eder, he was killed by his father, Lazarus Abeles, on March 21, 1694. The boy, Eder says, held fast to his wish to take up the Christian faith. The father was jailed and strangled himself with his tefillin. Simon was buried with great pomp in the Teyn Church. The entry warns that Eder's report is one-sided.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-mont: Abraham of Montpellier commented on the greater part of the Talmud. His comments on Hullin and Ketubot are quoted by Jacob ben Moses of Bagnols, who wrote between 1357 and 1361, and by Menahem di Lonzano, of the late sixteenth century. He has been wrongly taken for the father of Solomon ben Abraham of Montpellier, the famed anti-Maimonist of the mid thirteenth century. Isaac de Lattes places Rabbi Abraham in the generation after Solomon, whose father is named without the rabbi title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrass-joshua-o: Joshua Osias Abrass, also called Pitzi, was a noted cantor born in Austria about 1820. He sang in Tarnopol from 1840 to 1842. He then served in Lemberg from 1842 to 1860. From 1860 to 1883 he was chief cantor of the great synagogue of Odessa, where he died in 1883. His hymns and songs for Sabbaths and feasts came out at Vienna in 1873. His daughter became a known Russian singer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-absalom-the-fat:
Absalom was the third son of King David. He was born in Hebron. His mother was Maachah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur. The entry tells how his half-brother Amnon wronged his sister Tamar. David did not punish Amnon. Two years later, at a feast, Absalom had his men kill Amnon. Absalom then fled to his grandfather in Geshur. He stayed there three years.

Joab helped bring Absalom back to Jerusalem. In time father and son made peace. Absalom used his good looks and charm to win the people. He rose in revolt and drove David out of the city. The entry follows the war from the Bible account. It then adds rabbinic views of his fate. Some say he has no share in the life to come. One tale still has a voice from heaven spare him as David's son.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achbor-mouse-72: Achbor is a name borne by two men in the Bible. The first was the father of Baal-hanan, king of Edom. His name is listed in Genesis xxxvi. 38 and 39. Some see in it a trace of totem belief, tied to finds of clay mice. The second Achbor was a son of Michaiah. King Josiah sent him to ask the prophetess Huldah about the found book of the law. He is also named as the father of Elnathan. A seal find backs his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-nathan-ma:
Nathan Marcus Adler was chief rabbi of the British empire. He was born at Hanover on January 15, 1803. He died at Brighton on January 21, 1890. He was the third son of Marcus Baer Adler, chief rabbi of Hanover. Born under the English crown, he held British status from birth. He read widely in Hebrew, classics, and modern tongues. He studied at four German schools of high rank.

In 1830 he became chief rabbi of Oldenburg. Within a year he held the same post at Hanover. London's chief rabbi died in 1842. A split in the flock made the choice of a heir a grave step. Fifteen men sought the post. Adler won, and took office on July 9, 1845. He worked first to lift Jewish schooling in England. Jews' College opened on November 11, 1855, with him as its first head. His books treat law, prayer, and old texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-ahai-i-929:
Aha I was a tanna of the second century and a junior contemporary of Simon ben Yohai, appearing with him and others of the fourth and fifth tannaitic generations in halakic disputations. He is best known as a halakist, though he also appears in Haggadah.

Commenting on Exodus xiv. 15, he has God tell Moses that Israel would be saved for Moses' sake, since without his prayers they would have been destroyed for idolatry. From Deuteronomy vi. 7 he derived a duty to keep set hours for studying Torah, rather than leaving study to chance opportunity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akiba-baer-ben-:
Akiba Baer ben Joseph was the son of Joseph Hanoks, a Talmudist and cabalistic writer. He was among the Jews driven from Vienna in 1670. The refugees settled in Bavaria to spread Talmudic learning there. Poor at first, he wandered as a teacher through Bohemia and parts of Germany. His learning and his preaching won him welcome everywhere.

He served six years as rabbi at Zeckendorf, near Bamberg. With Isaac Seligman he issued a small midrashic work, "Pi Shenayim," at Sulzbach in 1702. His chief fame rests on a cabalistic comment on the daily prayers. It appeared at Wilmersdorf in 1688, in five parts matching the letters of his name. Later posts took him to Schnaitach, where a false charge put him briefly in prison, and then to Gunzenhausen and Ansbach. He also wrote popular tales of the patriarchs and of God's deeds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ali-b-abraham-a: Ali ben Abraham al-Tawil was a Karaite scholar in the twelfth century. He worked at Ramleh in Egypt. He wrote a commentary on the Bible. That work no longer survives. His name stayed unknown for a long time. It came back to light through a printed chronicle by Al-Hiti. That chronicle lists him among the Karaite doctors of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-hasida-th: Amram Hasida, called the Pious, was a Babylonian sage. He taught in the fourth century. He was a peer of Rabbi Nahman. His surname comes from an act at a hard test. To flee a sin he raised a false cry of fire. Shame fell on his peers for that cry. He told them shame here beats shame in the world to come. A tale says a shaft of fire left his body. The men of the exilarch's house mocked his strict ways. Their rough sport made him gravely ill.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apella-1629:
Apella is a name, real or invented, that Horace gives to a Jew known for extreme credulity. Roman writers treated credulity as a Jewish trait, and Horace's line, let the Jew Apella believe it, made the name a byword for a gullible man.

Scholars long read the name as a coined insult built from Greek and Latin parts. Geiger and Renan accepted that reading, the entry says, but later writers showed it to be false. Apella was in fact a common Greek name of the time, short for Apollodorus. Josephus, Cicero, and Petronius all name men called Apella, and it may not be a Jewish name at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archelaus-1729:
Archelaus was a son of Herod the Great and king of Judea, born about 21 B.C. to the Samaritan Malthace. At fourteen he was sent to Rome for schooling, and he came home after two or three years with his brothers Antipas and Philip. Intrigues by Antipater had meanwhile blackened him to his father.

Herod first changed his will in favor of Antipas, the youngest son. Four days before his death, though, the dying king named Archelaus to the throne and made the others tetrarchs only. Why he switched is not known for sure, the entry says. Archelaus's foes blamed a palace intrigue that worked on the weakened king. The entry then follows his rule and fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artaxerxes-iii-:
Artaxerxes III, called Ochus by the Greeks, was a son of Artaxerxes II. After removing the rightful heir Darius, he took his father's throne in the autumn of 359 B.C. and reigned until the summer of 338. Babylonian lists give him twenty-one years. Greek accounts stretch the reign longer, and the entry judges them wrong.

Cruelty and force define his rule here. He opened it by killing relatives who might threaten him. With the eunuch Bagoas and the Rhodian captains Mentor and Memnon, he held a breaking empire together by bloodshed and fraud. He crushed the Sidonian revolt in 345 to 344 and, after failed tries, subdued Egypt in 343 or 342. Josephus links a clash with his Jewish subjects to these same campaigns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-ben-jacob:
Asher ben Jacob ha-Levi, a Talmudic word scholar, lived at Osnabruck in Prussia toward the end of the thirteenth century. He studied under Samuel ben Baruch of Bamberg. His notes on parts of the Mahzor, the festival prayer book, survive in manuscripts at Munich, at Oxford, and in a private collection. In them he scolds the men of France and the Islands of the Sea for tampering with the prayers.

His fame rests on a smaller Aruk. In 1290, in the space of five weeks, he made a shortened form of that great dictionary for his nephew Isaac ben Eleazer ha-Levi. The copy runs to 142 folios and follows the Regensburg manuscript. He added words on the liturgy that the large Aruk lacks. Buxtorf later built his Hebrew lexicon on this manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-saul-:
Saul Cohen Ashkenazi was a religious philosopher of German descent, as his surname shows. Born in Candia in 1470, he died at Constantinople on May 28, 1523. He was a disciple of Elijah Delmedigo, who turned his attention to philosophy. His chief work is Sheelot, Questions, a philosophic treatise in the form of questions put to Isaac Abravanel.

Abravanel's replies were printed with the questions at Venice in 1574, together with philosophic essays by other authors. Saul Cohen also wrote an epilogue to his master's chief work, Behinat ha-Dat, printed at Basel in 1629. The entry rests on Geiger and on Steinschneider's catalogue. It gives a student of Delmedigo asking hard questions across the grave of his century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-assault-and-bat:
Assault and battery is an English law term for injury to the person, a crime known from the earliest stages of law. Property and contract disputes came later in social growth, the entry argues, but injuries to the body always demanded a settler. In ancient law, redress took the form of payment to the person wronged, not punishment by the state, and Talmudic law keeps that shape throughout.
