Many peoples let even a slayer buy his way out with wergild, man-money paid to the heirs. Mosaic law halts that practice: no ransom shall be taken for the life of a manslayer, Numbers chapter 35 commands. The entry's core texts are Exodus chapter 21 and Leviticus chapter 24. Read straight, they teach retaliation: eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azubah-2229: Azubah is the name of two women in the Bible. One was a daughter of Shilhi. She was the mother of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, as the first book of Kings and the second book of Chronicles both report. The other Azubah was a wife of Caleb, the son of Hezron. She is named in the family lists at the start of the first book of Chronicles. The entry gives no further facts about either woman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-dob-b-samu: Dob b. Samuel Baer was a Polish Ḥasidic writer of the late eighteenth century. He wrote "Shibḥei ha-Besht," a set of legends told in Ḥasidic circles about Israel Ba'al Shem-Ṭob, the founder of Ḥasidism. His son Judah Löb printed the book after his death, in 1815. The entry says Baer was son-in-law to a man who had served Besht as secretary for years. That tie gave him rare first-hand word on the movement's start, so the book holds great value for its history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamberger-selig:
Seligman Baer Bamberger, whose Hebrew name was Isaac Dob, led the Orthodox party in Germany as a Talmudist of the old school. He was born at Wiesenbronn, Bavaria, on Nov. 6, 1807, and died at Würzburg on Oct. 13, 1878. Sent to the yeshibah at Fürth at fifteen, he earned a rabbi's diploma in five years. He then opened a shop, since making a living from Torah did not fit his pious view.

Trade bored him and shrank, yet pupils came from all over Germany anyway. The entry follows his stand for Orthodoxy in Bavaria from 1836 and his later post at Würzburg. His books include a guide for Torah scribes and a textbook on ritual slaughter from 1863. One short work, on the three chief duties of Jewish housewives, ran through many editions. A pamphlet of his also set out the Talmud's stance toward non-Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barki-or-called: Isaac ben Elijah Barḳi was a writer who flourished in the seventeenth century at Salonica. According to Azulai, he was a pupil of Ḥayyim Shabbethai, who died in 1647. Little is known of his literary activity. One decision of his appears in his teacher's responsa, "Torat Ḥayyim," printed at Salonica in 1722. Another opinion on ritual questions stands as an appendix to Samuel ben Isaac Sardi's "Sefer ha-Terumot." He also annotated the Arba'ah Ṭurim. Those notes are given in Michael Cohen's "Moreh Ẓedek," Salonica, 1655.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baskets-2629:
Baskets of four kinds are named in the Old Testament, but the text does not state how their shapes differed. The entry works through each Hebrew term in turn. One was a carrying basket linked with bondage in Egypt and with hauling clay for bricks.

Other terms point to a small dish-like basket for offerings and cakes, a deep basket for grain and tithes, and a coarse covered basket for fruit. A final note treats the Greek word used in the New Testament for the baskets of leftovers. The Greek term in the Gospels may also have named a measure of about two gallons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bee-2729:
Bee is named often in the Bible, and wild bees clearly abounded in Palestine. The entry doubts that proof exists for Hebrew bee-keeping in Bible times. A verse in Isaiah about the Lord hissing for the bee is read by some as a call to the hive, but the entry questions that reading.

Honey was an export good and a staple of Hebrew cooking. A swarm stands in poems for a hostile army, and the bee's small work with sweet yield wins praise in Sirach. The name Deborah comes from the word for bee. Modern hives of earth and straw close the piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berchin-jonah-b: Jonah Borisovich Berchin wrote on early Russian Jewish history. He was born at Krichev, in the government of Mohilev, in 1865, and died at Moscow in August 1889. Raised in strict orthodoxy at his uncle's house, he learned Hebrew tongue and letters there. He then studied at farm and technical schools at Minsk and Riga. Sickness struck him in 1888 and sent him to Moscow for care. His studies, printed in Russian journals, dealt with old documents and with Jews at Kiev and at the Moscow court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernheim-hippol: Hippolyte Bernheim, a French physician and nerve specialist, was born at Mülhausen, in Alsace. He trained in his home town and at Strasburg, taking his medical degree in 1867. He taught and practiced at Strasburg until the city passed to Germany in 1871. He then moved to Nancy and became a clinical professor there. When its medical faculty took up hypnotism about 1880, he grew eager for the work and soon led in it. His books treat typhoid fevers and the use of suggestion in healing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-betrothal-in-ta:
Betrothal in Jewish law is not a modern engagement. A modern engagement can be broken freely. Bible and Talmud knew no such thing. Once agreed, the match bound both parties fully. The pair counted as man and wife in law. Only actual living together waited. A formal divorce alone could end it.

The entry traces how practice later changed. A twelve-month gap once split betrothal from home-taking. For widows and widowers it was thirty days. Jews later combined both rites in one ceremony. A looser engagement custom then grew up. The entry also covers betrothal gifts and rings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenfeld-j-c-: J. C. Blumenfeld was a Russian poet. In 1836 he settled in Odessa. There he joined its Hebrew literary circle. S. J. Abramowitch belonged to that circle. Blumenfeld helped Abramowitch's career notably. The entry gives no birth or death dates. His chief work is "King and Priest." It appeared in London in 1839. Dialogues in prose alternate with verses there. Kings and priests scheme to enslave humanity. Rome and the Church compact to degrade Israel. The book shows power yet wanders wildly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonfed-solomon-: Solomon ben Reuben Bonfed was a rabbi at Saragossa and a poet. He lived at the end of the fourteenth century and the start of the fifteenth. His diwan still survives in manuscript and holds history as well as verse. Bonfed was present at the controversy of Tortosa in 1413-14. Many poems speak to men who took part there. The diwan also answers a convert's letter defending Christian dogmas point by point.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandeis-bezale: Bezaleel ben Moses ha-Levi Brandeis was a Bohemian rabbi and author. He died about 1750 at Jung-Bunzlau. There he served as district rabbi and head of a Talmudic academy. His father had been rabbi at Mayence in Germany. Bezaleel wrote festival sermons and homiletic notes on the Pentateuch. His son Baruch Judah printed that work at Prague in 1786. Its title, Zedah-Baruk, joins the family name to the book itself in the son's edition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brodski-3729:
Brodski is a family that has produced many rabbis and notable men over three hundred years. It is a branch of the Schor family. Meir Schor of Brody settled in Kiev's government and took the name Brodski from Brody.

Meir's five sons all grew very wealthy in time. The Brodskis are now held the richest Jewish family in Russia. Israel, who died in 1889, settled in Kiev and gave largely to charity. His sons Lazar and Leon lead the Russian sugar industry from there. They own 22 sugar factories, including 3 refineries, the entry counts. Abraham of Odessa served long as vice-mayor of that city and founded benevolent institutions there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buol-schauenste: John Rudolph, Count von Buol Schauenstein, was an Austrian diplomat born Nov. 21, 1763. He served as ambassador at The Hague in 1790, at Basel in 1792, and later at Dresden. In 1816 he became president of the federal council at Frankfort. When riots struck the Jews of Frankfort on Aug. 9 and 10, 1819, he called the council together. He also called out federal troops to guard the Jews, since the city militia could not be trusted. His liberal views clashed with Metternich, who had him recalled in 1823. He died in Vienna in 1834.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calitas-3929: Calitas was a Levite who had married a foreign wife. The entry is brief and rests on the books of Ezra and First Esdras. At Ezra's urging, Calitas put away that wife. Ezra's book gives his name in other forms, Kelaiah and Kelita. He may be the same Calitas who helped Ezra explain the Law to the people. Nehemiah gives that helper's name as Kelita. The entry leaves the match as a likely one, not a certain one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cardinal-or-car: Judah ben Isaac Cardinal was a translator who lived at the end of the twelfth century and the start of the thirteenth, probably in southern France. A traveler named Joseph ben Baruch asked him for the work. Cardinal turned Judah ha Levi's Cuzari from Arabic into Hebrew for him. Joseph's trip from France to Jerusalem by way of Egypt fell in 1211. The version is now lost but for a few small fragments. Two later commentators on the Cuzari are known to have used it in their own work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castelnuovo-sam: Samuel di Castelnuovo served as secretary of the Jewish community of Rome. He lived at the end of the sixteenth century and the start of the seventeenth. He edited, and probably rendered into Italian, two liturgical works printed at Venice in 1609. One was Judah ha-Levi's hymn Mi kamoka, sung on the Sabbath before Purim. The other was Moses Rieti's Ma'on ha-Shoalim. Castelnuovo's name also appears in a legal ruling by Reggio on the ritual bath.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coblence-adolph:
Adolphe Coblence, a French army surgeon, was born at Nancy on May 11, 1812, and died in Paris on Sept. 18, 1872. He entered army service in 1832 as an assistant surgeon at Metz and rose fast. Baron Larrey made him head of the clinic at the Hotel des Invalides, where he also took his medical degree.

Duty in Algeria followed, then cholera work at Oran in 1849 that won him a gold medal and the Legion of Honor. He gave up a Bayonne post to serve in the Crimea and nursed typhoid cases in quarantine. Honors rose again after Magenta and Solferino in 1859. Blindness struck in 1863, and he retired to Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-contempt-of-cou:
Contempt of Court covers disrespect before a public authority, or disobedience of its orders. Courts everywhere may punish both, the entry begins. In Jewish law, judges could answer disrespect with stripes or the lesser ban. Insult to the judges themselves fell under the law against insulting the learned.

The working branch is disobedience. A summoned man who refuses to come is put under the lesser ban once the messenger reports the refusal. If he simply fails to show, the ban falls the next day. He clears himself only by submitting and paying the writ's cost. From the tenth or eleventh century, courts added pressure by halting worship in his synagogue. No writ compels witnesses, the entry ends, so the common attachment for absent witnesses is unknown to Jewish codes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-craniometry-472:
Craniometry sets out the methods of measuring skulls to fix their shape. Its key figure is the cranial index. That index divides head width by head length and multiplies by 100. A head 153 wide and 186 long gives an index of 82.26. Above 80 the form is called brachycephalic, or broad. Between 75 and 80 it is mesocephalic. Below 75 it is dolichocephalic, or long.

The article then applies the method to Jews. Few Jewish skulls had been measured, so most data came from the living. Tables list 100 skulls by origin and observer. A set of 345 heads of Jewish women found 77.97 per cent brachycephalic. The figures for men, the entry says, agree with those for women.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crown-of-the-la: Crown of the Law is a coronet set on the upper ends of the handles of a Torah scroll. It is usually gilded silver, with bells and a Hebrew inscription. Sometimes the crown is double. The same device, often held between two lions, ornaments the scroll's mantle and the Ark curtain. It stands for the majesty of the Law. Its first use is hard to date. In geonic times the reader of the last chapter on Simḥat Torah wore a crown, like a bridegroom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-d-israeli-isaac:
Isaac D'Israeli was an English author, born at Enfield, Middlesex, in May, 1766. He died at Bradenham on Jan. 19, 1848. He was the only son of Benjamin D'Israeli. His first print piece, in Dec., 1786, defended Dr. Johnson's character. A verse Defense of Poetry followed in 1790. An attack on Peter Pindar drew wide notice and opened literary doors to him.

His fame rests on Curiosities of Literature, first issued in 1791. Volume followed volume until a sixth appeared in 1834. Calamities of Authors and Quarrels of Authors mined the same rich vein. The books hold much lively matter on authors' lives, not always reliable, the entry warns. Later writers drew on them freely. Oxford made him a doctor of civil law in 1832.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniel-book-off:
Daniel, Book of, is one of the books of the Old Testament. Its first six chapters tell events of Daniel's life. Its last six hold his prophecies. The first part shows the heathen world empire cannot last forever. The second shows Israel founding that empire through the son of man. The book mixes two tongues. From chapter two, verse four, to the end of chapter seven it runs in Aramaic. The rest is Hebrew.

The entry weighs why the language shifts mid-book. One view says the author gave the Chaldeans their own speech, then slipped on in the tongue he knew. Another says the Aramaic part concerned all peoples. Chronology takes long space too. The siege of Jerusalem in Jehoiakim's third year is tested against Kings and Jeremiah. Nebuchadnezzar's part in the attack is weighed line by line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deborah-5029: Deborah was a Jewish weekly newspaper in the German language, founded in 1855 at Cincinnati, Ohio. Isaac M. Wise and Max Lilienthal started it for German immigrants who had not yet mastered English. It served as a German supplement to the American Israelite. As English-speaking Jews grew in number, the paper lost ground. Wise kept it going until his death on March 26, 1900. The last weekly issue came out on April 6, 1900. A monthly revival ran from January 1901 to December 1902, then stopped.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-detmold-samuel-: Samuel Detmold was an Austrian educator and translator who lived at the end of the eighteenth century and in the first half of the nineteenth. He joined the team of scholars who put the Bible into German, published at Breslau from 1822 to 1827. Detmold translated the books of Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and the Chronicles for that edition. He wrote a Hebrew primer called "Moreh Derek" (Guide of the Road), printed at Vienna in 1815. The entry warns that some printed statements about him are hardly right.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drohobiczer-isr:
Israel Nahman ben Joseph Drohobiczer was a Talmudic scholar and preacher of Stanislaw. Ghirondi instead places his origin at Ostrog, Russia. He studied under Israel Ba'al Shem-Tob. After serving as rabbi and school head in several German towns, he traveled to publish his books. He died at Safed early in the nineteenth century.

Drohobiczer spent years at Leghorn, where his works were printed, before going on to Palestine. His Emet le-Ya'akob is a set of funeral dirges. Hemdat Yisrael comments on Ecclesiastes and on works of Elijah ha-Levi. Pekuddat ha-Melek, in two volumes, holds new readings on Maimonides. Dirges appear in that collection as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eder-edar-5429: Eder, or Edar, is a name the Bible gives to four different subjects, and the entry keeps them apart. First comes a place near Bethlehem, where Jacob camped beyond the tower of Eder on his way to Hebron. The tower's name means tower of the flock, likely a lookout against robbers. Second is a town in Judah toward Edom, matched with a ruin five miles south of Gaza. The last two are men: a Levite of David's day and a Benjamite chief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-eliezer:
Eleazar ben Judah of Bartota was a scholar of the first and second centuries. He was a pupil of Joshua ben Hananiah and a peer of Akiba. Few laws and fewer homilies carry his name. His fame rests on his giving to the poor.

The entry tells how he lived by that motto to the point of excess. He gave away all he had so often that fund raisers hid from him. Once, while shopping for his daughter's wedding, he chased down the raisers. They were gathering a marriage gift for two orphans. That pair comes first, he cried, and gave them all his money. The tale adds that he kept one small coin. With it he bought wheat, and the storeroom was found full to bursting. He then gave that grain to the poor as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-of-toul: Eliezer of Toulouse was a French tosafist. He died about the year 1234. In his youth he worked as a tutor. His post was in the house of Hezekiah ben Reuben of Boppard. That scholar was rich and learned, the entry notes. Eliezer's glosses on one tractate are still quoted. Zedekiah Anaw cites them in his own book of customs. Other quotes in his name may come from that same source. Nothing more of his work or life is told here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emden-hermann-s: Hermann Seligmann Emden was a German engraver and photographer. He was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on Oct. 18, 1815. He died in that same town on Sept. 6, 1875. Love of art showed in him from his early years. Lack of funds barred him from a full art schooling. He learned his craft as a lad in a print shop. His cut of Pope Pius the Ninth made his name. He was among the first to set up a photo studio at Frankfort.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-erech-5829:
Erech was the second of four Babylonian cities that Genesis credits to Nimrod. Its site is now called Warka, on the left bank of the Euphrates. The entry places it about halfway between Hilla and Korna. Ruins there spread over an area six miles around.

Digging at Warka was still slight when the entry was written. The oldest finds bear the names of kings of Ur who held the city. Many coffins, mostly of the Parthian period, show the site later became a burial ground. A creation story credits the god Marduk with founding Erech. The city is also the center of action in the Gilgamesh epic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fiorentino-solo:
Solomon Fiorentino was an Italian poet born at Monte San Savino, Tuscany, on March 4, 1743. He died at Florence on Feb. 4, 1815. He studied at Sienna and began to write there. The reaction of 1799 put him in prison. When freed, he lived in poverty at Sienna and Florence. He later took a chair of Italian literature at Leghorn. Jews of that city had offered it to him, and he taught there until 1808.

Fiorentino's chief work is a set of elegies written after his wife died. He also wrote a poem for a grand duke's crowning and a teaching poem on the soul. He translated Hebrew prayers into Italian. His exchange of sonnets with Corilla Olimpica became famous. His son Angiolo taught Hebrew at Leghorn and Florence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-foreign-attachm:
Foreign attachment is the seizure of a debtor's property in a place where the debtor cannot be found. He has fled or lives elsewhere. The practice grew up in most lands from the needs of trade. It sits uneasily with the rule that no one should be condemned unheard. The Talmud records mixed views on making such an exception. Later authorities held the exception needful for the safety of trade.

The entry then sets out the Jewish procedure. The holder of a proven bond may seek payment in the debtor's absence. If the court's messenger can reach the debtor and return within thirty days, notice must go out first. If not, the debt may be taken at once from lands or movables. The creditor must swear the proper oath. Three facts must be proved: the bond is genuine, the debtor lives too far off, and the property is truly his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-godefroi-michae:
Michael H. Godefroi was a Dutch jurist and minister of justice born at Amsterdam on Jan. 13, 1814; he died at Würzburg on June 27, 1882. At thirty-two he became judge of the provincial court for North Holland, and in 1848 he entered the second chamber of the States General, sitting until 1881. His new code of judicial practice won him the Order of the Netherlands Lion.

In February 1860 he accepted the justice ministry, becoming the first Jew to hold a cabinet post in Holland, while openly keeping his faith and leading the Jewish consistory. He used his place to press for Jewish equality abroad, tying Dutch trade treaties with Switzerland and Rumania to guarantees for Jews there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottlieb-abraha:
Abraham Gottlieb was a civil engineer and contractor. He was born at Tauss, Bohemia, on June 17, 1837. He died in Chicago on Feb. 9, 1894. He graduated from Prague University in 1861. Railroad work in Austria came first. In 1866 he emigrated to America and settled in Chicago. By 1868 he was chief engineer of the American Bridge Works.

In 1877 he became president of the Keystone Bridge Company. His bridges crossed the Susquehanna, Ohio, and Missouri rivers. His Plattsmouth bridge was the first steel-truss bridge built in America. He also supplied ironwork for Chicago's Masonic Temple. He served as chief engineer of construction for the Columbian Exposition. He resigned in September 1891 once its main buildings stood well along.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guglielmo-benja: Benjamin Guglielmo was an Italian dancing-master. He worked in the fifteenth century at Pesaro. His teacher was Domenico di Ferrara, whose "Liber Ballorum" of 1460 names him. Guglielmo wrote his own treatise on dancing, "Trattato dell' Arte del Ballare." It is one of the earliest such works still in existence. In it he cites dances devised by himself and by one "Giuseppe Ebreo." The entry gives the treatise's later editions but no facts about his life beyond his craft and city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guillaume-of-au:
Guillaume of Auvergne was a French scholastic. He was bishop of Paris from 1228 to 1249. He helped found Christian scholasticism in the thirteenth century. He knew Hebrew literature well. He never names Maimonides, yet the "Moreh Nebukim" shaped his thought often. He followed Maimonides on the symbolism of sacrifice and the reasons for the commandments.

The Jewish thinker he prized most was Solomon ibn Gabirol. He cited the "Fons Vitæ" as "Fons Sapientiæ" and took its author, Avicebron, for a Christian. Still, his stance toward Jews was harsh. Through his influence the Talmud was burned at Paris in 1242. He blamed the Bible's silence on some dogmas on Jewish narrowness and moral decay.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hambro-joseph-7:
Joseph Hambro, born at Copenhagen on Nov. 2, 1780, was an aulic councilor to the King of Denmark who died in London on Oct. 3, 1848. He began with a Hamburg firm, then ran his father's business as general agent. He built a London branch and spread his trade across northern Europe. By 1820 he was spoken of as the richest man in Copenhagen.

The king made him a Knight of the Dannebrog. Late in life his health broke, and he lived a time in Italy. He married a Christian and had his son baptized. In 1831 he moved with his family to London for good. He kept some distance from congregational affairs, yet he stayed a synagogue member to the last and was buried in the Great Synagogue's cemetery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hana-b-hanilai-:
Ḥana b. Ḥanilai was a Babylonian scholar and philanthropist of the third century, junior to Huna I and Ḥisda. The Talmud pictures his open hand: he kept scores of bakers making bread for the poor, and his hand was ever in his purse for the needy. His house had doors on all sides so a traveler could enter with ease. No guest left it hungry or empty-handed.

He even left food outside at night, so the ashamed could take it in the dark. In time his house fell to ruin. Ḥisda, moved at the sight, heard 'Ula's comfort: God's own sanctuary fell too, and both would be restored. Rich and learned as he was, Ḥana stayed humble. He once offered to take a shovel from Huna's shoulder in the street, and Huna refused the honor at such a cost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazzan-eleazar-: Eleazar ha-Hazzan was a precentor who lived at Speyer toward the end of the eleventh century. He taught Samuel the Pious. He may be the same man as Eleazar, son of Meshullam the Great. That Eleazar gave many notes to a Narbonne writer on Chronicles around 1130. Eleazar also taught Shemariah ben Mordecai of Speyer. The entry is short and the identity point is left open. Two learned journals are cited for the little that can be said about him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-helin-jacob-mos: Jacob Moses ben Abraham Helin, born about 1625, was a Polish Talmudist. He studied at Lublin under noted teachers and married into the family of a Satanow rabbi. He died about 1700. His work "Yede Mosheh" comments on the Midrash Rabbah with sharp notes. It points out the Talmudic sources from which the legends are drawn. His son Abraham published it at Frankfort on the Oder in 1705. A second edition came in 1713. The work is now printed in all editions of the Midrash.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-fischl-7:
Fischl Hirsch was a Hebrew bookseller who died at Berlin on June 5, 1899. About 1860 he settled at Halberstadt and founded a Jewish printing and publishing business. He soon left printing to sell Hebrew books and manuscripts alone.

Nearly blind, Hirsch still traveled widely gathering old prints and manuscripts. He sold them to major Hebrew libraries in Europe. The British Museum gained most of its early Hebrew books through him, the entry says. The Bodleian and Amsterdam's Rosenthal library also owed him key gains. He moved to Frankfort about 1885, then to Berlin about 1891. His last British Museum visit came in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-humanists-7929: Humanists were scholars who revived the culture of antiquity and the study of classic books. The movement rose in Italy in the fifteenth century, then spread to France, Holland, and Germany. There it won great influence and cleared the way for the Reformation. Hutten and Reuchlin stand out as its leaders, both men of Luther's time. Reuchlin pushed the study of Hebrew into German universities. He also defended Hebrew books against Pfefferkorn and argued for the Jews. Humanism eased Jewish life under harsh medieval laws.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-jau-jacob-6:
Jacob ibn Jau was a silk maker at Cordova who rose high at the court of the calif Hisham. He died about 1000. He and his brother Joseph found a lost sum of money in the palace. They spent it on fine silks and woven flags for the calif and his minister Al-Mansur, gifts of a kind Spain had never seen.

Al-Mansur made Jacob prince and chief judge of all Jewish communities in the califate. Jacob could name judges and rabbis and set Jewish taxes. Guards and a state carriage marked his rank. When he would not squeeze large gifts from his people, Al-Mansur jailed him for a year. The calif freed him, but his prestige never came back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-verga-solom:
Solomon ibn Verga was a Spanish historian and physician of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. His kinship to Judah ibn Verga is unclear, but he was not Judah's son. Spanish towns sent him to raise ransom money for the prisoners of Malaga. He lived at Lisbon as a Marrano and saw the massacre there with his own eyes.

In Turkey he wrote the Shebet Yehudah, a record of Jewish persecutions across lands and ages. It holds accounts of sixty-four persecutions, plus debates and customs. He asks why Jews, above all Spanish Jews, suffer most, and he does not hide Jewish faults. His son Joseph finished the work. Printed in Turkey about 1550, it spread in many tongues. One critic warns that parts belong to legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-asher: Isaac ben Asher ha-Levi, called Riba, was a Tosafist who lived at Speyer in the eleventh century. He was son-in-law of Eliakim ben Meshullam and a pupil of Rashi. His tosafot are the first known, cited as "Tosafot Riba" in the "Temim De'im," in the printed tosafot and in the "Tosafot Yeshanin," and often quoted with no name. He also wrote a commentary on the Pentateuch, which is lost. It lives on only in quotes by the "Minhat Yehudah" and Jacob Tam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaacs-myer-sam:
Myer Samuel Isaacs was an American lawyer born in New York City on May 8, 1841. He joined the New York bar in 1862 and became a judge of the Marine Court in 1880. City affairs held much of his time: reform law work, help in creating Seward Park, and a hand in founding the Citizens' Union in 1897. He also worked for better housing for the poor.

In Jewish life he helped found body after body. The list runs from the Board of Delegates of the American Israelites in 1859 to the United Hebrew Charities in 1873 and the Educational Alliance in 1889. He was a founder of the Montefiore Home and president of the Baron de Hirsch Fund from 1890. In 1881 he called the meeting that planned relief for the Russian exiles. He was also tied to the "Jewish Messenger" from 1859 to 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-of-kefar-:
Jacob of Kefar Neburaya was a Judaeo-Christian of the fourth century. His village is likely Nabratain, north of Safed, where his tomb is shown. Before he embraced Christianity he was well known as a haggadist, and the Rabbis approved two of his teachings. In the school at Caesarea he read one verse in Habakkuk as a rebuke of simony, and on that day he marked out Isaac b. Eleazar as fit for the rabbinate.

At Tyre he was consulted on points of law, but his rulings were not accepted. He held that the slaughter rules apply to fish, and that a Gentile woman's son may be circumcised on the Sabbath. For those rulings R. Haggai ordered him flogged. Jacob argued, then admitted he deserved it. His heresy stayed mostly unknown; only Isi of Caesarea plainly counts him among the Judaeo-Christians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jassy-jaschi-85:
Jassy, also written Jaschi, is a city of Rumania that held the oldest and largest Jewish community of Moldavia, whose capital it once was. Old gravestones there reach back to 1467 and 1549. Set on the trade road between Poland and Turkey, the town drew Jewish merchants early, and their number grew after it became the capital in 1565.

The long history that follows is marked by attacks and flight. Cossack forces harmed Jews at Jassy in the mid sixteen hundreds, and refugees from Poland added scholars to the town. Later sections tell of plunder, forced payments, and great fires, among them a fire in July 1822 that burned five synagogues and hundreds of Jewish houses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-johannesburg-87:
Johannesburg is the largest city in the Transvaal and the chief center of Jewish life in South Africa. Its Jewish community is put at 12,000 in a total of 120,000 people, the largest share outside Aden and Gibraltar in the British empire. From the town's birth on the gold fields at the end of 1885, Jews have formed about a tenth of the white population.

Some eighty-eight pioneers formed the first Jewish body on July 10, 1887, and a synagogue plot was bought the next year. Splits soon made rival congregations, one of which President Kruger opened in person. By 1903 the town had a Jewish school of 400 pupils, aid and loan societies, an orphanage league, Yiddish papers, and 829 burials in the Jewish cemetery ground.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-davi: Joseph ben David Heilbronn of Eschau was a German Masorite who lived at The Hague in the eighteenth century. The Masorah is the set of notes that guards the exact text of the Hebrew Bible. His book Sefer Mebin Hidot, printed at Amsterdam in 1765, is called an important work on that subject. An appendix answers a critic named Asher Worms. In 1769 he also edited prayers for the feast of Simhat Torah and other special days, under the title Seder Tefillot li-Yeme Simhat Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kahn-robert-912:
Robert Kahn was a German composer and pianist. He was born at Mannheim on July 21, 1865. He studied at Mannheim with Ernst Frank and Vincenz Lachner. At Berlin his teacher was Friedrich Kiel. At Munich he worked with Joseph Rheinberger. After time in Vienna and Berlin, he moved to Leipsic in 1890. There he founded a ladies' choral union.

In October 1898 Kahn joined the Königliche Hochschule für Musik in Berlin. He taught theory and composition there. The entry lists his works in detail. They include an orchestral serenade. They also include piano quartets and trios. He wrote a string quartet and two violin sonatas. One choral work sets voices with orchestra. His pieces for female voices earn special praise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-karpeles-gustav:
Gustav Karpeles was a historian of literature and an editor. He was born on Nov. 11, 1848, at Eiwanowitz, in Moravia. He studied at Breslau and at its Jewish theological seminary. He chose journalism for his career. He worked on the staffs of several German papers. In 1883 he settled in Berlin.

At Berlin, Karpeles became editor of the "Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums" in 1890. He woke new life in the Jewish literary societies of Germany. He is best known for his work on Heinrich Heine. He edited Heine's works in four editions. He also wrote a shelf of studies on Heine's life and times. His wider output covers Goethe, Börne, and a history of Jewish literature. He even wrote comedies for the stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kings-books-of-:
The Books of Kings form the fourth book of the Prophets, the second division of the Hebrew Bible. They give a history of the kings of Judah and of Israel. The story runs from David's last days to Zedekiah's capture by Nebuchadnezzar. The work divides into I Kings, with twenty-two chapters, and II Kings, with twenty-five.

The entry summarizes the contents chapter by chapter. It then turns to a critical view. The books are a compilation, not an original composition. The compiler cites sources such as "the book of the acts of Solomon." He judges each king by his attitude to the Deuteronomic law. The entry dates the work's final form to the Exile. It also finds signs of an earlier edition from before the monarchy fell.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohn-samuel-942:
Samuel Kohn, a Hungarian rabbi and author born at Baja on Sept. 21, 1841, was grandson of that town's rabbi, Götz Schwerin Kohn. He studied at the Jewish theological seminary and the University of Breslau. Called to Budapest in 1866, he was the first to preach sermons there in Hungarian. He helped found the Hungarian Literary Society and led it for years.

Prolific writing fills the second half of the entry. Kohn published on the Samaritan Pentateuch, on Hebrew manuscripts in Budapest, and on the history of the Jews in Hungary. His study of the Sabbatarians appeared in Hungarian in 1889 and in German in 1894. From 1898 he also lectured on homiletics at the Budapest rabbinical school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kronenberg-stan: Stanislaw Leopold Kronenberg, a Polish-Russian financier born at Warsaw in 1846, died there in 1894. He was a brother of Leopold Kronenberg. Two years in France brought study of political economy and a doctorate at Paris. In the Franco-Prussian war he helped defend Paris and left with a lieutenant's rank and the Legion of Honor. On his father's death he took over the family trade and railway interests in Warsaw. Bank and line presidencies followed. A war memoir by him appeared at Paris in 1871.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-languedoc-hebre:
Languedoc, an old province of France with capitals at Toulouse and Montpellier, held many strong Jewish communities by the year 506. Under Visigothic kings the Jews suffered, yet less than across the Pyrenees. Local Christians often shielded them from harsh laws. An expulsion order in 672 sparked a general rising and soon failed.

Favor and harm then alternate. Carolingian kings gave Jews lasting land rights, and counts of Toulouse even placed Jews in public office about 1170. The Albigensian crusade brought bans on such office from 1209. Royal rule later crushed Jews with taxes and prison. The entry ends with the expulsion of 1394, which closed nearly all its communities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leidesdorff-wil:
William Leidesdorff was one of the earliest settlers in California. He was born about 1802, perhaps at Szathmar, Hungary, and died at San Francisco on May 18, 1848. He left home at about fifteen, and his family never heard from him again. He reached Yerba Buena in 1840.

Leidesdorff built wide trade links with the States and became the town's richest man. He served as vice-consul, alcalde, council member, and city treasurer, and he set up the first American public school there. He died without a will. His estate, worth a million and a half by 1854, drew rival claims that courts never settled in favor of any kin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-ben-gersho:
Levi ben Gershon, called Ralbag and Gersonides, was a French thinker, Bible commentator, mathematician, and physician. He was born at Bagnols in 1288 and died on April 20, 1344. He came from a family of scholars. Little is known of his life beyond his stays in Orange and Avignon.

Before he was thirty, Levi began the "Milhamot Adonai," the work of philosophy that made his name. A ban on teaching philosophy to the young did not stop his early training in all its branches. Isaac de Lattes praised his range: Bible and Talmud commentaries, plus logic, physics, metaphysics, mathematics, and medicine. Later writers held that he had no equal on earth in those fields.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-nathaniel-:
Nathaniel Levi, an Australian merchant and politician, was born at Liverpool, England, on Jan. 20, 1830. In 1853 he went to the gold-fields of Victoria. In 1858 he settled in Melbourne and joined the firm of John Levi & Sons.

In 1860 Levi won a seat in the Legislative Assembly for Maryborough. He was the first Jew elected to Parliament in Victoria. He worked to end the tea and sugar duties and to tax unused land. In 1892 he moved up to the Legislative Council. He founded "The Melbourne Daily News" in 1885. For years he led the Melbourne Hebrew Congregation as treasurer and president.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewis-samuel-99: Samuel Lewis, an English money-lender and philanthropist, was born in Birmingham in 1837. He died in London on Jan. 13, 1901. He began work at thirteen. He sold steel pens, then opened a jeweler's shop. At last he entered money-lending, the trade his name is tied to. He became the most fashionable lender of his day. Nearly every noble house in Britain is said to have dealt with him. He left nearly twenty million dollars. Five millions of it are to go to charity when his widow dies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lisser-joshua-f: Joshua Falk Lisser was a leading rabbi and Talmud scholar of the late eighteenth century. He served as a judge at Lissa while David Tebele was chief rabbi there. In 1782 he sat on the council that condemned and burned a letter by Naphtali Herz Wessely. He wrote notes on small Talmud tracts, with fixes to the text, printed at Dyhernfurth in 1788. His notes on one tract were later reprinted in the Wilna edition of the Talmud in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loveman-robert-: Robert Loveman was an American poet born at Cleveland, Ohio, on April 11, 1864. He was educated at the University of Alabama and lived at Dalton, Ga., in 1904. He published five volumes of verse between 1889 and 1903. Their titles run from simple Poems to A Book of Verses and The Gates of Silence. His work won praise from critics of his day. The entry cites Who's Who in America and other reference books as its sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-aseh-bereshi:
Ma'aseh Bereshit and Ma'aseh Merkabah, the work of Creation and the work of the Chariot, are treated together in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. The two Talmudic terms name the secret doctrine of the universe. The first rests on the opening chapter of Genesis. The second rests on Ezekiel's vision of the divine chariot.

The article stresses how closely this teaching was guarded. It could not be discussed in public at all. The Mishnah allowed the Creation teaching before two hearers at most, and the Chariot before only one. Even chapter headings went only to a school head of cautious temper. Stories warn of the danger, including a boy consumed by fire for grasping a verse too soon. Inquirers could ask about the six days of Creation, but not about what came before. The entry opens a careful window on Judaism's oldest mystical lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malea-maleha-me:
Meir de Malea, chief tax farmer of Castile, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. He served King Ferdinand III, winning favor by honesty and zeal for the state. Learned in the Talmud, he was praised by Nahmanides as the great prince, the learned Don Meir. His title, almoxarif mayor, marked him as the crown's chief revenue officer.

The article follows the office into his sons' hands under Alfonso X. Don Zag and Don Juzef inherited their father's post and the kingdom's tangled finances. Zag provisioned the king's army and leased all customs and taxes. For two years his partnership paid the crown 80,000 gold maravedis yearly. His fall came when the king's rebel son seized money Zag had gathered for the army. Alfonso had Zag dragged through the city and executed in 1280. The entry shows the heights and deadly risks of Jewish court finance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marli-samuel-ra:
Samuel Raphael ben Mazliah Marli, an Italian Talmudist and liturgist, is the subject of a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906, written by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn. Marli lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. According to S. D. Luzzatto, his family name may mean "of Arles," pointing to French roots before the move to Italy.

The entry records that Marli headed the yeshivah, or rabbinical school, at Mantua. It also places him among the rabbis drawn into the heated dispute over the ritual bath, or mikwah, of Rovigo. A brief bibliography points readers to older Italian and German reference works. The piece preserves basic facts about a scholar whom later sources mention only in passing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-me-asha-10529:
Me'asha is one name worn by three Palestinian teachers, and a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and M. Seligsohn separates them. The first is a tanna known from a single reference in the Mishnah, who lived in the days of Hillel's descendants. The third is a fourth-century amora whose sayings appear in both Talmuds, a companion of Samuel ben Isaac and Zera.

The middle Me'asha gets the warmest telling. A grandson and pupil of Joshua ben Levi, poor and frail, he had himself carried to the synagogue on Saturdays so that he could preach. He is remembered for a vision seen in a three-day trance: a world of confusion, he reported, where people honored here are held in contempt. From Isaiah he drew the lesson that one who shuts his eyes to indecent things becomes worthy to see the face of the Shekinah, God's presence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-josep: Menahem ben Joseph ben Hiyya was gaon of Pumbedita from 858 to 860. Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein give him a three-sentence notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry is candid about his weakness. He was likely raised to the gaonate for his father's sake. It was not, the writers suggest, for his own merit. He spent his short tenure in dissension with a rival. The rival was Mar Mattithiah ben Rabbi. That man was his superior in Talmudic learning. The quarrel ended only with Menahem's death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messiah-hebr-ha:
Messiah, from the Hebrew Ha-Mashiaḥ, meaning the anointed one, is the name for the ideal king of the Messianic age. Joseph Jacobs and Moses Buttenwieser wrote the long Jewish Encyclopedia article on the subject in 1906. It follows the word and the idea from the Old Testament through the prophets and into later Jewish writing.

The article shows that in the Bible the title first belongs to reigning kings and anointed priests, and even to Cyrus of Persia. Isaiah gives the fullest early picture: a scion of Jesse who rules in righteousness and brings peace, not war. Later sections treat Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the servant songs of Deutero-Isaiah, the Apocrypha, and Alexander the Great hailed as a deliverer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milcah-10829:
Milcah is a two-part name entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn. It sorts out two different women of the Bible who share the name. Neither gets a story of her own here; the entry is a signpost built from three verses of Genesis and one of Numbers.

The first Milcah, daughter of Haran, married her uncle Nahor and bore eight sons, the youngest being Bethuel, father of Rebekah. Ibn Ezra, the entry notes, doubted the uncle marriage, arguing her father was a different Haran from Abraham's brother. The second Milcah is simply listed as the fourth daughter of Zelophehad, with her sisters, in the census of Numbers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mole-10929:
The mole of the English Bible is a translation problem wearing fur. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz show this in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Isaiah's ḥaparparah is traditionally rendered mole. Leviticus offers ḥoled, probably a weasel. It also offers tinshemet, which the ancient versions took for a mole but which is likely a lizard or a bird.

Zoology settles it. The true mole does not occur in Palestine at all. Isaiah's burrower must be the mole-rat, Spalax typhlus. It is common among ruins and stone-heaps and mole-like to the eye. The Talmud calls the creature eyeless, and Aristotle and Pliny agree. The Talmud blames it for damage to grain. It counts its appearance in a dream, with the bat and weasel, as a bad omen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-nahma:
Moses ben Nahman of Gerona, called Nahmanides or Ramban, was a Spanish Talmudist, exegete, and physician born in 1194. The Jewish Encyclopedia article on him is by Joseph Jacobs, Wilhelm Bacher, and Isaac Broydé. He began writing compendiums of rabbinic law at sixteen, defending Alfasi's decisions against their critics.

Nahmanides revered the early authorities and resisted the new habit of explaining away the Bible's wonders. Yet in the fight over Maimonides' works he played the conciliator, and both sides rejected his compromise. Later he wrote the Iggeret ha-Kodesh on marriage and the Torat ha-Adam on mourning and burial. He died in Palestine about 1270.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muranyi-armin-1:
Armin Murányi was a Hungarian lawyer and journalist born at Asszonyfa on May 8, 1841. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied medicine at Vienna for three years, then turned to law, taking his degree at Budapest in 1866. Jews could not then practise law in Hungary.

The king gave Murányi special leave to open a law office at Györ in 1867, and he became the most popular lawyer in Trans-Danubia. In 1880 he moved to Budapest and turned to literature. He founded the weekly Hungarian Housewife and the daily National Journal, and edited the Illustrated Family Paper for twelve years. He died at Budapest in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehunya-ben-ha-:
Nehunya ben ha-Kanah was a tanna called the Great. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first and second centuries. He was a contemporary of Johanan b. Zakkai, not his pupil. Ishmael b. Elisha learned at his feet.

Nehunya was rich, with a large train of servants. Yet meekness and a forgiving heart set him apart. He credited those traits for his long life. He read the whole Torah by one rule of reading. That rule, general and particular, passed to Ishmael's thirteen. His famed saying praises the yoke of the Torah. Who takes it sheds the yoke of kings and worldly care. Cabalists also tie key prayers to his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-niddah-menstruo:
Niddah is the treatise on the menstruous woman. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. Ten chapters hold seventy-nine paragraphs in total. Leviticus chapter fifteen sets its base rule.

A menstruous woman is unclean for seven days. Her touch defiles the objects she contacts. Later custom added seven clean days after the flow. A ritual bath alone then restores her purity. Childbirth rules from Leviticus twelve fill much space. Colors of discharge and blood spots get close study. Caesarean birth and puberty's signs are treated too. The Gemara adds the famed angel of the womb tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunez-ribiero-s:
Samuel Nuñez Ribiero was a Marano physician of Lisbon. Cyrus Adler and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His family stood high in that city. He himself served as a court physician. The Inquisition still denounced and seized them all.

His medical skill proved the family's deliverance then. Release came chained to two resident officers. They watched the house against relapse into Judaism. His mansion on the Tagus entertained Lisbon's first families. At one dinner he plotted the great escape. An English brigantine's captain agreed to carry them off. London received them, then Georgia drew them on. They reached Savannah in 1733, a month after founding. The trustees grudged Jews their land grants there. Six farms nonetheless were allotted to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-david:
David ben Abraham Oppenheim was an Austrian rabbi and book lover. The board and M. Seligsohn wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms in the year 1664. He died at Prague on September 12, 1736. He read at Metz with Gershon Oulif as a youth.

David wed the girl of a rich court agent of Hanover. His uncle Samuel left him a vast sum of wealth. So he rose to lead the Jews of his lands. In 1691 he was named rabbi of Nikolsburg. He was also made chief rabbi of Moravia then. In 1702 he became chief rabbi of Prague. He ran great trade deals on the side as well. His famed store of books is praised in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pashur-11929:
Pashur is the name of two men in the Book of Jeremiah. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Both men were priests tied to the Temple in Jerusalem. Both came into conflict with the prophet Jeremiah.

The first Pashur, son of Immer, beat Jeremiah and put him in the stocks. Jeremiah answered that Pashur would die in captivity in Babylon. The second Pashur, son of Melchiah, served King Zedekiah. He asked Jeremiah about the siege of Jerusalem. As Temple governor he later had Jeremiah thrown into prison.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perez-b-menahem:
Perez ben Menahem was a rabbi at Dreux in France. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the twelfth century. In old age he still took part in a great synod. The record of him is brief but real.

That synod met before 1160 under Jacob ben Meir. Meir is better known as Rabbenu Tam. Perez's son wrote a long poem for the binding of Isaac. It ran to forty-five verses in all. Perez himself likely wrote Sefer Perez. That lost book held notes on the Masorah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-picciotto-haim-:
Haim Moses Picciotto was a communal worker from Aleppo. He was born in 1806 and died at London in 1879. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came to England about 1843 and plunged into Jewish affairs.

Picciotto pushed for a Jews' College and served its council. He helped found a society spreading religious knowledge. He sat for years on the Board of Deputies. In 1859 war sent him to Morocco with relief funds. His report there founded schools at Tetuan and Tangier. His son James wrote sketches of Anglo-Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poitou-12229:
Poitou was an old province of France with Jewish towns from the twelfth century on. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They name towns such as Niort, Bressuire, and Thouars. Scholars from the province joined a synod at Troyes about 1166.

Much of the article tells of hard rule under Alphonse de Poitiers. He expelled Jews from Poitiers and other towns in 1249. He freed Christians from interest owed to Jews. He laid a poll tax on the Jews in 1268. A year later he forced them to wear a badge. The entry shows how one ruler squeezed a small community step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prague-12329:
Prague is the capital of Bohemia and an old home of Jews. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote its long article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was the first Bohemian city where Jews settled. A record of the year 906 names them there. The Jew Ibrahim ibn Jacob found them at its slave market.

Pethahiah of Regensburg set out from Prague in 1187. He was bound on his trip to the East. In 1254 King Ottocar set rules for the Jews of Prague. Those rules were summed up again in 1269. They fixed the interest a Jew might take on loans. The article follows the community through bans, taxes, and growth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rafram-ii-12529:
Rafram II was a Babylonian amora of the seventh generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Rafram studied under R. Ashi and often put questions to him. He was also a colleague of Rabina II.

The article says Rafram followed R. Gebiha as head of the academy at Pumbedita. He held that post from 433 until his death in 443. Short Talmud notes show where his name appears in debate. A closing note points readers to Halevy's history of the early sages. The entry helps place one late Babylonian teacher in his school and time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ree-hartvig-phi:
Hartvig Philip Ree was a Danish merchant and author born on October 12, 1778. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Fredericia, Jutland. He died in Copenhagen on October 1, 1859.

The article says he took over his father's Fredericia business. He grew rich in shipbroking, sugar, cocoa, and clothing. Yet he found time for Jewish philosophy and literature. In 1814 he became Denmark's first Jew with full citizenship. Aarhus owed its first synagogue to his generosity. He paid its costs for several years himself. He also wrote hymns and a study of Psalm headings. Three of his sons receive their own entries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rose-arnold-jos:
Arnold Josef Rosé was a Rumanian violinist born in Jassy on October 24, 1863. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his short entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He built his career in Vienna, then a center of European music.

Rosé entered the Vienna Conservatorium at ten and studied with Karl Heissler. In 1881 he debuted with the Vienna Philharmonic, playing Goldmark's violin concerto. A year later he founded the Rosé Quartet, which toured widely in Austria and Germany. By 1888 he was concert-master at the Bayreuth festivals, a leading post for a violinist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rufina-12929:
Rufina was a Jewess of Smyrna who lived about the third century of the common era. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote her entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Her name survives in a Greek inscription found at Smyrna.

The inscription calls Rufina ruler of the synagogue, an office she held herself. She built a tomb for her freedmen and her household slaves there. Anyone burying another body in it owed heavy fines, the text warns. The entry notes hers is the only known case of a woman holding that office. Her wealth is plain from the tomb she provided.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salkinson-isaac:
Isaac Edward Salkinson was a Russian Hebraist who became a Christian missionary. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Wilna, he died at Vienna on June 5, 1883.

As a youth Salkinson set out for America to enter a rabbinical seminary. In London, missionary agents persuaded him to forsake Judaism and be baptized. Ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1859, he settled at Vienna in 1876. There he turned great English works into Hebrew verse and prose. His versions include Paradise Lost, Othello, and Romeo and Juliet. His Hebrew New Testament appeared after his death, in 1886, under Ginsburg's care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-moses-13:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Moses Samuel. He was an English author, born in London in 1795. He died at Liverpool in 1860. Samuel won a strong name as a Hebrew scholar. He was also known as an authority on rabbinical literature.

At Liverpool he published an Address to the Missionaries of Great Britain. That pamphlet firmly protested groups that tried to convert Jews. He also wrote on the position of Jews in Great Britain. He helped edit a monthly magazine called The Cup of Salvation. Samuel pushed hard for Jewish emancipation, full civil rights for Jews. He translated the Book of Jasher. He also translated Mendelssohn's Jerusalem, printed at London in 1838.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulmann-ludwi:
Isidore Singer and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Ludwig Schulmann. He was a German philologist and writer. Schulmann was born at Hildesheim in 1814. He died at Hanover on July 24, 1870. He studied philology at the University of Göttingen. He then taught for a time in his home town.

From 1842 Schulmann pushed for trained Jewish schoolteachers in Hanover. His efforts bore fruit on November 7, 1848. A seminary for Jewish teachers opened in Hanover that day. The school still exists in 1905. Schulmann also edited newspapers at Hildesheim and Hanover. He kept his last editorship until his death. His books include Talmudische Klänge, a set of poems from 1856. He also wrote tales in North German dialect. He signed some pieces with the pen name Justus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sibyl-13629:
Sibyl names the women who prophesied in frenzy in the ancient Greek and Roman world. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on them. Greeks and Romans knew no prophets in the Jewish sense. Their inspired speech came through sibyls instead, the entry says.

Ancient sources disagree on the sibyls' number and homes. Plato speaks of only one sibyl in his writings. Aristotle and Aristophanes mention several of them. Varro lists ten sibyls, including some from the East. Pausanias gives a list of special Jewish interest. His four include a Libyan sibyl and Herophile of Marpessus. Demo of Cumae leads Roman history's sibyl tales. Fourth stands the Hebrew sibyl herself. The entry links pagan prophecy to Jewish tradition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soest-latin-sus:
Soest, in Latin Susatum, was a city in Westphalia, Prussia. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews of Soest are named as early as the mid-thirteenth century. They paid eight marks a year to the Archbishop of Cologne. In 1349 they suffered badly in the Black Death persecution.

Later the city council kept Jews to two families at most. In 1510 some passing Jews were jailed, then freed on oath. A Jewish physician won their release by his petition. Permits in 1541 let two Jews stay for ten years. They paid gold up front and a yearly tribute for the right.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sosa-simon-de-1:
Simon de Sosa was one of the wealthiest Maranos in Portugal. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived in the middle of the seventeenth century. He joined a plot led by the Archbishop of Braga. The plotters meant to burn the royal palaces in Lisbon.

They also meant to murder King John IV and seize the queen. The plot was detected in time to stop it. Sosa was executed with the other conspirators for his part. Two probable kin of his are named in the entry. Isaac de Sosa Brito wrote letters that still survive. Gabriel de Sosa Brito was a famed mathematician and cosmographer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-henry-abr:
Henry Abraham Stern was a Christian missionary born in Hesse-Cassel in 1820. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Unterreichenbach on April 11 of that year. At seventeen he entered a trading house in Hamburg. He moved to London in 1839 and was baptized in 1840.

Stern sailed in 1844 to found a mission to Jews in Chaldea and Persia. He worked as a missionary for more than forty years. His travels covered Mesopotamia, Persia, Arabia, and Turkey. In Abyssinia he won many Falashas to Christianity. King Theodore held him prisoner there from 1863 to 1867. An English force under Sir Robert Napier freed him. The entry follows a missionary career across three continents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhum-b-elieze:
Tanhum ben Eliezer was a Lithuanian rabbi and merchant. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He was born in 1746, son of Rabbi Eliezer of Orle. He succeeded his father in the Orle rabbinate. He died at Grodno on January 12, 1819.

Tanhum later served as head of the court at Grodno. His father had been called there as rabbi. When Tanhum failed to win Grodno's rabbinate in 1791, he turned to trade. Business brought him great success instead. Tradition says Poland's last king trusted him. Emperor Alexander the First also thought well of him. In 1818 his signature led the Wilna delegates' resolutions. They chose deputies to represent Jews at St. Petersburg. His writings survive only in manuscript under one title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tennessee-11329:
Jewish life in Tennessee, town by town, is the subject of this article. Cyrus Adler and Max Samfield wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Tennessee joined the Union in 1796. A few Jewish traders settled near the Holston River in 1778.

The first congregations formed at Memphis and Nashville. Chattanooga Jews settled in 1858 and organized Mizpah around 1890. An Orthodox congregation, B'nai Zion, followed there. Knoxville had two Orthodox congregations and new aid societies. Nashville families arrived in 1845 and built Magen David in 1854. Each town section gives rabbis, societies, and population counts. Together they show small Southern communities taking root.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teplitz-14329:
Teplitz, a town in northern Bohemia, had Jews documented as early as 1414. Isidore Singer and A. Kurrein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The community gained a burial ground and synagogue in 1480. In 1583 it paid the town yearly for free use of the baths.

Hard years followed during the Counter-Reformation. Jews without fixed business were expelled in 1667. The rest were confined to the Judengasse. They also had to wear a large white ruff. Joseph's decree of toleration ended the badge in 1781. After 1848 the community grew and built factories. A grand new synagogue rose in 1883.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todros-ben-mesh:
Todros ben Meshullam, called Todrosi, was a Provençal translator born at Arles. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked early in the fourteenth century. In 1337 he lived at Trinquetaille. There he finished translating Aristotle's Rhetoric into Hebrew.

At twenty he rendered Alfarabi's philosophical sayings into Hebrew. He also translated parts of Avicenna's great Najah. Averroes drew most of his labor after that. He translated Averroes on the Rhetoric and the Poetics. Three shorter Averroes treatises came from his pen too. One asks whether God knows details before creation. His odd signature, of the seed of the Jews, puzzles scholars. Some think he feared confusion with a converted relative.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trumbull-henry-:
Henry Clay Trumbull was an American Christian Orientalist and Sunday-school leader. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Stonington, Connecticut, in 1830, he died at Philadelphia in 1903. He became a Sunday-school missionary in 1858. In 1875 he took charge of the Sunday School Times.

He made that paper influential even among scholars. Ill health sent him traveling in 1881. He visited Egypt, Arabia, and Syria on that tour. He identified the site of Kadesh-barnea during the journey. His monograph on that site appeared in 1884. The Blood Covenant, in 1885, argued sacrifice began as covenant. W. R. Smith later developed that theory further. The Threshold Covenant followed in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valentin-gabrie:
Gabriel Gustav Valentin was a German physiologist born at Breslau in July 1810. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Valentin took his medical degree at Breslau in 1832 and first worked as a doctor there. In 1836 he became professor of physiology at the University of Bern in Switzerland.

Valentin won the Grand Prix of the Institut de France in 1835. His prize work compared how animals and plants develop. He later wrote on blood and its flow, on nerves and muscles, and on digestion. His textbook of human physiology went through several editions. He also edited a journal of anatomy and physiology for seven years. The entry lists his many books and shows a busy research career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-volozhin-14729:
Volozhin is a Russian town in the government of Wilna. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there in the mid fifteen hundreds. Most of the town's people were Jews. Its fame rests on a great rabbinical school. That school ran until 1892.

Hayyim ben Solomon founded the yeshibah in 1803. He was a pupil of the Gaon of Wilna. The school opposed the rising Hasidic movement. It stressed deep, orderly Talmud study instead. Only proven Talmud students could enter. Support came from communities across Russia and beyond. The entry tells how one small town shaped Jewish learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-nethaneel-:
Nethaneel Weil was a rabbi and Talmud scholar. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Stühlingen in 1687. He died at Rostadt on May 7, 1769. His uncle adopted him at Prague as a boy.

Young Nethaneel won leave to hear Prague's top lectures. His teacher offered him his niece in marriage. He taught in Prague, where pupils numbered in thousands. His pay as assistant rabbi stayed scant. Maria Theresa's 1744 expulsion edict drove him out. He then led the Black Forest rabbinate. At Carlsruhe he finished his great commentary in 1754.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wreschen-15029:
Wreschen is a town in Posen, three miles from the Russian line. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Lewin wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish group once ranked among the largest in south Prussia. The group felt the great attacks of 1648 to 1651 in full.

Sad to say, all its old papers burned in 1873. The fine old wood synagogue burned in that fire too. The old grave yard has been shut for forty years. Most of its old stones can no longer be read. The entry names the top men the town still recalls. Two were rabbis of the Mirels kin line. A third was the famed Bible scholar Meir Lob Malbim. One rabbi gave a Hebrew hymn to a Prussian general.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yudan-ben-manas:
Yudan ben Manasseh was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One rule of his lives on in the Jerusalem Talmud. Two tale words of his live on in the Babylon one.

Both tale words turn on one verse read two ways. That verse stands in the First Book of Samuel. He praised the clean speech of the Bible in one line. Even the marks of foul beasts are named with care, he said. The clean marks of those beasts are named first of all. That neat line of his is oft quoted in tale books. It stands in more than one midrash on the Law. The entry rests on the great tale study of Bacher.
kittredge-witchcraft-old-new-england-192:
George Lyman Kittredge was a Harvard man of great weight in his field. His Witchcraft in Old and New England came out in 1929. The book sweeps the trials of both Englands over three hundred years. It is the chief grave study of its theme in English.

Kittredge holds that belief in witchcraft was the norm, not a craze of fools. He works from court rolls, tracts, and tales of the day. Salem takes its place in a long, wide tale, not as a lone blot. The book still rules the study of Anglo witchcraft in the past.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-1:
Nathaniel Bowditch translated Laplace's Mecanique Celeste into English, with volume one reaching print in 1829. Laplace, often called the Newton of France, had summed up the math of the heavens. Books one and two cover balance, motion, and universal gravitation. Bowditch filled the margins with his own famed commentary.

His notes explain hard steps and correct or extend the French text. The translation taught American readers celestial mechanics at the highest level. It also made Bowditch's name as a scholar in two fields. Volume one begins a four volume set. The scale of the project still impresses. Patient readers gain a master class.
larsen-passing-1929:
Nella Larsen published Passing in 1929, a short novel about two childhood friends who meet again as adults. Irene Redfield lives as a Black woman in Harlem with her husband and sons. Clare Kendry passes as white and has married a racist white man. Their renewed friendship brings risk to both homes.

Clare longs for the Black world she left behind. Irene fears Clare's secret and her pull on Irene's husband. Tension builds toward a shocking final scene at a party. Larsen leaves key questions open for the reader to judge. The novel is a classic study of race, identity, and danger in America.
lenin-what-is-to-be-done-1929:
Lenin published What Is to Be Done in 1902, and it founded the Bolshevik idea of the party. The text here is the 1929 International Publishers version, from the Little Lenin Library. Russian socialists were split over how to organize against the tsar. Lenin answers with a call for a vanguard party of trained revolutionaries.

Workers alone, he argues, reach only trade union demands, not full socialist consciousness. A tight, disciplined party must bring that consciousness from outside. His attack on freedom of criticism as a slogan runs through the book. The argument shaped communist parties across the world. It remains Lenin's most debated early work.
lewis-dodsworth-1929:
Sinclair Lewis published Dodsworth in 1929, the mature masterpiece of his middle period. Lewis set it in Zenith and then across Europe, where he had been living part of each year. He wrote Sam Dodsworth with more sympathy than any hero since his earliest work.

Sam, a blunt automobile manufacturer, retires and takes his wife Fran on the European tour she craves. Fran, terrified of aging, hunts youth and aristocratic flirtation from London to Berlin. Sam, at first lost among the ruins and manners, slowly finds his own second life. The marriage comes apart in scenes of unusual fairness to both sides. Many readers now rank Dodsworth as Lewis's finest novel.
lewis-mind-world-order-1929:
Mind and the World Order, published in 1929, is C. I. Lewis's outline of a theory of knowledge, the book that founded conceptual pragmatism. Lewis, a Harvard philosopher, asks how the mind's own concepts shape the world it claims merely to find.

His answer: the a priori is pragmatic, made rather than found. Concepts are made by us, chosen for their use, yet once chosen they bind experience without exception. Knowledge is the reading of the given through such schemes. The argument joins Kant to Peirce in an original synthesis. The book influenced a generation of American philosophers and logicians.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-3-1929:
Book Three of Nicholson's Mathnawi came out in 1929. R. A. Nicholson gave Rumi's vast poem a full English dress with the Persian text. This book holds Books Five and Six of the poem. With it, the tale part of his set is done.

Rumi's tales grow more deep and wild as the poem nears its close. Love of God burns through tales of beasts, kings, and poor dervishes. The poem breaks off at the end, cut short by Rumi's death. Nicholson's notes clear the dense web of Sufi signs for the reader.
mckay-banjo-1929:
Claude McKay, the Jamaican-born poet of the Harlem Renaissance, published Banjo in 1929. McKay had wandered through America, London, and Soviet Russia before settling for a time in Marseille. He set the novel on that city's rough waterfront, among sailors and drifters from every shore.

The hero, Banjo, leads a loose band of Black seamen who play music, dodge work, and argue about race and art. His friend Ray, a Haitian writer, gives the talk a serious edge. Little plot holds the scenes together; the pleasure is in the talk, the music, and the port's mixed life. Banjo became a key novel of the Black Atlantic, read across three continents.
mo-tzu-mei-1929:
Yi-Pao Mei translated the works of Mo Tzu into English in 1929 as The Ethical and Political Works of Motse. The Mozi is the founding book of Mohism, the school that rivaled Confucianism in ancient China. Mo Tzu, who lived after Confucius, taught universal love in place of love graded by kinship.

The works attack wasteful funerals, aggressive war, and belief in blind fate. They prize merit in office, plain living, and proof by benefit to the people. Mei's version, in the Arthur Probsthain Oriental Series, was the first complete English Mozi. Mohism later faded in China, which makes the book doubly precious. It preserves a whole school of thought in its founder's own terms.
murad-the-unlucky-and-other-tales-pg2129:
Maria Edgeworth leads this set with Murad the Unlucky, an Eastern tale. The Limerick Gloves and Madame de Fleury complete the contents. An introduction traces Edgeworth's life from her birth in 1767. Her father held estates at Edgeworthstown in Ireland.

He wed three times and taught his son by Rousseau's Emile. Maria learned at Derby and London schools. Holidays brought her to Thomas Day, who wrote Sandford and Merton. Such a home made tales a tool for teaching. V1 praised the morals as gentle and the telling as first-rate, fit for young readers then and now.
newton-principia-motte-1729:
Isaac Newton's Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy appeared in English in 1729, in Andrew Motte's translation. The Latin Principia of 1687 had set out Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation. Motte's version was the first in English, and it carried Newton to readers without Latin.

Newton showed that one law of gravity governs falling apples, the Moon, and the planets alike. He derived the paths of comets, the tides, and the shape of the Earth from a few stated laws. The math is hard, and Motte kept it close and plain. This translation shaped how the English-speaking world learned the founding work of modern physics.
objections-to-phrenology-being-the-subst: Objections to Phrenology gathers papers by David Drummond, tied to the Calcutta Phrenological Society, and dated 1829 in the record. The full title calls the book the substance of a series of papers communicated in Calcutta. The hosted sample holds only a digitization notice from a scanning project, so it preserves no readable content from the book itself. The title alone states the stance: a case against phrenology, argued before readers in India. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
observations-on-the-phrenological-develo:
Thomas Stone published this short book in 1829. It studies the heads of Burke, Hare, and other killers. Phrenology claimed that skull shape reveals character and talent. Stone gives measurements of thieves held in Edinburgh Jail and Bridewell. He also gives measurements for people from England, Scotland, and Ireland.

Stone presents his facts as evidence against phrenology itself. The title promises a series of facts that undercut the system. Readers meet a once popular idea tested by its own method. The hosted sample preserves only the title wording in readable form. Most pages survive as garbled scan text. The record lists 75 pages with illustrations.
openalex-w1493890929:
Rommy von Bernhardi, Laura Eugenín-von Bernhardi, and Jaime Eugenín wrote this review. It appeared in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience in July 2015. All three authors work at Chilean universities. Aging is the main risk factor for brain degeneration, they note. Microglia are the brain's own immune defense cells.

In aging, microglia change form in ways that suggest activation. Such activation can lead to harmful brain inflammation. That inflammation is now accepted as part of disease, they write. The review gathers evidence on microglial failure in aging. It links cell dysfunction to diseases that destroy memory.
openalex-w2008789929:
Joseli Oliveira-Ferreira, Marcus Lacerda, Patricia Brasil and colleagues reviewed malaria in Brazil. Their overview appeared in Malaria Journal in 2010. Malaria remains a major health problem in Brazil. Case numbers had fallen greatly since the 1940s. The authors summed up the current picture.

Nearly all cases now occur in the Amazon Basin. The main mosquito vector lives across most of the country. One parasite species causes most registered cases there. The milder vivax species dominates, yet it still causes much illness. Rapid settlement of the Amazon raised case numbers again. Crowded new settlements made standard control harder to carry out. The review covers that history and the control challenge it leaves.
openalex-w2019183229:
Sophie Bonnet, Julien Dekaezemacker, Kendra Turk-Kubo and colleagues measured nitrogen fixation deep in the Pacific Ocean. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Bacteria that fix nitrogen turn gas into a form life can use. Most such work had focused on sunlit surface waters.

The team sampled from the surface down to great depth. The site was the eastern tropical South Pacific. Fixation occurred in dark waters as well as sunlit ones. Per litre, dark layer rates were low. Spread over the deep layer, they formed most of the total. Gene tests confirmed nitrogen-fixing microbes lived there. Added amino acids boosted fixation in the low-oxygen zone.
openalex-w2022091129:
Julia Reisser, Boyan Slat, Kim Noble and colleagues measured how floating plastic spreads through surface waters. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2015. Tiny plastics are common across the ocean surface. Wind and waves mix them into the upper water column. Most counts come only from the very surface.

The team used a new multi-level net in the North Atlantic Gyre. It sampled from the surface down to five metres. They worked at twelve sites in the gyre. Plastic amounts fell sharply with depth.
