Statistical screening picked the telling variables, then five machine learning methods competed to predict severity, judged by a standard accuracy curve. Antibody G subtypes, rarely used in triage, anchor the approach. A validated score could flag fragile elders for early intensive care.
pmc-10732029:
Kamran Abbasi and co-authors, writing for more than two hundred health journals, urge leaders to treat climate change and nature loss as one health emergency, in work from twenty twenty-three. The editorial says the two crises are split in talks and research, and that split is a grave error.

Heat, drought, fire, and flood wreck plant life and soil, which then store less carbon and warm the world more. At the same time, healthy land and seas can heal and pull carbon back down. Some fixes help one side yet harm the other, so plans must be joined. Native land care gets a key role in the call. The piece speaks to the United Nations, leaders, and health workers.
pmc-10735629:
Naomi Meinertz, Jeong Eun Lee, and Megan Gilligan argue that family care programs in the United States too often leave out minority families. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. Women do most family care work in the home. Minority families face higher rates of poor health and stress. Yet most support programs were built and tested with White families.

The authors review care programs and check whether the known ones work for non-White families. They find that results broken down by race and ethnic group are rare. That gap can hide uneven results and deepen unfair gaps in care. The paper also looks at newer programs built for set groups of families. It calls for care programs shaped with diverse families from the start.
pmc-10736829:
Wu and six colleagues link social traits to aging related gene activity in older Americans in twenty twenty-three. Certain gene programs in blood cells respond to stress, DNA damage, and cell aging. Social and environmental exposures can tune those programs. The team asked how age, sex, and race or ethnic group relate to three such scores.

They used RNA data from a national sample of two thousand six hundred eighty adults aged fifty-five and older. Older age linked to lower scores on an inflammation related program and a cell aging program. Women scored higher on parts of the stress response program than men. Black and Hispanic adults showed lower cell aging scores than White adults. Adjusting for health habits and conditions changed the results little.
pmc-10737429:
Ashley Kuzmik wrote this research paper, published in 2023, about the family members who care for people with dementia when those patients leave the hospital. It looks at what drives the anxiety, depression, and burden those care partners feel at discharge.

The study drew on 434 patient and care partner pairs in a family-centered care program. A patient's behavior and mood symptoms were tied to all three outcomes in care partners. Living in the same home was linked to more depression in the care partner. Worse patient function was also tied to depression. The paper argues that discharge planning should weigh the patient's behavior and function, not just medical needs, to support the family member taking over care.
pmc-10738129:
Alexis Bender, Kiera Chan, Riley Hunt, and Molly Perkins interview clinic staff about merging substance use and HIV care into one service, in a 2023 study. The two conditions feed each other: drug use raises viral loads, hurts adherence, and kills. The team spoke with 21 providers and 15 administrators across Georgia, many serving older or rural patients. Both groups saw integrated care as a real benefit, above all easier access with fewer disruptions.

What integration meant, though, varied by respondent. Barriers piled up in space, staffing, budgets, and thin chances to collaborate. Most providers, outside the most integrated clinics, struggled to place patients into solid addiction treatment. The authors argue integration is vital for aging patients, and name what blocks it.
pmc-10738229:
Kristine Talley and co-authors shared a 2023 report on a geriatric case competition for health science students. Teams from many fields plan care for a simulated older patient with a complex mix of conditions. Health students most often learn within their own disciplines. That leaves them poorly prepared for the team-based care that frail older adults need.

Two university programs ran the competition in 2022. Each team had a coach and one month to build a care plan presentation. Judges scored the presentations on teamwork skills. The top teams from each site then met in a live online final. Of 132 students who took part, fifty-four completed an evaluation form. Their ratings were good to excellent. In their own words, two themes led: the value of patient-centered care, and the power of the team.
pmc-10738629:
Christina Victor and Dorothy Yen study a UK scheme called Happy to Chat, which encourages people to talk with strangers in public places. Their 2023 study draws on interviews with 23 people aged 51 to 88 who took part in the scheme early that year. The work focuses on older adults after the Covid-19 lockdowns.

The authors find that experiences differ by age and gender. People over 65 were more willing to chat, and spent more time doing so, than those aged 51 to 64. Men felt more sure than women about handling the risks of talking to strangers. The findings feed into training materials and chat aids meant to help older people feel safe starting conversations.
pmc-10738929:
Kengo Watanabe and co-authors shared a 2023 study of what lifespan-extending treatments do inside mouse tissues, read through many molecular lenses at once. A few dietary and drug approaches are known to extend mouse life and hold off age-related diseases. Their actions in the body were still unclear. The team asks what core cell processes they all share.

They pooled three kinds of data: metabolite readings, protein readings, and gene activity readings, from a large aging-study consortium and earlier publications. Three analysis tools read the haul. One checks how stable the ranking of cell processes stays. One networks genes that rise and fall together. One maps the metabolic grid of the body. Lifespan treatments kept the rankings more stable and shifted the flow of metabolites. One process stood out across treatments: how fats are burned. More treatments and more tissue types confirmed the story.
pmc-10742529:
Huanle Guo and co-authors study in 2023 why some maize plants load their kernels with cadmium, a toxic metal. Cadmium in farm soil can enter the food chain and harm health. A gene called ZmHMA3, which moves heavy metals inside the plant, was known to set how much cadmium corn grains collect.

The team compared proteins in kernels of a normal line and a mutant with the gene knocked out, under metal stress. The mutant stored more cadmium and switched on more stress proteins. The protein shifts pointed to different pathways in each line, covering sugar use, nitrogen handling, and defense chemistry. The work maps how this one gene shapes the plant's response to the metal.
pmc-10745929:
Huafeng Shi and four co-authors find a recipe tweak that slows how fast hot carriers cool inside perovskite crystals, a property solar cells can exploit. Their study came out in 2023. Perovskites are leading materials for cheap, efficient light devices, but their excited electrons usually shed energy as heat within moments.

Adding about ten percent extra cesium during crystal growth strained the crystal lattice. Light itself then expanded the lattice, canceling the strain. Under that balance, the coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations dropped by about seventy percent. Carriers kept their excess energy about three and a half times longer than usual. The work reveals a new role for the cesium ions that sit in the crystal's corners. It also offers growers a practical knob for tuning device behavior.
pmc-10747229:
Tao Zhang and Yong Liu prepare a clear flame retardant for epoxy resin in a 2023 study. Epoxy is used in optics, lighting, and energy gear, where a flame retardant must not cloud the material or shift its color. Their new compound is built from a known phosphorus based retardant family.

Resin loaded with seven percent of the compound passed a standard burn test at the top rating and kept ninety four percent of the clear resin's light transmission. Heat release fell by about a third and smoke by over a quarter, compared with plain resin. The compound also improved heat stability. Tests showed it works both in the gas phase and in the solid char layer.
pmc-10747329:
Pavla Šabacká and co-authors model supersonic air flow around sensors inside a specialized electron microscope, in a 2023 study. The microscope works across pressure regimes, and probes inserted near its nozzle disturb the very flow being studied. Shock waves form differently at normal pressure than near the edge of vacuum.

Using mathematical-physics simulations, the team compared flat-ended and pointed sensors under a ten-to-one pressure ratio, run two ways: ordinary atmospheric pressure before the nozzle, and a low pressure of ten thousand pascals. They tracked detached and conical shock waves and how the sensor shape bends them. The boundary regime matters because continuum physics itself starts to fray there. Results guide sensor design so measurements disturb the specimen chamber as little as possible.
pmc-10754529:
Liyuan Hao and co-authors review, in a 2023 paper, a protein that helps liver cancer evade the immune system. The protein, called PD-L1, sits on cells and can switch off immune cells that bear its partner receptor. Drugs that block this brake, immune checkpoint inhibitors, work on advanced liver cancer, but their benefit varies greatly by person. High levels of PD-L1 may be a main factor behind weak responses.

The review walks through levels that control the protein's amount, from gene variation and epigenetic marks to changes made after the protein is produced. It also asks which cell type in the tumor environment carries the PD-L1 that matters most, a point not settled. Beyond its immune role, PD-L1 can promote tumor growth and drug resistance on its own. The authors close with natural compounds and drugs that shift PD-L1 levels in this cancer.
pmc-10758129:
Louie Cris Lopos, Urbashi Panthi, Igor Kovalchuk, and Andriy Bilichak review microRNAs as levers to engineer better wheat. Yields are plateauing while heat and drought worsen. Wheat's huge three-part genome makes editing protein genes very hard. MicroRNAs, tiny regulators that repress many genes at once, offer a side door.

The team survey how tuning microRNA expression could address stress tolerance and the tissue culture bottleneck that blocks transformation of elite varieties. MicroRNAs are highly conserved, so their targets are easier to call across the genome's copies than protein genes are. The review weighs evidence for specific microRNA families in development and stress responses. It closes by judging where this strategy could in fact move wheat forward.
pmc-10764229:
Thinzar Aung and Mi Jeong Kim review drinks made from wheat, from brewing craft to health effects. Their review was published in twenty twenty-three. Demand is rising for drinks that do more than refresh, and wheat brings fiber, phenolics, and calming amino compounds.

Wheat flour fills bakeries, while germ and bran are usually side streams; both can enrich drinks. Yet wheat has drawn little attention as a beverage base next to its food uses. The review walks through making methods, taste, and biological activity of wheat drinks. It also weighs the sustainability angle and the hurdles the niche faces. The authors aim to guide design of non-alcoholic, plant-based functional drinks from a staple grain.
pmc-10769129:
Wenjun Bai, Zhe Wang, Junwei Liang, and Hualiang Deng pool trials of a Chinese herbal formula for irritable bowel syndrome. The syndrome causes gut pain and changed bowel habits with no clear cause. The formula is built on two core herbs and is widely used by practitioners of Chinese medicine. The team searched seven data bases for trials up to May 2023.

Twenty-four trials with 3,768 people met the bar for the pool. The formula gave more relief of overall gut symptoms than placebo or Western drugs. Scores for illness severity also fell more with the formula. A check that weighs how much proof has built up backed both results. The authors see promise, above all for the diarrhea form, but note weak proof and call for stricter trials.
pmc-10769529:
Wei Han, Dianxing Feng, and Shutong Dai report the full mitochondrial genome of a beetle used in forensic work. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The beetle feeds on carrion, so its presence on a body can help date a death.

The genome runs seventeen thousand five hundred fifty-six letters long. It holds thirteen protein-coding genes, twenty-two transfer RNA genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and one long noncoding stretch. Its letters lean heavily toward A and T. Family tree analysis places the beetle close to two burying beetle species in the same subfamily. The authors say the sequence gives forensic and evolutionary studies a firmer reference for this species.
pmc-10783629:
Philippe Roudot and a large team of co-authors present software for tracking particles in three dimensions, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. Dense 3D movies of cell innards defeat older tracking tools. Their package, u-track3D, extends a trusted 2D frame into full volume.

Tests across microscope types and a standard contest set matched rival tools, including deep learning ones. A moving window view lets users inspect live 3D action in flat views. An automatic score grades each track's trustworthiness, replacing eyeball checks. The toolkit aims at fair, hands-off study of molecular motion.
pmc-10823429:
Yankai Luo and a large team test a plant extract as chicken feed additive in a 2024 study. White feather broilers dominate world poultry output, but reliance on antibiotics raises drug resistance concerns. The extract comes from a traditional Chinese herb with germ fighting traits and no known resistance risk.

Birds were split into a control group and two groups fed low or high doses of the extract for thirty five days. Growth did not change. Gut microbe checks showed both doses shifted the gut community in ways linked to more amino acids and certain fatty acids in the meat. The authors say the extract could improve meat flavor and nutrition as a greener alternative to antibiotics.
pmc-10850029:
Welsh, Goberdhan, O'Driscoll, and co-authors set out updated guidance for studies of extracellular vesicles, known as MISEV2023. Vesicles are tiny parcels that cells release, loaded with cargo from their cell of origin. Their contents can change how other cells behave.

Those traits make vesicles promising as disease markers and even as treatments, and interest has grown fast. Fast growth, though, can mean uneven methods between labs. The guidance, from basic to advanced approaches, sets shared standards for isolating and reporting vesicles. Common rules help results from different groups add up instead of clashing.
pmc-10922929:
Nicholas Mallek, Elizabeth Martin, Lisa Dailey, and Shaun McCullough warn that a common dosing shortcut itself changes lung cell cultures, in a two thousand twenty-four paper on toxins. Air-liquid interface cultures of human bronchial cells are the workhorse for testing inhaled stuff.

Many test chemicals cannot be delivered as aerosols, so the research team pipette liquid onto the cells' air-exposed surface. The authors show that liquid application alone reprograms the transcriptome, redirects signaling pathways, boosts inflammatory cytokine release, and weakens the epithelial barrier. Anyone reading exposure tests with this method must subtract the liquid's own effects first. The paper supplies starting infrastructure for respiratory testing labs.
pmc-11538329:
Vivekamanickam Venkateswaran leads a team on small wind turbine aerodynamics. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with horizontal axis turbines. Random airfoil shapes were tested for the small scale design.

Glide ratios were compared across the foil set. The best foil was picked for blade design work. Chord and twist options were then tuned for output. Lift, drag, and power curves came from momentum math. Varied air densities were run through the models. Flow simulation checked the results at attack angles. A Weibull view mapped wind speed frequencies.  Results matched well between the two methods.
pmc-11564129:
Giovanni Briganti and co-authors give an overview of network analysis for mental health research. Their 2024 paper explains how graphs can map links among mental health traits, such as mood, sleep, and worry. The field has grown fast, and new tools have spread before many readers could follow them.

The authors walk through main model types, from networks that change over time to networks built from panel data. They also cover networks that include treatments, hidden traits, and factors that shift link strength. Bayesian networks get a section on causal claims from snapshot data. The paper closes by asking how network models and theories of mental illness can shape each other. It serves as a bridge for clinicians and analysts alike.
pmc-11570929:
Huiqing Yang, Xin Zhang, and Bo Xue review new insights into cellular senescence and chronic wounds. Their 2024 review covers non-healing wounds such as diabetic foot, venous leg, and pressure ulcers that burden patients and health systems heavily.

Healing slows with age partly because cells become senescent, and high glucose, reactive oxygen, and persistent inflammation all drive that state. The review covers senescence characteristics, stressors and signalling pathways, and links to typical chronic wounds. Current and future treatment strategies form the fourth section. Anti-ageing therapy might influence healing in theory, but molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood, which the authors aim to clarify.
pmc-11573729:
Yadav Ghimirey, Raju Acharya, and Jeffrey Mintz recount wild mammals in Nepal's Annapurna Conservation Area with camera traps and careful math. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Simple counts can miss shy species, so richness figures may mislead the managers who rely on them.

A twenty seventeen camera survey recorded twenty-one mammal species. The team then fit models that account for imperfect detection, since a species can be present yet never photographed. The model put true richness near twenty-six species, meaning about five were likely missed. It also estimated how often sites were used and how rarely animals were caught on camera. Richness seemed to rise with certain habitat features. The work shows why detection-aware methods give truer guides for conservation choices.
pmc-11585529:
Xiaorui Tian and four colleagues found a loop of RNA that helps kidney cancer shrug off a key drug. The drug, sunitinib, is a mainstay for renal cell cancer, but tumors learn to resist it. The loop, named hsa_circ_0072732, was spotted in RNA data sets and proved to be a true closed circle: it shrugged off enzymes that chew loose RNA ends. Lab tests then linked it to drug failure.

The loop blocks ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by rust-like fat damage. With that death path shut, cancer cells survive sunitinib that should kill them. Tests tracked cell growth, death signals, and fat-damage markers to make the case. The twenty twenty-four study names both a target and a test: cut the loop, or read it in blood, and resistant kidney cancer may lose its shield.
pmc-11588329:
Heba Marey and six colleagues published a 2024 study that compares satellite measures of carbon monoxide during wildfires. In September 2020, the western United States saw extreme fires. The smoke sent out almost three times the carbon monoxide of an average year across the past two decades.

Three space instruments watched the smoke: MOPITT, IASI, and TROPOMI. Each reads the air in its own way, so their numbers can differ. The team set the three records side by side over North America. They checked where the tools agree and where they part. Knowing the gaps helps scientists trust satellite data on fire smoke and air quality.
pmc-11592929:
Marco Macagno and a large team published a methods comparison in two thousand twenty-four on detecting a gene switch in tumours. The MGMT gene's promoter, when silenced by methylation, predicts response to a common chemotherapy drug. A trial sorting bowel cancer patients needed a reliable test for it.

Two digital PCR methods were compared on metastatic bowel cancer samples. One, Methyl-BEAMing, mixes droplet amplification with flow counting and is highly sensitive. The other, droplet digital PCR, is more automated and handles many samples with little operator input. The study reports that the two methods' results agreed closely, supporting either for trial screening. Full numeric detail sits in the paper's results section.
pmc-11593329:
Shuai Fan and nine co-authors review drug targeting of a growth-factor receptor in cancer in a 2024 paper. The receptor drives core pathways that control cell growth, specialization, and survival. When it is altered, those pathways can lock on, fueling division, blocking cell death, and aiding spread. The review explains how the receptor switches on and catalogs the kinds of alteration found in tumors.

It then gathers current therapies aimed at those alterations, drug by drug. The authors aim to give future treatment design a clear map of which drug fits which defect. The piece is a reference review for oncology researchers and clinicians.
pmc-11595729:
Moulias and fourteen colleagues test blood vessel function after COVID-19 in twenty twenty-four. The virus appears to damage the endothelium, the lining of blood vessels. Such damage may precede clots and heart complications. The team used a fingertip tonometry device to measure vessel response.

Twenty-three patients were compared with twenty-two matched controls. The patients' vascular response index was clearly lower two months after discharge. The gap was visible during hospitalisation and lasted six months. Over half the patients met the dysfunction threshold while hospitalised. Rates of clots, heart events, and death did not differ significantly. The authors conclude vessel dysfunction after COVID-19 can persist.
pmc-11600929:
Vandana Apurva Das and her five co-authors, publishing in 2024, compare the genomes of two bacteria that help apple trees grow, hunting the features behind their gift. Both strains belong to the Bacillus family and were already known to promote plant growth. The team read their full genomes side by side, looking for mobile DNA, borrowed genes, and fresh sequence motifs.

Both genomes carry islands of foreign DNA and intact virus remnants, signs that gene swapping with other microbes stocked them with useful traits. Those imports appear to underwrite survival tricks, adaptation, and the growth-promoting chemistry itself. The team also found new DNA motifs tied to core physiology and metabolism. The authors frame the comparison as a mechanistic sketch of how helpful soil bacteria evolve their talents, useful for designing sustainable orchard treatments.
pmc-11604929:
Minsik Kim and a large team test ways to remove human DNA from frozen airway samples. Their methods study from twenty twenty-four supports metagenomic sequencing for microbiome work. Human DNA dominates these samples and drowns out microbial signals. Standard gene fragment sequencing gives coarser results than full metagenomics.

The team compared five depletion methods across three sample types. Nasal swabs, cystic fibrosis sputum, and lung wash samples were included. Untreated samples were almost entirely human reads. Depletion raised microbial reads and the range of species found. Effects varied by sample type and method. Freezing harmed some bacteria, but a protective additive helped. One kit-based method caused the least harm.
pmc-11607429:
Anna Delgado-Tejedor and co-authors published this molecular biology study in 2024. Chemical modifications sit on the ribosomal RNA inside bacterial ribosomes, the machines that build proteins. Whether those marks change when conditions change was unknown. The team used nanopore sequencing, which reads native RNA strands, to survey the marks after exposing bacteria to a range of antibiotics.

First they built a new analysis pipeline, NanoConsensus, that calls marks with very few false alarms across types and coverage levels. With it, they found that antibiotics strip or shift marks near the ribosome's A and P sites, the pockets where transfer RNAs dock during protein building. Each drug left a distinct pattern. The authors suggest this shift may feed into resistance. They offer it as a general tool for tracking RNA mark changes in any species.
pmc-11607829:
Wenjun Zhang and others studied a protective immune switch in 2024. One disease attacks the spinal cord, eyes, and brainstem. Antibodies trigger that demyelinating disorder. Microglia arrive early at injury sites. They drive lesion formation in tissue. A surface protein called CD22 was tested.

Blocking CD22 made brain inflammation worse. Myeloid cells also behaved more harmfully. Two signalling proteins sat downstream here. A blocker drug reversed the harm. Mice improved greatly with that inhibitor drug. CD22 thus restrains damaging cell activation. The switch was previously unrecognised here. New immune therapies may target it in the years ahead.
pmc-11608029:
Fu, Xing, Yang, Liu, and Ma studied this marker in twenty twenty-four for nerve damage in diabetes. The marker divides fasting C-peptide, a sign of how much insulin the body still makes, by the years a person has had diabetes. Nerve damage in the feet and legs is a common and serious complication. The team asked whether the ratio flags patients at risk.

The study compared eight hundred sixteen patients, half with nerve damage and half without. Patients with damage had lower ratios on average. A high ratio acted as a protective factor even after other risks were taken into account. The ratio also predicted nerve damage better than either of its parts alone. The authors propose it as a cheap screening aid.
pmc-11609629:
Allison Barrett leads a large team evaluating an engineered T cell therapy for digestive cancers, in a preclinical study published in two thousand twenty-four. The target is claudin 18.2, a junction protein abundant on gastric, esophageal, and pancreatic tumors. Such solid tumors often suppress immune attack with TGF-beta signals.

The candidate, AZD6422, is a chimeric antigen receptor T cell armored against that suppression. Armoring is meant to keep the cells active inside hostile tumor environments. The paper reports the therapy's preclinical development and testing. It examines how the engineered cells behave against tumors carrying the target. Work of this kind precedes any human trial. The authors position the candidate for indications where effective treatments remain scarce.
pmc-11611829:
Zheyuan Ding and colleagues trace how China's COVID control policies bent the curve of a different disease: hand, foot and mouth disease in Zhejiang Province. The childhood enterovirus illness normally peaks each spring and summer. The team collected a decade of case data and compared case composition and weekly seasonality across control stages, using interrupted time-series regression to estimate policy effects.

Cases skewed toward children living separately from parents, and the usual spring-summer peak simply did not occur in twenty twenty. The disease's biennial peak periodicity was disrupted for a year, and the twenty twenty-three summer peak ran higher than in other years. During strict control, the shares of kindergarten children and two-to-four-year-olds were relatively low, consistent with closures suppressing transmission. Pathogens shifted too, with enteroviruses other than the two classic types becoming dominant in increasing proportion.
pmc-11612229:
Hiba Ibraheem led a team that made, in two thousand twenty-four, new hydrazone drugs and probed how they might act. The group has known worth in care. The team built their set in three steps, then ran lab tests and computer sums.

First, hydrazine met a carbonyl compound in warm ethanol to form the base, called H1. Next, H1 met indole to form a Schiff base, H2. In step three, H1 met thiophene to form H3. Tests with light and with magnets checked each new drug. H2 and H3 fought cell harm from rust-like stress, more so at higher dose. They also slowed the growth of three germs: Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Candida albicans. The sums showed firm holds on target sites in cells. That firm hold marks the set as a lead worth more work as a drug for colon cancer.
pmc-11612529:
Koichiro Matsumura and a team including Takahiro Tabuchi ask whether a health phone app nudges people with untreated high blood pressure to start medication. Their real-world cohort study was published in twenty twenty-four. Getting such patients onto drugs early prevents later heart and vessel disease.

The team mined a large database joining health checkups, insurance claims, and app records, mostly from working-age people and their families. The app logs weight and steps and sends tailored health tips. Patients whose hypertension was found at checkup were followed to see who began drug treatment. The analysis tests whether app use quickened that start. A tool that moves people from knowing to treating could close a common gap in blood pressure care.
pmc-11616129:
Ateeq Almuwallad and four co-authors interview Saudi paramedics about the strain of handling adult trauma. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Little was known about the specific hurdles these front-line crews face.

Twenty paramedics from the national Red Crescent service spoke in online interviews. They described friction in coordinating care and in getting accurate patient information at the scene. Keeping confidence and readiness up was a recurring strain. Crews said they build skill on their own through courses, drills, and peer talk. Their asks were plain: cleaner handovers, more staff, relief from burnout, and public awareness that helps rather than hinders. The authors turn the voices into concrete fixes for daily practice.
pmc-11616229:
Ivo Leist and colleagues published a 2024 paper on Pheno-Ranker, a software toolkit for comparing phenotypic data. Phenotypic data describe a person's observable traits and symptoms. Such comparisons are essential for disease studies, patient grouping, and linking genes to traits.

The toolkit works with the Phenopackets and Beacon standards set by the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health. These standards store and share genomic and phenotypic data in a consistent format. Matching patients across such files is still difficult because older methods do not fully support the formats. Pheno-Ranker computes how similar two records are, which helps researchers find matching patients and spot patterns across large collections of health data.
pmc-11618029:
David Korda, Andras Bibok, and Attila Doros lead a team reporting Hungary's first run of double-vein embolization, a trick to grow the liver before major liver surgery. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Removing much of the liver is only safe if the remnant can handle the load. Blocking veins on the side to be removed redirects blood and swells the keeper side.

Sixteen procedures were performed at one university center over eighteen months. Every procedure succeeded technically, with no major complications. Nearly all patients went on to their planned resection. The remnant grew substantially in both volume and share within weeks. Function scans showed matching gains in clearing power. One patient died of liver failure after surgery, a sobering footnote. The authors judge their results in line with the international literature. The technique now has a Hungarian foothold.
pmc-11619429:
Carolina Dertzbocher Feil Pinho and co-authors pool results on guided exercise and youth fitness. Their 2024 review covers children and teens aged seven to seventeen. Fitness is a key health mark at that age, but the best way to train it is debated.

The team searched major databases for trials that compared structured, supervised exercise with no exercise. Trials had to measure strength, heart and lung fitness, or speed. The authors then pooled the results and tested which factors shaped the gains. Age, sex, body mass, and training choices such as weekly sessions all came into the analysis. The review gives coaches and health staff a grounded sense of which programs raise fitness most, and for whom.
pmc-11619629:
Liu and four co-authors test plant-fat solvents to dissolve a poorly soluble natural compound, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Xanthone has health promise but dissolves badly in water. Classic solvents raise safety and green concerns. The team tries mixes of two triglyceride fats as a greener option.

Solubility peaks at a set mix ratio and climbs steeply with heat. A local-composition model fits the data with very low error. The model shows the two fats interact most strongly with each other. Dissolving is driven mainly by heat uptake, not disorder. The compound keeps its molecular form after dissolving, though crystal traits shift. Results support fats as solvents for water-shy compounds.
pmc-11626029:
Jiwon Kim and four colleagues published a 2024 study on spotting diseases of the orchid Cymbidium kanran. Four fungi cause much of the harm to this orchid. Telling them apart by eye is slow and hard, even for experts, so growers need a fast lab test.

The team built a single test that finds all four fungi at once. They designed four pairs of DNA markers, one per fungus, each giving a band of a distinct size. The test can detect as little as 0.1 units of DNA from each fungus. Trials on sick orchids showed the test works in practice, giving growers a quicker way to name the problem and act.
pmc-11630829:
Chodnekar and Tsetskhladze wrote a review in twenty twenty-four on human trials that use CRISPR gene editing. Gene editing promises cures for inherited diseases, but trial progress needed a stocktake. The pair searched seven trial databases up to March twenty twenty-four. They found eighty-two trials that used CRISPR in patients. They sorted the trials by disease, country, treatment type, and year. Quality checks used a standard ten-item tool for study appraisal.

The United States and China lead in trial counts by a wide margin. Cancer is the top target, with blood diseases next in line. Trial starts peaked in twenty eighteen in their count. Few trials run in Africa, Asia beyond China, or South America. The authors say current trials barely tap the method's full scope.
pmc-11631729:
Linlin Xiao and co-authors look at sites where locally advanced rectal cancer came back, and ask if elective nodal irradiation could be left out under total neoadjuvant therapy. Their 2024 study reviews patients whose cancer came back after surgery.

One hundred twenty-six patients took part, with one hundred eighty-six lesions that came back. They were read next to the imaging from when the cancer was first found. Most cases that came back sat in the pelvic cavity. They were centred in mesenteric and presacral regions. A large majority of patients had lesions that came back in zones of high risk, or in zones first thought to be at risk. Levels of a tumour marker at the start, and the type of adjuvant therapy, each forecast, on their own, if the cancer would come back in key regions. The data aim to hone target areas for radiotherapy.
pmc-11632029:
Korhan Kollu and five colleagues test whether tryptophan breakdown products can flag delirium in older patients in intensive care. The study followed 120 patients over sixty in a medical intensive care unit. In their first twenty-four hours, blood levels of tryptophan and five products made from it were compared between patients who did and did not develop delirium.

Patients with delirium were older and had higher scores for other illnesses. Their tryptophan was lower. Ratios of kynurenine and quinolinic acid to tryptophan were much higher. The kynurenine ratio was the strongest single predictor. One ratio kept a borderline link on its own in the adjusted analysis. The authors say these early blood markers could flag high-risk patients for preventive care.
pmc-11635229:
Peihong Hu, Bo Tian, Hang Gu, Haoran Liu, and Qiang Li build a model that reads lung tumor tissue images to forecast patient outlook. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Older methods predict survival in lung adenocarcinoma poorly, and a newer immune marker called TIGIT may help.

The team drew clinical data and tissue images from a public cancer atlas. Gene checks first confirmed that TIGIT levels carry forecast value. Software then cut the images into parts and pulled out hundreds of measured features. Three selection methods narrowed the features down, and a regression model turned them into a score. Chart tests judged how well the score foresaw TIGIT levels and outcome. The approach could give prognosis from slides alone, sparing extra gene tests.
pmc-11636029:
Liselott Årestedt, Fredrik Uhlin, and Ann Catrine Eldh evaluate ways of getting kidney care teams to involve patients as partners, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Nine Swedish kidney units tried three routes: no support, a participation toolkit sent to managers, or the toolkit plus six months of coaching for local facilitators.

Control sites never took up patient participation at all. Toolkit-only managers liked the materials but never put them to use. In the coached group, five facilitators engaged with the support program and valued what it taught about preference-based participation and about implementation itself. Interviews, recordings, and context surveys fed the mixed analysis. The lesson: handing over a tool is not enough; people need guided help to change practice.
pmc-11636529:
Yan and five colleagues review early cells found in the meniscus, a pad of tissue in the knee, in twenty twenty-four. The pad cushions the joint and helps guard it from wear. When it tears, healing is slow and the joint can break down. Cells that can grow and turn into other cell types may aid repair.

The review sorts how labs find and pull out these cells from knee tissue. It covers the marks on their surface and where in the pad they seem to live. Most work so far pulls the cells out and puts them back in animals. The authors say more study is needed before use in patients.
pmc-11637329:
Hideyuki Kabasawa and eight co-authors test a feed given during dialysis for patients who lack food. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. People on long-term dialysis can drift into poor nutrition. The feed, ENEFLUID, is pumped through the dialysis line three times a week. They run the trial at many centres, by lot, with open labels.

Forty patients with mild to mid malnutrition are split, half fed and half not, for twelve weeks. The main blood marker of protein state does not differ between groups. Protein intake holds up better in the fed group, where food protein rises while it falls in the control group. No ill events occur.
pmc-11639029:
Qiaozhi Hu and five co-authors review studies that use machine learning to warn of bad drug effects from health record data. Their review and pooled study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Bad drug effects harm many patients, and records hold rich clues to who is at risk. The team searched four large bases for work that built such warn tools for more than one drug effect at once.

Ten studies fit the brief, with twenty methods in use. Tree-based random forest was the most used method by far. Top scores came when that method was paired with ways to fix skewed data. Long stays, many drugs, and admit type were the top risk clues. The pooled score sat in a fair range.
pmc-11640429:
Sekelj Fures and co-authors measure a pain-linked peptide in children with headache. The peptide, CGRP, is well studied in adult migraine but less in children. The team drew blood between attacks from three groups. Groups held 66 children with migraine, 59 with tension headache, and 53 healthy peers. Children were split by age at first headache.

Migraine cases had higher CGRP than both other groups. Tension cases and healthy peers did not differ. Children with migraine without aura had higher levels than those with aura. The gap was clearest when headaches began between ages 7 and 12. The authors say CGRP marks child migraine, with shifts by type and onset age.
pmc-11640529:
Leão and colleagues test in twenty twenty-four whether warming eggs late in incubation changes broiler chickens after hatching. Eggs were kept at the standard setting or warmed for a few, half-day, or full-day stretch across three late days. Chicks then grew under normal farm conditions to market age, while the team tracked hatching, growth, body traits, gut form, and heat responses.

A full day of warming cut hatch rates and later growth and feeding. A brief warming raised a heat-shock protein in the liver and quickened breathing, hinting at better heat coping. Mid-length warming only quickened breathing. Carcass traits, gut shape, and nutrient use stayed unchanged across groups. The authors call brief warming possibly helpful, long warming harmful.
pmc-11641729:
Kinga Markowska and four co-authors shared a review in twenty twenty-four. It is about how bacteria that live without oxygen talk to each other. They do so inside biofilms. Anaerobic biofilms drive stubborn infections. They grow on implants and in inflamed guts. Their residents coordinate through chemical shouts called autoinducers. Those signals steer sticking, maturing, and dispersal in the film.

The review lists the signal families these groups use. They run from acyl-homoserine lactones to autoinducer-2, which is near-universal. Peptide signals are in the set too. Quorum signals switch on virulence and antibiotic resistance as well. That is why jamming them draws drug developers. The jam is called quorum quenching. Enzymes that degrade signals are one response the survey covers. Decoys that block receptors are an other. The authors frame communication itself as the target for treatment.
pmc-11641829:
David Putzer and six co-authors chart the early learn curve for robot-aided full knee swaps at one hub. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Three past-master surgeons each did fifteen robot swaps with one knee set and arm rig. Time marks for prep, cut, and pack steps were taped, plus worry, joy, and trust polls.

Forty-five of fifty set cases were done. Mean cut-to-close time sat past an hour and a half. Robot steps sped by up to near a third from first five to last five cases. Prep sped too. Worry fell and trust rose with case counts. The team gives train marks for new users.
pmc-11643429:
Salueña-Berna and three co-authors make clean hydrogen from scrap metal and water in this twenty twenty-four study. The gas is a prized fuel, yet most routes to it are hot, high-push, or hard to tame. Their route runs at low push with no heat step at the start.

Inside, pressed scrap discs with a trace of lye drip-feed water drop by drop. Each drip sets the gas flow, so the rate stays in hand at all times. The team tuned disc type, lye share, and grain size for best yield in tests. Fine grain raised yield yet cut the peak flow rate in their runs. Waste left is a solid that sells back for reuse, and cost per weight came out low.
pmc-11643829:
Patrycja Filipek and co-authors present a 2024 chemistry study of light-active compounds built on a double thiophene core. The molecules glow more strongly when they clump together, a trait called aggregation-induced emission. Such glow can reveal hidden fingerprints.

The team designed and made a family of these compounds with a cyanoacrylate part. Computer math explained why the reaction picked one path, and the energy levels. Glow was tested across water mixtures from none to nearly all water. Chain length in the molecules changed their traits. Tests covered fingerprint imaging and colour-changing electrochromic materials.
pmc-11644429:
Andreea Munteanu and eleven co-authors check clove essential oil against cancer cells in dishes and in computer models, in a two thousand twenty-four pharmacology paper. Clove oil is rich in eugenol, long suspected of anticancer activity.

Steam distillation yielded oil that was three quarters eugenol. Formulations with Tween-20 or PEG-400 carriers killed melanoma, colon, and skin cancer cells most effectively at the tested dose, sparing noncancerous cells comparatively. The oil disrupted mitochondrial respiration and uncoupled energy making, consistent with a rise in reactive oxygen species. Docking model runs nominated the enzyme PI3K alpha and the minor constituent calamenene as a surprisingly strong binder, hinting synergy among the oil's components.
pmc-11644729:
Ioanna Prapa and her team test a good germ sent free or fixed on nuts from the pistachio tree, in rats with diabetes. Their 2024 study maps shifts in gut germs and in the blood in the wake of four weeks of feed with the strain put forth as a good one.

Twenty-four male rats, sound or with diabetes, got one of the two forms of the germ. Blood, waste, and gut flesh were checked at the end. Rats with diabetes that got the nut-fixed cells had grades of a burn mark much more low than rats that got free cells. The fixed form cut counts of set gut germs in beasts with diabetes too. Both forms brought those germ groups in waste and in gut flesh back to norm. Shifts tied to Lactobacillus are told in more depth in the finds.
pmc-11645529:
Forhad Ullah and co-authors report three cases of a rare tumor surgery in this 2024 paper. The tumors are mediastinal paragangliomas, a type of neuroendocrine tumor. These three grew into the space between the aorta and the lung artery. That spot sits close to vital heart structures, so removal is hard.

All three patients were women. Diagnosis used blood and urine tests, scans, ultrasound, and biopsy. Each tumor was removed with the help of cardiopulmonary bypass, which takes over heart and lung work during surgery. Removal was complete in all three cases. Long term follow up found no return of the tumor. The cases support bypass as a useful tool for this surgery.
pmc-11649529:
Jules Hancox and five colleagues published a drug safety study in two thousand twenty-four on street opioids and the heart. Nitazenes are powerful synthetic opioids driving a new wave of the overdose crisis. Beyond breathing suppression, their toxic effects were barely known.

The team used machine learning tools to screen five nitazene compounds against a heart potassium channel called hERG. Block of that channel can trigger dangerous heart rhythms. All five compounds were predicted to block it at low concentrations. The authors warn of a real risk of rhythm disturbance from these drugs. They call for full cardiac safety testing as the compounds spread.
pmc-11650529:
Rasul and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on energy balance across world food systems. Farm systems once returned more energy than they used. Modern systems lean on fossil fuels, flipping that balance. The team compute energy return on investment for regions worldwide. Globally the ratio rose over recent decades but stays below one. Low-income regions still net-produce energy, though their edge shrinks with wealth. Rich regions are net energy sinks despite recent gains.

Food processing takes the largest share of system energy. Livestock products use most inputs yet give few calories back. Fertilizer takes a smaller share than processing. The authors flag food security and climate stakes in the imbalance.
pmc-11653829:
Yanru Qiu, Shuang Han, Yu Ji, Zhixian Lu, and Xuan Huang present a study from two thousand twenty-four on a blood test kit for clot risk in cervical cancer. The kit measures a complex that forms when clotting starts, called the thrombin-antithrombin complex. High levels can warn of venous thromboembolism, a dangerous clot in the veins.

The team looked back at one hundred seventy-seven cervical cancer patients treated at one hospital. Twenty-seven had developed clots and one hundred fifty had not. They compared the new marker with other clotting measures across cancer stages. A group of eighty healthy people served as a baseline.
pmc-11655029:
Ondi Crino and co-authors test how heat and a stress hormone during egg development shape an Australian lizard for life, in work published in 2024. Rising global temperatures expose developing animals to more heat. Mothers can also pass stress effects to offspring through hormones in the egg, and the two forces may interact.

Eggs of the delicate skink were dosed with low or high amounts of the stress hormone and incubated at cool or warm temperatures. The team tracked development time, size, and survival to adulthood, plus adult hormone levels and cell energy use. The two treatments did not interact, but each shrank body size at hatching on its own, and the smaller size lasted into adulthood. Low-dose hormone exposure also raised adult baseline stress hormone levels.
pmc-11655829:
Nicole Brown and co-authors followed women treated for early breast tissue changes at a large United Kingdom screening center in two thousand twenty-four. Atypical ductal hyperplasia and lobular neoplasia are not cancer, but they raise later breast cancer risk. Best follow-up and prevention plans remain uncertain.

Of one hundred seven women diagnosed from two thousand ten to two thousand eighteen, most returned to routine screening and a third got enhanced screening, a share that grew over time. About fourteen percent developed breast cancer over a median of nearly ten years, most of them after year five. Incidence was well above the general rate. The authors urge screening for at least ten years and preventive therapy talks.
pmc-11662329:
Schweng and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a study measuring how cats walk after two kinds of hip surgery. Total hip replacement swaps the joint for an implant. The older alternative removes the femoral head and neck instead. The team searched clinic databases for cats treated more than six months earlier. Nine cats per group came for re-examination and gait analysis. A pressure plate measured ground reaction forces as cats walked. Owners also rated activity and gait changes by survey.

Replacement cats loaded the operated leg more strongly. Their left-right symmetry was better on most force measures. Removal-group cats had smaller muscles and less joint motion on the operated side. Replacement cats showed no significant side-to-side differences on those measures. Owners also rated replacement outcomes better for activity and gait. The authors say the data aid decisions on feline hip disease.
pmc-11669329:
Hossain and co-authors present the Oligopool Calculator for large genetic library work. Oligopools let labs build and test huge part libraries at once. Design of primers, barcodes, and overlaps gets hard at scale. Their suite designs many thousands of oligos end to end. It also parses billions of barcoded reads fast.

New tricks include symmetric barcode design and adaptive primer trees. The tool designed over four million barcodes in 1.2 hours. Primer sites for one million oligos took fifteen minutes. Read analysis ran near 500 million reads per hour. All tests ran on an eight-core desktop machine.
pmc-11671929:
Howe and colleagues ask what makes drug plans work for grave mind ill at home in this twenty twenty-three review. Grave mind ills lean on drugs as their main care arm. Fit drug use asks for joint, folk-first work tween sick and staff.

Inside, three score works fed a tale built with sick and staff groups. The tale runs from first name of ill to trust tween the two sides. Shared picks and free fact swaps then lead to fit drug use. Backed picks and trust stand as the tale's twin base stones. Shame and fair reach cross groups are named as next asks.
pmc-11672429:
Francisco Fábio Oliveira de Sousa and co-authors describe lab work, published in twenty twenty-four, on tiny particles made to fight germs in wounds. The particles pair zein, a corn protein, with soaps built from amino acids. The team hoped the mix would kill germs while doing less harm than the soaps alone.

Tests showed the particles killed a wide range of bacteria and yeasts and broke up biofilms. The soaps also slowed skin enzymes tied to aging, and the effect grew once the soaps sat inside the particles. The team checked harm to human skin cells and to a small water creature used in safety tests. The work points to a safer way to use strong germ-killing soaps on skin.
pmc-11673829:
Olga Butranova and colleagues mined Russia's national side-effect database for cases of drug-induced lung fibrosis. Scarring of the lungs has many causes, and medicines are among the commonest. The pharmacoepidemiologic study covered spontaneous reports from January twenty nineteen to May twenty twenty-four. In total 1,308 reports of pulmonary fibrosis were identified. The average patient was about fifty-nine years old. Death was reported in about thirty-one percent of cases.

Cancer and immune-modulating drugs accounted for over half the culprit reports. Hormonal, nervous system, and respiratory drugs followed at a distance. Rituximab and methotrexate topped the individual drug list. The twenty twenty-four analysis shows regulators which drug classes deserve the closest lung monitoring when prescriptions are written.
pmc-11675729:
Garavito, Pena-Venegas, and Castellanos analyse starch based food packaging in developing countries in twenty twenty-four. Plastic pollution is a heavy burden where recycling systems are weak. Starch offers a cheap, widely available base for biodegradable packaging. Most prior work stops at lab scale formulation.

The authors trace the full value chain, from raw material conditioning to storage. They detail challenges, equipment, and process conditions at each stage. Moisture resistance stands out as the key trait for the final product. Single use plastic dominates food packaging in farm based economies with rich biodiversity. A full process view should help scale starch packaging there. That would help protect vulnerable regions from plastic waste.
pmc-11676329:
Umberto Lupo and co-authors introduce DiffPaSS in a 2024 paper, a method for pairing protein sequences that interact with each other. Interacting proteins tend to resemble each other across species, because they share an evolutionary history and must keep complementary binding surfaces. The pairing task can be framed as finding the matching that gives the best similarity or coevolution score.

DiffPaSS uses differentiable soft scores, so the pairing can be optimized directly without hand-tuned settings. On a benchmark dataset of prokaryotic proteins, it outperformed existing methods that optimize the same scores. The resulting pairings also helped predict the structure of protein complexes. The method does not require the sequences to be aligned first, and the authors also applied it to unaligned T-cell receptor sequences. The software is available as a Python package.
pmc-11676729:
Nasrin Abbasi Gharibkandi and five colleagues published a nanomedicine study in two thousand twenty-four on treating triple-negative breast cancer. This aggressive cancer lacks the usual hormone targets but often displays the EGFR protein. A radioactive particle aimed at that marker was built and tested.

Palladium-109, which emits beta particles and Auger electrons, was layered onto fifteen-nanometre gold particles and attached to the antibody panitumumab. The particles bound EGFR-rich cancer cells, entered them, and partly reached the nucleus. Cell metabolism fell in step with dose. The authors say the in-generator design mimics a proven terbium approach while adding punch. Cell work only so far; animal studies would come next.
pmc-11677129:
Tseng and co-authors track germ loads in spit tests for term dams on Paxlovid. Paxlovid pairs two drugs to curb the COVID germ in hosts. Term dams with the germ split in two arms in the work. One arm took Paxlovid, and one arm took no germ drug. Spit and nose germ loads were set side by side per host. Shifts in spit loads post care got the chief care in reads.

In sum, 37 term dams sat in the two arms of the work. The drug arm held 17 dams, and the bare arm held 20. Spit marks ran high next to nose marks in the drug arm. Post care, spit loads fell by 13.40 steps in that arm. The bare arm saw a shift of minus 1.59 steps in spit. Spit tests thus track drug work in such hosts.
pmc-11678629:
Miljana Jovandaric and co-authors review how plant-based food shapes the gut microbiota and helps ward off chronic disease. A gut community out of balance, dysbiosis, is tied to illness in children and adults. The microbiome forms before birth, and its makeup shifts with genes, food, and surroundings. The chief cause of dysbiosis, the authors say, is poor diet: short breastfeeding, too little fresh fruit and vegetables, and too much processed food.

A diet of grains, legumes, fruit, and vegetables is linked to lower risk of cancer, heart disease, stroke, rheumatoid arthritis, high blood pressure, asthma, allergies, and kidney stones. Gut germs ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids, which calm inflammation and shape the community itself. Fiber-rich diets also sharpen insulin response. A plant diet rich in fiber guards health because gut germs turn fiber into compounds that cut oxidative stress.
pmc-11678729:
Chengxing Wang leads a team of twelve authors doing unglamorous but essential groundwork: finding stable reference genes for gene-expression studies in a predatory flower bug. Orius nagaii eats thrips, mites, aphids, and moth pests, making it a prized biocontrol agent, but its molecular responses to prey are barely studied. Quantitative PCR results are only as trustworthy as the housekeeping genes used to normalize them.

Ten candidate genes were tested across developmental stages, tissues, temperatures, and host conditions, with stability judged by four algorithms combined in one ranking tool. Pairs of ribosomal protein genes won in most settings, with one gene, RPS10, appearing in nearly every winning pair. The validated pairs now anchor future expression work in this predator.
pmc-11679529: George Calin and nine board members of the journal Non-coding congratulate Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun. The two won the twenty twenty-four Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The prize honored their discovery of microRNAs. It honored their work on post-transcriptional gene regulation too. That work revealed a layer of control over gene expression in complex organisms, not known before. The editorial marks the moment for a journal devoted to non-coding RNA. It celebrates the founding insight as it reaches science's top honor.
pmc-11679729:
Musallam Al-Mazrouei and colleagues test shop-bought beef in Oman for germs, and find cause for concern, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Meat spoils fast and can carry disease, yet its safety in Omani shops was barely measured. The team sampled thirty-three packs of local and imported beef from six hypermarkets.

Counts of total bacteria in every sample topped the limit set by the Gulf food safety body. Coliform bacteria showed in nearly all samples, local and imported alike. The gut germ Escherichia coli showed in about four fifths. Lab identification named spoilage species that sour meat, and also species able to sicken people, including one tied to hospital infections. The authors call the report an eye-opener: they urge stricter hygiene and better handling from slaughter to shelf, in Oman and across the Gulf.
pmc-11685129:
Muhammad Azeem Ashraf, Samson Maekele Tsegay, Nida Gull, Muneeba Saeed, and Hussain Dawood study what makes blended learning work for medical students in Pakistan, in a 2024 paper. Blended learning mixes classroom teaching with online study. The team surveyed 275 medical students. They modeled how grades relate to self-steered learning, tech skill, trust in teachers, and the backing students feel from their school.

Students who managed their own learning well earned better grades. That self-management also carried much of the benefit of teacher trust and tech skill into better results. Feeling supported by the institution strengthened several of these links. The authors urge schools to build teachers' skills and to favor group learning, arguing that both feed the habits that lift student performance.
pmc-11689229:
Carolyn Pickering and four co-authors study abuse of older adults with dementia, by sex and disability. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses reports from family caregivers at three time points over a year. Caregivers covered more than four hundred fifty people with dementia. Most care recipients were women. The team tracked physical harm, verbal harm, and neglect.

Women needed more help with daily tasks and were more often in wheelchairs or beds. In a simple model, women faced less neglect than men. But women who could not leave a chair or bed faced more neglect. The authors say sex and disability must be read together, not apart.
pmc-11689629:
Evan Plys and six co-authors test a mindfulness phone app for dementia caregivers. Their twenty twenty-four trial sorted eighty stressed caregivers into two groups. One group used the Healthy Minds app. The other heard podcasts. The team checked if the trial could run well, and if the app built mindfulness skill, its proposed path to less stress and low mood.

Most aims for sign-up, data, and follow-up were met. Users liked the app and found it sound, but many did not reach the weekly time goal. Those on the app did gain mindfulness skill. They also showed clear gains in stress and mood in their own group scores over time.
pmc-11689829:
Heba Aldossary, Holly Kouts, and Mary Dolansky report, in twenty twenty-four, a front-line tool to boost age-friendly care. Clinic staff at MinuteClinic sites built a short form with eight questions. Patients fill it out while they wait for a visit. The questions map to four core aims of age-friendly care. The aim is to let patients state needs and wants before the visit starts.

Kits went to more than a thousand clinic sites. About ninety staff who used the form gave feedback after four weeks. They rated it easy to use and of good use. Their trust in doing the age-friendly steps rose, and visits took less time.
pmc-11690729:
Chelsea Kline, Matthew Baumgart, and Shelby Roberts report on a summit held in two thousand twenty-four about lowering the risk of dementia. In May two thousand twenty-three, a public health center funded by the CDC held the first such summit in Atlanta. It drew two hundred thirty public health workers, scholars, and researchers.

Six sessions walked through the levels at which prevention can act. They ran from personal skills and community teaching up to provider training, coalitions, office practice, and law. One more session covered social factors that shape health. Early feedback found most attendees judged the summit useful for their work.
pmc-11691029:
Kafayat Mahmoud, Deborah Carr, and Jarron Saint Onge published a study in 2024 on how marital status shapes end-of-life experiences among older adults in the United States. Many older people experience discomfort or care that conflicts with their preferences near death. Marriage is known to protect health, yet its role at the end of life had not been tested.

The researchers used thirteen waves of a national aging trends survey. They compared married, remarried, divorced, widowed, and never married people. The married group did not fare best on every measure. Widowed and remarried people were more likely to rate their care as excellent or very good, and widowed people were more likely to receive care that matched their wishes. Divorced people had worse pain management, while remarried and never married people felt less sadness. The differences did not vary by gender.
pmc-11691229:
Esteban Zavaleta-Monestel and co-authors published this review in 2024. It covers multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow. The disease is the second most common blood cancer in the world. It long had a grim name as fast and fatal. The review traces how care has changed over the past decade, with new drug families that hit the cancer more precisely.

The families include drugs that block the cell's protein shredder, lab-made antibodies that mark cancer cells, and drugs that rally the immune system. Steroids and mixed regimens that strike several paths at once also feature. The authors note longer calm periods, slower return of disease, and better daily life. They close with hope that a cure may come, plus a call for more study.
pmc-11691829:
Samar Assadi Khalil and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on life-space mobility in older adults. Life-space mobility means how far people move through daily life. It ranges from their rooms to their homes, neighborhoods, and towns. A wide life space is associated with quality of life and well-being. The researchers asked whether the factors behind it differ below and above the age of seventy-five.

The team assessed 242 adults aged sixty-five or older who lived at home and could move independently. For the younger group, participation in daily activities and a timed walking test best explained life-space mobility. For the older group, confidence in balance, cognitive scores, and the same walking test were the leading factors. The findings show that what drives mobility changes in later life, so support should change with age as well.
pmc-11692729:
Taghreed Alotaibi, Judith Sixsmith, Roseanne Cetnarskyj, and Mei Fang published a study in 2024 on older adults in Saudi Arabia who move from hospital care back to care at home. The country has shifted toward home-based care for older people with long-term care needs. The shift followed a sharp rise in hospital beds occupied by older adults who did not need acute care.

The researchers gathered views from older adults, caregivers, and health care professionals at King Saud Medical City. They used interviews, focus groups, observation of care, and analysis of documents. Culture, family, and national health care policies all shaped how the transition went. Barriers included rules separating men and women, which made it hard to plan care as one team. No standard follow-up plan was in place, and care was fragmented across groups. The authors urge a single coordinated system to manage the transition.
pmc-11692929:
Theresa Sivers-Teixeira and co-authors describe a training program that links two workforces in long-term care in a 2024 paper. Certified nursing assistants give most daily care to nursing home residents, yet they often struggle with the hard behaviors that come with decline. That strain lowers residents' quality of life and assistants' job satisfaction. Ombudsmen, the advocates who field residents' complaints, know the failure points well.

A university geriatric program trained ombudsmen to teach an age-friendly curriculum to the assistants. The four-lesson course was built with the local ombudsman program. It aims to raise the assistants' geriatric skills where they work. The paper tells how the partnership was formed and what the training covered. The model turns complaint handlers into teachers, spreading scarce geriatric expertise.
pmc-11696429:
Benedikt Judmann leads a team that asks if tumor balls suit tracer tests. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses three D cell balls. Such balls may bridge flat cell tests and live animal work.

Tracer work for therapy has used these balls with success. Tests for diagnostic tracers in balls were still missing. The team made a new tracer and tested its binding. Results in balls were weighed against flat cell tests. Flat tests gave the binding strength in two states. The work checks if balls are a sound test bed.
pmc-11697429:
Niroj Dahal and co-authors published a methods paper in 2024 on picking participants for qualitative studies. Such studies, common in social science and education, rest on who gets picked to take part. The right pick differs by method, and guides on the topic are scarce.

The authors draw on their own work across seven methods, from life-story inquiry to field ethnography. For each method, they spell out how participants are chosen and why the logic differs. Case study and grounded theory, for instance, pick for contrast and theory growth, not head counts. The paper offers practical tips for new and seasoned researchers alike. It also lists points to weigh before any pick is made. The aim is more thoughtful, better-justified choices.
pmc-11698929:
Solanilla-Duque and co-authors grade food safe plans in town cow kill shops in Colombia. Colombia has firmed rules to set food safe marks for such shops. The health arm made INVIMA the lead for meat checks there. That rule weighs build state, kill steps, and safe webs in shops. It also aims to sort the stock of town kill shops in the land. The work backs plain ways to lift safe marks in 47 shops.

Safe maps were built on the HACCP frame and land rules. Scores span build, clean, and green traits of the shops. A Leopold grid served as the watch tool for those scores. Just 32 percent of shops met the base marks in the pool. Gear and waste webs showed the most grave gaps there. Proof of thin staff facts joined the gap list.
pmc-11700529:
Satoshi Anai and co-authors report the case of a 73-year-old man with lung cancer who responded strikingly to a two-drug targeted therapy. Their report appeared in 2024. The man arrived with worsening breathlessness and breathing failure. Scans showed widespread shadowing in his right lung. A biopsy confirmed lung adenocarcinoma carrying a gene change called BRAF V600E. He was weak and needed oxygen to keep his blood levels safe.

After careful discussion and consent, the team started the drug pair dabrafenib and trametinib despite the risks. His breathing and scans improved markedly. He stayed on the treatment with no major side effects, and the disease remained stable. The authors present the case as early evidence that targeted drugs can help even frail patients when the gene match is right.
pmc-11700729:
Passing a camera into the lungs is a mainstay of lung medicine, but sedation for it carries its own risks. Dean Kellogg, Diego Maselli, Kevin Proud, Eusondia Arnett, Larry Schlesinger, and Jay Peters set out a protocol that skips sedation in healthy volunteers. Numbing comes only from lidocaine, given as a mist, by atomizer, and through the scope itself, at well under the toxic dose.

One of the team first tried the method on himself and reported discomfort of one to two on a five-point scale. The study then ran the full protocol in volunteers at a Texas research unit, washing the lungs to collect immune cells for research. The letter gives the dosing steps and safety checks meant to make such studies kinder to volunteers.
pmc-11716129:
A team led by Ramon Casanova published this study in two thousand twenty-five on spotting dementia risk in people with mild thinking problems. The team used a math tool called UMAP, which flattens many measures into a flat map that the eye can read.

The data came from a Wake Forest Alzheimer's center cohort of five hundred forty-two adults. For each person the team fed in test scores, blood markers, brain scans, and age. A trained sorter then drew a line between healthy adults and people with dementia, and that line marked out a high-risk zone. People with mild problems who fell in that zone had worse scores and marker levels. The work points to a simple way to flag who needs close watching.
pmc-11722129:
Kylie Alexander leads a large team in tracing how a stress hormone spike after spinal cord injury drives bone growth in muscle. The paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Such stray bone, called heterotopic ossification, can grow large near joints after harm to the brain or cord, for reasons that were not known.

In mice, cord injury sends corticosterone up at once, and that spike proves causal. Giving the hormone or a like drug alone starts bone in hurt muscle, even with no cord harm. Mice that lack the hormone's receptor do not grow the bone after injury. Clinic drugs that block the receptor stop it too, which hints at a shield for victims of severe nerve harm.
pmc-11723529:
A team led by Gennady Atroshchenko measured how fast surgeons new to robots learn heart surgery tasks in a wet lab. Trainees practiced three tasks on pig tissue: closing an upper heart chamber, freeing a chest artery, and stitching a valve ring. Scores from expert robotic surgeons set the bar.

Fifteen novices took part, some heart surgeons and some not. Most hit mastery in about half an hour to an hour per task. Prior open heart experience made little difference to speed of learning. On one task, non-heart surgeons scored lower on fine skill ratings. The authors back wet lab practice as a fast route to robot skills.
pmc-11727829:
José Hernández-Rodríguez leads a thirteen-author team characterizing a severe fever-and-muscle-pain syndrome, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Protracted febrile myalgia strikes mainly children with familial Mediterranean fever. Its imaging and tissue features were barely documented.

The team reviewed adults with the fever disease at their reference center, where over half reported muscle pain. One detailed case of the protracted syndrome, affecting calves and Achilles tendons, anchors the report. Published cases, over a hundred, were gathered for comparison. Biopsy evidence highlighted inflammation of fascia and its small vessels as novel features. Naming the tissue pattern helps clinicians distinguish the syndrome from infections and other myalgias.
pmc-11728229:
Benjamin Seybold and a team of co-authors measure how quickly anesthesiologists learn ultrasound-guided neck blocks for carotid surgery. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Regional anesthesia suits this operation well, but the learning curve for newcomers was uncharted.

Records covered eighty-three patients at a German district hospital after the technique launched. Nine experienced anesthesiologists, new to this specific block, trained briefly and were supervised for their first six cases. Patients were grouped by how many blocks their doctor had already done. The main measure was block failure: pain, restlessness, or rescue drugs. Complication rates were tracked beside it. The grouping lets the authors say how many supervised cases competence actually takes.
pmc-11728329:
Krzysztof Żaba and co-authors published this study in 2024 on 3D-printed steel. The parts were M300 steel made by a laser melting method known as DMLS. The team asked how laser power and surface finish change the steel's fight against rust. They ran both fast and long rust tests, and read the surfaces with fine imaging and element scans.

The printed steel proved prone to rust in harsh settings. Higher laser power mostly lowered its rust defense. Raw, unpolished parts resisted rust better at first, yet lost more mass over long soaks. Heat made rust worse. Photos after the tests showed eaten, pitted surfaces. The authors advise shielding such parts when they must work where rust is a threat, and they note print settings matter as much as polish.
pmc-11732329:
Joseph Jon Yin Wan and his three co-authors report, in a 2024 pilot study, whether a surgical robot can run a full spine fusion procedure, not just place the screws. Robot help in spine surgery has mostly stopped at screw placement. This team used a robotic arm platform for the whole minimally invasive fusion, including slipping the spacer cage between vertebrae. Twenty-nine patients were planned for the procedure at one center by one surgeon.

Two cases were dropped when the software failed to start. One patient needed a second operation after a cage migrated. At six months, no screws had loosened in any patient. Screw accuracy and complication rates matched the center's conventional navigation-guided results. The authors call the workflow feasible, while warning about start-up pitfalls and the limits of robotic cage placement. Bigger studies of outcomes and cost must come before wide adoption.
pmc-11733629:
Jannis Engel and six co-authors probe the hidden views of men with compulsive sexual behavior toward pornography. They use reaction-time tests in place of surveys. The disorder is new to the world list of diseases and looks like addictions in brain and in how men act. What patients say they feel may differ from what automatic associations reveal.

Forty-seven men with the condition and thirty-eight controls took an implicit association test that paired images of porn with feelings. The group with the disorder linked the images to positive feelings far more strongly. Those implicit scores also tracked reported problem behavior and how strongly the men respond to sexual excitation. With excitation and inhibition measures, the associations split the two groups. The findings back addiction-like workings below conscious report.
pmc-11745029:
Annie Swanepoel argues that ADHD and autism are natural human variations shaped by evolution, not disorders, in a commentary from twenty twenty-four. People with these traits lead the neurodiversity movement, which stresses their strengths. In the right settings, such minds can do better than typical ones.

Swanepoel writes that the science of how species change over time backs this view. Traits that stayed through natural selection likely helped single people or groups in some past settings. Keeping those gains in view supports this lens as truly useful for helping our species thrive. The piece is a position essay. It sets the movement's case, and the case from evolution, against the disorder label.
pmc-11770829:
Tareq Alotaibi and eleven colleagues published a cohort study in two thousand twenty-four on breathing support and hospital stay for extremely preterm babies. Heated humidified high-flow nasal cannulas help these infants breathe. Whether receiving one relates to longer hospitalisation was the question.

Records covered babies born before twenty-eight weeks at one tertiary hospital from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-two. Babies who received the cannula stayed ninety-nine days on average, versus forty-two point five days for those who did not, a statistically strong gap. The authors caution that sicker babies likely receive the support, so the device itself may not lengthen stays. They recommend prospective trials to untangle cause and effect.
pmc-11777429:
Lawrence Wackett and Serina Robinson argue that the best path to breaking down PFAS is to build the microbes for the job in the lab. PFAS are long-lasting fluorinated chemicals that pollute water and soil. They persist because their carbon-fluorine bonds are very strong, and because the fluoride released when bonds break can poison the microbes themselves. Waiting for nature to evolve a solution faces too many hurdles, they say.
