Their plan has three steps. First, build bacteria that survive very high levels of fluoride. Second, design and screen enzymes that cut carbon-fluorine bonds in more of these chemicals. Third, set up conditions where eating PFAS rewards the microbe, so evolution favors the trait. The review reads as a prescription: a sequenced recipe for turning a stubborn pollution problem into a solvable engineering one.
pmc-11790429:
Shaaf Ahmad, Kaleem Maqsood, Farwa Liaqat, and Nabila Roohi tested whether two blood proteins can flag how severe COVID-19 will be and who may die. Scarring of the lungs after severe illness is a lasting risk. They recruited two hundred forty patients and healthy people at two hospitals in Lahore, Pakistan, and followed patients for two months.

One protein, decorin, fell as illness grew worse, and survivors held higher levels than those who died. The second, biglycan, rose with severity but did not split survivors from others. The authors say the pair, decorin above all, may help spot patients at risk of lung scarring early.
pmc-11810929:
Yura Choi and co-authors test context dependent memory in daily life with a phone app, in work from twenty twenty-four. Memory often improves when the place at recall matches the place at learning. Lab tests dominate this field, so real world proof was scarce.

The app tracked GPS spots for five weeks as people lived their normal days. Participants were then asked to recall where they were at a set date and time, picking from all spots visited. The context effect held in the wild. Rarely visited spots gained most from a matched context. For rare spots, longer stays in the place grew the benefit further. The method lets memory be studied in genuine settings.
pmc-11971929:
Amine Benmoussa and co-authors published a 2024 case report of a rare pairing. Amyloidosis, a stiff protein laid down in tissue from a loose light chain, appears alongside a slow blood cancer, follicular lymphoma. The stiff deposits most often come with a bone marrow clone. A lymphoma is a rare partner for it. The case shows how hard the pair is to spot and treat.

The case is a man of sixty-seven, with no past illness of note. He arrived run-down, with a voice growing rough in steps, hard swallowing, and a large mass in the back hall of the throat. A biopsy reading showed the slow lymphoma. Four rounds of a lead drug combination did not move it. Three more of a second combination left it in place. A fresh biopsy then showed the lymphoma gone, but the stiff deposits there, of the same chain kind.
pmc-12663129:
Shoko Matsumoto and eleven colleagues followed HIV treatment outcomes in North Vietnam through a period of big changes. Funding was shifting from donors to social insurance, the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted care, and dolutegravir-based regimens were expanding. The twenty twenty-five prospective cohort enrolled 2,233 people with suppressed viral load at eleven facilities. Follow-up ran from late twenty nineteen into twenty twenty-three.

Viral suppression stayed above ninety percent and care retention above eighty-seven percent throughout. New viremia occurred at 3.2 cases per hundred person-years. Only 1.4 percent of participants carried drug resistance mutations, and none involved dolutegravir. Of those who switched to dolutegravir, 15.4 percent later stopped it, mostly because clinics ran out of stock.
pmc-12664229:
Huseyinoglu and nine co-authors published a study in twenty twenty-five on a test used in glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. The test measures chemical silencing of a gene called MGMT, which predicts how patients respond to the main drug. Labs lacked a firm line between silenced and active.

The team studied one hundred one patients treated between twenty oh eight and twenty twenty-two, all with surgery plus combined drug and radiation care. Curve analysis set the best cutoff at a low fraction of one percent, and the test sorted patients well at that line. Patients above the line lived a median of twenty-four months, twice the twelve months of those below it. Wide surgical removal also predicted longer life on its own. The authors say the cutoff is ready for use at their center, pending checks elsewhere.
pmc-12690829:
Jana Niemann and co-authors study how birth control care in Germany can harm the people it should serve. Wide promotion of the pill raises questions about side effects, true choice, and pressure to use it. The team spoke online with nineteen former pill users and six gynecologists. They read the talks through theories of symbolic, structural, and slow violence.

Three forces formed a cycle in the accounts. Drug and medical knowledge held the top place, while counsel on other methods stayed thin. The pill was favored over other options as a matter of routine. Over time, that cycle harmed users in slow, hard-to-see ways. The authors urge broader counsel, gender-aware research, and better training for doctors.
pmc-12695929:
Yung Jee Kang and co-authors predict in 2025 survival after mouth cancer surgery with deep learning. Standard staging gives rough odds but ignores much about the patient. The team trained models on records of 1,018 patients treated between 1996 and 2020.

Inputs ranged from age and lifestyle to scan values, invasion depth, and treatments given. Their best model, a deep network sorting patients into outcome groups, reached strong accuracy and matched predicted survival to observed survival closely. It beat classic statistical models and a random forest. The authors say such tools could sharpen personal prognosis and planning, though the low sensitivity for deaths shows room to improve.
pmc-12705029:
Reenaa Mohan, Jenifer Florance Mary, and three co-authors test whether training allied health students lifts leprosy knowledge. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, uses a before-and-after design. Leprosy control suffers from low public awareness and heavy stigma. Seventy-four lab and nursing students join group sessions.

Tests before and after training measure what changed. Knowledge scores rise by a clear, significant margin. Group discussion also surfaces the stigma students see around them. The authors argue frontline workers can carry awareness into communities. Early detection depends on that groundwork. Training, in their reading, is a cheap lever for control programs.
pmc-12705129:
Jason den Duijn and a large international team test whether patients' own devices can reveal decline before a hospital visit, in a 2025 study. Many emergency patients worsen gradually at home, with resting heart rate creeping up and daily steps falling. Phones and watches already record both, if clinicians can gather them.

Thirty-four hospitals across four countries ran a coordinated flash-mob study, enrolling acutely ill arrivals and pulling their device histories. The question was feasibility: can such data be collected fast, across systems, at scale? Baselines from healthy days could flag how far a patient has slid, sharpening admission decisions. The study design itself, many sites collecting the same data on the same plan, is the experiment's backbone.
pmc-12706529:
Bailin Li and five colleagues published an evolution study in two thousand twenty-five on a class of single-celled organisms called Spirotrichea. Their family tree stayed contentious because single-gene studies and sparse data conflicted. The team built the first broad multi-gene framework for the group.

Four genetic markers, body traits, and RNA structures were combined, including nineteen brand-new sequences for a scarce gene. The class resolves into four main lineages, with one group branching earliest. Several disputed placements were settled, including a reclassified order bridging two subclasses. Habitat shifts, such as sea to fresh water, lined up with the tree's splits. The authors argue ecology helped drive the group's diversification.
pmc-12708629:
Shiba and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on boron compounds that boost proton beam therapy. Nuclear reactions between protons and boron can raise cell killing in tumors. Two reaction paths exist, one via each boron isotope form. Which path sensitizes better was unclear. The team treat two human cancer cell lines with proton beams. One boron form is enriched in one isotope; the other keeps natural mix. Survival doses are compared across the setups. The enriched form gives the stronger boost in both cell lines.

Enhancement is modest but consistent in their measures. The natural-mix form barely helps at all. The authors back the enriched form for clinical study. They call for more work before patient use.
pmc-12717329:
Aanchal Preet Kaur and colleagues published a tumor immunology study in 2025. They studied how radiation changes immune cells in tumors. Radiation plus T cells can control leftover cancer. Regulatory T cells expand after radiation and block control. The team used three-dimensional tumor models and live tracking. They watched macrophages and monocytes after radiation doses. Two surface molecules, CD80 and CD86, rose sharply. Common alarm pathways did not drive that rise. The finding was unexpected for immune activation markers.

Blocking those molecules improved tumor control after radiation. It also reduced regulatory T cell expansion greatly. Fewer helper T cells entered tumors under blockade. Inflamed myeloid cells seem to invite suppressive cells. Cutting that invitation freed killer T cell control. The work suggests a new combination treatment idea. Timing with radiation will need careful testing.
pmc-12717629:
Schindele and a large team linked jobs to nose and sinus cancer across the Nordic countries in twenty twenty-five. This cancer is aggressive with a poor outlook, and workplace exposures are a known driver. The team used census and cancer registry data from five countries.

From nineteen sixty-one to twenty oh five, five thousand seven hundred ninety-nine cases were registered. Male woodworkers stood out, with incidence about eighty-four percent above average across all five countries. For one subtype, adenocarcinoma, their rate was five and a half times average. Female woodworkers also showed raised rates, though on only ten cases. Shoe and leather workers in Denmark and smelting workers in Norway also ran high. The authors name woodworking, even with soft wood, a high-risk occupation.
pmc-12718229:
Sandau and coauthors review joint self-care for heart pump patients and partners. A durable heart pump needs daily care at home for years. Partners share much of that care load with patients. Joint care science for pump pairs is still young.

Frameworks for family care exist for other long illnesses. Few have been used for heart pump pairs so far. Most pump studies are small and describe tasks in words. What helps or blocks joint care stays poorly known. The team sums up current proof on pump self-care. They offer frameworks to guide next pump pair studies.
pmc-12719229:
Portner and a large team build a learning network from analogue memory devices in twenty twenty-five. The devices, called memristors, hold and change values like the links between brain cells. Most past designs used them for just one part of a learning task. Here they store the link weights, work out updates, and pick the next move.

The network learns by reward, much like animals learn from treats and failures. It steered through two maze tasks, one on a grid and one water maze. All training took place inside the memory itself, with no data shuttled in and out. The team calls it a first step toward full in memory learning machines.
pmc-12721729:
Khanh Long Nguyen, Quang Khanh Chu, Duc Tien Doan, and Thanh Tung Nguyen describe a fully digital rebuild of both dental arches for one patient, in a 2025 case report. The patient, a 69-year-old man, had teeth beyond saving. Full-arch implant work is hard because fit, bite balance, and function all have to come out right. The team placed six implants in the upper jaw and five in the lower jaw using a stacked surgical guide.

Bone scans, mouth and face scans, and planning software set the implant positions, and a precision system checked them. What sets this case apart is that records of the man's actual jaw movements guided how the bite surfaces were shaped, for both the trial teeth and the final set. The finished zirconia teeth worked well, pleased the patient, and caused no problems during follow-up.
pmc-12722429:
Mohamed Hany, Ehab Elmongui, and Walid El Ansari build, in a 2025 study, a risk score that forecasts whether a stent will fail to close a leak after weight-loss surgery. No such forecast tool existed before. They used records for 250 patients at one center to build the model, then tested it on 150 patients at another hospital.

About three in ten stents failed in both groups. A lean statistical model beat ten other machine learning methods. Eight health factors, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and body mass index, drove most of the forecast. The team turned the model into a simple point score that doctors can use at the bedside.
pmc-12729229:
Zhe Lu and seven co-authors deliver stem cells through the nose in a Parkinson's study from two thousand twenty-five. The disease kills dopamine neurons deep in the brain, behind a barrier most cells cannot cross. Muse cells, a hardy stem cell type, home to damage unusually well.

In a lab barrier model, an inflammatory signal raised a lipid cue that loosened the barrier and let muse cells through. In mice modeling Parkinson's, nose-delivered muse cells reached the brain better than ordinary stem cells. Once there, they could turn into cells bearing the key dopamine enzyme. The authors present the nose route and the homing signal as a delivery strategy worth developing. Human work remains ahead.
pmc-12729529:
Tiziana Fragasso and five co-authors review how artificial intelligence is entering care for tetralogy of Fallot, a serious heart defect present from birth. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Patients need watching and treatment across their whole lives, with late risks to the heart's rhythm and pumping.

The review follows the patient journey from before birth to adult follow-up. Machine learning tools now aid imaging, surgery planning, monitoring during operations, and intensive care. Wearable and implanted devices feed long-term data. The authors see a future where images, records, genes, and live data merge for tailored care. They also flag open problems: small data sets, opaque models, rules, and ethics.
pmc-12732229:
Meng-Feng Tsai and co-authors test whether a bedside ultrasound within an hour of arrival speeds emergency care for belly pain, in a 2025 study. The team reviewed 6,866 admitted patients at a Taiwanese medical center. About 1,500 got the early scan; the rest got none. Weighting balanced age, triage, vital signs, and other illnesses between the groups.

Early scanning came with a 14 percent shorter emergency stay. It also raised the odds of follow-up CT imaging by 44 percent, yet total costs fell five percent. Among patients who skipped CT, emergency costs dropped most; among those scanned further, admission costs fell. The authors say a quick first look helps doctors sort belly pain faster and cheaper, even when it prompts more imaging.
pmc-12733029:
Samira Comtesse and three co-authors tested a score that selects which mental health patients benefit from gene-based drug testing, in a study published in 2025. Such testing can tune drug choice, but cost and vague selection rules hold it back. The score weighs a patient's drug list, side effects, and drug level readings. The team read records for 92 patients with depression at one hospital in Frankfurt.

The base score did track who benefited from testing, by a set benefit score. A revised form, which weights body drug facts more and side effect blame less, sorted patients with more precision but no more raw power. A score of four or more marked real benefit. The revised form did the same in a group from Prague. The authors call for live trials to prove the revision.
pmc-12733829:
Anton Minaev and colleagues compared medicines and surgery for a swapped heart ventricle in 2025. Some hearts pump body blood with the right ventricle. That ventricle weakens over time badly. Its inlet valve also leaks severely. No proven drug standard exists here. Surgical replacement is the alternative path.

A stepwise combined approach was assessed. Modern heart failure drugs came first. Elective valve replacement followed for suitable patients. Ventricular function improved after optimisation. Surgery proved safe in that sequence. Significant leakage did not recur afterward. Pharmacotherapy belongs in management plans now. Timing surgery after drugs seems wise.
pmc-12735429:
Rosengren and colleagues reviewed which patients develop severe leptospirosis in twenty twenty-five. This bacterial infection, spread through water contaminated by animal urine, can turn life-threatening. Definitions of severe disease varied across studies, generally meaning death or a complicated course.

Thirty-five articles met the review's criteria. Older age was linked to severity in seven studies. Bedside warning signs included abnormal lung examination, low blood pressure, low urine output, jaundice, and altered mental state. Routine blood counts and kidney and liver tests also flagged high-risk patients. The clinical picture varied by region, but low blood pressure and lung or kidney involvement predicted trouble everywhere. The authors suggest folding these simple indices into early risk tools, especially for resource-limited settings where most severe cases occur.
pmc-12736129:
Luo and coauthors ask if lab drug tests predict cure in a lung illness. The illness comes from a slow germ group that is hard to treat. Doctors pick drugs in part by the dose that halts the germ. The team asks if that dose truly tracks patient outcome.

They reviewed care records in China from 2018 to 2021. The set held 209 patients who started drug care. Most were around age 60 at the time of care. The team split patients by drug dose test results. They then weighed dose levels against cure rates. Clear links could help doctors choose drugs with more care.
pmc-12737529:
Paepa Tohaia, Amber Young, and four colleagues ask whether online maps and booking systems actually help pregnant women get vaccinated, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The research centers Māori and Pacific hapū māmā, pregnant women, in Aotearoa New Zealand, and follows kaupapa Māori methodology.

The team ran focus groups with seven pregnant women and interviewed forty healthcare professionals, then analyzed the transcripts thematically. Three themes emerged from the women's accounts. Awareness of the online tools was limited. The tools need to be accessible and user-friendly in practice, not just in principle. Deeper findings concern trust and how services present vaccination choices. Maps and booking sites are meant to lower barriers by showing nearby clinics and open slots. The study finds the promise is not yet matched by lived experience, and it points to what would make these tools fit for purpose.
pmc-12745329:
Guo-qing Song, Jirapa Jaikham, and Weiqi Wang review genes that control flowering in trees and other woody plants, in a 2025 paper. Breeding woody plants by crossing is slow because young trees may take years before they can bloom at all. Speeding up that first bloom would speed up every breeding cycle.

Over the past twenty years, researchers have mapped much of the gene network that triggers flowering. Editing or boosting key genes in that network can shorten the young phase sharply, an approach nicknamed FasTrack breeding. The review gathers what is known about the main flowering pathways and lists candidate genes for editing. It aims to give breeders a base for faster improvement of orchard, forest, and other woody crops.
pmc-12747329:
Patricia Azevedo and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, whether a common insecticide alters gut microbes in a Brazilian stingless bee. The insecticide, imidacloprid, is widely used in Brazil and harms bees at lethal and sublethal doses. Gut microbe disruption after exposure has been reported, but short-term sublethal effects in stingless bees were unclear. The team fed forager bees two very low concentrations for up to forty-eight hours. They sequenced a bacterial gene to profile midgut communities, comparing hive bees, exposed bees, and controls.

No clear changes in diversity or composition appeared after exposure at either dose or time. Hive bees differed from lab controls, though. That gap was tied to one bacterial family and likely reflects the shift to artificial lab conditions, not the insecticide.
pmc-12747429:
Romane Milcamps and nine co-authors show how cardioviruses disarm a key antiviral alarm by jamming the cell's nuclear traffic. The kinase PKR normally senses viral double-stranded RNA and halts protein production. The viral leader protein blocks PKR, interferon, and transport through the nuclear pore all at once, and mutations suggested the tricks are linked.

The leader recruits host kinases that tag pore proteins and choke transport. Viruses engineered to disrupt transport by different routes still inhibited PKR, cementing the connection. Imaging showed that when transport fails, a share of PKR retreats into the nucleoli and stays inactive there. The finding reframes PKR inhibition as a side effect of sabotaging the nucleus.
pmc-12753729:
Hatem Abdelaty and Moataz Mohamed assess what it would take to electrify every transit bus in Canada. Their national study was published in twenty twenty-five. Battery electric buses promise deep cuts in transit emissions, but no full country-level accounting had been done.

Using open data from one hundred and two transit providers, the team counted fleet, chargers, power needs, and costs. A fully electric fleet would need about seventeen percent more buses and a modest slice of national power output. Emissions would fall by more than ninety-two percent, and the social cost of carbon would drop by a like share. The authors call the switch technically feasible and financially manageable. Their open method can be reused by planners elsewhere.
pmc-12756029:
Meiyuan Lin, Yuan Gao, and Jun Deng published a case report in 2025 on one lung cancer patient. The tumor carried a gene fusion that often responds to targeted pills. The patient also had high levels of a marker tied to immune therapy response. Two targeted pills were tried in turn.

Both pills failed fast, with the cancer growing again within a short span. Fresh gene tests guided the switch each time. The team then gave a dual-action antibody drug plus standard chemotherapy. That mix brought a good response in this patient. The authors say this is the first report of that drug in such a case. They offer it as a lead for doctors facing the same drug resistance.
pmc-12767229:
Tuo Wei leads a team testing a traditional Chinese herbal formula against diabetic kidney disease, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The disease slowly scars the kidneys and leaks protein into urine. The formula, called Suyin Detoxification Prescription, had shown early promise in patients. The team paired a patient trial with computer mapping of its active parts and lab tests in diabetic mice.

Patients on the formula showed lower blood creatinine and less protein in urine than controls. The mapping tied the formula's parts to a receptor called FXR and to disease paths in the kidney. In mice, the formula cut inflammation markers in kidney tissue, and its benefit largely vanished when FXR was removed. The authors say the herb mix guards the kidney in part through that receptor.
pmc-12771229:
Yao Zhu and colleagues report a case series testing the safety of a portable nitric oxide generator for newborns with persistent pulmonary hypertension, a neonatal emergency that can kill. Standard inhaled nitric oxide comes from cylinders on large fixed gear, capping treatment during transport and in smaller hospitals and delaying a critical intervention.

The portable generator, made in China, makes the gas on site. The study pulled records of seven newborns treated with it over two months, grading age and sex, vital signs, blood gases, ventilation signs, and oxygen levels before and after therapy. All seven patients lived, with few side effects while it was given, and oxygen measures rose a lot after treatment began. Seven babies cannot settle efficacy, but the series answers the first question for a new device: can it be used safely where cylinders cannot follow?
pmc-12776229:
Lihua Yao and Xiaozhong Wang study a telomere protecting protein in acute myeloid leukemia in a 2025 paper. The protein guards the ends of chromosomes and keeps the genome stable. Its role in this blood cancer was poorly known, so the team measured its levels in patient samples and tested what happens when it is suppressed.

The protein was much higher in leukemia patients than in healthy people, and high levels tracked with worse clinical traits, such as high white cell counts. Database checks linked high levels to poorer survival. In lab and mouse tests, suppressing the protein slowed leukemia growth. The authors propose it as both a warning marker and a possible treatment target.
pmc-12784929:
Hao Dong and a large team of co-authors build variants of a propolis compound against liver cancer, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. They made twenty-eight versions of caffeic acid phenethyl ester and tested each on two liver cancer cell lines. One variant, WX006, beat the parent compound clearly.

WX006 scrambles metal balance inside the cells, sparking two metal-linked death modes. Modeling points to a block on a key breathing-chain part, draining the cell's energy carrier. Gene and chemical maps backed the dual strike on metabolism and metals. Animal checks then tested how well the variant works in living tumors.
pmc-12788529:
Gowrishankar Sekar and co-authors link vaping to mouth lesions in young urban Indians. Their 2025 study compares a few hundred adults in their late teens to mid thirties, split evenly between e-cigarette users and non-users. Each person received a standard mouth exam and answered a structured questionnaire.

Users showed clearly higher rates of a white patch condition and of mouth ulcers than non-users. Daily users carried about double the lesion risk of lighter users, a dose pattern that strengthens the case for cause. Awareness was low: only a small share of users knew vaping could harm the mouth, fewer in proportion than among non-users. The authors call for warning efforts aimed at young users.
pmc-12804829:
Cranes lift the heavy pieces of construction, and when they fail, workers die. With reports piling up, spotting true causes by hand is slow. Jinlong Zhao and co-authors build an automated route through the pile. They mined the text of 203 crane accidents in China from 2011 to 2022, weighted the words to build a checklist of causative factors, and linked the factors into a network. Network analysis picked out the key factors, and a structural modeling method then chained them into a step-by-step accident sequence.

Two factors stood out as central: cross parallel operation, where crews work in overlapping zones, and insufficient safety management. The team checked their accident chain against a real tower crane accident and found it reasonable. The method turns a mountain of reports into a short list of pressure points for targeted safety management.
pmc-12807929:
Wu and ten co-authors published a study in twenty twenty-six on how microbes shape the aroma of wine made from Jinggang honey pomelo, a large citrus fruit from China. Fruit wines gain much of their scent from the yeasts and bacteria that ferment them, but how rivalry among those microbes steers the scent was unclear.

The team fermented pomelo flesh with a partial starter and tracked the microbes and scent chemicals over time. Seven microbe groups took turns dominating as acidity, alcohol, and sweetness shifted. Chemical analysis picked out seventeen scent compounds that matter most for the smell. Two microbe groups, one bacterium and one mold, linked most strongly to the flavor compounds. The authors conclude that competition between fungi and bacteria is a key hand on the aroma dial. That insight could let winemakers steer scent on purpose.
pmc-12808329:
Sathiyamoorthy Murugesan leads a team that reviews printed catalysts for biomass. Their review from twenty twenty-five deals with turning biomass into value chemicals. That shift cuts need for fossil stock and its harms.

Most chem making still uses old style catalysts, they note. Three D printing can shape pore form and flow quite freely. That can raise site access, mass flow, and reuse counts. Past reviews stuck to small molecule reactions for most part. This one centers on biomass change in full depth. Metal, acid, enzyme, and light systems are covered.
pmc-12815729:
Yayue Liu and five colleagues published a stent study in two thousand twenty-five on narrowed neck arteries reopening after treatment. A stent can prop open the carotid artery, but the vessel sometimes narrows again inside it. Two stent designs, closed-cell and open-cell, may carry different risks.

The team reviewed two hundred fifty-seven procedures at one hospital, split almost evenly between the designs. Overall narrowing rates did not differ clearly. The closed-cell group started with tighter blockages and needed more widening steps, yet ended with less leftover narrowing. The authors then compared which patient and procedure factors predicted renarrowing within each design. Their point is that risk factors should be read per design, not pooled.
pmc-12819229:
Hongfei Zhang and co-authors report a solitary fibrous tumour of the chest wall, with Doege-Potter syndrome as a linked state. Their 2025 case report stresses talks with a team from more than one field, and embolisation of blood vessels before surgery.

A man in his mid-fifties came in with breathlessness when he put his body to work, with dizziness, and with low blood sugar that came back time and time again. He also had low potassium. Scans found a very large mass in the chest wall, and a biopsy made the tumour type clear. After three cycles of drug therapy used as a set, embolisation cut loss of blood in surgery by a large share. Surgeons took out the tumour, with part of a lung lobe and part of a rib. The blood sugar and potassium problems cleared up. At follow-up, the tumour had not come back.
pmc-12820029:
Go Hashimoto and colleagues ask whether lean body mass predicts short-term outcomes after ischemic stroke, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Muscle mass's influence on recovery has been unclear. The team used a lean body mass index as a muscle surrogate. Data came from a Fukuoka stroke registry covering over ten thousand patients.

Patients were grouped into sex-specific lean mass quartiles. Outcomes at three months included poor function, dependency, and death. As lean mass rose, all three outcomes became less common. Adjustment for clinical factors and fat mass kept the association intact. Higher lean mass meant lower odds of poor outcome and mortality. An interaction with diabetes appeared for functional outcomes. Muscle mass, the authors argue, is a prognostic factor distinct from fat.
pmc-12820129:
Pritam Chakraborty and co-authors published this computing study in 2025 on self-driving vision in India. Road scenes there mix dense traffic, blocked views, and weak lane marks. Models trained on tidy Western streets often fail in that mess. The team built IndiVNet, a model that labels each pixel of a road scene by kind. Its encoder widens its view step by step, catching both fine detail and broad context.

On an Indian driving data set, the model beat both classic and transformer rivals on the standard overlap score. On a British street set it scored higher still, showing it can travel across settings. The authors stress speed as well as accuracy, since a car must decide in real time. They offer the model as a region-aware base for driving in hard, mixed streets.
pmc-12821929:
Young and coauthors weigh costs of two calm-down drugs for children before surgery. Fear before anesthesia is common in young patients. One drug is the usual care choice in most hospitals. The next drug is a sleep hormone sold for home use.

A large trial split children to one drug or the other. Cost logs came from case forms in that trial. Care was judged from a health service point of view. The team tracked drug, staff, and stay costs for each child. Gains were weighed as calm scores and smooth surgery starts. The study gives leaders a cost base for drug choice.
pmc-12822129:
Eight researchers led by Muskan Garg mapped what computer-science studies say about sex gaps in memory and thinking decline. They searched major databases for work in journals and meetings of their field, from two thousand to twenty twenty-five. Only seventeen full papers met their rules.

Most studies came from North America and Europe, and most used standard statistics or machine learning at a single site. The team found the field mostly describes broad sex gaps rather than testing why they arise. Few studies use designs that can probe cause. The authors call for richer data work on the roots of these gaps, which hit some groups harder than others.
pmc-12824229:
Xiaopeng Li and colleagues show that broken body rhythms worsen fatty liver disease in mice. Their study from twenty twenty-five feeds mice a high-fat diet. Circadian disruption is a known risk factor for this liver condition. The cell death pathway behind that link was unclear.

Four groups separated diet effects from rhythm disruption effects. Combined disruption plus fatty diet produced the worst liver state. Fat buildup, liver function, and inflammation were all measured. Tissue staining showed deeper structural damage in combined groups. A chain of death-signalling proteins switched on more strongly. That chain links rhythm loss to liver cell death directly. Shift workers face a human version of this risk pattern.
pmc-12828029:
Michael Spantios and six colleagues published a 2025 brain imaging study of kendo players, practitioners of a Japanese martial art fought with bamboo swords. Kendo embodies a Zen ideal, and mindfulness, calmly observing thoughts and sensations without judging them, is close to that ideal.

The team used fMRI scans during an auditory oddball task, where listeners pick out rare tones. Their framework was the triple network model, which describes how the brain switches between its resting network and its task network through a salience network. They predicted that kendo players would switch networks more efficiently than non-players. The study tests whether long martial arts practice reshapes the brain's network control in measurable ways.
pmc-12829329:
Emara and six co-authors test a deep learning tool that reads two kinds of eye scans to spot diabetes eye harm early, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Eye harm from diabetes is a top cause of lost sight that can be prevented. Most tools use just one scan type, so each sees only part of the damage. The new tool fuses both types for a fuller view.

They built the test on two hundred twenty-two paired scans picked for sharp quality. One part reads color photos of the back of the eye. The other reads layered depth scans. A weighting step stresses the most telling areas. The fused tool was right in about nine of ten cases. The team calls the results early and urges tests on larger groups.
pmc-12830029:
Chan and co-authors report early safety results for a liver cancer treatment in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The cancer cannot be removed by surgery, and many sicker patients are left out of trials. The study tests a two-drug immune regimen as first treatment in groups with a poorer outlook.

Ninety-eight patients were included in this early check, drawn from groups with weaker liver function, lower daily function, or a blocked main vein. Serious side effects tied to treatment were limited, and the rate of severe ones was under one fifth. Two percent of patients died from effects linked to the drugs. The authors say the safety pattern matches an earlier trial and looks manageable, while the study continues.
pmc-12836829:
Wezzie Nyapigoti and five co-authors ask what fair pay and benefits for research participation mean to the many groups touched by studies in Malawi. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Global ethics rules say participants should be repaid for time, travel, and trouble. What counts as fair on the ground is still contested.

The team ran ten group discussions and seventeen interviews across rural and urban projects. Ethics reviewers and researchers shared one textbook understanding of compensation. Some community members, though, read payments as damages for harm suffered. Others complained that promised study benefits never reached their villages. Unequal pay across studies also left some feeling devalued. The authors urge clearer talk with communities before studies begin. Fairness, they show, is a local judgment, not a tariff.
pmc-12837529:
Ying-Yi Zhang and a large team test cell therapies meant to revive failing ovaries in mice. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Early loss of ovarian function is a rising cause of infertility, and stem cell treatments have shown promise with uneven results.

A chemotherapy drug was used to damage mouse ovaries. Three cell products were then placed into the ovaries at matched doses: cord-derived and fat-derived stem cells, plus a mixed fat cell fraction. Function and tissue checks judged the repair. Gene and protein reads traced how the cells act, pointing to delivery of oxidoreductase enzymes as a shared mechanism. The side-by-side test helps show which cell source earns further study for women with this condition.
pmc-12840029:
Jurys and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a case-control study of cancer patients living with a tracheostomy. The surgery opens a breathing hole in the neck and changes appearance and speech. The team compared one hundred fifty such patients with matched patients treated without the surgery. Matching covered age, sex, tumor site, and disease stage. A survey measured social withdrawal, self-consciousness, and how others seem to react.

Patients with a tracheostomy reported far higher social burden overall. They endorsed stigma-related items much more often than controls. Women and younger patients in that group struggled most. They avoided social settings more and felt less confident in public. Differences by age and sex were minimal among controls. The authors urge routine psychosocial support after treatment.
pmc-12852129:
Deependra Rastogi and six colleagues published a computing study in two thousand twenty-five on spotting brain tumours in MRI scans. Fast, accurate tumour detection guides treatment and improves patient outcomes. The team combined a deep learning network with classic sorting methods to raise accuracy.

They used a network called Xception, pre-trained on other images, to pull features from the scans. Two setups were tried: trimming the network's top layers, or freezing all of them. Five classic classifiers then labelled the features. On a public dataset of brain scans, the best pairings sorted test scans correctly about ninety-nine times in one hundred. The authors say such hybrid systems could support doctors, though checks on hospital data come first.
pmc-12913929:
Rozi Rozi and eight co-authors published a vaccine study in twenty twenty-five on protecting mice against Aeromonas hydrophila, a fish pathogen that also infects people and shrugs off antibiotics. Their candidate is a single outer membrane protein, Omp34, given with adjuvant in three injections. A killed whole-cell vaccine served as the comparison.

Antibody subclasses, lysozyme activity, and white-cell respiratory burst were tracked for six weeks. A lethal challenge then tested real protection. One immune measure, the nitroblue tetrazolium burst assay, tracked survival closely enough to serve as a correlate of protection, a shortcut for future vaccine testing without lethal trials. The authors frame the work within One Health, where fish farms and human clinics share the same microbial enemy.
pmc-13082629:
Shimazu and a large team test an influenza drug in ducks infected with deadly bird flu in twenty twenty-six. Highly pathogenic avian influenza threatens wild and captive rare birds. Treating valuable captive birds could support conservation. Baloxavir marboxil is an approved flu drug in human medicine.

Sixteen young ducks were infected with an H5N1 strain. Groups received daily drug doses starting two days after infection. All ducks on the two higher doses survived. Virus shedding fell significantly compared with untreated birds. A follow up dosing study linked drug exposure to shedding reduction. Blood levels of the active form predicted the benefit best. Treatment within forty-eight hours cut both deaths and virus output.
pmc-13092229:
Huimei Chen, Zhe Lin, and eight colleagues pool trial evidence on whether a diabetes drug class raises fracture risk in type one diabetes, in a meta-analysis published in two thousand twenty-six. The drugs are SGLT2 inhibitors, developed for type two diabetes and increasingly added to insulin therapy in type one. Bone safety worries have trailed the class since early signals in other populations.

The authors searched four major databases for randomized trials of these drugs as insulin add-ons in type one diabetes. Fracture risk was the primary outcome. Sugar control measures, other benefits, and wider safety indices came second. They pooled odds ratios, split analyses by dose, and graded each trial's risk of bias with the standard Cochrane method. Adjunct therapy in type one diabetes is a balancing act of tighter control against new risks. A careful fracture verdict helps clinicians weigh it.
pmc-13126729:
Rodríguez and a large team release Heartbeat, a dataset pairing fetal heart scans with clinical records. Congenital heart disease is the top cause of infant death from birth defects. AI tools for early spotting are held back by small, low-grade datasets and few that mix scans with records.

Heartbeat gathers data from many centers, anonymized, from 2019 to 2023. It holds standard fetal heart views, such as the four-chamber and outflow tract planes. Matching clinical metadata travels with each scan set. The authors aim to speed early detection research with this shared, multimodal resource from Colombia.
pmc-13149229:
Marcus Larnyoh and five co-authors test whether common drugs, antibiotic or not, change how bacteria swap resistance genes. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Bacteria pass resistance through plasmids, small DNA rings handed cell to cell in conjugation.

The team measured drug strengths against a lab strain, then ran mating tests with three plasmid types. At low, sub-killing doses, several drugs boosted gene transfer in a plasmid-specific way. A blood pressure drug more than doubled transfer of one plasmid and quadrupled another. A heart drug also nudged transfer up. Some drugs instead cured cells of their plasmids, broadly or selectively. The authors warn that everyday medicines may quietly shape resistance spread.
pmc-13153729:
Pierre Gillotay and co-authors study a cell defense switch in the thyroid gland, in work published in 2026. The gland makes hormones that steer growth and body burn rate in nearly all tissues. Making those hormones needs peroxide, which strains the gland with oxygen harm that must be held in check. The switch, called Nrf2, turns on genes that clear such harm.

The team broke the switch in zebrafish embryos and in mouse stem-cell thyroid models. Both showed a shared flaw in hormone making. In fish the flaw may stem from poor iodine tagging of the hormone base. In the lab models it may stem from making too little of that base.
pmc-13157629:
Farah Shahzad and colleagues published a case report in 2026 about side effects of a cancer drug. The drug, nivolumab, helps the immune system attack tumors. It can also make the immune system attack healthy organs. One man had taken it for five years for a lung lymphoma.

He arrived with fever, fast heartbeat, nausea, and belly pain. Tests showed mild liver injury, and scans found bowel inflammation. Infection tests came back negative. Doctors blamed the drug and stopped it permanently. High-dose steroids brought rapid improvement within days. He left hospital on a tapering dose of steroids. The case warns that such harm can arrive very late.
pmc-13158729:
Marije Vink and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-six, patient-reported outcomes after hip and knee replacement in private versus public hospitals in the Netherlands. Private hospitals now do more of this surgery there. The team used the national arthroplasty register, which tracks joint replacements. Cases from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-three totaled more than one hundred seventy thousand. Outcomes included pain scores, quality of life scales, and hip and knee function scores, before surgery and at set points after.

They also compared travel distance to the hospital as a measure of access. Models adjusted for factors that could bias the comparison. The title reports the core result: no difference in patient-reported outcomes between sectors. Full methods and endpoint choices are set out for the three replacement types.
pmc-13162029:
Shikhar Bindal and four co-authors report reuse of torn-off skin as a full graft to cover a grave leg peel wound. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-six. Peel wounds rip skin from deep tissue, often in road crashes, and the skin loses blood flow. Care is most often staged, with skin swaps late in the course.

Their patient, a man of sixty-four, had a vast peel on the right leg. After bones were fixed and dead tissue cut out, sound skin was trimmed of fat and laid back as a graft at once. Part of the graft died and needed a thin graft patch. By three months the leg was fully skinned, with fine use and looks.
pmc-13165029:
Guan, Wang, Yin, Hao, and Ji model how nylon affects an explosive, in work from twenty twenty-six. The case is a nylon jet piercing reactive armor, which can trigger a violent blast. The explosive is RDX, a common military compound.

Computer simulations of reacting molecules and quantum calculations traced how RDX breaks down with heat. Breaks start at a few known bonds and paths. Adding nylon lowered the energy bar for the first bond break and gave hydrogen atoms that start a second path. Free radicals from both materials then react together. Lab results matched the model. The work explains a trigger that armor design must handle.
pmc-13175029:
Kristina Bright leads a 2026 study of microbes and carbon cycling in alpine soils in the Swiss Alps. Streamside zones run from wet flats near streams to drier slopes, and oxygen levels shift with that moisture. In oxygen-free flat soils, organic carbon may pile up because microbes are thermodynamically constrained, limited by energy rules.

Using shotgun metagenomics, reading all DNA in a sample, the team compared microbe communities across two catchments. Flat soils held more carbon and more diverse microbes, with greater potential for breathing without oxygen, using nitrate, iron, or sulfate instead. Slope soils were less diverse and shaped by other soil traits. Redox state, the authors show, steers carbon fate.
pmc-13179729:
Alfredo de Jesús Garza Guerra and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on how often autism goes unspotted in adults who seek mental health care. Autism lasts across the whole life span, yet adult clinics still miss it often. Traits get blamed on other conditions, and some adults learn to mask how they think and act.

The review drew on studies from 2010 to 2025 found in three large databases. It finds that adult autism takes many forms, often mixed with anxiety, low mood, or other issues. That mix leads doctors to settle on the wrong label and delays real help. The authors urge clinics to ask about childhood development and to judge traits in context. Their frame aims to help doctors build a fuller, fairer picture of each patient.
pmc-13185029:
Kavya and four colleagues run a trial for a severe headache after spinal anaesthesia in twenty twenty-six. The headache can follow a caesarean birth and slow recovery for new mothers. The trial tested two drugs given as a mist through a nebuliser. It compared them with a salt water placebo.

Ninety-six women with moderate to severe headache took part at one centre. All got standard care and stayed lying flat for three days. Both drugs cut pain scores at twenty-four hours compared with placebo. The benefit held at forty-eight and seventy-two hours. One drug, dexmedetomidine, worked fastest and gave the strongest relief. Side effects were mild and rare. The authors call for larger trials that allow early movement.
pmc-13193529:
Leonardo Oliveira and a large team of co-authors published a scoping review in 2026 on cell-based shots for osteoarthritis, a joint disease that wears down cartilage. The shots use cells taken from body fat or from bone marrow. The team looked only at treatments the United States drug agency allows.

The team searched five databases and found 84 studies with close to ten thousand patients. Most studies tracked the knee, and most followed patients for a year or less. Almost all studies asked patients how they felt, but few used scans or X-rays. The authors say the field lacks strong trials and clear rules, and they call for shared reporting rules so future studies can be compared.
pmc-13195029:
Ahmad Bavali-Gazik and four co-authors built an AI triage model for chest pain in the emergency ward. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, starts from crowd harm: packed wards delay care and raise deaths, most of all for heart cases. Hand triage errs too oft. Their model joins routine triage facts with auto reads of ECG images. Six hundred records of patients with suspected heart signs formed the base.

The build ran in three phases: triage facts alone, ECG alone, then both as one. Scores were set against true outcomes in the first day. Readers who run wards get a tool to flag the true heart risk at the door, where minutes count most.
pmc-13195429:
Getasew Shitaye leads a 2026 review of the protein corona, the layer of proteins that coats tiny particles entering the body. A particle's biological identity is set not by its bare surface but by this corona, which forms from the fluids around it. The corona remains a major challenge for nanomedicine, medicine at the tiny scale.

The review explains how particle traits and the body environment shape corona formation. It then argues the field urgently needs standard, high-resolution methods. Standard methods would let results be compared and reproduced across labs. The review also explores untapped potential. Such particles can speed or slow the protein clumping behind brain diseases. The corona itself shapes that process, opening intervention ideas.
pmc-13197329:
Lawson McLean, Lawson McLean, and Senft surveyed who leads neurosurgery training across Germany in twenty twenty-six, looking for gaps by gender and by region. Training directors shape both teaching quality and the future workforce, yet their makeup had not been charted nationwide.

The team gathered public data from all seventeen state medical chambers. Of three hundred twenty-nine training directors, only twenty-six were women, under eight percent. That share looked similar in the former West and former East. Shared training licenses, where several sites train together, were far more common in the West. The authors link that gap to the West's larger private hospital networks rather than to teaching culture. Only about a third of sites could offer the full seventy-two months needed for certification. They call for mentoring and clearer promotion paths to widen the leadership pool.
pmc-13200729:
Elio Escamilla-Vega and colleagues published a 2026 developmental biology study of the small-spotted catshark, a cartilaginous fish. Their subject was a special population of embryo cells that builds much of the face in vertebrates. These cells are well studied in bony animals but poorly known in sharks and their relatives.

Combining detailed molecular and anatomical work, the team found that the basic genetic toolkit of these cells is much the same across jawed vertebrates. Differences in face shape arise mainly from how the cells' descendants behave later. The study gives evolutionary biologists a reference point for how faces diversified.
pmc-13202429:
Fruit peel waste becomes a water-cleaning material in a 2026 study led by Tra Huong Do, which turns Lansium domesticum peel into porous activated carbon. The research article uses a combined hydrothermal and phosphoric acid activation to build a mesopore-rich carbon for removing methylene blue dye from wastewater.

Despite only moderate surface area, the carbon adsorbed large amounts of dye in the authors' tests, which they attribute to accessible pores and oxygen-rich surface chemistry. Careful statistical comparison of models favored the Sips isotherm and pointed to a multi-step uptake process. The work shows careful pore design can partly compensate for low surface area in adsorbents made from farm residues.
pmc-13202529:
Cooling without gas compression could use magnetic materials, and a 2026 study from Dimitar N Petrov characterizes a gadolinium oxide for that role in deep cold. The research article profiles the disordered double perovskite Gd2MnZnO6, made by solid-state reaction, for its magnetocaloric effect near its magnetic transition.

Diffraction showed an orthorhombic crystal structure for the compound before magnet testing began. Under strong applied fields, the material produced a large entropy change and useful cooling power in the authors' tests. Analysis suggested short-range ordering from competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic forces inside the compound. The authors propose it as a promising option for cryogenic magnetic cooling.
pmc-13203029:
Living beside dogs for twenty thousand years may have left marks on human biology, and a 2026 commentary from Jamshid Faraji proposes how to look for them. The article defines an epigenetic archaeology of human-dog companionship, asking whether shared homes shaped stress regulation, immunity, and social-emotional biology.

Faraji and Gerlinde A S Metz treat DNA methylation and other gene-regulatory marks as records of early-life environmental calibration rather than inheritance. Drawing on genomics, neuroscience, microbiome research, and ancient DNA methods, they outline a testable guide. It would compare epigenetic patterns in ancient populations with archaeologically inferred dog co-residence, while controlling for ecology and demography.
pmc-13210529:
Abdelrahman Gadallah and four co-authors build an antibiotic-loaded scaffold in a 2026 study. Their scaffold mixes bioactive glass with a natural polymer and carries streptomycin at several loadings. It was made by a directional freeze-drying route and checked with imaging and spectroscopy before and after lab tests. Bacteria tests covered four common germ types, both major classes.

The scaffolds showed a highly connected pore structure, long-lasting antibacterial action, and a strong ability to form bone-like mineral in lab fluids. Compared with bead carriers, scaffolds hold their shape better and their pores favor steady drug release and tissue joining. The authors present the system as promising for bone work, pending more biological study.
pmc-13210629:
Gianfranco Picone reviews the pairing of metabolomics with machine learning in two thousand twenty-six for sharper chemical detection. Metabolomics profiles the small molecules in a sample all at once. Its data are huge and tangled, which pushed the field toward learning algorithms that can sort signal from noise.

The review walks through the full workflow: how samples are prepared, how raw data are cleaned, and which learning models, guided or unguided, do the classifying. It stresses how results are validated so findings can be trusted and repeated. Uses span food science, environmental monitoring, clinical diagnosis, and exposure studies. Open problems include data quality and models that explain themselves. The author points to explainable tools and joined data types as next steps.
pmc-13212029:
Peng Wen and co-authors compared two tests for tuberculosis of the pleura in two thousand twenty-six. The pleura is the lining around the lungs, and this form of the disease often has very few bacteria, so standard tests miss many cases. The team ran a prospective study of suspected cases.

Patients gave sputum, pleural fluid, and biopsy samples for targeted sequencing, the Xpert test, and culture. Sequencing had higher sensitivity than both rivals in each sample type, while staying fully specific in the small non-disease group. It found many cases that culture and Xpert missed. The authors place it as a second-line test in a tiered plan, not a first test for all.
pmc-13214429:
Ashish Sharma and a large team test in 2026 whether a licensed sleeping pill can also slow Alzheimer's-type brain damage in mice. The drug blocks orexin, a wakefulness signal, and poor sleep is known to raise levels of the amyloid protein that forms plaques.

Mice bred to develop plaques received the drug, a comparison sedative, or plain vehicle for several weeks, starting before or after plaques appeared. The orexin blocker improved sleep with less daytime drowsiness and prevented sticky fibrillar plaque build-up, while the comparison drug only trimmed early diffuse deposits. Brain immune cells clustered around plaques and ate more amyloid under the drug. Removing those cells erased the benefit entirely.
pmc-13215429:
Ellen E. Towers and co-authors published a 2026 systematic review of the biology behind having post-traumatic stress disorder and alcohol use disorder together. The review asks whether the combined condition has its own molecular, genetic, brain, and cognitive signature.

From nearly four thousand papers screened, only 14 studies qualified because each compared the combined group with controls or with one disorder alone. Hormone studies found no pattern unique to the combined condition. Genetic work reported shared risk between the two disorders in female twins, and brain studies found lower metabolite levels, weaker white matter, and smaller hippocampal volume. The authors stress that the underlying studies are few and skewed toward male veterans.
pmc-13216129:
Miaomiao Fan and co-authors present a 2026 prospective study of blood metabolic markers measured before illness and later risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Most earlier metabolite studies sampled patients after diagnosis, which cannot separate cause from consequence.

The analysis drew on UK Biobank, following 262,363 adults after excluding those with missing measures or prior disease. Thirty-nine certified biomarkers, measured by a high-throughput nuclear magnetic resonance platform, were tested against new cases of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis recorded through July 2023. The design lets prediagnostic chemistry speak to disease risk rather than to the effects of illness or treatment. The authors frame the work as a step toward earlier risk detection.
pmc-13216329:
Saskia Brummer and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of balance in children, asking which body measures and activity habits predict steady posture. Good balance underpins safe play and sport, and childhood obesity has been tied to poorer stability.

Ninety-five children aged seven to eighteen completed computerized balance testing and reported their activities. Statistical factoring sorted activity into five domains such as daily movement, cycling, and sports club participation. Older age and greater height generally tracked with better scores, while overweight and obesity linked to weaker measures, and weaker physical education grades linked to poorer directional control. One hopeful interaction appeared: sports club activity softened the link between obesity and slow motor responses. The authors stress that models explained only a modest share of the differences.
pmc-13217029:
Nicholas I-Hsien Kuo and co-authors present a 2026 study building cardiovascular risk equations from ordinary Australian general practice records. The equations replace a calculator adapted from New Zealand data that had never been validated locally.

The dataset linked records from 680 practices for 850,216 adults, among whom 33,578 cardiovascular events occurred over about five years. Sex-specific models with twenty-eight predictors discriminated well, with C statistics of 0.803 in women and 0.772 in men, and leaner twelve-to-fifteen-variable versions performed nearly identically. Calibration held across age, income, and smoking groups, and geographic validation across ten health networks was consistent. The authors propose embedding the equations in practice software for automatic, real-time risk scoring.
pmc-13218129:
Edda Weimann and co-authors explore what switching from charcoal to electric cooking would mean for child health in Uganda, in a 2026 qualitative stakeholder study. Charcoal smoke and cooking injuries are major preventable causes of illness and death among children in low- and middle-income countries. Electric cooking could cut both risks, but adoption is slow and the policy conditions behind it are poorly understood.

The team interviewed 51 stakeholders in Kampala between September and November 2023, drawn from government, development partners, civil society, private companies, universities, and experienced users. Stakeholders saw electric cooking as safer than charcoal, with less smoke and fewer hazards, but judged the child health gains indirect and dependent on broader conditions. They named unreliable electricity, high appliance prices, power cost worries, fragmented policies, and deep-rooted cooking habits as the main barriers. Child health rarely figured explicitly in energy policy, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-13218529:
Wen Sun, Sihan Yu, and Zhengye Jiang propose a way to detect islanding in distributed power generation, in a 2026 engineering study. Islanding happens when a generator keeps feeding loads after disconnecting from the grid, a serious fault that protection systems must catch quickly. In systems with generators, the signals dilute, and standard detectors develop blind zones where they miss the event.

The team built a simulation of a grid-connected distributed generation system in MATLAB and Simulink, under the IEC 61850-7-420 standard. They recorded voltage and current waveforms at nodes under islanded and grid-connected operation. Those waveforms became time series, time-frequency spectrograms through a short-time Fourier transform. A convolutional neural network trained on spectrogram features learned to classify system state. On a held-out test set the method reached an accuracy of 99.84 percent, and the authors report a much shrunken non-detection zone compared with standard approaches.
pmc-13219429:
Masaharu Takarada and colleagues report that heat leaves cells far more slowly than conduction predicts, in a 2026 study. Dye thermometers have revealed temperature differences inside cells, but the physics behind them was a mystery, since heat in surroundings should spread and fade almost at once. The team set out to watch heat dissipation.

A fluorescent polymer thermometer, read out by lifetime imaging microscopy, mapped temperatures inside cells while an infrared laser warmed them. After continuous heating, a cell's average temperature relaxed over seconds, far slower than in same-sized artificial liposomes filled with solution. The slowdown depended on the cell's internal structures and molecules, ruling out fluid physics. The authors conclude that cells dissipate heat by a non-diffusive process unlike textbook conduction. They frame the result as a foundation for a proper thermodynamics of the living cell, where warmth may be a functional signal rather than noise.
pmc-13221329:
Wendy Argelia García-Suastegui and co-authors screen suspended matter in Mexico's Atoyac River for polymer-like material, in a 2026 early study. The river receives industrial, farm, and household discharges along the studied stretch. Water came from six sites across a 43-kilometer section representing different land uses.

Infrared spectroscopy, sharpened by math-based separation of overlapping signals, found bands matching common plastics such as polyethylene and polystyrene types. A strong signal near textile sites pointed to sulfonated compounds linked with dyes. The authors stress that, without removing organic matter first, results suggest polymer-like signs rather than proving tiny plastic particles. Still, the method offers a fast screening baseline for a heavily polluted river.
pmc-13221529:
R Kavitha, Ravi Samikannu, and Nyagong Santino David Ladu model a complex nanofluid flowing over a porous stretching sheet, in a 2026 numerical study. The fluid blends three behaviors: plastic yield, shear-dependent viscosity, and elasticity. Radiation, magnetic fields, heat-driven particle drift, and chemical reaction all act on the flow at once.

Governing equations were converted to ordinary form and solved with a fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. More radiation and stronger Brownian motion lowered temperature, while thermophoresis raised it. Stronger magnetic fields slowed the fluid through Lorentz forces. Results for friction and transfer rates appear in graphs, extending theory for industrial cooling and coating processes that use such fluids.
pmc-13222029:
Ami Takeuchi and co-authors study how the cutting and rejoining of gene messages helps plant cells forget their old identity and form callus, in a 2026 paper. Plant cells are famously flexible, and the splicing of pre-mRNA is part of that flexibility. The team worked with a mutant Arabidopsis plant that fails at callus formation and root regrowth when warm.

The faulty gene proved to be the plant's version of a yeast splicing helper. Its failure only blocked callus growth when a plant hormone, a cytokinin, was in the growth medium. Gene scans showed wall-building genes switching up and cell-cycle genes switching down. Splicing faults clustered in fat metabolism genes, and the mutant's special membrane fats ran low. A fat synthesis blocker hit the mutant extra hard. The authors conclude that splicing steers the identity reset through fat pathways, under hormone control.
pmc-13222229:
Benjamin Kelvington and co-authors propose broken DNA repair as an overlooked mechanism in autism spectrum disorder, in a 2026 review. Large genetic studies already implicate repair genes in some autism cases. Smaller studies report extra DNA damage in blood and other tissues of autistic people and even their parents.

Chromatin remodelers tied to autism also help repair DNA, giving the two stories a shared hinge. Repair failure might also connect autism with later neurodegenerative disease and help explain sex differences in diagnosis. The authors call the mechanism a leading candidate needing systematic study, with possible benefits for autistic people and those who support them.
pmc-13222629:
Fan Bu and co-authors survey new drug therapy for depressive disorders, in a 2026 practice-focused review. Many patients never reach lasting remission on standard drugs, most of all in treatment-resistant and bipolar depression, where slow onset and side effects erode value. The search drew on major sources plus drug-regulator and gene-guidance documents.

Newer options covered include NMDA-targeting rapid agents, a cough-drug combination, brain-active steroids, psychedelic therapy, and kappa-opioid blockers. Equal weight goes to using existing drugs better: reusing old drugs, add-on therapy, sensible pairings, dosing order, and follow-up guided by scores. Progress, the authors argue, depends as much on smarter selection and monitoring as on novel molecules.
pmc-13225029:
Na Hu and colleagues review a 2026 account of endoplasmic reticulum stress in rheumatoid arthritis, the autoimmune disease that inflames and destroys joints. The endoplasmic reticulum folds proteins inside cells, and overload there triggers a rescue programme with three main sensor branches. Evidence now places that stress response at a crossroads of inflammation, metabolism, and cell survival in the joint lining.

Early on, the response helps cells adapt and restore balance. When it stays switched on, it instead amplifies inflammation, helps aggressive joint-lining cells resist death, and encourages bone-eating cells. Because effects differ by disease stage and cell type, the authors favour precisely tuned treatments over blanket suppression of the pathway.
pmc-13226829:
Alushika Jain, Nikita Bora, and Amit Toshniwal report a 2026 case of mucormycosis, an aggressive fungal infection, arising on the tongue of a 34-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes. The disease usually attacks the sinuses or lungs in people with weakened defences, so a primary tongue site is highly unusual. He had endured fifteen days of pain and trouble eating, with a dead-tissue ulcer on the side of his tongue.

Biopsy showed the fungus's broad, ribbon-like threads branching at right angles, confirming the diagnosis. Treatment combined tight blood-sugar control, surgical removal of dead tissue, and a lipid-wrapped form of amphotericin B. He recovered well, and the authors stress fast recognition of atypical mouth lesions in diabetic patients.
pmc-13226929:
Shao and co-authors feed a food part, DMG, to hens in heat rounds and check gut harm. Heat rounds strain the gut of yellow-feather hens in farm runs. In sum, 180 male hens of 35 days split in three arms. One arm sat in mild air on the base feed in the trial. One arm took heat rounds on the base feed in the trial. One arm took heat rounds with DMG at 0.1 percent in feed.

A seven-day heat ramp led to 14 days of heat rounds. Heat sat at 32 to 35 marks in the round spans. Marks span growth, rear heat, gut shape, and flare counts. Path parts for TLR4 and NF-kB got reads in the gut. A coat part, MUC2, joined the reads in the same bits. Dish tests on gut cells backed the hen finds in the lab.
pmc-13228129:
Paris, Bell, and Hoffmann tested mosquito traps in this study from twenty twenty-six. The devices use a trick: visiting females pick up a growth-blocking chemical and carry it to other breeding spots. Two rival products were compared in large mesh tents. The mosquitoes were two urban species that breed in hidden containers around homes.

One station cut adult emergence more strongly than the rival trap, though both beat plain water cups. Lab tests then separated the ingredients worn by the stronger station. A fungus that infects insects drove most of the adult deaths. The growth blocker alone also raised deaths, but more modestly. The authors say pairing both agents gives the traps their bite.
pmc-13230329:
Viktoria Barna and colleagues combine in 2026 trial results on how planned exercise changes blood markers of bone rebuilding. Their review kept only randomized trials lasting more than two weeks in healthy adults. Twenty-four studies with more than twelve hundred people covered endurance, power, and mixed training at varied intensity.

Endurance work alone did not move osteocalcin, a marker of bone formation, in the pooled data. High-intensity training did raise osteocalcin levels clearly, though certainty for that finding was only moderate to low. Power training and mixed programs showed no clear osteocalcin change, and bone density stayed flat across types. Endurance training did lower body mass index. Matching exercise type to a bone goal needs more than general activity advice.
pmc-13233029:
Juan José Aguirre and co-workers wrote a 2026 study of Trypanosoma lainsoni, a parasite first found in north Brazil and later seen in Argentina. The team studied the parasite's kinetoplast DNA. That DNA is a net of tiny rings called minicircles. The rings hold guide RNAs that steer the editing of gene messages inside the cell's mitochondria.

Working with three Argentine isolates, the team read the minicircles using two kinds of sequencing. Each ring held two fixed zones set across from two changeable zones, and the team rebuilt the full editing steps from the guides. The changeable zones showed that the three isolates are distinct local types. A PCR test built from the ring DNA now lets labs spot this parasite with more confidence.
pmc-13233129:
Thaddaeus Castaneda and Amer Afaneh published this surgical study in 2026. It compares two scans used to diagnose acute cholecystitis, a sudden inflammation of the gallbladder. Ultrasound is the usual first test, while CT is often added when the picture is unclear. The authors reviewed 224 adults who had their gallbladder removed between 2020 and 2025 and whose tissue confirmed acute disease, then checked the scans against what surgeons found.

CT caught about 71.5 percent of cases, against 59.6 percent for ultrasound, and agreed more often with the findings in the operating room. In patients who had both scans, the two disagreed in about a fifth of cases. Both tests did worse on the most severe, gangrenous form of the disease. The authors still place ultrasound first, with CT as a back-up that adds real value in selected patients.
pmc-13233329:
Yin Mei Chan and colleagues published a 2026 biomaterials study on scaffolds that help Schwann cells grow, a step toward repairing peripheral nerves. Schwann cells support nerve regrowth, and they respond to both the softness of their surface and chemical signals attached to it. The team synthesized a new family of degradable copolymers and spun them into aligned fibers.

Two bioactive peptides, RGD and YIGSR, were attached to the fibers using click chemistry, with control over where and how densely each peptide sat. Cells on YIGSR-bearing scaffolds showed stronger activity of a laminin receptor, and softer peptide-decorated materials raised cell proliferation. Pairing mechanical tuning with precise chemistry gives designers a modular platform for nerve repair materials.
pmc-13233929:
Jade Dunot and colleagues reported a 2026 study naming a little-known brain peptide as a contributor to Alzheimer's disease. The peptide, AETA, is clipped from the same precursor protein that yields amyloid-beta, and it tunes a receptor type central to memory. Comparing post-mortem human brain tissue, the team found AETA levels significantly higher in Alzheimer's patients, especially women.

A new mouse engineered to overproduce AETA echoed the human picture. Females showed more support and immune cells in the hippocampus without open inflammation, altered synaptic gene activity matching vulnerable human brain regions, weaker receptor signaling, lost dendritic spines, and memory problems. Male mice largely escaped these effects. The authors propose blocking AETA signaling as a fresh strategy against early synaptic decline.
pmc-13235129:
E. Wilhelm and co-authors interviewed in 2026 patients who had received stem cell transplants from donors at centres in Regensburg and Tel Aviv. Aftercare after such transplants lasts for life because late complications are common. Forty-seven patients with a median age in the late fifties shared where communication with their care teams broke down. Interviews were analysed with a structured qualitative framework.

Many patients felt overwhelmed during consultations, which hindered early reporting of graft-versus-host symptoms. Psychosocial strain, memory problems, and topics felt as taboo, such as sexual health, often went unraised by either side. Broken chains between providers also lost information along the way. Patients described leaning on nurses and social networks to fill the gaps. The authors recommend communication training, prompt sheets for patients, and checklists for doctors.
pmc-13236729:
Sauli Vuoti and co-authors analysed in 2026 immune cell levels and growth markers in tumours from nearly four hundred patients with advanced breast cancer. Records spanned treatment years 2020 through 2024 across the major disease subtypes. Four proteins that drive cell division were measured alongside the density of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes. Survival without progression and overall survival were tracked against those markers.

Low immune infiltration independently predicted progression within the first two years in the whole cohort. Every growth marker, when high, tracked with shorter progression-free time in the results. One marker, MCM2, showed the strongest effect among the four division proteins. Immune levels meant opposite things in different subtypes, helping in triple-negative disease yet signalling worse outcomes in hormone-driven disease. No prognostic value appeared for immune levels in the HER2-positive group. Combining both marker families may refine risk estimates, the authors propose.
pmc-13236829:
Kırlak Kara and colleagues build a small sensor for a major peanut allergen, a protein called Ara h 1. Peanut allergy is a rising global problem and can kill, so food makers need fast, trustworthy checks for traces. Their sensor uses a shortened aptamer, a crafted DNA strand that grips the target protein, set on gold particles over a printed electrode.

Binding changes an electrical signal, giving a reading without a full lab. Shortening the aptamer can sharpen that grip and cut costs. A portable sensor like this could screen foods at factories or borders, catching contamination that labels miss and that allergic consumers cannot afford to meet.
pmc-13237529:
Mohamed Sheeraz Mohamed Azhar and co-authors evaluate a digital symptom triage service inside a British acute oncology unit. Their 2026 service evaluation covers patients on anti-cancer drug therapy, who can decline between visits while services rely on reactive helplines. The platform maps daily patient check-ins to green, amber, and red urgency tiers drawn from national nursing guidance.

Over ten weeks, a few dozen patients joined and none withdrew. Daily check-in completion ran above ninety percent. Alerts were grouped into episodes so the workload numbers reflect real clinical effort. The team tracked engagement, response times, escalation paths, and safety signals. The aim is earlier sight of trouble, with triage sorted before the phone rings.
pmc-13238029:
Liébana and colleagues measure how well pneumococcal vaccination protects at-risk adults against pneumonia severe enough for hospital care. Pneumonia caught in the community is a leading cause of illness in adults with chronic conditions. Vaccine benefit is proven in older adults, but evidence for younger at-risk adults has been scarce, leaving policy on shaky ground.

The team ran a case-control study across Spanish centres for the years 2020 to 2024. Adults from eighteen to sixty-four with risk conditions who were hospitalised with pneumonia were compared with matched controls. Comparing vaccine histories between the groups yields a real-world effectiveness figure for an age band guidelines often overlook.
pmc-13238529:
Ronan M. G Berg and fellow editors introduced a 2026 special issue of Experimental Physiology devoted to exercise as medicine.
