Their framing treats planned exercise as a therapy for people who already have disease, judged by the same standards as drugs: indication, dose, effectiveness, mechanism, and safety. The editorial carefully separates the concept from the older Exercise is Medicine campaign, which mainly urges clinicians to promote activity.

Within their framework, lab studies explain how exercise changes pathways and organ-to-organ signaling, while properly designed trials weigh harms against benefits with drug-level rigor. It earns no automatic pass for being natural. The issue gathers work from inner workings to randomized trials. The editors present the cross-field blend as the field's defining feature.
pmc-13239029:
Xiyu Yang and a large team built a thirteen-gene signature in 2026 for osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone cancer of the young. The signature predicts which patients will resist chemotherapy and fare poorly. Resistance is the main barrier to better outcomes, and dependable markers are scarce. The team compared gene networks in resistant and sensitive tumors, then tested the resulting risk model in four independent patient cohorts.

High-risk tumors grew fast, carried unstable genomes with many mutations, yet paradoxically shut immune cells out. Single-cell and spatial data showed the high-risk cancer cells were stem-like, huddled at oxygen-starved dead zones, and in heavy conversation with surrounding stroma. Drug predictions confirmed resistance to first-line agents. The authors offer the signature as a clinically usable marker that also exposes new treatment angles.
pmc-13239429:
Yongli Ni and colleagues report a 2026 trial of a gentle pain relief method for premature babies during eye checks. Screening for retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of early birth, is uncomfortable, and drug-free comfort measures are preferred for fragile infants.

One hundred babies born between 32 and 36 weeks were assigned to either a dummy or a combined sensory approach. That approach paired oral glucose for taste, a recording of the mother's voice, and gentle massage before and during the examination. Babies receiving the combined method showed lower pain scores, better comfort ratings, and steadier oxygen levels. The authors recommend it for similar screening settings.
pmc-13239529:
Dedius E Peter and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a qualitative study on childhood kidney injury in rural Tanzania. Acute kidney injury can progress quickly in children, causing dangerous acid, potassium, and fluid build-up, and early spotting at small clinics is vital yet poorly documented in low-resource areas.

About twenty health workers at primary facilities will share experiences through semi-structured interviews lasting up to an hour. The study is framed by Donabedian's model, which links care structures, processes, and outcomes. Thematic analysis will run alongside data collection. Findings will go to participating facilities and district and regional health authorities to guide improvement.
pmc-13239829:
Lu Han and colleagues uncover a chain of events driving bowel inflammation in a 2026 laboratory study. In inflammatory bowel disease the cell-cleaning process called autophagy falters, and the team traced the problem to a tagging enzyme, RNF31, that marks a master switch protein for destruction.

Cell and mouse experiments showed the tagging silences the switch, stalls cleaning, and wakes an inflammatory complex named NLRP3. A synthetic curcumin-like compound called CM-C1 breaks the harmful pairing, restores cleaning flow, and calms inflamed intestines in the mouse model. Gut microbe balance also improved. The authors nominate the compound as a multi-action treatment candidate.
pmc-13240229:
Venugopal's team in Hyderabad used twisted laser beams to tell molecular mirror images apart. Splitting mirror-image molecules matters greatly in drug making and testing. Older methods lean on the spin of light alone. The team added orbital angular twist from ultra-short pulses and paired it with mass spec.

Tests on the two mirror forms of camphor showed sharply split ionization and fragmentation. Combining spin and orbital twist boosted chiral selectivity up to fourfold. Pulses lasted only a few hundred femtoseconds each. The method needs no chemical pre-treatment, a scalable way to probe handedness in complex samples.
pmc-13240629:
Lai's team at the University of Alabama at Birmingham surveyed children with disabling conditions about telehealth exercise programs. Community activity is hard for many of these children to reach. The survey went to families in a community wellness program. Fifty-two replies from children aged five to sixteen were analyzed.

Social barriers were the most common obstacle, ahead of psychological ones. Families favored one or two sessions weekly, lasting thirty to 45 minutes at beginner level. Live video calls and prerecorded videos tied as favorite formats. Over ninety percent had suitable technology at home, and the authors suggest brief seasonal programs as a starting dose.
pmc-13241929:
Leticia Amaral Corrêa and co-authors publish a 2026 translation study of a back pain knowledge questionnaire for Brazil. Low back pain is the country leading cause of disability, yet tools measuring what patients believe about it lag behind current guidelines. The team adapted the Back pain Knowledge and Beliefs Survey into Brazilian Portuguese.

Psychometric testing covered content, structure, and consistency. The adapted version scored acceptably on internal consistency and reliability. Its structure held up when checked across groups, supporting fair comparison between populations. The authors conclude the Brazilian version can measure evidence-based understanding of low back pain. Clinicians can use it to spot beliefs that block self-management before tailoring education to each patient.
pmc-13242029:
Debela A Efa and co-authors report a 2026 survey of community knowledge about cystic echinococcosis in Ethiopia. This parasitic disease passes between dogs, livestock, and people, and Ethiopia is heavily affected. Baseline understanding in communities had rarely been measured.

Over three hundred people across several regions answered the survey. Risky habits were common: dogs roamed freely, home slaughter was routine, and infected offal was fed to dogs. More than half of respondents showed limited knowledge and unsafe practices. Vets scored highest. Farmers and rural residents scored lowest, and schooling strongly predicted safer behavior. The authors recommend tailored education, regular dog deworming, and better slaughter services fitted to local conditions.
pmc-13242429:
Laércio Mariano-Fernandes and colleagues used computer modeling to hunt for new drug candidates against Leishmania, the parasite behind leishmaniasis. Their paper appeared in Archives of Microbiology in 2026. They started from beta-lapachone, a compound from the lapacho tree, and tested a family of related molecules. Docking tests checked how each one fit several proteins the parasite needs to survive.

One offshoot, called LPI3, stood out by binding well to more than one target at once. Later modeling suggested its protein complexes stay stable, and its predicted safety and uptake traits looked good for a drug. Current drugs for this disease are costly, slow, and facing resistance, above all in infected dogs that keep it spreading. LPI3 is offered as a lead compound for real lab testing.
pmc-13242629:
Filip Filipsky and colleagues show that a nuclear scaffold protein quietly protects B cells from DNA damage. Their study appeared in HemaSphere in 2026. Lamin B1 lines the inside of the nucleus and helps organize the genome, but germinal center B cells dial it down while they deliberately mutate their antibody genes. The team built mouse and cell models with reduced Lamin B1 and mapped where DNA breaks appeared.

Cells short on Lamin B1 carried extra DNA damage and scrambled gene activity. Break mapping found hotspots that were not random: they clustered near gene start sites and near control regions governing protein production. In patients, low Lamin B1 levels in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma tracked with worse outcomes. The protein thus looks like a guardian of exactly the genome regions B cells can least afford to break. Its loss may help explain how some lymphomas arise and progress.
pmc-13243029:
Shengyi Zhao and colleagues review programmed cell death in gouty nephropathy in this 2026 article. The condition is kidney damage caused by long-term high uric acid, the same chemical buildup behind gout, and its causes are still poorly studied.

The review explains how five forms of controlled cell death act together in the sick kidney rather than alone. Some quietly remove kidney tubule cells, others burst cells and drive swelling, and one involves iron-linked damage to cell fats. The authors argue that drugs aimed at these death pathways could protect the kidney beyond the usual approach of simply lowering uric acid levels.
pmc-13243729:
Jochem Nelen and colleagues hunt for a fresh drug scaffold against a kinase tied to inflammation in 2026 work. The target, called p38α, helps drive inflammatory and brain diseases. Past blockers mostly failed in trials because they hit too many other targets or caused harm.

The team screened a compound library with three docking tools at once and took the shared top hit. Chemists then gathered look-alike compounds and tested how small changes altered strength. Several reached very high potency in lab assays, and models showed a stable fit in the target pocket. The lead compounds stayed stable in plasma and spared almost all of 468 other kinases tested. The scaffold now merits animal and safety study.
pmc-13243829:
Xiaohan Huang and Shengcai Zheng trace lung infection burden tied to air pollution among women of childbearing age in 2026. Women aged 15 to 49 face added risk from body factors, social gaps, and smoke in the home. The authors ask what drives their burden and how fair the load is across countries.

They draw on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data and project trends to 2051. Population growth drove most of the global rise, while richer regions saw shifts in disease patterns lead instead. Death risk peaked at ages 45 to 49 and fell for cohorts born after 1975. Inequality between places widened over three decades. Cleaner air could cut outdoor-linked death rates sharply by mid-century, the models suggest.
pmc-13247529:
Agarwal, Mithal, and Balakrishnan recount a diagnosis missed for nearly a decade, in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. Their patient, a twenty-six-year-old woman, first presented at eighteen with sparse periods and was labeled with polycystic ovary syndrome. Infertility workups later showed her pituitary was not driving her ovaries, and over the years she developed insulin-dependent diabetes and then sudden, life-threatening heart failure requiring an urgent transplant.

Genetic testing finally named juvenile hemochromatosis, a rare inherited iron-loading disease, caused in her by a homozygous change in the hemojuvelin gene. The authors' lesson is blunt: a cheap, routine ferritin blood test, never done, would have flagged iron overload years earlier. They urge screening young patients with this symptom cluster before organs fail irreversibly.
pmc-13247829:
Reinhardt, Panayides, and Riley built a chemical sponge for cleaning up flowing reactions in this 2026 RSC Advances paper. In continuous-flow synthesis, leftover amines contaminate products, and a solid scavenger packed in-line can trap them. The team decorated high-surface-area SBA-15 silica with aldehyde groups through a three-step surface chemistry, confirming the coating with a battery of analyses and a color test.

The material's loading matched commercial resin scavengers, and it survived flow conditions. A twenty-two-run designed experiment varied solvent, flow rate, temperature, and amine concentration; only the solvent mattered significantly. Hydrophobic solvents gave near-total capture, while acetonitrile screened the interaction and cut efficiency to about three quarters. The authors present the scavenger as a ready in-line purification tool for flow-chemistry libraries.
pmc-13248329:
Zhang and co-authors examined how a mother's fat levels late in pregnancy affect her calf's muscles, in a 2026 animal study. Dairy cows release non-esterified fatty acids into the blood before calving. The team grouped sixty Holstein cows by those levels and examined muscle from their calves at birth and at one month.

Birth weight did not differ between groups. Still, calves from higher-fat mothers had lighter leg muscles and shifts in markers tied to mitochondria, the cell's energy units, and to inflammation. Tests on cultured muscle cells pointed the same way. The authors say late pregnancy metabolism may quietly shape offspring muscle development.
pmc-13249529:
Zelelew, Wondie, and Ashagire counted birds in a sacred Ethiopian church forest, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. The Tara Gedam Monastery forest survives as a grove amid farmland that expands each season. Working two hundred survey points across wet and dry seasons, the team divided the forest into edge, middle, and interior zones and measured its trees.

They logged ninety-four species and more than twenty-three hundred individual birds. Numbers swelled in the wet season, yet the species list stayed remarkably steady, marking the grove as a year-round refuge. Against expectation, edges held the richest bird life. Insect eaters and omnivores dominated, and the authors urge protecting the forest's layered structure, edges included.
pmc-13250229:
Huang and co-authors uncover a new way tumors shut down killer T cells, centered on a protein called VSIG4. Their 2026 Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer paper matters most for cold tumors like pancreatic cancer, where current immune drugs often fail. Earlier work tied VSIG4 to tumor growth, but not to how it controls T cells.

The team found that VSIG4 grabs a helper protein that moves amino acids, starving T cells of glutamine and scrambling their ion flows. Removing that block restored nutrients and ion balance, reviving the antitumor response.
pmc-13250329:
Victor Correia and colleagues describe a rare device complication in this 2026 case report. Brain fluid shunts drain excess fluid to the belly and are widely used, but the tubing can sometimes pierce the bowel, a dangerous event.

Their patient, a 29-year-old man with a shunt fitted in 2018, arrived with the tube coming out of his anus. He recalled earlier episodes of the tube slipping and foul fluid discharge. Scans suggested the tube had migrated into the gut. Surgeons opened the belly, removed the tube, and repaired the colon, while brain surgeons removed the upper part. Recovery was smooth, and the authors stress quick joint action.
pmc-13250429:
Saad Berreta and a large team define how much improvement actually matters to patients after knee microfracture surgery. Their 2026 Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine study follows seventy patients treated for cartilage defects between 2013 and 2018. Outcomes were tracked for at least five years using standard knee function scores.

The team set two kinds of thresholds: the smallest change patients can feel, and the score level where symptoms feel acceptable. Roughly two thirds of patients reached the meaningful-change threshold on most scores, and about half reached an acceptable state. Starting with worse scores made meaningful change more likely, while lower body weight, milder joint wear, and smaller lesions favored acceptable outcomes. pmc-13251429:
Neelam Dhiman and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a fast automated assay that names gram-negative bacteria in blood samples and finds their drug resistance genes. Such infections can kill, and slow culture methods delay the right drug choice. The assay checks for nineteen bacteria and eight resistance genes in about two hours.

The multi-site study used fresh, pre-picked, and lab-made samples, more than thirteen hundred in all. Agreement with standard methods was high for nearly all targets, and near perfect for ruling targets out. The most common germs matched known patterns. Some off-target bacteria did cross-react, a flaw the authors note. Speed of this kind can sharpen early treatment choices.
pmc-13251729:
Utsav Ratna Tuladhar and three colleagues published an imaging study in two thousand twenty-six on judging aneurysm risk from wall stiffness. A swollen abdominal aorta can burst without warning. Width alone is a poor guide, because the wall's material strength matters too.

Errors stayed tiny in simulation, and stiffness ratios matched in the physical models. An older step-by-step method scored similarly but ran far slower. Once trained, the network gives near-instant stiffness estimates, which the authors hope will sharpen rupture forecasts.
pmc-13254429:
Qiu and co-authors review six patients whose immune systems attacked their brains in anti-GAD65 autoimmune encephalitis. Steroids and immunoglobulin controlled seizures in most patients during acute care. One patient, the first reported with three different brain antibodies, improved markedly despite severe disease. Tissue showed both antibody and T-cell attack patterns, pushing the authors toward personalized, multi-marker care.
pmc-13255929:
Samrah Jawed and colleagues pilot a digital decision support tool in telehealth clinics in a 2026 study. Pakistan faces doctor shortages, worsened when trained female doctors leave work after marriage or childbirth. The Sehat Kahani platform lets female doctors consult from home, and a support tool for fever illnesses was added. The team surveyed 30 female providers at five clinics in Sindh and held three focus groups.

About 43 percent used the tool several times a day, mostly alongside their own judgment rather than alone. Half trusted its advice, and satisfaction and ease of use were generally positive. Focus groups explained the patterns and barriers behind the numbers.
pmc-13256829:
Aqsa Qayyum and co-authors report in 2026 that fermenting pumpkin puree with lactic acid bacteria sharply raises its anti-diabetic activity in lab tests. Pumpkin already carries useful compounds, and fermentation was tested as a cheap way to unlock more of them for functional foods.

pmc-13257129:
Jihye An and Jeehyun Lee report a 2026 consumer study of how young Korean adults perceive fizzy drinks. Carbonation shapes liking, yet its texture is hard to describe in words. Focus groups and free-sorting tasks were combined to capture that experience.

Participants grouped drinks mainly by fizz strength and flavor, and they pinpointed where in the mouth bubbles and tingling were felt. Cooling was the most chosen texture term, followed by carbonation itself and bite. Overall fizziness also ranked high, and each leading term reached statistical significance. Descriptions mixed sensation with precise oral location, which gives product teams richer language. Beverage developers can use the vocabulary to design and test new drinks. The findings come from young adults in one country, so wider checks are still needed.
pmc-13257529:

Livestock housing corrodes concrete early, partly through toxic gases moving into the material. Ordinary concrete and a porous lightweight version were compared for heat flow, strength, water uptake, and gas permeability.

The lightweight material conducted almost no heat compared with ordinary concrete, yet absorbed vastly more water. Gas permeability was tested with oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide under pressure. Ordinary concrete peaked slightly higher on the top reading, with carbon dioxide giving the largest flow for both. Agricultural engineers gain data for matching wall materials to barn conditions rather than defaulting to standard mixes.
pmc-13257929:
Magdalena Olson and colleagues link feeding mode with infant night sleep across the first year in a 2026 study. Nearly two hundred Phoenix-area infants were followed at six ages from three weeks to one year. Parents reported night sleep, feeding style, night weaning, and bed sharing at each visit.

pmc-13258729:
Stacy V. Lu, Susan M. Gross, and Allison L. West study infant feeding decisions among parents with developmental disabilities in a 2026 mixed methods project. Eighteen parents in the United States completed a survey, and seven also gave repeated interviews. Feeding covered breastfeeding, formula use, and starting solid foods near six months.

Strong fixed beliefs about breastfeeding influenced some decisions. Medication use also entered feeding plans for several parents. Findings argue for direct, tailored feeding support and care settings that affirm disability rather than work around it.
pmc-13258829:
Manhou Xu and colleagues map plant carbon storage across mountain grasslands in a 2026 field study from the eastern Loess Plateau. Eight subalpine meadows spanned elevations from about seventeen hundred to nearly three thousand meters. Carbon in shoots and roots was estimated by plant group.

Total storage followed a U shape along elevation, dipping in the middle range. Roots held nearly three quarters of all stored carbon. Broad leaf herbs stored the largest share, followed by sedges, with grasses last. Species diversity helped carbon build up in herbs and sedges. Soil phosphorus worked against storage. Land managers see elevation and plant mix as levers for grassland carbon.
pmc-13259229:
Yan Zhang, Xiaoyu Gong, and Xiaoyang Yuan fuse brain wave and blood flow signals for thought decoding in a 2026 paper. Electrical signals give precise timing while near infrared light tracks slower oxygen changes. Fixed late fusion wastes the links between the two streams.

Encoders first learn each signal family, then align pairs to capture long range cross links. A routing module weighs how strongly the two signals couple for each sample. Accuracy topped ninety nine percent on two mental tasks under their test protocol. Added noise hurt the new design far less than a fixed fusion rival. Assistive technology gains a decoder that adapts when one signal degrades.
pmc-13259329:
Yuan Gao and coauthors halve a rice herbicide dose with a spray helper in a 2026 study. The helper mix disrupts leaf wax so the weed killer enters barnyardgrass more easily. Greenhouse tests and two years of field trials checked control, soil health, and yield.

Residues in grain and soil fell under the reduced strategy. Soil carbon, available potassium, and microbe diversity all rose. Grain yield increased significantly as well. Rice farmers gain a lower chemical route that pays back in soil quality.
pmc-13259629:
Leandro L. Coutinho and coauthors map how nitric oxide locks advanced cancers into sugar burning metabolism in a 2026 review. Two inflammation enzymes cooperate to sustain that state in tumors and their support cells. Early macrophage work showed nitric oxide blocking energy production in neighboring cells.

At signaling levels, the gas disables key steps of oxygen based energy release. Cells shift toward fast glycolysis, glutamine use, and protective reducing power. Chemical locks on gene control then stabilize the cancer program. The two enzymes feed each other in a self strengthening circuit. Cancer biologists gain an integrated engine model linking inflammation to tumor metabolism.
pmc-13260029:

APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and may also matter in Parkinson's disease. The authors suggest autophagy-boosting strategies could help astrocytes clear harmful protein.
pmc-13260229:
Dimitrios Raptis and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of once-weekly versus daily basal insulin in adults with type 2 diabetes. Time spent in the target glucose range improved by 1.86 percent, and the odds of reaching an HbA1c below 7.0 percent were higher, with an odds ratio of 1.32. Rates of serious low blood sugar episodes did not differ significantly. The main gain is fewer injections, the authors say.
pmc-13260329:
Kun Sirisopana and colleagues followed in 2026 men whose kidney failure was treated with a transplant, tracking sexual function and sex hormones across the first year. Erection problems and low testosterone are common in men on dialysis. Their study enrolled 28 men who received a living-donor kidney between 2019 and 2021.

A symptom score for aging males eased from the first month onward. Bioavailable testosterone, the share the body can use, rose by six and twelve months, and luteinizing hormone fell and stayed lower. The authors read this pattern as the new kidney restoring testicular function.
pmc-13260829:
Alia A Melegy and co-authors present a 2026 study of magnetic nanocomposites for removing toxic hexavalent chromium from water. Chromium in this form is a harmful pollutant. Uptake was fast and reached exceptionally high levels, eight hundred to nine hundred fifty milligrams per gram, above most reported in the field. pmc-13261029:

pmc-13262729:
Tuomas Sipilä and co-authors work out how two receptor systems cooperate in blood vessel cells in a 2026 journal article. pmc-13263229:
Samar H Elagamy and co-authors review artificial intelligence in analytical chemistry in a 2026 journal article. Machine learning can separate overlapping spectra, spot patterns, and predict how compounds behave in separations.

The authors call for explainable methods tied to chemical reasoning.
pmc-13263329:
Mike T. Zuendel and co-authors argue in a 2026 commentary that the word dementia should be retired from medicine and public life. Dementia is the general term for severe decline in memory and thinking. Its Latin roots mean, roughly, without mind.

The authors say the label itself now does harm as a public health problem. It threatens a person's sense of identity and can deter people from seeking care early. It can also discourage patients from joining research studies. In their view, the stigma attached to the word adds avoidable suffering on top of the illness. They argue retiring it is a public health necessity, not a matter of politeness.
pmc-13263529:
Joseph Ladines-Lim and colleagues ask whether drug-resistant staph blood infections still kill more readily than susceptible ones. pmc-13263729:

pmc-13263929:

pmc-13264129:

pmc-13264729:

pmc-13264929:

The authors say the tool was not built for narrowing, but training a version for it could aid stroke workups.
pmc-13266229:

Several acts did relate to how much treatment people completed. The authors map contact patterns for future guidance research.
pmc-13267629:

pmc-13267729:

pmc-13267829:

pmc-13268229:

pmc-13268629: Vitria Wuri Handayani and colleagues publish a 2026 correction to their study on deep learning for estimating age and sex from jaw-focused head X-rays. pmc-13269029:

pmc-13269329:

pmc-13269829:

pmc-13271429:

pmc-13271729:

pmc-13271929:

pmc-13272329:

pmc-13272429:

pmc-13272629:

pmc-13273129:

They frame the event as a One Health warning, joining rodent ecology, climate change, tourism, and global travel.
pmc-13273229:

pmc-13273529:
Ye-Seul Lee leads a 2026 study of acupuncture-related therapies as an add-on for Parkinson's disease, using Korean national health insurance data. Such therapies here include acupuncture, electrical acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping, and herbal formulas at Korean medicine clinics. The team matched 23,454 users with the same number of non-users and followed records to August 2018.

Users took less levodopa, the main Parkinson's drug, but used more medicines for sleep, anxiety, and depression symptoms. Users also had a slightly lower risk of death from any cause over the long term. The authors warn that the observational design and varied exposure mean these links should not be read as proof of benefit, and call for randomised sham-controlled trials.
pmc-13273729:
Oliwia Grząsiak-Kraj and colleagues reviewed gut hormone changes after major pancreatic surgery in a 2026 systematic review. Pancreaticoduodenectomy removes the duodenum and part of the small gut, rerouting food in ways that can change incretin hormones. These hormones help control blood sugar after meals.

Six studies with 134 participants met their rules from searches up to March 2026. One hormone, GLP-1, generally rose after meals following surgery, especially where food emptied faster or reached further gut segments. The other hormone, GIP, appeared in fewer studies and showed no consistent rise. Other hormone and sugar measures varied a lot. A cautious pooled check of two surgical variants hinted at higher early GLP-1 with the classic operation, but the data were too thin to confirm.
pmc-13273829:
Satoru Taguchi and co-authors combined stem cell derived dendritic cells with an oncolytic virus against bladder cancer in a 2026 mouse study. Oncolytic herpes virus kills tumor cells and stirs immunity, and dendritic cells should amplify that effect by presenting tumor material. Making dendritic cells from each patient is impractical, so stem cells offered a standard supply.

Their induced pluripotent stem cell dendritic cells matched marrow derived ones in surface markers, antigen uptake, and T cell stimulation in lab and animal tests. In a bladder cancer model, adding these cells to a virus engineered to release interleukin-12 greatly improved tumor control. Tumors filled with T cells, and local dendritic cells matured. The authors propose the pairing as a practical, clinic ready strategy.
pmc-13274229:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued a 2026 safety evaluation of a food enzyme made by the fungus Rasamsonia emersonii, strain FGB. The product, made by DSM Food Specialties, carries three activities that break down plant fibers and is meant for four food manufacturing processes. European food law requires such enzymes to pass a safety review before use.

Genetic damage tests raised no concern, and a ninety-day rat feeding study found no harm at the highest dose tested. Estimated intake in European diets stayed far below that dose, giving a safety margin of at least 376. The enzyme matched two known respiratory allergens, so an allergy risk cannot be fully excluded, but the panel judged it low and found no safety concerns.
pmc-13274929:
Nguyen Le, Huy Vo, and Thien Nguyen present a 2026 journal article on a faster algorithm for mining strong patterns from uncertain data, such as sensor readings that come with probabilities. The task is finding the top few closed frequent itemsets, compact summaries of what items appear together. Existing methods crawl depth-first and find strong patterns late, wasting effort.

Their algorithm, TUFCI, instead searches best-first, always expanding the most promising candidate next using a priority queue. Strong patterns surface early, the quality bar rises fast, and the search can stop safely sooner. Checking whether a pattern is truly closed also gets cheaper. In experiments, TUFCI significantly outran depth-first rivals and needed fewer closure checks, especially on dense data sets.
pmc-13275229:
Lifang Ma and colleagues studied how small vessel disease burden affects early recovery after ischemic stroke in a 2026 retrospective cohort from Beijing. Damage to the brain's smallest vessels is common in stroke patients and may worsen outcomes. The team combined scan markers into one burden score and added whole body clinical patterns.

They reviewed 474 consecutive patients admitted during 2024, most of them men with a median age of sixty-seven. Only a small share left hospital with severe neurological deficit. Higher total small vessel burden raised the odds of that poor outcome, as did high homocysteine levels. One traditional Chinese medicine pattern, named phlegm-heat fu-excess, showed the strongest link. A small deep infarct type was the leading single scan marker. The authors urge caution, since few poor outcomes limit model stability.
pmc-13276529:
Zilong Tian authored a 2026 review on a new twist in cancer drug design: attaching a toxic payload to a PD-1 antibody. PD-1 blockers release the brakes on immune cells so they attack tumors, but many patients' cancers resist them. Antibody-drug conjugates instead use an antibody as a guided carrier for a cell-killing drug.

The review examines how joining the two ideas might beat resistance while boosting immune attack on tumors. Design choices dominate the discussion: which target to bind, which payload to carry, and which linker joins them, since each shapes benefit and harm. Combining these conjugates with other treatments may strengthen responses further. Stubborn problems include uneven target levels across a tumor and linkers that break too early. Tian frames the field as promising but still working out its safety and design rules.
pmc-13277229:
R Harini leads a 2026 computer-based study of gene variants that may change how the diabetes drug metformin works in polycystic ovary syndrome. The syndrome affects hormones and metabolism in about one in ten women of childbearing age. Metformin response varies, in part because transporter proteins move the drug into the liver and out through the kidneys.

Using several prediction tools, the team screened gene variants in three transporter genes and flagged fourteen as likely harmful. Some sit on the protein surface and may affect binding; others are buried and may affect folding. All were predicted to weaken protein stability. No lab tests were done, so the flagged variants are priorities for later bench work.
pmc-13277529:
Xiaoli Han leads a 2026 study of vehicle-to-grid technology in China, where electric cars send power back to the grid when needed. Such flexibility can support renewable energy, but real user willingness matters. The team ran a choice experiment with 1,412 electric vehicle owners and measured what payment owners would accept.

The study estimates vehicle-to-grid could supply up to three hundred forty-eight gigawatts of flexibility, over eleven times current national storage capacity. In emergency demand programs it looked cost-competitive, at about half the accepted price of standard storage. Willingness varied widely by region and fell in winter cold. Policy and market design must fit driver behavior, not just battery math, the authors argue.
pmc-13277629:
Xiaohui Ma leads a 2026 review of the JR blood group system, a little-known part of blood typing. Its sole marker, called Jra, sits on a protein named ABCG2 that moves substances across cell walls. The system was formalized in 2012, after the marker itself had been reported decades earlier.

People who lack the marker can form antibodies that cause harm in transfusion and in pregnancy, including anemia and jaundice in newborns. The same protein also affects uric acid handling, which links it to gout, and helps guard the brain and resist some cancer drugs. The review gathers the system's spread, biology, and clinical weight for transfusion and maternity care.
pmc-13278429:
Yeseul Choi leads a 2026 review warning that new fungal threats can emerge from the environment as the climate warms. Most invasive fungal infections once came from a small set of known genera. Warmer conditions may select fungi that tolerate heat, letting soil species survive in human bodies, while more immune-weakened patients raise the stakes.

Candida auris, a drug-resistant yeast that existed in the environment long before its recognition, is the lesson case. A second candidate, Rhodosporidiobolus fluvialis, turned up in blood samples from two severely ill patients in China who died despite antifungal treatment. Finding such fungi early, before wide clinical impact, is the authors' central plea.
pmc-13279329:
Vitaly Ryazanov and colleagues published a 2026 review of microbial community transplantation, moving microbes on purpose to restore balance in a disturbed system. The best-known medical form is fecal microbiota transplantation, used against stubborn Clostridioides difficile gut infection, but the authors range far wider. Their survey covers trials in metabolic and neurological disorders, vaginal microbe transfer, and applications well outside medicine.

In agriculture, researchers engineer soil microbe mixes to protect crops and clean polluted land, and farmers transplant microbes in livestock and even wild species. Fish farms use added microbe mixes to keep fish healthy, while cleanup teams deploy them to restore habitats and polluted land. The authors group these fields under a One Health framework linking people, animals, and nature. They flag open problems around how long effects last, cost, side effects on wildlife, and the lack of standard methods, arguing the strategy is promising but not yet routine.
pmc-13279429:
Yuyang Yuan and Yong Sun published a 2026 review mapping the broad risks artificial intelligence brings to agriculture, using plant protection as their example. Most research celebrates AI's gains in yield and pest control, they argue, while harms accumulate across social, technical, and ecological layers. Their review uses a social-technical-ecological systems framework to organize those harms and each layer's responses.

Social risks include farm job losses, widening inequality, and exclusion of farmers who cannot access the tools. Technical risks range from faulty devices and wrong model decisions to opaque black-box reasoning and network security holes. Ecological risks cover biodiversity loss, uncertain climate effects, and new forms of pollution. Their remedies pair farmer livelihood support and equity with demands for accuracy, transparency, and security in the technology itself, plus biodiversity goals in design. Above all, they urge governance so one layer's gains do not quietly export damage to another.
pmc-13279529:
Carlos V. Serrano and colleagues give a 2026 review of single cell tools in atherosclerosis, the artery clog illness that drives heart attacks. New tools read gene use cell by cell, map open DNA and place cells in tissue space. Past bulk tests ground up whole plaques and hid cell variety. The review sums how these tools redraw plaque biology.

Single cell reads found new states of immune eater cells and of smooth muscle cells that line vessels. They also found worn vessel skin signatures and small clone groups of immune T cells. Joining gene, DNA access, protein and place data traced paths that drive plaque growth. Those paths point to cell exact drug targets. The authors see new markers and more precise tests ahead for artery care.
pmc-13279929: Zewen Zhang and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their Scientific Reports study of Epimedin C, a plant compound, in asthma airway swelling in mice. The error was in figure order: Figure 2 ran as Figure 3, Figure 3 as Figure 5, Figure 5 as Figure 6, and Figure 6 as Figure 2. The notice reprints the four figures in their right order, with captions on lung tissue change, immune cell shifts and the signal path named in the title. No data or findings change.
pmc-13280829:
Rafaella Moreno Barros and colleagues published a 2026 review of natural biopolymers as inks for three-dimensional bioprinting aimed at bone regeneration. Bone can heal itself, but defects larger than about two centimeters or involving more than half the bone's circumference overwhelm that capacity and leave permanent damage. Bioprinting builds scaffolds in layers from cell-laden gels called bioinks. Natural polymers appeal because the body tolerates them, they break down, and they resemble the matrix cells live in.

The review weighs each material on flow, strength after printing, and performance once implanted. Strategies to fix weaknesses include chemical modification of the polymers, blending in nanomaterials, and systems that respond to their surroundings. Obstacles are vascularization, since bone needs blood supply, plus structural stability and immune reactions. The authors frame the field as past proof of concept and now wrestling with the steps that decide whether printed scaffolds reach operating rooms.
pmc-13281329:
Svetlana Novikova and colleagues described a combined heart surgery method in a 2026 report. The patients had both heart chambers failing at an advanced stage. Each got a pump that helps the main heart chamber push blood. At the same time, a new valve was placed through a balloon, with no large chest cut. Sixteen high-risk patients had the paired procedure from 2022 to 2023. Nine had the valve set inside an old fake valve, and seven in their own valve ring.

All sixteen procedures were completed. Blood flow measures stayed steady over time, with no major leaks around the new valves. No valve slipped, clotted, or broke down in the checks. Fifteen of sixteen patients lived past the first month, and three in four lived to one and two years. One patient later got a full heart transplant. The authors call the pairing workable for repeat-surgery patients.
pmc-13281429:
Hanna Holst and colleagues studied team learning in local clinics in a 2026 paper. Health students from unlike fields can train together to learn teamwork. Such training is well studied in hospitals but less in first-line clinics. Thirty-five people took part: fourteen students, sixteen patients, and five supervisors. The team mixed surveys with long talks and read both side by side.

All three groups said team training kept the patient at the center. Students took on more duty step by step as they learned to work across fields. Supervisors found they could step back to let students grow more self-reliant. Patients' views, the team found, pushed students toward whole-person care. The authors say first-line clinics are rich ground for team training. They argue it can raise care quality where most people first seek help.
pmc-13281929:
Shota Inoue and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a man with Takayasu arteritis, a rare inflammation of the aorta and its branches that usually strikes young women. He survived two false aneurysms. The 20-year-old arrived with fever, cough, and coughing blood. Scans showed a 57 millimeter pseudoaneurysm of the ascending aorta pressing on the pulmonary artery. He underwent replacement of the aortic arch; tissue examination then confirmed the arteritis diagnosis.

He went home on day thirteen, only to return six days later with fever, fatigue, and back pain. Imaging found a second pseudoaneurysm where a graft branch had been sewn to the carotid artery, a failure the authors link to still-inflamed tissue. A catheter-placed stent graft sealed it. Steroid treatment began the next day, and he moved to rheumatology care two weeks later. The case argues for fast surgery and early inflammation control.
pmc-13282129:
Mashael S Mahnashi and co-authors present a 2026 case report and literature review on a fluid-filled growth in a child's neck that appeared later than usual. Such growths, called lymphatic malformations, are present from birth. They stem from faulty lymph vessels, the channels that drain tissue fluid. Most show at birth or in early childhood. Their patient was a seven-year-old girl with a painless swelling on the left side of her neck.

The swelling had grown over nine months, without infection or injury before it. Examination found a soft mass that could be pressed in, at the back of the neck. Magnetic scans showed a many-chambered cystic lesion matching the large-cyst type. Surgery removed it, tissue tests confirmed the diagnosis, and recovery went smoothly. The authors remind doctors to consider this birth lesion in school-age children too.
pmc-13282329:
Clara Luna Marina and co-authors present a 2026 study comparing tiny cell packets in the blood of young and senior dogs. The packets, extracellular vesicles, carry proteins and small RNAs between cells and may mark ageing. The team drew blood from twenty-four healthy dogs in Brazil's Federal District. They isolated the packets by spinning and filtering, then measured their number, size, shape, and cargo.

Senior dogs produced fewer packets, and theirs varied more in size, with a larger share of big ones. Total protein and fat content per volume of blood fell with age. Yet fat per packet rose, suggesting the packets' makeup is remodelled over life. Levels of several small RNAs also fell, two of them markedly. The authors say these stable blood changes could help study age-related disease in dogs, a species that ages alongside its owners.
pmc-13282429:
Leyla Noroozbabaee and co-authors describe a 2026 modelling study of salt and water transport in the kidney's proximal tubule, using an energy-based method called bond graphs. The proximal tubule is the first reabsorbing stretch of the kidney's filtering units. Bond graphs map energy exchange across domains in one consistent scheme. The team built membrane and compartment modules and coupled them into a full model.

Their model holds four fluid compartments bounded by five membranes. It tracks five chemical species, including sodium, potassium, and glucose, and six key membrane transporters. A new step treats fluid volume itself as a model variable, letting volume changes feed back on transporter activity, as happens in the real tubule. Each process respects thermodynamics, the rules of energy balance. The authors released the model as open-source software. They present it as a flexible base for virtual experiments on kidney transport.
pmc-13282529:
Jane Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 arts-based report on heart health experiences in the Moosonee community in Ontario, made with Indigenous partners. Indigenous people in Canada face far higher cardiovascular disease rates than the general population, alongside colonial legacies. The team held a sharing circle in Moosonee to learn how culturally safe care access could improve. They used two-eyed seeing, a framework that holds Indigenous and Western knowledge together.

Four themes emerged: heart health is more than metrics; honouring traumas; removing stigma through relationship building; and solutions starting with the community. Community insights were transformed into a graphic report, honouring storytelling as a way to preserve knowledge and foster healing. The authors describe storytelling as shifting power, letting community members speak in their own voices within systems that have silenced them. The report models partnership between a Toronto health network and the regional Indigenous health authority.
pmc-13283329:
A cattle abortion parasite both triggers and suffers from a host danger sensor, Mengge Chen's mouse experiments show in 2026. The parasite is Neospora caninum, a major cause of cattle loss worldwide. No good drug or vaccine exists, so host defense paths matter greatly.

Mouse immune cells were infected to study a danger sensor called AIM2. Infection raised sensor levels, cell death, and release of a key inflammation signal. A binding protein called GBP5 proved vital for full sensor firing. Mice lacking AIM2 held more parasites but survived better in the tests. Less inflammation cut tissue harm even as parasite control fell. Defense strength and disease harm must be balanced.
pmc-13283829:
Antimo Cutone, Giusi Ianiro, and Claudia Fiorillo introduced in 2026 a journal research collection on iron gone wrong in the body. Iron is vital for DNA building, nerve insulation, and cell energy, yet loose iron sparks harmful oxygen reactions that damage fats and feed inflammation. The editorial frames iron dysregulation as a pathogenic amplifier that turns local metabolic trouble into spreading damage.

Five studies make up the collection, three research papers and two reviews. In acute settings, a form of iron-driven cell death called ferroptosis drives injury after stroke and in damaged lungs, and the pieces name marker proteins and protective compounds. In chronic disease, iron imbalance feeds slow, progressive harm. The editors argue the field has moved from scattered findings to one joined framework.
pmc-13284429:
F. Berglund and co-authors test an online therapy for prolonged grief in a 2026 Swedish feasibility study. Grief-focused cognitive behavioural therapy can help after a death, yet proven options remain scarce in Swedish care. The team offered eight weeks of internet-delivered therapy to 14 adults who met criteria for probable prolonged grief disorder.

Ten people finished post-treatment talks and surveys, and most found the program helpful and moving, with broad satisfaction reported by the authors. Scores for grief, trauma stress, and depression fell through follow-up at four months, though the small group limits firm claims. The authors say a larger randomized trial is now needed to test whether the therapy truly works.
pmc-13285029:
Awadh M. Alahmari and colleagues compare stroke patients in a Saudi National Guard community across two eras roughly thirty years apart. Their 2026 study draws on registry records from 2013 to 2024 and on older published data from 1982 to 1992. Care, scanning technology, and the population itself all changed greatly between those periods.

The modern group held 3,436 patients, against 500 in the earlier group. Death after stroke fell sharply, and bleeding strokes became less common. Meanwhile high blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking all rose markedly among patients. Because the data sources differ, the authors treat comparisons cautiously. They argue that prevention aimed at metabolic risks deserves urgent attention.
pmc-13285829:
Dmitry Kobylkov and Giorgio Vallortigara explore the brain basis of a built-in pull toward upward motion in a 2026 study of young chicks. Living things can move against gravity, while loose objects only fall, so upward motion serves as a cue for life. New chicks turn toward such motion without any training, and the team hunted for the neurons behind that pull.

Electrodes in a higher brain region, the nidopallium, recorded from chicks one week old while cameras and motion sensors tracked their gaze. Most direction-tuned neurons in that region favored upward motion over downward motion. Group activity from those neurons also matched what each chick did next, beat by beat. The match ties a basic survival skill, spotting living things, to a clear signal in the young brain.
pmc-13285929:
Eleftherios Mylonakis leads a 2026 follow-up analysis of antibody treatment timing in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. The drug pair casirivimab and imdevimab had already helped patients who lacked their own antibodies. This study asked whether days from first symptoms to the single infusion changed the odds of death or a breathing machine.

The data came from a large placebo-controlled trial run across six countries during 2020 and 2021. Patients treated within four days of symptom start fared better than those treated later, after age and other factors were counted. The timing edge looked strongest in patients aged 50 to 70, while older age itself raised risk in every group. One wider test set showed the same lean with weaker force, which keeps early dosing as the safer bet.
pmc-13286229:
Daniela Coutiño leads a 2026 brain imaging study of glaucoma damage along the visual pathway. Standard diffusion scans blur spots where nerve bundles cross, which can hide or fake injury in the optic chiasm. Patients whose two eyes suffered uneven glaucoma damage offered a built-in test bed for sharper methods that split crossing bundles apart.

Scans covered 31 patients and 31 healthy peers with four grades of diffusion analysis, from basic to bundle-splitting. Every method found altered tissue signals in the nerve, chiasm, tracts, and radiations of the visual system. The sharper measures also tracked eye clinic readings such as nerve layer thickness and field loss from the worse eye. The team reads the match as proof that bundle-wise scans can follow this slow, spreading decay in living patients.
pmc-13286329:
Femke Groen and a broad Dutch team lay out a study protocol for timing self-care advice in joint wear in a 2026 design article. Guidelines urge education and self-care before surgery for hip and knee osteoarthritis, but generic apps rarely stick. Their e-cOAch study will build data-driven models that pick both the moment and the flavor of advice for each person. Programs cover activity, sleep, and weight, with a no-program period as the yardstick.

Six hundred Dutch adults will rotate through all three programs plus the control stretch, each lasting twelve weeks in random order. App check-ins every two weeks feed forecasts of drops in daily physical function. Funding landed in 2023, and 520 volunteers had signed up by submission. The models are destined for a smarter second version of the app, tuned for users with low digital skills as well.
pmc-13286429:
Mauricio E Perez Pachon and Alfredo E Hoyos Ariza challenge a safety study of a rib-reshaping technique in a 2026 letter to the editor. The RibXcar procedure sculpts ribs with an ultrasonic tool, and the original article claimed a favorable safety profile from a survey of 113 plastic surgeons. The letter writers argue the design cannot carry that claim: a recall-prone survey is not a complications analysis.

Their arithmetic disputes the headline numbers directly. Adding the major events in the published table yields about 9%, not the 2.6% the text calls low, and percentages leave nearly 1% unaccounted. With every respondent using the same tool, no comparison statistics were even possible, they note. Aesthetic success claims rest on surgeon self-report without patient measures. They ask the journal for a rebuttal or a correction with honest denominators.
pmc-13286829:
Molly Ahern and co-authors gather trial evidence on whether eating fish improves children's micronutrient status. Their 2026 systematic review searched three databases for studies of children aged two to fourteen comparing fish eaters with low or non-fish eaters using blood or urine markers. Seven studies qualified, six of them randomized trials, covering nine nutrients.

Only vitamin D could be pooled across studies, and fish eaters showed a modest advantage in over a thousand children. Results for iodine, iron stores, hemoglobin, vitamin A, calcium, and B vitamins were mostly flat or inconsistent. Study quality varied. The authors judge the vitamin D gain possibly too small to matter clinically and call for stronger trials on the other nutrients.
pmc-13286929:
Baohong Lu and co-authors model how a university teacher's personality relates to how engaged their students are in class. The 2026 study surveyed 154 teachers across China with standard questionnaires on the Big Five traits, emotion regulation habits, and perceived classroom engagement. Whether students lean in may depend partly on who stands at the front.

Personality as a whole predicted engagement strongly, and openness to experience carried the heaviest weight in the model. Emotion regulation carried about a third of the personality effect, acting as a bridge between stable traits and classroom outcomes. Handling emotions by rethinking situations looked especially valuable. Training teachers in emotion management, the authors suggest, could lift engagement.
pmc-13287129:
Ahmed Abdelsamad and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026 comparing two keyhole approaches to removing part of the pancreas and duodenum. Their question was how surgeon experience, gained case by case, changes results for robot-assisted work versus standard laparoscopy.

Pooling 25 studies, with 20 used for pooled numbers covering 4,764 patients, the authors report that both routes need a similar number of cases before performance steadies. Outcomes improved in later practice, with shorter operations and fewer leaks and conversions. Robot work showed a few early-phase advantages, but the authors conclude that broad superiority is not supported.
pmc-13287529:
Yingtong Xu and co-authors report a 2026 study that sorts out eleven variants in the CYP21A2 gene. Changes in this gene cause most cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a hormone disorder present from birth. Many rare variants carry an uncertain label, which leaves families and doctors unsure what they mean. The team combined population data, protein structure models, and lab tests in human cells.

Two variants behaved like common harmless changes, and two more looked likely harmless. Three variants cut enzyme activity below 20 percent and were classed as disease-causing. Three others kept about 40 to 45 percent of normal activity, fitting a milder form of the disorder. Structure models showed how the harmful changes block the enzyme or break its partner contacts. The results give clinics a clearer map for reading test results.
pmc-13287829:
Anna Blach and colleagues report in 2026 a woman aged 25 who first arrived with sudden mental symptoms and was treated for a presumed mental illness. Her state then worsened. Spinal fluid tests found antibodies against the NMDA receptor, a severe immune brain condition, and scans showed growths on both ovaries called teratomas.

She also carried a strep throat infection at the same time. Care combined antibody infusions, high-dose steroids, removal of both ovarian growths, and plasma washing. She improved and left hospital after a long stay. The authors stress pelvic scanning and infection checks in young women with sudden mental symptoms and decline.
pmc-13288029: Pablo S Paolinelli and co-authors issued this 2026 correction for their article on access to molecular studies in gliomas in low-resource countries. The notice is a correction only, replacing a wrong funding statement and adding no new research content. The corrected statement says Servier Argentina paid the article processing charge. It also says the funder played no part in design, data work, writing, or the choice to publish. The original article has been updated to match.
pmc-13289029:
Rong Mu and colleagues map the partner proteins of a bacterial signal-making enzyme in a 2026 study. The enzyme DacA builds c-di-AMP, a messenger that many gram-positive bacteria cannot live without. Known regulators were few, so the team fished for partners in Streptococcus mutans, a tooth decay bacterium. Pull-down tests plus mass spectrometry produced candidate lists under two conditions. Six candidates appeared in both lists.

Modeling and a split-luciferase test confirmed one partner, a likely calcium transporter called SMU_723. Three amino acids at the contact surface proved key, since changing them broke the binding. Breaking the partnership lowered messenger levels inside the cells. Bacteria missing the transporter copied several traits of bacteria missing the enzyme, though in milder form. Those traits included slow starts, weak acid handling, and poor colonization in a fly model. The link ties calcium balance to signal control.
pmc-13289929:
Jiaxin Peng, Jing Chen, Zhipu Qian, Mingzhang Han, and Ling Chen test a 2026 dietary compound, ergothioneine, for slowing the slide from acute kidney injury to chronic kidney disease. Acute injury often seems to heal, yet many patients drift into lasting damage and scarring. A cisplatin mouse model that mimics that slide was used, with compound treatment, tissue review, blood tests, and single-cell gene reading.

Treated kidneys showed better function numbers and less injury and scarring under the microscope. Gene patterns in tubule cells moved partly back toward normal, with energy pathways in mitochondria recovering ground. Lab tubule cells also kept more energy and membrane strength with less oxidative harm. Mitochondrial protection anchors the proposed benefit.
pmc-13290129:
Rihua Xu and co-authors compare a flipping technique for fibroid removal through the vagina in a 2026 study. The approach, called vNOTES, operates through a natural opening and leaves no belly scars. Large or high fibroids near the top of the uterus are hard to reach that way. The flipping method turns the uterus to bring those fibroids into view. Records covered 42 flipping cases and 46 standard cases at two hospitals.

All operations in both groups finished successfully. The flipping group actually handled bigger uteruses and removed more fibroids, including ones at the fundus. That reach cost longer operating time and greater blood loss. Catheters also stayed in longer after flipping procedures. Pain stayed low and scars absent, matching the standard approach's known benefits. The authors conclude that flipping widens which fibroids this scar-free route can treat. Case selection should balance reach against bleeding risk.
pmc-13290629:
Sleep trouble, anxiety, and loneliness in older adults form one tangled web rather than three separate problems, Xiaonan Li and Lin Mao show in a 2026 network analysis from Nanchong, China. They mapped symptom-level links in community-dwelling elders to find which symptoms hold the web together.

A total of 1,637 older adults completed sleep, anxiety, and loneliness scales. Nearly all symptoms correlated positively, and the network's core nodes were two sleep items and one anxiety item, while bridge symptoms connecting the clusters again mixed sleep and loneliness items. A Bayesian network put one loneliness item at the top, pointing toward ten others, and men's and women's networks did not differ significantly. Li and Mao propose the core and bridge symptoms as the smartest targets for combined prevention.
pmc-13290729:
Printing living scaffolds from hydrogels has matured into a toolbox with clear trade-offs, Chao-Ming Su and colleagues review in 2026. Their survey covers two decades of 3D bioprinting for tissue engineering, with landmark earlier work added for context.

The authors compare light-based, extrusion-based, and inkjet printing on resolution, fidelity, material range, and cell friendliness. Natural and synthetic hydrogels play complementary parts, one bringing biological activity, the other printability and strength. Newer tough and composite designs, from double networks to nanocomposite reinforcement and gradient structures, aim to fix the classic weakness of printed gels. Applications now span wound healing, cartilage and bone repair, and vascularized tissue, while scale-up, blood supply, reproducibility, and regulation remain the gates to the clinic.
pmc-13290829:
A cheap lab model of Alzheimer's cholinergic loss gets a tuned recipe from Muhammad-Safuan Zainuddin and colleagues in 2026. Human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells can be coaxed into neuron-like cells with retinoic acid, but few published protocols actually produce the cholinergic traits that define the disease's target neurons.

The team first reviewed 23 such studies from 2000 to 2025 and found only about 30% even reported cholinergic markers. They then tested a simplified acid-only protocol across serum levels and durations. Seven days at 10 micromolar retinoic acid with 1% serum gave the strongest result: mature shapes, long branched neurites, and raised activity of the enzymes ChAT and AChE. Zainuddin and colleagues offer the setup as a low-cost first-pass platform for screening Alzheimer's stressors and drugs.
pmc-13290929:
Caring for a child with disability measurably dents caregivers' own quality of life in Australia, Benojir Ahammed and colleagues find in a nationwide study from 2026. Using Longitudinal Study of Australian Children data, they linked children's disability profile, its type, count, and mix, to caregivers' health-related quality of life scores.

A quarter of children had at least one disability. Their caregivers scored significantly lower on overall quality of life than other caregivers, and lower on both physical and psychological summary dimensions, even after income and background adjustments. Physical, sensory, and mental-health disabilities, and having several at once, each tracked with lower caregiver scores. Ahammed and colleagues argue support services should target these families first, and their numbers can feed value-for-money studies of caregiver programs.
pmc-13291129:
Garlic and its active compounds get a careful look as helpers against age-linked wear of bones, joints, and muscle in a 2026 review led by Nana Cheng. Conditions such as osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, disc degeneration, and muscle loss are rising as populations age, and standard drugs often ease symptoms while adding side effects and failing to reverse damage.

Compounds in garlic, including allicin and several sulfur-bearing molecules, show anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions in the studies gathered here. They also tune key cell pathways that govern bone turnover, cartilage balance, and muscle upkeep, which in turn slowed disease progress in many reports. The authors frame garlic compounds as a base for add-on treatments, while the evidence base still needs stronger human trials.
pmc-13291729:
Yanmao Wang and co-authors test a digital training system for stiff elbows after surgery, in a 2026 trial. Patients had arthroscopic release for post-traumatic elbow contracture at a Shanghai hospital. One group trained for twelve weeks through a digital platform with tailored exercises and teaching videos. The other group trained conventionally with physiotherapists in outpatient clinics. Elbow range of motion at twelve weeks was the main outcome.

Patient-rated arm function, pain, and quality of life scores were equivalent too. Nearly everyone finished the program in both arms, and adverse event rates were similar. Digital care cost about 7,400 yuan less per patient on average. The authors call the system a viable, cheaper alternative for this rehabilitation.
pmc-13292329:
Miranti Pangastuti and a large team present a 2026 case series on pemphigus foliaceus wearing an unusual disguise: pus-filled lesions instead of the classic erosions, scales, and crusts. Only two such patients appeared across twelve years at their service. One was an 18-year-old Sundanese woman, the other a 57-year-old Javanese man, and both showed heavy neutrophil infiltration under the microscope.

Direct immunofluorescence settled the diagnosis by revealing IgG deposits between the skin cells in both patients. The young woman improved on cyclophosphamide at 100 mg daily. The man failed sulfasalazine, then improved on corticosteroids with azathioprine plus psychotherapy. The authors warn that pustular breakouts can hide this immune blistering disease and urge the fluorescence test when the picture misleads.
pmc-13292429:
Victoria H Arrandale and co-authors pool a 2026 systematic review and meta-analyses on workplace vapors, gases, dusts, and fumes as causes of chronic lung disease. An earlier thoracic society statement blamed work exposures for 13 to 15 percent of COPD. Searching five databases through February 2025, the team kept studies with at least fifteen exposed cases and a comparison group.

Exposed workers showed consistently higher risk: pooled estimates of 1.51 for spirometry-defined COPD and 1.83 for chronic bronchitis in the combined results. The link ran slightly stronger in non-smokers and weaker among women. The authors conclude workplace exposure adds to smoking's harm rather than merely overlapping it.
pmc-13292829: Ahmet Eken and co-authors published a correction in 2026 to their review on inherited immune flaws in the LCK gene and T cell signaling. The notice fixes a single drawing error in Figure 2 and leaves the text and findings unchanged. In the first version, a molecule in panel B was labeled as the wrong class, shown as MHC I when it should have been MHC II. The online HTML and PDF files now carry the fixed figure. Only the print copy and early PDF downloads still hold the error.
pmc-13292929:
Patrick Münzer and a large team map, in a 2026 study, how fats in neutrophil membranes change as these immune cells cast out DNA traps. Those traps, called NETs, help fight germs but also drive many diseases.

The team counted 1048 fat species in human neutrophils and watched them shift as trap formation began. Several fat families rose or fell sharply, and two trigger routes for trap release followed distinct paths. pmc-13293229:
Taeyeon Koo and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, how older adults in South Korea view digital health devices. South Korea is aging fast, and such devices promise personal health support, yet uptake among older people stays low.

A total of 349 adults aged 65 and older from welfare and community sites near Seoul answered questions based on an expanded acceptance model. Ten traits were measured, from usefulness and ease to privacy and price concern. The team used component analysis and grouping methods to sort people into shared outlook profiles. Such profiles could help makers and clinics tailor devices to distinct older users.
pmc-13293429:
Jiale He and co-authors run, in a 2026 soil experiment, simulated irrigation to track how arsenic moves in dry farmland soil in Xinjiang, China. Watering with arsenic-rich groundwater can load topsoil with the toxic element over time.

The team varied drying strength, acidity, and salt in the water, then measured arsenic in soil water and on membranes placed in the soil. All three factors shaped arsenic spread in the top 10 centimeters of soil. Weak drying let arsenic travel farther, while higher acidity change and salt pushed it deeper down. Less salty, less alkaline water may keep arsenic near the surface, where risk can be managed.
pmc-13293629:
Kasturi Krishnamoorthy and colleagues describe a puzzling fracture case in a 2026 report: a forty-two-year-old man whose bones broke after a minor fall from standing height. Breaks of that kind in a younger man call for a search for hidden causes. His history held severe depression, alcohol misuse, and long self-neglect, and he arrived underweight, weak, and largely dependent on a wheelchair.

Care brought together bone specialists, dietitians, and psychiatrists, with blood tests confirming serious malnutrition. Treatment with the antidepressant venlafaxine lifted his mood and appetite quickly, and he gained weight and recovered much of his function. A refeeding complication during recovery underlined how depleted he had been. The authors argue that unexplained fragility fractures deserve a whole-person assessment, since treating the underlying driver can change the outcome.
pmc-13293729:
A targeted drug faces a preclinical test by Sarah Ottum and colleagues in 2026 against a rare ovarian cancer that barely answers standard chemotherapy. Low-grade serous ovarian cancer needs new targets, and a surface protein called TROP2 offered a possible entry point.

The drug, datopotamab deruxtecan, curbed tumor growth sharply in a mouse graft model from a heavily treated, drug-resistant patient, with no major toxicity seen. Control mice lived a median of 22 days, while treated mice had not reached that mark by day 50.
pmc-13294229:
Maria Ormhøj leads a 2026 comparison of artificial scaffolds for growing tumor-specific T cells for cell therapy. Scaffolds present antigen plus growth signals outside the body. Growth, killing power, and single-cell profiles were compared head to head.

Gene scores showed stronger cytotoxic programs and weaker dysfunction marks. A favorable cell product profile supports trials of the new scaffold.
pmc-13294329:
Mohamed Zahir Alimohamed and coauthors call for national genome projects across Africa in a 2026 article on genomic equity. African peoples hold the deepest human genetic diversity, yet only 0.15% of genome-wide association participants come from Africa in the cited barometer. Skimpy data weaken disease gene hunting and personalized care both locally and worldwide.

Political, funding, and social hurdles slow progress, alongside stigma and thin public understanding. Skilled scientists and working labs already exist on the continent. Concrete steps cover priority setting, funding, policy alignment, and public engagement, so genome programs serve national health needs rather than imported agendas.
pmc-13294929:
Yu Yamamoto, Hiroshi Mizumoto, and Hiroaki Fukuzawa report severe stomach bleeding in a newborn baby in a 2026 case report. The full-term infant vomited a large amount of fresh blood at just 15 hours old, with no clear risk factors. Gentle measures alone usually settle such bleeding within days.

Bleeding continued despite conservative care, causing shock and anaemia in the baby. A large blood clot inside the stomach made camera inspection unworkable, so surgeons opened the abdomen to stop the bleeding. They found widespread surface damage and several bleeding ulcers, and the baby recovered well after the operation.
pmc-13295229:
Yeo Wool Kim and colleagues map what researchers actually measure when they study health in adults with cerebral palsy, in a 2026 scoping review. Better care has stretched life expectancy for people with this lifelong movement condition, so adult health needs now stretch far beyond childhood services. The team searched nine databases, finishing in May 2025, and sorted every reported outcome into domains, sub-domains, and the instruments used to measure them.

From nearly seventeen thousand records, 159 studies qualified. They covered four domains and sixty-seven distinct outcomes measured with 348 different instruments, a sprawl that makes comparing studies hard. Physical outcomes dominated, while mental, social, and overall well-being drew less attention, and tools designed specifically for cerebral palsy were rare. Most samples skewed young, leaving older adults understudied. The authors urge broader age coverage and shared measurement choices across the field.
pmc-13295329:
Weining Sun and colleagues show how a sulfur-based molecule shields a hardy bacterium from oxidative attack, in a 2026 study of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The germ survives the peroxide bursts that immune cells and its own metabolism throw at it. Sulfur chemistry was suspected in that defense but not proven. The shield is sulfane sulfur, made by an enzyme that handles sulfide.

Bacteria making the sulfur stood up to hydrogen peroxide better, not by mopping the peroxide up, but by tagging cysteine sites on proteins, a change called persulfidation. One target is OxyR, the master switch for antioxidant genes, whose tagged form grips DNA in a new way and turns defenses on. Sulfur signaling, the authors say, quietly runs this germ's antioxidant program.
pmc-13295829:
Noudy Eleryan and colleagues study self-care needs in musicians with playing injuries in a 2026 article. Playing-related muscle and joint problems limit many performers, yet music-specific health support is scarce. An online survey and small focus groups with British musicians explored barriers, helpers, and digital wishes.

One hundred musicians answered the survey and ten joined focus groups. Two thirds kept playing through symptoms, and repeated episodes were common across the group. Poor music-specific teaching during training, cost, and time blocked self-care most. Musicians asked for clinicians who grasp performance demands, tailored advice per instrument, peer support, and digital tools with reminders and tracking.
pmc-13296029:
Evelien B van Kempen and co-authors interview, in 2026, Dutch parents whose young children were admitted with fever from serious bacterial infection. Knowing what finally prompts parents to seek help could improve a planned health app for families.

Fifteen parents described acting when illness looked abnormal, through single alarming signs such as breathing trouble or changed awareness, or through familiar patterns and lingering fever. Many already knew official red-flag symptoms. Work pressures and hard-to-reach GP care sometimes delayed visits. The authors say parent-focused tools should build on what parents notice while easing access barriers.
pmc-13296329:
Katalina Llanos-Azócar and co-authors expose, in 2026, red sea urchins to warmer water to see how heat stress ripples through the animal. Farmed urchins face rising seas, so the team track feeding, gut microbes, DNA damage and gene activity under thermal strain.

Heated urchins lost gut microbe variety while opportunistic bacteria gained ground. DNA damage rose and genes tied to stress, immunity and cell death switched on. The authors say warming disrupts the animal at several levels at once. Knowing the weak points should help farms build hardier urchin production as the climate warms.
pmc-13296629:
Hyung-Suk Yi and colleagues compare three treatments for nipple tissue death after nipple-sparing mastectomy in a 2026 study. Patients using it also reported less pain and greater satisfaction, with the clearest benefit in larger wounds. Average time to starting further therapy shortened, although the share of patients formally delayed did not differ significantly. The authors recommend a larger randomised trial across centres.
pmc-13296929:
Assiya Boltaboyeva and a large team build an explainable machine-learning tool that flags likely sleep disorders at hospital admission in a 2026 study. Sleep apnoea often goes undiagnosed in inpatients, and frailty overlaps with it through shared biology. Their models drew on nearly ten thousand hospital episodes from a public intensive-care database.

Five model types were trained on admission-time information spanning frailty scores, early vital signs, and basic patient details. The strongest performer separated patients with sleep-disorder diagnoses well, catching most true cases in held-out testing. Importance analysis put frailty and overall illness burden at the top, matching the classic apnoea picture. Explainability was a design goal throughout.
pmc-13297029:
Emmeran Bieringer and colleagues use engineered bacteria to turn a sugar acid into mucic acid at high yield in a 2026 biotechnology paper. Mucic acid serves as a chelator and a building block for bio-based polymers. Wild bacteria oxidise the starting material too weakly, so a modified strain carrying an extra enzyme was used.

At a mildly acidic setting, resting cells converted a concentrated feed almost completely within forty-eight hours. Product levels passed one hundred grams per litre, at near-total yield by moles. Simple cooling crystallisation after removing the cells recovered most of the acid at good purity. The authors present the route as a cost-effective, sustainable production option.
pmc-13297129:
Davide Vurro and co-authors print, in 2026, organic memory devices that mimic synapses for brain-like computing, using aerosol jet printing instead of heavy factory methods. Both the active polyaniline ink channel and the conducting electrodes were printed on glass and on flexible film.

Tuned printing gave strong on-off current ratios above a hundred and fast switching, matching on rigid and bendable supports without peeling. Channel thickness and evenness proved decisive for switching behaviour. The authors say the low-waste printing route can scale flexible memory parts for energy-sipping, bio-inspired computing circuits and systems.
pmc-13297929:
Keyhole surgery for deep endometriosis brought lasting gains in daily life, not just pain scores, in a 2026 multicenter study led by Andrei Manu. Records covered 837 patients treated at two referral centers from 2018 to 2024, most with advanced disease, and 39.7% needing part of the bowel removed.
