The team compared dialysis and non dialysis patients treated with a modern balloon valve.

Among 3,189 treated patients, 143 were on dialysis, and matched groups of 139 each were compared. Dialysis patients had far higher five year death rates, with most deaths within three years and over half from non cardiac causes such as infection. Heart failure returns and strokes did not differ clearly. Leaky tricuspid valves flagged higher death risk.
pmc-13311029:
Ke Gao and colleagues design a light vision model for citrus picking robots in a 2026 study. Orchard scenes hide small fruit in clutter, which causes missed picks and false alarms. The team built a detection transformer that fuses traits across scales while staying light for field robots.

A large kernel attention block pulls global, local, and texture cues at once. A linear attention encoder sharpens fruit focus against leaf noise, and a two way pyramid neck joins deep and shallow traits to recover hidden fruit. Against the base model, the design cut millions of parameters and lifted accuracy scores by clear margins on orchard tests.
pmc-13311129:
Mitsuyoshi Abe and colleagues describe in 2026 a brain aneurysm that burst five years after the heart infection suspected of seeding it. A 57-year-old man had earlier suffered streptococcal heart-valve infection with embolic strokes, then received a replacement mitral valve. He now arrived with sudden loss of consciousness and right-sided weakness while on blood thinners.

Scans showed bleeding in the left posterior cerebral artery territory with blood inside the ventricles and fluid build-up in the brain. Angiography found a small aneurysm on a distant branch of that artery, but its vessel was too twisted and narrowed for selective catheter treatment. Surgeons drained the ventricular blood endoscopically, and coils then closed the parent artery segment. No rebleeding followed, though the patient left with severe disability. Such delayed rupture is rare, and blood cultures were negative this time.
pmc-13311329:
Cahyo Budiman and colleagues present a 2026 dataset on how a malaria parasite protein, Pk-FKBP35, binds a tail piece of the heat shock protein Hsp90. The protein is a possible target for new malaria drugs.

Full-length protein and three trimmed versions were made in bacteria and purified. Shape checks confirmed the pieces folded well. Enzyme tests showed the full protein and two versions could twist their target bonds, while one version could not. Surface binding tests measured how tightly each version grips the MEEVD tail piece. The data give drug designers a firm base on this parasite protein.
pmc-13311829:
Josef Finsterer and Claudia Stollberger write a 2026 letter questioning whether e-cigarettes alone explain a young man's brief atrial fibrillation. The case they discuss involved a 26-year-old with dizziness and palpitations after heavy vaping.

The authors list rival triggers that deserve fuller checks, from mineral imbalance and hidden heart defects to thyroid-like states, poor sleep, caffeine, stress, and hard exertion. They also note that vaping can provoke coronary spasm, so artery anomalies merit thought if symptoms return. Genetic causes of the rhythm disorder form a third point. Their message: pin the blame only after the field is cleared.
pmc-13311929:
Alia Jebri and Raja Boussessi describe, in a 2024 letter, a training model for ultrasound-guided sciatic nerve block that costs less than five pounds to build. Novice trainees must practice nerve blocks before touching patients, yet commercial phantoms are expensive, which puts them out of reach in many low-income and middle-income settings. Their substitute uses an opened chicken breast to stand in for the muscles behind the knee.

Ground turkey forms the two nerve branches, wrapped in a glove finger to mimic the nerve sheath, while intravenous tubes filled with ultrasound gel serve as blood vessels. During a session with anesthesia residents, a standard linear probe showed the nerve and its two branches joining, and trainees could watch needle placement in real time. The model survives repeated use across a day, giving teachers a cheap, faithful way to build scanning and needling skill.
pmc-13312529:
Daniel Zarate and colleagues apply, in a 2026 longitudinal study, machine learning to forecast which social media users slide into problematic use. Earlier research on such compulsive engagement had produced inconsistent correlates, so the team let algorithms compete to predict risk over time from a wide pool of personal measures.

Data came from 276 adult users in Australia, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and Canada, scored on the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Random forests beat four rival models at predicting follow-up risk. The strongest signals were the person's own starting addiction score, anxiety including COVID-related anxiety, low agreeableness, and disengagement coping such as avoidance and escapism. The authors argue that early symptoms, persistent anxiety, and unhelpful coping keep problematic use going, and that interventions should target those levers.
pmc-13312829:
Dongyan Ding and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, breathed-in bacteriophage endolysins as a fresh weapon against drug-resistant lung infections. These infections kill at high rates, especially hospital-acquired pneumonia, and the antibiotic pipeline has stalled. Endolysins, the enzymes phages use to burst bacterial walls, kill quickly and rarely breed resistance.

The review covers the major resistant lung germs, from Staphylococcus aureus to Klebsiella pneumoniae. It covers how endolysins work, how they amplify antibiotics, and how they chew through biofilms. Given by inhaler, the enzymes reach high levels right where the infection sits, clearing bacteria in animal pneumonia models with little body-wide harm. The authors flag stability and production scale as the remaining hurdles, and argue that better aerosol systems could make endolysins a standard partner or stand-in for failing antibiotics.
pmc-13313229:
Sherjeel Hashmat leads a 2026 field study on whether a helpful bacterium can shield pea crops from cadmium, a toxic metal that fouls farm soils. Cadmium breaks plant signals, cuts nutrient flow, weakens green pigment making, and harms the use of light for growth.

Peas faced cadmium at 250 and 500 micromolar doses, levels tied to real polluted fields, with or without the bacterium Acinetobacter schindleri strain SR-5-1. Poisoned plants showed lost green pigment, high stress markers, and poor nutrient signals. Plants given the bacterium kept more pigment, raised their stress-fighting enzymes, and showed less fat damage in cells. They also took up less cadmium in roots and leaves. The results back microbe seed treatments as a green way to grow food on tainted land.
pmc-13314229:
Yurma Metri and colleagues feed, in a 2026 trial, thin-tailed sheep on combinations of a protein-rich forage shrub and a mushroom-farming waste product. Tithonia diversifolia supplies protein, while fermented oil palm frond baglog, the spent substrate of mushroom cultivation, offers cheap fiber. Sixteen young male sheep were randomized to four diets holding concentrate constant while the shrub and baglog traded places from sixty percent shrub down to twenty.

No diet changed microbial protein synthesis significantly, and rumen conditions stayed balanced across groups. The lowest-shrub, highest-baglog diet nevertheless posted the best numbers almost everywhere: the highest microbial nitrogen supply and purine derivative totals, dry matter digestibility of 87.13 percent in the reported results, and the fastest growth at 81.25 grams per day. The authors recommend that mixture as a sustainable ration that converts an agricultural by-product into sheep performance without disturbing rumen fermentation.
pmc-13314329:
Adel S El-Hassanin and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, titanium dioxide nanoparticles as a cleanup agent for soil and water spiked with two ring-shaped aromatic hydrocarbons, naphthalene and phenanthrene. These combustion-born pollutants persist in the environment and threaten health. The team tested the nanoparticles, then dosed contaminated water and soil at three concentrations, with and without sunlight, measuring what gas chromatography said remained.

More catalyst meant more cleanup, even in the dark. In water without light, naphthalene removal climbed from 21 percent at the lowest dose to 92 percent at the highest. In soil, the second pollutant's removal rose from 44.63 percent to 73.53 percent across the dose ladder in the reported figures. Performance depended on light availability, catalyst dose, and which pollutant was targeted. The authors claim the first demonstration that modest, safe nanoparticle doses can remediate even subsurface soil, where sunlight-driven methods usually fail, at low cost.
pmc-13314729:
Liang Zhao and co-authors report two cases of a stripe-like skin rash arising during biologic therapy, in a letter published in 2026. Lichen striatus is a line-shaped rash of unknown cause, with bumps that follow Blaschko lines on one side of the body.

As biologic drugs spread in immune diseases, such rashes may follow them. The first case was a 20-year-old man with severe eczema for over 10 years. His skin cleared fully within 3 months on dupilumab, a drug that blocks the IL-4 and IL-13 path, by the times given in the report. Four months later, quiet red bumps rose on his left forearm. Tissue study showed mild surface thickening, dead surface cells, and immune cells around upper skin vessels, with no mouth or nail disease. Paired with a second case and past reports, the letter warns skin doctors to watch for this pattern.
pmc-13315529:
Nahla Ennejjari and a large team report in 2026 a case of autoimmune pancreatitis appearing in several separate spots, with loss of pancreatic function and raised pressure in one vein segment. They also review published work on this uncommon pattern of the disease.

Autoimmune pancreatitis comes in two types, one tied to IgG4-related disease and one more limited to the pancreas and often linked with bowel inflammation. Diagnosis rests on tissue, scans, blood tests, other organ signs, and response to steroids. Multi-spot disease is hard to spot because scans can look much like pancreatic cancer, so careful checks matter before treatment is chosen.
pmc-13315629:
Adrien Paschier and colleagues compared eye antiseptics in the lab in 2026 for killing germs tied to conjunctivitis and lid inflammation. Propamidine 0.1 percent was tested against hexamidine, cethexonium bromide, and picloxydine on five Gram-positive bacterial strains at set contact times from 2 to 15 minutes.

All products killed bacteria, with strength varying by strain and time. Propamidine acted fast, reaching its peak reduction within two minutes against Staphylococcus epidermidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Propionibacterium acnes. A drop of more than five log units counted as bactericidal. Such speed data can guide choice of antiseptic before eye care or surgery.
pmc-13315729:
Mingjun Ma and a very large team show in 2026 how the gene regulator EZH2 creates a cholesterol weakness in ovarian cancer that a drug can hit. Ovarian cancer is the deadliest gynecologic cancer, mostly through spread, and EZH2 is often raised in tumors and tied to metabolic change.

High EZH2 levels marked both primary and spread tumors and tracked with poor outlook. Silencing EZH2 cut tumor growth and spread. The regulator switched on an NF-kappaB and Rap1A path and reset cholesterol handling through SREBP2 and TMED10. The team then identified napabucasin as a compound that exploits this metabolic dependence to suppress spread.
pmc-13316429:
Erhan Yarar sets out a 2026 framework paper on how cell membranes may shape joint signaling among three receptor families: cannabinoid receptors, smell receptors found outside the nose, and TRP channels. The core claim is cautious: shared presence in a membrane patch does not prove true higher-order teamwork.

His method, named MECS-BER, locks one membrane starting state, one near outcome, and one three-part assembly before any test begins. Gates check that each arm is engaged, and a statistic called kappa tests whether a three-way effect beats pair-only math. Practice matrices and simulations prove the logic works, but real biology verdicts await full datasets. Kidney niches are sketched as first test grounds, with no assembly claimed as proven.
pmc-13317029:
Érica Torres de Almeida Piovesan and co-authors link, in a 2026 Brazilian study, town-level dental service coverage with oral health in five-year-olds. Data came from the national oral health survey SB Brasil 2023, merged with town coverage records over time.

Towns fell into four coverage paths, from always-low to always-high. Children in towns with medium-high or medium-low coverage had lower odds of the painful fallout of untreated decay than those in always-low towns, with odds ratios of 0.59 and 0.63 in the adjusted models. Always-high towns showed the lowest odds of needing urgent care. About eighteen percent of child differences traced to town gaps, backing wider public dental coverage.
pmc-13317929:
Kiruthiga K and colleagues present, in 2026, a small pilot study of immune cells inside womb cancers. Tumour-associated macrophages can shape how a cancer behaves, and their location within the tumour may carry meaning. The team used a marker called CD68 to highlight these cells.

Seven stored tissue samples from a medical college in India, collected during 2024, were stained and examined. Patients averaged about 63 years, and the endometrioid subtype was most common. Macrophages clustered mainly in the supporting stroma, with fewer inside the tumour or at its invasive edge. No link appeared between cell location and tumour grade or stage. The authors recommend larger studies with extra markers before drawing conclusions about prognosis.
pmc-13320029:
Omer Mohammed and co-authors pool studies on a sugar lowering drug class after valve repair in a 2026 review. A new heart valve placed through a leg vessel fixes a tight valve, yet heart failure risk and other harms linger after the fix. Whether the drug class, first built for diabetes, also guards these patients was the question.

Six studies with 35075 patients in total, one trial and five records studies, were pooled with checks for bias. Drug use tracked with lower rates of major heart events, heart failure hospital stays, and death from any cause in the pooled counts. Proof grades stayed low, though, due to mixed study types. A firm trial is needed to settle whether the gain is real.
pmc-13320329:
Shohei Okusa and co-authors survey drooling in Parkinson disease at a Tokyo hospital in a 2026 study of body system burden. Extra saliva pooling is common in this illness yet poorly tied to gut, bladder, and swallow faults in past work, and few patients know shots exist that can dry the flow. Forms plus records for clinic patients over three months in late 2025 gave the data.

Among 208 patients, 116 met the study mark for drooling, and they skewed male with longer illness and higher drug doses. Drooling tracked solo with both body system scores and swallow scores after wide checks. Yet only about a third of droolers saw it as a problem, and very few knew of the shot option. Three drooler types split by burden level may guide tailored care.
pmc-13320429:
Yusuke Ota and co-authors grow slime films inside hospital waste water in place in a 2026 study of drug resistance. Hospital drains are feared as hot spots where germs trade drug proof genes, yet the live part those films play was ill defined. Films grown in real drain flow were read by gene scans, voice scans, and culture next to the free floating water crowd.

Films held more mass and more of a key drug proof gut germ than the water itself, and they packed a wider set of top tier proof genes. Transfer ready gene carriers ran hot in films and voiced more there too. Culture proof of a feared proof gene showed in four film strains and one water strain. Films act as stores that may seed spread.
pmc-13321029:
Valentina Mastrorilli and a large team test a paired treatment for long standing spinal cord injury in a 2026 animal study. Injury leaves lasting inflammation, scar glial growth, neuron loss, and myelin damage, causing weakness and nerve pain. Botulinum toxin type A eased harm in early injury, but its value in the chronic phase was untested.

Mice with severe chest level injury received electrical muscle stimulation on a set schedule, then a single spinal dose of toxin or salt water 15 days after injury. Recovery was tracked for up to 60 days, along with nerve pain and tissue measures for glial shape, neuron survival, and myelin proteins. Milder injury groups were also included to judge breadth.
pmc-13322829:
Siyuan Yang, Lei Wang and Jianyun Nie examine mitochondria as a treatment target in triple-negative breast cancer, in a 2026 article. This cancer type lacks the three usual receptors, spreads early and often resists standard drugs, leaving few targeted options.

Mitochondria help drive growth, spread and drug resistance by running several fuel pathways at once, covering oxygen use, fat burning and glutamine use. Their division, fusion and recycling also shape whether tumour cells live or die, and they influence immune responses and cell death routes. The authors weigh small drugs, nano-scale delivery and drug pairs against these weak points, while noting problems of selectivity, flexible metabolism and slow progress into clinic use.
pmc-13322929:
Haoran Gao and colleagues compare two endoscopic routes for broad-based lumbar disc herniation, in a 2026 retrospective study. Records cover 184 patients with single-level disease treated between June 2023 and October 2024, split between the transforaminal route and the interlaminar route, with the same mecobalamin regimen after surgery.

Pain scores at three months formed the main outcome, alongside disability scores, operating measures and complications. The interlaminar group had lower pain at three months and lower disability at three days, plus shorter operations, fewer X-ray checks and more disc material removed. Nerve function improved in both groups without a clear gap, and overall success and complication rates were alike.
pmc-13323029:
Yaoqiang Zhu and co-authors test treated fishpond sediment as a cleaner for metal-contaminated soil, in a 2026 plant study with spinach. Soil carried chromium, copper and zinc together, and amendments included plain sediment and sediment carrying zinc oxide or silica nanoparticles.

Both plain and treated sediments cut the share of each metal that plants could take up, with the zinc oxide version working best in their measures. Metal levels in roots and shoots fell, while photosynthesis and chlorophyll improved and stress signals eased. The authors infer that root uptake control linked to cytoskeleton-related processes may take part, though they relied on indirect signs rather than direct cell images.
pmc-13323229:
Jorge Robalino-Diaz and co-authors study how uneven data across sites weakens federated anomaly detection, in a 2026 analysis of Internet of Things and medical device networks. Training without centralising data protects privacy, yet sites differ strongly in what their sensors record.

Their hybrid dataset held 71,980 behaviour traces drawn from three public sources, with 22,698 traces used for testing. A central model scored near-perfect detection, while the federated version kept high overall discrimination but missed many true anomalies, with recall falling hardest in medical device data. Calibration also worsened. The authors warn that a strong headline score can hide failure where detection matters most, in clinical settings.
pmc-13323329:
Liping Li, Zhonghua Zhang and Lin Zong survey artificial intelligence in neurovascular surgery, in a 2026 narrative review spanning diagnosis, intervention and long-term prediction. Tools covered include machine learning, deep learning, computer vision and language processing applied to scans, records and operating room inputs.

Algorithms help spot large vessel blockages, describe aneurysm shape and separate bleeding types with speed and precision. Models also predict rupture risk, stroke recovery and complications after treatment. Surgical uses run from planning simulations to robot-assisted work and live guidance, though most operating room studies stay early or single-centre. Bias, weak general reach, opacity, privacy and regulation remain the main barriers the authors list.
pmc-13323729:
Deng and coauthors link a brain gene to anxiety-like acts in mice. Anxiety is marked by high stress response and poor mood control. Brain zones and stress hormones both help set anxiety levels. The gene at issue is full in the brain and shapes nerve growth.

Mice that lack the gene in the brain showed clear shifts. Young mice grew stray starter cells in a key memory zone. New nerve cell growth in that zone fell in adults. Adult mice acted more anxious but learned at a normal pace. Old mice stayed anxious and also learned less well.
pmc-13323929:
Christos Savvidis and Ioannis Ilias write a 2026 letter to the editor on clock and microbe misalignment in fatty liver disease. They respond to work by Rusman and others on gut microbes in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, published in the World Journal of Experimental Medicine.

Beyond which microbes live in the gut, timing matters: the gut-liver axis runs on daily rhythms shared between host clocks and microbes. Social jetlag scrambles metabolite timing, weakens the gut barrier and worsens liver injury in their account, with bile acid signalling knocked off rhythm. Time-restricted eating heads the clock-based fixes they cite, said to reprogramme liver gene activity and cut liver fat.
pmc-13324129:
Changhao Le and co-authors compare brain responses under two robot-assisted therapy modes after stroke, in a 2026 study using near-infrared brain imaging. The study enrolled 23 chronic stroke patients and the same number of matched healthy controls, who performed upper limb tasks in active movement mode and mirror therapy mode.

A 48-channel system tracked activation across frontal, motor and sensory areas, plus hemisphere balance and resting connections with eyes open and closed. Both groups activated widely under both modes in the reported tests, with task effects in the target regions. Activation levels were set against arm function scores to probe brain-behaviour links. The authors aim to guide which robot mode suits which stage of stroke recovery.
pmc-13324629:
Subrahmanian Sathiavageesan and team compared two antigenic variants of membranous nephropathy head to head for the first time. Their 2026 retrospective cohort contrasted 17 patients with NELL1-linked disease against 24 with PLA2R-linked disease diagnosed in the same period, using time-to-event analysis with remission, complete or partial, as the primary outcome. PLA2R disease is the most common variant, followed by NELL1, yet direct outcome comparisons had been few.

NELL1 disease carried a favorable prognosis: higher remission rates, faster time to remission, more spontaneous remission, and less treatment-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Prior exposure to usual indigenous medicines was more common in the NELL1 group, a link the authors note for further study. They argue that antigen-specific outcome research can sharpen prognosis and guide treatment choices in membranous nephropathy, rather than treating all variants alike.
pmc-13326429:
Xu Zhu and co-authors simulate spine straightening surgery for severe ankylosing spondylitis kyphosis in a 2026 modeling study. Choosing which vertebra to cut changes the loads on screws and cages, and a wrong pick risks hardware failure.

Finite element models cut at T12, L1, L2, or L3, each with screw-rod fixation and a fusion cage. Total shift fell step by step down the spine, from 6.88 mm at T12 to 2.26 mm at L3 in the models. Peak screw stress peaked at L2, near 191.35 MPa, yet stayed under device limits throughout. The L3 cut gave the steadiest build with well-spread stress. One case fed the model, so wider checks are needed.
pmc-13326629:
Fabian Kerwagen, Maximilian Bauser, and Stefan Störk write a 2026 editorial on hearing congestion in heart failure through the voice. Fluid buildup drives hospital returns, yet symptoms and weight checks catch its shifts poorly.

The editorial discusses a pilot study by Riehle and colleagues on AI voice analysis in acute heart failure care. Across two centers in Germany and the United States, 79 patients gave daily voice samples until discharge. Their natriuretic peptide levels started high, at 9400 pg per mL, and they shed about 5 kg over a mean stay of 7 days. A learning model told admission from discharge voices. The editors weigh promise against proof still needed.
pmc-13328029:
Peng Dai and co-authors profile acute pancreatitis across three data layers in a 2026 study. The sudden pancreatic inflammation mixes immune turmoil, metabolic rewiring, and gut microbe shifts that single-method studies see only in part. Blood gene activity, plasma metabolites, and stool microbes were measured in 15 patients and 15 matched healthy controls.

Gene profiling found 4,776 altered genes, including 409 immune genes clustered in inflammatory pathways. Metabolite testing found 296 altered compounds. Nine of them separated patients from controls with AUC values above 0.75 in their screen. Microbe makeup and function also shifted clearly. Joint profiling may yield marker panels that sort patients earlier and more sharply.
pmc-13328329:
Nhung Phuong Doan and colleagues explored how death, dying, and the body are perceived in Vietnamese culture. Their 2026 qualitative study sat inside research on minimally invasive tissue sampling in Vietnam. It ran 59 interviews and five focus groups with informants, health professionals, community stakeholders, and bereaved relatives. Western views of death have dominated the literature, leaving a gap in Asian cultural perceptions and their implications for end-of-life practices.

Attitudes varied from acceptance to fear and anxiety when discussing death. A good death was usually seen as dying at home with family near, with no worries or regrets, and keeping the body intact. The body holds sacred meaning and is handled with great care. The authors conclude that death and dying in Vietnamese culture are a communal family affair, and that end-of-life care and tissue sampling must account for cultural aspects to gain acceptability.
pmc-13328629:
Taslima Khanam and co-authors examine privacy risks in shared brain-signal learning in a 2026 study. Brain-computer systems use EEG signals that can reveal personal traits. Federated learning trains models without gathering raw signals in one place, yet attackers may still guess who took part.

The team built a federated motor imagery system and tested four attack types, covering records, features, model updates, and client identity. Plain federated training gave weak protection on its own. Adding differential privacy cut attack success a lot, most of all for update and identity attacks. A strict setting protected best but hurt accuracy. A middle setting gave the best balance, the authors conclude.
pmc-13329229:
Sandeep Dey and co-authors reply in 2026 to a letter about their trial of pain relief for spine fusion surgery. The trial tested ropivacaine alone and with added dexmedetomidine or morphine in back muscles. The reply thanks the letter writer and answers two queries about rescue fentanyl use and pain scoring.

On rescue use, Dey clarifies that fentanyl ran only while pain scores stayed at or above the set limit, and stopped once pain fell below it. Nearly all patients needed rescue at some point, the reply states. On scoring, the authors give time-weighted average pain scores for the three groups and note group differences. The morphine mix group showed the lowest average among the values reported.
pmc-13329329:
Ke-Yun Chao and a large team compare three tools for Chinese to Japanese translation in clinic visits in a 2026 study. Language gaps can harm safety and fairness when skilled interpreters are scarce. The team recorded heart and lung outpatient visits between December 2024 and November 2025 and translated the spoken exchanges with ChatGPT, Google Translate, and UD Talk.

In total, 20 visits with 2,450 exchanges were checked. Skilled medical interpreters scored accuracy, and Japanese-speaking lay readers scored satisfaction. ChatGPT scored a median of 5.0 on both scales in the reported results, ahead of the other two tools at 2.0 in those summaries. The authors suggest such tools can aid multilingual care as a support, not a replacement.
pmc-13329729:
Neda Nikpour Rashidabad, Ashley D. Keiser, and Masoud Hashemi study perennial living mulches of clover and grass in a 2026 report. Mixes varied from pure clover to pure Kentucky bluegrass, with or without added root fungi. The team measured leaf traits, growth, carbon and nitrogen in shoots and roots, and forage quality.

A clover-heavy mix gave the most shoot growth and leaf colour in the reported results. With fungi added, that mix also held the most shoot carbon and nitrogen. Fungi lifted photosynthesis and root size across treatments. Clover gave more protein, fat, and calcium, while grass gave more dry matter and fibre traits. Pairing legume and grass with fungi balanced yield and quality best, the authors conclude.
pmc-13330629:
Mengqin Tao and colleagues trace how early lead exposure drives anxiety and low mood in mice in a 2026 study. Dams drank water with 100 ppm lead from pregnancy through weaning, and pups kept drinking it to day 60 after birth. Behaviour tests and brain checks focused on the medial prefrontal cortex.

Exposed offspring showed anxiety and depression-like behaviour plus neuron shape damage in that brain area in the reported results. Lead shut down a pathway where AMPK supports ACSS2, cutting a chemical tag on histones that keeps synapse genes on. Restoring the pathway with a supplement rescued synapse proteins and eased behaviour. The authors nominate boosting ACSS2 as a treatment idea.
pmc-13331229:
Ryo Nogami and team tell of surprise intercostal fusion that steadied a thoracic fracture dislocation. Their 2026 case paper presents a 50-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis and a total T10 fracture and dislocation. Such fractures challenge surgeons through long-segment stiffness and severe shifting. Urgent back fusion ruptured the dural sac and fully cut through the spinal cord. The thecal sac was tied off and an instrumented T10 to T11 fusion done without much shifting or enough bone mass.

Within six months, wound opening from a pressure sore exposed the implant, forcing removal. During that second surgery, clear osseous bridging between the tenth and next ribs appeared to steady the spine. The team concludes that thoracic fractures in ankylosing spondylitis do not always allow full repair or hardware fusion, and that natural intercostal fusion can steady the spine when a construct fails.
pmc-13331429:
Shahram Majidi and colleagues set out a 2026 focused guideline on clot removal for strokes from blockages in medium and small brain vessels. The writing group worked for the Society of Vascular and Interventional Neurology and reviewed studies from January 2015 through February 2026. The guideline weighs when the vessel procedure helps and when it does not.

Searches covered PubMed, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library, plus hand checks of key study lists and meeting reports. Trials, pooled analyses, and subgroup results were weighed for safety and benefit, and an expert panel agreed the advice. Routine clot removal for these smaller-vessel strokes is not backed by present proof, the authors conclude. They do judge it reasonable for disabling strokes from a dominant second branch of the middle cerebral artery.
pmc-13332429:
Flurina Staubli and co-authors tested freeze-storable cartilage modules for rebuilding jaw bone in a 2026 large-animal study. Their approach copies natural development: a soft cartilage template is placed in a defect and remodels into living, vessel-fed bone, a route barely tried in the face, where bone normally forms directly.

The modules are devitalized cartilage that keeps the instructive signals in its matrix without needing living donor cells. In ten goats with clefts on both sides of the upper jaw, one side received a module and the other the standard graft of the animal's own hip bone. Scans and tissue measures showed the module side regrew and remodeled bone no worse than the graft side early on. In rats, modules kept their bone-forming power after 9 months in frozen storage, supporting an off-the-shelf product for facial repair.
pmc-13333529:
Hao Zhou and colleagues review in 2026 whether the brain's daily rhythms can be harnessed to restore movement after stroke. Stroke leaves more survivors with motor disability than any other condition. Standard rehabilitation plateaus for many, because fatigue, thin intensity, and flagging motivation cap what practice can do.

The reviewers assemble evidence that circadian and ultradian rhythms govern neural plasticity and the feedback loops that rebuild motor control. So the same training may land differently depending on the brain's rhythmic state. They survey studies tying sensorimotor rhythms and motor-network connectivity after stroke to recovery trajectories. They examine neurofeedback and EEG-based modulation techniques that try to steer those rhythms. Gaps remain: the causal chain from rhythm to recovery is not fully mapped, and ward-ready protocols lag the laboratory findings. The authors pitch rhythm-aware rehabilitation as a layer on top of conventional therapy rather than a replacement.
pmc-13333629:
Qianxue Wei and co-authors looked back at a combined treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. They tested chemotherapy plus immunotherapy given before radical radiotherapy, a sequence meant to shrink tumors early and improve control.

The team reviewed 60 patients with stage IIIA to IVA cancer treated between June 2022 and July 2024. Thirty received the combined approach and thirty received radiotherapy with or without chemotherapy. Response in the combined group reached 93.3 percent before radiotherapy and 100 percent afterward. Two-year progression-free survival was higher with the combination, at 82.5 percent against 66.0 percent for the comparison group, and bowel side effects from radiation were less common. Immune side effects stayed mild, supporting further study of this sequence.
pmc-13334429:
Ohood Sallam and co-authors tested two bacteria-killing viruses as food safety tools in a 2026 study. Phage SW03 targets Salmonella enterica and phage CF03 targets Escherichia coli O157:H7, and the team checked how they perform inside real foods under storage conditions.

SW03 came from municipal sewage and CF03 from camel feces. Both were applied to artificially contaminated beef, chicken, and lettuce held at 4 and 21 degrees Celsius, with heavy starting loads for a stringent test. Antibacterial action showed within 4 hours and deepened by 24 hours. Lettuce at room temperature gave the largest cuts, around 4.0 log units for SW03 and 3.5 for CF03. Activity persisted in the cold, though weaker, and both phages also reduced biofilms. The work supports phage biocontrol for fresh foods.
pmc-13336229:
Emylly Lopes Theodoro and co-authors mapped oral problems linked to long COVID in a 2026 scoping review. Mouth symptoms receive little attention next to fatigue and breathlessness, yet they affect eating, speaking, and quality of life.

Following the JBI method, the team searched six databases for primary studies in Portuguese, English, and Spanish published between March 2020 and December 2024. Fifteen studies were analyzed descriptively. The most frequent findings were taste changes, dry mouth, chewing difficulty, gum bleeding, periodontitis, and changes in the teeth themselves. Age, other illnesses, and social inequality influenced how long symptoms persisted, and women were affected more often. The authors call for multiprofessional care and clearer dental guidelines for long COVID patients.
pmc-13337029:
Yeonsu Jeong and colleagues blend two ferroelectrics to strengthen memory films in a 2026 study. Pairing two-dimensional CIPS nanosheets with a ferroelectric polymer lets their dipoles reinforce each other. A balanced solvent mix spread the sheets evenly and helped the polymer form its active crystal phase.

The hybrid film gained nearly 75% more remnant polarization while needing a 15% lower switching field than the plain polymer in reported measures. Transistors using it as the gate layer kept data beyond 10,000 s and endured over 300 switching cycles in device tests. Light could also partly reset the filler, giving multi-level optical memory. Cooperative dipoles may power flexible, low-energy memory and logic.
pmc-13337429:
Jian Wang and colleagues untangle an infection that impersonated cancer in a 2026 case report and literature review. A 53-year-old Chinese man with untreated hepatitis B arrived with cough, chest pain, and back pain. Scans showed a lung mass, swollen lymph nodes, and widespread bone lesions glowing on PET imaging, a picture that screamed metastatic lung cancer.

Repeated biopsies found no cancer. Gene sequencing of lung wash fluid and spine tissue instead identified Mycobacterium kansasii, spread through lungs and bones. Immune testing then revealed autoantibodies against interferon-gamma, an acquired immune defect that invites such infections. Treatment was complicated by liver trouble and high hepatitis B levels. The case warns against anchoring on cancer when scans mislead.
pmc-13337729:
Vijay Sundarsingh and colleagues argued in a 2026 viewpoint that knowing trial headlines is not the same as understanding evidence in critical care. Randomised trials and guidelines now shape bedside decisions, yet trainees often learn headline results without grasping design, methods, or fit to individual patients. Uncritical adoption can mislead practice and expose patients to harm.

Borrowing Richard Feynman's distinction between labels and understanding, the authors urge critical appraisal as a core clinical skill. Headline driven reading, they warn, hides context, limits, and harms. Training that teaches appraisal alongside results would help clinicians judge when evidence applies, when it does not, and what uncertainty remains.
pmc-13339029:
Jiho Shin and colleagues review new routes to zeolite pore structures once thought out of reach in a 2026 perspective. Zeolites serve in catalysis and capture, yet standard hot-water synthesis misses many feasible frameworks. Unusual chemistries are now opening those gaps.

Five routes are highlighted, from rebuilding crystals for tiny pores to phosphonium-guided ultra-open frameworks. One family holds fewer than 13.2 framework atoms per volume unit in the reported density measure, marking extreme openness. Uses include drying, carbon capture, and cleanup. Cost, scale-up, and guide chemical waste remain hurdles, but the expanded toolbox reshapes what zeolites can do.
pmc-13339629:
Sarah J. Madlener and colleagues shine light on sodium pyruvate clusters to mimic aged sea salt air particles in a 2026 study. Pyruvate gathers in such aerosols, and salt surroundings may change its light chemistry. Tiny clusters were made by electrospray and weighed with high precision.

Ultraviolet spectra, light-driven breakup rates, and collision tests mapped the paths. Clusters mainly shed whole sodium pyruvate units, while rarer breaks ran about a hundred times slower as reported. Light first cut a carbon bond, sometimes passing an electron to a neighbor and releasing carbon dioxide. Quantum calculations assigned the light bands behind each step.
pmc-13339829:
Evangelos Smith and a large team use liquid crystals to sense nitrogen dioxide on metal surfaces in a 2026 study. Nitrogen oxides harm air quality, and cheap optical detection at low levels is wanted. A common liquid crystal coated gold, silver, and copper films.

The crystal lay flat on gold and copper but stood upright on silver before exposure, as microscopy and infrared data showed. At 10 ppm nitrogen dioxide in nitrogen gas, alignment flipped in metal-specific ways as reported, with gold showing a reversible switch. Theory linked flips to gas binding. Crystal films could thus report invisible surface chemistry by eye.
pmc-13340129:
Jusail CP and colleagues profile immune responses in human leptospirosis using multi-omics in a 2026 study. This neglected waterborne disease varies widely, and blood immune signaling during acute illness was little known. White blood cells from confirmed patients and healthy controls were compared.

Gene profiling found over 5,800 changed genes, mostly raised, tied to inflammation paths such as TNF and interferon signaling as reported. Protein data and network analysis highlighted shared immune factors. Whole-blood and cell infection models checked key factors directly. The integrated picture names host signals that could become severity markers or treatment targets.
pmc-13340729:
Federico Sacasa and Cristian Geovanny Pereira Santana reported a complex gut bleeding case in 2026 in a 78 year old man. Lower gut bleeding in older adults most often comes from diverticular disease, yet other pathology can hide alongside it. The patient arrived with painless bloody stools and shock from blood loss while taking clopidogrel.

After stabilisation, colonoscopy found a sigmoid diverticulum with an adherent clot, treated by injection and clipping. The same examination noted an ulcerated ileocecal valve, and further enteroscopy showed terminal ileal ulceration matching Crohn disease plus an incidental Meckel diverticulum. Finding the silent diseases shaped later care and surveillance.
pmc-13341229:
Preparing a glide path before root canal shaping affects instrument damage, in a 2026 study by Merve Gökyar and colleagues. Sixty extracted lower molars were split into three groups of 20: rotary glide path, manual glide path with a steel K-file, or none.

Each canal was then shaped with a fresh nickel-titanium rotary file, imaged by scanning electron microscopy before and after. Tip bending was the commonest starting flaw everywhere. After shaping, canals without a glide path showed more microcracks, and blade distortion, surface pitting, and fractures also differed clearly between groups. A prepared glide path, by either method, appears to spare the shaping file.
pmc-13341429:
Sleep, body signals, and mood together separate depression from health in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Di Jiang's group. The 101 people fell into healthy (47), subthreshold depression (30), and major depression (24) groups, assessed by questionnaires, overnight sleep recording, heart rate checks, and eye tracking.

Groups differed on many symptom scales plus sleep timing scores and a rhythm index. After adjustment, anxiety score, a dream-related questionnaire score, and longer REM latency stayed tied on their own to depressive status. A combined model reached an AUC of 0.942, barely above the clinical-only model at 0.930, suggesting fancy measures add little beyond good symptom scales.
pmc-13341529:
A stubborn scarred esophagus is treated with a new combination in a 2026 case report by Xinhui He and colleagues. The 21-year-old man developed severe narrowing along the whole esophagus after accidentally swallowing acidic toilet cleaner, and 13 earlier endoscopic procedures had failed to hold it open.

Doctors paired balloon dilation with transplantation of acellular dermal matrix, a scaffold material, in a first reported use for this problem. The procedure succeeded and brought clear short-term relief with better quality of life. One case cannot prove a therapy, but it offers a fresh option where repeated dilation alone keeps failing.
pmc-13343529:
Prabhdeep Kaur and Jesús Rivera-Nieves set out a standardized stool transplant protocol in 2026 for triggering gut inflammation in mice that lack interleukin-10. Such mice develop colitis only through their microbes, but timing swings wildly between facilities, and drug tricks used to sync disease also injure the gut lining.

Recipient mice aged eight to ten weeks receive repeated oral doses over nine weeks from donor mice whose double gene knockout breeds a colitis-driving microbial community. Disease arrives evenly across cohorts without chemical triggers, keeping the mechanism purely microbial. The platform suits tissue, immune, and microbiome follow-ups and gives bowel disease researchers a steadier test bed for microbe-based treatments.
pmc-13343929:
Sharon K. Kuss-Duerkop and co-authors grade a targeted sequencing test for tuberculosis germs in 2026. Fast, accurate naming of mycobacteria and their drug resistance guides early care. The Deeplex Myc-TB assay reads many gene targets straight from sputum or grown isolates. The team benchmarked it against standard methods.

Across 78 isolates and 102 sputum samples, the test stayed fully specific, wrongly naming nothing. Sensitivity for the tuberculosis complex reached 92.7 percent in isolates and 97.6 percent in sputum, though rarer slow-growing species from sputum scored lower, and many sputum runs for those species came back invalid. Resistance calls matched reference results about 92 percent of the time, rising near 97 percent without unclear variants.
pmc-13346029:
John F Shepherd, Caroline W Maloney, and Paul L Linsky review robot-assisted chest surgery in children in 2026. Robots spread fast in adult thoracic work but slowly in pediatrics. Chest-center removals suit the robot's precise hands in tight spaces. The team gathered every study and case report on patients under 18.

Twelve reports made up the whole evidence base, a thin shelf, yet all pointed the same way: operations finished safely with few complications and rare switches to open surgery. Fans cite steadier vision, finer dexterity, and better surgeon ergonomics than camera-only surgery. The authors judge the approach feasible and safe while calling the literature too sparse for strong claims.
pmc-13348029:
Runjie Xia and colleagues hunt overlooked toxins in lake algal blooms. Their study came out in 2026. It uses a fragment-search method. Blooms in Muskegon, Michigan, supplied a fraction library. Two new micropeptins were isolated from it. One bears a stretched tyrosine unit. A known acid was also confirmed. Combined spectral tools did that work.

A network query language tagged whole peptide classes. It also tagged their tweaks across all fractions. Coverage widened beyond hand-picked isolates. One new compound slowed a human enzyme. That enzyme ties to exposure effects. Lake Erie field samples held recurring micropeptins. They held no microcystins, though. Toxin checks that watch microcystins alone are thus challenged.
pmc-13349929:
Julia Haldina and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a brain signal method for measuring vision without relying on a patient's own answers. Standard acuity testing needs cooperation, which fails in young children, people with cognitive problems, or suspected faking.

The P300 wave appears when a person consciously sorts a rare target from common stimuli, so tests can use ordinary eye-chart shapes such as Landolt Cs. Unlike earlier visual potentials that track only the first steps of seeing, this signal reflects conscious perception. It matched real acuity losses in lazy eye better than older methods. The authors present it as a useful partner to standard electrical vision testing.
pmc-13350129:
Kaizhi Wen and colleagues tested a six-herb traditional formula, Huyan-I, against kidney ageing and scarring in a 2026 study. The patented mix is used clinically for early chronic kidney disease, where cell ageing and the inflammatory signals aged cells release drive damage.

Chemical analysis found 211 ingredients, with dozens detected in the blood of treated mice. In naturally old mice and aged human kidney cells, the formula cut aged cell counts and ageing markers, calmed a STAT3 and NF-kB driven inflammatory chain, and eased tube injury and scarring. Computer predictions had pointed to exactly that pathway, giving the traditional remedy a defined mechanism to test further.
pmc-13351529:
Peng Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 case report with a literature review on hot spots in adaptive radiotherapy for cervical cancer. A patient treated on the Ethos system, version 2.0, developed areas of excess dose inside the target during daily adaptive sessions. The team links the problem to the target edge sitting near the collimator leaf boundary.

When the target sits that close, leaf movement is limited and dose shaping loses flexibility. Jiang and colleagues propose a revised online workflow that corrects the target shift before planning. The fix lowered the chance of hot spots and offers a practical reference for safer, more stable adaptive treatment.
pmc-13351929:
Mai Taguchi and co-authors build a high-throughput platform to mutate F1-ATPase, the rotary motor that makes ATP, and watch single molecules spin. Single-molecule rotation assays reveal how residues couple chemistry to motion, but testing mutants one by one is slow. Their 2026 study combines cell-free protein synthesis with a multiplexed rotation assay, completing the whole cycle within ten hours.

Two positions were mutated exhaustively. At the catalytic base position, almost every substitution destroyed activity; only aspartate, which keeps the crucial negative charge, worked partially. At a second conserved position near a proposed phosphate exit tunnel, variants were tolerated more broadly, with activity tracking side-chain size and water-avoidance. Smaller substitutions there increased the inactive fraction, suggesting the tunnel matters for occasional phosphate release linked to inhibition rather than routine turnover. The authors present the workflow for rapid mutational profiling of rotary enzymes.
pmc-13352429:
Paola Verachi and co-authors surveyed fenretinide, a synthetic retinoid studied for decades as a cancer care and preventive agent, in a 2026 survey. Lab work has shown broad action against tumour cells and their surroundings, and early safety results looked encouraging. Medical use, however, has been held back by poor solubility and low absorption, which produced uneven results in people.

The review traces the compound from lab studies through medical trials, covering the many targets it affects and the reasons its promise has not yet translated into routine care. It also surveys newer mixes and hand-off ways intended to beat the absorption problem. The result is a useful guide for teams weighing whether this long-studied drug deserves a fresh medical push.
pmc-13352829:
Rapeepat Narkbunnam and four colleagues map how daily step counts relate to health in 2,603 Thai adults aged sixty and over. Wrist accelerometers measured steps for a week, and outcomes spanned quality of life, knee function scores, and physical performance tests such as timed walking and repeated sit-to-stand.

Every outcome improved monotonically with more steps. Those walking over fifteen thousand steps daily outperformed the lowest group by margins exceeding clinically important thresholds, with the strongest associations past age seventy-five. A target of six to nine thousand steps looked both meaningful and attainable. The authors propose step count as a practical, scalable metric for healthy aging strategies across Asia.
pmc-13354029:
Abdulaziz Al Shaibani and colleagues report two pelvic kidneys paired with a two-horned womb in 2026. Both kidneys sitting in the pelvis is exceptionally rare, and shared developmental roots link kidney and womb anomalies. A 37-year-old woman with no urinary history presented with left flank pain.

Ultrasound showed both kidneys in the pelvis and a 5 mm non-blocking left kidney stone. Pain relief and fluids were advised, and a scan six months later confirmed the stone had passed. MRI during pregnancy mapped kidneys in the presacral and pouch spaces with unusual vessel origins. Kidney tests stayed normal throughout, and she delivered by planned caesarean at 37 weeks and 3 days without complications.
pmc-13355229:
Moshe Z Shapiro and co-authors studied in 2026 whether social factors shaped use of health monitoring among World Trade Center responders. The program offers regular checks to people who helped after the attacks, whose illness rates link to income, race, and other social factors. Records for 15,515 members from 2008 to 2024 were compared across groups.

Visit timing differed by less than a month across race, income, schooling, and other traits, which the authors call a strong result. Black and Hispanic members in fact came slightly sooner than white and non-Hispanic peers. The authors note the group still has fewer women, older people, and people of color than the wider public.
pmc-13355529:
Maria Ilyas and co-authors write a 2026 letter on low magnesium in patients taking oral EGFR blocker drugs for cancer. Low magnesium is a known effect of the injected forms of these drugs, but whether the pills cause the kidney to waste magnesium was unclear. The team reviewed 43 patients at one Florida center who started the pills from 2014 to 2024.

Eight patients developed low magnesium within a year, seven of them on one older drug. Yet on close review, every case had another cause, such as chemotherapy, water pills, gut losses, or acute illness. None met the bar for kidney wasting caused by the pill itself, which suggests other factors explain most cases.
pmc-13355729:
Christine M Pfeiffer and co-authors report in 2026 how blood folate forms changed in Ethiopian women given salt fortified with iodine and folic acid. Folate shortage causes anemia and raises the risk of spine birth defects, and Ethiopia has very high rates. Women got plain iodized salt or salt with a lower or higher folic acid dose for about six months.

All measured folate forms rose in step with dose, with the main form rising about fivefold at the higher dose and about threefold at the lower dose. No gaps appeared at the start. The pattern matched earlier supplement trials, backing double-fortified salt as a way to lift folate status.
pmc-13356529:
Ruben Peralta and others updated injury brain injury classification for surgeons, in 2026. Old Glasgow Coma Scale categories give doctors a shared language, but they capture too little of the biological heterogeneity, imaging variation, and contextual factors that shape results. A richer plan was needed for trauma and acute care practice.

In January 2024, a National Institute of Neurological Illnesses and Stroke working group put forward the Medical-Markers-Imaging-Modifiers plan, known as CBI-M. The review explains its rationale, structure, and power uses. Surgeons gain a classification that integrates medical, biological, imaging, and contextual information into decisions and research.
pmc-13356729:
Álvaro Gimeno Peiró and co-authors present a 2026 clinical image case of a 55-year-old man diagnosed with pulmonary artery intimal sarcoma, an extremely rare cancer often mistaken for a lung blood clot. He had five months of chronic cough and general symptoms, and scans showed a large left lung mass pressing into the chest center and the pulmonary trunk, with tumor clot.

Instead of surgery, the team used an ultrasound-guided scope through the airway to take needle samples from the left upper lobe bronchus, with no complications. Cell tests showed a poorly differentiated high-grade sarcoma with a gene change that fit the diagnosis. The authors highlight the method for patients who cannot have surgery.
pmc-13358829:
Michael H Udin and co-authors study the scaffolding inside lung tumors in a 2026 paper. Some lung adenocarcinomas spread to lymph nodes while others, at the same stage, do not. The team asked whether the pattern of collagen, the tough protein that gives tissue its frame, differs between the two kinds.

They examined tissue from 120 patients treated at a Buffalo cancer center, using stains and a light-based imaging method to map fiber layout. Tumors that had spread showed collagen fibers lined up in one direction, while others crossed in a crisscross. Ordered fibers may give cancer cells a road out, a clue that could one day flag spread-prone tumors early.
pmc-13360429:
Charlotte E. J. Toomes and co-authors review new lab models of multiple myeloma in a 2026 paper. This blood cancer grows inside bone marrow, where the tissue around the cancer helps it spread and resist drugs, yet flat lab dishes copy that setting poorly. The disease is still incurable, so better models matter for testing treatments.

The review covers 3D and engineered platforms that mimic the marrow's mix of cells, bone, and blood flow more closely. In these settings, cancer cells act more as they do in a patient, including how they answer or resist drugs. The authors argue that such models can sharpen early drug screening and safety checks. They may also reveal new drug targets and speed the path to better care.
pmc-13363329:
Nursulu Nurpeissova and colleagues present a 2026 social study on national identity, gender roles, and state stability in Kazakhstan. Post-Soviet states face pressure to forge a shared identity while views on gender shift. The team surveyed 284 mostly young urban participants and ran three focus groups, then modeled which attitudes best predicted a sense of national stability.

A blended outlook, national uniqueness joined with gender integration, was the strongest predictor, and national identity alone also helped. Views on gender roles by themselves showed no direct link. Focus groups explained the pattern: equality framed as foreign import drew pushback, while equality woven into the national story won support. The authors advise reformers to root gender policy in the country's own narrative.
pmc-13363829:
Lan Ju and colleagues report a 2026 gene hunt for long mesocotyls in sorghum, the seedling stem that pushes shoots up through deep soil. Deep sowing helps sorghum reach moist ground, but only if seedlings can emerge. Scanning 232 varied sorghum lines genome-wide, joined with gene activity reads, the team singled out one switch gene, SbERF60, whose natural promoter variants raise its activity and lengthen the stem.

Tests that raised or lowered the gene confirmed it drives elongation, and moving it improved deep-sown emergence in rice as well. The authors offer the gene and its promoter variants as direct targets for breeding sorghum that stands up reliably from deep planting, a need that grows with machine sowing.
pmc-13365129:
Sheng Cheng and co-workers test in 2026 a blood mark that may spot fresh Epstein Barr germ ill in youth fast. The germ drives gland fever type ills, but sure tests can lag. The team checks a small cell waste protein in 129 ill youth next to 130 youth with plain cold type ills.

The mark ran high in the ill group and rose with germ load in the blood. A test chart shows strong call power at a set cut line, with high catch of true cases. A sun vitamin ran low in the ill group as well. The mark could speed triage.
pmc-13366929:
Peng Zhang and co-workers scan in 2026 the brain nets of folks with bulimia, a binge and purge eat ill, for faults in how nets split and join. Past work read lone spots, which misses net wide tales. The team reads rest scans from 85 ill folks and 71 well kin with graph math.

Ill nets show weak links in and cross nets, with more split at whole brain rank. One core net, the day dream net, joins more with kin nets and splits less. Its join rank ties to low mood scores. Net scale faults may sit back of core eat ill signs.
pmc-13367329:
Ambre Baillou and co-workers build in 2026 the first single cell map of horse blood guard chief cells, the cells that start immune acts. Horse types of these cells were not well set, which blocks work on horse immune ills. The team reads gene use cell by cell in blood from two horses.

All main types show: two guard types, a plasm type, plus rare seed and shift forms. Trait marks match past flesh marks for most types. One type splits in two, one half set to leave blood and wake T cells more. Kin maps link horse types to pig, man, and mouse kin.
pmc-13369629:
Howard Cohl and Michael Schlosser work in 2026 on trans forms and sum rules for two way basic hyper geo series, a deep math field of set sums. Their start points are two fresh finds on such series, built on old Bailey rules for one way kin. From those starts they draw new cases not yet in print.

Square and cube sums for the two way sets come out in plain form. Low rank trans forms fall out by set choice of the terms. The work adds to a long line of sum lore used in physics and number work.
pmc-13371029:
Muhammad Zahid and co-workers link in 2026 blood marks of clot lean and rust stress to small vessel harm risk in type two sugar ill. Such harm drives kidney, eye, and nerve loss. The team reads 200 such folks at one Pakistan site, split by harm risk from care and lab checks.

High risk folks run high on three clot marks and a rust harm mark, and low on four guard marks. The rust mark sets the groups part most in their checks. Joint clot and rust marks could flag who needs guard care first, the team holds.
pmc-13373229:
Ji Yang and co-authors published this eye study in 2026 on pterygium, a fleshy growth that creeps over the surface of the eye. The growth is most common where sun is strong, and surgery is the usual fix, yet it often grows back. The team asked whether genes tied to cuproptosis, a form of cell death driven by copper, play a part in the growth.

They scanned gene activity in growth tissue and in healthy tissue from the eye's clear cover. Nineteen genes tied to copper death were found, and eight of them worked at changed rates in the growth. Machine learning picked three genes as the best flags for risk, and lab checks backed the picks. The genes also tracked with immune cells in the tissue, which may point to new drug targets.
pmc-13374829:
Youssef and colleagues report a case of melanosis ilei, a dark pigmentation of the small intestine's final section, caused by iron tablets, in a 2026 case report. A 42-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia on oral iron had colonoscopy and gastroscopy in her anemia workup. Both examinations were unremarkable until the scope was advanced into the terminal ileum. There, distinct to confluent dark brown patches gave the lining a peppered, speckled appearance unlike healthy pink mucosa.

Biopsies confirmed the diagnosis: the tissue held macrophages, scavenger cells, stuffed with pigment in the layer beneath the surface. Clinicians attributed the change to her iron supplementation, a recognized benign cause of this pseudomelanosis. Youssef stresses the practical point: recognizing the pattern spares patients misdiagnosis as intestinal ischemia, dying bowel that demands urgent surgery. It also avoids unnecessary surgical consultations and intense workups for a harmless finding that needs no treatment.
pmc-13376729:
Marshall and colleagues revisited the Wells-Riley model in 2026, a classic tool for estimating airborne infection risk indoors. The model takes inputs such as how much infectious material a sick person sheds, room ventilation, the number of infectors, and time spent inside. The team rebuilt it in probability form so each input could vary or carry uncertainty, as real settings do.

Under that treatment, each person's infection risk becomes a spread of values rather than one number, and the authors derived its shape under standard assumptions. Using plain average inputs in the classic model can mislead in set directions: doubt about shedding, time, or breathing rate pushes risk estimates too high. Wobble in ventilation can push them too low. The team also ranked which input drives the spread when two vary at once, giving modelers a sharper sense of where better data matter most.
pmc-13378029:
Mahnoor Khan and co-authors published a 2026 review on multiple myeloma, a cancer where plasma cells grow out of control in the bone marrow. The disease often returns after treatment, and cancer cells can escape by losing the target that therapy aims at. Care has shifted from standard chemotherapy toward immune-based treatment and four-drug starting regimens.

The review brings together approved CAR-T therapies, in which a patient's own T cells are changed in the lab to attack cancer, with those four-drug regimens. It weighs trial findings on whether combining the two could deepen responses and keep remission longer. Readers also get the main limits that remain, plus practical next steps and barriers to wider use.
pmc-13380529:
Irem Soyler and co-authors report a 2026 study on how high-frequency sound waves kill a common food-poisoning bacterium, E. coli, and how the bacteria fight back. At low power the killing mechanism was unclear. The team tested whether damage came from reactive chemical species or from physical force.

One sound frequency produced more reactive species inside the bacteria and more membrane damage than another. Adding a green-tea compound greatly boosted the killing effect and damaged the cell surface further. Bacteria pre-treated with sound became weaker against later heat and chemical attack. Mutant tests showed one defence system, tied to a protective chemical inside the cell, was especially important for survival.
pmc-13380729:
Anneroos E Nederstigt, Samiksha Sardana, Francine Rodrigues Ianiski, and Marc P Baggelaar report a 2026 study of a fatty tag that cells attach to proteins during inflammation. The tag, called long-chain S-acylation, can be added and removed, and it controls where proteins sit and how they signal. Its role in macrophages, key immune cells, was not well mapped.

Using labelled building blocks and a chemical capture method, the team mapped the tags in lab-grown macrophages before and after an inflammatory trigger. Tag patterns changed with activation, including new tagged forms tied to inflammation. Blocking tag removal or addition changed which inflammatory messengers the cells released. The findings mark the tag as a control point in inflammation.
pmc-13380829:
Ziad Farih, Nadia El Wadidi, and Youssef Naji report a 2026 case of primary syphilis found by chance during a dental visit. Syphilis is rising again worldwide and can appear in unexpected places, including the face, where it is easily missed. Their patient was a 43-year-old man who came for a routine dental check.

While examining the outside of his face, the dentist found a painless, firm ulcer on the left side of his forehead. Blood tests confirmed syphilis. The authors argue that a systematic look outside the mouth should be part of every dental visit. Dentists may be the first to spot early signs of infections that affect the whole body.
pmc-13382829:
Mohammed A. Al-Haiqi, Choon-Fu Goh, and Wen-Da Oh make a coconut-shell biochar loaded with iron and magnesium for pulling paracetamol from water in 2026 work. The nitrogen-doped material beat versions with one metal or none, showing a clear joint effect. The best mix held about 13.8 percent iron by weight.

That version took up close to 158 milligrams of the drug per gram and had a large surface area. Tests of speed and uptake fit standard models well, and theory work pointed to stronger surface binding. Several forces joined in holding the drug, which supports the char as a green option for cleaning drug-laced water.
pmc-13386629:
Man Chen's team built immune profiles to tell gut graft-versus-host disease from viral diarrhea after stem cell transplant, in a 2026 study. Diarrhea after allogeneic transplant, mainly from gastrointestinal graft-versus-host disease or viral infection, demands fast etiologic distinction for proper care. The team followed 232 transplant patients at Beijing Lu Daopei Hospital from 2021 to 2024.

Fifty-eight patients developed biopsy-confirmed post-transplant diarrhea, 34 with graft-versus-host disease and 24 with viral enteritis. Immune profiles were measured a week before onset and at weeks 4 and 5 after transplant, with LASSO and logistic models built at single and multiple time points. Dynamic immune profiling may aid early distinction and guide intervention after transplant.
pmc-13386829:
Mingwei Peng and colleagues trace flu A(H3N2) evolution in Hubei, China, from 2017 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Surveillance data and gene sequences for two surface proteins frame the analysis. Flu followed normal seasons before 2020, nearly vanished for two years, then surged back after mid-2022.

Several lineages shared the stage before the pandemic, while single dominant clades ruled the return. Population size had already shrunk by late 2019, before COVID measures began, the models suggest. Selection mostly pruned variation, with a few antigen sites adapting, which can guide vaccine strain updates and preparedness planning.
pmc-13389929:
Jillian E Hardee and colleagues examine, in 2026, how reasons for drinking and self-protective habits jointly shape alcohol outcomes in college students, and whether the pattern differs by sex. Students who drink hazardously face high risk, yet men and women may use protective strategies differently.

Data from 109 students with hazardous drinking were tested against four outcomes covering amount drunk, drinking days, and drinks per occasion. Men reported higher values across the drinking measures, and the analysis probes how motives such as seeking enhancement interact with strategies and sex. Campus health researchers gain a more detailed model for tailoring alcohol programmes, since advice that works for one group may miss the motives driving another.
pmc-13390029:
Jordi Minnema and colleagues present, in 2026, a machine learning model that predicts how chemicals harm water species, built for use in formal risk assessment. Regulators face thousands of marketed chemicals with too little toxicity data to judge safety for aquatic life.

The model predicts toxicity across many species, and those predictions are assembled into species sensitivity distributions, a standard tool that shows the range of species responses to a chemical. The authors focus as much on trust as on accuracy, since assessors will only use model output they can defend. Environmental regulators and modellers gain a pathway for filling data gaps while keeping the reasoning behind a safety decision open to scrutiny.
pmc-13390129:
Zhenghong Chen and colleagues review, in 2026, how animal models are built for pigmentary skin disorders, conditions where skin gains or loses its normal colour. The group covers vitiligo, melasma, and darkening after inflammation, which share distressing visible effects though they are rarely life-threatening.

Causes span sun and chemical triggers, hormone shifts, stress, and skin injury, so no single model fits all. The review sorts published methods for creating each model, compares what each model captures well, and tracks recent progress in the field. Dermatology researchers gain a practical guide for choosing a model that matches the human condition they study, rather than adopting the most common model by habit.
pmc-13390429:
Guodong Zhou and co-authors build, in 2026, a duck vaccine that borrows tiny membrane bubbles from Salmonella to display proteins from a second pathogen. Riemerella anatipestifer causes severe blood infection and membrane inflammation in waterfowl and heavy farm losses, while antibiotic resistance keeps growing.

Three surface proteins from the duck pathogen were mounted on outer membrane vesicles shed by a mutant Salmonella strain. Ducks given the vesicles mounted strong antibody and cellular responses. After challenge, survival reached four fifths for two of the protein displays and seven tenths for the third. Poultry veterinarians gain a flexible vaccine platform that could be adapted to other waterfowl diseases without growing the target pathogen itself.
pmc-13392329:
Joe Khodari's team laid out sound-scan findings telling apart feline large-intestinal gland cancer from high-grade lymph cancer. Both cancers appear as through-wall dark swelling with lost wall layers. Forty-four cats with gland cancer and thirty-eight with lymph cancer and complete abdominal sound scans were reviewed.

Gland cancers, mostly colon or ileum-colon, tracked a median twenty-three mm long with nine-mm walls, while lymph cancers tracked about forty mm with fifteen-mm walls. Swollen nodes were common in both, blockage more frequent in gland cancer, and median life span data help doctors weigh sound-scan patterns in diagnosis.
pmc-13392629:
Funda Atila, Mehmet Çetin, and Didem Aksu grew elm oyster mushrooms on wheat straw mixed with used tea leaves or used coffee grounds. The question matters because brewers discard huge amounts of both materials that might otherwise enrich mushroom beds.

pmc-13395429:

pmc-13395829:

People judged success by neatness, accuracy, speed, and fixing errors, not just finishing. Many wrote less, switched tools, or leaned on tech. Frustration and lost independence shadowed the loss. pmc-13396029:
Xin Sun and colleagues combined large-scale chemical and protein profiling to map the body changes behind high uric acid, a state called hyperuricemia, in a 2026 study. From the same data the authors picked candidate blood markers that could flag the condition earlier than uric acid alone.
pmc-13396229:

The path may serve many germs and bendy rocks. The paper bares a new way life can eat motion itself, far from sun and food.
pmc-13396329:

pmc-13396729:

pmc-13396829:

pmc-13397329:

Trials differ in recipes, measure success differently, and rarely follow patients long, while each operation makes its own demands of healing tissue. pmc-13397729:
Brigitte Vogl-Lukasser and Christian R Vogl trace how farm homegardens in Eastern Tyrol, Austria have changed across almost a century. These small plots, once tended by hand near the farmhouse, hold clues about vanished plant uses and rural habits.

pmc-13398129:
Zehao Hong and colleagues uncover a self-reinforcing loop that powers triple-negative breast cancer, a form with few drug targets. Their 2026 study hunts membrane receptors feeding the Hippo/YAP growth switch, which stays stuck on in this disease. Screening gene data and drug-annotated receptor lists, then silencing candidates one by one, landed on the endothelin receptor EDNRA.

The receptor and YAP each switch the other on, so cutting the loop at EDNRA offers a fresh point of attack.
pmc-13398529:
Tien Tran Phung Dung and Huan Nguyen Ngoc review outcomes of Hartmann's surgery for perforated bowel diverticula. Their 2026 study covers 96 patients treated at Cho Ray Hospital between May 2020 and April 2025. The operation removes the diseased sigmoid colon and brings out a stoma, avoiding a risky join in an infected belly, but reversing it later is notoriously hard.

Perforated sigmoid and rectosigmoid disease brings abscess and peritonitis at high rates, so the balance between a safe first operation and a tough reversal shapes counselling. The authors lay out that balance with figures from a busy Vietnamese centre.
pmc-13398629:
Xianfei Cao and co-authors build bendy electronic sensors whose layers heal, realign and recycle themselves. Their 2026 study stacks functional layers from clashing polymer backbones that share the same dynamic chemical bonds. Interfaces are the weak point of layered flexible devices: they peel, misalign after damage and resist recycling.

Shared bonds weld layers almost as strongly as solid material, while the mismatched backbones let layers find their register again after a cut. Sensors built this way, carrying nanospheres, conductive media and magnetic particles, self-assembled under magnetic guidance and regained function after heat treatment. The design points to wearables and soft machines that can be repaired instead of binned.
pmc-13398929:
Valeria Pecce and colleagues show a tiny RNA helping thyroid cancers remember how to soak up iodine. Their 2026 study works on BRAF p.V600E mutant cancers, where a stuck growth pathway strips cells of their thyroid identity and shuts out radioiodine therapy. Drugs against the pathway can restore identity, but tumours find workarounds.

Restoring it in mutant cell lines revived thyroid-specific genes and proteins, moved the iodine importer back to the cell surface and raised iodine uptake, confirmed in organoids. The group also probed its links to shape-shifting EMT genes, hunting a steadier redifferentiation route.
pmc-13399729:

Tested externally on 5,507 participants from the American ARIC study, the score's distribution stayed close to the original, with Jensen-Shannon distances as low as 0.10 reported. The authors propose whole-body damage scores as a basis for personal monitoring and pattern-matched care.
pmc-13399829:
Papakostas and co-authors describe, in 2026, a hardware-sparing way to fix a lateral extra-articular tenodesis during ACL reconstruction, an add-on procedure that reduces graft failure and rotational instability. The flap is cut about 8 to 10 millimeters thick and 8 to 10 centimeters long. It is routed to fixation in the isometric zone, leaving a smoother surface on the lateral femoral condyle. An incision of roughly 5 to 8 millimeters marks the approach between the condyle's upper and lower borders. The authors argue the simplification keeps strong fixation while reducing irritation and convergence risk.
pmc-13400229:
Qilin Wang and colleagues isolated a soil bacterium that eats the banned antibiotic chloramphenicol and traced the genes that let it do so, in a 2026 environmental microbiology study. The authors offer CS1 and its gene cluster as a mechanistic foundation for bioaugmentation of contaminated soils.
pmc-13400729:

Some prophage regions encoded bacteria-dissolving enzymes that might themselves become treatments. Family tree analysis showed high prophage diversity. pmc-13400829:

Each is judged on nutrition, environmental cost, scalability, regulation and public health, with limitations stated plainly. Cross-cutting obstacles include fragmented rules, consumer wariness, energy use and unequal access. The authors favor a combined, evidence-first portfolio over any single fix.
pmc-13400929:

All were sampled within a day of admission. Five messengers carried cut-off values for severe COVID-19. All six measured messengers distinguished the inflammatory syndrome well. Its thresholds ran higher than those for severe infection. Ages spanned infancy to seventeen years.
pmc-13402229:

pmc-13402329:

pmc-13402629:

pmc-13402729:

pmc-13402829:

pmc-13403029:

pmc-13403429:

pmc-13403729:

pmc-13404129:

pmc-13404329:

pmc-13406729:

pmc-13408129:

pmc-13409329:

pmc-13409629:

pmc-13411329:

pmc-13411629:

pmc-13411729:

pmc-13412429:

pmc-13413529:

pmc-13414529:
