That withholding effective treatment from older adults on blanket safety grounds is not supported by the trial record.
pmc-13414629:
Marcia A. Docherty, Andrea L. Taylor, and Josh T. Duncan describe a refreshed transition program for new nurses at Island Health, evaluated in 2026. The health system has run the program since 2005 and rebuilt it for graduates entering practice during pandemic recovery, covering cohorts from 2022 to 2024.

Evaluation followed repeated Look, Think, Act cycles with graduates and other users shaping each round. Engagement, once scattered between almost zero and 36 percent, rose to between 14 and 61 percent. Graduates leaving within a year fell from 7 percent in 2021 to 4 percent in 2023. Casual positions also dropped sharply by 2024, which the authors credit to deliberate relationship building.
pmc-13415429:
Hiroyuki Tokue and co-authors build a planning framework for bleeding from the inferior epigastric artery, an abdominal wall vessel, in 2026. They reviewed sixty-two patients treated with catheter embolization, sorting cases into four types by the collateral route feeding the bleed. Types covered isolated wall bleeds, postpartum cases, pelvic fracture cases, and puncture injuries.

Embolization stopped bleeding on imaging in every case, yet clinical success averaged about 82 percent. Pelvic fracture cases fared worst, near 56 percent, and supplied all three rebleeds. A simple score using fracture type, a clotting disorder, and very low blood pressure tracked failure risk in steps.
pmc-13415529:
Zijuan Wang and a large team uncover a repair module built around the small protein tag UFM1, in 2026. Cells fix double strand DNA breaks by several routes, and non-homologous end joining is a fast, direct one. The team built a light activated UFM1 probe to catch its weak binding partners.

Mapping showed UFM1 touching core repair factors, including a floppy tail of the XRCC4 protein. A partner protein, Ku70, carries the UFM1 tag and helps XRCC4 lock the repair complex onto damaged DNA. Patient cells with defects in this tagging system repaired breaks poorly. The work links a little studied tag to genome protection and disease.
pmc-13416829:
Bingqing Wang and colleagues mine insect genomes for piggyBac transposons in the order Hymenoptera, in a study published in 2027. These mobile DNA pieces can cut and paste themselves, and labs use them as tools to move genes. Bees, wasps, and ants matter for farming and nature, yet their transposons were little explored.

Across 287 species, elements appeared in 137 genomes and fell into four groups. Tests showed two transposons, from a cuckoo bee and a mason bee, moved DNA about as well as a top engineered version. Attempts to boost them further gave mixed results. The pair adds strong new tools for genome work.
pmc-13418429:
Melis Selamoglu and colleagues survey family physicians in Istanbul about e-cigarettes as quit smoking aids, in a 2026 cross sectional study. Responses came from 243 doctors, collected online between August and October 2022. Most felt responsible for helping patients quit and trusted current medicines, yet views on vaping were strongly negative.

About four fifths rejected e-cigarettes as cessation aids or as safer than cigarettes. Worries centred on addictiveness, gateway effects, and health harm. Over half lacked confidence in their knowledge or in answering patient questions. Most would not recommend vaping even after other methods failed. Training and guidance are the authors' prescription.
pmc-13418929:
Alisha Dhiman and colleagues show that one part of a chromatin-opening machine is required for breast cancer cells to change form and spread. The machine, called SWI/SNF, comes in three forms, and the team focused on the PBRM1 part found only in the PBAF form. A growth signal normally pushes breast lining cells toward a loose, mobile state that seeds spread.

Cells missing PBRM1 could not finish that shape change in lab tests. Mouse breast tumors without the part also failed to spread to distant sites. The same pattern held across several mouse models of the disease. Blocking the PBAF form could therefore offer a new line of attack against metastatic breast cancer, the stage that drives most deaths from the disease.
pmc-13419929:
Hallas and colleagues propose widening drug safety watch: beyond side effects, to the way medicines are used. Side effect reporting misses misuse that no single clinician can see, such as odd doses, strange treatment lengths, or relapse patterns spread across a system. Their 2026 concept paper names the practice DU-Vigilance, drug utilization vigilance. It models the practice on signal detection. Real world datasets are screened without a prior suspicion, and anomalies surface for expert review.

The data would come from prescription registries, health records, and insurance claims, scanned continuously, since misuse patterns shift over time. The tools are borrowed from drug use research, but the stance is new: hypothesis generating rather than checking known worries. An anomaly is a question, not a verdict, and subject experts judge which ones matter. Folding this watch into pharmacovigilance, the authors argue, could catch prescribing problems years earlier and lift the quality of care.
pmc-13421129:
The Pan American Health Organization issued this 2026 outlook on the El Niño climate pattern expected during 2026 and 2027 and the health risks it brings across the Americas. Warm ocean conditions can drive both drought and flooding in different places at once.

The outlook divides the region into two broad patterns. Northern South America, Central America, the Caribbean, and the Amazon face hotter, drier conditions. Those conditions raise risks of drought, water shortage, food insecurity, wildfires, heat illness, and mosquito-borne disease. Parts of Ecuador, Peru, southern Brazil, Colombia, Paraguay, Argentina, and the southern United States face heavier rain, with flooding, landslides, displacement, and waterborne disease. Because the worst health effects often arrive in the year after onset, the organization urges sustained monitoring and early preparation, especially where poverty and weak services already strain health systems.
pmc-13421229:
Gao-Feng Liu leads a ten-author team investigating, in a 2026 study, a long non-coding RNA called MNX1-AS1 in non-small cell lung cancer. Long non-coding RNAs do not build proteins, yet they can steer gene activity, and earlier work had left this one's role in lung cancer unclear.

The team measured MNX1-AS1 in 40 paired tumour and healthy lung samples and found it raised in tumours, where higher levels tracked with poorer outlook. Silencing it in two lung cancer cell lines reduced growth, migration and invasion. The RNA works by soaking up a small regulatory RNA, miR-218-5p, which frees a gene named COMMD8 to act. Tumour growth in mice confirmed the chain, marking the pathway as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13421329:
Rima Baalbaki leads a very large collaboration reporting, in 2026, experiments on how new particles form in the atmosphere from gases released by ocean plankton. At CERN's CLOUD chamber, which simulates atmospheric conditions, they tested methanesulfonic acid — a breakdown product of a marine sulfur gas — whose role in particle birth was unclear.

Below minus ten degrees Celsius, the acid formed new particles with ammonia as effectively as sulfuric acid does, and the two acids together formed mixed clusters that nucleated faster still. It also drove particle growth at near-maximum rates in cool, humid air. Global simulations suggest the process boosts cloud-forming particles, especially over polar oceans, and may have mattered in the pre-industrial atmosphere.
pmc-13421529:
Armando Tripodi and co-authors guide clinicians through the clotting tightrope of liver cirrhosis in a 2026 review. A scarred liver makes too little of both clotting and anti-clotting factors, leaving patients balanced on a narrow edge. They can bleed during procedures yet also form dangerous clots. The authors reviewed the current literature to support real decisions.

Their guidance starts with the tests: the standard prothrombin time and its partner do not describe clotting in cirrhosis and should not be used to predict bleeding. Patient and procedure factors judge risk better. Because procedure bleeding is uncommon, blanket preventive measures are often wasted. The review turns to when anticoagulant drugs help or harm. It is a practical map for a famously confusing corner of liver care.
pmc-13422329:
Taco Jan Prins leads a five-author case report, published in 2026, of a pregnant Karen woman on the Thailand-Myanmar border who arrived unable to walk, sit or drink unaided. Wilson's disease, an inherited failure to clear copper, was destroying her liver and brain; untreated, it is fatal, and successful pregnancies with symptoms this advanced are rare.

Her year-long decline, with the tell-tale copper rings in her eyes, pointed clinicians to the diagnosis despite scarce tests. Zinc treatment began at once, switching later to a copper-binding drug once it could be sourced. She delivered a healthy full-term girl, and after a year of treatment most symptoms had melted away while the baby thrived. The authors champion careful physical examination where laboratories are few.
pmc-13422829:
Jiaying Li leads an eight-author team surveying China, in a 2026 study, on whether the public would accept large language models in healthcare — and whether acceptance is fairly shared. Nearly thirty-six thousand adults across one hundred fifty cities rated their acceptance after a standard explanation of what these systems can do.

Average acceptance sat near sixty-four on a hundred-point scale, lower among people with chronic conditions and falling with age. Higher social status, prior digital-health use, self-confidence, warm neighbourhood ties and digital health literacy all nudged acceptance up, while loneliness and financial strain pulled it down. Tree analysis profiled the groups likeliest to refuse. The authors warn that uneven acceptance could widen health inequities as the tools spread.
pmc-13422929:
Mohamed and colleagues gather in 2026 what patients and clinicians actually think of virtual hospital care, hospital treatment delivered to patients at home through digital links. They drew only on qualitative studies, which record experiences in people's own words.

From more than fifteen thousand initial records, nineteen studies survived screening, covering 514 clinicians and 215 patients, mostly in high-income countries. Five themes shaped experience: whether the care felt valuable, confidence and readiness to use it, and digital and health literacy. The therapeutic relationship at a distance and the infrastructure behind it completed the five. The reviewers conclude that acceptance depends on tailoring the service to each person's needs, training clinicians properly, and designing the model together with its users. They flag a near absence of evidence from poorer countries.
pmc-13423029:
Ivan Bivolarski, Martin Dimitrov, and Hristo Dechev review how daily body-clock gene networks shape prostate cancer, drawing on RNA sequencing studies published through 2026. Their article links disrupted circadian rhythms with androgen receptor signaling, shifts in transcript forms, and pathways tied to metabolism and drug resistance.

Sequencing data, the authors argue, can reveal time-based gene patterns even in tumor samples collected without timing records, thanks to newer computing methods. They close by weighing chronotherapy, the idea of timing treatment to match biological rhythms, as a route toward more personal care. Clinical use remains limited, so the review frames circadian transcript patterns mainly as a guide for future trials and biomarker work.
pmc-13424029:
Henry Bair, Molly Orlick, and Zeba A Syed review how GLP-1 receptor agonists, the widely used diabetes and weight-loss drugs, affect the surface of the eye. Most eye reviews of these drugs focus on the retina, so the authors instead treat the tear system, lids, and cornea as one metabolic surface unit and weigh repair against unwanted reshaping.

Animal work is most encouraging: one drug cut tear-gland inflammation and scarring and improved tear flow and corneal healing in preclinical tests. Human evidence is still thin and observational, with diabetic cohorts showing less dry eye among users. Reports from weight-loss patients hint at tissue changes around the eye that need watching, the authors caution.
pmc-13424529:
Huang and colleagues report a 2026 lab study of naringin, a citrus compound, as a helper for chemotherapy in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer of the upper throat. They tested whether naringin makes cancer cells more sensitive to the drug paclitaxel. 

Naringin showed a trend toward lowering the paclitaxel dose needed to halve cell survival, while it did not change sensitivity to two other common drugs. The gene search pointed to AKR1C3, an enzyme, as the likely mediator: naringin raises its level in the cells. Forcing the enzyme up or blocking it with a drug shifted the paclitaxel response, which supports its role. A food compound that sharpens one drug, through a named enzyme, is a focused research lead.
pmc-13425029:
Shraddha Uprety and colleagues published a 2026 letter describing itching as an overlooked sign of leprosy. Their patient was a 57-year-old woman with a severely itchy red plaque on her forehead that had lasted six months. Biopsy showed granulomas around skin structures and nerves, while stains for acid-fast bacilli stayed negative, and the team diagnosed tuberculoid leprosy from the combined clinical and tissue findings.

Readers learn why itch can mislead clinicians toward other skin conditions and delay care in areas where leprosy remains common. The authors link the symptom to nerve injury and inflammatory mediators, note dry skin from sweat gland damage, and describe starting multidrug therapy planned for six months.
pmc-13425129:
Helge Einar Lundberg and colleagues test whether daily Jarlsberg cheese, fermented with a named bacterium, shifts bone health in older adults. Fifty-seven postmenopausal women and men aged 55 or more took part, all with bone density scores between minus 2.5 and 0 and none on bone drugs.

All received calcium and vitamin D, while one group started cheese at once and the other after a 16-week delay, each eating it for 32 weeks. Bone markers and density were checked every 16 weeks, and total osteocalcin rose in the cheese group. The trial gives a food-based lead worth a larger test, not yet a proven bone treatment.
pmc-13425529:
Wang and co-authors widen the job description of a small brain nucleus in this 2026 narrative review. The entopeduncular nucleus, a main output station of the basal ganglia and the rodent counterpart of part of the human globus pallidus, is filed under motor control in most textbooks. The review argues it equally integrates emotion, mood, and sleep.

The authors synthesize rodent experiments using light- and drug-based circuit control, recordings, and tracing. They add human imaging and stimulation studies. Together these describe the nucleus as a convergence hub for five signaling systems. The systems run from dopamine to endocannabinoids. Its projections to the lateral habenula, a disappointment-processing center, regulate aversion, addiction-related behavior, and mood, while specific cell circuits govern anxiety. Its disruption is tied to depression, anxiety, and Parkinson's movement problems, and the authors nominate the nucleus as a target for neuromodulation.
pmc-13426029:
De Roy and colleagues published a 2026 study on how spine facet cartilage is built and behaves. Facet joints guide spine motion, and their cartilage wears in patterned ways. The team mapped one sheep joint surface point by point for this work. They paired squeeze tests with measures of thickness and key tissue parts.

Upper facet cartilage proved thicker and richer in a water-holding tissue part. Strength measures matched between upper and lower facets despite those build gaps. At lower facets, thicker spots relaxed under load in a distinct pattern. At upper facets, the water-holding part tracked the same relaxing behavior closely. Such maps may show which joint zones face the highest wear risk. Sheep joints served as the test model for these detailed maps.
pmc-13426229:
Yonne Peters and colleagues tested a probiotic milk drink in Barrett's esophagus in a 2026 single-arm pilot study of 23 patients. Barrett's tissue and its cancer successor are linked with an inflamed esophageal microbiome dominated by Gram-negative bacteria. Participants drank a fermented milk product containing Lactobacillus casei strain Shirota twice daily for four weeks.

Afterward, metaplastic lining showed significantly more Gram-positive Firmicutes without a change in total bacterial amount, and the Gram-positive to Gram-negative ratio rose as Proteobacteria fell. Shifting the esophageal community toward a friendlier profile could, with further testing, become a low-risk adjunct in Barrett's care. A drink a day is a light ask for most sick men and women, so a clear win here could spread fast in real wards and clinics.
pmc-13426729:
Dharmendra Kumar Pipal and colleagues report a woman whose large kidney cyst came back after a simpler needle treatment, and review similar published cases. Her cyst, a fluid-filled sac, measured about 8 by 10 centimetres and pressed on her left kidney.

The 46-year-old had six months of dull back pain and a swollen belly, and scans showed her kidney working at only 30 percent strength. Doctors first drained a litre of fluid and treated the sac lining, yet the cyst returned within about a month. Surgeons then removed the cyst wall through small cuts using ultrasonic scissors, finishing in 60 minutes with no complications. Pipal presents this keyhole approach as safe and effective for large cysts that return.
pmc-13427229:
Jiapeng Zhang and colleagues describe a molten salt method that recovers palladium, a scarce metal used in car catalysts and electronics, without acid baths. The route first locks palladium into a calcium compound, then uses molten calcium iodide to free the metal.

Computer calculations showed charge moving from calcium to palladium, giving the compound a stable, partly ionic bond structure. The compound barely lost mass when heated to very high temperatures, confirming its heat stability. In the molten salt at high heat, iodine attacked the calcium and left pure metal behind within one hour. The recovered palladium reached about 99.5 percent purity by weight, pointing to cleaner recycling of spent catalysts.
pmc-13427529:
Pooja Kushwaha and Sangita Mukhopadhyay show a tuberculosis protein fragment easing experimental colitis by removing mast cells in a 2026 mouse study. A peptide derived from the Mycobacterium tuberculosis PPE2 protein improved dextran sulfate induced colitis across weight loss, disease activity score, colon length, and the inflammation marker myeloperoxidase. pmc-13428029:
Robert Rauschkolb and colleagues grew five long-lived herb species in gardens at five Central European sites to see how leaf and root traits shift within one species. Traits are measurable features, such as height or leaf dryness, that hint at how a plant grows.

After up to four growing seasons, the team measured shoots and roots and compared them with local weather and soil data. Taller plants tended to have less branched roots, and dry leaves matched dry roots, linking above- and belowground parts. Soil nutrient levels, more than weather, drove most of the shifts seen within each species. Rauschkolb warns that leaf traits cannot stand in for root traits, so studies should measure both on site.
pmc-13428229:
Dadson and colleagues report a case in which a new kind of PET scan helped decide whether joint inflammation after Lyme disease had turned into true autoimmune arthritis. The usual glucose based PET scan showed inflammation without saying whether infection or autoimmunity drove it.

The team scanned her with a tracer that targets VAP-1, a vessel molecule that guides white cells into inflamed tissue. Uptake lit up the same joints and persisted after antibiotics, which pointed to ongoing immune activity rather than leftover infection. The diagnosis became seronegative rheumatoid arthritis triggered by the Lyme bacterium. The scan backed stepping up to disease modifying therapy. The tracer also exposes patients to less radiation than the glucose scan, suiting repeat checks.
pmc-13428429:
Herr and colleagues published a 2026 study on spotting immune therapy effects early with ultrasound. Some cancer drugs free the immune system but work slowly and unevenly. The team tested bubbles that stick to a blood-vessel growth marker in tumors. They used a mouse model of bowel cancer for the test.

Mice on dual immune therapy showed far lower tumor blood flow by week one. Bubble binding to the vessel marker also dropped sharply under therapy. Tissue checks confirmed more tumor cell death and more immune cells inside. Treated tumors also grew fewer and smaller blood vessels over time. The scans flagged response well before size changes alone would show it. A blood-free scan like this could spare patients repeated biopsies.
pmc-13429129:
Yun-Qiang Yue and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, nanoparticles harvested from a magnolia flower remedy against ulcerative colitis in mice. The flower buds, called Xinyi in Chinese medicine, yield tiny exosome-like particles when boiled into a decoction. Such plant particles survive digestion and carry active compounds. The team isolated and profiled the particles, then ran dish tests and a mouse colitis experiment with daily oral dosing for two weeks.

The particles carried flavonoids and other plant chemicals known for calming inflammation. In dishes they mopped up damaging molecules and pushed immune cells toward a healing mode. In mice they eased weight loss, protected colon length, lowered disease scores, and shifted gut microbe mixes. Computer docking and protein checks pointed to the pathways involved. A traditional remedy gains a modern, testable form here.
pmc-13429729:
Melisa E. Gülseren and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, an infrared sensor that listens to radio waves instead of light. Tiny vibrating radio-frequency devices, called RF MEMS, can be tuned to absorb specific infrared colors when paired with patterned surfaces. Earlier designs tracked shifts in vibration frequency. The new design watches changes in electrical impedance, the resistance a circuit presents, and ties them by formula to sensing strength.

The detector reached very high responsivity at room conditions, responding to infrared power down near a trillionth of a watt. It picked out a narrow color band around a chosen wavelength in the mid-infrared. Response time sat under a millisecond. Because a matching network can retune it, one chip could serve many sensing jobs. On-chip chemical fingerprinting for medicine and environment checks is the stated direction.
pmc-13430529:
Debora Freitas Silva and a large team packed an essential oil from an Amazon tree into tiny capsules in 2026, then tuned the recipe with a planned set of tests. The oil comes from breu branco, a plant valued in local use. Bare oil can break down fast, so the shell aims to keep it stable and active longer.

The capsules came out round and small, with a tight size spread, a strong load of oil held inside, and steady form over time. Skin cell tests showed good match with living tissue at most doses. Free oil failed to stop a common skin germ, while the capsules held it back at a low dose. The capsules also sped skin cell movement in a scratch test and calmed one key swelling signal, which supports wound care use.
pmc-13430829:
Afnan Sultan and co-authors asked in 2026 how much vast pre-training helps transformer models that forecast traits of new drug-like molecules. Such models often learn first from millions of unmarked molecules held in large public banks. The team tested whether a bigger first diet truly lifts scores on lab traits that govern how a drug moves through the body.

Across seven data sets, growing the first diet past a few hundred thousand molecules brought no gain. A small second step worked far better: tuning on at most four thousand molecules close to the task, with side targets drawn from basic chemical traits, lifted scores on every set. A mid-sized model tuned this way matched or beat far larger rivals. Plain chemical feature sets stayed strong as a base for fair checks.
pmc-13432729:
Frank Hülsemann and co-authors compared lab routes in 2026 for spotting fake urine used to cheat doping and forensic tests. Fake products mimic real urine, and cheats may blend the two. The team ran three routes blind: a steroid scan, an atom-weight method for carbon and nitrogen, and a marker-based liquid scan.

All routes caught pure fake samples. The steroid scan flagged fakes by their lack of body-made steroids. The atom-weight route shone on blends: fake urine's atom marks sat far outside the human band, and half-and-half blends still read as off. The marker scan caught blends rich in fake share. The authors pitch atom weights as a strong partner when steroid reads leave doubt.
pmc-13432929:
Jia-Xin Wang and co-authors set out a trial plan in 2026 to test a classic Chinese herbal drink against lasting fatigue after COVID. Fatigue ranks among the most common tails of the illness. Old books record the drink, and fresh lab work backs its power to ease tiredness. The trial will run at one Beijing hospital.

One hundred patients with post-COVID fatigue will draw by lot into drink or fake-drink groups for eight weeks of care, with a month of watch after. Score keepers and math hands stay blind to who got what. A fatigue impact scale leads the reads, joined by mood, worry, sleep, life quality, and a timed walk test. The plan hews to care-as-planned math. The team frames the trial as firm proof on short-term gain and safety.
pmc-13433729:
Man Li and colleagues review immunotherapy for pancreatic cancer driven by KRAS mutations, one of the most aggressive gut cancers. Over 90 percent of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas carry KRAS mutations, which drive tumour growth and reshape the surroundings into a cold, immune-suppressed zone.

Dense scar tissue, dysfunctional immune cells, and a distinct metabolic state blunt checkpoint inhibitors, the main immunotherapy class. The review traces how KRAS builds that cold zone and surveys combination strategies to thaw it, pairing checkpoint drugs with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted drugs such as KRAS G12C and G12D blockers. Oncologists get a strategy guide for a cancer where immunotherapy alone has largely failed.
pmc-13434129:
Prabhat Tiwari led a 2026 field study in Bundelkhand, India, on farms that mix fruit trees, timber trees, and grass for animal feed. Two tree mixes were grown at two spacings during 2024 and 2025. The work asks which mix gives more feed, better feed quality, and more stored carbon.

The mix with custard apple gave taller grass, more green feed, and more dry feed than the mix with pomegranate. It also gave more crude protein in the grass. Wider spacing helped grass growth, while close spacing raised tree mass and stored carbon. The results point to a farm plan that feeds stock well in dry years.
pmc-13434429:
Junxian Du offers an intrusion detector for factory Internet of Things gear on 5G nets, where weak processors and shaky links raise cyber risk. Older hybrid deep-learning detectors struggled here, so a lighter, smarter design was needed.

The detector joins federated learning with attention to a light MobileNetV3 net for feature reads and a mini-transformer for sequence reads. Feature choice by mutual information, plus self-attention layers, lifts key traffic traits like packet size and flow time while dropping redundant ones. Factory operators get a shared detector that learns across devices without pooling sensitive traffic in one place.
pmc-13436429:
Xiangru Cheng and coauthors chart how intermittent fasting rewires jumping genes in mouse tissues in 2026. Mice fasted sixteen hours daily for four months. Gene reads cover liver, skeletal muscle, and cortex, with locus level counts for transposable elements.

The liver answered loudest, with 5,359 jumping genes shifted. Muscle shifted 620, while cortex barely stirred. Modules link jumping genes to nearby host genes that move in step. Liver modules center on metabolism and protein making, while muscle modules center on contraction and chromatin. Jumping genes may act as local dials for fasting gains.
pmc-13437629:
Suye Sun, writing alone in 2026, examined whether university counselors' guidance of student values can lower psychological crisis risk. Chinese campuses face rising student distress, and most research maps risk rather than protection. The first surveyed 800 undergraduates on counselor guidance, sense of meaning, resilience, and crisis vulnerability. The second ran a six-week workshop in sixteen classes, with 319 students completing it, against ordinary mental health lectures.

In the survey, stronger guidance tied to lower vulnerability, through two channels of similar size: students built more meaning in life, and more resilience. In the workshop, the guided group improved more than the lecture group, with gains in meaning and resilience again carrying the change. Sun is frank about limits: the trial was logged internally but not publicly registered ahead of time, so its tests count as exploratory. Registered repeats with longer follow-up must confirm the pattern.
pmc-13438629:
Chenyan Zhou's team developed a hybrid method in 2026 to infer ice loads on polar ship structures from strain readings. Knowing true ice forces is vital for safety, but few sensors and high noise make the inverse problem ill-posed, and older methods traded peak accuracy against smooth background fidelity. Green kernel functions linked strain response to impact loads, and a hybrid penalty mixing L1 and L2 norms was tuned by an information criterion and solved by coordinate descent.

High-fidelity simulations of an ice-class vessel section plus scaled model tests showed the method kept impact peaks while preserving low-amplitude background continuity. Naval engineers get a more physical load estimate for design and monitoring. Full-scale ship trials will test the method in real ice.
pmc-13438729:
Aradhana Chhabra, Riya Kalra, and Kanu Goyal write to qualify a study of hippotherapy, therapy on horseback, that varied the sitting surface under children with special needs. They welcome the question as practical and unexplored. Their 2026 letter then raises five cautions about how the original findings should be read, starting with a classic statistical trap.

The textured surface group improved its own ten-meter walk scores, yet the change did not beat the other groups' changes, so comparative benefit is unproven. One thirty-minute session also cannot show what repeated practice and motor learning would do. Balance, a headline outcome, improved in no group at all, a null the letter says deserved more weight. The children ranged from three to eighteen with mixed conditions, which blurs who exactly benefits. The authors close constructively: bigger, tighter, longer studies can settle whether the horse-rider interface truly shapes rehabilitation gains.
pmc-13439029:
Xin Huang and Jie V Zhao use genetics in a 2026 study to test whether alanine, an amino acid found in meat, plays a causal part in mental illness. Alanine helps move energy between muscle and brain and feeds into brain chemicals tied to mood and thought. Early work gave mixed signals, with some small studies hinting at help for schizophrenia and others raising worry for mood disorders.

The pair applied Mendelian randomisation, a method that uses genes fixed at birth as a stand-in for lifetime alanine levels. They drew gene data from large genome studies covering more than 115,000 people in the UK Biobank. Outcomes covered major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, anxiety, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with checks split by sex. Readers can follow how gene-based tests sidestep many traps of small observational studies.
pmc-13439529:
Sharonmercy Okemwa's team tracked sugary drink intake in 2026 among Kenyan women and teens aged ten to forty-nine, a group with thin evidence despite higher health risks from sugary drinks. Two rounds of national tracking nutrition surveys were analyzed by home place, with odds models for drivers. Over half of women reported sugary drink intake, a bit higher in towns than villages.

Intake peaked among women aged twenty to twenty-nine, those in union, college-schooled women, and richest households, with city living and higher schooling raising odds. Policy makers get a targeting map: taxes, labeling, and schooling should reach urban, schooled, and wealthier consumers, not only the poorest. The cross-sectional design limits causal claims.
pmc-13439629:
You and colleagues examine healthy lifestyle and survival in a modern combined syndrome in this 2026 analysis of two large cohorts. Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome describes the intertwined burden of heart, kidney, and metabolic disease. The team scored lifestyle across seven factors, from smoking and diet to sleep and social connection. They covered over 300,000 affected people in the UK Biobank, plus about 9,800 in a United States cohort.

Each step up the lifestyle score was tied to roughly a fifth lower risk of death in the British cohort. That held overall and for cardiovascular death, with hazard ratios near 0.81 in the fitted models. The United States data showed smaller but similar protection. Physical activity and low sedentary time stood out as the strongest individual factors in both cohorts, and the benefit was greatest when the syndrome was still at an early stage.
pmc-13439829:
Zimmermann and colleagues studied in 2026 how a blood protein called resistin interacts with smoking and sex in depression risk. Resistin is a hormone-like protein from fat tissue linked to inflammation and insulin resistance. The team assessed depressed patients with two symptom scales, one standard and one designed for men.

Higher resistin levels went with a higher risk of major depressive disorder, but the pattern depended on sex and smoking. The link was strongest in women who smoked or had quit smoking. Resistin did not track how severe depression was once present. Alcohol use, in contrast, was the strongest predictor of masculine depression symptoms on the men's scale. The authors argue that prevention should pay special attention to women who smoke and carry metabolic risk.
pmc-13441029:
Hussein Biganeh and colleagues isolate phenolic compounds from the plant Diarthron lessertii and test them against cervical cancer cells, reporting in 2026. Plant phenolics are a rich hunting ground for cancer drug leads. Chromatography pulled nine compounds from shoot extract, spanning lignans, a biflavonoid, a bicoumarin, and five flavonoids, each identified by magnetic resonance and mass readings. A standard viability assay graded their killing of HeLa cells.

One lignan, epinortrachelogenin, hit hardest, halving cell growth at a moderate dose. Reporter tests showed the same compound selectively switching on FOXO3a, a forkhead protein that can order cancer cells to die or stall. Computer docking placed the lignan snugly in the protein's binding pocket, matching the laboratory signal. The authors nominate the compound as a lead for FOXO3a-targeted drug design, pending wider testing.
pmc-13442629:
Sayada Momotaz Akther and colleagues study root-zone microbes in two bermudagrass types under drought in a 2026 paper. One grass type bears drought well, while its twin wilts fast. The team joined chemical scans of root leaks with full gene reads of soil microbes to see how the two halves talk.

Two leak goods, riboflavin and a carboline compound, tracked with a microbe called Massilia putida near tolerant roots. The authors read the pattern as grass-led tuning of its soil crew through chemical signals, a route seed breeders may exploit.
pmc-13443129:

pmc-13443329:

Blocker drugs against the enzyme have reached lab and early clinic stages, a sign of translational pull. Gaps span thin human data and off-target risks. The authors set ranked research aims, from better blockers to clearer maps of who gains most from the drugs.
pmc-13445429:
Han Gong and colleagues review how the body's stress hormone system goes off track after ischemic stroke and drives later harm, in a 2026 narrative review. The system, run from brain to adrenal glands, shapes metabolism, immunity, and mood. Its role in stroke after-effects has drawn less notice than the brain injury itself.

Over months, a system stuck on high can reshape circuits for feeling and thought, feeding depression, anxiety, and poor memory. The review ties these threads into one frame and points to hormone control as a care target.
pmc-13445529:
Hari Shankar Meshram and colleagues model how many organ transplants India needs each year, now and by 2040, in a 2026 study. Transplant is the surest cure for end-stage organ failure, and India runs the world's third largest program, yet no one had sized the unmet need across organs. Supply covered only about seven in a hundred kidney cases and under two in a hundred liver cases. pmc-13445729:
Yanhong Liu and Xingguo Xiao present a 2026 case report of liver vein blockage and multi-cavity fluid buildup caused by chronic arsenic poisoning from a traditional medicine. pmc-13445929:
Mete Ucdal and Evren Ekingen present a 2026 case report of odd nerve-drug deadly syndrome in a 71-year-old comfort care patient, a risky drug reaction that eluded classic rules. pmc-13446329:
Xiaoqing Yuan and colleagues build a diagnostic model for limited mouth opening in jaw joint disorders, joining two scan types, in a 2026 study. A jaw that will not open past a set span wrecks chewing, speech, and daily comfort. Records covered two hundred twenty-six patients, most of them women in their mid-twenties, with four hundred fifty-two joints scanned in all.

Four signs carried the model: age, flattening of the jaw condyle, head height, and a jaw disc slipped forward and stuck. Split into training and test groups, the model sorted limited opening from normal with fair accuracy in both. Fit checks and benefit curves also looked sound. The authors offer the tool for sorting each patient's risk and shaping care to the joint's own state.
pmc-13447829:
María-Isabel González-Siso and coauthors apply a 2026 broad math model to full growth rates of Escherichia coli across heats from 29 to 45 degrees Celsius. Glucose ran from a tenth to 2 percent. The model splits a key time, a glucose-tied balance factor, and a heat-led peak rate.

Doubling times matched printed values. The split tool aids control of helpful and harmful germs in brewing, dirty water, and biofilm settings.
pmc-13447929:
Haonian Li and colleagues study a 2026 investigation of how steel reinforcement shapes bonding and cracking at ultra-high-performance to normal-strength concrete joints, the weak wet joints in precast bridges. Larger bars, longer anchorage, and ribbed bars raised strength and slowed crack widening, while two failure modes appeared in reinforced specimens. Bridge designers gain practical rules for tougher wet joints.
pmc-13448129:
Kwang Nam Jin introduces a July 2026 special issue on essential thoracic trauma imaging for a Korean radiology journal. pmc-13449329:
Robert and co-authors review hair as a double record of environmental chemical exposure. The shaft stores pollutants built up over time. The living follicle offers cells in which body damage can be read. Proving which exposures cause disease is hard. Illnesses emerge decades later, making fast working biomarkers in exposed people valuable.

pmc-13450229:
Hanne Sagsveen Hjorthaug and colleagues map in 2026 the cell types of the thymus lining, the tissue that teaches T cells to tolerate the body's own proteins. pmc-13450529:
Bell and co-authors tracked a regional Australian clinical trials unit in Victoria from 2011 to 2022 to learn what drives growth outside metropolitan centers, where trial access for remote patients lags. pmc-13450629:
Nan Ding and co-authors track in 2026 how a targeted breast cancer drug spread through Dutch care over a decade. Use climbed from under a tenth of patients in the first year to about four fifths by 2018, then held flat. Older patients and those with lower incomes or hormone-linked tumors got the drug less often in the flat years. The authors say the gaps point policy makers to where equal access still fails.
pmc-13451629:
Ferreira and Stocker build a new rat model to separate the jobs of one hormone receptor in thirst and blood pressure. The hormone angiotensin II acts through its type 1a receptor to drive drinking when blood volume falls. The 2026 study uses CRISPR gene editing, a method that cuts DNA at a chosen site. With it, the team deletes that receptor in rats, since mice respond oddly to the hormone.

The knockout rats ran a resting blood pressure about ten points lower than normal, at the same heart rate. pmc-13451929:
Huang and colleagues describe three new species of the congrid eel genus Gnathophis from deep waters off Taiwan in 2026, based on 130 specimens. pmc-13452229:
Ting Peng and a large team map in 2026 how early birth reshapes a newborn's brain networks by the due-date age. Resting brain scans came from a large Chinese cohort, 107 babies born early and 62 born on time. The team read the webs both as still maps and as shifting ones, at whole-brain and node levels.

pmc-13452629:
Lian and colleagues pool the evidence on pairing dupilumab, a lab made antibody drug, with house dust mite immunotherapy for atopic dermatitis, a long lasting itchy skin disease. Immunotherapy trains the immune system with tiny doses of the mite allergen, the trigger found in house dust. Only four studies with 138 patients met the bar, and just one was a randomized trial. The pair showed no clear gain in skin severity at 6 or 12 months. A hint of benefit appeared at 18 months, but the authors rate that evidence as very low in certainty. pmc-13453029:
Lei Xu, Shuang Peng, Zhongjun Huo, Zhixiong Fang, and Yuqing Chen report a case of severe chickenpox pneumonia where the airway itself showed the disease. Their 2026 case report follows a 35 year old man with diabetes whose breathing worsened five days after his rash began. By then most of his skin spots had crusted over, hiding the usual clue.

pmc-13453729:

pmc-13453829:

pmc-13454029:

pmc-13454229:

pmc-13454329:

pmc-13454529:

pmc-13454829:

pmc-13455229:

pmc-13455629:

pmc-13457729:

pmc-13457829:

pmc-13458029:

pmc-13458929:

pmc-13459329:

pmc-13459429:

In that layout, belonging flows through physical exercise and then a growth mindset, the belief that abilities can develop, before reaching mental health. pmc-13459629:

pmc-13460329:

pmc-13461029:

pmc-13461329:

pmc-13461729:

The editorial also urges early diagnosis from childhood and teamwork across dentistry, paediatrics, and primary care.
pmc-13461929:

pmc-13462029:

pmc-13462229:

Together they show how psychological insight can shape clinical work, health service design, and public health planning. The editors stress that modern health systems are complex and needs keep shifting across the lifespan. They call for care models that are joined-up and sensitive to context, serving individuals, professionals, and whole communities alike.
pmc-13462429:
Rui-Zhi He, Min Zhou, Yong-Jun Chen, and Xing-Jun Guo compare, in a 2026 records study, three drug plans meant to shrink advanced pancreatic cancer enough for surgery. Most cannot be removed at diagnosis. Conversion therapy downsizes the tumor until an operation is possible. About thirty-eight percent of patients converted to candidates. The strongest mix, modified FOLFIRINOX, converted the most, near fifty-three percent, ahead of both rivals near a third. Among converted patients, most achieved clean-margin removal, and a third showed major tumor kill. The authors recommend it for fit patients and flag a normalized tumor marker and good nutrition as good signs.
pmc-13462529:
Chunkai Li and colleagues study, in a 2026 analysis, how dryness reshapes soil microbes' abilities by changing the balance of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in soil. Two hundred natural ecosystems across the world's biomes supplied soil measures and gene catalogs from shotgun sequencing. As sites grew drier, the ratios between those elements shifted downward consistently. Gene pools shifted with them, in a coordinated move.

Genes for building cell material, copying RNA, making proteins, and moving cargo inside cells became more common. The pattern reads as a switch from a tearing-down lifestyle to a building-up, drought-resistant one. The authors link element ratios to microbe function across biomes, offering a frame for predicting how drying will reorganize soil life. Such reorganization carries consequences for how carbon and nutrients cycle through ecosystems.
pmc-13463229:
Caminero and Oreja-Guevara reviewed in 2026 a testing problem in multiple sclerosis care that affects safety decisions for the drug natalizumab. Blood tests for antibodies to the JC virus help judge the risk of a rare brain infection called PML in patients on this drug. Many weak positive results on the newer test also faded or flipped back over time. The authors advise reading clashes in context, using antibody strength, persistence over time, and the patient's full picture, not binary cut-offs alone.
pmc-13463629:
Filipa Godoy-Vitorino reports on the first Puerto Rico and Caribbean Microbiome Symposium, held in San Juan in February 2026. More than two hundred researchers, trainees, and partners attended. Talks covered microbes in human health, cancer, infection, diet and immunity, wild ecosystems, and data methods.

The meeting launched the Puerto Rico Center for Microbiome Sciences as a regional hub for multiomics work, meaning studies that read genes, proteins, and small molecules together. Student talks and mentor links sat at the center of the program, alongside plans for shared training across the islands. Readers get a record of a new network tying Caribbean labs to partners worldwide.
pmc-13463929:
Alshahrani and colleagues audited Saudi Red Crescent records in 2026 to measure how often bystanders start CPR. CPR means the chest compressions that can keep a person alive after the heart stops outside a hospital. A strict rule counted CPR only when the registry explicitly credited someone other than the ambulance crew. The records covered cardiac arrests attended in the first half of 2024.

Among the 5,271 classifiable cases, bystander CPR was documented in just 646. That is about 12 in every 100 arrests. Witnessed arrests carried more than five times the odds of bystander CPR. Each extra minute of ambulance response slightly lowered the odds. Wide regional gaps persisted after adjustment. The authors call for dispatcher coaching, wider public training, and cleaner registry forms.
pmc-13464329:
Candelario and colleagues evaluated in 2026 a Los Angeles County experiment in who gets heard in policy. The Reentry Health Advisory Collaborative, founded in 2020, pays people once in prison to advise the safety-net health and justice systems. Three years in, the team surveyed collaborative members. They also surveyed the agency staff, nonprofits, and policymakers who work with them.

All eight members replied, along with 30 collaborators, about six in ten of those asked. Both sides credited members' firsthand experience with sharpening programs. It kept attention on root causes and tailored services to real community conditions. Members described gains in motivation, peer support, and leadership skill. The friction points were power and money. Members felt their influence on big decisions was limited, officials varied in openness, and funding was insecure. Respondents urged earlier involvement in pivotal decisions and steadier grassroots engagement.
pmc-13464729:
Greta Romano leads a team that reads whole genomes of RSV from Italy's 2024-5 season, the first under a national baby protection program. The antibody shot nirsevimab now shields newborns, so tracking virus change matters early. Eighty-eight positive airway checks from two regions went to full sequencing.

Within type A, one lineage led with about two thirds of strains, while all type B strains shared one lineage. Genes for surface and copying parts varied most across the set. No changes known to blunt the antibody shot appeared anywhere, a reassuring first-season read.
pmc-13465329:
Nikhil Raj Selvaraj and eight co-authors craft a family of thiazolone compounds and test them against Alzheimer's-like damage in cells and fruit flies. Oxidative stress and amyloid clumps drive the disease's neuron loss. Their microwave-fast chemistry yielded a series built on a sulfur ring core.

In flies bred to make human amyloid, 3n eased movement and behavior faults. Computer fits placed the compounds inside the acetylcholinesterase pocket, and lab tests confirmed dose-linked blocking of that enzyme. Drug-likeness scores looked clean across the set.
pmc-13465529:
Lindsay A Wilson compared methadone and buprenorphine in 2026 for pregnant patients with opioid use disorder, weighing newborn outcomes. Both drugs are deemed safe in pregnancy, yet head-to-head evidence stayed thin. The review pooled 27 studies covering 14,978 buprenorphine-exposed and 8,358 methadone-exposed pregnancies, reviewing trials and cohort studies apart.

In cohort data, buprenorphine linked to lower risks of preterm birth, low birthweight, small size for age, and withdrawal treatment, with risk ratios from 0.48 to 0.82. No clear gap appeared for withdrawal diagnosis or stillbirth, though stillbirth was rare. The pattern favours buprenorphine for newborn outcomes, while the authors note cohort gaps mean trials and careful advice still matter.
pmc-13465729:
Cong and colleagues published a 2026 study on keeping Sichuan pepper fresh in storage. The spice is prized for its numbing heat and bright scent, both quick to fade. The team tested cold rooms, nitrogen gas, yellow LED light, and all three together. Storage ran for 60 days, with checks on flavor and health-linked plant compounds.

Cold air at five degrees and zero oxygen slowed losses the most in early screening. Yellow light best protected the numbing compound on its own. The three methods combined beat every single method by a wide margin. Losses of two key plant compound groups fell by about half versus plain storage. The combined setup needs no chemical sprays, which suits food sellers well.
pmc-13466129:
Piotr Zawadzki and Łukasz Pierzchała tune a light-driven cleaning process that strips color from the dye methylene blue, in a 2026 water treatment study. Their method activates persulfate salts with visible light, helped by glucose, to create aggressive radicals that attack the dye. A statistical design tested how acidity, glucose dose, salt level, and starting dye strength interact.

Best results came at a fairly acidic setting with set doses of each ingredient, reaching about sixty-three percent color removal at the middle dye level. Reaction speed followed a simple first-order pattern across runs. Scavenger tests showed both sulfate and hydroxyl radicals at work, and the process stayed effective across a tenfold range of dye strengths.
pmc-13466229:
Zheng and colleagues search biopsy tissue taken before treatment for a gene pattern predicting whether ulcerative colitis patients will respond to anti-TNF therapy, in 2026 gastroenterology research. Ulcerative colitis is chronic bowel inflammation, and anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab fail many patients. The team combined gene activity data from three independent patient cohorts totaling 79 people, prioritizing patterns that recurred across cohorts over single genes that replicated poorly in past studies.

When each dataset was held out in turn, the signature still separated non-responders, with a pooled effect size of 1.36 in standardized units. Pathways for inflammation, TNF signaling, and tissue remodeling dominated the non-responder pattern, while energy-production pathways marked responders. Zheng presents the tissue state, measured before any drug, as a reproducible guide for choosing therapy.
pmc-13466329:
Iftikhar ud Din, Daud Khan, and Tayeb Denidni design a flat patterned surface that soaks up microwaves in three separate bands, in a 2026 engineering study. The pattern pairs a square metal ring with two nested ten-sided resonators on a common circuit board material backed by metal. Target bands sit inside the S, C, and X ranges used by communication systems.

Simulations tuned the shape until absorption topped ninety-nine percent at each of the three peaks. Field maps and current patterns showed the coupled metal parts trapping energy inside the structure, where it fades as heat. Symmetry keeps performance nearly equal for either wave orientation, and absorption held steady for signals arriving at angles up to sixty degrees.
pmc-13466529:
Karumbi and colleagues built a core outcome set for newborn research in Kenya in 2026, testing whether a rich-country set could be adapted instead of starting fresh. A core outcome set is the agreed minimum every trial should measure. None existed for sub-Saharan Africa, where newborn deaths remain high. Twelve outcomes made the final set. Five won instant unanimous backing: survival, hospital stay length, feeding and growth, thinking ability, and vision problems. Five were Kenya-specific, reflecting local costs and family burdens. The study shows adaptation works, but only with genuine local reshaping.
pmc-13466729:
Shun Nakahara, Bradley Fujiuchi, Toru Nakata, and Lorrance Majewski describe a fungal brain infection hidden behind low blood sodium in an older man, in a 2026 case report. The seventy-seven-year-old had taken the immune-damping drug fingolimod for multiple sclerosis for fifteen years. He arrived after four weeks of growing confusion, with no fever and no classic neck stiffness signs.

The authors warn that in patients on such drugs, low sodium and muddled thinking may be the infection's main mask.
pmc-13466829:
Huang and Li reviewed a 2026 account of small cell carcinoma of the cervix, a rare but highly aggressive cervical cancer making up only one to two percent of cases. It invades early, spreads readily, and returns often despite treatment. High risk human papillomavirus, especially type 18, is recognised as a core driver.

Tumour diversity, treatment resistance, and spread are tied back to those molecular features throughout. The authors propose a closed loop model where laboratory research answers clinical questions and clinical practice feeds questions back.
pmc-13467129:
Rizwan Barkat and colleagues check two suspects for clots forming inside a graft after planned aortic arch replacement, in a 2026 records study. The frozen elephant trunk operation leaves a fabric tube where clots appear in about a tenth of patients. Transfused blood products and the choice of clot-preserving drug were the suspects, since both shift clotting balance.

Every non-emergency arch replacement at their center from 2017 to mid-2025 entered the analysis, with clots defined on follow-up scans. Neither transfusion volumes during or after surgery nor the choice between aprotinin and tranexamic acid tracked with clot formation. Known drivers such as aneurysm disease and graft position remain the likelier explanations, which refocuses prevention efforts.
pmc-13468129:
Samuel Haeuser and co-authors image in 2026 the protected edge channels of the topological material ZrTe5 at the nanoscale, using a cryogenic near-field infrared microscope of their own design. Such helical edge modes promise charge transport without the usual energy loss, but watching them directly at high frequencies has been difficult. The experiment ran at 1.8 kelvin under magnetic fields up to 5 tesla while scanning the crystal surface.

A magnetic field made the edge channels brighten in the infrared signal, a signature the authors read as the edge states electric polarizability switching on. Remarkably, that high-frequency response survived magnetic conditions that normally shut down edge conduction at low frequencies. The images also showed a two-lane reorganization of the edge channels. Direct views of how these edges behave in real use help teams judge them for low-loss electronics.
pmc-13468329:
Taiwo Musa Adeniji and colleagues present in 2026 a soft-template recipe for nanoporous gold with pores at several size scales at once. Spongy gold made by dissolving away a partner metal offers huge surface area and excellent conductivity for sensors, catalysts, and energy devices. A single pore size, however, forces a trade-off between surface area and how fast fluids can move through. Their method uses a polysaccharide polymer as a mold alongside metal reduction, annealing, and chemical dealloying.

The result is a self-supporting gold monolith whose structure visibly spans two length scales, with larger channels feeding fine nanopores. The authors describe the route as reliable, simple, economical, and environmentally friendly, with room to scale up. Optimizing area and transport together matters most in flow-through uses such as biosensing, biofiltration, and catalysis, which are the applications they name.
pmc-13468429:
Vega-Baudrit, Lopretti, and Orozco published a 2026 review on a hard measurement problem. Their subject is nanoplastics, plastic bits far too small to see, in drinking water. Following a set review method, the authors screened records and kept 22 studies for close reading. Common tools such as standard infrared scans proved too coarse for true nanoscale bits. Newer laser and heat-based methods each help, but each misses some key detail. No single method gives size, shape, plastic type, and amount at once. The authors call for shared test samples and paired methods before rules are set.
pmc-13468529:
Xiaochen Zhang and six colleagues published this 2026 scoping review of OpenCap, a free smartphone-based system that captures human movement without the markers and camera arrays of laboratory motion capture. Only 23 of the 51 studies had benchmarked it against gold-standard systems, and most enrolled few participants, so the authors warn against broad claims. They call for larger validation datasets, tougher tracking under occlusion, and sensing before OpenCap's accuracy can be assumed across populations.
pmc-13468929:
Shi and colleagues design a portable sensor measuring the dielectric constant of materials, a property describing how a substance stores electrical energy, in 2026 electronics research. Their probe is a short-ended transmission line built on an air coplanar waveguide, with a parallel resistor at its input. Different materials resting on the probe shift its resonance frequency, where its reflection peaks. Reading that shift lets the system work out the dielectric constant without outside lab gear.

Tests on six materials, powdered solids and liquids, confirmed the device could measure dielectric constants accurately. The authors analyze when the frequency-to-constant conversion stays valid, and which interference factors, such as resistor drift and material losses, threaten precision. Shi calls the sensor a simpler, more precise alternative.
pmc-13469729:
Ziyan Zhang and co-authors issue a correction in 2026 to their 2021 Sensors paper on rebuilding and tracking the surface of a silicone heart in three dimensions. The notice concerns only the reference list of the original study. A set of citations numbered in the original list was judged unrelated or unsuitable for the work and has been removed.

The correction republishes the amended references so the record points to sources that match the study topic. Nothing in the notice alters the original experiments, the surface reconstruction method, or the reported findings. Readers citing the heart study should follow the updated reference list.
pmc-13469829:

Five themes emerged, covering the program aims, wanted functions and design, content, acceptability, and use after discharge from the unit. Parents and staff sometimes weighted features differently, which the mapping process made visible. The authors say these user insights will guide building and refining the program. Later studies are planned to test usability, feasibility, and effects.
pmc-13470029:
Xu and colleagues in the United States asked in 2026 what deep space rays do to blood vessels more than a year after the dose. Moon and Mars crews will soak in mixed rays that Earth's shield blocks. Apollo crews hint at more heart deaths, but long term proof is thin. The team dosed plaque prone mice with a NASA mixed ray field, and kept a gamma group as Earth like gauge. The mice lived on plain feed to old age.

Vessel skin over the plaques told a worn tale in the space ray group. Two seam marks that keep the skin tight and sound sat far below plain marks. The loss points to a leaky, weak skin long after the trip dose. Plaque checks sat in the same frame of harm. The authors warn that heart risk plans for deep space crews must count this slow vessel wear.
pmc-13470329:
Axelle E. Deroubaix and colleagues mapped a plant immune module in 2026 linking surface-triggered and intracellular immunity in Arabidopsis. pmc-13471329:

Personalized choices, they argue, are now the central challenge.
pmc-13471429:
Bhandari and colleagues measured how widespread canine distemper, a contagious and often fatal viral disease, is among free-roaming dogs living around Bardiya National Park in Nepal. Their 2026 survey collected blood samples from 91 dogs in the park's buffer zone and tested them for virus antibodies.

Just over half the dogs carried antibodies: apparent prevalence was 52.75% of the sample, and an adjusted true prevalence came to 53.28% after correcting for test error. Dogs older than 72 months showed the highest rate at 80% seropositivity, though no factor reached statistical significance. Because these dogs roam where tigers and leopards live, the authors warn the virus sits enzootic, steadily present, as a spillover risk to wildlife.
pmc-13472729:

A random forest model with forward selection reached 89.8 percent accuracy on held-out folds and produced a compact panel of just 13 genes. That panel kept a held-out accuracy score, measured as area under the curve, of 0.960 in the same data. On two independent cohorts of 500 and 159 tumors, accuracy reached 74.8 percent and 69.18 percent respectively in external testing.
pmc-13472929:

One branch models smooth motion over time, a second highlights repeating periodic patterns, and a third catches brief sudden changes linked to diarrhea. It beat the tested baseline models by up to about nine percentage points, while its trainable fusion head held only about 1.3 million parameters, a small size for deployment. The authors present the model as an efficient tool for fine-grained livestock health monitoring.
pmc-13473129:
Dong and colleagues studied soil organic carbon in 2026 in the salty farmland of China's Yellow River Delta, comparing bare land with land where wheat followed rice in rotation. Wheat growing changed soil water, salt, and nutrient patterns and generally raised enzyme activity. Statistical modeling singled out one enzyme, sucrase, as the key driver in the wheat system. In bare land, a different enzyme and available phosphorus mattered more, showing the two systems run on different controls.
pmc-13474829:
Zhenyan Li and Lin Liu study nursing-linked risks in 2026 for pancreas inflammation after a bile duct scope procedure. Overall, just under seven percent developed the complication, and most cases were mild. A combined risk model is offered for bedside triage.
pmc-13475629:
Phuntsho Wangdi and a team of co-authors compare stress among school students in Bhutan, with and without a mindfulness and yoga program. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The program draws on Bhutanese traditional practice and runs in selected schools to support student well-being.

The team surveyed one thousand thirty-five students in grades nine to twelve across four schools. pmc-13476229:

Raising frequency cut the time to reach mid force by about a quarter. Wireless soft muscles suit light robots and wearables.
pmc-13476329:
Soo Yeon Lee and a team of co-authors watch bacteria break down biodegradable plastics in compost, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Four plastics went into a forty-one-day aerobic compost fed with treated sewage sludge. The team tracked surface damage, germ growth, and the genes at work.

All four plastics cracked and drew germ films, with PHB and PBAT hit hardest. PLA drew the least growth. The plastics barely shifted the overall germ mix but boosted a few genera. Genes for breaking PHB ran most abundant. The compost matured fully with no germs of concern found.
pmc-13476729:

Between September 2024 and January 2026, the unit enrolled 400 admissions from 359 patients, about 77 percent of those eligible. Newborn admissions numbered 227, spanning extremely early births to full-term babies, and child admissions numbered 173. The records cover 3,600 patient days and over 20,000 manual notes, amounting to about three terabytes of data. pmc-13477129:

Short-term deaths were rare and similar in both groups, and ten-year survival also showed no clear gap. The authors argue that care should follow each patient's anatomy and overall risk rather than valve shape alone.
pmc-13477529:
Yazid Abualkebash and colleagues studied blood inflammation scores in anal cancer in 2026. The cancer is rare, and outcomes vary widely. Standard care pairs chemotherapy with radiation. pmc-13478329:

pmc-13478529:

The model matched permit and building patterns in time and space, offering a portable planning aid for uncertain recoveries.
pmc-13478629:

pmc-13479729:

pmc-13479829:

pmc-13479929:
