Standard error measures judged accuracy on the test years. The authors present the hybrid as a first application of this design to provincial tuberculosis planning.
pmc-13480029:
Vincent Legros and co-authors present a 2026 study of heart stoppage outside hospital caused by a burst brain aneurysm. Cases were drawn from twelve French intensive care units for the brain between 2014 and 2024. Among nearly sixteen thousand bleed admissions, 164 patients arrived alive after this type of arrest, and the team tracked their brain recovery at six months.

Only eight patients, under five percent, reached a good level of recovery. Most died, and about two in three met brain death within about a day. Shorter low-flow time and less use of adrenaline tended to appear in survivors, yet no single factor proved decisive on its own. Drain placement, pressure checks, and aneurysm repair were more common in those who lived. The findings stress both the grim odds and the value of organ donation planning.
pmc-13480229:
Abdullah Mohammed Al Farqani and colleagues report a 2026 series testing an extra-large replacement lung valve in four patients. Their outflow tracts had stretched too wide for standard catheter valves, leaving surgery as the usual path. Each patient had severe backward leak through the lung valve and a swollen right heart chamber.

Inflating a test balloon during the procedure showed a usable landing ring near 32 millimetres in every case, despite wider scans at rest. The team placed a custom 35-millimetre balloon valve, adding stents first where the tract bulged and going direct where a narrow waist held. All four placements succeeded, the leak vanished, pressure gaps stayed low, and no major harm followed. Live sizing during the procedure may open catheter treatment to patients once ruled out by size alone.
pmc-13480529:
Erfan Oftadeh and co-authors describe a 2026 greener way to forge carbon-nitrogen bonds with a palladium catalyst. Nature runs its chemistry in far from pure water, so the team tried couplings that sit on strongly basic water made with potassium hydroxide, dubbed dirty water. The base comes built in, which removes a separate dosing step.

Reactions ran fast, and the thick basic layer kept fragile groups such as esters and nitriles safe by holding the organic partners out of full solution. The same basic water served again in later runs, keeping waste scores very low. Side-by-side checks against recent routes with palladium, nickel, or copper in organic solvents favoured the water method on waste and ease. Enzyme steps could even run in sequence in the same pot. The team sees room to extend the trick to other bond types.
pmc-13480729:
Yang Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 smart window that shifts among three states using heat and light alone. Buildings burn huge energy on cooling, and glass that admits heat freely makes the load worse. Their film pairs light-driven molecular motors with liquid crystal polymer, so sun and warmth themselves flip the window between clear, mirror-like, and frosted modes.

Visible light passage swung by about three quarters across modes, while heat-carrying infrared swung by about half. Building simulations showed clear cooling savings across cities with varied climates. Since no wiring or steady power is needed, the film suits retrofits as well as new builds. The triple-state range beats the usual clear-or-dark choice that older smart glass offers.
pmc-13483229:
Al-Dujaili and team compared two gases for squeezing more oil from the Asmari rock formation in southeastern Iraq. Their 2026 simulation study focused on the Abu-Ghirab field, where water for the usual flooding method grows scarce as the climate dries. The team modeled pumping carbon dioxide or nitrogen into the reservoir, a method that keeps pressure up and pushes oil toward wells without the gases fully mixing into the oil.

Carbon dioxide raised the oil production rate far more than nitrogen did in the modeled scenarios presented. Wells on the flanks of the field produced over 5,000 barrels per day, beating wells on the crest. Wells near the fault kept the cleanest output, with water making up roughly 18 percent of flow. Nitrogen sharply inflated the gas-to-oil ratio, a drawback Al-Dujaili weighs against its easier supply.
pmc-13483529:
Chuai and colleagues searched in 2026 for gene markers tied to neutrophil extracellular traps in the intestinal scarring that can follow long-running ulcerative colitis. These traps are web-like structures that immune cells cast out, and they can drive fibrosis, meaning harmful tissue thickening. The team mined public gene data from colitis patients.

They found 99 trap-related genes with changed activity, then used machine learning and network analysis to narrow the list. Three genes, IL1RN, MUC1, and SERPINA1, emerged as a marker panel linked to immune signaling and the gut's protective mucus layer. Their activity tracked with several immune cell types in patient tissue. A mouse model of the condition confirmed all three genes were unusually active in scarred intestine, supporting the panel for diagnosis research.
pmc-13485629:
Mark R. Marshall and others ask why lowering the sodium level of dialysis fluid failed to shrink heart muscle in a recent trial, despite improving other tests. In 2026, the causal analysis re-examines home and satellite hemodialysis patients, tracing paths from treatment assignment through fluid volume, blood pressure, weight gain, and medication dose to left ventricular mass.

Fluid volume strongly drove heart mass, and blood pressure during and between sessions had modest effects, while weight gain between sessions and drug dose had none. Lower-sodium fluid cut weight gain and slightly reduced drug dose but did not move fluid volume or blood pressure, the actual drivers. The analysis explains the trial's surprise and redirects focus to fluid and blood pressure control.
pmc-13488129:
Bowen Zhang and colleagues test adding low-dose esketamine to pain control after major pancreatic surgery in a 2026 randomized trial. The operation, which removes the head of the pancreas and nearby tissue, often leaves patients with severe pain and low mood. Eighty patients received patient-controlled pain pumps with either a standard opioid alone or the opioid plus esketamine, a drug related to ketamine that can lift mood.

Depression rates on day three were similar between groups in the main comparison. Mood score change by day five favored the esketamine group, patients pressed the pump less often, and total opioid use was lower with the added drug. Two inflammation markers also fell at different time points. The authors call the mood benefit possible, not proven.
pmc-13489629:
Ting Liu and colleagues test a blended teaching model in endocrinology training in a 2026 quasi-experimental study at a Guangdong hospital. The model fuses problem-based learning, where students work through clinical cases, with a six-step lesson frame that runs from opening hook to summary. Records from 2022 to 2025 covered 285 students, split between the blended cohort and a conventionally taught cohort at the same hospital.

The blended group scored higher on every graded component, including written exams and total score, in the reported comparisons. Satisfaction also ran higher on all ten survey items, with the biggest gaps in creativity, clinical thinking, interest, and communication. Attendance tracked strongly with exam success in both groups. The authors back wider adoption in competency-based training.
pmc-13490429:
Anliang Huang and others use graph learning on lipid chemistry to explain why triglyceride levels alone predict pancreatitis poorly. In 2026, the study launches DeepLipiDecipher, a network model that joins lipid chemical structures with energy connections, and tests it in 433 people with high blood fats or hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis. Some patients with severe lipid elevation stay well while others with modest elevation become critically ill.

The model distinguished pancreatitis cases with a rightness score of 0.810, beating standard machine learning. Risk tracked a structural pattern of many-double-bond and ether-linked fats rather than total fat mass. Causal analysis implicated ceramide buildup through one enzyme and peroxidation driven by another, pointing to a new immunometabolic target for preventing advance to organ injury.
pmc-13490729:
Saeed Aldarwish and others test whether a difficulty score for laparoscopic liver surgery also predicts troubles across surgery approaches. In 2026, the look-back study covers 168 patients who had anatomical liver resection between 2014 and 2018 at a tertiary center, stratified by the IWATE score. Open procedures used a modified score subtracting one point as an exploratory adjustment.

Higher difficulty independently predicted more after surgery troubles and more revision surgery, with strong predictive rightness for both results. Laparoscopic cases showed less blood loss, fewer transfusions, and faster recovery. The authors propose IWATE as a universal before surgery risk tool, pending forward-looking testing.
pmc-13492329:
Hiro Kawata and others report the first merged use of left bundle branch pacing with leadless left ventricular heart lining pacing. In 2026, the case concerns a patient who had not responded to standard cardiac resynchronization therapy, which paces both ventricles through a coronary sinus lead. About a third of such patients fail to respond.

Adding a wireless heart lining electrode inside the left ventricle to left bundle branch area pacing narrowed the QRS complex clearly and a lot improved pumping function and heart failure status. The authors propose this merged plan for selected patients who remain nonresponders to standard resynchronization or conduction system pacing alone.
pmc-13493729:
Rachele Danieli and others compare two SPECT/CT camera systems for testing lutetium-177 action after radiopharmaceutical therapy. In 2026, the study scans a phantom with printed kidney and spine inserts mimicking patient action one day after a standard dose. It tests both a ring-shaped CZT system and a standard dual-head sodium iodide system, then confirms results in patients.

Total action deviated by thirteen percent on the ring system versus zero on the standard system, yet tumour and kidney quantification after correction was slightly better on the ring system. Background action was badly overestimated on the ring system, and reproducibility was lower. The authors suggest longer scans for the ring system and caution about low-uptake regions.
pmc-13493829:
Zalewski and co-authors examine whether narrow-spectrum LEDs could light roads more cheaply at night. After dark, drivers' vision sits in the mesopic range between daylight and darkness. Standards are written for brighter, daylight-like vision, so lamps are judged by rules that may waste energy at night. In the 2026 laboratory work, the team tested LED chips emitting single colours from blue-green to orange-red and computed how much light vision actually gets from each at low brightness.

For chips between green and yellow-green, useful light output rose as the scene got dimmer, the opposite of what standard ratings suggest. A yellow-green lamp and one blended spectrum each promised up to a fifth better energy efficiency than old sodium streetlights at the lowest levels modelled. The authors call the option worth developing, not yet proven on real roads.
pmc-13495229:
Chaofan Zhang and a large team chart, in a 2026 study, how quinoa and its wild kin adapted to high altitude in the Chenopodium genus. Quinoa splits into highland and lowland forms, yet the genetic and regulatory roots of that split were hazy. The team re-read the genomes of 558 samples from twenty species and added gene activity data from 295 of them.

The data showed rich diversity, uneven change in the crop's two subgenomes, and gene flow between species. A wild relative had fed helpful variation into farm quinoa, above all in stress and defense genes. Both farm and wild forms bore matching marks of selection for altitude, hitting shared genes for nutrient transport and flowering time. A huge map of gene control switches tied one switch, near a clock gene, to deletions common in highland plants. The authors offer the resource for breeding tougher quinoa.
pmc-13495429:
Annalisa Maraone and colleagues measure, in a 2026 study from Rome, demoralization in people with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Demoralization is a state of helplessness and lost hope. It overlaps with depression yet is not the same, and it may call for different care. The team recruited 43 adults from a clinic and scored how severe the illness was, plus demoralization and depression, with standard scales.

Both low mood and demoralization were widespread. The state reached a serious level in nearly nine in ten patients. A subgroup showed strong demoralization without matching depression, proof the two can part ways. It deepened as obsessions grew worse. The authors argue that spotting this state can sharpen the picture and tailor therapy beside standard treatment. They call for longer studies on how it steers the course of the illness.
pmc-13498429:
Joerg Klepper, Lucia Kiesel, and Eva Runkel report in 2026 that movement episodes in a rare glucose transport disorder can last far longer than textbooks describe. The condition limits how glucose reaches the brain, and exertion can trigger sudden muscle tightening, mainly in the legs. Published episodes usually run 20 to 30 minutes, yet families increasingly described attacks lasting hours.

Among 60 patients seen at one centre over four years, 26 experienced exertion-triggered episodes despite a special high-fat diet used as treatment. Eighteen had episodes under an hour, while eight had prolonged attacks lasting from over an hour up to a full day. The authors stress that these long episodes resist diet treatment and place a heavy burden on patients and families.
pmc-13498929:
Ciaran Moore and five co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-six on mouth health in older adults with head and neck cancer or pre-cancer mouth spots. The team searched four databases across six decades of work. A set framed ask weighs harm rates in the old with illness against the old with none and the young with illness. Just eight studies made the final cut.

Finds clash across the eight. Two studies gave older patients better life quality scores after care than younger ones in some fields. Two others found no age gap at all. One ties age to dry mouth after radiation in a straight line. No data at all cover the pre-cancer spots. The team calls the proof thin.
pmc-13499729:
Matthew Todd and co-authors summarise in 2026 the landmark cardiology trials of 2025, drawn from the year's major international heart conferences. Heart medicine moves quickly, and clinicians need a filtered view of which results should change practice or shape future guidelines. The team screened trials presented at leading cardiology meetings and kept those with the highest likely impact and broad relevance across the field.

More than 80 key trials were identified in total. Highlights included challenges to the standard year of dual blood-thinning therapy after stenting, plus new drug-coated balloon data. Valve replacement and closure device updates featured too, alongside advances in heart failure, muscle disease of the heart, and prevention. Trial names and designs are catalogued by subspecialty, giving clinicians a single map of a crowded year and researchers a guide to where evidence shifted most.
pmc-13500429:
Akihiro Usui leads a 2026 multicentre Japanese analysis of whether free cancer cells found in wash fluid during bowel cancer surgery predict return of disease differently by tumour side. Data came from a prospective observational study of stage II and III colorectal cancers removed with curative intent, now reanalysed by right-sided versus left-sided origin and by wash cytology result. A total of 1,500 patients qualified, split between right and left sides.

Fewer than one patient in twenty-five had positive wash cytology in the reported share. Among those who relapsed, positive cytology, deep tumour stage, and right-sided location each independently predicted spread within the abdomen. Cytology-negative patients on the left fared worse on relapse-free survival than those on the right, while overall survival matched. Once relapse occurred after positive cytology, right-sided patients survived for a shorter time.
pmc-13500629:
Shunshun Liu and Prasanna V Balachandran build in 2026 an active learning workflow that predicts a key strength descriptor in refractory high-entropy alloys, exotic mixes of several heat-resistant metals in equal shares. The descriptor, misfit volume, captures how much each atom's size and electronic character distorts the crystal, and crude averaging rules miss the local relaxation that matters. Their loop couples quantum-level calculations with ensemble machine learning across 126 five-element alloys, choosing which compositions to calculate next for maximum information gain.

Analysis plots showed atomic size mismatch driving the descriptor directly, while differences in electronegativity, the pull atoms exert on electrons, partly compensated electronically. Feeding the learned values into a mechanistic strength model reproduced measured yield strengths well across diverse compositions in the reported checks. The workflow promises cheaper screening of alloys for jet engines, nuclear systems, and power plants.
pmc-13500829:
Aparna Chaudhuri leads an eight-author team with a 2026 computational design of a peptide vaccine meant to cover all four dengue virus serotypes. Dengue spreads by mosquito bite in the tropics, and the licensed vaccine protects unevenly across serotypes. Working in software, the team screened the viral envelope protein for short fragments, called epitopes, that the immune system can recognize. Candidate fragments between 45 and 65 amino acids were checked for immune visibility, allergy risk, and toxicity before assembly into one construct.

The final construct scored 0.7991 on an antigenicity scale and was predicted non-allergenic and non-toxic. Docking showed it binding strongly to immune receptors TLR2 and TLR3 and to antibody chains, with energies near minus 13.9 to minus 11.3 kilocalories per mole. Simulated immune responses showed raised B-cell and T-cell activity, and codon optimization suggested the construct could be produced in E. coli. Laboratory and animal testing remain ahead.
pmc-13501629:
Barış Baydemir leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 biomechanical study of what makes freestyle swimmers fast over a short sprint. Twelve licensed male swimmers aged 18 to 25, each with at least three years of competitive experience, had their body measurements recorded and their best 25-metre freestyle times documented. Stroke count, stroke length, stroke frequency, and glide time were extracted from recordings with Kinovea, a two-dimensional motion analysis program.

Swim time correlated significantly with all three technique measures. Higher stroke frequency and longer glide time went with faster times, showing negative correlations. Longer stroke length, by contrast, went with slower times in this group, a positive correlation the authors flag for individual technical review rather than a general rule. They recommend that training programmes develop stroke rate, stroke length, and glide use in balance instead of chasing any single parameter.
pmc-13501729:
Mira Miraturrofi'ah leads a four-author team with a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of family-centered communication for parents of premature babies. Babies born early face high risks, above all in low-resource settings, and coaching families to talk and take part in care may help families care better and improve outcomes. Evidence so far is scattered, so the team lays out its full plan in advance, following PRISMA-P guidance. The review is registered in PROSPERO.

Eligible studies will test communication programmes delivered by health staff to parents or caregivers of preterm babies without major conditions. Designs range from randomized trials to observational studies. Five databases will be searched using a Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome framework, with two reviewers screening, appraising, and extracting data separately. Results will be combined in narrative form under SWiM guidance, with meta-analysis where the data allow and GRADE ratings.
pmc-13501829:
Lili Zhu leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 comparison of two childhood lung viruses in Wenzhou, China. Human metapneumovirus and respiratory syncytial virus both cause acute lower respiratory infections, a leading killer of young children. Hospitals there tested 15,772 admitted children during 2021 and 2022 with a multiplex PCR panel. Some 889 children, 5.6 percent, carried the metapneumovirus, while 2,196, or 13.9 percent of those screened, carried RSV in the same testing round.

The two infections looked different at the bedside. Metapneumovirus patients were older, with a median age of 2.5 years against 1.6 years, and more often had underlying conditions. Their fevers ran longer and hotter, and blood markers of inflammation, including C-reactive protein at 14.18 against 7.80 milligrams per litre, ran higher. RSV patients showed more breathing distress signs. Chest imaging in the metapneumovirus group showed more consolidation and collapsed lung segments.
pmc-13503829:
Damodharan Palaniappan leads a team that built a screening tool for diabetic eye disease, in a 2026 paper. The disease is a top cause of sight loss that can be prevented if caught early. Screening must work across cameras and clinics, yet past models often fail on new data sets and miss rare severe stages.

Their tool builds on a transformer design that reads images in patches at several scales. Prep steps boost contrast so faint lesions stand out. Training weighs the rare classes more, so severe stages are not swamped by mild ones. Across three public data sets the tool scored accuracy near 97 percent, with strong recall of advanced disease. The code is shared in public for checks by others.
pmc-13503929:
Jianjun Zeng, Ziyang Cheng, and Yanqiang Cui track four ecosystem services in China's Shule River Basin from 1980 to 2020, in a 2026 study. The services are water yield, soil keeping, carbon storage, and habitat quality. A standard model suite simulated each service across the basin.

Water yield and carbon storage rose over the four decades, while soil keeping slipped slightly and habitat quality dipped a touch. Rich service zones cluster in high mountains at the basin's south edges; poor zones sit in the dry northwest. Rain, water loss to air, and height best explained where water yield was high. Slope ruled soil keeping. Land use, climate, and terrain mattered far more than people or wealth in shaping the patterns.
pmc-13505029:
Naema Ibrahim, Abdiqani Abdikadir Mohamoud, and Abdirahman Omer Ali study why patients start dialysis at the main hospital in Hargeisa, Somaliland, in a 2026 paper. Rich countries often start dialysis on lab numbers found in routine care. The team expected Somaliland starts to be driven by symptoms, given late presentation and thin early care.

Records covered 123 new dialysis patients over two years. Poisoning symptoms from kidney failure led: a stomach form of uremic illness in about 44 percent, and a brain form in about 29 percent. Nearly all patients came from the home region of the hospital. Men more often showed the stomach form, women the brain form. The authors call the pattern a sign of crash-landing starts and urge wider early screening.
pmc-13507129:
Jingwen Zhang leads a 2026 team that adds transcript awareness to rare variant hunting in heart and lung traits. Genes can make several transcript versions, and standard tests that use one version can miss real effects. Their method tests each version, then combines results into one gene score while keeping false alarms in check.

Simulations showed power close to knowing the best version in advance. Applied to whole-genome data from over 240000 people in the All of Us program across 129 traits, the method found eleven new gene links and recovered forty-seven known ones. For the TTN gene, it pinpointed the N2B version as the strongest tie to heart muscle disease.
pmc-13507229:
Carlos M Vallez, David Contreras, and Mario Castro build, in 2026 work, an interpretable probability framework for demand in BiciMad, Madrid's dock-based bike share system. Demand swings with hour, weather, station, and day type, yet records show only part of true demand. Their model generates synthetic trips under stated assumptions so planners can test ideas safely.

Trip distances follow one standard curve family, while hourly counts use another that allows extra spread and responds to rain and day type. Checks against 2018 data showed well-calibrated uncertainty bands. A 2019 consistency check even exposed systematic timestamp errors, later confirmed by the provider. The tool serves demand study and data auditing, not full operations simulation.
pmc-13507829:
Long Li, Haiyi Cheng, Guangzhao Jin, and Rize Jing report a study from two thousand twenty-six on internet use and mental health among older adults in China. As public services move online, many older people feel forced to use the internet. The authors ask whether use that feels pressured helps mood as much as use that is freely chosen.

They drew on survey data from more than five thousand adults aged fifty and older. About twenty-seven percent of users fell into the pressured pattern. Voluntary use linked to fewer depressive symptoms, partly because it made people feel younger than their years. Pressured use showed no clear benefit over nonuse. The authors urge support for self-driven digital participation rather than forced adoption.
pmc-13508229:
Rajdeep Jajoriya and six co-authors hunt gene regions that shape rice straw quality, aiming to make straw better feed and industrial material, in 2026 work. Rice straw is produced in huge amounts, but its fiber and silica make it hard for animals to digest. The team measured straw parts in 207 diverse rice lines plus 25 farm varieties. Traits covered silica, lignin, cellulose, plant size, and lab digestibility. A genome scan on a subset of lines used dense DNA markers.

High silica tracked strongly with poor digestibility, while lignin effects shifted with other components. The scan found 33 marker links spread across the genome for these traits. Several landed near known genes for silica uptake and fiber building. Certain gene versions cut silica by up to about one sixth and lignin by about one quarter. Breeders could use those versions to raise straw value without harming the grain crop.
pmc-13509229:
Zeng and colleagues compare tiny parcels released by the back of the human eye in 2026 research on retinal disease. These parcels, called extracellular vesicles, carry proteins between cells and reflect the state of the tissue that made them. The team collected vesicles from the macula, the central region used for sharp vision, and from the peripheral retina of donor eyes, asking whether their cargo differs by region.

Explants from four non-diseased donor eyes were cultured, and vesicles were isolated and checked by electron microscopy and particle tracking. The particles measured between 119 and 140 nanometers across, confirming they were small vesicles in both regions. Protein profiling then showed a clear regional split: macular and peripheral samples separated in both the vesicle data and the surrounding fluid. Pathway analysis linked macular vesicle proteins to functions that may explain why the macula is prone to disease.
pmc-13510829:
Raymundo A. Munoz and colleagues review a simpler urine diversion used after bladder removal for muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The method, single-stoma cutaneous ureterostomy, brings both urine tubes to one skin opening and skips any bowel surgery.

The standard alternative, an ileal conduit, uses a piece of bowel and carries more surgical burden, the review notes. Newer refinements of the older method show shorter operations and faster recovery than the conduit in early data. The option appeals most for older or frail patients, where cutting operative burden matters most. Problems still needing watch include narrowing of the opening, catheter dependence, infections, and long-term kidney health. Munoz stresses that randomised trials are lacking, so most evidence comes from small backward-looking studies.
pmc-13512829:
Martinez-Zujeros and colleagues published a 2026 study on recovery paths of older hospital patients. Rehab wards treat elders whose daily abilities vary wildly at admission. The team clustered 957 patients by how their independence scores moved over time. Records came from one geriatric rehab unit between 2019 and 2025.

Four recovery profiles emerged from the machine-learning grouping in the study. Two groups regained independence well and showed strong bounce-back overall. The other two stayed limited by chronic damage or severe impairment. Walking ability and muscle strength traced the same split across profiles. Stable groups could guide tailored rehab plans for each new arrival. Check methods agreed, which supports the profiles' stability over resampling. Walking category and muscle testing joined independence scores in the records.
pmc-13514429:
Xindi Feng and Zhongjun Wang published a 2026 engineering study on why screwdriver bits snap. The bits are made from alloy steel. Fractures looked uneven in failed batches. Microscopy examined the broken surfaces closely. Computer simulations modeled heating and twisting stresses.

Two flaws combined to weaken the bits. Low heating left the steel structure uneven. Low furnace carbon thinned the surface hardness. Soft surface layers became crack starting points. Quenching and service stresses then drove cracks onward. Uniform, hard tempered steel performed best. The findings translate into concrete factory settings. Better heat treatment should cut field failures.
pmc-13514729:
Li and colleagues fed young pigeons in 2026 to learn how the energy and protein mix in feed shapes meat and gut health. The birds were gray-feathered King pigeon squabs weaned early, a stage when chicks shift from crop milk to solid feed and react strongly to diet. The team varied both feed factors at once.

In a trial with 216 squabs, the team crossed three energy levels with three protein levels, giving nine diets. More energy raised belly fat, while protein level changed carcass traits and gut enzyme strength, which shows how well food is broken down. The two factors often acted together rather than alone. Gut microbe samples also split by diet: the richest, lowest-protein feed favored Lactobacillus types, while the leanest, highest-protein feed held a wider mix of microbes.
pmc-13515029:
Huizhen Yang and her team boost a wave-front fix tool for lens and mirror kits that work with no wave-front gauge. Their 2026 study adds a new step-by-step math tweak to the known SPGD method.

Bendy mirrors are the main fix tools in such kits, and slow work by the old method holds back fast fix in real time. The team built a kit with a mirror of ninety-seven parts to test the new method at more than one level of rough air. In tests on a screen, fix speed rose by more than half on a mean score when set next to the old method. Tests with real gear showed a small but clear gain. Tests with rough air that kept on changing showed the new method fit the change well and stayed firm, which backs its use in real time.
pmc-13516229:
Nicolò Bisi and Abdallah Hamze compare two ways of attacking cancer with one molecule in a 2026 medicinal chemistry review. Tumours dodge single drugs through backup pathways and resistance. The authors walk through cancer target pairs where both designs exist.

Across the paired examples, switching from blocking to destroying improved tumour killing in more than eighty-five percent of cases, lengthened action, and beat resistance mutations. The catch is the linker, the strap joining the molecule's two ends: its length and shape decide whether both proteins can be dragged to the shredder together. Bisi and Hamze distil practical linker strategies, offering chemists a working entry point for designing multi-target degraders.
pmc-13517129:
Maria Michailou and seven colleagues audit vaccine coverage among kidney patients and their families in a 2026 hospital study. Chronic kidney disease raises infection risk, yet vaccination lags, and the cocooning idea, shielding patients by vaccinating their households, is barely studied here. The team recorded coverage for sixty-three dialysis patients, fifty-three children with kidney disease, and their relatives at one Greek university hospital.

Coverage was thin almost everywhere. Dialysis patients reached sixty-two percent for flu but only a quarter for pneumococcal vaccine and almost none for tetanus-pertussis boosters. Children with kidney disease managed just twenty-one percent for flu and zero for COVID-19, though their flu rate still beat healthy controls. Relatives fared little better, leaving the cocoon full of holes. Michailou's team calls for targeted catch-up drives and for teaching families that their own shots protect the patient.
pmc-13517629:
Wen and colleagues measured heavy metals in 2026 in surface waters of the Meili Snow Mountains glacier basin on the southeastern Tibetan Plateau. The team analyzed nine metals, including vanadium, chromium, arsenic, and cadmium, across glacier meltwater and downstream rivers and assessed the risks to ecosystems and health.

Metal levels ran higher in glacier meltwater than in downstream rivers, which the authors attribute to local geology plus air pollution carried in from surrounding regions. Statistical source analysis grouped the metals into three associations pointing to mixed natural and human-made origins. Ecological risk came out low, and non-cancer health risk stayed within safe limits, though children were more susceptible than adults and arsenic contributed most of the risk. The authors offer the results as a baseline for water management on the plateau.
pmc-13517829:
Sartore and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what makes domestic cats aggressive, weighing inherited causes against environmental ones. The team gathered the current evidence on inherited roots of feline aggression and on the life conditions that interact with that inheritance.

Sartore concludes that aggression is best seen as a trait with many causes, shaped by genes and environment together rather than by any single factor. Comparing studies is hard because teams define types of aggression in different ways and measure behaviour with varied tools. Sharper shared definitions, the authors argue, would help vets and owners prevent problems earlier, manage cases better, and improve cat welfare. The review sets out what is known and where the evidence still conflicts or runs thin.
pmc-13518829:
Alys Peisley and nine colleagues map the structure of Kir7.1 in 2026, a potassium channel tied to inherited eye disease and, unusually, to appetite control in the brain. Blocking it in brain slices woke up receptor-bearing neurons, and in living animals the blocker curbed food intake and caused weight loss. Peisley and co-authors also confirm the channel and receptor sit close together on the cell surface.
pmc-13518929:
Qahl and a large team compare five green plant extracts against N-acetylcysteine, a standard protective drug, for shielding liver cells from a classic toxin. Carbon tetrachloride reliably injures the liver through runaway oxidation, making it a standard test bed. Their 2026 experiments used a mouse liver cell line, poisoning the cells and then treating them with extracts of moringa, arugula, broccoli, mint, or celery. They tracked survival, liver enzymes, oxidation markers, and inflammation.

Moringa won among the plants, keeping the most cells alive and pulling the leaked liver enzymes closest to normal values. Arugula ran second, and the rest protected moderately in the reported assays. Moringa also best restored the cells' own antioxidant enzymes and nearly matched the drug at cutting a key fat-damage marker. Arugula and moringa led at suppressing two inflammatory signals.
pmc-13519029:
Mélanie Chester leads a seven-author team pinning down functional puberty in female laboratory mice in 2026, a milestone usually guessed from vaginal opening and cell smears. True reproductive maturity means first ovulation, which external signs may not track. The team combined daily smears, hormone measurements, and an ovarian scoring method that reads follicle and corpus luteum development.

Individual mice varied widely. Ovulation, by the ovarian score, arrived between days 36 and 54 after birth, averaging about day 44, with no correlation to vaginal cytology. Hormone surges appeared in some ovulating females but matched neither smears nor scores in time. Chester and colleagues conclude puberty unfolds gradually and unevenly, so single external markers mislead.
pmc-13520529:
Caorui Lin and colleagues identify in 2026 a mitochondrial protein called ERAL1 that restricts hepatitis B virus, extending its known antiviral role from RNA viruses to a DNA virus. Liver samples across disease phases showed ERAL1 sharply reduced, especially during immune-active illness.

Raising ERAL1 in cell and mouse models suppressed virus copying and cleared nearly three fifths of a key viral surface marker in animals. The protein binds a mitochondrial adaptor called MAVS and boosts its clustering, switching on downstream defence pathways. Loss of ERAL1 in patient livers may therefore weaken natural control, making restoration an appealing treatment idea.
pmc-13521529:
Chishi and colleagues report a 2026 study of regenerative treatment for dead, immature permanent teeth in young patients.  Regenerative therapy uses a scaffold inside the root to restart development. The team compared two scaffolds made from the patient's own blood: standard platelet-rich fibrin and its injectable form, in 38 patients.

Both groups gained root length and wall thickness over twelve months, with no clear difference between them. The injectable form, however, healed the area around the root tip better: every case succeeded, against about nine in ten for the standard form, and infection scores fell further. Most roots showed ongoing maturation without yet closing at the tip. An injectable scaffold is easier to place in narrow young roots.
pmc-13521929:
Wangbiao Guo and colleagues imaged the sheathed swimming tail of the cholera bacterium inside intact cells at near-atomic detail. The tail, a flagellum wrapped in membrane, drives the germ through water and into the human gut.

Their structures show the motor anchors to the outer membrane through fatty rings without punching a pore through it. Ring parts act as sliding bushings, letting the tail spin fast yet seal shut when the tail is shed. The motor's spinning units switch on through a specific protein contact, not by gripping the cell wall as long assumed. Guo links this build to the germ's gut survival and lasting colonisation.
pmc-13522429:
Yukti K Agrawal, G Varadharajulu, and Suraj Kanase compare two forms of arm rehabilitation after stroke in a 2026 experimental study. Twenty-four survivors aged thirty to fifty took part, with one group doing bilateral arm training alone and the other adding rhythmic sound cues from a metronome. Sessions lasted thirty-five minutes, five days a week, for four weeks.

Both groups improved on standard measures of arm impairment and hand function. Gains were larger when sound cues were added, with bigger rises on both the impairment scale and a practical arm test. The authors present cued training as a low-cost option that clinics could add to usual stroke rehabilitation, while noting the small size of the trial.
pmc-13522529:
Fatemeh Nourmohammadi and colleagues examine a gene regulator that helps esophageal cancer cells act like stem cells in a 2026 study. This cancer of the food pipe is a leading cause of cancer death, and stem-like leftover cells can survive treatment and regrow tumors. Patient data, cell experiments, and mouse grafts were used to test the regulator EZH2.

Higher EZH2 activity raised stemness markers, boosted colony and sphere growth, and helped cells divide, move, and resist two chemotherapy drugs. It also reduced programmed cell death. In mice, extra EZH2 sped tumor growth, spread to the lungs, and blood vessel formation, while blocking it slowed progression and improved survival. The findings support EZH2 as a possible target for new treatment strategies.
pmc-13523229:
Irene Marcilla-Toribio leads a team linking distance to urban parks with psychological resilience in Spanish adults in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nearly three thousand adults from primary care centers across nine regions completed a validated resilience scale, and the distance from home to the nearest park was calculated. Analyses adjusted for age, education, income, marital status, social support, and mental health.

People living farthest from a park scored lower on resilience than those living close or at middle distance. Each increase in distance tracked slightly lower resilience overall. Split by sex, the association was clear in men and absent in women. The authors highlight accessible urban green space as a possible support for mental resilience, with attention to gender differences in how that benefit appears.
pmc-13523529:
Chandrashekar K. Dhanush and others report a 2026 whole genome analysis of a multidrug-resistant E. coli strain taken from seafood in Mumbai, India. The strain belongs to sequence type 167, an emerging clone that can cause infections outside the gut. It carries a gene, blaNDM-5, that confers resistance to last-resort carbapenem antibiotics.

Lab testing showed resistance to 26 of 33 antibiotics tried, matching predictions from the genome. Sequencing placed the strain in serotype O101:H9 and phylogroup A, and it carried many virulence genes suggesting potential to harm humans. Resistance genes covered several drug classes, and mutations explained quinolone resistance. The authors warn that fecal contamination of seafood can spread such resistant clones through the community and call for monitoring of the supply chain.
pmc-13525929:
Arturo Flores Morales and co-authors present a case report and literature review, published in 2026. The patient was a 62-year-old man. He had an Amyand hernia. In this rare form, the appendix sits inside a groin hernia sac. His right groin and scrotum hernia had gone untreated for ten years. He presented with swelling and dark skin. His bowel was blocked.

Emergency surgery found more damage. Cecum, appendix, and small bowel reached far into the scrotum. The cecum had burst. Fournier gangrene was present, a fast-spreading infection that kills tissue. Surgeons removed damaged bowel and made an ileostomy. One testicle was removed. The scrotum was cleaned repeatedly over a 33-day hospital stay. The patient survived. Bowel continuity was later restored.
pmc-13527129:
Kim and colleagues explain in 2026 how even trace moisture in factory dry rooms damages a leading solid battery material called LPSC, short for an argyrodite lithium thiophosphate chloride. The material conducts lithium ions well and is soft, making it a top choice for all-solid-state batteries, yet humid air quickly spoils its surface.

Combining computer modeling with depth-profiling X-ray analysis, the team traced a five-step decay path. Water first sticks to sulfur-rich spots, then oxygen swaps in for sulfur and migrates below the surface. The surface ends as an oxygen-rich layer that breaks into several lithium compounds and turns porous. That layer failed to protect the material, and ion conductivity fell by 36 percent within three days.
pmc-13528029:
M. Ndu and five colleagues explore how research institutes can practice solidarity in global health in a 2026 paper. Global research still leans on uneven funding, credit, and data control. The team interviewed 75 stakeholders across the field in 2024 and 2025. This paper draws on thirteen talks with institute leaders.

Five themes came out of the leaders' accounts. Solidarity-driven research should produce fair, tangible results. It should honor how relationships and effects unfold over time. It needs flatter ways of working, a fair split of burdens and benefits, and deep listening. The authors argue solidarity is a living practice, not a fixed slogan. Institutes must reshape hiring, funding, authorship, and partnership habits to live it. They frame institutes as moral actors with real power to change the system.
pmc-13528129:
Muhammad Ruslin and eight colleagues review immersive reality training for dental students in a 2026 systematic review. Immersive reality blends virtual and augmented worlds for hands-on practice. Three databases were searched for studies from 2014 to 2025. Thirteen studies comparing immersive training with classic methods qualified.

Across the studies, students trained faster with the new tools. Procedures took less time once learned. Errors dropped as well. Knowledge and skill scores improved versus traditional teaching. Gains showed most clearly for complex tasks like oral surgery and extractions. The authors call immersive tools a strong support for engagement and skill building. They still want bigger trials with shared measures. Dental schools weighing the cost get a mostly positive verdict here.
pmc-13528229:
Zhou and colleagues use the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans to find the switch by which a mild fast early in life buys a longer, hardier old age. The phenomenon, hormesis, means a small dose of stress protects against larger ones, but the gene-control mechanism was unclear. Their 2026 study lands on a tag placed on histone H3, the spool protein DNA wraps around: acetylation at one specific position, which loosens the spool and switches nearby genes on.

Fasting raised that tag on genes for burning fat, giving the worms an alternative fuel, and, crucially, on antioxidant defence genes, mopping up the damaging oxygen by-products that fat burning itself creates. Removing any of the three partner proteins that delivered the tag broke the lifespan benefit in the reported experiments. The authors cast the tag as a memory of early hardship, written into gene control and cashed in across the whole lifespan.
pmc-13528429:
Nurşah Ersezen and colleagues made new lab antibodies that block PD-L1, a checkpoint protein tumors use to hide from immunity. Published in 2026, the study produced 25 PD-L1-targeting antibodies, screening cell lines for target binding and cross-checks, then testing binding, blocking, and gene sequences. Checkpoint blockade has reshaped cancer care, but better antibodies remain valuable.

Most clones hit monkey PD-L1 without touching other checkpoint proteins, and staining confirmed binding to PD-L1-bearing cells alone. Only two clones paired ultra-tight binding with effective blocking of PD-1 and CD80 links, and one emerged as the drug hopeful on binding strength, blockade, and unique sequence. The authors present it as on par with anti-PD-L1 antibodies now in clinics. Readers get a pipeline from bench clones to a drug hopeful.
pmc-13530229:
Roger M Krzyżewski and colleagues examine in 2026 which brain malformation traits force vessel-blocking treatment into several stages. Tangled artery-vein clusters in the brain often need repeated embolization sessions to close fully. Records covered 117 patients treated with curative intent at one center.

Half the group needed more than one session, averaging under two sessions per person. Prior bleeding was less common among staged cases, while supply from certain deep arteries and a location in the parietal lobe appeared more often. Small lesion size sharply lowered the odds of staging, while parietal location raised them, supporting anatomy-led planning.
pmc-13531129:
Takeshi Matsubara and co-authors published a study in 2026 on lung infection after food-pipe surgery. Pneumonia is a major risk after removal of the gullet for cancer. When it is suspected, doctors culture spit to guide drug choice. The germ mix in that setting was poorly mapped.

The team reviewed 150 patients who had the surgery from 2014 to 2026. Forty-four developed pneumonia of a grade needing treatment. All forty-four cultures came back positive, yielding sixty organisms in all. Gram-negative germs made up more than two-thirds of the finds. Three-quarters of cases held germs that standard drugs can target. Rates of pneumonia were higher in the robot-assisted surgery group. The authors caution that cultured germs show spread, not proven cause.
pmc-13531829:
Habibollah Mahmoodzadeh and Sayyed Mohammad Reza Hakimian test in 2026 a budget-friendly way to support breast implants using the patient own skin layer. Sixteen patients covering 21 breasts received immediate reconstruction above the chest muscle, with hand-meshed dermal grafts taken from the belly or a breast. Preparation added about 36 minutes.

Minor skin wound problems appeared in ten breasts and healed with simple care. Two implants were lost, both in patients exposed to radiation around the surgery window. The series shows the technique can be done, while flagging wound burden and radiation as concerns needing bigger studies.
pmc-13532429:
David J Schneider and colleagues report in 2026 on a platelet test after heart attack. Platelets are small blood cells that help form clots, and a surface mark called Fc gamma RIIa can be counted with a lab test. The study enrolled 749 people in hospital with a heart attack who had at least two risk factors.

More risk factors meant more heart attacks, strokes, and deaths over one year. Within each risk group the platelet test still split people into higher and lower risk groups. Readers see how a blood mark could help doctors weigh clot risk against bleed risk when they choose care.
pmc-13532529:
Yuki Kamiya, Yingzhe Wang, and Keisuke Morishima present in 2026 a way to build tiny hollow hydrogel tubes ring by ring. Thick lab-grown tissue needs vessel-like paths, yet tubes at the small arteriole scale are hard to make because hydrogels are soft. Surface tension holds a stable oil and gel border inside a narrow channel.

Ultraviolet light sets one ring at a time, and stacked rings form a tube whose width follows the light position. Straight, curved, and branching tubes were made, plus tubes with more than one material. Readers get a flexible route toward vessel networks for grown tissue.
pmc-13534429:
Changshu Pan and colleagues run in 2026 sixteen model tests on how reinforced embankments fail under rainfall. Extreme rain is growing more common and damages such earthworks used for roads and water projects. Tests varied rain strength, slope, and the number of reinforcing layers in a custom rig.

Pressure in soil water and soil stress both showed depth and slope effects, though in opposite ways for water pressure. Failure grew step by step from water entry and softening through gully growth to full collapse. Loss of soil suction, not a pressure spike, drove the breakdown, guiding safer designs.
pmc-13534629:
Samarth Godara and colleagues present in 2026 AgriTrack, a framework that tracks farm pest movement using farmer helpline data in India. Manual pest surveys are costly and slow, which limits large-scale watch. Fourteen years of call centre data held over 36 million farmer queries from across the country.

The system tracks pest movement within and across seasons, extracts key date shifts, and forecasts farmer information demand with deep learning. A case study followed termite pests in wheat across India and matched real patterns well. Stakeholders gain timely, low-cost insight for targeted pest action.
pmc-13534729:
Muhammad Arsalan, Xiaojun Yu, and Muhammad Tariq Sadiq develop in 2026 a reinforcement learning optimiser that slows tumour growth with combined radiation and chemotherapy while easing toxicity. Many dosing plans chase short-term shrinkage alone and ignore patient comfort. Their model joins tumour, immune, and healthy cell dynamics in one system.

A smoothed control method paired with a policy learning algorithm adjusted doses in simulation. The hybrid plan cut chemo and radiation doses sharply versus baselines while holding tumour suppression and speeding it slightly. Total treatment intensity fell by over nine tenths in model runs.
pmc-13536129:
Hein Thu, Kaung Khant Tin, and Aung Thura Htoo measure hospital access amid war in Myanmar, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They tracked all 330 townships across sixteen quarters from twenty twenty-one to twenty twenty-four. Travel time to the nearest of sixty-eight general hospitals was weighed by population.

Conflict events came from a database of nearly thirty-six thousand battles and blasts. Facility attacks were counted apart. The team asked whether fighting clustered where access was already worst. They also summed person-years lived under both poor access and heavy conflict, a double burden measure.
pmc-13536529:
Herman G van de Werfhorst argues in 2026 that sociogenomics, the study of genes and social rank, must face core theories of inequality directly. Findings on gene-environment interplay and parental genetic nurturing are often read in unlike ways. One view stresses efficient sorting of people into roles, while another stresses how society builds which traits get rewarded.

Simulations that split context-linked from context-free genetic variation show the field cannot separate these views with current methods. Some starting assumptions about genetic differences can never be tested, yet they are always required. Scholars should state those assumptions plainly when they interpret genetic links to schooling or earnings.
pmc-13536629:
Fatemeh Ahmadinia and colleagues test in 2026 whether bitter orange flower capsules ease anxiety around childbirth and postpartum blues. The plant is used traditionally as a calming agent in Iran. One hundred anxious pregnant women were split into capsule and placebo groups for six weeks spanning delivery.

Anxiety scores fell in the capsule group both at delivery and two weeks after, unlike the control pattern. Blues at two weeks were also less frequent with the capsules than with placebo. The authors recommend the capsules for anxious mothers, within this trial setting.
pmc-13536729:
Yu Gao and colleagues build a computer model to predict low blood pressure after surgery in people with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study. Low pressure during recovery can cause serious harm, yet tools tailored to this group are scarce. Records from more than 44,000 past and recent surgical patients supplied training data, narrowed to 13 key predictors. Fourteen model types were trained and compared, with explanations for each prediction.

A random forest model performed best across training, internal, and later patient groups, and held up in an outside hospital check. Blood loss during surgery, age, heart failure, sleep apnea, and body weight ranked as top predictors. The authors present the tool as a practical aid for sorting risk before surgery and tailoring watchful care afterward.
pmc-13538329:
Coni and five co-authors ask if a cell fuel aids or harms bowel cancer in this twenty twenty-six review. The fuel sits in a chain that fast tumors tap to grow and spread. Some proof casts it as a growth aid, while other proof casts it as a guard.

Inside, the review traces how the fuel feeds a growth loop tied to a top cancer gene. Joint blocks on that loop curbed tumor growth in lab models more than lone blocks. Yet high doses of the fuel can kill cells, and it may shield the gut wall from sores. The pair of roles makes dose and place key, the team says. They weigh how the fuel might still be used with care in cures.
pmc-13538529:
Raju Vidap and colleagues present a brain-inspired spiking network for edge gesture reading from muscle signals in a 2026 study. Standard deep models need offline training and heavy power, blocking tiny wearable devices. The design uses memory-like synapses with self-adjusting updates, ongoing learning that guards old gestures, and short-horizon prediction from spike timing. Muscle-surface signals from hand movements supplied the test stream.

Sorting accuracy ran high, with a matching strong combined score and very low forgetting of earlier gestures. Short-ahead prediction also scored well. Average energy per decision stayed tiny, suiting low-power edge hardware. The authors argue that unifying adaptation, retention, and prediction in one spiking design answers the drift of personal muscle patterns over time.
pmc-13538929:
Lucy McGill and colleagues drew on first-hand accounts of receiving an ADHD diagnosis as an adult. Published in 2026, the systematic review screened 10,357 records down to 21 studies and wove their findings into themes. More adults now seek ADHD labels, yet the lived side of the process was poorly mapped.

Three threads ran through the accounts: ties to self, ties to others, and ties to systems. Diagnosis often landed as a turning-point moment for the self, sparking life review that could breed self-kindness but also grief, anger, and a shaken sense of self. It eased talks with others yet exposed people to stigma and hard choices about telling. Clinics, meanwhile, brought hurdles, waits, and uneven follow-up care. The authors call adult diagnosis a process tied to relationships that can both affirm and shake up.
pmc-13540229:
John Robert White and five colleagues argue, in a 2026 ethnobotanical study, that crop research should look at whole plant genera rather than single species. Indigenous growers often manage several related plants together, and those shared practices can shape the gene pools of all of them.

Fieldwork with the Runa community of Mondayacu in Ecuador combined interviews, observation, and walks focused on the genus Xanthosoma, whose starchy roots are eaten widely. One historically important species is no longer grown there. Another, called lalu, draws responses from destruction to careful keeping for medicine, animal care, and ritual. Herbarium records and literature place these local habits in a national frame.
pmc-13540829:
Jian-hang Xue and four colleagues measure, in a 2026 survey in Xiamen, China, how much four groups at high risk of hepatitis C actually know about the virus. Reaching the global goal of eliminating viral hepatitis by 2030 depends on such groups understanding transmission and cure.

A standard national questionnaire reached 1,621 people across men who have sex with men, drug users, female sex workers, and patients facing invasive procedures. Overall awareness reached about seventy-seven percent, highest among men who have sex with men and lowest, near half, among procedure patients. College education strongly predicted adequate knowledge in most groups. Gaps centred on curability, hidden infection, and new drug risks.
pmc-13540929:
Libo Zhu and seven colleagues hunt, in a 2026 study, for microbial signatures in the uterus that mark endometriosis, a painful inflammatory condition affecting about one in ten women of reproductive age. Diagnosis is often delayed for years, and a non-invasive test would help.

No single microbe survived strict correction as a biomarker, and the well-known Lactobacillus varied widely among individuals. A combined feature set, merging faint signals with machine learning picks and a dysbiosis score, classified proliferative-phase samples moderately well. Secretory-phase models did worse, so the authors stress cycle-aware sampling.
pmc-13541929:
Caroline Gao and co-authors offer a hands-on tutorial on ensemble clustering, in a methods paper from 2026. Clustering sorts mixed data into subgroups, a tool used widely in psychology and psychiatry. Single clustering runs can be unstable, so their results may not repeat or travel well to new data.

Ensemble clustering merges the answers from many runs, which may use varied algorithms, settings, or data samples, into one consensus. The tutorial sets out the core ideas and the main ways to build the parts and merge them. It walks readers through R libraries with worked examples and tuning advice. Tests on simulated and real-style data show the merged results hold up better than single runs.
pmc-13542129:
Zhiming Guo and colleagues build a scoring framework in 2026. The field is engineering evaluation. The framework judges how well a process can evolve over time. Car door stamping served as the test case. Older methods handle shifting, uncertain data poorly. That gap motivates the design.

Three parts string together in the system. An indicator set rests on the plan-do-check-act cycle. A weighting scheme mixes entropy weights with a cloud model. The cloud model captures fuzziness and randomness together. An improved ranking method then orders the options. A divergence measure separates options near the ideal. Five real stamping schemes scored across a wide range. Their order matched production logic.
pmc-13542229:
Anna Szymczak-Graczyk and colleagues report a 2026 study, part laboratory work and part computer modelling, on how layered perlite concrete beams respond when one face is heated. Perlite is a light volcanic material valued for insulation, and such beams are increasingly used in energy-saving buildings. Their model links heat flow through the beam thickness to bending behaviour, using a shear-deformable beam formulation with an added axial term.

In the laboratory, a concrete and perlite sandwich beam was warmed on its upper surface to 35 degrees, and measured midspan deflections over time matched the model well. The match shows the calculation captures the delayed bending that slow heat conduction causes in mixed materials. A further purely numerical example, with stiffness falling as temperature rises, shows the framework can extend beyond the simple linear case, though that extension was not tested in the laboratory.
pmc-13544129:
Paula Rojas-Garcia and eleven co-authors ask whether quick in-clinic testing changes how patients feel during a respiratory infection. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. A large parent trial had already shown the testing did not cut antibiotic use or speed recovery.

The parent trial enrolled over two thousand six hundred patients. Tests at the visit covered inflammation markers and common germs. Patients filled a standard quality-of-life form on days one, fourteen, and twenty-eight. Utility scores were converted into quality-adjusted life gains. Static and dynamic analyses compared the testing and usual care arms. Even where prescribing stayed flat, small differences in felt well-being could still matter for policy.
pmc-13545229:
Mei Yi and colleagues build in this 2026 study a risk score for prostate cancer based on genes from cancer-associated fibroblasts, the support cells that surround a tumor and help it grow. Such scores aim to predict which patients will relapse and how they might respond to immune therapy.

Using single-cell and bulk gene data from public databases, the team found two fibroblast types tied to patient outcomes. Five genes survived statistical screening and formed the final signature. Patients scored low risk lived longer, while high-risk patients relapsed more often in outside datasets. High-risk tumors also showed heavier immune cell infiltration and more activity in growth and spread pathways. The authors propose the score as a guide for prognosis and treatment planning.
pmc-13546629:
Jing Xiang and co-authors compare two drug delivery routes for older patients with advanced lung cancer, in a 2026 study. Standard care pairs chemotherapy through the veins with an immune drug, but many older patients cannot bear it. The alternative threads chemotherapy into the bronchial artery feeding the tumor, then blocks it, keeping the drug local. The team reviewed 81 patients over 65 treated either way at one hospital, all also getting the immune drug.

The artery group was older and frailer, yet response rates ran slightly higher. Survival times, with or without disease progression, did not differ between the groups. Blood-cell suppression hit the vein group far more often, while breathlessness was commoner in the artery group. No treatment-related serious events appeared. The authors see the local route as a fair option for frail elders.
pmc-13547329:
Aliakbar Dehno Khalaji and Kasim Sakran Abass synthesized in 2026 a new composite material for pulling dye pollution out of wastewater, combining chitosan from crustacean shells, starch, and iron oxide particles. They tested it in batch experiments against two common industrial dyes, the orange methyl orange and the blue methylene blue, tuning conditions for the best removal.

At its best the material removed about 99 percent of the orange dye and about 98 percent of the blue one. The capture pattern fit models describing a single layer of chemically bound dye on the surface. After five rounds of washing and reuse, removal still stayed above 92 percent for both dyes. The authors present the composite as a cheap, repeatable cleaner for dye-laden water.
pmc-13547629:
Hye Mi Lee and colleagues described in 2026 a Merkel cell carcinoma, an aggressive skin-related neuroendocrine cancer, that appeared as a large mass under the jaw with no skin lesion at all. The tumor almost always starts in sun-exposed skin, so a primary growth in the submandibular region is exceptionally unusual. Their patient, an 86-year-old man, had a painful neck mass that grew over three months to roughly seven by five centimeters.

Imaging placed the mass at the submandibular gland with no lymph node spread, and a needle biopsy confirmed the cancer type. The report walks through the diagnosis, surgical handling, and early recovery. The authors urge doctors to keep this cancer on the list for fast-growing submandibular masses even when the skin looks clean.
pmc-13548529:
Rudy Celeghin and colleagues examine gene changes that disrupt RNA splicing in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, a heart muscle disease, in a 2026 study. Many such changes sit outside the usual splice sites and stay labeled as variants of uncertain significance, which limits what doctors can tell families. The team gathered candidate variants from 200 affected people and tested them several ways.

Computer prediction, heart tissue data, and laboratory minigene tests were combined, then matched against family segregation records and standard classification rules. Faulty splicing was confirmed for nine of twenty variants, and sixteen of the twenty could be reclassified once all evidence was joined. Certain heart genes, including DSP and DSG2, carried an excess of these variants. The work shows how pairing prediction with bench testing can turn uncertain findings into clinically usable answers.
pmc-13548629:
Xin Zhang and colleagues look for a blood marker that separates better from worse outlooks among pancreatic cancer patients whose scans show stable disease, in a 2026 retrospective study. Scan categories judge chemotherapy response crudely, and stable disease hides wide variation. Among 182 patients on first-line chemotherapy, the team tracked the tumor marker CA19-9 every eight weeks alongside imaging, focusing on those whose marker started high and whose scans stayed stable.

Most patients landed in the stable group, and their survival resembled that of patients whose tumors had visibly shrunk. Inside the stable group, patients whose marker fell by at least thirty percent from its starting level lived longer without progression and longer overall than those without such a fall. The authors propose the thirty percent cut as a cheap extra layer for judging prognosis when scans look unchanged.
pmc-13550029:
Cécile Pinault and colleagues show that umbilical cord jelly stem cells can make fat after all, if the metabolic menu is right, in a 2026 study pairing a literature review with experiments.
