The team tested four induction mixes varying sugar and insulin, reading fat buildup with machine learning assisted imaging. Marrow cells fattened readily under the standard recipe, while cord cells lagged. Extending the induction and enriching metabolic support unlocked a delayed but clear fat response in cord cells, with sugar and insulin reinforcing each other. The authors propose a standardized yardstick for comparing fat potential across cell sources.
pmc-13550429:
Shivendra Verma and colleagues chart the hormone response to sugar in a rare diabetes caused by a calcified, stone-filled pancreas, in a 2026 physiology study. Fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes destroys insulin production, but its effects on glucagon and gut incretin hormones were murky. Nine patients and six healthy volunteers each took glucose by mouth and, on another occasion, by vein at a rate matched to copy the same blood sugar curve.

Patients ran high glucagon at rest and after oral glucose, and glucagon exposure was larger by mouth than by vein, a route difference absent in controls. Two hormones from the lower gut surged, while the upper-gut hormone GIP lagged. Insulin-linked C-peptide and pancreatic polypeptide stayed deeply suppressed by both routes, confirming severe gland failure. The authors describe a distinctive hormonal fingerprint for this diabetes type.
pmc-13550529:
Jiraporn Sirison and colleagues blast two green microalgae species with ultraviolet-C light to make them richer for food and fuel at once, in a 2026 cultivation study. Stress can push algae to stockpile valuable compounds. Cultures of Desmodesmus quadricauda and Scenedesmus dimorphus received up to three hours of UV-C, then grew for fourteen days while the team tracked biomass, pigments, protein, and fats.

Both species grew more biomass after irradiation, peaking at different doses. Cancer-fighting carotenoid pigments and protein rose, protein by up to about a third. Fat content and productivity crested at one hour of exposure, reaching up to nearly double the untreated level. The fat mix shifted toward oleic acid. The prized omega-3 DHA also appeared for the first time. Biodiesel from the fats met the cetane standard but failed cold-flow requirements, so the authors call for more tuning.
pmc-13553429:
Yue Ma and five colleagues test an advanced imaging workflow for brain tumor surgery planning, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Meningiomas can entangle critical blood vessels and venous sinuses. Surgeons need the vascular map before the first incision.

Seventy-two patients with confirmed intracranial meningiomas were reviewed retrospectively. All had microsurgical removal between two thousand twenty-three and two thousand twenty-six. Their planning used three-dimensional rotational angiography fused with other imaging. The authors judged the workflow's technical feasibility and the anatomical information it yielded. Decision support value was also assessed. Where tumors hug the skull base, such fused images can change the surgical approach. The study sizes up whether the extra angiography earns its place.
pmc-13554129:
A Andres F Ramirez and L Alberto J Lamadrid forecast air pollution from New York power plants in 2030 as green energy grows, in a 2026 study. They built their method on hourly records from 2019 across the state grid. Federal pollution archives and forecast tools from a national energy programme filled the gaps. The aim was a method that grid planners can reuse in running studies.

Future cases vary how much wind and solar power joins the mix. Swings in that green supply change how hard fossil plants must run, and thus what they emit. The authors lay out steps linking past plant behaviour to future cases. Planners can use the output to weigh climate goals against local air quality before choices are locked in.
pmc-13554229:
Yulong Chen leads a five-author team breaking tunnel models to learn how rock bolts hold layered stone together in a 2026 study. Blocks of rock-like material held a round hole crossed by bedding layers, laid flat or upright. Seven support schemes were fitted, from sprayed concrete to steel arches and bolt patterns. Cameras watched the hole walls fail under squeezing, and CT scans mapped cracks afterward.

Full bolt patterns and slotted steel pipes gave the biggest strength gains. Sprayed concrete and arches pressed the walls and stopped flakes from spalling off. Upright bedding gained more strength from support than flat bedding. Scans showed bolts compacting cracked zones, halting cracks, and bending their paths. That grip lifts the load the broken rock can still bear.
pmc-13554329:
Roma Fe Mabanag and co-authors compared neck surgery outcomes in patients with sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle, according to how many levels were fused. The operation, anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, treats worn neck discs, and patients may fare worse when more levels are involved. Using a health database, the team matched patients pairwise and tracked complications from three months to two years.

Multilevel patients used more rehabilitation and more opioids in the first months, and their fusions failed to knit, a problem called pseudoarthrosis, more often. By one year they reported more new swallowing difficulty. The gaps persisted rather than fading with time. The authors urge risk assessment, counseling, and monitoring for sarcopenic patients facing multilevel surgery. The study cannot say the extra levels cause the harm, since sicker patients may need them. It does quantify what surgeons should warn about.
pmc-13555629:
Kai Ye leads a six-author team crafting an injectable corn-protein gel to mend torn shoulder tendons in brittle bone in a 2026 study. Rotator cuff repairs often fail when osteoporosis weakens the tendon-to-bone joint. Their gel carries niacin, a vitamin, inside tiny carbon spheres that also convert light to gentle heat. Electron-beam treatment set the gel's structure without harsh chemicals.

Gel extracts pushed bone-forming cells toward bone and tendon stem cells toward tendon in dishes. Signs of cell aging fell, and harmful oxygen species dropped inside cells. In rats with brittle bones, gel plus near-infrared light rebuilt the joint's cartilage zone and strengthened the repair. Skin wounds also healed faster with richer blood vessel growth and calmer inflammation.
pmc-13555929:
Ruth B Mbwambo leads a sixteen-author team mapping variation in a malaria parasite gene eyed as a vaccine candidate in a 2026 study. The gene, called phistb, helps the parasite survive inside red blood cells. Genomes from more than fourteen hundred samples across Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and Ethiopia were drawn from a public database. Filtering left 1,312 samples for analysis.

Two thirds of infections carried a single parasite strain, with Ethiopia highest on that measure. Among single-strain samples, eighty-eight gene versions appeared, two of them dominating. Kenya showed the richest diversity of the four countries. Populations barely differed from each other overall, with no clear geographic structure. Rare variants ran in excess in most countries, hinting at recent expansion.
pmc-13556029:
Veethika Nayak and four colleagues mapped in 2026 what research connects hospital falls to the wellbeing of the staff who work there. Burnout, low professional fulfilment, poor work settings, and weak organisational culture can all erode care, yet their link to falls had not been gathered in one place. Following established scoping methods, the team searched five databases and also checked whether fall-prevention trials measured staff wellbeing at all.

Seventy-eight studies qualified from more than eleven thousand records, most of them observational and focused on nurses in acute hospitals. Burnout tracked with more falls, job satisfaction with fewer, and better work environments also helped. Culture findings were mixed, with supportive leadership protective and toxic leadership harmful. No fall-prevention trial in the Cochrane set had built staff wellbeing into its design, a gap the authors highlight.
pmc-13556229:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study of a tiny viral protein that blocks plant immunity in two separate ways.  Cucumber mosaic virus fights back with its 2b protein. The team built virus versions with shortened 2b proteins to separate the protein's skills.

One shortened protein could still grip small RNAs and long viral RNA, and it blocked the amplification route run by the host enzyme RDR6, but not the RDR1 route. The other shortened protein could not grip RNA, yet it blocked the RDR1 route by binding that enzyme directly. Only in plants whose own defense was crippled could a fully disarmed virus thrive, proving both skills matter in real infection. One small protein thus runs two separate counter-defenses.
pmc-13558329:
Wei Li and four colleagues reviewed in 2026 how minimally invasive tension band methods for kneecap fractures have evolved. The classic operation wires the broken patella so that muscle pull presses the fragments together, and newer versions do the same job through small incisions. Their review searched three databases to December 2023 for clinical studies of these percutaneous techniques, with or without camera assistance.

Four families of technique emerged: plain tension band, wire-based, screw-based, and strong suture versions. Against open surgery, the gentler methods generally won on operating time, hospital stay, pain, joint recovery, and scar appearance. Two questions stay open: many patients still need a second operation to remove hardware, and whether adding a joint camera helps enough to justify it remains disputed. The authors warn that most studies are small and retrospective, so enthusiasm should stay measured.
pmc-13558529:
Valentin Herber and six colleagues measured in 2026 how accurately a dynamic navigation system places dental implants. The system tracks instruments live against a merged plan built from a 3D scan and a mouth scan, aiming to beat freehand placement. Their prospective study covered 109 implants in 76 patients placed by five experienced surgeons at four centres, with deviations checked by matching scans taken after surgery to the plan.

Average angular error came to just over three degrees, and the implant tip landed about a millimetre from its planned spot on average. Every deviation measure beat freehand benchmark goals drawn from the literature by a clear margin. No serious device-related harm occurred, and surgeons rated the system highly for satisfaction. The authors conclude that navigation delivers true-to-plan, safe placement in experienced hands.
pmc-13558629:
Jing Zhang and Siti Zuraidah Md Osman tested in 2026 a game-based language module in vocational education, a setting where game learning is rarely studied. Their quasi-experimental design taught sixty students with the game module for six weeks. Sixty-six peers followed ordinary instruction. The team then compared achievement, enjoyment of the foreign language, and learner autonomy, with interviews adding texture. Flow theory, the psychology of full absorption, framed the module's design.

The game group finished with clearly higher achievement and enjoyment scores. Autonomy, the habit of directing one's own learning, did not differ between groups. Students praised the module for building language skill and allowing flexible, personal pacing, while criticising thin game features and technical glitches. The authors conclude that well-built games lift results and mood in vocational language classes, even if self-direction must be taught apart.
pmc-13559129:
Wenting Wang and colleagues examined whether the volume of red blood cells transfused during children's heart surgery predicts harm afterward. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 19,081 patients aged 14 or younger who had operations with cardiopulmonary bypass. Children were grouped by weight-adjusted transfusion volume, from none up to more than 34.5 mL/kg.

About 44.5 percent of the children received red cells during surgery. After adjustment, the team found no steady linear rise in risk with volume; a threshold pattern fit better instead. Volumes above the top cutoff were tied to longer mechanical ventilation, more acute kidney injury, and more combined complications. Small volumes, curiously, were linked to fewer of those outcomes than no transfusion at all. The authors suggest a workable transfusion range may exist and that volume per kilogram deserves attention in surgical planning.
pmc-13559629:
Jinzi Liang and six colleagues published this 2026 study on whether adding radiation, with or without chemotherapy, after surgery helps patients with head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma. That is a rare salivary-type cancer that has not spread. Guidelines recommend postoperative radiation for high-risk cases, but evidence is mixed. The authors reviewed patients treated with curative surgery between 2011 and 2023 and sorted them into surgery-only, radiation, and combined chemoradiation groups.

The cohort held 114 patients, 35 surgery-only, 42 radiation and 37 chemoradiation, followed for a median of 51.0 months across the study. No significant differences appeared between the groups in overall survival, progression-free survival, local control or distant spread. Nerve invasion by the tumour predicted worse survival, with a hazard ratio of 3.425 for death. Within that subgroup, radiation did improve local control over surgery alone. Adding chemotherapy showed no clear advantage over radiation alone.
pmc-13560129:
Xin Li and colleagues model poor prognosis in invasive aspergillosis, a dangerous fungal infection, using records from a general hospital in Anhui. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 307 patients diagnosed between January 2019 and March 2024. Thirty-nine patients had unfavorable outcomes, against 268 with favorable ones, and detection of the infection had climbed in the last two years.

Four factors survived selection as independent risks: longer intensive care stay, higher C-reactive protein, higher blood glucose, and kidney failure. A nomogram built from them predicted poor outcomes with an area under the curve of 0.810 in the group's analysis, and bootstrap checks kept the figure close. Calibration agreed well between predicted and observed risk. The team also released the tool as an interactive web application. The authors present it for early risk sorting and faster intervention in high-risk patients.
pmc-13561929:
Wangda Li asks whether fancy balance and foot-pressure tests can outpredict one simple questionnaire for ankle trouble in badminton players, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The questionnaire, the CAIT, scores felt ankle instability. Players across seven centers were tested, then followed monthly for a year to see whose ankles gave way, resprained, or ached on.

The answer was largely no. The baseline questionnaire alone predicted the year's outcome better than a six-measure equipment model. Adding the equipment numbers to it gained nothing, and decision analysis showed no consistent benefit. Most outcomes were the persistence of instability already visible at baseline, not new breakdowns, which flatters any baseline score. Among players starting with good scores, prediction was weak all round. The author advises against buying the gear for screening: the cheap form already holds what the sensors add.
pmc-13562529:
Haichao Xing and five colleagues uncover a route by which brain tumours pump out the main drug used against them. Temozolomide often fails in glioblastoma, and high levels of a protein called ARL13B mark patients at greater risk. Working from public tumour datasets and lab experiments, the 2026 team traced how the protein is controlled and what it does. A signalling pathway known as ERK/P90 switches the gene on, with a factor named C/EBPβ doing the direct work at its start site.

Once active, ARL13B made tumour cells shed more tiny vesicles from their surface, and those vesicles carried drug out with them. Less drug stayed inside the cells, so treatment weakened. Blocking the ERK/P90 pathway restored the drug's effect in the experiments. The authors nominate both the pathway and ARL13B itself as targets that could rescue a standard therapy many patients currently fail.
pmc-13562629:
Wenhui Yan and colleagues show how to steer soil microbes so plants can unlock phosphorus, a nutrient often locked in organic matter. In the soil around roots, a few keystone species shape the whole microbial community, but nudging them has proved hard. The team used simple synthetic root secretions, a mix of luteolin, myristic acid, and glucose, to reshape the microbes around plant roots. Their 2026 study tracked which species rose to dominance.

The mix boosted one bacterium, Domibacillus indicus D99, into a keystone role and raised an enzyme that frees phosphorus from soil compounds. Partner bacteria then fed on its byproducts, dividing the available food rather than competing, and the partnership raised both enzyme activity and plant growth. The authors present this as a route to managing soil microbiomes for farming, using ecological roles rather than brute-force inoculation.
pmc-13562729:
Xiaoxiao Kong and colleagues produced a fine-grained daily temperature map for the Tibetan Plateau, a region often called the Third Pole for its sensitivity to climate change. Existing daily land-surface temperature products are too coarse, at a kilometre or wider, to capture glacier forefields, thawing slopes, and patchy landscapes. Their 2026 dataset fuses satellite and reanalysis data to give gapless daily mean temperatures at 100-metre resolution for 2019.

Checked against ground stations, the dataset's errors averaged about 3.1 degrees, with a strong match to observed temperatures, and it beat a 1-kilometre product by roughly half a degree. The finer detail reveals slope, land-cover, and temperature contrasts that coarser maps blur. The authors offer the dataset for studies of permafrost, glacier melt, and the region's energy balance.
pmc-13563729:
Cyrine Bennasrallah and nine colleagues survey what drives breast cancer checking among women at primary care centres in Monastir, central Tunisia. Screening uptake lags despite national campaigns. Their 2026 cross-sectional study questioned 439 women between May and October 2023 with a purpose-built questionnaire. Most, 80.6 percent, had heard of breast self-examination, and 53.1 percent said they did it monthly. Among the 192 women over 45, only 35 percent had ever had a mammogram.

Knowing about self-examination was the strongest single predictor of doing it, with adjusted odds above six, and family history of the disease plus older age also helped. Mammography followed a chain: women who examined themselves and women who knew the recommended starting age were far likelier to have been screened. The authors call for targeted teaching that connects the two habits, since awareness, more than access alone, seems to move behaviour in this group.
pmc-13564129:
Ashley Foster, Cora Ormseth, Jacqueline Grupp-Phelan, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It checks whether the triage score given to children arriving at emergency departments with behavioral health crises predicts how much care they actually use.

Drawing on a national survey, the team estimated 3.6 million such visits against 52 million other pediatric visits. Behavioral health visits stamped with the least urgent scores still used multiple resources a third of the time, double the rate of other visits. Nearly half of behavioral visits arrived at the most acute levels, yet over half of those children went home. Within behavioral visits, the score did not predict waiting time to see a provider. It did predict resource counts, modestly. The authors say a triage ruler built for physical injury misfits mental health crises in both directions.
pmc-13567129:
Daniela Posta and eight co-authors give, in two thousand twenty-six, the first full account of pecan oil grown in Eastern Europe. Pecan is a new oil crop in the region, while walnut is well established there. The study compares the oils from both nuts side by side.

Samples came from Romania and the Republic of Moldova, and oils were pressed with heat. The team measured kernel makeup, fatty acids, and how the oils changed over twenty days of storage. Most pecan oils were rich in one polyunsaturated fat, while walnut oils were rich in a different, single-bond fat. One pecan sample broke that pattern for reasons the study could not pin down. All oils stayed below the set limit for early spoilage.
pmc-13569529:
Hana Amer and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study across four South Australian hospitals, how inpatients feel about collaborative pharmacist prescribing. In that model, pharmacists and doctors build medicine plans together and pharmacists then prescribe. Two hundred patients answered, half served by the joint model and half by doctor-only prescribing.

Feelings and views were compared between the groups, with written notes analyzed for themes and rating scales summed side by side. Shared decision-making sits at the center of the model, so patient views are the test that matters. Hospital managers weighing wider pharmacist prescribing get direct evidence on whether patients feel involved and respected under the newer arrangement.
pmc-13570429:
Haihang Ao and colleagues pilot, in a 2026 animal study, patches made from processed human skin tissue to rebuild narrowed ureters in three miniature pigs. Ureters are the tubes carrying urine from kidney to bladder. Long narrowings are hard to repair by joining cut ends, so the team replaced a two-centimeter segment with a rolled tube of the material over a stent.

At forty-five days all three pigs showed open channels on imaging and scope checks, with new lining, organized collagen, fresh blood vessels, and early muscle regrowth. Gene data supported repair activity. Only three animals and short follow-up limit the claim, yet the approach could one day free patients from needing their own tissue grafts.
pmc-13570629:
Jing Zhang and five co-authors built tiny carriers to treat a harsh form of breast cancer. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with triple-negative breast cancer. A germ that can settle in these tumors makes them grow faster and resist care. The team loaded the carriers with silver, a plant compound, and a gene silencer. A ring shaped marker on the carrier helps it find the tumor.

The carriers aim to kill germs and lift the tumor's block on the immune system at once. The team checked size, drug load, and how much drug got trapped inside. Old single drug care is held back by poor aim and fast loss from the body. Readers see a plan that hits germ, tumor, and immune block in one dose.
pmc-13570829:
Junjun Xu, Ziyan Zhang, Liuyang Yu, and Yi Feng hunt, in twenty twenty-six, for mitochondrial genes that causally shape sleep disorders. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been linked to poor sleep, but which genes matter was unclear. Their multi-omics Mendelian randomization design uses gene-linked variants as natural experiments. Data came from a Finnish genome bank, other genome studies of sleep subtypes, and molecular trait maps for methylation, expression, and protein levels. Brain tissue data from a reference atlas checked tissue-specific effects.

The scan flagged many genes at the methylation level, fewer at expression, and a handful at protein level. Two genes stood out with opposite, subtype-specific roles: one protective in sleep apnea, one raising daytime sleepiness risk. An epigenetic control mechanism for the first gene was also identified.
pmc-13571729:
Yuhang Yi and co-authors tune a fermentation that boosts the antioxidant power of a medicinal orchid. The plant, Dendrobium officinale, is both food and medicine in China. Lactic bacteria fermentation can free its helpful compounds and add new ones. Nine learning models were raced against a classic surface method to find the best brew settings.

One boosting model won with near-perfect fit scores over the classic method. The tuned brew raised radical-scavenging power without harming cell life in dish tests. Chemical reads showed deep reshaping of the plant's molecule mix. Thirty-one flavonoids rose, and rich phenolic acids grew in step. Alkaloid paths also shifted in marked ways under the bacteria.
pmc-13572529:
Xiaofan Yu, with ten colleagues, reports a 2026 study of gene activity behind eggshell formation in laying hens. Shell quality drives farm profits, and thin or cracked shells waste eggs and raise costs. The team tracked how mineral builds up across three stages, from before it starts to the fast growth phase.

Gene reads from the uterus, the organ where the shell forms, were grouped by stage and network pattern. Early on, a protein called ovalbumin ran high and may stop crystals from forming too soon. In the fast phase, shell matrix proteins plus calcium pumps and carriers worked together to hold calcium steady. Calcium in uterine fluid rose over time, then held flat through the fast phase. The gene map offers targets for breeding and feed plans.
pmc-13573329:
Xiaomeng Gu, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 pooled review of bone marrow stem cells for heart attack care. A heart attack kills heart muscle, and reopening the artery cannot bring dead cells back. Stem cells from a patient's own marrow may help repair the damage, and many small trials have tested that hope.

The review pooled 25 trials with 1,822 patients, split between cell treatment and standard care. The cell group gained on the heart's pumping share, with a mean edge the authors report as clear. A wall motion score also improved in the cell group. Chamber sizes and scar size showed trends toward gain, but none reached clear proof. Major bad heart events did not rise with cell treatment. The authors say long-term gains in heart shape remain open and need stronger trials.
pmc-13573429:
Riki Tanaka and colleagues asked what, at age 12, predicts whether adolescent self-harm will persist rather than fade. Most teen self-harm is transient, but a minority repeat it and need intensive care, and the social environment's role in persistence is poorly understood. Their 2026 study followed 1,501 children in the Tokyo Teen Cohort, recording self-harm at ages 12, 14, and 16.

About 13 percent reported transient self-harm and 3.5 percent persistent self-harm. A mother's depressive or anxious symptoms and being female predicted persistence, while companionship with the mother protected against it. Depressive symptoms and psychotic experiences predicted both transient and persistent self-harm. The authors call for care for maternal mental health and support for mother-child bonds as prevention.
pmc-13575129:
Talhi Amar, Djeffal Selman, and Ghoul Abdelhamid optimize chromium plating on steel in this 2026 paper. The steel is 42CrMo4, and the bath uses trivalent chromium. Conditions that smooth the surface do not always cut wear or save energy. The hardest preparation also shifts the best operating range. Five goals must be balanced at once.

The team turned lab data into a five objective decision problem. Goals covered roughness, wear, energy use, efficiency, and hardness. Curves were interpolated through the measured sweeps of current and temperature. Three swarm and evolutionary optimizers searched the same space. Robust settings that serve all goals fairly were identified. The method targets wear resistant coatings with lower energy demand.
pmc-13575929:
Anna M Newen leads a 2026 immunology study on how the body deletes self-reactive B cells before they cause autoimmune disease. B cells that target the body's own tissues arise during development. Some later sharpen their attack through a process driven by the AID enzyme, raising the risk of diseases such as lupus.

Using mice engineered so a cell-death step could be blocked at chosen stages, the team separated early from late checkpoints. Blocking the step early let self-reactive cells survive, diversify, and drive kidney damage with lethal disease. Blocking it after activation raised self-reactive cells and antibodies yet caused little tissue harm. The authors propose a model of deletion spread across stages, where early checkpoints carry the main protective weight.
pmc-13576129:
Ali Zamlout and six colleagues compare two modern operations for haemorrhoids in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Classic removal surgery works but brings marked pain and slow recovery. The review pits laser haemorrhoidoplasty, which shrinks the tissue with laser energy, against LigaSure removal, which seals and cuts with a heated device.

Five studies covering 461 patients were pooled. Laser patients reported less pain on day one, returned to routine life about 5.75 days sooner, and had shorter operations and hospital stays. LigaSure patients faced a lower recurrence risk, with a gap of 12 percentage points. Rates of bleeding, infection, urine retention, and clotting were similar. The authors rate certainty in the pooled results as very low and ask for stronger trials.
pmc-13577529:
Saher Fatima Awan and co-authors build an explainable stacked model to predict diabetes, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Early spotting of diabetes can head off heart and kidney damage. Past models chased accuracy while leaving their reasoning opaque.

Three base learners feed a boosting meta-learner in the stack. Scaling, feature ranking, and synthetic balancing prepared the classic Pima data set. Accuracy hit eighty-six percent, beating recent rivals. Two explanation tools then showed which features drove each call, locally and globally. The authors pitch the pairing for trustworthy clinic use.
pmc-13578329:
Hamid Reza Roosta, Sajad Azizabadi, and Seyed Hossein Mirdehghan grow three bell pepper types in a soil free film system. Their 2026 greenhouse study, set in Iran, tests which feed mix suits each type. Roots sat in a thin stream of liquid feed, a setup called nutrient film technique. Three feeds were tried: a classic standard, a Dutch mix, and a mix advised by a United States agency.

Plant type and feed both shaped growth, yield, and fruit quality. One pepper paired with the agency mix piled up the most growth and the heaviest fruit. A second type kept the richest green color on the standard feed. A third used light most ably under every feed. Fruit firmness and vitamin C also rose on the agency mix.
pmc-13578529:
Christopher W Roy and colleagues test a free running heart scan that needs no breath holds or heart wires, in a 2026 study of 45 patients born with heart defects. Standard scans split the heart check into flat movies and still three dimensional views, each with its own setup. Their five dimensional method records the whole heart while sorting beats and breaths after the fact, using a standard contrast dye.

The new scan ran faster than both older methods. Its measures of heart chamber size tracked the standard movie method closely, though small offsets appeared. Graders scored its overall quality above the still three dimensional scan, and longer bits of the heart arteries stayed visible. Sharpness on those arteries still favored the older still scan, a trade the authors note.
pmc-13578629:
Four authors present a lab platform dated two thousand twenty-six that mimics heart injury after a blocked artery reopens. The injury brings a surge of oxidative stress followed by sterile inflammation, where the immune system reacts without germs. How that sequence harms the human heart's mechanics is poorly defined.

Their two-hit model combines vessel cells, heart muscle cells grown from stem cells, and tiny three-dimensional heart organoids. The first hit is oxidative priming, and the second is the fluid shed by dying immune cells. Vessel cells switched on alarm pathways and died. The heart cells survived but remodeled in unhealthy ways.
pmc-13579829:
Brototo Deb, Timothy Lim, Ian K Everitt, and Carl G Streed audit how clinical calculator tools handle sex and gender, in a 2026 review of the MDCalc site. Such tools guide daily care, and a muddled sex or gender input can skew their advice. The team screened eight hundred twenty one tools in May 2025 and kept those asking for sex, gender, or both.

Eighty four tools qualified, and nearly all forced a two way answer. Most labeled the input as sex, the rest as gender. One in five mixed the two up, pairing a label with answer choices that meant the other thing. Source papers showed the same mix up in a quarter of cases that stated how data were gathered. Most tools carried medium or high weight for care decisions, raising the stakes of the muddle.
pmc-13580029:
Bescós-Ramo and co-authors build wound dressings that release two germ-killing drugs in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The base is a soft gel made with a common medical polymer. One drug is bound into the gel itself, while a second drug is soaked into it afterward.

The soaked drug leaves in a quick burst, which can kill germs right after a wound occurs. The bound drug then leaks out slowly, and faster in acid conditions, giving long cover against new infection. Tests showed strong action against two tough germs, including a drug-resistant staph type. The gels did not harm cells at doses that killed germs, so the authors see promise for wound care.
pmc-13581629:
Alessandra Mangone leads a team on adrenal lumps found on both glands. Their study from twenty twenty-six tracks a single center group. Such lumps are found more as belly scans grow common.

First shows vary a lot in hormones, scans, and traits. Guide books give no clear path for the both gland type. Records of non surgery cases over many years were reviewed. A smaller set had full data and long follow up. At start, just over half showed mild cortisol excess. A share of the rest grew that trait with time.
pmc-13582129:
Sammy J S Wrede, Ines-Maria Gärtner, and Achim Mortsiefer scan workplace health programs for how much they build health, not just dodge risk, in a 2026 scoping review. The lens is salutogenesis, a frame that asks what makes people thrive: feeling life makes sense, joining in, setting goals, having variety, and gaining power over one's work. Five databases gave up 128 intervention studies from 2014 to 2024.

Each program was scored on how many of the five principles it wove in. Overall uptake landed mid range. Empowerment, variety, and sense of coherence appeared most, while taking part and goal setting lagged far behind. Programs with personal coaching or self management tools scored highest, and mixed programs aligned best overall.
pmc-13582629:
Xiongwei He and seven colleagues build a vision model that counts young maize plants in crowded fields, in a study dated twenty twenty-six. Dense seedlings overlap, so plain counting tools often miss plants or count them twice. The team improved a fast detector, YOLOv8n, in three ways. A new attention block keeps small plants from fading against the background. A smarter loss function ties class scores to box quality for packed targets.

A final filter adjusts how it removes duplicate boxes based on local crowding. On their own field dataset, the model beat the base version on every score while adding almost no extra size. Top-end accuracy rose the most. The authors offer it as a tool for precise farm counts.
pmc-13586029:
Roshan Kumar, Babak Pakbin, Mona Roshan Singh, and Bharathi Muruganantham introduce a journal collection on the microbiome in cancer therapy. Fast gene reading has shown that the microbes living in and on the body shape the soil a tumor grows in, tune the immune system, and sway how well treatments work. The editors gathered work on using that knowledge, from helpful-germ therapies to computer models that mix host genes with microbe data.

The collection holds 24 papers across research, reviews, and syntheses. One strand shows that cancer-linked microbe shifts turn up in spit, stool, and blood at once, not just in the gut. Another builds stool and spit classifiers that can flag bowel cancer without a scope. Liver and bile duct cancers also feature, where microbe and chemical profiles together may sharpen forecasts. The editors frame microbes as both markers and levers for future care.
pmc-13586229:
Akiko Yamakawa and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study validating a blood biomarker panel for frailty in older adults. Frailty creeps in through weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slowness, and inactivity. Objective, low-burden tests could catch it earlier than clinic exams.

Biobank participants were classed as robust, pre-frail, or frail by standard criteria. Blood tests, ageing factors, and gene activity were mined together. Hundreds of signals linked to frailty at first pass. Focused models tied a handful of candidates to specific frailty parts, especially muscle weakness. Checking the panel across samples refined it for real screening use.
pmc-13586829:
Sandra López Gordo and colleagues describe a diagnostic trap in severe pancreatitis in this two thousand twenty-six case report. Necrotizing pancreatitis destroys pancreatic tissue and can bleed. One feared cause of bleeding is a pseudoaneurysm, a ballooning weak spot in an artery wall. In this patient, scans suggested a pseudoaneurysm of the splenic artery. Closer study showed something else: an organized blood clot with an abnormal artery-to-vein channel inside.

That look-alike is the pitfall of the title. Treating a clot as if it were a pseudoaneurysm could lead to the wrong procedure. The authors walk through how the two differ on imaging and in behavior. Their report alerts radiologists and surgeons to double-check before acting. Rare mimics matter most when the stakes are life and death.
pmc-13588129:
Muhammad Nadeem Khan, Atif Haroon, and Hazrat Bilal test urine germs from sick children in Pakistan. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, focuses on Escherichia coli, the top cause of urinary infections. The children, aged one to twelve, all had other health conditions. Such children face higher risk when drugs fail.

Samples came from nine hundred forty-one outpatients over one year. The germ grew in about thirty percent of samples. Standard disk tests show which antibiotics still work on each strain. The team also screens for a trait that breaks down many penicillin-type drugs. Multi-drug resistance is a named worry. Local data like this guide first-choice treatment.
pmc-13589929:
Jing Zhang leads a 2026 study of liver scarring, a slow harm that can lead to liver failure and liver cancer. The work centers on SNX3, a protein that sorts cargo inside cells. Levels of SNX3 were high in scarred liver from both patients and mice. Zhang and the team used mice bred so the gene could be cut or raised in liver cells.

Cutting SNX3 in liver cells shielded mice from scarring, while raising it caused scarring on its own. The protein holds back a growth signal called TGF-beta1 from being broken down, so more of it leaves the cell. That signal wakes nearby star shaped cells, which lay down scar tissue and make yet more signal. Blocking the signal path eased the harm, marking SNX3 as a drug target.
pmc-13591029:
Zuleyha Akin, Ozlem Akin, Seyhan Hidiroglu, and Ozlem Tanriover survey adults in Turkiye about ingrown toenail care in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Ingrown nails are common, painful, and prone to come back. Foot care methods that fix them without surgery are little known to the public.

Over eleven hundred adults aged eighteen to sixty answered an online survey in two thousand twenty-three. About one in six reported chronic ingrown nails, and two in five had episodes now and then. Over half had never heard of podology or its nail brace methods, and few had ever visited a podology center. Chronic cases tracked with female sex, hard physical jobs, poor footwear, diabetes, and family history.
pmc-13592629:
Maria Lamarca leads a team checking whether sex changes how people with psychosis respond to metacognitive training. The group therapy targets thinking biases behind delusions and related symptoms, and men and women often present differently. Harmonized records from an international consortium covered 573 people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders who took the training in clinics or studies. Symptom scales tracked positive, negative, general, and total scores over time.

Symptoms fell across every domain for the whole group. Yet the pace and size of gains matched between men and women, despite different starting profiles. Sex did not steer the trajectory of change on any scale. Lamarca and the team read the training as broadly usable, while urging finer study of sex linked factors beyond the simple male female split.
pmc-13592729:
Malak El-Ramly and Casey Fowler present a review from twenty twenty-six on bacterial toxins that shut down the ribosome, the cell's protein mill. These toxins snip a key spot on the ribosome's large RNA. Ricin from plants and Shiga toxin from bacteria are the famed cases. The review stays with the bacterial side of the family.

Shiga toxin's role in the worst gut infections gets a full tour. A fresh find is a set of such toxins in Spiroplasma, bugs that live in other hosts and guard them from parasites. Wide genomes hold many more of these toxin parts, some in complex builds once thought plant only. The team wagers the family began in Streptomyces soil bacteria.
pmc-13593629:
Chase McDonald and Cleotilde Gonzalez introduce two open-source tools meant to make experiments with mixed teams of people and AI agents easier to run. CoGrid is a grid-world simulation library with both NumPy and JAX backends, while the Multi-User Gymnasium turns those simulations into live web-based experiments.

The web layer can host any number of human and AI participants together, using either a central server or peer-to-peer connections with rollback netcode that smooths out network delay. Case studies in the paper show how the pairing works in practice. The authors aim the tools at researchers studying social decision making, psychology, and cognition, fields where how AI behaves alongside people matters more than how it scores alone.
pmc-13594029:
Pei-Tien Chen and a team of co-authors review nanoimprint lithography, a way of stamping nanoscale patterns into material with a mold instead of projecting them with light. Because the pattern is copied mechanically, the method sidesteps the diffraction limits that constrain optical lithography and can print features under ten nanometers wide.

The review traces three decades of development and compares the main variants, including heat-based, ultraviolet, step-and-flash, and roll-to-roll versions, weighing how each scales to factory production. Mold design, resist materials, and surface choice all decide whether the printed pattern stays faithful. Applications highlighted include metalenses with high efficiency, low-loss silicon light circuits, and flexible photonic sheets made over large areas. The authors frame the technique as a bridge between laboratory precision and industrial output.
pmc-13594729:
Alexander Lazzaro and eleven colleagues traced how first-line treatment for multiple myeloma changed across two decades of United States veterans' care. New approved drugs have multiplied, making choices more complex and adoption uneven. Clinical trials often exclude older and sicker patients, limiting what they say about real practice. The twenty twenty-six retrospective study covered 20,135 newly diagnosed patients in the Veterans Affairs system from two thousand to twenty twenty-four.

Because VA care is largely equal-access, cost fades as an explanation for treatment differences. The team examined which regimens patients actually received over time and how outcomes moved with them. Survival gains from novel therapies have not been shared equally across populations. Documenting real-world patterns helps clinicians judge whether everyday care matches what modern drugs make possible.
pmc-13595229:
Deepika Manoharan leads a team on a rare low calcium gene disorder. Their case series from twenty twenty-six is set in North East England. The disorder, ADH1, comes from activating CASR variants.

It brings low calcium, low hormone, and high urine calcium. Care aims at safe calcium levels to guard the kidneys. Adults with proven gene faults were reviewed over years. Most cases ran in families in this small group. Kidney harm hit most, with stones and calcium deposits. Two kin progressed to kidney failure and death.  Low magnesium was common in the group as well.
pmc-13597829:
Jin and six colleagues characterize a bacterium that frees phosphorus in soil in twenty twenty-six. Plants need phosphorus, but much of it sits locked in soil compounds. The strain was taken from soil around soybean roots. The team studied its traits with lab, genome, and chemical methods.

The strain released large amounts of soluble phosphorus in lab tests, mainly under acidic conditions. Its genome holds genes for phosphorus uptake and processing. Chemical profiling showed it makes several organic acids, which likely drive the release. In pot tests, adding the strain with a locked phosphorus source more than doubled available soil phosphorus. Plant biomass did not change in those tests. The authors see promise for farm use to raise phosphorus supply.
pmc-13598729:
Maria Skallerup Andersen and colleagues measured pain sensitivity with standardized sensory testing in thirty-five people with newly diagnosed Parkinson's disease who had never taken dopamine medication, matched against thirty-five healthy controls. Pain is a common early non-motor symptom, and removing drug effects let the team see the disease's own sensory fingerprint.

Pinprick testing found heightened mechanical pain sensitivity in the patients at every body site, whether or not they lived with daily pain. Pressure pain thresholds also ran lower across most regions, confirming early pressure hypersensitivity. Brushing the skin, which probes a different pain pathway, showed no group difference, and only a few patients showed its abnormal signature. The authors conclude the raw pain-carrying system is already turned up in early Parkinson's, before any treatment, while gentler touch processing stays intact, making these measures candidate markers of altered processing.
pmc-13599029:
Michael Veldeman and five co-authors study how the brain guards its blood flow in the first hour after a bleed around the brain. In health, the brain holds flow steady as pressure shifts; after such a bleed, that guard may fail. The team re-read data from rats in which a vessel was pierced to mimic the bleed. They tracked blood pressure, skull pressure, and blood flow on both sides of the brain.

On average, the guard held in the first hour. Still, time spent past a danger line rose after the bleed and rose with skull pressure. Two ways of scoring the guard often disagreed. The paper refines how early failure should be judged.
pmc-13599429:
Yuqi Han and six colleagues describe a 2026 computer-designed test that detects active coronavirus infection by sensing one of the virus's own enzymes. Standard PCR tests find viral RNA, yet RNA can linger for weeks after a person is no longer infectious. The enzyme targeted here, called 3CL protease, is needed for the virus to copy itself, and its shape barely changes across strains, making it a steadier signal of live virus.

On computers, the team designed short protein pieces that this enzyme cuts, shaped so they match no natural viral protein. They built these pieces into two reporter proteins: one gains a glow when cut, the other loses it. Either way, the change in signal reports how much active enzyme is present. The authors offer the design as a flexible tool for screening treatments and picturing infected cells, ready to adapt if a new coronavirus appears.
pmc-13602429:
Jonathan G Quicke leads a seven-author team arguing in 2026 that Australian waiting list policy blocks good trials of elective surgery. Randomized trials are the standard for judging operations, yet only about one in five surgical trials recruits on time and on target. Long public waiting lists are part of the problem. When a patient joins a trial, their queue place can conflict with the trial's treatment timing, and services are left to improvise.

Treating trial patients exactly like everyone else can wreck a study's design, while quietly prioritizing them can break waiting list directives. Both workarounds trouble the authors ethically. They propose a third option: policy that openly justifies prioritizing trial participants. Two scenarios built around a knee replacement trial, facing a national median wait of 265 days, carry their argument. Transparent rules, the team contends, would let surgical research proceed without ethically awkward choices.
pmc-13603629:
Manuela Moriggi and a team of co-authors hunted for blood signs of a muscle wasting disease. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with a type of muscular dystrophy that varies a lot by person. No firm blood marker tracks how bad it is. The team thought cell stress and fat harm reshape a class of fats in the blood. They tested that idea in muscle samples and blood.

They read gene activity in arm muscle from mild and severe cases and healthy peers. They also checked small sacs shed by cells into the blood. The fat shifts in blood tracked how severe the disease was. Readers get fresh leads for a blood test to watch this disease.
pmc-13603929:
Miriam Tenuzzo and co-authors report the first find of the mcr-1 gene in a wild red fox, in work published in 2026. That gene confers resistance to the antibiotic colistin. Drug resistance spreads among people, animals, and the environment. Foxes live close to humans and range widely, so they mark resistance well. The fox lived in Italy with dense cattle farming and heavy farm drug use.

The team grew bacteria from fox droppings, screened them for resistance genes, tested drug response, and read the genome. The gene sat inside the chromosome of an Escherichia coli strain. The strain stayed borderline sensitive to colistin but resisted several drugs used on livestock. Farm use of colistin in the area was near zero, yet overall drug use was high. That pattern points to spread by co-selection rather than pressure from that drug.
pmc-13605729:
Adrian Boloș and co-authors published a 2026 study on treating bad breath in older dental patients. In this age group, halitosis rarely has one cause. Tongue coating, gum inflammation, denture films, and dry mouth often stack together. Treatment that fixes one source may leave the others untouched. The team compared three care pathways in a prospective cohort of ninety-four patients aged sixty-five and older.

Patients were assigned by their dominant problem. One group got gum debridement plus tongue cleaning. Another had denture biofilm managed. A third received restorative and prosthetic maintenance. The researchers tracked breath improvement and asked whether shrinking tongue coating explained the gains within each pathway. The design treats halitosis as a bundle of causes, not a single fault. Its lessons are practical: match the cleaning to the mouth, and watch the tongue, a quiet mediator of whether treatment works.
pmc-13605829:
Craig Eling, Jennifer Stinson, and six co-authors interview families about finding health information online for children's joint diseases. Their qualitative study, from twenty twenty-six, sits in Saskatchewan, Canada. Ten caregivers and seven adolescents with rheumatic disease take part. Phone interviews explore how they search, judge, and use web health content.

One theme: online reading adds knowledge without burdening busy clinicians. Families develop habits for spotting trustworthy pages. Gaps and confidence vary widely between them. The study uses an interpretive description method with constant comparison. Findings can shape clinic handouts and portal design. Digital skills emerge as part of disease self-management.
pmc-13607329:
Lee and colleagues show in twenty twenty-six that cold air reshuffles where B cells sit in the body, through a stress-hormone pathway. Immune cells patrol between blood, spleen, and marrow, but how everyday stressors move them was unclear. Mice kept in the cold, or given a steroid drug, lost B cells from the blood and their spleens shrank, without the cells dying.

Labelled-cell transfers showed the missing B cells had moved into the bone marrow. Cold raised the stress hormone, which boosted a homing receptor on B cells; blocking that receptor largely stopped the migration. The authors propose the marrow as a sheltered reservoir during stress, saving energy for heat-making. The pathway may matter for B-cell autoimmune disease care.
pmc-13609929:
Vasconcelos and co-authors compare two ways to finish a set in biceps training in this 2026 study. One approach pushes every set to failure, where no more reps are possible. The other stops with one to three reps still in reserve.

Nineteen trained adults trained both arms differently for eight weeks, one arm per method. They did preacher curls twice a week at 70 to 80 percent of their one-rep maximum. Both arms gained muscle thickness and strength. The estimated differences between methods were tiny, and the uncertainty ranges covered zero in both directions. Sex-specific checks showed the same pattern. Stopping short of failure built just as much arm muscle and strength here.
pmc-13611429:
Guangda Xu and You Dong present a 2026 study of robots for risky work in power substations. Gas-insulated substations are compact and trusted, but their gas can form toxic by-products. Tasks such as gas pressure tweaks put workers at risk. The team built a robot setup that shares control between the machine and a human operator.

The setup runs on a standard robot platform with a six-joint arm. A vision system with an attention boost spots small parts, and a motion system runs the arm's path. The level of machine control can shift as the task demands. On the test task of gas pressure work, the robot finished over 90 percent of runs on its own, even as scenes changed. The work points toward safer upkeep for power sites.
pmc-13612329:
Wanchun Xue, Jianhua Zhang, and Zhiyu Chen test whether treadmill running rewires a key brain output station in Parkinsonian mice. The substantia nigra pars reticulata helps gate movement, and dopamine loss distorts their electrical behavior. The team lesioned mice with the toxin 6-OHDA, then ran one group on treadmills daily for six weeks. Patch-clamp recordings probed parvalbumin-lineage neurons in the output nucleus.

Exercised mice moved better on open-field and rotarod tests than sedentary mice. Their output neurons also looked healthier: input resistance, firing threshold, evoked firing, gain, and adaptation all shifted back toward normal. Total parvalbumin protein did not differ between groups, so the change was functional rather than a protein-level rescue. The authors read this as a circuit-level mechanism for exercise benefit in Parkinson's disease. Treadmill training, they suggest, retunes the neurons that dopamine loss leaves misbehaving.
pmc-13612629:
David Leblang and Dennis Wesselbaum present a 2026 global study of loneliness, using survey replies from 218,048 adults in 148 countries in the 2023-2024 Gallup World Poll. More than one adult in five said they felt lonely. Rates were highest in low-income countries and in Sub-Saharan Africa, even though the emotional cost of loneliness looked heavier in richer parts of the world.

Better health, more schooling, a larger household, and having a job each went with lower loneliness, though the links shifted from place to place. Lonely adults reported lower well-being, more bad feelings, and a stronger wish to move abroad. The authors argue that plans to ease loneliness need to fit local conditions, not one global mold.
pmc-13612829:
Liu and colleagues reported in twenty twenty-six the discovery of tiny DNA stretches that act as master switches for genes, which they named Methylation Mesa. Chemical tags called methylation usually quiet genes, and removing tags from the well-known promoter regions switches genes on only unevenly.

Scanning twenty-four full methylation maps from human and mouse samples, the team found narrow stretches with an outsized grip on gene activity. Each stretch runs just tens to hundreds of letters long and keeps a conserved shape. They also built a precise editing tool that strips tags from a chosen spot more cleanly than older methods. Erasing tags at one mesa switch woke a sleeping cancer-guard gene so strongly that tumors shrank in living animals. The mesa even reshaped how the chromosome folded around it. The authors see these switches as prime targets for diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-13613329:
Jihen Krichen and co-authors look for factors that predict complications after surgery for liver hydatid cysts, in work published in 2026. The cysts come from a parasite and remain a public health burden in regions where they are common. Surgery is the main treatment, but leaks of bile after surgery are a frequent problem.

The study reviewed 107 patients with 168 cysts treated at one Tunisian hospital over eight years. Most patients had conservative surgery. About one patient in six had a complication, and bile leak was the most common. Two factors predicted specific complications on their own: warning signs on scans before surgery, and problems arising during the operation itself. The authors frame risk sorting as a public health tool for using surgical resources well.
pmc-13613629:
Cara Ghiglieri and colleagues reviewed how a standard framework for judging health care acceptability is actually used in research. The framework asks how people who give and receive care feel about a treatment or program. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team searched major databases and trial registries for studies since the framework appeared. They included finished studies, protocols, and trial records that used the framework for patient-facing care, and they charted how and when acceptability was assessed.

Use of the framework has grown and spans many care settings. Most teams assessed acceptability after care was delivered, often with questionnaires given once to patients. Studies based on interviews used the framework more during analysis. Reporting often left out which parts of the framework were used, which makes studies hard to compare. The authors propose a reporting checklist to make future use clearer and more consistent.
pmc-13614929:
Giselle Coelho, Alejandro Rabinstein, and W. David Freeman review in 2026 what long spaceflights do to the brain and nervous system. Months without gravity, plus radiation, raised carbon dioxide, and isolation, shift fluids toward the head and change the brain's structure and blood flow. Known effects include a syndrome harming the eyes and brain, balance problems, faintness on standing, and clouded thinking.

The authors gather the current proof into one frame based on how blood vessels in the brain behave under these stresses. They weigh fixes now in development: machines that pull blood back toward the feet, artificial gravity, better brain monitoring, and even controlled low-body-temperature rest. For planners of deep-space missions, the review maps the dangers crews face and the tools most likely to keep their brains safe.
pmc-13615029:
Priya Nigam and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a sexual health education program for Philadelphia teenagers called Proud Teens of Philly. About a quarter of the city's sexually transmitted infections occur in teens. Birth rates among underserved youth there run more than double the national average. The program recruited through schools, churches, and community groups and delivered eight one-hour online sessions.

In the 2021-2022 school year, 650 students aged 12 to 18 took part, following two established curricula. Surveys before and after measured knowledge of infections and birth control, attitudes, confidence about consent and condom use, and life skills. Comparing matched answers showed what the course changed. For a city trying to close health gaps among Black and Latino youth, the results show whether community-based teaching shifts both knowledge and attitudes.
pmc-13615429:
Pyae Aung leads a team reporting real-world results for cannabidiol, a cannabis-derived medicine, used as an add-on treatment in adults with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, a severe epilepsy that begins in childhood. Four patients died of causes unrelated to the drug, and 86 percent were still taking it at last follow-up.

Across all seizure types, 59.5 percent of patients had at least half their seizures cut at six months, rising to 67.1 percent at last follow-up. For drop seizures, which fling patients to the floor, half responded by six months and 61.5 percent by the end. pmc-13617029:
Daniel Callow and eight co-authors follow daily rest and activity patterns in older adults in this two thousand twenty-six paper. A person's rest-activity rhythm captures how regular and how sharply divided their days are. Broken rhythms have been tied to cognitive decline. The team used week-long wrist recordings in one hundred sixty-nine older adults who began the study without major cognitive impairment. Many were measured again in later years.

They split each person's average rhythm from their off days at each visit. Outcomes covered thinking tests, blood biomarkers, and clinical change. This split shows whether steady habits or single bad stretches matter more. The work may turn a cheap wrist sensor into an early warning tool for brain aging.
pmc-13617229:
Anneka Anderson and nine colleagues report a 2026 qualitative study of how Maaori and Pacific families in Auckland, New Zealand, experience echocardiography during rheumatic fever care. Seventeen participants shared their experiences, and the analysis found four themes: communication, engagement, access, and the role of kaiaawhina. Families described what helped them get scans done and what got in the way, from clear explanations to practical barriers in reaching services. The authors say these insights can guide child- and family-focused models of care that improve both experience and service delivery across Aotearoa New Zealand.
pmc-13618229:
Xiaoying Zhang and co-authors study how lung cancer cells survive the shear stress of the bloodstream, in a research paper from 2026. Most cancer cells that enter the blood die fast, torn by flow or cut off from support. The few that live can seed new tumors, so their survival tricks matter.

The team built a lab flow system that mimics blood shear and profiled cancer cells under flow, attached, and still states. A chain of signals stood out: stress raised reactive oxygen, which acted through CD44 to switch on a protein called ezrin. Once on, ezrin braced the cell's outer frame and turned on survival pathways. That dual role kept cells intact and alive under flow. The authors suggest the chain as a target worth testing in more realistic models.
pmc-13618929:
Yusuke Sakamoto and four colleagues present a case of a newborn whose thigh bone broke during cesarean delivery. This baby was managed conservatively with a Pavlik harness, the strapping used for infant hip problems, avoiding anesthesia and surgery.

The ultrasound visualized callus formation and the correction of deformity in a manner comparable to the radiographs, which matters because newborns are vulnerable to radiation and follow-up can require repeated images. The authors suggest ultrasound could reduce how many radiographs these infants need. That gives a radiation-free monitoring option, while the harness's other advantages, from shorter hospital stays to easy diaper changes at home, support the conservative route.
pmc-13619129:

The authors stress that most human evidence comes from small, early, often uncontrolled trials with short follow-up. Results also vary with cell source, dose, and delivery route. Standard production methods and better trials, they argue, must come before such therapies can join routine, personalized care.
pmc-13619629:

Six involved syndromes that raise leukemia risk directly, including changes in TP53 and extra chromosome 21, while three involved syndromes tied to solid tumors. Most of these diagnoses were new to the families. Findings led to tailored health checks for eight of the nine children and changed treatment for four. The authors call the yield modest but useful, and they note that how wide a panel should run depends on local counseling resources.
pmc-13620129:

pmc-13620429:

The planned review will follow standard scoping methods.

The team will search five databases plus gray sources for studies from around the world. Two reviewers will screen and chart each study on their own using a tested form. The map should show current teaching practice and where the gaps lie, guiding better training for future nurses and midwives.
pmc-13620829:
Gianfranco Puddu, Marco Piras, Stefano Congia, and Shashank Kaushik present a case of shoulder bone destroyed by spread kidney cancer. Two years on, his shoulder scores showed fair function, enough for daily activities, and no pain. He lived three years after the operation. The authors argue that a half replacement, rather than a total joint swap, can match the needs and life expectancy of such patients well.
pmc-13623129:
Isabela Fernanda Rodrigues de Oliveira leads a school-based study asking what daily habits cost teachers and other education staff in Brazil in quality of life. The authors hope the findings push healthier routines and better workplace policy.
pmc-13623929:

For demographers, measuring concepts precisely is the precondition for predicting behavior; this 2026 paper supplies the ruler for one pivotal generation.
pmc-13624029:

pmc-13624829:

Seven already sit on the World Health Organization's essential medicines list. Listing the rest, the authors argue, could steady supply and payment, and some products may deserve full approval as medicines.
pmc-13626229:

Across yaw angles and blade speed ratios used by commercial machines, they measured forces and power. The blade speed that gives peak power changed with yaw angle, which means standard control rules built for aligned flow should be revised. Force changes with angle also depended strongly on blade speed. A unified model they present matched the lab behavior well. The authors offer it for turbine design and wind farm control.
pmc-13626829:
Daniel Eriksson and eight colleagues, publishing in 2026, use Sweden's national registers to ask whether autoimmune diseases share their genes in families. Connective tissue diseases grouped together, gut diseases together, and hormone gland diseases together. Nerve diseases barely cohered. No single universal autoimmunity factor appeared. Families of patients, the authors advise, deserve watching for the cluster cousins of a first disease.
pmc-13626929:

The authors place the cases in a rising pattern: this yeast increasingly infects patients whose immunity is weak, above all those with central lines or blood disorders. They share the series so clinicians spot the culprit sooner.
pmc-13627029:

The effect also held for strains that were still sensitive to fluconazole. The authors probe how the pair kills the yeast. Repurposing a known drug could widen options against resistant fungi.
pmc-13628229:

Over a hundred twenty patients treated with the modified method were compared with about a hundred earlier patients treated the conventional way. Serious leaks fell from about a quarter of patients to under a tenth. Major bleeding also dropped. The joining step itself took less time, though total operating time held steady. Adjusted and matched analyses kept the leak advantage. The authors suggest the method eases stress on the pancreas tissue.
pmc-13628429:

Checks then ran each month for six months.

Just over half the patients did have worm infections. Strongyloidiasis was the most common proven cause. Blood counts went back to normal for nearly all within three months of treatment. A patient's exposure past helped sort worm cases from other causes. The authors back worm treatment as the standard first step in such regions. Other causes should still be checked at the same time.
pmc-13628529:
Julian Burkhart and six colleagues found a gentler way to recover germanium from its oxide. Germanium is a scarce element vital for fibre optics and heat-sensing devices. Their 2026 study uses vapour transport, which carries a solid through the gas phase for collection elsewhere. The driver here is hydrogen-bearing gas, not harsh halogens.

Pure hydrogen cut too hard and stalled the transport. Natural gas fouled the product with carbon. A mix of ten percent hydrogen in argon, helped by water vapour, hit the balance. It recovered most of the germanium within half an hour. It kept working when scaled up threefold. The same setup pulled germanium from a silica mix like fibre waste. The silica stayed behind.
pmc-13629229:
Laurine A. Mathieu and five colleagues raised great tits from city and forest eggs under identical conditions to separate inherited change from flexible adjustment in urban birds. Published in 2026, the common garden experiment hand-reared nestlings from unincubated eggs, then paired the adults by origin in breeding aviaries and recorded their reproduction.

Under shared conditions, the earlier laying seen in wild city birds vanished, showing that timing is a flexible response to environment. Egg size, though, stayed smaller in city-origin females, evidence of genuine genetic divergence. Clutch size flipped entirely: city females laid larger clutches than forest females in the aviary, the opposite of the wild pattern. The authors describe this as hidden evolution working against the visible trend.
pmc-13630729:
Ryan Ahmed and colleagues published a review in 2026 on light therapy for healing skeletal muscle. The method shines red or near-infrared light on injured tissue. It is painless and drug-free, which makes it attractive for rehabilitation. Yet clinics still use it inconsistently, and results vary between studies.

The review gathers more than two decades of animal and human research. Light acts on an enzyme inside mitochondria, the cell's energy centers. That raises energy output and sends controlled stress signals. Those signals can wake repair cells and grow new blood vessels. Effects follow a two-way dose pattern: too little or too much fails. The authors urge standard dose reporting and pairing light with exercise.
pmc-13631229:
Yuteng Zhang and five colleagues propose a cheaper way to certify layered pipes and shells. The goal is proof they will not collapse under outside pressure. Their study appeared in 2026. Proving collapse resistance for offshore flexible pipes normally demands full-scale pressure chamber tests. The other route is detailed models. Those miss the stresses locked in during making.

Their method squeezes a flat plate sample in a benchtop rig. It works backwards to an equivalent material law. That law quietly absorbs cold work, leftover stress, friction, and flex. It then drops into a simplified computer model of the whole structure. Tested on flexible pipe carcasses and reinforced plastic pipe, predictions matched detailed simulations. They also matched chamber measures. The authors pitch it as a general qualification shortcut.
pmc-13631929:
Hande Işıl Akbağ and five colleagues asked whether kefir, a fermented milk drink, helps hand-reared baby pigeons grow. One exception appeared in Homing pigeons, where the kefir group ate more and weighed more than the plain artificial milk group. Blood tests at twenty-eight days differed mostly by breed. Only total protein and albumin levels responded to the feeding treatments.
pmc-13632529:
Meiling Jiao and six co-authors trace how one germ in a lone patient lost its drug grit in part, by a cut in a gene pack. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, reads germs taken in a row.

Grit to the strong class of germ drugs is oft held as a firm trait. But packs on loose gene rings can shift form, and spawn kin germs that part in their grit. Three germs from one stay were read: two with grit, one sans. Two came from one wound swab. Reads of lone germ sets showed firm states in each. A long gap was found in one ring's text, twixt two like marks. That gap held the grit pack.
pmc-13633829:
Wajdi Alnajada and eight colleagues review outcomes after radiotherapy for localized prostate cancer, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Radiation offers cure rates comparable to surgery for many patients. Biochemical failure, a rising PSA signal, warns that disease may be returning.

The retrospective cohort covered ninety-one patients treated at Jordan's Military Cancer Center. Treatment years ran from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-five. Failure was defined by the Phoenix criteria, PSA rising two points above its lowest value. The authors measured how often failure occurred, when it appeared, and which factors predicted it. Such local outcome data helps military and regional centers benchmark their results. It also informs follow-up schedules for survivors.
pmc-13633929:
Marta Parellada-Vendrell and five colleagues studied why women delay seeking help during acute coronary syndrome, a sudden blockage of heart blood flow. Their study, written in Spanish, took place in the cardiac care unit of a large referral hospital. They enrolled eighty women who had survived such an event over one year.
